The beauty-meets-wellness industry is now worth a combined $6.8 trillion, and peptides, found in products from injections to viral, low-cost lip balms, are among its most prized compounds. Academics at Northeastern University warn that peptide usage is racing ahead of its safety and efficacy track record. Their concerns follow an FDA meeting on the future of a group of peptide compounds, a cause championed by Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Peptides have become the leading craze in "biohacking" and "longevity." U.S. peptide-related searches reached 10.1 million per month in January, a fivefold jump since 2020, and roughly 1 in 8 Americans now take GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, which are FDA-approved peptides. The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met on July 23 to consider broadening access to at least four previously banned peptides, letting specialized pharmacies compound customized medications for prescribed patients. HHS press secretary Emily G. Hilliard said the FDA will weigh the committee's recommendations, consult the United States Pharmacopeia, and develop a proposed rule, followed by public comment before a final rule. That rule may include all, some, or none of the substances proposed for the 503A Bulks List. In February, Kennedy had announced that roughly 14 of 19 banned peptides could be moved off the FDA's restricted list, the largest reversal in U.S. peptide regulatory history. Valerie Aparovich of OnSkin, a cosmetologist, aesthetician and biochemist, said topical peptides such as Matrixyl and Argireline carry "a high safety profile" and support collagen production, though she cautioned that much research comes from companies selling the ingredients rather than independent investigators. Real-world harm has been reported. In 2025, authorities investigated why two women fell critically ill after receiving peptide injections at a booth run by a California physician, unlicensed in Nevada, at a Las Vegas festival. Karthik Achari, founder of PepMD, who spoke at the FDA meeting, said being authorized to prescribe a peptide and being qualified to do so are different things, and the current system does not distinguish them. He noted there is abundant anecdotal evidence but little usable controlled data, and stressed the vote "doesn't authorize anything," since formal rulemaking could take over a year. Still, he argued a regulated pathway is "categorically safer than a grey market." Dr. Neil Panchal of Longevitix agreed, saying that without licensed access, patients migrate to gray-market vendors selling material of unverified purity. Northeastern professor Mansoor Amiji said that apart from GLP-1 agonists by Eli Lilly and Novo and other FDA-approved peptides, there are no preclinical or clinical studies showing safety and effectiveness of the "hyped" peptides. Influencers claim peptides can speed injury recovery, boost performance and slow aging. Amiji warned that even topical use risks dangerous systemic absorption, calling placebo responses the "best-case scenario" and serious reactions the worst. His colleague Steve Kates said the approval bar of efficacy, manufacturing validation and toxicology has not been cleared, adding that peptides' complex manufacturing has historically made them hard to produce at scale.

La Salle rowing coach Ivo Krakic was frustrated that the app he used to track rowers' stroke length and force from the team's ergometers stored data in different places, so he paid the app's developer $500 for a fix that would put it on one screen. That caught the attention of rower Will Tran, a senior computer science major who rows in the second varsity eight. Tran thought he could have done the job in 20 minutes and saw a gap in the market, so he built his own app, RowIQ. RowIQ is a data ecosystem that uses artificial intelligence to pinpoint where and how rowers can improve. It processes data from Concept2 ergometers, smartwatches, and RowIQFuel, Tran's nutrition app, and will eventually collect data from on-water rowing monitors. Tran says the aim is to give rowers a complete picture of their training with "data that's never been seen before," since races are sometimes won by hundredths of a second. Rowers can form groups so coaches see an entire team's data in one place and spot trends in under a second, helping with lineup decisions. Krakic says it gives good feedback on a rower's curve and power transfer, lets the team match indoor performance to on-water performance, and puts La Salle "a little bit" ahead. In the last two months the app has passed 1,000 downloads and shows strong retention, with top users logging over 200,000 meters per week. Tran says clubs are signing on and about 70 new athletes are onboarded daily. Tran initially worked alone but, lacking time for marketing, assembled a team with rowing backgrounds. Some Penn lightweight crew members are building a telemetry system to centralize RowIQ's data, and former Harvard lightweight rower Zarret Mills consults. Sergej Čipak, a former La Salle teammate who returned to Serbia to study electrical engineering, started part-time and now leads development while Tran handles the big picture. Tran can now pay Čipak, which he never expected to do at 22. He describes this as a "yin, yang": rewarding to support someone through his creation, but a source of constant pressure to keep working because Čipak relies on him. Čipak, who works full-time at a company outside his intended career path, says he plans to keep working on RowIQ. Amid an AI boom in which venture firms like Y Combinator and Antler fund students and companies like Palantir and xAI encourage dropping out, Tran says he has seriously considered taking the fall semester off to join an accelerator like Y Combinator and return to school later, though he probably won't. He has already turned down a summer internship at a data analytics company. For now he plans to balance school, Division I rowing, his relationship, and RowIQ. Krakic says you can't tell Tran no, because the more you say something is impossible, the more he tries to prove you wrong.

Even wealthy clients who can afford top advisors are asking AI chatbots such as Claude and ChatGPT for portfolio recommendations and tax advice, wealth management leaders told CNBC. Matthew Fleissig, CEO and cofounder of Pathstone, a registered investor advisory with $185 billion in assets, said ChatGPT is "the single largest investment advisor in the world right now." Firm leaders say AI second opinions can help clients ask informed questions and have deeper conversations with advisors. Pamela Lucina, head of family office solutions at Northern Trust, first noticed clients double-checking the firm's advice with AI about 18 months ago; clients have said they will put their questions to AI before asking the firm, often testing for specifics or evidence the firm has done such work before. Many prospective clients also use LLMs to decide whether to hire Northern Trust. Previously only billionaires typically requested formal proposals, but Lucina estimates about half of clients now do, even some with as little as $100 million, sometimes using LLMs to formulate highly specific questions. She said this makes meetings more efficient, shifting talk from information sharing to desired outcomes. Michael Zeuner, managing partner at WE Family Offices, first saw clients feeding portfolio recommendations into LLMs about five months ago and is considering running every recommendation through Microsoft Copilot so advisors can anticipate client questions. He sees it as a positive second set of eyes that keeps clients engaged. The risks include incorrect advice and leaked personal information. Zeuner said clients may struggle to tell hallucinations from real insights; an LLM might invent details of an uploaded trust document, or ChatGPT told one client two ETFs were identical when both tracked the same index but one was equal weight and the other cap-weighted. Lucina said an LLM got the math wrong on capital gains tax savings examples; she finds AI good for poking holes in ideas but "more often than not, especially on the advice side, it's wrong." Clients using personal accounts, even paid ones, risk exposing identifying information, whereas firms typically use enterprise plans with strict data protections. WE Family Offices' agreement with Microsoft Copilot ensures its data is never used to train public models. Morningstar's Sean Dunlop said wealth advisories, especially those targeting the mass affluent, will have to do more to justify fees. Wealth management stocks have pulled back as AI encroached, citing an Altruist AI tax planning tool released in February and an OpenAI personal finance feature launched in May. He thinks AI is unlikely to wipe out traditional managers; service levels will improve, fewer advisors may be needed for a possibly larger asset pool, and some customers will go it alone. At minimum, it should raise the floor for advisors. Fleissig said LLMs offer analysis but not actionable advice, describing them as "semi-objective tools" unsuited to subjective decisions. They also cannot secure access to deals such as a pre-IPO Anthropic funding round, which depends on relationships. Vince Lumia, a 27-year Morgan Stanley veteran overseeing more than 16,000 financial advisors, said the value of human advisors is easily overlooked in bull markets but returns in volatile times, when larger clients want advice.

The author, after years of experimenting with Docker containers on a home server, lists the ones they would reinstall first if they had to rebuild from scratch. The choice is based on daily dependence, not popularity or flashy features. Uptime Kuma is a 24/7 watchdog that continuously checks whether self-hosted services are online, notifies the author if one goes down, and shows their status on a single dashboard. It also monitors SSL certificates so the author gets a warning before they expire. It is lightweight and easy to maintain, and it gives confidence that the server works even when not actively in use. Portainer is a visual Docker management interface. The author still deploys with Docker Compose, but Portainer provides a dashboard to view running containers, check logs, monitor resource usage, and restart services from a browser instead of the terminal. It is especially useful when rebuilding a server and installing several containers at once, and it makes updating stacks and managing volumes less intimidating. It saves small amounts of time every day. Paperless-ngx is the author's digital filing cabinet for invoices, warranty cards, bank statements, tax documents, and user manuals. It organizes documents automatically, and built-in OCR makes every file searchable by word or date. Tags and custom document types keep a growing collection tidy. The author says it has genuinely changed how they manage documents. Immich automatically backs up every phone photo and video to the home server, reducing dependence on cloud storage. It offers facial recognition, location search, albums, and an easy timeline, so old photos can be found quickly. The author keeps full control of the library without a subscription, accesses it almost daily, and treats it as the main way to organize and revisit years of memories rather than just a backup. Home Assistant is the control center of the author's smart home. It connects lights, switches, sensors, and other devices from different brands into one interface and supports automations, such as lights turning on in the evening and notifications when certain sensors trigger. Because it runs locally, most automations keep working if the internet connection goes down, which the author appreciates more than expected. The author concludes that a useful server doesn't need dozens of containers, just a handful relied on every day to stay organized, protect data, and ease server management. Everything else is optional and can come later, and with this foundation in place, adding new services becomes less stressful.

New technologies are letting Ukrainian drone operators, who are high-priority targets for Russia, control drones from relatively safer locations hundreds or even thousands of miles away. Interceptor drone and other uncrewed aerial system operators increasingly use satellite connections that allow them to work far from the launch site, potentially even from another country. Makers describe this as a key way to protect pilots. Wild Hornets, for instance, has developed technology that lets pilots fly its interceptor drones from hundreds of kilometers away. However, the aircraft still often have to be brought to a launch site and prepared, so soldiers are still needed closer to the danger, at least for now. Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who is now a lessons-learned analyst with Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," said satellite communications allow pilots to be placed anywhere with a stable internet connection. But "this doesn't remove the need for the ground groups, people who actually attach the explosive, put the drone outside of the bunker, et cetera." Troops may still need to transport, unload and assemble drones, attach explosives and communications equipment, and position them for launch. Efforts are underway to use ground robots to launch interceptors and first-person-view drones, but these robotic motherships are not yet ubiquitous along the front lines. Zhluktenko said keeping everyone involved in a drone operation far from the fighting is "impossible so far." On more traditional missions using radio-frequency-controlled drones, operators generally must stay closer to their drones. Units try, when possible, to move operators farther back, even at the expense of capability. Zhluktenko called this a "very tough balance" between safety and getting the work done. Protecting operators is critical because Russia often treats them as top targets, according to soldiers, operators and military officials. Ukraine's drones destroy more Russian targets than any other weapon, and one operator can fly repeated missions to collect intelligence and launch attacks. Then-defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in April that "the pilot is no longer tied to the position," with control taking place from a protected environment in Kyiv, Lviv, or even abroad, which increases interception effectiveness, minimizes risk to operators and allows capabilities to scale without being tied to the front. Ukraine is investing heavily in drones, ground robots, AI and autonomous systems to keep soldiers away from intense fighting and to offset Russia's manpower advantage, including replacing tasks such as front-line logistics with robotic systems. The defense ministry has said ground robots' primary task is to replace soldiers in the most dangerous areas. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in April that Ukraine's ground robot force had carried out more than 22,000 front-line missions over the previous three months, meaning lives were saved that many times. Then Commander-in-Chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi said in October that Ukraine was prioritizing high-tech systems to reduce soldiers' presence on the battlefield. Zhluktenko said the ultimate goal is fewer people at direct risk, but for now it is not total robotic warfare.

It's hard to imagine Microsoft turning in a better earnings report. Not only did the tech giant post strong growth in its AI-powered Azure cloud-computing business, it also refrained from raising its capex-spending forecast. Investors went nuts over the report, pushing Microsoft shares up 16%, their biggest single-day jump since 2008. Microsoft's market success did well to lay out a blueprint for hyperscalers hoping to get investors excited again: Show that you're starting to monetize AI, and don't revise your spending projections upward. If you do that, investors will reward you. It also reinvigorated a market that sold off sharp on Wednesday following Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's post-FOMC address. Here's a rundown of the gains across the market: - S&P 500: 7,438.72, up 1.7%. - Dow Jones Industrial Average: 52,209.57, up 1.2%. - Nasdaq 100: 28,106.35, up 3.4%. The chipmaking sector — which has been the foremost lightning rod for AI-spending jitters — got a particularly big boost. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index soared 8%, while Micron, Intel, and AMD each spiked double digits. Microsoft's market-moving earnings report contrasted sharply with that of its fellow hyperscaler Meta. Meta issued a disappointing sales forecast while simultaneously raising capex projections. Its stock fell 8%. Meta-specific concerns aside, Microsoft may have just shown the market that there's a fine line hyperscalers can walk in their spending strategy, one that allows them to both remain competitive and project at least some image of capital discipline. Jeff Fratarcangeli, the managing principal of Fratarcangeli Wealth Management, told Business Insider earlier this week that it's a line he hopes to see more companies walk in the future. While he doesn't think it's prudent for companies to pull back on capex, he said firms can acknowledge investors' concerns. "I kind of want to see them play both sides of that," Fratarcangeli said. "They can say things in a fashion that doesn't necessarily irritate the investors," he continued, "yet still say they're going to be competitive."

Federal regulators are clearing the way for robotaxis to operate without steering wheels or eventually even brake pedals as the rules start to catch up to the evolving technology. Amazon’s fully autonomous Zoox vehicles got approval Thursday to begin charging customers for rides in the specially designed boxy cars that feature four inward-facing seats once they secure state and local approval. Zoox has already been offering free rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco since last year. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration also proposed a rule last month to allow robotaxis to operate without brake pedals, but that proposal is still pending. Administrator Jonathan Morrison said his agency wants to clear the way for the safe development of autonomous vehicles. “By removing unnecessary barriers to innovation, developing industry guidance, and providing strong enforcement oversight while we create performance requirements, NHTSA is taking a balanced approach to AV regulation,” Morrison said in a statement. “These advancements will ensure that the United States continues to lead the world in AV technology in a safe and responsible manner.” Zoox and Tesla are working to catch up to the industry-leading Waymo that already operates in multiple cities. Waymo is owned by Google’s parent company, Alphabet. Zoox CEO Aicha Evans said this approval is an important milestone for autonomous vehicles. “This achievement reflects a shared commitment to enabling innovation while maintaining the highest standards of safety,” Evans said. Amazon hopes to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robotaxis a year at a plant near Silicon Valley as it works to challenge Waymo. Amazon paid $1.2 billion to acquire self-driving startup Zoox. Initially, Zoox will only be allowed to deploy up to 2,500 vehicles without steering wheels over the next two years as it works to prove the technology is safe. The company said that more than half a million people have already ridden in its vehicles.

Microsoft's stock surged as much as 17% on Thursday to above $455, the largest single-day gain since 2008, when it rose 19%, according to Jefferies. The stock closed at $390.54 on Wednesday and briefly hit $456 Thursday, adding about $483 billion in market value. Going into earnings, it was down nearly 30% from an October 2025 high of $555, weighed down by investor doubts about returns on AI spending. The rally followed fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results that appeared to convince investors that CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood's strategy for turning an estimated $190 billion in AI spending this year into revenue growth is working. Nearly every metric beat expectations. Quarterly revenue was $90 billion, versus the $87.6 billion consensus and up $13.6 billion (17.7%) from a year ago. Earnings per share were $4.74 against the $4.24 consensus, with net income of $35.8 billion. Nadella announced that Azure crossed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time in fiscal 2026. William Blair's Jason Ader estimated fourth-quarter Azure revenue at $29.9 billion, up from $20.9 billion a year earlier. The 43% growth beat company guidance of 39% to 40%. Hood guided to 45% Azure growth for the quarter ending in September, above the 41% analysts expected, per BNP Paribas. Ader estimated fiscal-year Azure revenue at $104 billion, up from $75 billion. Microsoft's annual report disclosed that OpenAI accounted for $24.1 billion of fiscal 2026 revenue and still owes Microsoft $6 billion in accounts receivable. OpenAI has been a source of concentration risk and uncertainty for investors. Analysts estimated it drove roughly half of Azure's $30 billion year-over-year growth, and Stifel's Brad Reback noted the relationship is becoming less competitively additive as Google closes in. BNP Paribas's Stefan Slowinski, who has a $549 price target, put OpenAI at 23% of Azure's revenue and said Azure can keep growing above 40% as consumption-based pricing is phased in across Copilot offerings. He said the quarter showed progress toward revenue growth outpacing capex growth, "an equilibrium state" investors wanted. Other indicators were strong. Reback reported Microsoft 365 Copilot seats rose to 30 million, up 10 million in a quarter versus expectations of about 6 million. Commercial remaining performance obligations rose to $678 billion from $368 billion a year ago, which Ader called "tremendous demand visibility across enterprise and AI workloads." Operating cash flow was $55.4 billion, $6.7 billion above consensus, despite $41 billion in quarterly capex. Reback, who rates the stock "hold," raised his price target from $400 to $450. Hood guided to more than $50 billion in capex next quarter and announced an accounting change extending the useful life of data center buildings to 25 years from 15. This will shift some future finance leases into operating leases, lowering reported capex; with 2026 spending plans of $190 billion unchanged, the new classification would allow reporting $175 billion.

The U.S. Air Force’s F-47 program has begun its engineering and manufacturing development phase and will fly in the coming years, a service official said. The program, described as “extreme teaming” with industry partners, entered the phase with “unprecedented maturity,” Gen. Dale White, director of Critical Major Weapon Systems, said in a Wednesday keynote address at an event in Dayton, Ohio. The engineering and manufacturing phase includes maturing, integrating and testing all parts of the F-47. It will produce a small number of test aircraft for evaluation and includes priced options for low-rate initial production. White did not specify the number of test aircraft being produced. The first Boeing F-47 is on track for its first flight in 2028. The Air Force plans to buy at least 185 F-47s, matching the size of the F-22 Raptor fleet it intends to replace. “The F-47 will fly in this administration,” White said during his speech at the Life Cycle Industry Days, hosted by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center. White, who also acts as direct reporting portfolio manager to the deputy defense secretary, is tasked with managing weapons systems, such as the F-47 and B-21 programs. In March 2025, President Donald Trump announced that the force will proceed with development of sixth-generation Boeing F-47s under the Next Generation Air Dominance program, or NGAD, intended to replace the F-22 Raptor. “In terms of all of the attributes of a fighter jet, there’s never been anything even close to it, from speed to maneuverability, to what it can have, to payload,” Trump said at the time, insisting that the aircraft will be built and in the air during his administration. “And this has been in the works for a long period of time,” he continued. “America’s enemies will never see it coming.” NGAD is a “family of systems” that includes the F-47 and Collaborative Combat Aircraft designed to achieve air superiority. The F-47’s modular design is intended to accommodate emerging technology and integrate long-range strike capabilities to counter threats in contested environments. The F-47 program was allotted $3.45 billion in fiscal year 2026 funding and over $5 billion in the fiscal 2027 budget request. Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

Amazon said it will raise this year's capital spending on technology, mostly artificial intelligence, by an additional 10% after reporting strong profits and net sales for its fiscal second quarter, helped by surging growth in its cloud computing unit. Sales at AWS rose 37% in the April-June period, up from 28% in the previous quarter and the fastest growth in 18 quarters. CEO Andy Jassy told investors that Amazon now expects capital spending of $220 billion, including outlays on robots, semiconductors and satellites. That is up from the $200 billion plan announced in February and well above last year's $128 billion. Jassy cited the higher cost of memory chips as the main reason. He said that even at $220 billion Amazon will lack the capacity to meet all demand this year, that he expects the same in 2027, and that "the demand we already have for 2028 is striking." Shares rose more than 9% in after-hours trading. Amazon offered a cautious sales outlook for the current quarter. Investors had been watching to see whether heavy AI spending is paying off, and worry such spending is eating into cash flows and may not be worthwhile if AI doesn't deliver promised productivity and profits. Amazon was among the last big tech companies to report. Alphabet reported better-than-expected revenue last week, driven by an 82% increase in its cloud business, but its stock tumbled as it raised its full-year capital expenditure forecast to $195 billion to $205 billion from $180 billion to $190 billion. Microsoft reported stronger-than-expected profit, with strong Azure growth, and did not announce a big increase in AI spending, which boosted its shares. Jassy said AWS is "booming," with its AI and chips businesses each topping run rates of $25 billion. Amazon set record Prime delivery speeds in the first half, with 40% more items delivered same-day or overnight. In April, Amazon signed big deals with OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, including a "major expansion" of its OpenAI partnership. Amazon faces higher tariff costs from President Donald Trump's trade policies, and rising shipping costs tied to the Iran war's effect on oil and fuel prices could cut into e-commerce revenue. Faster delivery, driven by robotics, AI and more efficient warehousing, helped Amazon surpass Walmart in February as the largest U.S. company by revenue, according to Fortune. In May, Amazon announced it was rapidly opening small order processing hubs in dozens of U.S. and foreign cities for 30-minute deliveries. In the first half, it more than doubled new customers for its online pharmacy, and same-day prescription deliveries rose nearly fivefold. Prime Day was moved up to June from July this year. Amazon reported net income of $62.65 billion, or $5.75 per share, for the quarter ended June 30, versus $18.16 billion, or $1.68 per share, a year earlier. Net sales rose to $200.6 billion from $167.7 billion, topping analyst expectations of $197.03 billion. Amazon expects net sales of $197 billion to $202 billion next quarter, while analysts expect $203.9 billion, according to FactSet.

A top Ukrainian diplomat told NBC News in a report published Thursday that Kyiv had brokered an agreement with Washington to share its drone technology, potentially allowing collaboration to improve drone models. According to NBC News, the deal involves "allowing Ukrainian-made weaponry to be sent to the U.S. for military testing and evaluation." An anonymous senior administration official and Ukraine's ambassador to Washington, Olha Stefanishyna, reportedly confirmed it, though it had not been publicly confirmed at press time and few other details were offered. NBC speculated it could hint at a growing U.S. munitions shortage after months of conflict with Iran, though the Ukraine war is distinct from Operation Epic Fury, America's operations against Iran. The report follows Ukraine promoting itself as a global drone heavyweight, both in resisting Russia's invasion and in countering cheap Iranian "Shahed" drones. President Volodymyr Zelensky offered Shahed experts to Gulf states facing Iranian attacks, and they are believed to be aiding Saudi Arabia. It also follows a cordial White House meeting between Zelensky and President Donald Trump, held before Zelensky attended the funeral of Sen. Lindsey Graham; both leaders called it positive and discussed paths to ending the war. The line between the Ukraine and Iran conflicts has blurred. Ukraine has long accused Iran of supplying suicide drones to Russia, but Zelensky recently suggested Russia is now aiding Iran. On July 25 he announced he would share intelligence on "Russia's new assistance to the Iranian regime," accusing Moscow of providing satellite imagery to help Iran target American military facilities in the Middle East and Gulf neighbors. He cited "a clear correlation between Russia's satellite imagery of these sites and Iranian strikes." Zelensky also revealed last week that Ukraine struck Iranian vessels in the Caspian Sea believed to be carrying military hardware for Russia, along with a warship. Iran reacted with outrage and threats of retaliation, claiming the vessels were not engaged in military activity. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Zelensky attacked an Iranian commercial vessel, killing a sailor, calling it a UN Charter violation done at Israel's behest to drag Europe into its war, and said it "CANNOT GO UNANSWERED." Ukraine had already played a role against Iran. In March, shortly after the Iran-U.S. conflict began, Zelensky visited the UAE and Saudi Arabia, which, along with Bahrain and Kuwait, were among the first targeted by Iranian strikes; Saudi Arabia and Kuwait continue to face them. The Saudi visit produced a defense agreement under which Ukraine would share expertise and systems with Saudi Arabia. Zelensky also offered help to American forces, telling the New York Post he wanted the U.S. not to see Ukraine as a country that merely asks for help. Trump replied at the time, "We don't need help. The last person we need help from is Zelensky."

Federal regulators are clearing the way for robotaxis to operate without manual controls like steering wheels or, eventually, brake pedals as rules catch up to the technology. Amazon's fully autonomous Zoox vehicles received approval Thursday to begin charging for rides once they secure state and local approval. Zoox has offered free rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco since last year, and the company said more than half a million people have already ridden in its vehicles. A rider in Las Vegas said the experience was scary at first but then "really cool," though the projected wait time kept changing. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) also proposed a rule last month to allow robotaxis without brake pedals, which is still pending. Administrator Jonathan Morrison said the agency wants to update regulations written decades ago, when a human driver was always assumed, because items like steering wheels, windshield wipers and side-view mirrors aren't really needed in an autonomous vehicle. He said NHTSA will still act as the "cop on the beat" to make sure this is done right. Questions remain about safety. The Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety group raised concerns about Zoox's plan to operate without a steering wheel or other standard controls, saying the company provided no detailed evidence that its vehicles could operate safely on public roads. The group's general counsel, Peter Kurdock, said there were "lots of promises" but no data behind them. Morrison said the technology promises to eliminate distracted or drunk driving, but robotaxis have had problems, from odd behavior like stopping in the middle of the road to passing school buses or interfering with first responders. NHTSA responded with investigations, recalls and calls to action, he said, adding that Americans shouldn't be terribly worried about robotaxi safety. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety said the limited crash data the government requires makes it hard to assess robotaxi safety. Most companies don't report miles driven, making crash rates impossible to calculate, and there is no clear standard for which incidents must be reported, so autonomous vehicle companies report many more minor incidents than human drivers do. The industry is expanding quickly. Zoox and Tesla are working to catch up to industry leader Waymo, which operates in multiple cities and is owned by Google's parent company, Alphabet. Zoox CEO Aicha Evans called the approval an important milestone. Amazon, which paid $1.2 billion to acquire Zoox, hopes to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robotaxis a year at a plant near Silicon Valley. Initially, Zoox may deploy up to 2,500 vehicles without steering wheels over the next two years while it works to prove the technology is safe.

Trump announced on Truth Social an agreement with Hamas leaders that he said would lead to "COMPLETE DISARMAMENT" of the group under a structured process. Whether it holds is uncertain: an Israeli official said the proposed terms were not acceptable, and a Hamas official and a diplomat said progress depends on Israel's response. Trump threatened to withdraw the nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general and restart the process once Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis leave office. Stephanie Garneaux of Portland, Oregon, has severe diastasis recti, a common pregnancy-related condition in which the abdominal muscles thin and separate, making movements like bending and stretching painful. After physical therapy failed, her doctor recommended surgery, but her Medicaid plan denied the request twice. She received a call this month that she had been waiting for. Topline. Jeff Bezos on Friday became the world’s third-richest person once again, reclaiming the ranking from Google co-founder Sergey Brin as Amazon’s stock accelerated at its fastest pace in four years, following a hotter-than-expected earnings report. Key Facts. Shares of Amazon surged about 14% shortly after trading opened on Friday, pacing the stock’s largest single-day gain since April 24, 2015 (14.1%). That burst followed Amazon’s quarterly earnings on Thursday, in which the firm reported $206.6 billion in revenue boosted by a 37% year-over-year surge in cloud sales to $42.2 billion, exceeding Wall Street’s estimates of $197 billion and $40.5 billion, respectively, according to FactSet. Amazon even raised its spending forecast this year to $220 billion, up from $200 billion, as CEO Andy Jassy said a majority of Amazon’s capital expenditures would go toward matching demand for AI, noting the firm was “unusually well-positioned for this AI inflection.” Tech firms have been increasingly scrutinized as they raise their projected spending to meet demand for AI, but Forrester analyst Tracy Woo wrote in a note Thursday that Amazon’s cloud sales growth was a “clear indicator” that its investments are “meeting market demand rather than outpacing it.” Forbes Valuation. Surging Amazon shares added $25 billion to Bezos’ net worth, estimated at $271.5 billion as of Friday morning. That ranks the Amazon founder as the world’s third-richest person between Google co-founders Larry Page ($279.3 billion) and Brin ($257.6 billion). tangent. Apple shares plunged 9% after the firm issued weaker-than-expected guidance for its current quarter, citing “supply constraints” as it now anticipates revenue growth between 9% and 11%, below estimates of 12%. Apple CEO Tim Cook, who spoke in his last earnings call at the helm of the firm, said Apple expects to “pay even higher memory costs” amid a global memory shortage. “If you look beyond September, we see the market pricing for memory continuing to increase, which could drive an increasing impact on our business,” Cook said. key background. Bezos and Brin have swapped spots among the world’s wealthiest people multiple times in recent weeks, as investors weigh incoming earnings reports and any signs of weakness in the global AI market. Most of the focus has centered on AI strategy from mega-cap firms, like Amazon, as they navigate an accelerating market and a shrinking memory trade. Earlier this week, Meta shares tanked while Microsoft rallied 15%, as traders took sides on either firm’s approach to their AI products.

Microsoft reported fiscal Q4 2026 results that beat Street expectations on overall revenue, Azure revenue and earnings. The stock rose more than 15% in the session before the report. With a market cap of $2.9 trillion, it could soon pass $3 trillion, though it remains down 5% year-to-date, and its dividend yield is 0.93%. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) rose 6.9% over the past five sessions, suggesting talk of software's decline may be premature. Revenue grew 18% year over year to $90 billion, beating estimates by $2.4 billion. The Intelligent Cloud segment, which includes Azure, grew 31.5% to $39.31 billion, with operating income up 31.4% to $15.96 billion and margins roughly flat. Azure revenue rose 43% against expectations of 39% to 40%. For the full year, Azure surpassed a $100 billion run rate for the first time, and commercial backlog nearly doubled to $684 billion, of which 30% will be recognized over the next year. Productivity and Business Processes revenue, which includes Microsoft 365 Copilot, rose 14% to $37.8 billion, with operating margin at 57.9% versus 57.4% a year earlier. CEO Satya Nadella said Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats, up from over 20 million in Q3. Azure and Copilot are both growing healthily while reporting operating margins above 40%, indicating returns on AI investment. Capital expenditure was $41 billion, up 70%, with guidance of $50 billion for Q1 and $175 billion for FY27. CFO Amy Hood said two-thirds of the quarter's spending went to short-lived assets such as CPUs and GPUs, as demand outpaces capacity and the company is capacity constrained for calendar 2026. The Android operating system has officially introduced automatic cloud backup functionality for locally stored documents, enabling users to automatically save files from internal phone storage directly to Google Drive. Rolling out broadly through Google Play Services version 26.26, this system feature addresses a long-standing data management gap, making it significantly easier for users to safeguard critical local files against potential device loss, theft, or sudden hardware failure. Users can configure the new feature by navigating to Settings > Accounts and backup > Google Backup on their Android smartphones. Within this menu, a new Documents category appears positioned between Photos and videos and Other device data. By default, the toggle switch remains disabled. Activating the feature immediately displays available cloud storage capacity alongside direct shortcuts to manage quota allocations or purchase additional Google One storage plans. When activated, the system automatically creates a dedicated root directory named “Android backups” within “My Drive”. Inside this directory, a subfolder labeled with the specific smartphone model name stores the captured files. The backup functionality supports an extensive range of file formats. Beyond conventional document formats such as .PDF, .DOC, .XLS, and .PPT, practical tests confirm that the process also backs up .ZIP compressed archives and .APK installer packages originating from the device’s main Downloads folder. Users should carefully monitor their cloud capacity, as all uploaded documents count directly against their total Google Drive storage quota. If the feature is turned off later, previously backed-up cloud files will not be deleted automatically. Crucially, the tool operates as a static security copy rather than a bi-directional real-time sync service. Edits made to a local document will not reflect in the cloud copy, nor will cloud changes modify local files. Overall, this feature provides essential protection for local receipts, contracts, and installers. Filed in . Read more about Android, Backups and Google Drive.

AI has become a standard part of modern software development, through coding assistants, code completion tools and AI-powered development environments, yet engineering organizations still struggle with developer productivity. About 65% of organizations report that engineering teams spend just 0–20% of their time on net-new innovation, with most capacity consumed by maintenance, migrations, reviews, operational toil and context switching. The problem is no longer access to AI tools but how organizations redesign software development around them. In an episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, Deepak Singh, vice president of developer agents and experiences at Amazon Web Services Inc., and Steve Tarcza, director of software development at Amazon, discussed the shift from AI-assisted coding to AI-native engineering workflows. Organizations using the same tools get dramatically different results. Singh said studies inside and outside the company show some teams gaining 15% to 30% in productivity while others gain three to 10 times or more. According to Singh, the highest performers rethink software development itself, redesigning planning, specifications, reviews and handoffs so AI agents become active participants throughout the lifecycle rather than being inserted into existing workflows. AI is evolving from a coding assistant into a collaborative engineering system. Context is becoming a key asset. Foundation models understand programming languages but not an organization's architecture, coding standards, operational practices or business priorities. Tarcza said teams that write down that knowledge, whether in steering files, documentation or specifications, unlock agents to take on much more work. Prompts alone are insufficient for production development; agents need structured knowledge, engineering intent and reusable organizational context. Trust underpins adoption. Tarcza said, "Trust is the currency of AI adoption," noting that if agents can't be trusted, nobody will use them. AWS is emphasizing specification-driven development, structured engineering context and automated reasoning techniques that identify ambiguity before code generation begins. The goal is software developers are confident deploying to production, which matters more as agents run longer tasks with less human oversight. AI is also expanding beyond writing code. Within Amazon, teams use AI agents to prioritize work, summarize Slack conversations, analyze tickets, generate specifications and automate parts of daily engineering operations, functioning more like teammates than assistants. Tarcza cited an Amazon retail feature called "Add to Order," which was delivered two months earlier than projected after the team adopted spec-driven development, placing AI at the center of planning, execution and implementation rather than only code generation. The author concludes that the first wave of generative AI accelerated individual tasks, while the next transforms software engineering itself. Organizations that merely layer AI onto existing workflows will likely see incremental gains, whereas those redesigning around specifications, trusted context, autonomous agents and AI-native processes may unlock far greater productivity and innovation. Competitive advantage is shifting from adopting AI tools to building organizations that know how to work alongside them.

The United States’ next-generation fighter aircraft program has reached a significant milestone. Boeing has begun manufacturing prototype aircraft for the F-47, the U.S. Air Force’s future sixth-generation stealth fighter. According to Air Force officials, the program remains on schedule, with the aircraft’s maiden flight expected in 2028. The progress marks the transition from years of design, research, and technology demonstrations to the construction of physical aircraft that will undergo rigorous testing before entering operational service. Centerpiece of US Air Force’s Next Generation Air Dominance program. The F-47 is the centerpiece of the U.S. Air Force’s Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program, an ambitious effort to secure American air superiority for decades to come. It is intended to replace the F-22 Raptor, which entered service in 2005 and remains one of the world’s most capable air-superiority fighters. Unlike previous fighter programs, the F-47 is not being developed as a standalone aircraft. Instead, it is designed to operate as the command platform of a networked combat system that includes autonomous drones, satellites, airborne sensors, and advanced communication networks. With prototype construction now in progress, engineers will begin integrating the aircraft’s complex airframe, propulsion system, avionics, stealth materials, and onboard computing systems. These early aircraft will primarily support developmental testing rather than combat operations. Flight-test campaign will evaluate fighter’s aerodynamic performance. The upcoming flight-test campaign will evaluate the fighter’s aerodynamic performance, stealth characteristics, software reliability, weapons integration, and overall mission capability before full-scale production begins. Future air warfare is expected to be far more complex than today’s conflicts. Adversaries are investing heavily in long-range missiles, integrated air-defense systems, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, and next-generation fighter aircraft. To maintain an operational advantage, the U.S. Air Force believes it requires an aircraft capable of surviving and fighting in highly contested environments. The F-47 is expected to address these challenges through a combination of low observability, long-range performance, powerful onboard sensors, and advanced data processing. Artificial intelligence is also anticipated to assist pilots by rapidly analyzing battlefield information, prioritizing threats, and coordinating missions with unmanned aircraft. One of the defining features of the F-47 concept is its ability to operate alongside Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA)—autonomous drones designed to fly with crewed fighters. These drones could perform tasks such as reconnaissance, electronic warfare, decoy operations, or missile strikes while remaining under the supervision of the F-47 pilot. This “manned-unmanned teaming” concept is expected to reduce operational risk and expand combat capability without placing additional pilots in danger. Officials have revealed that the F-47 program has entered its engineering and manufacturing development phase with unprecedented maturity. “The F-47 will fly in this administration,” said Gen. Dale White, director of Critical Major Weapon Systems. Military planners have increasingly focused on the Indo-Pacific region, where vast distances present major operational challenges. The F-47 is expected to have greater range than current U.S. fighters, allowing it to operate farther from friendly bases while carrying sufficient fuel and advanced weapons. Although official specifications remain classified, analysts believe improved endurance and fuel efficiency will be among the aircraft’s key advantages. Most technical details surrounding the F-47 remain confidential. Neither Boeing nor the U.S. Air Force has publicly disclosed the aircraft’s maximum speed, combat radius, radar systems, engine configuration, or weapons payload. This level of secrecy reflects the strategic importance of the program, which is intended to preserve the United States’ technological advantage in air combat. For Boeing, the F-47 represents one of the company’s most important military aviation projects in decades. Successfully delivering the aircraft would strengthen its position in the defence sector and reinforce its role as a leading supplier of advanced combat aircraft for the U.S. military. The program is also expected to support thousands of highly skilled jobs across Boeing’s manufacturing facilities and supply chain. The immediate focus is completing the prototype aircraft and beginning flight testing in 2028. Engineers will spend several years validating every aspect of the design before the fighter enters operational service.

Google Drive is free, with 15GB of storage, an office suite and sharing tools, and a Google One subscription expands it. The base plan adds 100GB for a couple of dollars, with 400GB, 2TB and 5TB tiers above it, and three of the four plans offer far more than extra storage. The article lists ways people underuse the service. First, Drive can hold almost any file type, not just documents and photos. The author stores ripped CDs and a friend's Minecraft server, and apps such as CookMate use Drive for backups. Second, files should be organized with folders, color-coding, renaming and the move function, since Drive won't do it automatically. Google also released an AI tool that sorts files into existing or suggested folders. Third, the built-in tools are underused: Docs, Sheets, Slides, Keep, a PDF viewer and Gmail. Docs can handle .docx files. The 400GB tier adds Gemini to Gmail, and higher tiers add it to Docs, Slides, Meet and Vids. Fourth, Google One's exclusive storage manager, available online and in the Android and iOS apps, shows what is in your trash and your largest files across Drive, Gmail and Photos. Fifth, Google Photos' Storage Saver Mode reduces image quality before upload, with negligible visible loss for photos and file sizes cut by up to 75%, though it is less suited to video. Sixth, Magic Editor, once Pixel-exclusive, is available to other Android phones with the 2TB tier or above. It can deblur faces, remove objects and improve lighting and saturation, though the author acknowledges criticism of AI content. Seventh, a Family Group lets relatives share expanded storage, some AI features and Google Store discounts for free. Storage is shared on an as-needed basis, so unused space isn't wasted. Plans such as Metro by T-Mobile include Google One, which can be shared this way. Eighth, Gemini usage limits rise with the tier: the 400GB plan doubles free usage, 2TB gives four times, and 5TB gives 20 times. It can answer questions, help write code, summarize files and make images with Nano Banana. Google uses shared information to train future models, so avoid sensitive or work documents. Ninth, NotebookLM, an AI note-taking and research tool, gets higher limits. Free accounts get three audio overviews, 100 notebooks and 10 reports per day, while the Ultra subscription raises those to 200 audio overviews, 500 notebooks and a thousand reports, plus more flashcards, quizzes, slides and video overviews. Students should follow their school's AI rules. Tenth, higher tiers unlock other Google AI products, including Antigravity, an agentic development platform that built an operating system running Doom at Google I/O 2026, along with Flow (video), Flow Music, AI Studio Project Genie and Dreambeans. Since subscribers are already paying for these tools, the author suggests trying them.

A U.S. natural hydrogen explorer is turning to cloud computing to speed up the search for underground hydrogen deposits, selecting a platform designed to process massive geological datasets in hours instead of days. Koloma has selected GeoComputing Group’s RiVA private cloud platform to power its exploration and analysis workflows. The platform is designed to tackle one of the biggest challenges in natural hydrogen exploration: processing and interpreting vast amounts of geological data quickly enough to identify promising underground deposits. Natural hydrogen, also known as white hydrogen, has gained attention as a potential low-carbon energy source because it occurs naturally underground and requires little processing after extraction. But finding commercially viable reserves remains data-intensive, requiring advanced computing infrastructure capable of handling complex geological models and decades of exploration data. According to GeoComputing, RiVA’s high-throughput architecture can cut processing times from days to hours while improving workflow efficiency. The platform also simplifies the deployment of geoscience applications, allowing exploration teams spread across multiple locations to access the same computing environment without building specialized IT infrastructure. Faster data, faster decisions. “As a data-driven natural hydrogen exploration company, we look to work with symbiotic partners in ways that will help accelerate global decarbonization efforts and usher in the next generation of global energy,” said Jerome Bellian, PhD, VP of Emerging Plays at Koloma. See All. Bellian said the company chose RiVA because it supports traditional oil and gas datasets and applications that can be adapted for the emerging natural hydrogen industry. “It is critical that we have the best-in-class technology to make the most informed decisions quickly, and RiVA is the only technology on the market that allows us to do this.” GeoComputing said its platform currently supports more than 200 petro-technical applications used across exploration and production activities. Each application is pre-tested and integrated into the platform to reduce deployment time and improve reliability for end users. Scaling hydrogen exploration. Koloma also expects the platform to reduce the burden on its internal IT team. “RiVA gave us the geoscience computing platform we needed without requiring us to build and support a costly specialized environment ourselves,” said Richard Haynie, Head of IT at Koloma. Haynie added that GeoComputing’s engineers remained involved beyond deployment, giving both IT staff and geoscientists direct access to technical support while allowing the company’s lean IT team to focus on business operations. In addition to supporting exploration workflows, the RiVA platform includes integrated disaster recovery capabilities intended to improve business continuity and protect critical exploration data. John Creevan, CEO of GeoComputing, said the partnership reflects a shared focus on using data-driven technologies to reduce exploration risks and costs while improving access to new energy resources.

One of the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturers is expanding its U.S. chip production with a new $1 billion investment in industrial gas infrastructure, as demand for advanced semiconductors continues to grow. Linde has signed a long-term agreement to supply ultra-high-purity industrial gases to the unnamed chipmaker’s manufacturing complex in Phoenix, Arizona. The company will invest $1 billion to expand its existing on-site gas production facilities, making it one of Linde’s largest investments for an electronics customer worldwide. The expansion will support two new semiconductor fabrication plants by supplying ultra-high-purity nitrogen, oxygen and argon, gases that are essential for manufacturing advanced chips in contamination-free environments. Alongside the U.S. project, Linde’s Taiwan joint venture, Linde LienHwa, will invest about $800 million to build new industrial gas and hydrogen production facilities for the same customer’s semiconductor manufacturing and advanced packaging sites across Taiwan. Supporting chip expansion. As part of the Arizona project, Linde will build, own and operate two new SPECTRA air separation units and related infrastructure. The new facilities will join three existing air separation units already operating at the Phoenix site. Air separation units produce industrial gases by separating atmospheric air into oxygen, nitrogen and argon. In semiconductor fabrication, these gases are used throughout manufacturing processes, including wafer processing, chamber purging and maintaining contamination-free production environments. See All. The new plants will use Linde’s SPECTRA technology, which the company says is designed to deliver the purity and operational reliability required for advanced semiconductor manufacturing. “Advanced semiconductor manufacturing depends on the reliable supply of gases at exceptional levels of purity,” said Armando Botello, President Linde Gases, US. Taiwan capacity expands. The Taiwan expansion mirrors the U.S. investment, reflecting continued growth in advanced chip production across two of the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturing hubs. Linde LienHwa plans to build several additional air separation units along with hydrogen production facilities to support new semiconductor fabrication and advanced packaging operations. The company did not disclose the identity of the customer, but described it as one of the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturers. “As global demand for advanced semiconductors continues to increase, this investment demonstrates Linde’s ability to deliver the purity, reliability and scale our customers require,” Botello said. He added: “We are proud to support our customer’s expansion in the United States and Taiwan and to further strengthen our long-term global relationship.” Industrial gases are among the critical materials required for chip production, alongside ultrapure water, specialty chemicals and silicon wafers. Modern semiconductor fabrication plants consume massive volumes of high-purity nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen to maintain the tightly controlled manufacturing conditions needed for advanced chips. Linde said the Arizona expansion represents one of its largest electronics-sector investments globally, while the combined U.S. and Taiwan projects underscore continued investment in semiconductor supply chains as chipmakers expand production capacity.

Cupertino, California, technology giant Apple warned in its 10-Q filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that it could face shortages of computing capacity when it comes to artificial intelligence and machine learning requirements. Apple's latest earnings report was notable for the firm outlining that supply chain constraints could affect its revenue growth in the current quarter. However, a deeper read of its SEC filings reveals that the firm is also concerned about the constraints in AI and machine learning computing infrastructure capacity. Apple Says Product & Services Launches Could Be Delayed Due To Computing Capacity Shortages. In its 10-Q filing with the SEC, Apple added a section about components and computing resources, which could count as risk factors to its business. The firm started off by outlining that its decision to limit sourcing for components and parts to a select group of suppliers exposes it to pricing fluctuations and supply shortages, which could affect its revenue. Apple specifically mentioned the ongoing shortage in the memory industry as it outlined that turmoil in the NAND and DRAM sectors "adversely affects the Company’s ability to obtain sufficient quantities of components and products on commercially reasonable terms, or at all." The firm then shifts to discussing computing capacity for artificial intelligence and machine learning applications. Unlike hyperscalers and its big tech peers, Apple has restrained itself from spending heavily on AI infrastructure or software development. Instead, the firm has opted to rely on infrastructure from others, such as Google. In its filing, Apple admitted that its artificial intelligence and machine learning services depend "on access to sufficient computing resources." The firm added that demand for this infrastructure had grown substantially and resulted in "constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs." According to Apple, apart from its own computing infrastructure, it also relies on third-party infrastructure to meet its computing needs, and it may be "unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, to meet customer demand." Consequently, the firm outlined that if it is unable to access sufficient capacity in time or at reasonable costs, then the functionality and availability of its products and services could be limited and the deployment of products and services could be delayed. While Apple's big tech peers such as Google and Amazon have developed custom in-house AI chips to run AI software, details about Apple's hardware have been scant. The firm runs AI workloads through its Private Cloud Compute (PCC) ecosystem. On this front it made an important announcement in June when it revealed that it had worked with Google and NVIDIA to extend PCC to NVIDIA's chips via Google Cloud. China is preparing new rules to restrict foreign access to its most advanced AI models, according to a Reuters report citing sources. The plans target top-tier, frontier-level systems rather than China's broader range of AI models. The move follows a year of expanding global reach by Chinese AI firms such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Zhipu, whose open-weight models (which anyone can download, run, and modify) have been widely adopted abroad. Chinese open-weight models overtook U.S. models in total Hugging Face downloads by August 2025 and made up seven of the platform's top ten most-downloaded models between November and December 2025. Alibaba's Qwen family surpassed 1 billion cumulative Hugging Face downloads by March 2026. Chinese state media and officials have not detailed the scope of the proposed restrictions. Earlier this month, Breitbart reported that China's "Kimi K3" model largely matched top U.S. models on many metrics. Arena testing showed it beat Anthropic's Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol in front-end coding, and outperformed Anthropic's Opus 4.8 in broader text ranking, while costing 40 percent less than comparable American models. Moonshot AI plans to release Kimi as an open-weight model on July 27, letting companies and governments customize it and run it on their own infrastructure instead of developer-controlled cloud services. Meanwhile, the U.S. Congress is considering the Remote Access Security Act (RASA), authored by Sens. David McCormick, Ron Wyden, Tom Cotton, and Chris Coons. It awaits consideration by a Senate committee and has not been scheduled for a floor vote. The bill would give federal regulators authority to license or restrict remote, cloud-based access to export-controlled U.S. technology. Some scholars have criticized its scope. Clark D. Asay of Brigham Young University said that, while worries about adversaries accessing American computing remotely are legitimate, the bill as written is "broad enough to burden allies and commercial users who pose no meaningful risks," pushing them to build their own solutions or use non-American AI providers. Oren Etzioni, professor emeritus at the University of Washington, warned that foreign customers could turn to China, costing the U.S. economic activity and "technological and political influence," and argued that export controls "cannot become America's entire AI strategy." The Trump administration has generally favored competing with China through the strength of American companies rather than restrictions alone. Its settlement approving Hewlett Packard Enterprise's acquisition of Juniper Networks was reportedly meant to strengthen a U.S. rival to Huawei. Under a July 2025 executive order, the Commerce Department launched the American AI Exports Program, inviting U.S. companies to propose full-stack AI packages for deployment with international partners. At the India AI Impact Summit in February, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios called American AI "the gold standard." The bill's fate could shape how far U.S. export policy extends into cloud computing as Beijing weighs its own limits on foreign access to its most advanced AI.

Bombardier's Global 8000, the fastest civil aircraft since Concorde, costs at least $78 million. It entered service in December and made its airshow debut at the Farnborough Airshow near London. The flight from Los Angeles to Farnborough took 8 hours and 46 minutes, the fastest time ever recorded between the two destinations; a commercial LA-London flight typically takes up to 10 hours. Its top speed is Mach 0.95, while Concorde could exceed Mach 2, or over 1,500 mph, and connected New York and London in under four hours. Bombardier's CEO, Éric Martel, and chief engineer, Stephen McCullough, say going supersonic isn't worth it. Martel said supersonic flight would be a niche and very expensive to certify. McCullough said going beyond the speed of sound requires a great deal of thrust and brings challenges of drag, friction and heat, and that the Global 8000 gets close enough to supersonic speed without those complications. To certify the jet's structural integrity for such speeds, Bombardier had a NASA F-18 follow the test aircraft. McCullough cited Concorde's hurdles: four Rolls-Royce Olympus engines with afterburning that burned huge quantities of fuel, and a delta-wing design needing a steep angle of attack at takeoff and landing, hence its drooping nose. Having worked at Bombardier for 37 years, he said there has always been talk of a Concorde replacement, but the economics and the compromises needed for that speed make it hard. He noted a couple of companies are trying. One is Boom Supersonic, which is building an airliner capable of Mach 1.7, about 1,300 mph. It chose to build its own engine, called Symphony, after major manufacturers declined to help; Rolls-Royce had a contract with Boom but decided not to prioritize commercial supersonic flight. Last January, Boom's scaled-down test aircraft broke the sound barrier without an audible sonic boom on the ground. A few months later, President Donald Trump signed an executive order lifting the ban on supersonic civil aircraft over land. The Global 8000 is named for its 8,000-nautical-mile range, enough for a 17-hour nonstop flight. Customers also expect superlative comfort, McCullough said: very good galleys for nice meals, a very quiet cabin, and more of what they have at home, including high-speed internet, comfortable seats, ample space, good views and a rear bedroom. The jet has the lowest cabin altitude of any private jet, reducing jet lag and dehydration. While cruising at 41,000 feet, the cabin feels like 2,691 feet, versus about 6,000 feet on newer airliners like the Boeing 787 or Airbus A350.

The PGA Tour once shipped its own servers by truck, rebuilding its data operation at each new course. David Provan, the tour's vice president of digital architecture, called the tour "a traveling circus." That setup illustrates a shift Amazon CEO Andy Jassy predicts at far larger scale: about 85% of global IT spending is currently for on-premise servers, an equation that "is going to flip in the next 10 to 20 years." Amazon's second-quarter results suggest the shift is happening faster than expected. AWS revenue hit $42.2 billion, up 37.6% year over year, its fastest growth in 18 quarters and the fifth straight quarter of acceleration. AWS added more than $4.6 billion sequentially, about 80% more than its previous largest quarterly increase, and now runs at a $169 billion annualized rate. Customer backlog stands at $496 billion. Jassy said AWS will "very possibly be a $1 trillion annual revenue business for us in time." Amazon stock rose more than 15% on Friday, even though Jassy raised 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $220 billion from $200 billion. William Blair analysts said the market would likely react more favorably than feared. The PGA Tour, an AWS sponsor that signed a new agreement during Amazon's first quarter, shows the mechanism: companies move existing infrastructure to the cloud, then stack AI on top. When it opened new headquarters about five years ago, the tour skipped fixed IT infrastructure and moved everything to AWS, including its ShotLink ball-tracking system, media archive, website, app and data distribution. It then layered AI on top. CFO Brian Olsavsky said customers seeking AI's benefits are accelerating cloud transitions, with AI investment bringing a corresponding increase in core consumption. Using an agentic AI platform on Amazon Bedrock, the tour creates about 150 betting profiles in about nine minutes and produces thousands of content pieces weekly. At the 2025 Players Championship it launched AI commentary giving a two-sentence summary for each of 32,000 shots. In 2026 it debuted "agentic production," a fully automated broadcast with camera selection and graphics driven by ShotLink data, plus a "favorite player hub" in its app. Provan said the tour shifted from pursuing "AI projects" to solving business problems, and now has "projects that use AI." Jassy described AI demand as a barbell: AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI and a few breakout consumer apps on one end, and enterprises gaining productivity and lower costs on the other. The middle, existing enterprise workloads that could use AI inference but mostly don't yet, will be "the largest absolute segment" over time. Val Henderson, CEO of consulting firm Caylent, called Bedrock's model choice, running Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI and Amazon's Nova with prompt routing to the most cost-effective model, AWS's key differentiator. Amazon said customers spent more on Bedrock in the second quarter than in all prior quarters combined since its 2023 launch, more customers joined in the past six months than in the first two years, and AWS's AI business exceeds a $25 billion annual run rate. Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, said enthusiasm has not peaked and that regulated industries such as healthcare, financial services, insurance and manufacturing are moving fastest, because years of focus on governance and data security make adding AI relatively cheap. Provan said AWS "has ridden shotgun with us the whole way."
