These capabilities strengthen the solution’s ability to operate with minimal human intervention while further reducing risk to Soldiers. Primordial Labs’ next-generation human-machine interface, Anura, transforms robotic systems into battlefield teammates, according to a press release. By distilling commander’s intent through intuitive, natural language commands, Anura scales the Soldier-to-robot ratio, reduces cognitive burden, accelerates training timelines, and enables heads-up, hands-free operation. Hybrid vehicle platform exemplifies how commercial technologies can be adapted. “The Harbinger hybrid vehicle platform exemplifies how proven commercial technologies can be rapidly adapted to meet the evolving needs of the U.S. military,” said John Harris, Co-founder and CEO of Harbinger. “By partnering with American Rheinmetall, we’re bringing together advanced vehicle platforms, scalable manufacturing, and proprietary battery technology to deliver autonomous-ready vehicles that reduce risk to soldiers while enhancing military operational effectiveness.” The contract includes the potential for follow‑on orders as the Army continues to evolve and modernize its autonomous logistics fleet.

Coal has long been associated with electricity generation, steelmaking, and carbon emissions. But a new technology unveiled in China aims to give the fossil fuel a very different role. Transforming it into high-value carbon materials used in industries ranging from energy storage to aerospace. The technology, presented at an industry conference in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province, converts ordinary coal into premium carbon materials through a specialized coal liquefaction process. Developers say the approach could significantly increase the economic value of coal while reducing emissions associated with conventional coal utilization. A different approach to coal utilization. According to the company, the technology was jointly developed by Zhaoqing Shunxin Coal Chemical Industry Technology Co., Ltd. and Guangdong Coal-based Carbon Materials Research Co., Ltd. It was reviewed by an expert panel organized by the China International Association for the Promotion of Science and Technology in October 2025, which assessed the process as having reached an internationally leading level and recommended accelerating its commercialization. Rather than burning coal for energy or converting it into fuels, the process focuses on extracting carbon-rich molecular structures that can serve as feedstock for advanced engineering materials. The developers say the technology is based on quantum chemistry, separating coal molecules according to their chemical structure and bond strength. Molecules with lower bond energies are converted into oil and gas, while highly stable aromatic structures are transformed into condensed-ring pitch. A carbon-rich precursor used to manufacture advanced carbon materials. See All. From coal to aerospace-grade materials. One of the most notable aspects of the technology is the range of materials it claims can be produced. According to the developers, the condensed-ring pitch can be used to manufacture carbon foam, carbon fibers, 3D graphene, super-activated carbon, and supercapacitor-grade activated carbon. These materials are widely used across sectors including aerospace, energy storage, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. The company also claims its carbon foam exceeds China’s Class A flame-retardancy standard and is suitable for military and aerospace applications. If these performance claims are validated at commercial scale, the technology would shift coal from being primarily an energy resource to serving as a raw material for high-performance engineered products. Environmental and economic potential. The developers also highlight environmental benefits. According to the company, approximately 60% of the carbon contained in coal can be converted directly into carbon materials rather than being released through combustion. The process is also claimed to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by around two tonnes per tonne of coal processed, while generating virtually no waste gas, wastewater, or solid waste. Economically, the approach aims to move coal further up the value chain. Instead of producing a commodity worth hundreds or thousands of yuan per tonne, the process is designed to generate advanced carbon materials that can command values ranging from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of yuan per tonne, depending on the final product. These figures were provided by the technology’s developers and have not been independently verified. Moving toward commercialization. The technology has already taken its first step toward industrial deployment. The developers announced a cooperation agreement with the state-owned China Pingmei Shenma Group to construct a 6,000-tonne-per-year coal-based carbon materials project in Henan Province. They also said several carbon products produced using the process have completed user testing with downstream manufacturers and are now ready for commercial-scale deployment. Although the technology still faces the challenge of proving its performance at industrial scale, it reflects a broader shift in how coal is being viewed. Rather than serving solely as a fuel, researchers are increasingly exploring its potential as a source of advanced materials, potentially opening new applications for one of the world’s most abundant carbon resources.

Legislation sponsored by state Sen. Michael Hastings, D-Frankfort, that is expected to help law enforcement with investigations into missing persons cases was signed into law. The new law, which takes effect Jan. 1, was signed by Gov. JB Pritzker on July 24 and is intended to accelerate the timeline for adding critical forensic data to state and national databases. Under current law, missing persons cases are entered into state and federal databases and may eventually receive additional identifying data. Senate Bill 2949 updates the process so that if a person remains missing for 30 days after a police report is filed, their dental record will be added to the Law Enforcement Agencies Data System, rather than waiting longer under previous practice, according to a news release from Hastings’ office. After 60 days, the bill would require dental records to be entered into the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System, the federal repository used to match missing persons with unidentified remains, according to the release. Dental records, including charts and radiographs, are among the most reliable tools when fingerprints or other identifiers are unavailable, according to the release. By ensuring dental data is available earlier, the law aims to improve identification outcomes and help families find closure.

The researchers said they searched three major research databases and analyzed a decade of published literature on collagen peptides, skin aging, and the molecular mechanisms connecting the two. The review's authors argued that previous research has focused too narrowly on well-known signaling pathways related to collagen production, and in doing so may have missed a more complete picture of how collagen peptides act inside cells. A review of this type synthesizes existing studies rather than running new experiments, according to the article. Collagen is a family of proteins that provides structural support to skin, bones, tendons, ligaments, and cartilage, according to Mercola.com. It accounts for about 30% of total protein in the body and as much as 70% to 80% of the protein in skin [1]. Collagen supplements are hydrolyzed, digestible forms of collagen derived from cows, fish, and chickens, usually sold as powders. The peptides in those powders are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, according to the article. Previous clinical research indicates that collagen supplementation can improve skin elasticity and hydration, although experts said the effects develop over time and are not a quick fix, according to a scientific review published in February 2026 [2]. The review identified five mechanisms by which collagen peptides may slow skin aging: According to the review, collagen peptides may help clear free radicals that damage skin cells, inhibit inflammatory processes, slow the breakdown of the skin's structural matrix and reduce pigmentation. Earlier skin-aging research has described similar pathways, including inhibition of matrix metalloproteinase enzymes and chelation of reactive oxygen species [3]. The review's authors said the lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways have been "significantly underexplored" relative to the collagen-production story that has dominated the supplement market. Mitochondria act as cellular power generators, producing the energy cells need to function, repair and renew, according to the researchers. Age-related decline in mitochondrial function is linked to reduced skin regeneration because skin cells lose the energy required to maintain healthy tissue. The review suggests collagen peptides may support mitochondrial activity, helping skin cells remain energized and functional over time. Lysosomes act as cellular cleanup crews, breaking down and recycling damaged proteins and cellular debris. When lysosomal function declines with age, waste accumulates and contributes to cellular dysfunction, the researchers said. The review highlights lysosomal activation as a key mechanism through which collagen peptides may help keep skin cells functioning cleanly. The article noted that many natural antioxidant compounds have been shown to support skin aging by targeting the same organelles, adding weight to the case for collagen peptides in this pathway. The review did not recommend a specific dose or product. It stated that the functional activity of collagen peptides depends on bioavailability, or how well the peptides are absorbed and reach target tissues, according to the article. The authors identified bioavailability as an area needing further research. The article recommends choosing a collagen supplement that is third-party tested, uses hydrolyzed collagen peptides, and is paired with complementary antioxidants such as vitamins C and E. A separate review published in May 2026 reported that collagen, vitamin C and vitamin E may work synergistically to support healthy aging across body systems [4]. Nutritional literature has also examined interactions between vitamins C and E in skin care [5]. Consumers should also consider sourcing. Many nonorganic collagen products are made from hydrolyzed CAFO cattle hides rather than beef bones, according to Mercola.com [6]. The takeaway, according to the article, is that collagen peptides may act on cellular energy systems and cleanup processes, two fundamental drivers of skin aging, placing collagen in the broader skin longevity conversation.

The Next Generation Of 3D Printing Is Here, And You Can Build It Right Now. For makers who know the pain of waiting hours for a desktop 3D printer to lay down hundreds of millimeter-thick plastic lines one by one, a faster solution to additive manufacturing would be most welcome yesterday. Standard consumer manufacturing at the moment forces users to compromise between build speed and surface resolution, making operators choose between visible layer lines or lengthy post-processing work. But there's been a breakthrough in open-source hardware and software that's going to completely upend how hobbyists and engineers create physical objects. The OpenCAL volumetric 3D printer brings Computed Axial Lithography out of high-end university research laboratories and kicks open the doors of accessibility for makers. We can now build a portable, maker-friendly volumetric 3D printer capable of producing fully formed solid objects in just a few seconds. Yes, you read that right. Unlike traditional additive 3D printers, which can be either resin or filament 3D printers, volumetric printing solidifies entire three-dimensional geometries simultaneously without moving along a vertical Z-axis. Originally requiring massive laboratory setups, this technique has now been condensed down into an open-source build that fits neatly inside standard checked luggage. The system relies on a blend of off-the-shelf electronics, custom software, and specialized photopolymer materials to enable high-speed digital light processing. The contained nature of OpenCAL looks like it could also avoid some of the health risks that current 3D printers have. Computed Axial Lithography creates 3D shapes in seconds. Traditional desktop manufacturing builds an object layer by layer, otherwise known as additive manufacturing. But Computed Axial Lithography approaches fabrication from an entirely different mathematical dimension. Instead of extruding hot plastic or curing flat cross-sections onto a rising build plate, OpenCAL rotates a glass cylinder filled with viscous resin while projecting a video through the container. A compact projector shines 450-nanometer blue light through the spinning liquid, delivering varying intensities of light patterns from multiple angles. As the container rotates, the intersecting light energy accumulates a specific radiation dose only in predetermined coordinates, hardening the liquid resin into a solid part in one go. This simultaneous light accumulation delivers unprecedented production speeds compared to standard desktop systems. In a demonstration of the portable rig posted on YouTube, researcher Taylor Waddell showcases a fully formed miniature space shuttle created in 20 seconds. Because parts harden without sequential slicing, finished components avoid the mechanical weak points and layer lines typical of standard prints. Once exposure completes, operators clean away uncured resin using high-speed rotational spinning or an isopropyl alcohol bath before placing the component in water for a final ultraviolet light cure under natural sunlight. This post-processing routine is very similar to existing wash-and-cure solutions used in resin printing today. Standard off-the-shelf components. Constructing an OpenCAL volumetric 3D printer relies on accessible hardware, basic hand tools, and a straightforward assembly process. A Raspberry Pi single-board computer manages the system, driving an attached LCD and streaming continuous MP4 video files directly to the blue laser projector without needing complex G-code translation. Without a doubt, this is one of the most creative ways to use Raspberry Pi hardware. Alignment is a top priority here, too, since the printer locks in alignment with a custom three-axis screw adjustment mount to position the light precisely at the cylinder's center point. To keep home fabrication safe, the project partnered with Formlabs and MatterHackers to distribute pre-mixed photopolymer resins at cost, preventing users from handling volatile chemicals. The liquid polymer reacts exothermically during curing, generating moderate heat during normal print cycles. But Taylor Waddell warned that exposing bulk resin vials to direct sunlight can trigger runaway chemical reactions reaching 230 degrees Fahrenheit. All that said, building an OpenCAL 3D printer carries an estimated price tag of $1,400 for just the materials, with the laser projector accounting for most of that expense. However, anyone can download firmware from the OpenCAL GitHub page and follow step-by-step guides from the official OpenCAL build documentation.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71), the U.S. Navy's fourth Nimitz-class supercarrier, is set to return to its homeport of San Diego in the coming days. It left Naval Air Station North Island on June 15 to lead the biennial Rim of the Pacific 2026 exercises near Hawaii, which began in late June and ended last week. More than 30 surface combatants, five submarines and nearly 200 aircraft took part. According to the San Diego Union-Tribune, the carrier will have a brief turnaround before a full deployment now expected to begin in September. The Navy currently has just one carrier in the Western Pacific, the Yokosuka, Japan-based USS George Washington (CVN-73), which began its deployment on May 10, 2026. Last Thursday it became only the fourth U.S. carrier to make a port call in Vietnam since 2018, and it is expected to leave Da Nang on Monday and resume a patrol that could last through the end of the year. It earlier visited Guam in mid-June, operated in the Philippine Sea, and took part in the Valiant Shield exercises with Japan's Maritime Self-Defense Force. Last week it transited the Luzon Strait into the South China Sea, becoming the first U.S. carrier to operate in waters claimed by China since January. Two Nimitz-class carriers, the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) and the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77), are deployed to the Middle East in the U.S. 5th Fleet and Central Command's area of responsibility, supporting combat operations against Iran. CVN-72 has been deployed more than 254 days as of Sunday and at sea 233 days without a port call, since a one-day Guam visit. If it stays out three more months, it will approach the record of 326 days for the longest deployment, set in May by USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78). This has fueled speculation that the Theodore Roosevelt will head to the Middle East if a final peace deal cannot be reached, allowing the Abraham Lincoln to go home. Those would be familiar waters for the "Big Stick," which will mark 40 years since commissioning this coming October. It was the Navy's first supercarrier built using modular construction. It deployed to the Middle East for Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm in 1991 and took part in Operation Enduring Freedom strikes on al-Qaeda in Afghanistan after the September 11, 2001 attacks. During the Global War on Terror it became the first carrier since the Korean War to embark a Naval Reserve squadron, Strike Fighter Squadron 201. It supported Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2005-2006 and deployed again to the Middle East in September 2008. During its 2015 round-the-world deployment, its air wing flew more than 1,800 sorties against Islamic State militants in Iraq and Syria under Operation Inherent Resolve, totaling 10,618 flight hours and employing over one million pounds of ordnance, including 1,085 guided munitions. A modernization beginning in July 2021 enabled it to embark the F-35 Lightning II. Its last Middle East deployment was in summer 2024, ending after 278 days.

MAINE—All good wildlife management starts with science, and all good science starts with data. That’s where you come in. Maine’s Wild Turkey August Production Survey invites community scientists to play a direct role in monitoring our state’s wild turkey population. Whether you enjoy watching wildlife from your window, spend time hiking, hunting, or exploring the outdoors, or just need an excuse to get outside, you can help. Each summer, Maine’s wild turkey hens are busy raising the next generation of birds. By reporting your sightings and observations, you’ll help our biologists monitor annual reproduction rates, track population trends, and make informed management decisions that support healthy, sustainable turkey populations for generations to come. The information collected helps ensure there are abundant opportunities for both wildlife watchers and hunters to enjoy Maine’s wild turkeys. It’s easy to participate! Whenever you see wild turkeys anywhere in Maine during August, simply report: Date and location of your observation. Number of adult females (hens) Number of adult males (gobblers) Number of poults (young turkeys) Estimated poult size relative to the adult hens. Every observation counts, even if you don’t see poults. Together, these reports provide a clearer picture of turkey productivity across the state and are an important part of Maine’s wildlife management. Ready to help? Report your turkey sightings online using the Wild Turkey August Production Survey.

Google Cloud has opened submissions for Agentic Cinema: The Blockbuster Hackathon, an online competition offering $75,000 for AI agents designed around film and entertainment workflows. Entries opened on July 27 and close at 10:00 p.m. GMT+1 on September 7, 2026. Participants must be above the legal age of majority in their country of residence, with some countries and territories excluded under the official rules. The challenge asks developers to build a functional agent or multi-agent system powered by Gemini and Google Cloud Agent Builder. Each project must integrate a product or Model Context Protocol server from IBM, Grafana, Parallel, ClickHouse or Replit. Despite the cinema branding, this is not a competition for AI-generated films. Entrants must create a working tool for a media and entertainment process involving filmmakers, screenwriters, studio crews or fans. Potential applications covered by the hackathon resources include script processing, video transcription, asset captioning, storyboarding, speech generation, sentiment analysis and production data management. Google Cloud also provides guidance covering deployment, function calling, external tools, database access, security and safety settings. Working software and public code required. A concept or technical demonstration alone will not meet the submission requirements. Entrants must provide a URL to a hosted project and a three-minute video demonstrating the agent working as built. The video must be publicly available through YouTube or Vimeo and presented in English or include English subtitles. Each submission also needs a public open-source code repository containing the source code, assets and instructions required to run the project. The repository must include a complete open-source license and demonstrate actual runtime use of Google Cloud and the selected partner service. Naming a partner technology in a README file is not sufficient. Its service must be imported and called in the project’s code. Participants must select one partner track and complete the Devpost submission form. Projects will be assessed against other entries using the same partner technology. Five partner tracks divide the prize fund. IBM, Grafana, Parallel, ClickHouse and Replit each have separate first, second and third-place awards. First-place winners receive $7,500, second-place winners receive $4,500 and third-place winners receive $3,000. The five tracks therefore account for the full $75,000 prize fund. First-place winners are also offered an opportunity for social media promotion. Judging will consider technological implementation, product design, potential impact and the quality of the idea. The organizers say projects should present a coherent product experience and demonstrate how the proposed system addresses a specific problem for a defined audience. The full judging panel has not yet been announced. Developers can use either a managed, low-code route or a custom software development kit. Available resources cover the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Builder, Agent Engine, the Agent Development Kit and Google Cloud services for deployment and data connectivity. Google Cloud is also offering eligible participants the option to request $100 in cloud credits. Approval is expected within one to five business days, while supplies last. Completed projects, demonstration videos, public repositories and Devpost forms must be submitted by 10:00 p.m. GMT+1 on September 7, 2026.

ZimaOS is a free, easy-to-use NAS (Network Attached Storage) platform, based on Linux and described as reliable and secure, that can serve as a local alternative to Google Drive. Its feature set can be expanded with apps. The author used Google Drive as primary storage for years but has been migrating away, especially for sensitive or important files. His reasons: he doesn't want his work used to train LLMs, and he has privacy concerns about storing material like bank account details, wills and contracts beyond his LAN. His best option is local storage. An external drive limits access to one computer, and sharing it over a network can be slow and insecure with some protocols. A NAS on the LAN offers a centralized repository for files, photos and media, and some options even let users add tools, including AI. ZimaOS is a lightweight NAS solution made for Zima's own hardware or off-the-shelf x86 computers. It can be installed on a spare desktop, a Raspberry Pi, or a virtual machine, and installs about as easily as any Linux distribution, taking a few minutes. Zima offers desktop clients for MacOS, iOS and Windows, though not Linux. The installation is text-based: download the .img file, burn it to a USB drive with Balena Etcher, insert the USB into the target machine, boot it, and follow the prompts. Afterward, the system shows how to access ZimaOS; the author pointed a browser on his local network to the address, accepted the license and created a local account, then reached the dashboard for customization. To add and share folders, open the Files app from the dashboard, click New Folder at top right, name it (for example, Photos), click the folder's three-dot menu and choose "Share via Samba." In the pop-up you can add members allowed to access the folder and add it to Time Machine for rollback purposes. After clicking Create, the final window shows how to reach the share: Linux or MacOS machines use a network address, while Windows uses a path such as \\192.168.1.62\Photos. To add users, such as family or business members, return to the folder in the Files listing, click the three-dot menu, select Manage Samba Share, then Add member > Create new member. Enter a username and password and click Create. Permissions can be set to Read or Read/Write, and the user is prompted for credentials when accessing the share. The dashboard's Apps section lets you search for and install apps for AI, media, productivity and more. Some AI tools also require the Open WebUI app; the author had Open WebUI running with Ollama in under a minute. The author calls ZimaOS an outstanding solution for expanding LAN-based storage, citing its simple installation, ease of use and many options, and recommends it for any home network.

Air taxis are nearer to reality thanks to new technology, competition and regulatory changes. Starting this summer, federally sanctioned pilot projects across the U.S. will let several makers of all-electric aircraft carry cargo, then passengers, in real-world tests. Paul Sciarra, executive chairman of Joby Aviation, says a Midtown Manhattan to JFK trip that now costs about $100 and takes 45 minutes to two hours could take under 10 minutes by air, eventually at similar cost. The aircraft are eVTOLs (electric vertical takeoff and landing), combining traits of helicopters, airplanes and drones. Joby's has six electric rotors that lift it vertically, then tilt to propel it forward, making a fraction of a helicopter's noise. It carries four passengers and a pilot up to 100 miles at altitudes as low as 1,000 feet. Joby, based in Santa Cruz, Calif., has a $7.6 billion market cap and backing from Toyota, Uber and Delta Air Lines. It plans tests in New York, New Jersey, Texas and Florida this year, starting with cargo, with nonpaying passenger tests expected in fall or winter. Archer Aviation of San Jose, backed by United Airlines, has a $3.7 billion market cap and hopes to begin commercial passenger service with its 12-rotor Midnight eVTOL in time for the Los Angeles Olympics in July 2028. CEO Adam Goldstein says L.A. suits air taxis because many short trips under 20 miles take over an hour by car. Archer was selected for testing in Florida, Texas and New York/New Jersey under the Trump administration's three-year Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing and Advanced Air Mobility Integration Pilot Program (EIPP), which lets companies test before obtaining FAA certification, provided their aircraft are in the certification process. Beta Technologies, backed by Amazon and GE Aerospace, completed the first EIPP flights in Maryland and Virginia on July 10 and is testing in seven of eight announced projects across 26 states, initially with a conventional-takeoff electric aircraft while developing an eVTOL. Boeing subsidiary Wisk Aero will test fully autonomous eVTOLs in Texas. Public acceptance may be a hurdle, as flying in not-yet-certified technology may worry people. Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Andres Sheppard notes eVTOLs' multiple independently powered rotors are safer than a helicopter's single overhead rotor, a single point of failure. Bain & Co. partner Mattia Celli says combustion helicopters are more complex and need more maintenance, and distinguishes real from perceived safety. Archer, Joby and Beta say their aircraft are undergoing extensive testing with specially trained pilots and are in the final stages of FAA approval, which would be the first new civil aircraft category certified in decades. Air taxis will likely fly below 4,000 feet on short routes, where space could get tight. Raymond James analyst Savanthi Syth says that with hundreds flying over a city, a more automated air traffic system will be needed. Last year Joby acquired helicopter operator Blade Air Mobility, gaining operations experience. Blade has flown as many as 200 flights a day in New York this summer and cut a helicopter trip to JFK to $195, comparable to Uber Black; analysts say eVTOL prices must fall to roughly standard ride-share levels. Sciarra argues air taxis could reshape where people live, how they reach jobs and access to medical care.

BROOMFIELD, Colo. and PARIS, Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Mana Battery, Inc., a developer of high-energy anode-free sodium-ion battery technology, and Saft, a wholly owned subsidiary of TotalEnergies and a global leader in advanced battery solutions for demanding industrial and mission-critical applications, today announced the signing of a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) to jointly develop, validate and pave the way toward commercialization of next-generation sodium-ion batteries. Under the agreement, the companies will combine Mana Battery’s proprietary electrolyte platform and anode-free sodium-ion cell technology with Saft’s market access and deep expertise in cell design, prototyping, manufacturing, testing and qualification. The collaboration will develop and validate cells and demonstrate the technology under the rigorous performance and safety conditions required by defense and critical-infrastructure customers. Anode-free sodium-ion cells are assembled without an anode active material; the sodium anode forms in situ during initial operation. This architecture delivers a step change in energy density over conventional sodium-ion designs while retaining the fundamental advantages of sodium chemistry: abundant, low-cost raw materials free of lithium, cobalt and nickel supply constraints, a resilient and geographically diversified supply chain, strong safety characteristics, and performance across an exceptionally wide temperature range. Those attributes align closely with the needs of the markets the collaboration targets. Defense platforms demand batteries that start engines and power systems in extreme cold, tolerate high heat, hold charge through months of standby, and meet stringent military safety standards. Aerospace and rail applications place a premium on safety, reliability and energy density. Meanwhile, the rapid build-out of AI and cloud computing infrastructure is driving unprecedented demand for datacenter backup power, and industrial uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems across critical infrastructure increasingly seek alternatives to legacy lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries that offer longer life, wider operating temperatures and enhanced safety. “Saft is exactly the partner we would design for this mission — a battery manufacturer with decades of experience qualifying cells for the world’s most demanding defense, aerospace, rail and industrial customers,” said Tyler Evans, CEO of Mana Battery. “This agreement validates the maturity of our electrolyte and anode-free platform and puts it on the fastest possible path from the lab to the field, where its energy density, safety and supply-chain advantages matter most.” “Sodium-ion is a strategically important chemistry for the industries we serve, and anode-free designs are its most promising frontier,” said Kamen Nechev, Chief Technology & Innovation Officer at Saft. “Mana Battery brings world-class electrolyte innovation that complements our cell design, manufacturing and qualification capabilities. Together we intend to bring safe, high-performance sodium-ion batteries to defense, aerospace, rail, datacenter and industrial UPS customers.” The collaboration builds on a technical evaluation the companies began in 2025. Financial terms were not disclosed. About Mana Battery. Mana Battery, Inc. is a U.S. battery technology company based in Broomfield, Colorado, developing high-energy sodium-ion batteries built on a proprietary electrolyte platform and anode-free cell architecture. Spun out of the University of Colorado Boulder, Mana Battery’s technology delivers energy density beyond conventional sodium-ion designs with self-extinguishing electrolyte safety and a supply chain free of critical-mineral constraints. Learn more at. Mana Battery Press Contacts. Sam Jaffe, VP of Business Development and Product. +1 (303) 502-4001 l. About Saft. Saft is a global leader in advanced battery technology, designing and manufacturing high-performance solutions for critical industrial applications. For over 100 years, Saft has delivered reliable, long-lasting energy systems used in safety, back-up power, and mobility across land, sea, air, and space. Saft is wholly owned by TotalEnergies, a multi-energy company that produces and sells energy in all its forms throughout the world, including oil and biofuels, natural gas and green gas, renewable energies and electricity. In a fresh report, Barclays claims that Google can earn as much as $252 billion in sales of its tensor processing units (TPUs) by shifting its business model. Google's TPUs are among the most widely used custom AI chips in the industry, and Barclays believes that the firm can further expand its platform by entering into joint ventures with asset managers Blackstone and Apollo Global, as well as chip designer Broadcom. Barclays Estimates Healthy Revenues But Limited Profit From Google's TPU Off-Platform Merchant Model. Google's TPUs are among the oldest AI chips in the market, and unlike NVIDIA, which sells its products to data center firms such as CoreWeave, the firm offers the TPUs through its Google Cloud business. Google's second-quarter earnings saw revenue from the Cloud business grow by a whopping 82% annually to touch $24.8 billion. The firm had made inroads into the AI computing infrastructure race before ChatGPT's public release. Google started using its in-house AI processors in 2015 to beat Amazon to the punch by three years. It made the TPUs available to external customers in 2018, with analysts from D.A. Davidson outlining in September last year that the business could be worth $900 billion. Now, a report from Barclays claims that Google can generate as much as $252 billion from shifting its TPU business from Google Cloud to an off-platform merchant model. This model should likely see Google create joint ventures with asset managers Apollo Global and Blackstone, along with custom AI chip designer Broadcom, to outsource TPU capacity and enable the combined entity to offer the chips for computing capacity. Such a move could lead to Google operating 11.5 gigawatts of TPU capacity, says the report, to generate the aforementioned revenue. The figures are estimates of 2028, and the report considers Google's joint ventures with Blackstone and others. The Blackstone deal was announced in May this year, through which the TPUs will be used to offer compute-as-a-service, or CaaS. However, the heavy lifting will be done by Google's joint venture with Apollo and Blackstone, says the report. In June, Apollo and Blackstone led a $35 billion AI infrastructure funding platform with Broadcom to deploy the TPUs. As per Barclay's estimates, the deal could contribute $20 billion to Google's revenue by the year's end and grow the contribution to $67 billion in 2027 courtesy of 3.2 gigawatts of deployed TPU capacity. An unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor is running a campaign against Apple iOS devices using a publicly leaked version of the DarkSword exploit kit, according to a July 31, 2026 analysis by Censys researcher Aidan Holland. Censys identified more than 100 web properties operated by the actor, most of them fake Amazon Web Services (AWS) sign-in pages on a domain that also hosts the toolkit. Hosting concentrates in Hong Kong but reaches into Japan, the United States, and Europe. DarkSword, detailed earlier this year by Google Threat Intelligence Group, iVerify, and Lookout, is a full-chain exploit kit believed to have been used by commercial surveillance vendors and suspected state-sponsored actors against targets in Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine since at least November 2025. It targets iOS versions 18.4 through 18.7, using watering holes to trigger now-patched vulnerabilities and run JavaScript that deploys the information-stealing malware GHOSTBLADE. A public leak of its source code has led other actors to adopt it. As of July 30, 2026, Censys found a "DarkSword Admin" login panel matching seven hosts across three countries, including one with Chinese-language field labels (38.22.89[.]117:8888). It also found a Singapore-based host (38.181.52[.]95) running three exploit-panel front ends and a Hong Kong host (103.106.190[.]217) bundling an Apple ID credential-harvesting decoy. Other panels are "Decode Dashboard," on 103.226.155[.]200, 103.226.155[.]201, and 202.8.120[.]249, and "C2 Control Panel," on 103.106.190[.]217. The attack flow is consistent: a victim visits an AWS-console impersonation subdomain or an Apple ID sign-in page, a malicious iframe loads JavaScript that fires the DarkSword chain, and GHOSTBLADE modules are deployed. The implant dumps keychain, iCloud, and Wi-Fi credentials and sweeps for files, and the data is packaged and sent to attacker-controlled endpoints. The attacker then logs into one of the panels to extract it. Censys concluded the cluster runs the leaked kit rather than a reimplementation, citing a shared staging-page hash and Russian-language code comments carried over from the leaked source. The now-inactive Singapore host also hosted an administration panel for Coruna, an older iOS exploit kit targeting iOS 3.0 through 17.2.1. Some evidence suggests a threat actor known as UNC6353 has used both kits against Ukrainian targets. Censys also found an open directory in Frankfurt (93.152.221[.]37) exposing the operator's tooling, including an SSH key comment "jkcing@apt," a web-content fuzzer, and references to a previously undocumented malware family called "Thorn C2." The C2 Control Panel login is visually distinct, with a near-black background, red accent, animated particle effect, the group name 亚太集团 ("Asia-Pacific Group"), and a Telegram contact link (hxxps://t[.]me/YATA0000). Censys called this the first direct contact channel recovered for the operator.

AWS has launched Strategy Insight, a tool aimed at opening up Formula 1's strategy "black box." For decades, the reasoning, math, data and risk behind pit-wall decisions, such as whether a driver pits or stays out, stayed inside the garage and headsets, leaving fans guessing. Strategy Insight, powered by AWS cloud and machine learning services, uses F1 live timing, telemetry and historical race data to build context around race strategy. It sits on top of the existing AWS and F1 system Track Pulse, which flags which live moments are worth explaining; Strategy Insight then builds the explanation. Fans will see a plain-language broadcast graphic translating, in real time, what a pit-wall strategist is working through. Ruth Buscombe, a former F1 race strategist who is now an F1 TV analyst and AWS technical advisor, says the tool replicates the experience-based analysis a veteran strategist does. It does not forecast what a team will do; it surfaces what is likely given current track action, tire degradation, traffic, weather, gap to the lead and more. Buscombe defines strategy as "making the best call you have with the information you have at the time." The tool launched at the Hungarian Grand Prix, a track where strategy shifts year to year. With few straights, major wind and heat effects on grip, and strategy often unclear until the opening laps, one-stop versus two-stop decisions are made while drivers are already racing. Buscombe cited Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes running P6 while chasing the lead, with tire data on the edge of a one-stop or two-stop call. The team could have covered the field and locked in fourth or fifth, or gambled on a one-stop to try to win. They chose to race for the win and stayed committed even after being re-passed by Lando Norris, the eventual winner, to secure third. Without context, this could look like a mistake; Strategy Insight is designed to explain exactly such moments. The launch comes after F1 President Stefano Domenicali said last week that fans don't care about data or "how you drive your car." The article argues the opposite, noting F1's audience has shifted heavily over the past decade, and that unlike lifelong fans of other sports, most F1 viewers lack strategy knowledge, which varies race to race. Buscombe says the tool is meant to serve viewers whether it is their first race or their 1,000th, given a demographic very different from the pre-Drive to Survive, pre-Liberty era. Buscombe says AWS handles the cutting-edge, live view of what teams are doing, while strategy can also be done with pencil, paper and knowledge. In the broadcast booth she has no engineering department or live telemetry, but AWS and F1 effectively serve as her strategy department; her aim is not to win the race but to "win the broadcast." From Hungary onward, fans will understand the data behind calls such as an undercut, giving the black box a measure of transparency.

Saad Hassan, a petroleum engineer specializing in data-intensive work, saw a foundational flaw in how drilling operations in the eastern deserts of Saudi Arabia were analyzed. Hundreds of sensors streamed data every second, yet analysts spread across eight countries spent a full working day producing a single performance report. In continuous 24-hour operations, Hassan argues, a report arriving eight hours late is "a post-mortem," not intelligence. Leading a cross-functional team, he built a platform that ingested a decade of historical operational data, cleaned and categorized it, and applied trained machine learning models to real-time streams. It flagged anomalies, compared current performance with historical baselines, and delivered KPIs to a live dashboard within minutes. Analysts freed from manual extraction could return to engineering work. Hassan's career began in an industry where bad data can cost lives, not just money. He says people have died and equipment has exploded in his field, which shaped how he builds systems. While peers relied on experience and instinct, he taught himself Python and wrote automated real-time alert systems, which were rudimentary but worked and inspired the larger platform. The results were substantial. Reporting time fell from eight hours to minutes, and downtime across monitored sites dropped by more than 30%. Some sites had been logging 240 hours of downtime per month, with each day costing $60,000 to $90,000; cutting 75 of those hours delivered major savings. His second platform unified thirty years of data held across four applications with different naming conventions and standards. Models trained on historically optimal operating conditions were deployed on live data across 20 sites, cutting an average of one full day of downtime per site. At $90,000 per day, monthly savings approached $2 million. No one lost a job: an operator who once monitored one site could now oversee ten, so the company scaled while its people stayed. Hassan is critical of public AI hype, such as chatbots and photo filters that look impressive but solve little. He measures value by societal benefit: less downtime means cheaper gasoline, and so cheaper goods that move by truck. Most machine learning talent, he argues, is concentrated on consumer apps, leaving AI's potential in critical operations largely unrealized. He is now moving toward consultancy, saying there is "no one-size-fits-all" and that each organization's data and operations need a tailored solution. He targets time-sensitive, high-consequence industries: aviation, mining, power generation, water treatment, and healthcare. The market, he says, needs engineers who understand both data and domain and have built systems under pressure, not another off-the-shelf product.

Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) shares jumped 15.51% on July 30, their strongest one-day performance in nearly two decades. The move added roughly $450 billion to its market capitalization, the largest one-day gain ever recorded by a U.S. company, lifting its valuation to about $3.45 trillion. The rally followed a strong fiscal fourth-quarter report showing Azure growth accelerating to 30% and evidence that heavy AI infrastructure investment is starting to lift profits. Before the report, Microsoft had lagged many Magnificent 7 peers such as Alphabet as investors worried capital spending was outrunning returns. The stock is up 0.81% year-to-date but down 6.98% over 52 weeks, though it is up 25% since the earnings release. It trades at 26.89 times trailing earnings (sector median 25.15) and 10.40 times trailing sales (sector median 3.57). It pays an annual dividend of $3.64, a forward yield of 0.81%. Quarterly revenue was $90.01 billion, beating the $87.71 billion estimate by 2.6% and rising 17.7% year-over-year. GAAP EPS was $4.81 versus a $4.22 estimate, a 14.1% surprise. Gross margin was 67.2%, down from 68.6%, while operating margin held at 45.1%. Free cash flow margin fell to 21.8% from 33.4%, reflecting the cost of scaling AI infrastructure and data centers. The Intelligent Cloud segment, 41.5% of sales, grew 31.6%, outpacing AWS's 28.4% but trailing Google Cloud's 81.8%. Recent partnerships broaden the business. A deal with French AI start-up Mistral expands AI capacity in Europe: Microsoft will use Mistral's Europe-based GPU capacity, and Mistral models are being added to Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, and Azure. A 3M partnership focuses on AI data center infrastructure, with Azure becoming the first announced hyperscale cloud provider to deploy 3M's Expanded Beam Optical technology. Microsoft and Databricks extended their partnership into the 2030s, with Databricks deepening its use of Azure Databricks and Azure Cobalt. The next earnings date is November 4. Analysts expect September-quarter EPS of $4.67, up from $4.13 a year earlier, or 13.08% growth. Guggenheim's John Difucci kept a "Buy" rating and $586 price target on July 27, implying 19.6% upside. Among 51 analysts, the consensus is "Strong Buy," with an average target of $547.45, implying 12% upside. The article concludes the jump looks justified for now given the results, cloud growth, and new deals. Shares can likely keep rising, though not as fast, and if Azure stays strong and AI spending keeps paying off, the stock looks more likely to rise than to give back all its gains.

Formula 1 (F1) engages over 800 million fans globally across digital platforms, F1 TV, social media, ticketing and merchandise. Its MarTech platform, Customer 360, captures these interactions to power personalization, segmentation and commercial strategy. The platform faced a bottleneck: according to Chris Roberts, Director of IT, every new data source required 6 to 8 weeks of manual engineering, creating an 18-month backlog to integrate 12 new sources. Matt Kemp, Head of Data Operations, wanted a repeatable, robust, reliable solution to improve efficiency and data quality. In early 2026, F1 and AWS built the Data Accelerator, which uses agentic AI on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to turn the platform into a self-managed, observable, unified data estate. It cut onboarding from up to 8 weeks to about 40 minutes of code generation plus hours of deployment. The team faced three problems: manual onboarding (schema mappings, pipelines, quality checks, GDPR classifications, governance policies); upstream feeds that changed columns, fields or schedules without notice, often during race weekends; and fragmented visibility, with no unified lineage across S3, Redshift, Airflow and DBT. The solution has six workstreams: agentic onboarding, automated schema evolution, unified data access via Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, end-to-end observability with root cause analysis (RCA) and a context graph, automated failure triage, and optimized customer identity resolution. Onboarding works in two phases. A team member uploads a Business Requirements Document to Amazon S3, triggering a Lambda function that invokes AgentCore Runtime. The agent generates configuration files, opens a GitHub pull request and creates a Jira ticket; an engineer reviews and approves. The agent then generates three linked PRs: AWS Glue application and infrastructure code, a DBT transformation framework, and governance policies including GDPR tagging. The agent analyzes every column, classifies it as personal, sensitive or pseudonymized data, and publishes tags to the governance registry in SageMaker Unified Studio. A single agent uses modular skills (schema mapping, data quality, governance, sensitive data classification) composed through multi-pass reasoning. AI agents handle 95% of the work. For schema evolution, the same architecture monitors upstream changes via Lambda and EventBridge, assesses downstream impact, generates code updates across repositories and opens a Jira ticket with linked PRs. Resolution now takes hours instead of days. SageMaker Unified Studio underpins a data mesh in which governance is declarative configuration, so one source definition publishes to the catalog and provisions access. Engineers, scientists and analysts now work in one governed environment. The observability layer shows lineage from S3 raw ingestion through processed layers to Redshift DBT stages as a color-coded graph with drill-down, refreshing every 15 minutes. RCA, augmented with business context and system topology as JSON, explains why a failure occurred, not just what failed. Identity resolution optimization cut processing time by 50% without changing the pipeline or accuracy, yielding fresher unified profiles. Security follows "AI proposes, humans review": least-privilege short-lived tokens, full audit trails, mandatory PR approval, agent-generated tests, rollback, VPC network isolation and encrypted credentials. Models run via Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.6) behind F1's AI Gateway. Results: roughly 99% reduction in time-to-value, the 18-month backlog cleared in weeks, and one developer took the solution from proof of concept to production in 4 months. The approach is replicable and domain-agnostic.

Alexander “Sasha” Rakhlin PhD ’06, the Distinguished Professor in Data, Systems, and Society at the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS); and a professor of brain and cognitive sciences at MIT, has been named the next director of the MIT Statistics and Data Science Center (SDSC). Rakhlin succeeds Ankur Moitra, the Norbert Wiener Professor of Mathematics, associate director of the IDSS, and a faculty member in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) who has been SDSC director since 2021. Philippe Rigollet, the Cecil and Ida Green Distinguished Professor of Mathematics and a core faculty member in IDSS, also served as interim director in 2024-25. “Sasha is one of the sharpest theoretical minds working in statistics and machine learning today, and also one of the most devoted mentors I know,” says Fotini Christia, the Ford International Professor of the Social Sciences and director of IDSS, which houses SDSC. “He has helped train an entire generation of interdisciplinary scholars through the Interdisciplinary Doctoral Program in Statistics (IDPS), while his own research keeps pushing the boundaries. The SDSC could not ask for a more fitting leader.” Rakhlin is the inaugural holder of the Distinguished Professorship in Data, Systems, and Society, an endowed chair created in 2025 by the generosity and vision of IDSS professor Richard “Dick” Larson, an “MIT lifer” and pioneer in operations research, queueing theory, and system optimization. “I am honored to take on this role,” says Rakhlin. “The strength of the Statistics and Data Science Center has always been its people — students, postdocs, and faculty from across MIT who bring sharply different perspectives to the most interesting problems of the day in statistics, machine learning, and AI. My goal is to support that community as it takes on the constantly evolving questions reshaping the field.” Rakhlin has been connected to the Statistics and Data Science Center as a visiting professor since 2016, before formally joining MIT in 2018 in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and IDSS. As the initial chair of the Interdisciplinary PhD in Statistics program at the SDSC, Rakhlin has seen the successful defense of over 75 IDPS PhD students across a variety of departments at MIT, including IDSS’ own Social and Engineering Systems program. “I have been fascinated by machine learning since my PhD work more than 20 years ago, drawn by its beautiful connections to statistics, probability, algorithms, optimization, and game theory,” says Rakhlin. “At the Statistics and Data Science Center, I work alongside colleagues who share this fascination and pursue these connections in many directions. The recent revolution in AI is extending this web into the sciences; it promises to accelerate discovery, and it raises new questions for statistics. Answering them demands a rigorous science of the tools themselves. As AI enters medicine, energy, and public life, its safety and security are, at their core, statistical and mathematical questions: quantifying uncertainty, providing guarantees, understanding failure, and resisting manipulation.” As Rakhlin puts it, the SDSC is built for this moment. “Statistics is a shared language across MIT,” he adds. “Through the Interdisciplinary Doctoral Program in Statistics, the center connects students and faculty from economics and political science to physics and engineering. Collaborations in areas from biology to nuclear fusion have shown how statistical thinking accelerates science itself.” As director, one of his goals is to deepen these interdisciplinary connections. He hopes to help make SDSC the Institute’s home for the rigorous foundations of data science and AI, and a bridge to the scientific and societal questions where those foundations are most needed. Rakhlin received his bachelor’s degrees in mathematics and computer science from Cornell University, and doctoral degree from MIT. He was a postdoc at the University of California at Berkeley in EECS before joining the University of Pennsylvania, where he was an associate professor in the Department of Statistics and co-director of the Penn Research in Machine Learning center.

Vibe-coding startup Superblocks announced a multiyear joint marketing agreement with Amazon Web Services (AWS) that lets its tool be embedded within the private clouds of AWS customers. An enterprise on AWS that subscribes to Superblocks can offer vibe coding to its business users, and the resulting apps will not send data externally to model providers or databases. Instead of creating external Supabase databases, the apps will spin up Amazon Aurora databases inside the company's private cloud, and they will integrate with Amazon Bedrock, AWS's AI app development/gateway/inference platform. As a result, the apps fall under IT's management and security rather than being rogue applications. Superblocks co-founder and CEO Brad Menezes told TechCrunch the aim is to "bring it to your data inside your private cloud," so data never leaves the customer's AWS account, with all of the auditing, encryption and network controls. AWS will also help sell Superblocks to enterprises, as it does for many Marketplace partners. An AWS spokesperson said it supports partners where it sees strong customer demand and alignment with how customers want to build. AWS does not yet have its own vibe-coding agent for business users. It has Kiro, an AI coding agent for developers, and Quick, an AI assistant for business users, but Quick is closer to Claude Cowork or Microsoft Copilot than to Lovable or Replit. The deal should boost early-stage Superblocks, which has 50 employees and raised $60 million total as of its Series A in May 2025, backed by Spark Capital, Kleiner Perkins, Meritech Capital and Greenoaks. The deal also reflects a broader trend: hyperscaler cloud providers are urging enterprise customers to separate AI models from the other scaffolding needed to run enterprise AI, and to buy AI harnesses (agentic apps), orchestration and security tools from them rather than from frontier model providers. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has recently pushed this message, telling customers to use multiple models to cut costs and avoid lock-in, and warning that AI labs may not be trustworthy for agent orchestration or app-level harnesses because they could use the data to study a business and later compete with it. Enterprises may not need such warnings, as many have already adopted multiple models, including frontier Chinese open-weight options. Menezes said this has flipped in about 60 days, from customers wanting a specific model, Anthropic, to wanting choice. Open models accounted for 29% of all traffic routed through Vercel's AI gateway last month. Menezes called a multi-model strategy across OpenAI, Anthropic and open source, currently Chinese but increasingly U.S. as well, "a must-have for the CIO," covering coding, customer service, HR and sales automation. He predicted that "any enterprise that is betting on a single model provider, that executive will be fired." Bringing vibe coding for business users into private, secure clouds could be a second wave after AI coding agents for enterprise developers. AWS called it "an emerging category with real momentum, and exactly the kind of innovation we support."

The surge places Amazon among an elite group of companies valued above $3 trillion, underscoring how rapidly investor enthusiasm has shifted toward technology firms building the infrastructure needed to power the next generation of artificial intelligence. AWS generated $42.2 billion in revenue during the quarter, significantly ahead of analysts' expectations of $40.54 billion. The results reflected accelerating demand from businesses investing heavily in AI applications, data processing and cloud infrastructure. Cloud computing has become one of the most important battlegrounds in the technology industry as companies race to develop and deploy increasingly sophisticated AI models that require enormous computing power. Fusion energy startup American Fusion Inc. has completed the initial phase of laboratory testing for its Texatron Fusion Engine, marking the transition of the company’s technology from years of engineering development into hands-on evaluation under controlled laboratory conditions. The first round of tests was carried out at the Center for Emerging Energy Sciences within the Department of Physics & Astronomy at Texas Tech University, where engineers and researchers evaluated key subsystems, instrumentation, and high-voltage operation of the experimental platform. While the tests did not demonstrate sustained nuclear fusion or net energy production, they represent an early engineering milestone as the company prepares for more advanced phases of development. What exactly is the Texatron? Unlike conventional power generation technologies, a fusion system seeks to generate energy by fusing light atomic nuclei together, the same process that powers the Sun. If commercialized, fusion promises abundant, carbon-free energy with significantly less long-lived radioactive waste than today’s nuclear fission reactors. American Fusion’s Texatron remains an experimental platform under development. According to the company, the current testing campaign focuses on validating engineering systems, including high-voltage hardware, plasma control, diagnostics, and instrumentation, before progressing toward more advanced experiments. In other words, the emphasis at this stage is on ensuring the machine operates as designed rather than demonstrating commercial fusion performance. See All. High-voltage systems and plasma controls put to the test. The company informed that the engineers successfully operated several critical components during the first testing phase. These included the Texatron’s remote ignition and control system, plasma switching system, and high-voltage power supply operating within a controlled vacuum environment. It also reported successful operation of the Texatron platform using non-radioactive fusion fuel, allowing engineers to evaluate system behavior without introducing radioactive materials during this phase of development. American Fusion also said it completed calibration and evaluation of radiation-monitoring equipment used throughout the testing campaign. According to the fusion energy firm, no measurable radiation was detected during the initial engineering tests, an expected outcome given the nature of the experiments conducted. Building the foundation for future testing. Beyond verifying individual subsystems, the first testing campaign generated engineering and diagnostic data that will help guide future refinements. American Fusion said the results compared favorably with several pre-test engineering expectations, although the company has not yet released detailed technical data. Engineers are continuing to analyze information collected during the testing campaign, with a technical summary expected following completion of the review. Future phases are expected to expand subsystem integration, diagnostics, instrumentation, engineering measurements, and additional evaluation of the Texatron platform. A long road remains for fusion startups. The announcement illustrates an important reality of fusion research: progress often comes through incremental engineering milestones rather than dramatic breakthroughs. Before any fusion concept can demonstrate commercially meaningful energy production, developers must first validate high-voltage systems, plasma control, vacuum hardware, diagnostics, and safety systems through repeated laboratory testing. Those engineering foundations ultimately determine whether more ambitious fusion experiments can be conducted reliably and safely. For American Fusion, the completion of this initial testing phase marks the beginning, not the end of that journey. While commercial fusion remains a long-term objective for companies across the industry, the Texatron program has now entered an active laboratory testing stage where future progress will increasingly be measured through experimental results rather than design concepts.

AI adoption is spreading beyond healthcare, automobiles and content creation into heavy industries such as steel. ArcelorMittal (MT), the world's second-largest steel producer, has extended its partnership with Microsoft (MSFT) to adopt Azure as its primary cloud computing platform. The company said the advances will let it turn data into a strategic asset, enabling faster, smarter decisions and sustained competitive advantage as its long-term digital transformation continues. Azure will be used to upgrade legacy IT systems and for advanced analytics, while Microsoft Fabric, Purview and Foundry will be used to improve cybersecurity. ArcelorMittal was founded in 2006 through the merger of Mittal Steel and Arcelor. Its businesses span flat and long steel, mining, automotive and electrical steel, renewable energy infrastructure products and downstream solutions, serving sectors such as automotive, construction, infrastructure, railways and shipbuilding. Headquartered in Luxembourg, it also serves as a Western hedge for steel procurement, where China dominates. The stock (ADR) has a market cap of $54.4 billion, is up 62% year to date, and yields 0.74%. Founder Lakshmi Mittal, whose family still controls most of the shares, built the company by acquiring near-bankrupt steel mills across North America, Europe, Latin America, Kazakhstan and Africa, modernizing them and restoring profitability. ArcelorMittal now has steelmaking operations in 14 countries and commercial operations in 126, with 2025 crude steel and iron ore production of 55.6 million tonnes and 48.8 million tonnes, respectively. Its vertical integration, owning much of its iron ore and metallurgical coal supply, has helped it keep unit costs lower than European and Asian peers who rely on spot purchases. The company also uses AI directly in steelmaking: neural networks analyze thousands of data points per second to predict the temperature and chemistry of molten metal, letting engineers anticipate thermal fluctuations hours ahead and use less coke and coal, while algorithmic scheduling optimizes machinery and logistics flow in its yards. The Boeing 737 is Boeing's most successful and longest-running jetliner family, introduced in the late 1960s as a short-to-medium-haul aircraft to complement the 707 and 727. It evolved through the Original, Classic, Next Generation (NG) and 737 MAX generations, with Boeing improving efficiency, economics and range while preserving commonality that cut airline training needs. Developing a family over such a long period, however, brought compromises. The 737-900ER illustrates this. It was developed to fix shortcomings of the NG family's longest member, the 737-900, which Boeing designed as a narrowbody carrying nearly as many passengers as the 757 with 737 economics and commonality. The -900's fuselage is 138 feet, two inches long, versus 110 feet, four inches for the 737-700 and 129 feet, six inches for the 737-800. But it kept the 737-800's exit configuration (four main doors, four overwing exits), capping it at 189 seats. The -900ER added two Type II doors behind the wing and a redesigned flattened rear pressure bulkhead allowing an extra row of seats, for up to 215 passengers in one class. It was commercially successful: according to ch-aviation, nearly 450 remain in active service, including with Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines. The stretch had costs. The aircraft has a longer take-off run than comparable narrowbodies and is more prone to becoming tail-heavy on the ground. An aircraft stays stable only while its center of gravity is ahead of the main landing gear. If forward cargo is removed or passengers move aft to disembark while baggage remains in the aft hold, the center of gravity can move behind the gear and the aircraft can tip onto its tail. More of the -900ER's structure sits behind the main gear than on shorter variants, and the flattened aft bulkhead shifted more weight rearward, tightening the limits. Several incidents show the risk. In 2016 a Ukraine International Airlines 737-900 tilted onto its tail after forward cargo was removed. In 2021 a United 737-900ER carrying the USC football team tipped backward during disembarkation in Lewiston, Idaho, with no injuries or significant damage. In 2025 a GetJet Airlines 737-800 operating for Wizz Air tipped back after flight W6 1749 from Gdańsk to Haugesund; no one was hurt, but the aircraft was withdrawn for fuselage repairs. To prevent this, ground crews use a tail stand ("pogo stick") under the aft fuselage near the tail cone, installed after arrival and removed before pushback. Common on military and cargo aircraft, it is also required on the 737-900ER, and may be needed for the 737-800, 737 MAX 9 and Airbus A320 family aircraft; a JetBlue A321-200 tipped back at New York JFK in 2023. The longer fuselage also reduces tail clearance during rotation, raising tailstrike risk. Because the -900ER already needs relatively high rotation speeds, pilots must carefully control pitch, leaving little margin for error. Overall, Boeing expanded the 737's capacity while keeping commonality, but within the constraints of a late-1960s design, making the -900ER more vulnerable to tipping if weight is not carefully managed.

Amazon Web Services Inc. today launched Kiro Crew, an autonomous workspace that keeps AI coding agents running all day and all night. AWS said it lets developers start a task, walk away and return when something needs review. Crew assigns multiple agents and their sub-agents to multi-step tasks that can run unattended, manages recurring jobs on a schedule, and uses a heartbeat to monitor the system until something needs attention. Crew also provides Apps, an interface that lets developers bring their own tooling and give individual processes purpose-built UIs and structure. An App can combine a custom user interface with agents, skills, schedules and backend services. Crew is built on Kiro, AWS' development environment that integrates agentic AI for software engineers, and extends the same agent infrastructure as Kiro's autonomous mode. The difference is scope: autonomous mode handles individual tasks within a single session, while Crew keeps working whether a developer is online or not, maintains memory across sessions, runs scheduled work and orchestrates multiple specialist agents. Because it is built on Kiro, Crew can read .kiro configuration out of the box, including steering files, skills and custom agents a user has already created. Amazon touted Crew as "self-learning and self-evolving." Persistent memory of preferences, active-project context and relevant history carries corrections into new sessions, including workspace- or project-specific guidance. For example, an agent repeatedly told to prefer one function over another would ingrain that guidance, and agents can pass along knowledge about a tool, such as an MCP server that fails on certain requests unless they are reformatted. Amazon stressed that agentic memory remains visible, so developers decide what Crew carries forward. Crew runs locally or remotely on developer hardware, allowing developers to view, audit and control it. An app and web dashboard offer a place to work with Crew across conversations, files, approvals, memory, schedules and Apps. Developers can also reach Crew through Slack, Telegram and Discord, letting them add or adjust tasks away from the dashboard or have an agent check in when something needs review. Crew's core is extensible, so the community can build an ecosystem of Apps and integrations. AWS said this community-driven capability became the core of Crew when it first emerged among Amazon's own developers, and that it will be preserved. Crew can also incorporate skills and configurations from other harnesses and orchestrators such as OpenClaw, Hermes and other open-standards-based platforms, so it can slot into a developer's toolset as an addition rather than a replacement that must be retrained. The Kiro Crew app for macOS is available for direct download or installation from the GitHub Repository, which also includes setup instructions for Linux and Windows and guides for connecting chat interfaces such as Slack, Telegram and WeCom.

Nvidia has launched Alpamayo 2 Super, an open reasoning model for autonomous vehicles that it says can analyze complicated driving situations, reason through what is happening around a vehicle, and decide what to do next. It is released on Hugging Face under the OpenMDW-1.1 license, a permissive Linux Foundation license allowing commercial use, fine-tuning, derivative models and redistribution. The license applies across the Alpamayo family, and Nvidia positions the model as a foundation for robotaxis, trucks, shuttles, delivery vehicles, tractors and other mobile robots. CEO Jensen Huang said the model should "think before it acts." The target is the long tail: rare, ambiguous situations such as a hesitating pedestrian, a vehicle half-entering an intersection, competing merges or unusual construction layouts. Rather than output only a trajectory, the model generates a chain-of-causation trace explaining its decision, identifies meta-actions such as yielding, stopping or changing lanes, creates reasoning labels for training and validation data, and answers visual questions tied to regions of camera images. It processes full-surround 360-degree camera coverage. Nvidia says the traces can integrate with its Halos safety-validation workflows and support AI safety work aligned with ISO/PAS 8800. The model can also autolabel proprietary fleet footage, which Nvidia claims can compress annotation cycles from months to days. Alpamayo 2 Super is the largest model in the family, three times the scale of the 10-billion-parameter Alpamayo 1.5 and Alpamayo 1. Because running it inside vehicles would be costly, Nvidia proposes distillation: use the large model in the cloud to produce reasoning traces, synthetic data and teacher outputs, then train smaller, lower-latency models for in-car use. Alpamayo 1 and 1.5 remain available as cheaper options. Open weights let companies adapt the models with proprietary fleet data and driving policies and keep the resulting intellectual property in-house. Nvidia reports that Alpamayo 2 Super ranks first among nearly 40 models on LingoQA, an autonomous-driving reasoning benchmark. On the Lingo-Judge metric it beat Qwen2.5-VL 72B by 17 points, Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro by 15.1 points and OpenAI's GPT-4o by 23.2 points. These are Nvidia-reported results, and benchmark performance does not establish readiness for public roads, where hardware failures, weather, unusual behavior and sensor limits matter. The model sits within a wider Nvidia toolset: AlpaSim for closed-loop simulation, AlpaGym for reinforcement learning at scale, Physical AI Open Datasets, open training recipes and autolabeling tools. Nvidia says the Alpamayo family has passed 500,000 downloads on Hugging Face, making it the platform's most-adopted open reasoning model family for autonomous driving. The release does not remove safety, regulatory and engineering hurdles, but it gives automakers, trucking companies, robotaxi developers and startups access to test whether reasoning models help vehicles handle ambiguous moments.
