Science drives human progress, but advancing it is costly, sometimes requiring billions of dollars and multiple countries pooling resources. Even negative results yield useful knowledge. Nine of the most expensive experiments follow. The International Space Station, announced in 1993 after a 1962 U.S.-Soviet discussion and including partners such as Japan, Canada, Spain and England, is estimated to cost $150 billion, including $3 billion in annual expenditures. Its first module reached orbit in 1998. The aging station has a potentially dangerous leak, and the project is expected to end in 2030 with deorbiting, adding another $1 billion. NASA's Apollo program, run from 1960 to 1972, cost $25.4 billion ($203 billion adjusted for inflation). It answered Soviet successes with Sputnik (1957) and Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 flight (1961) and President Kennedy's 1961 goal of a moon landing before the decade ended. Apollo 11 landed on the moon on July 20, 1969, and the program was succeeded by the Space Shuttle program in 1981. CERN's Large Hadron Collider, built from 1998 to 2008 for about $4.75 billion, is the world's largest particle accelerator, in a 17-mile tunnel more than 500 feet underground near Geneva. It was meant to probe string theory, other dimensions and dark matter, and it discovered the Higgs Boson in 2015. It is being shut down for an upgrade to the High-Luminosity version, expected to start between 2028 and 2030, with operations scheduled until 2041. A proposed collider nearly four times larger, costing an estimated $23 billion, is expected to begin construction by 2038. The Human Genome Project, run from 1990 to 2003 by the National Institutes of Health and international partners, cost $2.7 to $3 billion and mapped the euchromatic regions comprising over 90% of the genome; the remainder was completed by 2022. It also funded the ELSI program on ethical, legal and social implications. NASA's Curiosity rover, part of the Mars Science Laboratory mission, cost $2.5 billion and landed on Mars in 2012. Planned for two years, it is still operating after 14 years, collecting data. Skylab, launched in 1973 as the U.S.'s first space station, cost over $2.3 billion and studied long-term exposure to space and solar radiation, including X-rays. Riccardo Giacconi won the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics partly for related technology. Delays to the shuttle meant to keep it aloft doomed it; it broke up, mostly landing in the Indian Ocean, with debris in Western Australia, where the Shire of Esperance jokingly fined NASA $400 for littering. The Manhattan Project, led by Major General Leslie Groves and Robert J. Oppenheimer, employed up to 130,000 people at once and cost $2.2 billion, over $40 billion in 2026 money. It produced the "Fat Man" and "Little Boy" bombs, dropped on Nagasaki and Hiroshima in August 1945. Ocean Networks Canada's NEPTUNE, begun in 2007, cost $111 million Canadian ($79 million USD), with annual maintenance of $17 million. It uses 500 miles of optical cable to livestream the seafloor, holds the Guinness record as the largest undersea observatory, and includes crawlers named Wally and Wally 2. The National Science Foundation's Very Large Array, 28 radio telescopes acting as one, was approved in 1972 and completed in 1980 for $78.5 million (about $627 million in 2026 dollars). It images black holes and neutron stars. It is being upgraded to the Next Generation Very Large Array, expected to cost around $2 billion.

Summary. - Azure CTO Mark Russinovich got the original Doom running in MS Paint with an OLE clipboard hack. - Every frame is pasted into Paint as a genuine document edit. - Paint only displays frames while the engine does the compute. If you thought Microsoft's Azure CTO should have better things to do than getting classic FPS Doom to run in MS Paint, you'd be very wrong. Developed by Mark Russinovich, Microsoft Azure's CTO, DoomPaint runs the original shareware version of Doom using MS Paint as the monitor for the game. The project is powered by an OLE clipboard hack that allows Doom to run at a solid 35fps. "The actual Doom engine (ViZDoom) runs the real shareware DOOM1.WAD — with the BSD-licensed Freedoom WADs covering the episodes shareware doesn't ship — and renders headlessly," writes Russinovich on the project's GitHub page. "Every frame is placed on the Windows clipboard and pasted into Paint's canvas as a genuine document edit." Doom really can run on anything. 35fps is pretty good for MS Paint, right? Russinovich goes on to say that the game's low frame rate is part of DoomPaint's charm, and when you think about it, 35fps is pretty good as far as 90s gaming is concerned. There's even sound and music included in the MS Paint version of Doom. To be clear, Paint doesn't actually handle the compute side of the game and only renders it. If you want to try DoomPaint for yourself, you can find steps to get the game up and running in Microsoft Paint on Russinovich's GitHub page. Doom is famous for running on pretty much anything, ranging from gut bacteria to a pregnancy test. More recently, I covered a story where someone ported Doom to the Commodore 64, giving the already primitive-looking first-person shooter an even more pixelated look.

Chinese memory manufacturer CXMT was the fastest-growing memory company in the world in the second quarter, according to the latest data from Counterpoint Research. Like China's Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), CXMT has also shaped up to become a key player in the country's bid to develop semiconductor self-sufficiency. However, unlike SMIC, it is also capable of manufacturing the most advanced memory chips, with multiple reports claiming progress in being able to manufacture LPDDR6 memory chips. CXMT Led The Pie In Q2 Revenue Growth Due To Strong Domestic Demand, Says Report. Counterpoint's research outlines that during the second quarter of 2026, Samsung made a comeback in the global DRAM market. The firm's revenue as a percentage of the market sat at 39% during the quarter to make it the largest DRAM memory manufacturer in the world. The gain came at the expense of SK hynix, whose share dropped by 13 percentage points annually to sit at 26%. According to Counterpoint, the dip occurred despite SK hynix's revenue surging by 214% annually during the quarter. Crucially, Micron almost caught up to SK hynix when it comes to market share. The details show that its market share sat at 25% during the quarter as it almost overtook hynix to become the world's second largest DRAM supplier in terms of revenue. DRAM is a key component of the AI market as multiple layers are bonded together to create high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in advanced AI GPUs. As for CXMT, the Chinese memory company was the fastest-growing DRAM memory manufacturer in the world, says the research firm. During the second quarter, CXMT's DRAM revenue grew by a strong 716% annually. It was followed by Taiwan's Nanya Technology, whose revenue jumped by 690% in the quarter. The details suggest that the reason behind CXMT being the world's fastest DRAM supplier was strong domestic demand in China and capacity expansion. After its IPO earlier this year, CXMT is interested in aggressively expanding its memory production capacity. Reports have suggested that the firm is in the early stages of building a new manufacturing facility in Beijing. Additionally, consumer electronics giant Apple is also interested in procuring memory chip supply from CXMT due to the broader tightness in the market, which has forced it to raise product prices. Counterpoint's Vice President of Research, Neil Shah, linked the capacity expansion to CXMT potentially being able to reshape the global memory industry's landscape. Taking an optimistic tone, the executive stated that "the question is not about ‘how’ but ‘when’ CXMT will be able to break into the Big Three Memory Club.” Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

Philadelphia should use the Waymo testing period to get this right, not rush it. The pattern that is emerging is that problems that should have been caught during testing are instead being confronted when the autonomous vehicles have already been deployed. Waymo’s driverless cars have been rolling through Center City for almost a year now. Still with a trained specialist behind the wheel, still without a commercial launch date. Some of our local elected officials have expressed concerns about driverless vehicles on Philadelphia streets. Based on what has happened in other cities, their concerns are not unfounded. When it comes to deploying robotaxis, Philadelphia should slow down, not speed up. The pattern that has emerged across the country is that problems that should have been caught during testing are instead being confronted when the autonomous vehicles have already been deployed and are carrying passengers. Start with what happened in Austin, Texas, this spring. When a gunman opened fire outside a bar on Sixth Street, killing three people and wounding more than a dozen, several Waymo vehicles ended up blocking the emergency response. One sat sideways in the road as an ambulance tried to get through, with bystanders shouting at it to move, while a police officer worked the car’s speaker system trying to get a human being on the line. In San Francisco, fire crews and other first responders have had to physically take control of stalled Waymos to move them out of the way during emergencies. These aren’t isolated glitches. Federal regulators counted at least six incidents nationally in which first responders had to take control of a Waymo vehicle during an emergency. In July, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration told the industry that emergency scenes are not rare or extreme “edge cases,” and that an automated vehicle unable to interact safely with first responders is a danger to the public. That’s the backdrop against which Philadelphia is being asked to move forward. Councilmember Nina Ahmad gave voice to concerns after a City Council hearing in May. “Progress for the sake of progress isn’t enough. We need to look at the impact of that progress,” she said during a news conference. She wasn’t the only Council member who expressed reservations, or whose questions for Waymo went unanswered at the hearing. Under state law, PennDot holds the authority to certify these vehicles for full commercial service. City officials have said Philadelphia is preempted from regulating this technology at all. After Waymo vehicles became immobilized and helped bring San Francisco traffic to a standstill during the city’s July Fourth celebration, Mayor Daniel Lurie called for stronger statewide standards that verify that the autonomous vehicles’ systems can handle major events and emergencies before they are allowed to operate. His message was simple: “Prove it before you deploy it.” Here is the question I’d ask before this moves one step further in Philadelphia: Have the police officers, firefighters, and paramedics who will be on the street been trained, specifically and verifiably, to handle a car that will not pull over for a siren, will not respond to a hand signal or a flare, and has no driver to negotiate with? A first responder trained to deal with a human behind the wheel is not automatically equipped to deal with an empty vehicle that only takes instructions from a call center hundreds or thousands of miles away. Austin’s ambulance crews and San Francisco’s fire companies found out about that gap in real time, during emergencies — Philadelphia doesn’t have to. Cities where Waymo has already launched are the ones now writing the incident reports. The company cites a substantial reduction in serious-injury collisions compared with human drivers, and that’s worth weighing. But a strong overall safety record and a specific, unresolved gap around emergency scenes are not the same question, and cities where Waymo has already launched are the ones now writing the incident reports. Philadelphia has something Austin and San Francisco didn’t have when they signed up for driverless service at scale: time. This is the moment to apply Mayor Lurie’s standard: Prove it before you deploy it. Amy Witherite is a traffic safety advocate and founder of the Witherite Law Group, which has offices in Philadelphia.

Anthropic is building a team to design its own in-house AI chips as it faces surging demand for its models. The AI startup is hiring engineers to design custom chips for its Claude AI model, according to a job listing and a company statement. An Anthropic spokesperson told Business Insider that the company is building an in-house silicon team to design custom chips for Claude, the first time it has publicly confirmed the plans. They added that Anthropic would co-design hardware and models, allowing Claude to run faster and more efficiently "at the scale our customers need." The spokesperson said Anthropic has taken and will continue to take a "multi-chip approach" in which hardware from AWS, Google, Nvidia, and AMD will remain central to the AI lab's scaling efforts. Reuters previously reported that Anthropic was exploring the possibility of designing its own chips, while The Information reported last month that Anthropic had held talks with Samsung Electronics as a potential manufacturing partner. A recently posted job listing detailed Anthropic's plans for a "custom silicon team," with the company seeking engineers with expertise across a wide range of chip design and verification domains. The engineer position, which lists a salary range of $320,000 - $485,000, says candidates must be able to demonstrate "direct personal contribution" to the finalization and shipping of semiconductor designs. "This is a role for someone who has shipped silicon, has a realistic relationship with schedules, and is comfortable making consequential calls without a large organization behind them," the listing read. Designing an AI chip in-house is a costly and difficult process, but it can help companies to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, which dominates the market for AI accelerator chips. It also allows AI labs to customize their compute to fit their models' needs. Anthropic is the latest AI lab to move into designing its own chips. In June, rival OpenAI unveiled its own purpose-built semiconductor, dubbed Jalapeño, which it developed with Broadcom. Meta is also planning to put its next-generation AI chip into production in September, according to an internal memo reviewed by Reuters, and the CEO of AI startup Mistral has said the French company is considering building its own silicon.

Rumors about Apple's next budget phone, the iPhone 18e, point to small but real changes rather than a redesign. The biggest shift is a new chip and an unexpected RAM configuration, while most other specs, including the screen and camera, look set to carry over largely unchanged from the iPhone 17e. The e-series appears to be evolving into a calibrated gateway to the iPhone ecosystem, with just enough modern performance to stay relevant while leaving reasons to buy the standard, Air and Pro models. On timing, Apple usually launches e-series phones in spring after the fall flagship lineup, so the iPhone 18e most likely arrives in March or April of 2027. Unlike past years, it won't trail the regular iPhone: previous rumors suggest Apple will split its iPhone releases for the first time, with the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and the first foldable iPhone arriving this September, followed six months later by the iPhone 18, the second-generation iPhone Air and the iPhone 18e. Two analysts, Ming-Chi Kuo of TF International Securities (in June) and Jeff Pu of GF Securities (in late July), say the iPhone 18e will have 9GB of RAM, just 1GB more than the iPhone 17e. Both point to Apple's upcoming A20 chip powering it. That chip reportedly uses six 1.5GB memory dies instead of four 2GB ones, which produces the odd 9GB total. The A20 may also move to a 2nm manufacturing process from the current 3nm, bringing efficiency gains and modest speed improvements. The extra memory should help iOS 27 run Apple Intelligence features more smoothly, but not everything. Apple's most advanced on-device AI model requires 12GB of RAM. It could power the most exciting iOS 27 features, such as the more expressive Siri AI voices and more accurate systemwide dictation Apple announced in June. If the 9GB rumor holds, both the iPhone 18e and the regular iPhone 18 might miss out on those high-end AI features. Elsewhere, Chinese leaker Digital Chat Station says the phone will keep the iPhone 17e's 6.12-inch OLED screen at 60Hz, meaning no ProMotion or Always-On display. Some rumors suggest a switch from the notch to the Dynamic Island, though that has been heard before. The camera is expected to be a single 48MP rear sensor on the same Fusion camera hardware as the iPhone 17e, and storage options should remain 256GB or 512GB. A price increase looks likely. Macs and iPads recently became more expensive, and although Apple did not raise iPhone 17 series prices, component costs, especially memory chips, have climbed sharply. No concrete numbers have leaked; some outlets say the iPhone 18e will cost $650 to $700, but these are early guesses. Apple has confirmed nothing, though the pattern across analysts and outlets is consistent enough to take seriously.

China tightens drone exports, sanctions U.S. firms in latest tech retaliation. - Share via. Beijing is leveraging its dominance over global drone production as it spars again with Washington over widening U.S. curbs on technology and trade, unleashing a barrage of retaliatory actions on Wednesday in what it described as a “restrained” response. China’s Commerce Ministry stiffened controls on the exports of drones as it announced four sets of countermeasures to recent U.S. moves. It cited decisions such as the Federal Communications Commission’s ban on some foreign-made robots and power inverters and the blacklisting of more than 40 Chinese companies accused of using forced labor. The tit-for-tat standoff now pitting Beijing against Washington is reviving tensions between the world’s two biggest economies and straining their fragile trade truce. President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet President Trump in the U.S. next month, after agreeing to build a relationship of “constructive strategic stability” during their summit in the Chinese capital in May. Beijing has been particularly irked by the timing of U.S. sanctions against the 43 Chinese firms, which came just a day after Vice Premier He Lifeng held a video call with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer last week. The recent U.S. measures “seriously violated the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state and severely damage China’s legitimate rights and interests,” a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said in a statement. “China has no choice but to take necessary countermeasures in response.” But the spokesperson also signaled Beijing’s willingness to keep relations on track, calling its retaliation “generally restrained” while urging the US to immediately revoke its measures and return to consultations to resolve differences. As part of the retaliation package, sales to the U.S. of drones, their key components and related technologies listed on China’s dual-use export control list will be subject to “strict case-by-case review,” the ministry said. China is the world’s dominant manufacturer of unmanned aerial vehicles, with Shenzhen-based DJI Technologies accounting for about 70% of the U.S. commercial drone market as of last year. But the U.S. has moved to reduce that reliance. Last December, the FCC announced a ban on most foreign-made drones and critical components for unmanned aircraft systems. The prohibition applied only to new drone imports and sales and not those that had already been sold or were in use. On Wednesday, the Commerce Ministry also sanctioned six U.S. entities, including Applied DNA Sciences and Stratum Reservoir, for what it said was their involvement in US sanctions over Xinjiang. In addition, it sanctioned Compliance Testing for helping the FCC impose the measures against China. China will also conduct a foreign trade national security investigation, which takes aim at imported printers, copiers, and other office imaging equipment with imported software, the ministry said. Beijing’s retaliation comes amid reports of further U.S. curbs on Chinese technology and products. The FCC is drafting an order to ban Chinese-made data center components, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. Reuters earlier said earlier the U.S. government agency was considering barring imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers. “If the U.S. side insists on introducing new restrictive measures against China, China will take further countermeasures,” the Commerce Ministry spokesperson said in the statement.

Anthropic is building a team to design its own custom chips for AI usage. Business Insider was first to report on the news, but Anthropic has since confirmed with TechCrunch. The Claude maker said it is planning to co-design hardware and models to help its technology run faster and more efficiently. Last month, The Information reported that Anthropic was scouting Samsung as a potential partner for building such chips. Anthropic’s decision to design its own chips comes as demand for Claude rises while AI companies snatch up as many AI infrastructure deals as they can. For its part, Anthropic has inked deals with AWS, Google, Nvidia, and AMD to access AI computing hardware. But to really scale to meet the level of demand, relying on others clearly isn’t enough. Anthropic isn’t the first AI company to decide to build its own chip. In June, OpenAI unveiled its Broadcom-built Jalapeño chip, which is designed specifically for inference workloads. Google DeepMind has long relied on Alphabet’s TPU chips to power its AI models, while Meta has been developing its own MTIA accelerators for AI workloads. The company is seeking engineers with experience in chip design for its “custom silicon team,” per a job listing. This article has been updated to include confirmation from Anthropic.

On July 25, Jeff Dean spoke to 6,000 would-be founders at Y Combinator's Startup School in San Francisco. Dean, a legendary Google engineer, cofounded Google Brain, is chief scientist of Google DeepMind and Google Research, and is technical colead on Gemini. With frequent collaborator Sanjay Ghemawat, he wrote significant parts of Google's computing and search infrastructure. Asked what founders should tackle, he said to pick something you're excited about that would be useful, and described his own interest: an automated version of the scientific method, in which an experiment is proposed, implemented, evaluated, and results gathered. Running thousands of such loops, he said, could unlock advances in science, biology, chip design, and improved AI models. Unknown to the crowd, he was describing his own secret startup. Now official, after almost 27 years Dean is leaving Google, along with Ghemawat and two other top AI scientists, to found Discovery Loop. Google will take a stake, but the departures are a major blow as it competes in AI models. The other cofounders are Oriol Vinyals, VP of research at DeepMind and a technical lead for Gemini, and Quoc Le, a cofounder of Google Brain and key scientist behind AutoML-Zero, which uses machine learning to autonomously build AI products. Dean says the idea arose only a few weeks ago, and the four, long-time colleagues and friends, quickly joined forces after each seeing the possibility of automating scientific and engineering loops. Their road map makes Discovery Loop its own first customer: autonomous experiment loops will first improve the company's own machine learning algorithms, and that software will become the core of an AI system tackling other domains. Le says it might discover a different transformer architecture. The company then aims for superhuman advances in chip design, biology, drug discovery, and material design. Vinyals says a key focus is how models come up with new ideas to try, which they are not currently strong at. Ideas will initially be codeveloped with humans, with the goal of deep automation. The founders contend a few individuals might out-invent the largest research organizations, presumably as customers; the startup may also run its own loops to monetize breakthroughs. Structured as a public benefit corporation, the company raised funding with a simple pitch deck. Vinod Khosla, who met them on a Saturday to avoid tipping off Google, called them "the ultimate superstar team" and said Discovery Loop's premise is that AI is the researcher, not just a research aid. Khosla Ventures and Radical Ventures invested, along with a handful of other firms; amounts and valuation weren't disclosed. Radical managing partner Jordan Jacobs will join the board. Leaving Google was painful: Sundar Pichai tried over multiple meetings to get them to stay. They chose the freedom of a startup; Vinyals cited the inertia of large organizations. Google gave its blessing, an investment, and compute for the first year. Pichai said Google will remain a founding investor and Cloud partner and collaborate on a research framework for ML systems. The company has not begun hiring, which could mean more Google defections, or rented offices. Dean says he is the CEO because "everyone pointed at me." The mission is not novel, as many AI leaders claim AI will drive scientific discovery. The question is whether their work will match the talent gap they leave at Google.

A study by researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and the AdventHealth Research Institute found that a year of regular aerobic exercise made participants' brains appear younger, though the scientists cannot fully explain why. After 12 months of regular workouts, participants' brains appeared about seven months younger than at the start. "Brain age" is estimated by machine learning algorithms trained on thousands of brain scans to recognize the structural patterns typical of a given chronological age. A brain that looks older than its owner's actual age is a biomarker linked to higher risk of future cognitive decline, while a younger-appearing brain suggests a more resilient neurological future. The study focused on healthy, middle-aged adults, a group often overlooked in brain aging research. It enrolled 130 sedentary participants aged 26 to 58 and split them into two groups. One was a control group. The other followed the standard public health guideline of 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise weekly, such as brisk walking, jogging or cycling, a regimen designed to be achievable. After one year, MRI scans showed the exercise group's brains appeared, on average, nearly a full year younger relative to the control group's. Participants stuck to the program well, and their cardiorespiratory fitness improved significantly. However, analysis could not identify the cause. The degree of fitness improvement did not account for the change in brain age, and body weight, blood pressure and levels of key brain health proteins showed no significant or explanatory shift. The work builds on decades of neuroscience showing that physical inactivity contributes to age-related brain shrinkage. Research by Dr. Arthur Kramer at the University of Illinois used MRI to show that aerobic exercise could increase the volume of both gray matter and white matter. The new study suggests exercise can actively roll back brain aging, even in midlife. The focus on midlife is pivotal because most brain health studies target older adults after cognitive warning signs have emerged. The study posits that the 30s, 40s and 50s are a crucial intervention window, since midlife sedentariness predicts dementia risk decades later while the brain remains plastic at this stage. The researchers speculate that exercise may reduce systemic inflammation, enhance cellular energy systems or improve brain blood vessel health in ways current tests did not capture, or that the effect may be the sum of many synergistic changes. The practical takeaway is that the standard recommendation of 150 minutes of moderate activity per week appears to benefit the brain as well as the heart, requiring consistent, moderate effort rather than extreme athleticism. The study has limitations. Participants were generally healthy and well-educated, and the change in brain age, while significant, was modest. Longer studies are needed to confirm that a younger-appearing brain translates to a lower incidence of dementia decades later.

US researchers have created a machine-learning-guided method to design better electrolytes for sodium-metal batteries. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) team’s work could help make this low-cost energy storage technology more viable for large-scale applications. The study addresses a key challenge: the highly reactive nature of sodium-metal batteries, which affects their stability and fast-charging ability. According to researchers, by using AI alongside experimental testing, they identified promising electrolyte formulations that could enable batteries based on abundant sodium instead of scarce materials like lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Smarter sodium batteries. An MIT team has developed an AI-guided method for designing advanced electrolytes that could significantly improve sodium-metal batteries, bringing the low-cost energy storage technology closer to commercial use. The research focuses on one of the biggest technical barriers limiting sodium-metal batteries: the electrolyte. Alongside the anode and cathode, the electrolyte is one of the three essential battery components. It transports charged sodium ions between the electrodes during charging and discharging. However, conventional electrolytes often react with the electrodes, triggering unwanted chemical reactions that produce insulating byproducts, block ion movement, and shorten battery life. See All. The MIT team set out to engineer electrolytes that remain chemically stable while also enabling rapid ion transport. Achieving both has long been a challenge because improving conductivity typically comes at the expense of long-term stability. The researchers built on an earlier discovery involving a sulfonamide-based solvent called DMTMSA, which had shown exceptional chemical stability in lithium-metal batteries. They hypothesized that smaller molecules with similar chemical structures could deliver the same stability while allowing sodium ions to move more quickly through the electrolyte. According to the team, solvent size plays a critical role in ion mobility. Smaller solvent molecules form more compact shells around sodium ions, reducing resistance as the ions travel between the battery’s electrodes. Faster ion transport translates into quicker charging, higher power output, and improved overall battery performance. Intelligent electrolyte design. To accelerate the search, the team developed a machine-learning-guided molecular design pipeline. Within 24 hours, the AI system generated approximately 100,000 candidate solvent molecules. These were computationally screened based on structural similarity to DMTMSA, electronic characteristics, and other chemical properties before being narrowed to 200 promising candidates. From this pool, researchers selected 27 representative molecules for laboratory evaluation under identical testing conditions. The experiments identified a standout performer: a compact solvent known as DMFSA. The molecule combined the smallest molecular size among the candidates with superior electrochemical performance, delivering both fast sodium-ion transport and strong stability against degradation at the battery electrodes. The work introduces a new strategy for electrolyte engineering that combines machine learning with molecular design principles. Instead of relying on conventional trial-and-error materials discovery, the AI-guided workflow rapidly generates, filters, and prioritizes promising candidates for experimental validation, dramatically reducing development time. The researchers have already launched the next phase of the project, using DMFSA as the new starting point to discover even smaller and more efficient solvent molecules. Beyond sodium-metal batteries, the team believes the design framework could be applied to a broad range of next-generation battery chemistries. By optimizing solvent size and molecular similarity through AI-driven screening, the approach could accelerate the development of safer, faster-charging, and longer-lasting energy storage systems for electric vehicles, grid-scale storage, and other high-performance applications. “Because the concept is broadly applicable, its impact could extend well beyond sodium batteries and influence the design of a wide range of future energy storage technologies,” said Jinhyuk Lee, an associate professor of materials engineering at McGill University, in a statement.

By Ed Ludlow, Bloomberg. Amazon.com Inc.’s Zoox robotaxi division will start charging fares next week in Las Vegas, marking a first in the US for autonomous vehicles without driver controls. Zoox will charge Vegas customers starting Aug. 10, with fares calculated from a base rate, the company said in a statement Wednesday. The trip cost will also take into account distance and the duration of each trip. Zoox declined to reveal more fare specifics. Alphabet Inc.’s Waymo is the clear leader in US robotaxis, operating the largest commercial driverless ride-hailing service, with rivals including Tesla Inc. and Amazon’s Zoox looking to catch up. But unlike Zoox robotaxis, Waymo vehicles feature a steering wheel and pedals. Last month, regulators gave Zoox permission to deploy as many as 5,000 robotaxis on US roads over the next two years. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s temporary exemption also lets Zoox charge per ride. The full fare will be visible to riders prior to booking. To date, Zoox’s bug-eyed, boxy robotaxi has driven over 3 million miles on public roads. Prior to commercial launch, it carried 1 million riders across Las Vegas, San Francisco, Austin and Miami.

ZenaTech, Inc. (Nasdaq: ZENA), a provider of AI drone, Drone as a Service, enterprise SaaS and Quantum Computing solutions, announced on August 5, 2026 that it has filed five U.S. provisional patents covering acoustic fire suppression and aerial wildfire assessment technologies. Because nothing is discharged, it can work where conventional suppression cannot, such as electrical substations, data centers, archives, battery storage and home ember defense, with possible expansion into aviation, marine and industrial fire safety. Office for Disaster Risk Reduction. Grand View Research projects the global firefighting drone market will grow from $1.2 billion in 2024 to nearly $2.8 billion by 2033, a 9.8% CAGR. The ZenaDrone 1000 is a 7' x 12' multifunction autonomous AI drone that can carry up to 40 kg of payload, such as acoustics technology, and operate in coordinated swarms. NASCAR's Next-Gen car is arguably the most scrutinized race car in the sport's history, especially when it comes to aerodynamics. The effects of turbulent air, called "dirty air" in the racing community, have been exacerbated with the car, which does not race well at single-groove tracks where drivers are largely unable to get clean air on the nose of their car. That makes passing extremely difficult, especially since the way the flat underbody of the Next-Gen car produces thousands of pounds of downforce that keeps the cars glued to the racetrack. Mark Martin, a 40-time Cup Series winner who was a big part in helping NASCAR change points systems over the offseason, knows how he'd try to fix the car. "I would work with the smart engineers from the teams to make the underbody not work at all," Martin said on the latest episode of the "Dale Jr. Download." "I know why there's an underbody, because all the money was spent before there was one was getting out of control. I get it." "I'll just tell you: I want zero downforce in the front, or lift. You need the front to be virtually nothing. If it's nothing, it shouldn't lose anything [grip] when it gets behind a car." In the Next-Gen car, drivers must constantly find a way to get clean air to the front of their cars. Running in the tire tracks of the driver in front of them puts them directly in that car's wake, forcing them to lose grip and get out of the throttle. While aerodynamics have always been a focus for NASCAR teams, the Next-Gen car is arguably the most aero-sensitive and aero-dependent car NASCAR has ever raced. "I can tell you, I raced cars at Atlanta and Charlotte and all those places, I raced cars that were around zero [downforce in the front] or front lift, and you never, ever heard anything about aero-tight," Martin said. "There's a lot of complications, but the unwillingness to look at no downforce is really a problem. It's ate at me since 1995. I just know that the racing was better." Meta today launched Muse Code, a terminal coding agent available for macOS and Linux. Muse Code is in beta, and it is powered by Muse Spark 1.2, Meta's newest model. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse Code can accomplish complete software engineering tasks across large repos. It can plan out changes, write code, and validate results using multiple persistent subagents. Muse Code is Meta's equivalent of OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code, and it is Meta's first major push into agentic coding. There are several default skills available, such as /plan for turning a task into an approval-gated plan, /grill for stress testing a plan, and /goal for working toward the successful completion of an objective. Muse Code maintains an append-only local event log of every model call, tool run, approval, and edit, so it can resume where it stopped if it crashes. Muse Code can be used through the Mac's terminal after a one-command install, and there is no dedicated app available. The model is priced at $1.25 for 1 million input tokens and $4.25 for 1 million output tokens, but Meta is offering a discount for users who give the company permission to use their prompts and completions to train future AI models. With the Contributor tier enabled for Meta model training, Muse Spark 1.2 is priced at $0.10 for 1 million input tokens and $0.20 for 1 million output tokens. The Standard tier costs more and does not let Meta use prompts to train its models. The more affordable Contributor tier is rate limited at 60 requests per minute and 2,100,000 tokens per minute, while the Standard tier allows for 3,000 requests per minute and 4,000,000 tokens per minute.

Google is losing key AI researchers as its booming cloud business raises questions about its commitment to frontier AI development, according to CNBC. The company posted 82 percent second-quarter cloud revenue growth alongside a major AI shakeup: Chief Scientist Jeff Dean announced his departure after 27 years, and Demis Hassabis stepped down as Google DeepMind CEO to become the unit's chairman. Google published the influential 2017 transformer paper that enabled the generative AI boom, and now faces a resource dilemma. Advanced models demand massive upfront investment in computing power and research without guaranteed returns, while cloud growth outpaces Amazon and Microsoft. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said last month that 90 percent of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise, evidence Google can sell AI services to cloud customers. Some researchers are frustrated over compute access, sources said, as Google Cloud sells TPUs, its proprietary AI chips that rival Nvidia GPUs, to outside customers including Anthropic. Frustration runs especially high when Google announces large infrastructure commitments to rivals whose models compete with Gemini. Bureaucracy, with multiple layers of approval needed to move research into products, compounds this, making OpenAI and Anthropic more appealing to researchers who prefer laboratory work to commercial considerations. Dean is leaving with Google engineers Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le to start Discovery Loop, a Google-backed public benefit corporation that Dean said on X aims to automate machine learning, science and engineering to accelerate discoveries. Earlier prominent departures included Noam Shazeer, who left to join OpenAI. Breitbart News previously reported that The Information described Shazeer clashing with colleagues on internal forums over posts expressing personal beliefs, including that he doesn't believe humans "have an attribute called gender" and that "it is not okay to sterilize children." Shazeer is widely regarded as a founding engineer of the AI revolution; as a Google Brain researcher he co-authored papers that laid the foundation for the transformer architecture behind models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. Gil Luria, a D.A. Davidson analyst who recommends holding Alphabet stock, said the pattern is clear: "They're not interested in commercializing AI. They're interested in being part of history, and so they look at Anthropic, OpenAI or another startup as being the place where they can pursue history." Hassabis, who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google four years later, becomes Alphabet's newly created chief scientist, focusing on longer-term research and the societal implications of artificial general intelligence, plus more time at Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug discovery company that grew out of DeepMind. Koray Kavukcuoglu, DeepMind's technology chief and Alphabet's chief AI architect, takes over daily management and development of the next Gemini model; a person close to the team said he had assumed broader responsibilities from Hassabis over the past year. Kavukcuoglu told CNBC in May that Google aims to push the frontier while improving efficiency, with its Flash model delivering frontier-level capabilities while running four times faster than comparable models.

Security flaws in agent infrastructure from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google, and Vercel let untrusted or forged instructions reach an agent's tools without any check that a model turn had authorized them. In several attack paths the model never ran, so system prompts, content filters, and guardrails never intervened. Hedi Ingber and Aviyam Ivgi of Stealth presented the pattern, which they call CoreBreak, at Black Hat USA 2026. The vulnerabilities differ in conditions: AWS involved an authenticated remote request, Google's required attacker-controlled session events or user-authored function calls, and Vercel's required untrusted code already running in a Linux sandbox. Exposure is bounded by what each agent can already do. In the normal flow, the SDK sends the request and tool definitions to the model, which returns a structured tool call that the SDK executes. The vulnerable paths did not verify provenance between those steps and treated tool-call-shaped data as authoritative. AWS assigned CVE-2026-18830 (CVSS v4.0 8.6) to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore's InvokeHarness API. An authenticated user could put a tool-use block in the final message of a request, and the event loop would dispatch the tool without asking the model. AWS added server-side validation before July 31, 2026, applied automatically. The researchers say the open-source Strands Python code underlying the harness retains a comparable shortcut that skips model invocation when the latest message contains a ToolUse; it remained in the main branch as of August 5, 2026. A pull request to remove it was closed unmerged on June 19. Exploitability depends on whether untrusted callers can place such a block in the message history. AWS told the researchers this falls on the customer side of shared responsibility and responded with a documentation page, "Trusted Message History," telling developers to build history from their own application rather than caller input. Google's CVE-2026-18236 (CVSS v4.0 9.3) affects ADK for Python before 2.5.0. An attacker able to inject events into session history could forge a tool-confirmation approval, because the processor did not verify the tool belonged to the agent, required confirmation, or matched the original recorded call. A second fix in ADK 2.5.0, released July 16, 2026, rejects function calls in user-authored messages, closing a resumable-mode bypass. That second issue is not covered by the CVE. Vercel's flaws are CVE-2026-64650 (@ai-sdk/harness-codex through 1.0.28) and CVE-2026-64651 (@ai-sdk/harness-opencode through 1.0.27), both CVSS v4.0 6.3. The relay trusted any process whose command line contained an approved helper script path, so malicious code in the sandbox could invoke host tools such as secret lookups, deployments, and cloud API calls. Vercel now requires an exact, short-lived, one-time authorization tied to an observed model event. Fixes shipped July 10, 2026, in versions 1.0.29 and 1.0.28. Both CVE records contain errors. A separate June 10 fix hardened tool-approval replay against forged approvals. No advisory addresses whether any path was exploited before patching; the researchers have not released proof-of-concept code. Recommendations: upgrade to the fixed versions; treat conversation history, resumable events, confirmation responses, and tool-use blocks crossing external boundaries as untrusted; bind each invocation to the exact model event, tool, arguments, and session; and limit each agent's tools, roles, and credentials. This is not prompt injection: the model never gets a turn.

Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems, successfully launched its 13th Electron rocket of the year on August 6, 2026, deploying the latest satellite for multi-launch customer Institute for Q-shu Pioneers of Space, Inc. (iQPS), operator of the QPS-SAR Earth-imaging constellation. The mission, called 'The Grain Goddess Provides', lifted off from Rocket Lab Launch Complex 1 in Mahia, New Zealand, at 9:18 p.m. NZST. In February 1946, the U.S. Army unveiled ENIAC, a computer that could calculate an artillery shell's trajectory faster than the shell could reach its target. It weighed 30 tons and had 18,000 vacuum tubes and 3,000 switches. Six mathematicians, Kathleen McNulty Mauchly Antonelli, Jean Jennings Bartik, Frances "Betty" Snyder Holberton, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, Frances Bilas Spence and Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum, figured out how to program it. They had worked for the Army as human "computers," calculating trajectories by hand. With no programming languages, manuals or classes, they studied electrical diagrams, broke equations into thousands of steps and used cables and switches to guide calculations, helping create the profession of computer programming. History ignored them for decades. The article argues manufacturing faces its own ENIAC moment: the smart factory, with robots, sensors and AI that spots defects and predicts failures, is arriving before the workforce to run it exists. No single title has emerged for these jobs, but there are not enough people who can do them. A MAGNET survey of Ohio manufacturers found demand for technically trained, experienced workers at a seven-year high. Across four technical occupations alone, U.S. manufacturers are expected to add nearly 90,000 jobs over the next decade, even as automation eliminates entry-level jobs that once taught people how factories work. Computer programming took decades to develop career paths; manufacturing must build them now. The article proposes six steps: 1. Build a new first rung. Treat every entry-level hire as a future technician and create a visible in-plant pathway of skills and qualifying jobs from day one. 2. Build a culture of opportunity. One workforce study estimated 40% of current advanced-manufacturing skill requirements will evolve within five years, so training cannot be a one-time event. Map changing jobs and skills, give employees paid learning time, expect supervisors to identify people who can advance, and give experienced workers time to teach. 3. Stop hiring only for experience. The ENIAC women had never programmed but understood mathematics, logic and the problem to be solved. Hire for how people think, use job-related problems to assess candidates, and teach the equipment. 4. Train people before the technology arrives. Before approving a major purchase, ask who will run, fix and improve it and what training they need. Too often vendors give a few days of instruction and employees return to full workloads. Training should be part of the purchase, with protected learning time. 5. Use AI to capture tribal knowledge. In MAGNET's survey, 70% of manufacturers said they were transferring knowledge from retiring workers to younger employees. Recorded explanations from experienced workers, combined with maintenance histories and manuals, can form a searchable knowledge base. AI will not replace expert judgment but can preserve examples of it. 6. Build the pipeline through partnerships. Most small and midsize manufacturers cannot do this alone. Employers should agree on core skills, share hiring projections and commit to paid experience and jobs, while schools, community colleges and community partners build and support training. A factory tour cannot create a technician; a connected path from classroom to paid experience to a real job can. Just as ENIAC was a room of hardware until six mathematicians made it work, technology is reaching the shop floor faster than the people and career paths needed to use it. The next great breakthrough may be the path that teaches someone to run a machine.

Apple's attempt to use Chinese memory maker CXMT as leverage against Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix has backfired, with the two Korean chipmakers ending up with more pricing power rather than less, DigiTimes reports, citing South Korean and Chinese trade press. This year, Apple has explored CXMT and fellow Chinese chipmaker YMTC as potential DRAM suppliers, and had progressed to testing CXMT's chips as memory shortages pushed up the cost of almost all Apple devices. Apple hoped a credible Chinese alternative would pressure Samsung and SK Hynix into cutting their own prices, a tactic it has used before with OLED suppliers and contract manufacturers. CXMT is barred from EUV lithography tools under U.S. export controls, so it has to rely on older DUV equipment that, per a cost analysis cited by TechTimes, requires around 30% more wafer starts to produce the same output. That extra cost means matching Samsung and SK Hynix's prices is CXMT's floor, not a discount it's able to offer, so when Apple pushed for a lower LPDDR5X quote, CXMT turned it down and held pricing at or above the Korean suppliers' own rates. With that threat neutralized, Apple seemingly lost its main point of leverage. Digital Daily reports that Chinese device makers Huawei and Xiaomi have already locked up most of CXMT's output through long-term, high-price contracts, so the company doesn't need Apple's business badly enough to negotiate. The result is the opposite of what Apple wanted; without a credible cheaper alternative to point to, Samsung and SK Hynix face less pressure to lower their own prices, at the same time they're shifting production toward high-bandwidth memory for AI servers and tightening the broader DRAM supply. The setback comes after Apple's CXMT plans drew pushback, with politicians demanding Apple commit to not buying Chinese memory chips at all. In 1964 the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) subjected Oklahoma City to 1,253 intentional sonic booms over six months to gauge public attitudes toward supersonic flight. A University of Chicago survey of 3,000 residents found 73% felt they could live with the booms, but the test brought lawsuits, about 12,400 complaint calls, and compensation for window and wall damage. It helped set off events that doomed commercial supersonic flight over the US: Congress canceled funding in 1971 for Boeing's 2707, and in 1973 the FAA effectively banned civil supersonic flight over land by prohibiting speeds above Mach 1. Concorde, the only commercial supersonic airliner, flew from 1976 to 2003 and had no successor; only 14 entered service, and it was limited largely to New York–Paris and London routes. In June the FAA proposed new rules that would replace the speed-based standard with a noise-based one and repeal the 1973 prohibition, aiming to finalize them by mid-2027. The proposed limit is 0.11 pound per square foot at the surface, a moderate thump; the Oklahoma booms reached 1.6, over 14 times more. Two approaches aim to meet it. Boom Supersonic, of Colorado, relies on Mach cutoff, or "boomless cruise." The plane flies higher, generally above 30,000 feet, and at a speed calculated from the day's weather, so the shock wave bends upward and never reaches the ground. The concept dates to 1960s Lockheed Martin studies and 1970s NASA tests. Boom says it achieved it six times in two XB-1 supersonic flights, though it released no observational data. Its limits: only marginally faster than sound, typically Mach 1.1 (Boom says up to Mach 1.3), unavailable in some weather, and higher fuel use. Boom's planned Overture would carry 60 to 80 passengers at up to Mach 1.7 over water, cutting New York–Los Angeles to 3.5 hours, with passenger flights expected within four years and up to three times the fuel of today's airliners, run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, which remains below 1% of fuel use. NASA's approach, under its Quesst mission, is the experimental X-59, shaped to spread shock waves evenly so they reach the ground as a thump comparable to a car door closing about 20 feet away. It flew first in late 2025, went supersonic in June, and has reached Mach 1.4. Further measurements come later this year, then community testing modeled on Oklahoma City, with NASA aiming to inform International Civil Aviation Organization rules by 2031. Mission manager Peter Coen says unrestricted speed over land is needed for supersonic travel to be economically attractive, and that the X-59 is a data-gathering plane, not an airliner prototype. Boom CEO Blake Scholl calls Quesst "a waste of taxpayer money," saying a scaled-up version would be as long as a football field. Stanford's Juan Alonso says Mach cutoff can launch service sooner but cannot deliver Mach 2 to 2.5, and expects low-boom design to suit smaller business jets of 15 to 20 passengers. Scholl predicts even full booms may prove acceptable, possibly prompting further deregulation.

Meta has launched Muse Code in beta, a terminal-based AI coding agent built to handle complete software engineering tasks across large repositories, putting it in more direct competition with Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. It was released alongside Muse Spark 1.2, a coding-focused update to Meta's AI model family. The agent can plan changes, write code, run validation, and keep working across long tasks spanning a large codebase. CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced it on X, and Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in a CNBC interview Wednesday that it can be installed with one command and used for a wide variety of use cases. Muse Code relies on persistent sub-agents that maintain context and work in parallel, an approach aimed at longer development jobs rather than one-off code generation. Meta says Muse Spark 1.2 and Muse Code were developed and trained together, which Wang said improves coding performance. He declined to disclose usage figures for the Muse Spark models, saying "adoption has been exciting and strong." The model has posted competitive results on coding benchmarks including Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, and scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, within striking distance of models from established rivals. Price is one of Meta's main weapons. Muse Spark 1.2 starts at $1.25 per million input tokens under standard pay-as-you-go pricing. A contributor tier cuts that to $0.10 per million input tokens, more than 10 times cheaper, according to Wang. The tradeoff is that developers on that tier must opt in to letting Meta use their data to improve its models. Meta has also begun accepting requests for zero-data retention, which Wang called "a big enterprise feature that is important for folks." The distinction could matter for companies handling proprietary source code or sensitive information, and given Meta's data-driven advertising business, its handling of developer data is likely to draw close attention as Muse Code moves beyond beta. Developers will access Muse Code through the same Meta developer platform that hosts the Muse Spark API. Muse Spark 1.2 is also set to appear on OpenRouter, alongside models from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Z.ai, and other labs. The launch comes as coding agents become one of the most contested areas of the AI market. Claude Code has gained traction among developers who want an AI working directly inside repositories and terminals, and OpenAI has been pushing Codex deeper into software development workflows. There is also a financial dimension. Meta continues to spend heavily on AI infrastructure and data centers, creating pressure to turn that spending into products people will pay for. Its shares fell last week after it issued a lighter revenue forecast and reported shrinking free cash flow for the second quarter. Muse Code offers another way to monetize its AI research beyond consumer assistants and advertising. The key question is whether developers will switch on price. Wang has made the strategy clear: Meta does not need Muse Code to beat Claude Code or Codex on every benchmark. If it delivers comparable coding performance at a fraction of the cost, it may find a way into a developer market where Anthropic and OpenAI already have a head start.

Apple and its manufacturing partners are racing to secure enough mobile DRAM to complete production of the iPhone 18 Pro and its first foldable iPhone, with around $1 billion worth of unpackaged processors reportedly sitting idle as they wait on memory chips, according to semiconductor analyst Tim Culpan. With less than six weeks until the expected debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and the first foldable iPhone, widely rumored to be called the "iPhone Ultra," assemblers are working with Apple to hurry DRAM shipments, Culpan reports. Apple leans heavily on Micron for the memory but also buys from SK Hynix and Samsung. Apple and its assemblers are said to remain confident they can meet initial demand, though sources are concerned that online order wait times could stretch out while retail inventory dries up quickly. This year's iPhone lineup is set to introduce the "A20 Pro" chip, Apple's first chip built on TSMC's N2 process, which started shipping in volume earlier this year. Production is reportedly progressing well, with good volume and yields, but completed wafers are piling up because the DRAM needed to package them has not arrived. Because packaging cannot be completed without the corresponding DRAM, Culpan estimates that TSMC is currently sitting on roughly $1 billion worth of Apple processors that cannot move to the next stage of production. The bottleneck apparently threatens to ripple into the final stages of iPhone production. Main logic board assembly and final assembly are handled primarily by Foxconn and BYD in China, and delays in packaged processor deliveries could compress their production schedules even if Apple ultimately secures enough memory for launch. The squeeze reflects a broader memory shortage as AI infrastructure spending eats into global DRAM supply. Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged the pressure during the company's July 30 earnings call, saying Apple was "seeing some very significant constraints currently, with limited flexibility in the supply chain." The crunch already forced Apple to raise prices and shift production priorities, with Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reporting this week that Apple is steering buyers toward the MacBook Pro and away from the MacBook Air. Assemblers have reportedly been told that Apple plans to build around 200 million units combined across the iPhone 18, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Ultra over their lifetimes, with the Ultra accounting for less than 10% of that total. The rest is expected to be split evenly between the Pro and standard models. The foldable iPhone will likely cost more than $2,000, making it the most expensive iPhone Apple has ever sold.

Gov. Greg Abbott announces $16.8 billion SpaceX chip manufacturing plant in Texas. GRIMES COUNTY, Texas - SpaceX will build a massive, vertically integrated semiconductor fabrication plant in Grimes County, representing an initial capital investment of more than $16.8 billion and creating 3,000 jobs, Gov. Greg Abbott announced Thursday. Grimes County is about 40 miles northwest of downtown Houston and directly east of College Station. SpaceX announces major chip plant. By the numbers: The project, dubbed the "Terafab," will span 100 million square feet and consolidate the chip manufacturing process, including logic, memory, and advanced packaging, under a single roof. The facility is designed to scale up chip production for the company's space and terrestrial artificial intelligence needs. "Texas is where big ideas grow even bigger," Abbott said in a statement. "The first-of-its-kind Terafab facility will accelerate chip production in Texas at an unprecedented scale, create thousands of good-paying jobs in Grimes County, and expand economic opportunity for generations of Texans across Southeast Texas and beyond." To support the project, the state extended a $30 million grant from the Texas Enterprise Fund (TEF), a deal-closing incentive used to secure competitive corporate expansions. The Terafab also qualifies for economic incentives under the Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation (JETI) program, created by the Legislature in 2023 to draw large-scale industrial projects. The expansion further anchors SpaceX's footprint in Texas, where it already operates its global headquarters and Starbase launch complex near Brownsville, as well as a Starlink manufacturing facility in Bastrop. Elon Musk, founder and CEO of SpaceX, said the facility aims to bring cutting-edge manufacturing back to the U.S. while powering the company's futuristic tech needs. What they're saying: "We’re now embarking on the most epic chip-building effort — combining logic, memory, and advanced packaging all under one roof — in Grimes County, Texas," Musk said. "The Terafab is bringing cutting-edge manufacturing to America, creating thousands of high-paying jobs in the Lone Star State, and enabling us to produce AI chips at scale for use on Earth and in space." Local leaders welcomed the economic development, which will hire engineers, technicians, and plant operators. Grimes County Judge Joe Fauth III called the announcement a "generational change" for the area located northwest of Houston. School districts serving the rural area have also moved to approve tax incentive agreements with project entity TeraFab AI, LLC under the state's JETI program. Leaders from both the Anderson-Shiro Consolidated Independent School District and the Iola Independent School District cited long-term educational and financial benefits for local students and schools. Regional economic groups said they are preparing to bolster local infrastructure and workforce pipelines to accommodate the multi-billion-dollar buildout. Atlas Motion, a startup making motors for drones and robots, is emerging from stealth with $11.5 million in funding led by Greycroft, with participation from Also Capital, Enea Capital, Mana Ventures and Sunflower Capital, plus angels Jai Malik, CEO of AMCA, and Scott Sanders, CGO of Forterra. Its founding team includes alumni of Tesla, Mitre, Shield AI and Mach Industries. The company says it already ships 10,000 motors a month and will reach 40,000 a month by December, according to CEO Christian Mochen. It incorporated in February and shipped its first motor in under 60 days, and says current capacity is already committed. It has not named any customers, who are in defense, so demand cannot yet be independently verified. The central claim is that its proprietary engineering AI, Vector, can design a new motor in about 20 minutes, versus the weeks to months typical when cross-functional teams work in parallel. Vector, inspired by Tesla's Odin platform for self-testing across production lines, ingests a design's requirements, runs simulations normally done by hand, and generates the manufacturing packages. Mochen says it goes from specification to finished design in five to 10 minutes, with small tweaks afterward, and that output matches real hardware with "99 percent confidence." Atlas says it can move a new design into scaled production in six weeks, versus up to six months for the industry. Mochen says designs can even be generated during a first customer call. Mochen frames Vector as an accelerant, not a replacement: "AI isn't replacing engineering," but orchestrating critical decisions across the engineering toolpath quickly. Atlas calls its engineers "architects," who design from first principles and shape the inputs while the software covers the hard design work. The company injected compute into its manufacturing tooling and wired Vector through the process so it feeds ground-truth data back and improves over time. Atlas aims for near-zero cost of iteration. Changing over a production line for a variant is normally punishing, forcing suppliers into rigid catalog models; Atlas argues standardized raw-material inputs and a software-driven line cut changeover costs sharply. Mochen says this is why customers in places like India, Poland and Africa buy from Atlas even when China is an option, getting speed and flexibility with designs custom to spec. Atlas also pitches itself as a supply-chain play. Most of the world's drones and robots use Chinese-made motors and actuators, which Mochen calls one of the more severe vulnerabilities facing the United States, and he wants to restore American "sovereignty" over that capability. He says Atlas doesn't want to depend on government subsidies. It is also opening an online storefront so independent builders can buy production-grade motors directly. Engineering and prototyping are in Long Beach, California, but mass production is in the Philippines, a longtime U.S. treaty ally; Mochen cites that status and Atlas's trade accreditations as insulation, though importing finished goods still leaves tariff risk and some geopolitical exposure. Mochen says hardware moving at the speed of software will be the most critical part of the industry over the next five to 10 years. The article notes the speed claim warrants skepticism.

Building a data center is hard. Building a rocket that doesn’t explode on the way to space is harder. SpaceX (SPCX) CEO Elon Musk says that’s precisely why SpaceX believes it has an edge. Musk made that case during the company’s first earnings call as a public company, arguing that the engineering challenges behind reusable rockets make designing terrestrial data centers look almost simple by comparison. “As the saying goes, this ain’t rocket science. Well, actually, rocket science is literally our daily business,” Musk said on the call. “Rockets desperately want to blow themselves into tiny pieces.” He explained that SpaceX’s engineers spend every day solving one of the most difficult engineering problems imaginable: reliably getting massive reusable rockets into orbit without catastrophic failure. That’s why, in his view, building data centers doesn’t require an entirely new playbook. Why Musk Thinks SpaceX Has an Unfair Advantage. “If you apply a small amount of the engineering skill that goes into making gigantic rockets reach orbit on a regular basis reliably to terrestrial data centers,” Musk said, “this is like, frankly, the New York Yankees going in and playing a little league team.” Musk wasn’t suggesting data centers are easy. Rather, he argued they’re dramatically less complex than developing reusable rockets or the company’s Starlink satellites, which he described as “alien-level technology.” He also acknowledged that rocket science remains extraordinarily difficult, noting that even talented competitors continue to face launch failures. “But you’ll note that some of our competitors do in fact blow their rockets up,” Musk said. “That does not mean they’re incapable. In fact, I think our competitors are very smart people. But despite being very smart, the rockets still blow up.” His point was that if engineers can repeatedly solve problems at that level of complexity, designing power systems, cooling infrastructure, and server racks becomes a far more manageable challenge. From Space to AI Infrastructure. SpaceX is already putting that philosophy into practice. Musk said the company is building terrestrial data centers using many of the same engineering principles developed for Starlink. He has previously explained that the Starmind V1 compute design created for satellites—minus the solar arrays and radiators needed for space—can also be deployed on Earth, allowing the company to reuse technology across both businesses. As demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continues climbing, companies are racing to build the computing capacity needed to power next-generation AI models. While hyperscale data centers have traditionally been dominated by large technology companies, SpaceX is betting its aerospace engineering experience can become a competitive advantage in an entirely different industry. Investing in the Next Wave of AI. Artificial intelligence isn’t only reshaping established technology companies. It has also fueled growing interest in startups building the infrastructure and automation tools that could benefit from AI’s expansion. Whether SpaceX ultimately dominates data centers the way Musk predicts remains to be seen. But his message was clear: compared with convincing rockets not to “blow themselves into tiny pieces,” keeping rows of servers running looks like a much easier engineering problem. Doom Just Found Its Weirdest New Home: Microsoft Paint. DoomPaint is about what you'd expect from a wild port like this, because apps like Microsoft Paint can't accommodate an entire game engine inside of its interface. What's really happening is that Doom is being rendered in the background through ViZDoom, and each rendered frame is placed into the Windows clipboard and then immediately pasted into MS Paint. The visual results, combined with keyboard controls from within the Microsoft Paint app, allows DoomPaint to simulate the game as if it were being run inside an MS Paint container, as screenshotted below. The real engine is still doing all the heavy lifting, and Paint is quickly presenting new frames. Just last month, we covered a playable Doom port for the Commodore 64, that required a custom game engine to get working. There's even been DoomPDF and a project allowing lab-grown human brain cells to play Doom. Of existing releases, DoomPaint is most like DoomPDF, which uses its target "platform" as visual output for a real Doom port running in the background. This may be the first Doom port where AI-assistance took center stage, though. With Doom considered an American cultural landmark, Mark Russinovich's DoomPaint may mark a new era for these port projects, where AI helps enthusiasts find even sillier places to put Doom.

The author has used Docker as their go-to tool for self-hosting since starting a home lab, but after exploring Proxmox LXC containers, they now choose LXCs over Docker for most of their services. They expected LXCs to be a lightweight alternative to virtual machines, but found they offer the isolation of separate systems without the overhead of full VMs, while staying easy to organize and manage. Docker became hard to manage as the home lab grew. Running a few containers was easy, but with dozens, each application brought its own Compose file, environment variables, bind mounts, networks, and update process. Some needed custom ports, reverse proxy changes, or special permissions that had to be looked up repeatedly. Troubleshooting also took longer, requiring checks of container logs, Docker networks, and mounted volumes, and determining whether a problem came from the application or Docker. The author wasn't seeking a Docker replacement, only a setup that stayed manageable as the lab grew. LXC (Linux Containers) are lightweight system containers that share the host's Linux kernel but give each container its own isolated operating system environment, sitting between Docker containers and full VMs. The author now gives each important service its own LXC, which acts like a tiny Linux server with its own filesystem, users, packages, and services. Installation is more straightforward because they can follow official Linux documentation, using apt or installation scripts directly, rather than finding a Docker image or converting commands into a Compose file. Management feels natural: they can SSH in, restart services with systemctl, check logs with journalctl, and update packages as on a regular Ubuntu or Debian server. Proxmox makes LXCs easy to manage from one web interface, showing CPU, RAM, and storage use per container, with restarting, terminal access, and settings changes a few clicks away. New services are set up by creating an LXC from a Debian or Ubuntu template and installing the application. Because each service runs in its own container, changes don't affect the rest of the lab. Snapshots, taken before updates or configuration changes, allow a broken container to be restored in minutes. The built-in backup system lets the author back up and restore an entire LXC. The author hasn't abandoned Docker. They now choose the tool that fits the job rather than defaulting to Docker. Most long-running services live in LXCs, while a few Docker-first applications remain in Docker. This balance has made the setup easier to expand, simpler to maintain, and more enjoyable to work with. Proxmox is an open-source platform built on Debian Linux for server virtualization.

An autonomous vehicle is one that uses technology to partially or entirely replace the human driver in navigating from origin to destination while avoiding hazards and responding to traffic, according to the University of Michigan Center for Sustainable Systems. The terms "autonomous" and "self-driving" are often used interchangeably. SAE International defines six levels of automation, numbered 0 to 5. Levels 0 to 2 keep a driver in control, aided by features such as blind spot warning and automatic emergency braking. Levels 3 and 4 let the vehicle drive itself under certain circumstances but may require a human to take over. Only Level 5, which needs no human at the controls, is fully autonomous. Self-driving cars perceive their surroundings using radar, cameras and LiDar (light detection and ranging), plus artificial intelligence. Data goes to on-board processors that use software, algorithms and machine learning to command braking, steering and acceleration. The sensors detect lane markings, curbs, pedestrians, cyclists and other vehicles, but are not infallible and can be degraded by snow or heavy precipitation covering sensors or lane markings. Vehicles with a safety driver or no driver are used mainly by fleets. Kodiak Robotics and Aurora operate driverless trucks, possibly with monitoring engineers aboard, and Gatik runs autonomous trucks from warehouses to points of sale. Failures include Cruise, a former General Motors subsidiary, which shut down its robotaxi service after a car injured a pedestrian, and a 2018 incident in which a driverless Uber with a safety driver killed a bicyclist in Tempe, Arizona. Advantages include mobility for people unable to drive due to age or disability, and cost and efficiency gains for operators who need fewer employees and can run longer hours. Driver-assistance systems (ADAS) already reduce accidents and congestion, per a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration report. A University of Michigan study found efficiencies could cut lifetime energy use and greenhouse gas emissions by up to 9% versus conventional vehicles. Challenges include cost, safety concerns, weather, and the fact that the technology does not emulate human thought or instincts for split-second decisions. Removing humans eliminates distraction and emotion, but the vehicles cannot make ethical decisions; Germany passed a law prioritizing human lives over animals. Serious accidents have fueled community opposition. The highest automation available to consumers is Level 2: GM's Super Cruise, Ford's BlueCruise, BMW's Motorway Assistant and Tesla's Full Self Driving. Waymo runs robotaxis in 11 U.S. markets with plans for 21 more cities, including London and Tokyo. Zoox, partnered with Amazon, operates in Las Vegas and San Francisco, with Miami and Austin planned. May Mobility runs driverless Toyota Sienna minivans in 15 locations in the U.S. and Japan. Kodiak Robotics equips semi-trucks for Kroger and Ikea, and Einride's remotely operated electric pods deliver goods in Europe and North America. AI, through deep learning and computer vision, helps vehicles understand environments and predict other road users' behavior; a June 9 McKinsey report said generative AI has significantly accelerated ADAS and AD progress. McKinsey predicts ADAS and AD could generate $300 billion to $400 billion in the passenger car market by 2035. Anticipated effects include fewer accidents, reduced car ownership, automated logistics, less noise and pollution, and no parking tickets. However, McKinsey projects only 4% of new passenger cars in 2030 and 17% in 2035 will have Level 3 or higher automation, so full self-driving will likely remain mainly with fleets and commercial operators for the foreseeable future.

Why AI sandbox escapes are cybersecurity’s newest attack surface. Security researchers have spent the past year watching AI accelerate attacks that already exist. A harder question is whether AI can create attack techniques that didn’t exist before. An AI sandbox escape — where an attacker breaks out of the isolated environment meant to contain an AI assistant — is one of the clearest signs yet that it can. Joe Hladik (pictured), head of Zero Labs, the threat research arm of Rubrik Inc., the data security firm, built his team’s research practice around backup data — a source few others study. This year that focus turned to how employees use AI day to day, starting with the Copilot assistant used by roughly 20 million people and about 90% of the Fortune 500. “No one’s looking at backup data,” Hladik said. “We found it to be a viable place to find actual intelligence to act upon.” Hladik spoke with Krista Case at Black Hat USA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio.
