The writer was assigned to calculate how much she has saved by making cold brew at home, and found that her old habit was costly. Buying iced coffee at roughly $7 a cup, three to five mornings a week, came to about $28 a week, roughly $112 a month, or $1,344 a year. She had already started brewing at home with a $130 KitchenAid cold brew carafe (currently on sale for $100), which she says paid for itself in about a month. It has a 4.4-star rating on Amazon. She was first impressed by the unit's build. It arrives almost fully assembled, with a thick, weighty glass carafe, a brushed stainless steel handle and base, and a sturdy stainless steel pouring spout rather than a lightweight plastic one. Even her husband remarked on how nice it looked in the refrigerator. Brewing is simple: add grounds and water, refrigerate, and wait about 12 hours, so she brews overnight and has coffee ready by morning. The removable stainless steel filter has measurement indicators, and a pouring guide is included. Without the filter basket, the carafe works as a beverage dispenser, and with loose tea, fruit, cucumber or mint in the basket it can make infused water, iced tea or other chilled drinks, making it useful for entertaining. The standard carafe she owns holds 1.7 liters and measures about 8 inches deep, 7 inches wide and just under 7 inches tall, fitting comfortably in her refrigerator. A 38-ounce XL version offers about 35% more capacity at 8 inches deep, 7.2 inches wide and about 8.5 inches tall; it normally costs about $140 and is on sale for $120. She concludes the brewer has replaced her daily coffee shop runs, consistently produces cold brew she enjoys, and has earned a permanent place in her kitchen, with the savings a bonus. Reviewers echo these points. One calls it perfect for her family, praising its ease of cleaning and plastic-free glass and stainless steel construction, though she finds the spout pours a bit slowly. Others describe it as easy to use and clean and well made, and several say they are saving a lot of money on bottled or takeaway cold brew. One says it was pricey but the best kitchen purchase in years, with thick glass and hefty metal parts. Another notes coarse grounds are needed. A buyer who gave it to his wife says she has used it nearly daily since Christmas and stopped using her Ninja countertop machine.

Not all home internet connections are equal; the technology determines your experience, but your choice mostly depends on what is available at your address. Nearly half of US homes lack fiber, and one in three has only a single broadband provider. You can check availability by ZIP code or on the FCC's broadband maps. The FCC defines broadband as at least 100Mbps download and 20Mbps upload. Connection types below are ranked from most to least recommended. Fiber is the gold standard, with the fastest speeds, light-signal transmission and higher customer satisfaction. Providers like Ziply Fiber offer up to 50Gbps, though most max out around 1,000 to 5,000Mbps. Upload speeds typically match downloads, which no other type does. Top plans run about $100 or more monthly, while slower tiers cost $40 to $80, and fiber is likely the best value per megabit. Its only real drawback is availability: the FCC says it reaches only about 56% of US households, mainly urban. Cable is second, available to over 82% of households and often bundled with TV. Many providers offer gigabit downloads (about 940 or 1,000Mbps), but uploads usually top out at 20 or 35Mbps, and congestion can slow speeds at peak times. Plans meeting broadband minimums often start at $50 or less (Mediacom has a 300Mbps plan from $30), but promotional prices frequently rise afterward, though Xfinity offers a five-year price guarantee. 5G home internet uses cellular signals picked up by a router. It is popular for availability and affordability, with prices comparable to cable and simpler terms, including multiyear price locks. In the 2026 American Customer Satisfaction Index, T-Mobile scored 78% and Verizon 79%, better than most fiber providers. Speeds are not guaranteed; T-Mobile's All-In and Amplified plans list 170 to 498Mbps, and Verizon offers up to 1Gbps in some areas. Some plans use LTE. Fixed wireless requires a mounted receiver with line of sight to a tower, and obstacles can block the signal. Speeds typically run 5 to 50Mbps, below the federal broadband definition, so it mostly serves rural areas. In cities like New York and San Francisco, providers such as Google Fiber and Starry beam service to buildings and run Ethernet to units, sometimes reaching gigabit speeds. Satellite is the most widely available but the most expensive, averaging about $100 monthly, with faster plans at $120 to $200 plus roughly $15 monthly equipment fees. Speeds average 12 to 120Mbps. Starlink claims up to 400Mbps and is available in all 50 states, but a 2025 report found only 17% of its customers got FCC broadband speeds. Hughesnet has slower speeds and data caps and filed for bankruptcy in August 2026. DSL, which runs over copper phone lines, is a last resort for rural areas, with downloads of 5 to 120Mbps that vary by address at a flat price. CenturyLink charges $55 monthly plus a $17 equipment rental. It is cheaper than satellite but slower than Starlink. When choosing, consider usage (households that stream, game or upload should want at least 100Mbps down), cost, and whether promotional pricing outlasts the contract. Location is the biggest factor. Wi-Fi is not a connection type; it wirelessly distributes your provider's signal. Symmetrical speeds in a speed test suggest fiber; downloads of 200 to 940Mbps with low uploads suggest cable. A coaxial cable on your modem means cable; a phone line means DSL. The FCC raised its broadband definition in 2024 from 25/3Mbps, so many DSL and satellite services no longer qualify.

As software delivery accelerates and adversaries use AI to move faster, security and engineering teams can no longer operate in silos. They need shared context drawn from production data so both sides can prioritize risk and respond without friction. This friction was a major focus at Black Hat USA 2026. Data separation has historically created delays: security teams often lack production visibility, while engineering teams struggle to understand the security context behind requested fixes, according to Emilio Escobar, chief information security officer of Datadog Inc. "At Datadog … it has to be a unified context for both teams," he said. "If both people, both teams can see the same data, but from a different lens … they can solve the problems faster." Escobar spoke with theCUBE Research's Krista Case during a broadcast on theCUBE at Black Hat USA, discussing how shared context can break down silos while helping teams prioritize risk and validate detections. When both teams examine the same telemetry through different lenses, root-cause analysis accelerates. Escobar gave an example: security investigates a threat on a server while engineering troubleshoots sudden CPU saturation degrading a customer-facing function. The underlying cause, a crypto miner, is identical, yet without shared data the teams pursue separate problems and lose critical time. With the same data, he said, they would know exactly what happened and could solve the problem within minutes. Risk prioritization depends on the same joint visibility. A vulnerability on an internet-exposed critical business function with a known exploit must rank higher than a similar finding buried deep in the infrastructure with no active exploit path. Without runtime and traffic context, both items look equal on a backlog and create tension when engineering is asked to act. "Every security team understands that not every vulnerability should be treated the same," Escobar said. "However, where I think security teams lack is the context and the visibility to be able to understand why is one more important than the other, rather than just the rating and severity of the vulnerability." Deep runtime and application-level information remain the biggest visibility gap for many security teams, Escobar noted. Traditional tooling often stays at the surface, such as attack surface, external scans or infrastructure posture, while actionable understanding requires insight into what is happening inside the running application and supporting systems. He added: "How can you do more with what you have? The right agents for the right use cases, helping them actually close the loop — which is remediating problems rather than just telling you all the problems you have." I guess we are in an era where the zeitgeist is not to teach the man how to fish, but the AI model, ensuring that the AI lab - Anthropic in this case - would then nosh on a lifetime's worth of customized silicon chips. Anthropic is paying $500,000-$850,000 right now to research engineers who are teaching its AI models how to design silicon chips, but just a fraction of this renumeration to the silicon engineers actually building those chips, and that too with nearly identical skillset requirements We reported back in May that Anthropic's passing remarks on "logic chips" in relation to its evolving partnership with Samsung had unleashed a flood of speculation regarding a possible ASIC-related tie-up between the two. Well, just around two months later, Anthropic all but confirmed to Business Insider earlier this week that it indeed plans to build such a custom chip by acknowledging its ongoing efforts to assemble an in-house silicon design team, going on to add that it has and will continue to take a "multi-chip approach." As Anthropic continues to beef up its silicon design team, however, an interesting pay disparity has emerged, with the AI lab willing to pay between $500,000 and $850,000 per year to research engineers who are teaching its AI models how to design silicon chips, but just between $320,000 and $485,000 to the silicon engineers who are actually designing its first ASIC. What's more, this material pay disparity has emerged despite the convergent skillsets required for these two roles, including expertise on full ASIC/FPGA flow, RTL to tape-out, UVM/formal, physical design, PPA, DFT, and EDA tools. Of course, Anthropic is not the first AI lab to try to leverage AI models for chip design processes. After all, Moonshot's viral Kimi K3 model was recently able to design a viable silicon chip completely autonomously within 48 hours, producing a chip design with a 4.0 mm² area and a Nangate 45nm library, all by leveraging open-source EDA tools and building a GPU compiler from scratch. The virtual chip even managed to achieve over 8,700 tokens/second decoding throughput in simulation. Looks like even silicon engineers are not immune from the AI's roving wrath of obsolescence. Eaton, a U.S. power management company, has landed a $7 million contract from the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) to develop quantum computing tools aimed at protecting the nation’s electric grid from increasing cyber and physical threats. The company announced the two-year project on Thursday. Eaton will team up with Infleqtion and Pennsylvania State University to develop new quantum-powered ways to detect and respond to several grid failures at once. The research will use quantum computing, machine learning, and advanced visualization to help power operators spot vulnerabilities and handle disruptions. The goal is to make the grid more resilient as utilities deal with more severe weather, wildfires, cyberattacks, and other risks. Tackling a growing grid security challenge. A key part of the project is solving what engineers call the contingency problem. This means analyzing countless possible operating conditions to find weak spots in the power grid before anything goes wrong. Current reliability standards set by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) require transmission systems to keep working after two failures in a row, a standard called N-2 planning. Eaton’s research aims to go further by looking at several failures happening at once, so operators can better understand all possible risks. The company plans to use its power management experience along with quantum computing’s strength in handling complex calculations. By using a mix of quantum and classical computing, the company hopes to find grid vulnerabilities faster and more accurately, and suggest better responses. See All. “We’re facing unprecedented risks to electric reliability and security from extreme weather, wildfires, physical and cyber threats, and need tools that consider many failures at once,” stressed Sid Suryanarayanan, senior chief engineer, strategic partnerships and innovation at Eaton. “This AFRL-funded project pairs Eaton’s grid expertise with quantum and machine learning methods to bring faster awareness and more actionable control to critical energy systems.” Quantum and machine learning join forces. The project brings together experts from several organizations. Infleqtion will supply specialized quantum hardware, and researchers at Pennsylvania State University will contribute advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence skills. The team will work together to create new quantum algorithms, improve circuits for hybrid quantum-classical computing, and test them on different quantum hardware. They will also try to reduce computational errors, which is one of the main technical challenges for today’s quantum computers. The goal is to create practical tools that utilities can eventually use to improve infrastructure planning, support daily grid operations, and strengthen emergency response during major disruptions. Demonstration planned after two-year project. As part of the AFRL-funded effort, the research team will produce a proof-of-concept demonstration showing how existing quantum hardware, combined with newly developed algorithms and machine learning techniques, can address real-world electric grid challenges. The demonstration is expected to highlight how quantum-enabled technologies could help operators visualize complex grid conditions, evaluate multiple threat scenarios, and make faster operational decisions during emergencies. “At Eaton, we’re delivering next-generation solutions for intelligent power management that benefit critical infrastructure through our world-class engineering capabilities and our comprehensive approach to research and development,” said Dr. Christopher A. Herbst, vice president, strategic partnerships and innovation at Eaton. “This research will enhance infrastructure planning, daily operations and emergency preparedness, bringing unprecedented awareness, anticipation and response to strengthen infrastructure.”

Cloudflare is the latest company to join the race to build a new web browser. But instead of pitching a Chrome alternative to consumers, the internet infrastructure provider launched Kitesurf, a cloud-hosted browser designed specifically for AI agents. AI software is evolving from chatbots that answer questions to agents that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. Browsers are a critical part of this transition, as they’ll need to navigate the web and use websites, as humans do. Unlike traditional web browsers built for humans, a browser built for AI agents doesn’t care about visual elements, like themes, tabs, or browser extensions, Cloudflare explained in its announcement. A browser designed for AI agents needs to manage context windows, performance, token costs, and scalability. It also faces a different threat model because an AI browser could be subject to vulnerabilities like prompt injection attacks and more, the company noted. With Kitesurf, AI developers will be able to build software that can navigate websites, fill out forms, and complete other browser-based tasks, without having to build their own browser software. Cloudflare says it decided to build Kitesurf just 12 weeks ago, and it runs entirely on top of the company’s serverless platform, called Workers. Kitesurf is available for free while in beta in Browser Run, which lets developers programmatically control and interact with headless browser instances on Cloudflare’s network. For developers, Cloudflare’s pitch is that this enables AI agents to use the web more efficiently while using less computing power than Chromium, which keeps costs down. “Kitesurf is significantly more efficient in CPU and memory consumption than Chromium for common agentic tasks like screenshots and HTML extraction,” according to the company. The browser itself was built from other technologies, including a modular rendering engine from Blitz; Firefox’s CSS parser, Stylo; and Boa JS, a Rust ECMAScript engine. Everything else runs inside Cloudflare Workers. Although still new, Cloudflare says Kitesurf already passes around 215,000+ web platform tests, and it’s adding hundreds more, passing tests every week. Cloudflare also credited the open source Rust headless engine, Obscura, for inspiring it to develop Kitesurf, noting that the first proof of concept was a port of Obscura to Workers. The company said the browser correctly renders pages like TodoMVC, a popular benchmark application for comparing JavaScript frameworks, along with Wikipedia, Hacker News, the Cloudflare Blog, and much of the Cloudflare dashboard.

How Do Hot-Swappable Battery Packs Work? We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Most modern electronic devices use built-in battery packs. These components reduce e-waste (or at least the need to recycle batteries), but you have to plug them into a wall outlet or USB port every so often to keep them topped up and functional. However, a new trend is spreading across the entertainment peripheral industry, marrying the best of both worlds. Hot-swappable battery packs are a relatively new development in power technology that provide devices with a semi-infinite energy source without the need for power cords. Hot-swappable devices achieve this by using two batteries at once. The main power source is a removable battery pack. Once that runs low or dry, you just remove it, which is easy since, unlike the removable batteries that manufacturers once put in smartphones, hot-swappable batteries are easily accessible. Then you insert a fresh battery and charge the empty one. Again, depending on the device, the dongle that lets it communicate with your computer (or another device) can also double as a charging pad. The main hook of a hot-swappable battery device is its ability to remain connected during battery swaps. Even Xbox controllers, which keep a charge longer than PlayStation and Switch controllers, disconnect while swapping out their AAs. The secret behind the hot-swap system's feat is the aforementioned second battery. Unlike the removable power pack, this secondary battery is built into the device and takes over when the main battery is absent. Think of it like an emergency generator that provides electricity during a blackout. While this secondary battery keeps a device active, it will eventually run out of charge and should be recharged (often via a USB cable) during downtime. What devices use hot-swappable battery packs? Since hot-swappable battery packs are a relatively recent innovation, few devices use the system. If you want an Xbox controller that doesn't chew through AAs, you need either a proprietary rechargeable battery or rechargeable AAs (USB-rechargeable batteries are worth it in this situation). But given the devices that currently use hot-swappable batteries, game controllers that utilize them might not be far off. One of the first devices that comes to mind is computer accessories. Companies such as Glorious and Angry Miao have recently started selling mice with hot-swappable batteries, and rumors are swirling that SteelSeries' next mouse will also use this system. Headset manufacturers are also joining in on the hot-swap revolution. Glorious sells a headset with hot-swappable batteries, and SteelSeries claims headphones such as its Arctis Nova Elite have batteries you can swap out without losing connection ... so long as you complete the battery transfusion within eight seconds. Not really hot-swappable, but it's a start. Hot-swappable battery systems have also found a home in various industries. Hospitals and many of their hi-tech devices can't afford to lose power, so many medical centers have adopted medical carts, tablets, and other devices that run on hot-swap batteries. You can also find hot-swap battery packs in devices such as industrial tablets. Not only can these gadgets handle a fall, but they can also keep a charge for extended periods, which is a lifesaver for people who work outdoors or in remote locations. Depending on the success of current hot-swappable battery devices, we might see future products adopt the system. Fingers crossed that Project Helix uses them for its controllers.

Drone maker Modovolo is using quantum-inspired computing to speed up the design of its next-generation propellers. The technology, developed by quantum-accelerated simulation software company BQP, uses advanced computing methods to explore thousands of engineering designs on existing high-performance computing and GPU systems. Modovolo has integrated BQP’s BQPhy simulation platform into its engineering workflow to test a much larger number of propeller designs than traditional methods allow. The goal is to shorten the process of finding designs that can improve drone flight time and payload capacity while keeping manufacturing costs low. The companies say the approach has already been used to optimize Modovolo’s patent-pending 3D-printed propellers. Traditional computational fluid dynamics and structural analysis tools can make design optimization slow because engineers have to narrow many possible configurations into a manageable set. BQPhy’s QuantumNOW solver uses quantum-inspired algorithms on existing high-performance computing and GPU systems. BQP says this can compress tens of thousands of simulations into a fraction of the usual time and computing resources. For Modovolo, the immediate target was a set of 3D-printed propellers designed to maximize flight time and payload while keeping costs down. Thousands of designs, fewer delays. Modovolo had already built its own genetic algorithms for propeller optimization. But CEO Justin Call said traditional methods could take days to reach a single design on local servers, and some results had to be discarded when calculations became trapped in a local minimum. See All. “We have developed our own genetic algorithms for propeller optimization, which has produced some very high-efficiency designs,” Call said. “But relying on traditional optimization methods was incredibly time-intensive, due to the extremely large number of potential three-dimensional geometries for the propeller.” The challenge is not limited to the number of shapes that can be tested. Propeller blades have changing aerodynamic and structural conditions along their surfaces, creating a large design space with many variables. BQPhy is intended to let engineers examine more of them at once. CTO Arion Mangio said the platform supplied the computing capacity needed to expand that search. “BQPhy enabled us with the computational muscle, to explore an unprecedented number of design variables at once, solving our immediate performance bottlenecks and giving us a scalable engine to tackle our next generation of complex UAV systems.” From simulations to hardware. The companies say the optimization has already moved beyond computer models. Modovolo is applying the results to patent-pending, 3D-printed propellers, with the company reporting increases in flight time and payload lift capacity. That matters because Modovolo’s business model is built around performance per dollar. Its Lift drone is designed to carry payloads while keeping operating costs below competing systems. Faster optimization could let the company iterate on hardware more frequently without a matching increase in engineering time. The BQP-Modovolo work also illustrates a broader shift in engineering software. Quantum-inspired systems do not require a quantum computer to run; BQPhy is designed to operate on infrastructure manufacturers already use. That makes the technology easier to test in existing development pipelines. BQP and Modovolo are both part of the NY Ventures portfolio, linking the project to New York’s advanced-manufacturing ecosystem. For Modovolo, the immediate benefit is a faster way to search for better propellers. For BQP, the project shows how its simulation technology can be applied to physical engineering.

The addition expands the range of sensor suppliers able to connect to NVIDIA’s DRIVE hardware and software stack, according to company statements. DRIVE Hyperion is a production-ready autonomous vehicle computing architecture, and DRIVE AGX Thor is among the centralized computers used in the platform, according to reports [1][2]. NVIDIA’s sensor-processing approach also aligns with open standards such as OpenVX, which is used for performance-optimized computer vision in advanced driver-assistance systems, according to the book Embedded Vision: An Introduction [5]. The sensor is intended for use cases including advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving, and broader physical AI applications, the report stated [3]. Radar transmits an electronic signal that bounces off objects and returns to the receiver, according to Embedded Vision: An Introduction [6]. Pre-trained neural networks are used in self-driving systems to detect pedestrians, vehicles, and traffic lights, including their color, according to Hands-On Vision and Behavior for Self-Driving Cars [7]. The Uber partnership is intended to support scaling of its global autonomous fleet to 100,000 vehicles over time, starting in 2027, according to an earlier report [12]. The Apollo integration follows that open-platform approach, according to the companies. No customers using the integrated Apollo and DRIVE platform were named in the initial release. Replit CEO Amjad Masad says AI is making software engineering at his company more cerebral and fun. That's a surprising take, given the widespread concern about the so-called "SaaSpocalypse" and fears that AI is replacing coding jobs at software companies. Speaking on tech journalist Casey Newton's podcast, Masad said coding agents have changed the day-to-day environment at his company, freeing up engineers for more imaginative tasks. "You are trying a lot of things, you are ideating very quickly," Masad said. "Two years ago, everyone is hands on keyboard, you hear clicking all the time." "Now, actually, it's a lot more vibrant environment," he added. Others, too, have scoffed at the idea that AI could spell the end of the software industry. Jared Spataro, a Microsoft executive overseeing marketing for AI-powered workplace tools, earlier told Business Insider that he thinks that "the rumors of the demise of enterprise software are greatly exaggerated." Investors, meanwhile, have not been so buoyant. The notion that AI could let companies build their own software — instead of contracting the work out to dedicated software builders, like Microsoft — rattled the markets earlier this year. Software engineers themselves have said that coding with AI, while more efficient, quickly leads to burnout, and at least a dozen major companies have laid off workers, citing AI as a reason. This summer, Meta laid off nearly 1,000 software engineers. Mark Zuckerberg, however, attributed the cuts to the need to offset AI spending rather than to automation itself. Masad said that Replit, an integrated coding environment he cofounded in 2016, reached an inflection point in 2025 when Anthropic began releasing its Opus models. The models could write code more effectively than earlier ones. "My entire life mission around teaching people coding and making coding easier is changing," Masad recalled thinking at the time. "Everything that I work toward is kind of moot." Masad said Replit adapted by shifting its mission from teaching people how to code to making coding as easy as possible. The company built an AI agent to build programs from requests made in plain English, a process now known as vibe coding. Now, he said, Replit's engineers spend more time at the whiteboard, taking occasional breaks to send the next prompt to an AI agent. "You create a culture where it's fun to build things," Masad said. "You create a culture where it's not intense all the time."

The article argues that students heading into a new school term, especially computer science majors, should turn an old PC into a home lab. A home lab is better suited to certain tasks than a phone or laptop, and having one from day one means being ready for whatever comes up. Beyond running personal stacks, a home lab can be valuable for completing a CS major and can make college life easier to manage. Virtualization platforms like Proxmox are especially useful for anyone planning a career in system administration or DevOps. A job isn't guaranteed by graduation, but the hands-on experience is something even the best college likely won't match. Proxmox lets users launch many self-hosted, isolated virtual machines (VMs) and Linux containers (LXCs), and it is also good for learning and experimenting with software-defined networking (SDN) and distributed storage. Running a hypervisor as the home lab can provide an all-encompassing platform for almost everything needed in a CS major, and it may help with other subjects too. Kubernetes is described as king of learning for DevOps. K8s may be overkill for most home labs, but it is excellent for tinkering with workload scaling, rollbacks, and JSON scripting. Tools like Terraform and Ansible can also be tried, all through something like Proxmox. A home lab can also save money, since it can be built from parts already owned. A PC that is gathering dust or not needed during term can be reused. Before migrating to a dedicated setup, things can get messy: Python environments everywhere, games installed alongside code compilers, and projects spread across multiple drives. A hypervisor like Proxmox can replace the existing OS and provide a solid foundation for learning. The author says he wishes he'd had this in college, when he used a Windows 98 dev machine that later moved to Windows XP. A home lab can help with life management too. Students start accumulating expenses, paying taxes, and shopping for groceries, all alongside studying and social activities. Rather than tracking outgoings in a spreadsheet, a student could self-host an app that handles finances, groceries, taxes, and more. If no suitable app exists, Proxmox allows experimenting with building one. Powerful hardware isn't required. Compact mini PCs with an Intel N100 processor or single-board computers like the Raspberry Pi can run entire stacks, and a standard mid-tower gaming PC with a dedicated GPU and decent modern CPU works well. Proxmox runs on almost any system from the last decade or so. The author has run it flawlessly on a micro PC with an Intel Core i5-12100, a 1U server with an old Xeon, and an AMD Threadripper. Even Kubernetes can run on a single node for experimentation. An old laptop also works, though users going the used enterprise gear route should watch power draw, as such hardware can use considerable electricity when running 24/7, which is probably how Proxmox, scripts, and containers should be run.

China-based Hwatsing Technology has taken a significant step forward in electronics manufacturing by advancing wafer polishing, aiming to reduce reliance on foreign supply chains. Chinese chip developers continue to enhance their technical capabilities, achieving a new breakthrough in wafer polishing. Wafer polishing, also known as chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), is a manufacturing process that uses chemical reactions and mechanical abrasion to make semiconductor silicon discs ultra-smooth and flat. Manufacturers print, etch, and construct thousands of microscopic integrated circuits and transistors onto a single wafer before slicing it into individual microchips. The wafer serves as the base, or substrate, for producing integrated circuits, microchips, and other microdevices. As China’s top producer of semiconductor production equipment, Hwatsing Technology announced a new metrology system paired with chemical mechanical polishing equipment for six-inch wafers – a first for the country. A critical step in electronics manufacturing has made measurable progress. On Thursday, the partially state-owned Chinese company Hwatsing Technology announced an innovation in semiconductor manufacturing. The industry still depends on foreign suppliers for these complex processes. As the South China Morning Post notes, turning “a raw wafer into a finished chip requires multiple steps, including coating the surface with photoresist, etching intricate layers, and wiring microscopic transistors.” See All. In practice, wafers must move between separate polishing machines and inspection systems, which slows down production. The company’s new six-inch metrology system provides real-time measurements before and after polishing. It transmits live data to the control system to enable defect detection and ensure consistent output quality. With this integrated innovation, the company aims to improve wafer uniformity and reduce waste, addressing key production challenges. Because even a microscopic impurity can ruin an entire batch of chips, the manufacturing environment must be cleaner than an operating room. The company intends to target chips used in “power devices, microelectromechanical systems and sensors, mostly with mature processing nodes. Such devices are widely used in electric vehicles, industrial equipment, consumer electronics and telecommunications infrastructure,” according to the South China Morning Post. Could this development shift the global market in China’s favor? Verified Market Research describes the Silicon Wafers Market as a specialized, high-technology industry that supplies the essential “blank canvas” for the digital world. The South China Morning Post referenced the “advanced bottlenecks” that typically capture the world’s attention, such as EUV, or Extreme Ultraviolet lithography. ASML, a Dutch company, has a 100% global monopoly on manufacturing these machines. However, domestic companies such as Hwatsing are developing solutions for semiconductor processes like etching, chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), wafer polishing, and nascent immersion DUV systems. Some believe this could shift the global market, while others argue that “progress remains constrained in lithography,” a field dominated by ASML, which is currently barred from selling its most advanced systems to China. While these improvements enhance factory systems and reduce waste, wafers are just one piece of the geopolitical puzzle. As Santiago and Company concluded, “the primary bottleneck has shifted from wafer fabrication to physical integration.” Though Hwatsing remains the “undisputed leader,” according to the South China Morning Post, “the self-sufficiency rate for wafer metrology and inspection tools” doesn’t quite measure up—not yet, at least.

The author wanted to move notes and projects out of Notion's cloud and tested dozens of self-hosted alternatives for a similar experience with full data control. Some felt unfinished or too complicated, while a few impressed, and four stood out. AFFiNE was the closest to Notion. Its familiar interface made it easy to create pages, organize notes, build databases, and manage projects. It also includes a built-in whiteboard for visual brainstorming and planning, which worked surprisingly well alongside documents. Running it on the author's own server with Docker was straightforward. It is still under active development, so a few features are missing and there are occasional rough edges. It is an open-source, local-first workspace combining documents, whiteboards, databases, and AI. SiYuan does not copy Notion but offers many ways to organize and connect notes. It supports block-based editing, bidirectional links, backlinks, outlines, databases, and embedded content, plus document, outline, and graph views, daily notes, powerful search, and Markdown. Navigation stayed quick even with large note collections. Docker setup was simple and data stayed on the author's server. Its interface felt more overwhelming than AFFiNE's because of the number of features, but the workflow made sense with time. It is an open-source, privacy-focused personal knowledge management system and one of the most capable options for users who want more than basic note-taking. Docmost is not an all-in-one workspace; it focuses on team documentation such as internal wikis, knowledge bases, and documentation portals. Its clean editor supports Markdown, tables, code blocks, embeds, and rich formatting. It offers nested pages, spaces for different teams or projects, version history, and fast built-in search, along with comments and user management that suit teams better than many self-hosted note apps. The author found it the best self-hosted choice for team documentation. Outline was among the simplest tools tested, offering a fast, clean, collaborative, distraction-free writing experience. It supports nested documents, collections, Markdown, slash commands, rich-text formatting, embeds, and powerful search, with comments, version history, and permission controls for shared documentation. It feels responsive and closer to modern SaaS apps than many self-hosted alternatives. The author concludes that no single app is perfect for everyone, since each serves a different need, whether a personal knowledge base, a collaborative workspace, or a documentation platform, so it is worth trying a few. Most of these projects are free, easy to self-host with Docker, and actively improving, making them a good starting point for leaving Notion while keeping control of your data.

If you want quantum computing exposure without betting the farm on a pre‑profit science project, I think a case is building that Microsoft is the more interesting option right now. Microsoft is a $3 trillion AI stock whose own quantum roadmap has matured quietly in the background, and with sentiment cooled after a year of worry about AI spending, you’re getting that quantum upside at what looks like a multiyear valuation low instead of peak euphoria. Microsoft is already a quantum platform. Microsoft doesn’t market itself as a quantum stock, but its Azure Quantum materials read like a company that has spent years building a full stack. Azure Quantum is a cloud service where developers can run quantum programs today on hardware from partners such as IonQ, Rigetti, Quantinuum, and Pasqal, or on advanced simulators, using the same Azure environment they use for AI and high-performance computing. That matters. Quantum is not off in a lab. It’s already being wired into Microsoft’s mainstream developer tools and cloud workflows. In its quantum overview, Microsoft describes Azure Quantum as an “open, flexible, and future-proofed path” that adapts to how customers actually work. The company is effectively acting as the orchestrator, sitting between enterprise demand and multiple hardware providers. That is a very different position from a single hardware vendor trying to persuade the world to come and build on its island. Azure Quantum Elements and the long game. The part that really shifts the story for me is Azure Quantum Elements. In 2023, Microsoft announced this system with a bold goal: Compress 250 years of chemistry and materials science progress into the next 25. Quantum Elements combines Azure high-performance computing, AI models from the AI4Science team, and quantum capabilities to let scientists search a vastly larger design space for new materials and molecules than classical tools alone can handle. In its own words, Microsoft talks about speeding up some chemistry simulations by factors in the hundreds of thousands and expanding candidate materials from thousands to tens of millions. Customers are already using this stack to reshape their research pipelines today while preparing for scaled quantum hardware later. That is exactly the kind of “earn while you learn” model you want as an investor. The company now makes money from AI and high-performance computing while building the bridge to a future quantum supercomputer. Why this looks different from pure plays. Contrast that with the pure-play names. IonQ’s latest investor materials outline a roadmap to multimillion-qubit systems by 2030 and highlight its position as a full-stack quantum platform spanning computing, networking, and sensing. Rigetti is focused on superconducting hardware, touting a 108-qubit processor available through Amazon Braket and a letter of intent for up to $100 million in U.S. government funding. D Wave is selling a 4,400-plus-qubit Advantage2 annealing system, emphasizing connectivity, coherence, and energy-efficient processing for optimization and materials use cases. These companies are pushing the frontier and deserve credit for it. They are also, by design, narrow bets. Revenue is still modest, funding is lumpy, and their fortunes depend heavily on how quickly quantum workloads move from pilots to production. If you get the timing wrong, you’re exposed to both technology risk and capital markets risk. With Microsoft, quantum is one pillar inside a much broader AI and cloud story. Azure Quantum rides on top of a business that already generates massive cash flows from AI, cloud infrastructure, and software, and that can fund long-duration R&D in topological qubits without betting the company. If the quantum timeline slips, you’ll still be a leader in AI and cloud. If the timeline holds and Microsoft’s qubit approach works, you’re suddenly holding a stock that controls both the classical and quantum rails of the next computing era. To me, the practical takeaway is simple. If you want exposure to quantum, but you also care deeply about downside protection, Microsoft offers a more balanced way in than IonQ, Rigetti, or D Wave. You get immediate participation in AI and cloud, plus optionality on quantum computing that’s already being woven into real customer workloads, all at a valuation the market has derated from its AI peak.

Uncrewed aircraft are becoming more important to militaries, and defense departments are increasingly looking to air-taxi companies for help. Beta Technologies unveiled the MV250, an autonomous hybrid-electric cargo aircraft, at the Farnborough Airshow in July. Business Insider was there to see why the company believes it could be a valuable tool for the future battlefield. Beta initially focused on civil electric aircraft. But as militaries seek new ways to move supplies amid increasingly autonomous warfare, Beta has adapted its technology for a new customer. The MV250 can take off and land vertically, fly without a pilot aboard, and carry up to a ton of cargo into dangerous areas. Here's what it's like, and why it matters. Beta Technologies is one of several firms building air taxis — electric aircraft that can take off and land vertically. These eVTOLs operate like helicopters but make very little noise. So, they wouldn't annoy residents when flying over cities. Beta is also building an electric aircraft that takes off and lands conventionally, known as a CTOL. Earlier this year, Beta deployed its all-electric ALIA CTOL aircraft during NATO Exercise Aurora 26 in Sweden. It then adapted that technology into a military aircraft, the MV250. It is a hybrid-electric aircraft that can take off vertically and fly autonomously. "Why do we all want autonomy? I'm a pilot. No pilot wants to see their job go away," said Gen. Jim McConville, a former chief of staff of the US Army and a Beta board member. "But what we want to do is give commanders the ability to go into situations at extremely high risk." For example, in Ukraine, aerial drones and ground robots are increasingly being used for logistics missions that have become too dangerous for soldiers. Ukrainian officials have said that they want machines to eventually handle 100% of battlefield logistics amid a broader push to replace humans with robotics wherever possible. Instead of carrying pilots or passengers, it can transport up to a ton of cargo. The MV250's nose opens to reveal a cargo bay capable of carrying up to 2,000 pounds of equipment, medical supplies, munitions, or other critical cargo. Beta says it can take that payload to destinations within a 250-nautical-mile tactical radius, roughly 288 miles, and return to base. Beta says hybrid-electric power means it can fly faster and farther than a helicopter. A turbogenerator developed with GE Aerospace produces electricity for the MV250's motors. As well as the 1,300-nautical-mile repositioning range — when it isn't carrying a payload — Beta says it can generate power on the ground for equipment such as radar, antennas, and other vehicles. Beta says its bonded-composite fuselage could speed up production. The MV250's fuselage is bonded together rather than held with conventional fasteners. "That allows us to make this in a panini press, basically," Clark said. "You can make it inexpensively and meet the demands of the military." Beta says manufacturing cycle times could be measured in hours rather than months. It has also designed the aircraft without gearboxes, hydraulics, or articulating rotors, systems that can add maintenance demands. During earlier military exercises with Beta's all-electric aircraft, Clark said the company sent one maintainer and one pilot — and "the maintainer was bored." Beta thinks military demand could develop faster than the air-taxi market. Beta developed the technology behind the MV250 for civilian electric aircraft, but Clark said defense customers may adopt vertical-lift technology sooner. "Near-term defense, I think, will take a pace in front of civil in vertical lift, and then civil will overtake that," he said. Defense dominated this year's Farnborough Airshow as governments are growing more concerned about security. Defense companies made up about half of the roughly 1,600 exhibitors at this year's airshow, up from the roughly 40% share they usually represent. The event drew over 140,000 visitors, a 41% increase on the last edition in 2024. The shift reflects a scramble to rearm as wars have reshaped military priorities, including the need for cheaper drones, autonomous systems, and new ways to move supplies. NATO allies have also committed to raising defense and security-related spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, after President Donald Trump pressed them to spend more.

On August 7, 2026, Levi Strauss & Co. disclosed in an SEC filing and public statement that hackers gained unauthorized access to certain corporate data by compromising three company-issued employee computers through a social engineering attack. The breach was contained shortly after discovery, with no disruption to business operations and no evidence of consumer data compromise. The company said the incident is not expected to have a material impact on its strategy, operations, financial condition, or results of operations. No ransomware, ransom demand, or extortion attempt was reported, and no hacking group has claimed responsibility. Regulatory notification was filed with the California Department of Justice, and the investigation remains ongoing. Attackers manipulated employees into taking actions that enabled access to their devices, bypassing technical controls. There is no evidence that software vulnerabilities, brute-forcing, or missing patches were involved. The attackers exfiltrated unspecified corporate information; Levi Strauss has not disclosed what was taken, who the attackers were, or what tools were used. No technical indicators of compromise, such as malicious IPs, domains, or file hashes, have been published, which limits other organizations' ability to defend proactively. Similar retail-sector incidents have involved vishing, adversary-in-the-middle phishing portals that capture credentials and MFA tokens, and automation scripts for exfiltration, but there is no direct evidence these were used here. Some industry analysts have speculated about a link to the threat actor cluster UNC6671, known for vishing campaigns against help desks and IT support staff, in which attackers impersonate internal staff, direct victims to phishing portals, and manipulate MFA enrollment to maintain access. This attribution is circumstantial, unconfirmed by Levi Strauss or law enforcement, and low-confidence. The likely attack chain, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, may include vishing (T1566.004), impersonation (T1656), MFA request generation (T1621), valid accounts (T1078), and automated exfiltration (T1020), though this is based on patterns in other incidents rather than evidence from this case. The incident fits a broader surge in social engineering attacks on retailers, including recent breaches at De Bijenkorf, Mango, The North Face, Harrods, M&S, and The Co-op. The FBI and other authorities have repeatedly warned of their growing sophistication and frequency, and CrowdStrike reports a significant rise in vishing-based intrusions and cloud-oriented eCrime in 2026, with attackers using AI tools. Recommended mitigations, by priority: critically, strict identity verification for help desk and IT support interactions, especially password resets and MFA enrollment, including multiple verification forms and out-of-band confirmation. High priority: regular security awareness training on vishing and phishing, plus least-privilege access and monitoring with alerts for unusual MFA enrollment or removal. Medium: hardening help desk procedures, possibly requiring managerial approval for high-risk account changes, and updating incident response plans. Low: threat intelligence sharing with industry peers and law enforcement.

Boom Supersonic's Overture aims to revive commercial supersonic travel with a 64–80 passenger airliner that makes financial sense, having moved past the XB-1 demonstrator, which reached supersonic speeds in 2025. The article argues the real test is whether Overture can survive the economic realities that grounded the Concorde, which was government-subsidized and prioritized prestige over profit. Boom must certify a clean-sheet airframe and its own Symphony engine simultaneously, a process that has historically taken established giants over 10 years. Orders from United Airlines, American Airlines, and Japan Airlines total 130 conditional orders and pre-orders. These are non-binding, offer little protection against delays and cost overruns, and are best seen as a strategic hedge; the airlines are not banking their fleets on a 2029 entry into service. Analysts such as Forecast International are far more skeptical than Boom's timelines. No company, including Boeing or Airbus, has simultaneously certified a clean-sheet airframe and all-new engine on such a schedule, and many expect the 2030 target to slip into the 2030s. Operationally, Boom lacks a legacy supply chain, global maintenance, repair, and overhaul network, and decades of airport ground support experience. It targets production of 33 to 66 aircraft annually amid industry-wide backlogs. It has committed to 100% sustainable aviation fuel, whose supply is currently constrained. The Airbus A380 is cited as a warning: a specialized engineering masterpiece that became a burden when demand and costs shifted. Overture risks becoming a premium asset viable only on a few long-haul routes. As a hedge, Boom is using Symphony's core technology for industrial power generation in a program called Superpower, creating a revenue stream independent of Overture flying. Against existing options, Overture's halved flight times appeal to time-poor travelers, but its narrower fuselage cannot match the space, privacy, and sleep-friendly comfort of modern premium cabins on aircraft like the Airbus A350 or Boeing 787, and the market is moving toward more luxurious suites. Overture may therefore succeed as an ultra-niche time-saving tool coexisting with subsonic travel rather than replacing it. Regulation adds constraints. In July 2026 the FAA proposed a performance-based framework for overland supersonic flight, requiring operators to prove sonic booms stay below strict overpressure limits. Airports can still restrict operations over noise, and Overture must meet increasingly stringent ICAO noise standards. The article concludes that supersonic travel is technically possible but not yet economically inevitable. The key indicator is Symphony engine testing progress, not promotional renders; success requires reliable, maintainable engines with a lower cost-per-seat-mile than the Concorde. Airlines will likely stay cautious until they see concrete certification timelines and firm operating cost data as the 2029–2030 entry-into-service target approaches. Overture would succeed only by turning supersonic travel into a repeatable, scalable business, which has never been achieved.

Archer to buy Boeing’s Wisk, two other units for nearly 20% equity stake. Archer Aviation said on Monday it would acquire Boeing’s electric aircraft firm Wisk Aero and two other units, in a deal that will give the planemaker a nearly 20% stake in the air-taxi maker. The acquisitions, which also include drone maker Insitu and airspace-services provider SkyGrid, give Archer access to Boeing’s autonomous-flight technology, potentially bolstering its position in defense and commercial logistics. Archer shares rose about 14% in morning trading. It also marks Boeing’s latest effort to streamline its portfolio and sharpen its focus on its core commercial and defense aircraft businesses, while stepping back from its air-taxi ambitions. Despite years of investment and ambitious forecasts, the electric vertical takeoff and landing, or eVTOL, sector has yet to prove that air taxis can be certified, built at scale and operated at prices attractive to everyday customers. As commercial rollouts have taken longer than expected, companies have increasingly turned to military, cargo and government markets for nearer-term revenue and funding. Wisk has been developing an autonomous electric passenger aircraft. Under the deal, Boeing and Archer will establish a collaboration and technology-sharing agreement that preserves Boeing’s access to Wisk’s core autonomous-flight technology for use in its current and future commercial and defense aircraft programs. Archer, which has yet to generate significant revenue from its core business, will gain access to Insitu, a profitable defense business that generates more than $200 million in annual revenue. “We gain the ability to start generating significant revenue immediately in a major growth market,” Archer CEO Adam Goldstein told Reuters in an interview. “Demand for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) drones is probably the highest it has ever been, creating a major opportunity for a company that is already generating revenue and cash flow.” Boeing will receive Archer shares representing 19.75% of the air-taxi company’s outstanding Class A stock prior to closing and gain the right to appoint a director to the startup’s board.

Eric Schmidt and Suhas Mahesh argue that AI for science needs reasoning, not just data, and that AI agents modeling the human research process will accelerate discovery. Claims that science is nearly finished recur every few decades: Albert Michelson said in 1903 that physical science's facts "have all been discovered," and Stephen Hawking predicted in the 1980s that theoretical physics might be done by century's end. The same feeling has returned with AI, accompanied by a Nobel. In 2024 Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind won part of the chemistry Nobel for AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures by learning from experimentally measured shapes. Its success prompted a wave of startups building foundation models for biology, chemistry and materials, raising billions of dollars. The authors say AlphaFold may not be the best template for AI in science, because the conditions behind it are rare and could take decades to replicate elsewhere. It depended on the Protein Data Bank, roughly 170,000 validated structures that took 53 years of international cooperation and an estimated $21 billion of experimental work to assemble. Even where funding and access exist, comparable data is often scientifically impossible to generate. Protein crystallography is unusually replicable, which is why over 25 Nobel Prizes have relied on it, but most experimental science varies: cell lines drift, chemicals carry contaminants, lab humidity changes. Datasets consistent, accurate, precise and scalable enough to train neural networks in biology or most of chemistry would require new measurement methods and standards. A few fields, such as weather forecasting, much of genomics and limited areas of chemistry, may see AlphaFold-style breakthroughs, and government support for such datasets will be critical, as the US National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology has argued. For most questions, the authors point to agents: AI reasoning engines, powered by large language models, with access to digital or physical tools. Scientists have always reasoned under uncertainty, combining multiple imperfect methods and weighing them by their strengths and failure points; agents can now mimic this iterative process, greatly reducing the need for specialized datasets. They model the human process of discovery rather than being a new way of doing science. As an example, Google's AI Co-Scientist, announced in May, was asked how antibiotic resistance spreads between bacterial species. Sub-agents drafted hypotheses from the literature, critiqued them, ran tournaments to rank them and refined the winner. It concluded that resistance genes hitch rides on bacterial viruses, which was correct; Imperial College London researchers had spent a decade reaching the same result in the wet lab, and their paper, unseen by Co-Scientist, was still in peer review. Agents still hallucinate, judge inconsistently and have memory and input limits, but these barriers should fall. The authors expect three effects. First, agents log every action, offering a structural fix for the reproducibility crisis. Second, they will preserve a lab's whole history in a central repository, improving scientific memory. Third, and most important, speed: an agent that reads a thousand papers in an hour and designs 500 molecules lowers experimentation costs and frees researchers to pursue bold questions. The authors compare agents to rare, field-wide tools like calculus, statistical inference, spectroscopy and the computer, and say another such transformation is under way.

The author argues that the common advice to seed more brand content into Reddit threads misreads how large language models decide whom to trust. AI models aren't loyal to Reddit; they are starved of alternatives. When ChatGPT or Perplexity leans on Reddit for recommendation queries, it's because Reddit is one of the few large, easily parsed repositories of unfiltered, first-person "I actually used this" content. An analysis of roughly 30 million cited sources by Peec AI found Reddit, YouTube and LinkedIn dominate citations because they carry real user discussion, not brand messaging. The model is really asking where it can find a real person describing what actually happened, so Reddit is a proxy for trust rather than its source. Brands chasing Reddit placement are optimizing for the symptom instead of the cause. Trust matters more in generative search because, unlike a search engine that shows 10 blue links and lets readers decide, an answer engine synthesizes a response and puts its own credibility behind it. Any brand claim it repeats without independent backing is one it personally vouches for. A product page calling a jacket "the warmest on the market" has an obvious incentive problem; a hiking forum thread describing a Colorado winter in it does not, and models are increasingly built to weigh the second kind more heavily. Google's E-E-A-T framework (experience, expertise, authoritativeness, trustworthiness), drawn from its Search Quality Rater Guidelines, is the clearest public blueprint of what "trustworthy" means to a machine. Experience matters most, since raters weigh whether a reviewer actually used the product, and trust overrides the rest. Generative AI wasn't trained on E-E-A-T as a rule book but has absorbed the same logic. Seer Interactive, studying more than half a million LLM responses across 20 brands, coined "ghost citation": a brand's own content is cited as the source, but a competitor is named as the recommendation. Their tests suggest the model first decides which brand to recommend based on what it "knows" from training, then looks for a source URL. A Semrush study of nearly 4,000 domain appearances found 62% of AI citations carry no brand mention at all, a result of weak "entity-level" presence in training data, while strong public identity brought that rate near zero in some categories. A brand can do everything right on its own site and still be invisible when it matters, because citation and recommendation aren't the same system. This also explains why AI shopping assistants hedge. When a model can't find independent accounts to back a claim, declining to commit is the safer output; confidence tracks the density of verification behind it. Brands supplying only their own marketing copy hand the model the self-interested claim it is trained to discount. Most brands already have the raw material for machine trust: years of reviews, unboxing videos, community threads and creator content. This is the "experience" layer E-E-A-T asks for, and what generative engines weigh over brand copy. Nielsen research has long shown people trust word-of-mouth over brand advertising, and that now earns machine trust for structural reasons. The conclusion is to focus on trust, not visibility. Being found and being cited are necessary but don't get a brand recommended, because a generative engine won't stake its credibility on a claim it cannot independently verify. Brands should treat trust as something demonstrated by others, not asserted by themselves.

Apple briefly published a support guide in China explaining how Mac users can connect Alibaba's Qwen AI to Siri and Writing Tools, before pulling it entirely less than a day later. Reuters first spotted the Chinese-language guide on Apple's support site on August 8, which explained how eligible Mac users in mainland China could connect Qwen, Alibaba's family of generative AI models, to Siri and Writing Tools. According to the document, the extension required macOS 26.6 or later, needed users to sign into their own Qwen account, and specified that Alibaba was barred from using submitted materials to train or improve its models. Siri would be able to lean on Qwen for more detailed responses to certain requests, including analysis of photos and documents, while Writing Tools could use it to generate text and images. No equivalent guide was published for the iPhone or iPad. The setup closely mirrors Apple's existing ChatGPT extension available elsewhere, which similarly lets Siri hand off complex requests and gives Writing Tools a "Compose" option, all on an opt-in basis. By August 9, the guide had been removed. Chinese news aggregator ReadHub reported that the guide had disappeared from Apple's site, and TechNode reports that Apple's customer service told Chinese media it had received no notification of a new feature launch. Separately, tech analyst Liu Dingding told the Global Times that the takedown could reflect pending technical adjustments still tied to the regulatory process, rather than a full reversal. It's a similar pattern to what happened back in March, when Apple Intelligence itself briefly went live for some Chinese users before being pulled offline without regulatory approval. China maintains strict rules around releasing AI features, and in practice requires companies like Apple to partner with local providers. Apple originally lined up Baidu as its primary China AI partner, but by February 2025, reports indicated Alibaba had taken over as the lead partner after Baidu's models fell short of Apple's requirements, with Baidu shifted to a supporting role. Chinese regulators cleared Apple Intelligence for launch in the country in July, registering Apple's on-device AI service with the Cyberspace Administration of China. That approval covered the iPhone only, and Apple did not say whether or when the iPad and Mac would follow, making this week's brief Mac-specific guide the clearest signal yet on the Mac timeline specifically. It remains unclear when Apple will formally relaunch the Qwen integration for the Mac, or whether the guide's brief appearance points to an imminent rollout.

A US manufacturing company has produced a drone boat using large-format robotic 3D printing, highlighting how additive manufacturing is moving into maritime and defense applications. Florida-based Haddy built the TF-179 Drone Boat by using industrial robotic arms to deposit material layer by layer, rather than relying on traditional molding or machining methods. The approach is designed to speed up production while allowing manufacturers to create and modify complex vessel designs more efficiently. The company has also used the same technology to manufacture a hull for an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) and expand production capacity for a maritime defense division. Digital drone boat. The maritime industry is undergoing a shift in how vessels are designed, developed, and manufactured, with digital production technologies opening new possibilities for specialized platforms such as the TF-179 Drone Boat. The vessel was produced using large-format robotic additive manufacturing, a process that uses industrial robotic arms to build large structures layer by layer. Unlike conventional manufacturing methods that often rely on molds, machining, or assembling multiple prefabricated components, robotic 3D printing can provide greater flexibility during the design and production process. According to Haddy, the approach can also help shorten development cycles by allowing manufacturers to rapidly produce, test, evaluate, and refine new vessel designs. This flexibility is particularly relevant for unmanned and specialized maritime systems, where requirements can change quickly and production may need to adapt to specific operational needs. See All. “As demand grows for specialized maritime platforms, manufacturing methods must evolve alongside them. The ability to rapidly produce, evaluate, and refine complex systems is becoming an increasingly important advantage,” said Haddy in a post on LinkedIn. Haddy has not revealed who commissioned the TF-179 or what mission it is designed for. However, the company’s recent work shows growing expertise in rapidly producing unmanned vessels with robotic manufacturing, as demand for small, expendable maritime drones increases across the US defense sector, reports Defence Blog. Robotic maritime manufacturing. Haddy operates from a roughly 30,000-square-foot (2,800-square-meter) facility in downtown St. Petersburg, Florida, equipped with eight large-format additive manufacturing systems from Dutch robotics company CEAD. Seven of the systems operate on rails, extending their reach to manufacture especially large components. Founded in 2022, Haddy initially focused on custom furniture, architectural elements, and molds. The company has increasingly shifted toward defense manufacturing, using robotic 3D printing to produce drone hulls and full-scale boat structures, reports Defence Blog. Haddy’s manufacturing platform combines large-format robotic 3D printing, integrated milling, advanced materials, and digital production workflows to accelerate the development of large-scale hardware. The platform is designed to produce hardware in days or weeks rather than months, while allowing designs to be updated without restarting traditional tooling cycles. It can also support production ranging from prototypes to repeatable manufacturing runs and is intended for distributed and expeditionary manufacturing models. Haddy had earlier demonstrated the platform’s speed through the production of a 12-meter low-profile USV hull. The company says the structure was produced for rapid validation, water testing, and integration of mission systems. According to Haddy, the hull went from design to shipment in 10 days, making the process up to nine times faster than traditional hull production. The company also reports that its approach can reduce costs by 50 percent to 65 percent compared with conventional boatbuilding, highlighting the potential for faster and more flexible USV manufacturing.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are changing how enterprises hunt for fraud, moving detection beyond isolated transactions to reveal entire hidden networks of bad actors. The key advance is less about faster models than about a data structure built to expose relationships that traditional systems miss. This is playing out in pharmaceutical anti-counterfeiting work, where fraud detection is a common use case for graph-powered systems, according to Thomas Luu, director of global product security at Gilead Sciences Inc. His team investigates counterfeit drugs and fraud across Gilead's global commercial business, which required converting relational data into graph form to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated schemes. "With the implementation of graph neural networks with Neo4j, we were able to really surface these hidden networks and enable us to analyze our data to a level and to a scale that was not possible before because of human limitations," Luu said. "Fraud doesn't happen with just one transaction. It happens across a lot of entities, and a lot of these entities are hidden." He spoke with theCUBE's John Furrier at the Neo4j GraphTalk event. Before adopting graph technology, Luu's team relied on manual comparison across disparate, nuanced data sets, a process that depended heavily on individual analyst expertise and struggled to scale. The team now runs a three-layer detection model: rules-based logic for known patterns, traditional machine learning for statistical anomalies, and graph neural networks for uncovering relationship-based schemes that neither of the first two layers can surface. "We don't want to just rely on one technique," Luu said. "Rules are great, ML is great, but when you combine them with GNNs and the graph layer, that's when you start seeing things you never could before." Cleaning and unifying the data set the stage for automation, letting the team apply graph neural networks and graph machine learning once the underlying data was trustworthy. The payoff extends beyond detection speed: clustering algorithms built into the graph automatically group a main fraud actor with lower-volume auxiliary players whose signals would otherwise stay buried in aggregate data. The approach also makes findings easier to explain to investigators without technical backgrounds, since relationships between nodes are visually intuitive. "I always said the best fraudsters are the ones hiding in the averages, and they're hiding amongst peers and they're concealing their activity," Luu said. "The graph relationship — it tells you exactly what it is. It's very intuitive when you look at a relationship graph or a knowledge graph."
