Once a Home Assistant setup reaches roughly 50 or more devices (smart switches, energy monitors, motion sensors), clicking an entity's history or logbook can show a loading wheel for 5 to 10 seconds. The likely culprit is not CPU, Wi-Fi latency, or dashboard cards but the default single-file SQLite database. The proposed fix is to point the Recorder integration at a dedicated PostgreSQL instance, for example running in Docker on a local NAS. This offloads storage operations, gives sub-second history graphs, allows zero-downtime backups, and makes the system much more responsive. SQLite struggles at scale because of its architecture. It stores the entire state history in one flat file, so write-heavy activity such as power meters logging wattage every second causes lock contention that blocks reads when you render a history graph. It also has high overhead for frequent data manipulation operations: hundreds of inserts per minute back up the write queue. There is a hardware cost too, since continuous unbuffered state logging to an SD card, eMMC flash, or budget SSD on a Raspberry Pi or mini PC causes excessive wear and can lead to drive failure or database corruption during power outages. Clean SQLite backups often require stopping Home Assistant or disabling the recorder to avoid copying an active, locked file. PostgreSQL addresses these problems. Its multi-version concurrency control allows simultaneous reads and writes without blocking queries, so hundreds of sensors can write in the background while history dashboards render instantly. Running it on a secondary host, such as a NAS with NVMe caching or a homelab server, decouples I/O and compute, so the Home Assistant host's CPU and primary drive no longer suffer database disk thrashing. Scheduled, compressed database dumps can run 24/7 without stopping Home Assistant or pausing the event log. It also opens the door to external tools such as Grafana, Metabase, or the TimescaleDB extension for deep time-series analysis without affecting Home Assistant's runtime. Implementation has four steps. First, deploy PostgreSQL via Docker Compose, a dedicated NAS container, or the official Home Assistant add-on store. Second, create a database user and database with commands like CREATE USER homeassistant WITH PASSWORD 'YourSecurePassword'; and CREATE DATABASE homeassistant_db WITH OWNER homeassistant ENCODING 'utf8';. Third, update configuration.yaml so the recorder integration uses a db_url of postgresql://homeassistant:YourSecurePassword@POSTGRES_IP:5432/homeassistant_db, with purge_keep_days set to 10. Fourth, choose a migration strategy: start completely fresh or use pgloader. Home Assistant's default configuration is designed for frictionless, zero-configuration onboarding, but power users with growing entity lists quickly outgrow single-file databases. If you have 50 or more devices and notice lag, especially slow history graphs, spinning up a PostgreSQL instance and updating the recorder config should produce an immediate improvement.

Lyft (LYFT) reported a better-than-expected second quarter, with active riders passing 30 million for the first time and record gross bookings of $5.5 billion, up 23% year over year. Revenue rose 16% to $1.8 billion, and net income increased to $50.3 million from $40.3 million. Adjusted EBITDA grew 37% to $177.2 million, with the margin on gross bookings improving to 3.2% from 2.9%. Free cash flow was $319.6 million for the quarter and $1.1 billion over the last 12 months. Operationally, active riders rose 17% to a record 30.5 million, the seventh straight quarter of double-digit growth, and total rides rose 12% to a record 262 million. About 30% of North American rideshare rides are now tied to partnerships, an all-time high. That partner strategy may matter more as autonomous vehicles (AVs) develop. Lyft launched a fleet operation with Waymo in Nashville in June, plans an 80,000-square-foot AV depot there in October, and is extending its partnership with Curb into New York City. For the third quarter, Lyft guided gross bookings of $5.50 billion to $5.67 billion, roughly 15% to 19% growth, and adjusted EBITDA of $183 million to $203 million, with a margin of about 3.3% to 3.6%. The stock has risen to its highest level in six months, up about 5.37% over the last five trading days and 39.7% from its 52-week low of $12.46, but it remains about 31.2% below its 52-week high of $25.54. Market capitalization is $6.63 billion. Valuation is modest, at roughly 0.98 times price-to-sales, 23.62 times forward earnings, and a price-to-earnings-to-growth ratio of 0.97. The article attributes this to uncertainty over competition and AVs: analysts are split between viewing Lyft's partner approach as an advantage and viewing its smaller size as a vulnerability relative to Uber (UBER). Analyst reactions reflect that split. RBC's Brad Erickson kept an "Outperform" rating and raised his target from $18 to $20, citing a richer ride mix of partner rides, airport trips and higher-value transportation, and noting negative sentiment toward ridesharing despite its growth. Oppenheimer's Chad Larkin kept "Outperform" and a $20 target, noting the stock trades at about six times projected 2027 EBITDA and that better execution could cause short positions to unwind. BofA Securities' Justin Post raised his target from $17 to $18 but kept "Underperform," arguing the AV debate will matter more than earnings near term and favoring Uber for its scale and stronger balance sheet, though acknowledging Lyft could become a good AV distribution partner. Wells Fargo stayed at "Equal Weight" with a $19 target, citing higher prices and reliance on consumer incentives to drive demand. The consensus rating is "Moderate Buy," with a mean target of $19.33, implying 11.5% upside. The street-high target of $30 implies 73% upside over 12 months.

The author set out to replace a growing pile of note apps, and their subscription bills, with one tool that wants neither a subscription nor their data, and found it in SiYuan. SiYuan is an open-source, self-hosted knowledge management app that runs in Docker. The author went from pulling the image to having it open in a browser at localhost in about five minutes. A desktop app is available for those who want to skip the container. It uses Notion-style block-based editing, with a slash menu, headings, templates, embeds, databases and an AI assistant. Every block has a permanent ID, so a paragraph from one document can be referenced or embedded in another, and those references survive restructuring. Notion's synced blocks, by contrast, are tied to page structure and tend to break after big reorganizations. The author keeps a daily log, uses bidirectional links that work locally without a sync subscription, and has a global graph view similar to Obsidian's. Because it is self-hosted, everything stays on the author's PC with no account attached, and nothing leaves the container unless exported (options include Markdown). SiYuan's paid tier covers only its hosted sync, which the author doesn't need. The author discovered a built-in spaced-repetition feature while browsing the block menu, where a "Flashcard" option sits. You highlight the part of a block to hide as the answer and add the block to a deck. It uses FSRS, the same modern algorithm Anki recently adopted, running against the author's actual notes. Anki is free on desktop and Android, but its official iOS app costs $25, a paywall to using one deck across devices. SiYuan avoids that because it runs on the author's own server, and the flashcard block remains part of the original document. The author mainly uses it for design terminology they repeatedly re-look-up, which they say is a light load but enough to replace dedicated paid tools like Anki. For saving reading material, the author had abandoned Evernote after its free version became heavily restricted, effectively a demo, and fell back on browser bookmarks. SiYuan's official browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox clips the current page into a chosen notebook as an editable document made of regular blocks, which can be annotated or reused in other writing. PDFs can be dropped into a document and marked up, and the highlights become linkable references usable in other documents. The author notes Evernote locks that feature behind its Advanced plan at $249 a year, while SiYuan provides it for the cost of running Docker. The author concedes SiYuan is not a perfect one-for-one replacement: people deeply invested in Notion databases or with years of Anki decks will miss things. But the subscriptions mostly covered tasks that can be done in one place, on their own machine, for free.

Apple may introduce a photo authentication tool in iOS 27. Reference Image could be a new way to prove provenance in the wake of generative AI. We're looking forward to seeing the new artificial intelligence side of Siri when iOS 27 launches, but it appears that Apple may have additional tools in the works. In its analysis of the latest operating system beta, 9to5Mac noticed some signals that Apple might be working on a photo authentication feature. Apple Reference Image appears to be a tool that will verify that a photo was taken with an iPhone camera. To confirm that a photo is an iPhone capture, select sensor information and metadata for an image can be sent to Private Cloud Compute for verification. A new Reference mode will need to be enabled on an iPhone's camera in order for this authentication option to be available. Resources for checking an image's source in this age of AI slop is more critical than ever. Thus far, most of the tools involve putting a digital watermark onto generative AI creations, such as those in Apple's Image Playground and its other forthcoming image editing capabilities. Google also continues to expand its SynthID AI watermarking program. This approach of Reference Image to create confirmation of content's provenance could be a useful counterpart to those metadata watermarking efforts. Since all this is happening in an ongoing beta test, however, it's possible that Reference Image won't be included when iOS 27 does have its public rollout this fall.

Digital Science has launched two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for its Dimensions research platform, giving enterprise AI agents direct, license-aligned access to a large, interconnected database of scientific and technological information. The aim is to let AI systems retrieve and analyze current research data instead of relying only on general-purpose models whose training data may be outdated, incomplete, or hard to verify. The two systems are the Dimensions Semantic Search MCP and the Dimensions Analytics MCP. The semantic search service is built for precision retrieval across more than 40 life science domains. The analytics service connects agents to more than 430 million linked records covering publications, grants, patents, clinical trials, datasets, and policy documents. Together they combine detailed evidence retrieval with large-scale mapping of the research landscape. MCP is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to external tools and structured data sources. Rather than answering from internal parameters alone, an MCP-enabled agent can query an authorized data service, receive relevant records, and build a response from them. This can improve traceability and reduce the risk of plausible but unsupported claims. Because language models may not know about recent findings, new grants, emerging patent activity, or clinical developments, live database access lets agents retrieve information when needed. Existing Dimensions API customers can use the integrations without an additional license, according to Digital Science. The Semantic Search MCP searches by meaning rather than exact word matching. Keyword systems can miss relevant documents when terminology, abbreviations, chemical names, or disease classifications differ. The semantic system uses domain ontologies, structured representations of scientific terms and their connections, to find related evidence across publications, patents, grants, and clinical trials. For example, a search for "PFAS" could surface related substances such as PFOS, PFOA, and PFHxS, rather than only documents containing the exact abbreviation. The process maps terms to concepts, recognizes hierarchical and associative relationships, and retrieves passages, potentially at the section level of individual documents. Possible uses include drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, medical affairs, biotechnology, and regulatory intelligence, such as reviewing safety signals, tracing drug–disease associations, and monitoring therapeutic pipelines. The Analytics MCP links research outputs with the people, organizations, funding sources, and intellectual property tied to them. An enterprise agent could compare competitors in a therapeutic area, identify leading investigators, examine funder activity, or track trends across regions and technology sectors. Because record types are connected, a query can move from a publication to its authors, institutions, grants, patents, and related clinical trials without consulting multiple disconnected systems. Digital Science says the integrations are compatible with major AI platforms including Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, and work within existing enterprise workflows without custom integration. Research and development teams could use agents for competitive landscape analysis, funding intelligence, technology-transfer scouting, or horizon scanning using structured, verifiable records. Sebastian Schmidt, executive vice president of Enterprise at Digital Science, described the servers as a bridge between AI and authoritative research intelligence. Peter Haase, vice president of Knowledge Graph Technologies, said semantic retrieval lets systems search scientific concepts rather than depending on users to predict every relevant term. The launch reflects a broader shift toward connected AI agents that retrieve, interpret, and analyze live evidence. With appropriate licensing, provenance controls, and human oversight, such connections could speed access to research intelligence while keeping a clearer link between AI-generated conclusions and their supporting data.

Modern agriculture is high tech, and some of the same technology behind smartphone location services and car navigation is used to reduce waste and costs while boosting harvests. Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) is a generic term for related technologies including the U.S.-developed Global Positioning System (GPS). According to NASA, it can pinpoint a three-dimensional position to meter-level accuracy and time to the 10-nanosecond level, worldwide and 24/7, enabled by at least 24 orbiting satellites. Eric Shuman, head of global precision technology product management at CNH (owner of Case IH, New Holland and STEYR), said GNSS can determine a tractor's exact position in a field. Combined with automatic steering, GNSS-guided equipment helps farmers reduce overlap, avoid unnecessary passes and place inputs more accurately. More precise application of seed, fertilizer, crop protection products and other inputs can reduce waste and over-application, lower fuel consumption and improve field efficiency. Fewer tractor passes also mean less soil damage. Because many crops are planted in tight rows, guidance must be precise. Jason Blanchette, product manager of StarFire and AutoTrac at John Deere, noted that standard GNSS, like phone GPS, is typically accurate within a few feet, but in agriculture a few inches of error can mean seeds planted in the wrong place or spacing, emerging crops driven over, or an area sprayed twice while another is missed. Real-time kinematics (RTK), which uses data from a fixed base station, delivers centimeter-level precision. Shuman said it keeps equipment within 1.5 cm between each pass and within 2.5 cm repeating season after season. Blanchette said RTK with automated steering gives consistency and repeatability over hundreds or thousands of acres, letting farmers return to the same planting lines year after year, though lines can be adjusted. RTK can also be combined with field data on soil types, moisture, elevation and previous harvest results to fine-tune planting by section: fertile areas may get more seeds to maximize yield, while sandy, wet or less productive areas get fewer. The technology works at any scale. Kaleb Rulon, strategic marketing specialist at PTx, a division of AGCO, said operators of smaller, irregularly shaped fields worry about skips and overlaps in curved headlands, while those on large fields, such as in Kansas, worry about field efficiency and operator fatigue. The biggest gains come in large fields with long, repetitive passes. In Europe, where fields are smaller and more specialty items are grown, cost per acre is much higher, making it even more important to avoid running over standing crops and to place inputs exactly. Satellite-guided, self-steering tractors are far more precise than human operators, which can prevent double planting and driving over crops, reduce fertilizer and pesticide use, save time and raise yields. Rulon said several studies show fuel consumption can fall by 5-6% or more in typical operations. The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates U.S. farms spent $15.4 billion on fuel in 2024, so a 5% saving equals $770 million.

Researchers at the University of Birmingham and the security firm Fuzzware showed that a malicious SIM card can order the device it sits in to run commands of the attacker's choosing, which on cellular modules in EV chargers, industrial routers and car telematics units is enough to take the device over. Of 26 phones and modules tested, 9 accepted the command: six of eight modules and only 3 of 18 phones (the OPPO Find X5, OPPO Reno 14 F 5G and ASUS Zenfone 9). No iPhone or Pixel was affected. Five of the six modules were Quectel parts, three pulled from an EV charger, an industrial router and a car's telematics unit. The command is RUN AT, a standardised proactive command that makes the modem execute an AT command, effectively giving the card a general-purpose console. Marius Muench of Birmingham frames this as compliant with the standard rather than a break from it, so individual bugs can be patched but switching the interface off is each vendor's decision. Most modules also run a small application processor, usually Android on an ARM Cortex-A7, behind the radio, which the paper presented at USENIX WOOT in Baltimore calls "a rich attack surface to hostile SIMs." Attacks require a hostile card already in the slot, whether swapped by hand, inserted as an interposer, pushed by a compromised operator, or subverted in software or production. Unattended IoT gear is the likeliest target. On a commercial Autel EV charger (MAXI US AC W12-L-4G), the Quectel EC25AFXDGA module's atfwd_daemon passes attacker-controlled text into a shell call through an unsafe format string; a newline slipped past a character blocklist, yielding code execution driven entirely by SIM commands. On the OPPO Reno 14 F 5G, AT+COPS=0,,,0 pinned the phone to 2G, which lacks mutual authentication, and the owner could not reverse it by any settings change; other commands powered it down or shut off the modem. The team's tool, CATana, found 198 AT commands reachable through the SIM on that handset. A third case read arbitrary files off a Quectel EG25-G via a root TFTP daemon that does not check symbolic links, though that needs a malicious link placed on the filesystem first. Earlier work showed a hostile SIM could make a locked Android phone open a web page; Google patched that as CVE-2025-48618 in December 2025. All nine affected devices use a Qualcomm communication processor, though five other Qualcomm-based handsets did not accept the command, possibly due to vendor customisation. Qualcomm has built a hardened configuration that disables the interface by default and will be the default on future devices. Quectel says it mitigated the file-access flaw and is still working on the interface. Muench believes all Quectel EC25, EG25 and RM52xN modules are affected and others likely are. Quectel does not release firmware publicly, making exposure hard to verify, and no one has counted affected units. Reports went to Google, Oppo, Quectel, Semtech and Qualcomm in March 2026 and to the GSMA in May. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-57550 and CVD-2026-0122. Oppo and Google deemed it outside bug bounty scope; Semtech plans Qualcomm-written patches. As of August 10, no vendor had published an advisory and no exploitation had been reported. Fleet operators should ask suppliers whether RUN AT is enabled and can be disabled.

The Air Force spends billions of dollars each year sustaining its aircraft fleet, but maintenance has been mired in delays, depot backlogs, and shortages of workers and spare parts. To speed visual inspections, the service is turning to drones and robotics. Last month, Asylon, a provider of autonomous robotic platforms, announced a Phase Three contract with the Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex in Georgia. Joe Costa, a former senior Pentagon official now with the Atlantic Council, said maintenance backlogs already exist in peacetime and that wartime demand adds to them. Three Air Force depots, known as air logistics complexes, maintain aircraft such as the F-16, F-35, KC-135, and C-130: Ogden ALC in Utah, Oklahoma City ALC in Oklahoma, and Warner Robins ALC in Georgia. A recent Government Accountability Office report found that the share of aircraft maintenance delayed past original target dates rose from 31% in fiscal 2019 to 73% in fiscal 2024. Delays beyond revised target dates grew from 19% to 34% of aircraft over the same period. The depots have tried to fix staffing shortages caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, retirements, and resignations, but struggle to compete with higher private-sector pay. Diana Maurer of the GAO's Defense Capabilities and Management team said drones and robotics are worth exploring given the shortage of trained maintainers, though "the proof is going to be in the pudding." Under the agreement, Asylon will deploy its Guardian small drone and DroneDog Q-UGV, using its Range autonomy stack to navigate indoor hangars and DroneIQ software for command-and-control and data visualization. The DroneDog scans the underside of an aircraft while the drone scans the top, and the data is merged into one platform so airmen can decide on repairs. CEO and co-founder Damon Henry said this avoids building scaffolding for airmen to climb atop aircraft like the C-5, a safety concern, by automating data collection. The robots look for loose fasteners, dings, dents, corrosion, chipped paint, and anything that could cause damage in flight. One Guardian and one DroneDog can scan an entire aircraft, and the company aims for a full inspection in hours, versus days for people today. Henry said the technology could expand to other services' aircraft, commercial aircraft, warships, and facilities and buildings. The war in Iran adds urgency, since damaged systems will stress the depots when they return. A Congressional Research Service report from May says the Air Force has lost or damaged more than 40 manned and unmanned aircraft. Losses include four F-15Es (three shot down accidentally by Kuwait, one by Iran), an A-10, an E-3 Sentry, and about two dozen MQ-9 Reapers, while one F-35A was damaged and seven KC-135s were damaged or destroyed. Maurer noted that battle damage repairs are especially time-consuming and costly, and that AI, drones, and robotics could eventually help, though it is up to the Air Force whether to try new tools on a critical need. Nearly half the fleet is over 40 years old, and more than 60% of aircraft are over 30.

Investors have put hundreds of billions of dollars into autonomous vehicles over the past decade, and commercial robotaxis now carry paying passengers in multiple cities. The author, George Kalligeros, argues the next major opportunity may be the physical infrastructure needed to keep millions of such vehicles running, and the commercial real estate beneath it. He points to historical precedents: railroads created freight terminals, aviation created airports, mobile communications created cell towers, and cloud computing created data centers. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts the global commercial robotaxi fleet could grow from roughly 7,000 vehicles in 2024 to about 6 million by 2035, generating roughly $415 billion in annual revenue. Such a fleet would need a large physical network for charging, cleaning, inspection, tire service and maintenance. Kalligeros rejects the assumption that this will mean large, permanent depots on cheap land. Instead, infrastructure will need to minimize time and mileage vehicles spend out of revenue-generating operation. A study of California robotaxi operations, which analyzed more than 86 million Waymo miles across nearly 14 million commercial trips, found about 46% of mileage was driven without a passenger. Not all of this is avoidable, but at fleet scale each eliminated mile matters. This makes autonomous transportation a real estate story. Parking garages, lots, petrol stations, service centers and dealerships built for human-owned cars could become a distributed operating network for shared autonomous fleets. The key trait is centrality: a site inside or near a robotaxi operating zone offers proximity to revenue, valued by the minutes and miles it removes from servicing. A small, well-placed site could be worth more than a large distant one. Safety will determine how fast the market develops. Waymo reports that across more than 220 million fully autonomous miles, its vehicles had 94% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury or worse and 82% fewer injury-causing crashes than comparable human drivers, though these results come from one operator and will keep being tested. Kalligeros also questions whether early infrastructure should be permanent. Robotaxi networks are young, and demand, fleet density and regulations will shift, so permanent facilities risk being stranded. Portable, quickly deployable infrastructure lets operators and property owners learn before committing capital, and some locations will later justify fixed facilities. He argues the infrastructure opportunity is attractive because it doesn't require betting on which autonomy company wins; a fleet-neutral network could serve multiple platforms, like cell towers serving multiple carriers. Property owners could supply locations, infrastructure investors could finance deployment, private credit could fund equipment, and fleet operators could provide recurring utilization. His prediction is that within a decade, some of the most valuable autonomous-vehicle assets will be ordinary urban real estate that became indispensable nodes in the operating network. Kalligeros is co-founder and CEO of Aseon Labs, which builds distributed robotic pit stop infrastructure for autonomous fleets and has raised $10 million in seed funding. He previously co-founded Pushme, a battery-swapping network for shared e-scooters and e-bikes, later acquired by TIER-Dott.

Tons of aid from regional partners began arriving in Colombia on Wednesday as the search for survivors grew more desperate after a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck the country's west on Monday, razing buildings, buckling roads and crushing cars. The disaster has tested new president Abelardo de la Espriella's government and civil society groups providing aid. De la Espriella said Wednesday evening that at least 265 people died and nearly 500 were reported missing, though civilian-run databases put the missing at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families were affected. "Our efforts are focused on the disappeared," he said. Teams continued searching rubble in the hardest-hit cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo. Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours crucial for finding survivors, though that window can extend if trapped people have food and water. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder said rescuers continue to find signs of life under the debris and that "the next 20 hours are the most critical." In Pereira, rescuers pulled Daniela Largo alive late Tuesday after a 12-hour operation, while another man was pulled lifeless from a building in the same city. In the coffee-growing region, authorities have turned sports arenas, schools and public buildings into shelters for thousands of displaced people. In Pereira and Cali, families sleep in parks, some fearing aftershocks or building collapses, others with no homes to return to. Colombia's geological service has documented 130 aftershocks. Seismologist Rodrigo León Loya said a similar-magnitude quake in the same area is unlikely but more seismic activity cannot be ruled out, since Colombia is full of active fault lines. The response has been complicated in the epicenter region, Choco, by deep poverty and decades of civil conflict and forced displacement. The quake's true impact in the jungled northwest remains largely unknown because cell service is down and many communities are remote and reachable only by river. Giovanni Rizzo of the Norwegian Refugee Council said the earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation. Many aid groups were already in Choco supporting the 2016 peace accord and responding to violence by armed groups, and were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief, according to U.N. resident coordinator María José Torres. International aid is arriving. The U.S. State Department said disaster response teams began arriving Monday, and the U.S. offered over $15 million. Mexico sent two military aircraft carrying 19.5 tons of nonperishable food and 19 security force members to Pereira, plans another 39 tons, and has 255 military specialists and 20 dogs on standby. Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered two planes carrying 100 tons of aid. Pope Leo XIV expressed solidarity with Colombians and thanked those contributing to recovery efforts.

Cloud computing stocks, and ETFs that track them such as the GX Cloud Computing ETF (CLOU), have recently rebounded after a rough stretch, raising the question of whether a second wave of gains is underway. CLOU is seven years old and holds about 40 stocks, with only 10 accounting for nearly half its assets. The author likes it as a cloud computing pure-play, with no Magnificent 7 stocks among its top holdings. The ETF has actually declined in price over the past five years, showing how it has failed to keep pace with the other side of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, as hyperscalers and semiconductor companies have eaten into cloud stocks' business. The author argues those companies may not meet lofty market expectations, so CLOU may have been pushed down too far, creating a possible buying opportunity. After the pandemic, valuations in this area contracted as enterprise businesses tightened budgets, hitting cloud infrastructure and software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers. That is now stabilizing. The recent price action is driven by infrastructure demand from enterprise AI projects. Rather than replacing cloud computing, AI deployment requires large amounts of cloud-hosted compute capacity, storage, and data management. The first era of cloud growth was basic migration of legacy on-premises databases to remote servers; the current phase is driven by data density, as generative AI models and enterprise automation platforms need continuous access to high-performance computing clusters on public and hybrid clouds. CLOU covers the full ecosystem of SaaS, platform-as-a-service, and infrastructure-as-a-service, and as corporations move AI experiments into full production, recurring revenue for cloud infrastructure providers, data warehouse platforms, and observability software expands. Key risks include high multiples: trailing earnings of 22x would not be terrible, but investors are lowering the valuation levels they consider fair, and the days of paying 30x–40x earnings for cloud stocks are gone. Another risk is the hyperscalers. Amazon (AMZN) AWS, Microsoft (MSFT) Azure, and Alphabet's (GOOG) (GOOGL) Google Cloud capture a large share of infrastructure spending, pressuring margins of the smaller pure-play SaaS providers among CLOU's top-10 holdings. As a chartist, the author acknowledges these risks but sees emerging upside. The first big move off the lows is past, as the daily chart shows, but the weekly chart shows a breakout with fleeting yet powerful potential upside of perhaps 15% to 20%. Since the author believes nothing in the stock market is a buy-and-hold now, the trade can work if the broader market does not roll over. CLOU can serve as an "anti-AI-success" trade for short periods, but a big, sustained move would require a rising tide across the market. The author, Rob Isbitts, is a semi-retired CIO and former fiduciary investment advisor who holds no positions in the securities mentioned.

Unmanned aircraft-maker Swarm Aero has secured a $10 million government contract that will be primarily executed at its new Fayetteville research and manufacturing facility. As part of the contract with the Air Force Research Laboratory, Swarm Aero will preform research and development of its high-rate manufacturing process to manufacture aircraft parts for the U.S. Air Force. In mid February, Swarm Aero opened its Fayetteville Advanced Manufacturing Center in 80,000 square feet of industrial space once occupied by Key Tronic Corp. The company said its Fayetteville operations will eventually have the ability to produce thousands of unmanned aerial vehicles and will create up to 600 high-skill aerospace jobs over the next five years. "We're focused on the advanced manufacturing techniques that we intend to use for the future, and so this contract will be largely spent in Fayetteville on research happening right there," Spencer Rodriguez, vice president of operations and finance, said in a phone interview Tuesday. He said the Fayetteville operation employs about 10 workers with plans to add more soon, with hiring continuing to grow as operations scale up. Rodriguez said the Fayetteville facility will eventually be the center of Swarm Aero's primary operations. Last month, Fayetteville's City Council approved an ordinance detailing how it will handle non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) in part because of concerns over a non-disclosure agreement made between the city and Swarm Aero. In May, City Council members said they received threats online and through email after a 5-3 vote by the council allowing Swarm Aero to remain in its Fayetteville location, overruling an earlier decision by the city Board of Adjustments that the facility did not fit the property's zoning. Founded in 2022, California-based Swarm Aero, which makes large, unmanned aerial vehicles, has secured nearly $60 million in funding from various sources, the most recent $35 million in Series A financing lead by Two Sigma Ventures and Silent Ventures in March. The company has said Swarm's manufacturing approach extends well beyond a single platform, giving it the foundation to develop additional aircraft for defense, civil, and commercial customers. "Since our first engineering hire, Swarm has invested in manufacturing and design in tandem. We are not designing or even building one aircraft only to then start thinking about how to manufacture it at scale. We have designed our manufacturing processes to enable us to deliver aircraft at the scale our customers require," Peter Kalogiannis, chief executive officer and co-founder, Swarm Aero, said in a statement Tuesday. Cyberattacks against critical systems often leave defenders searching for clues outside the machine. Crytica Security wants to change that by monitoring what happens inside the device itself. The cybersecurity company has developed a compact security probe that detects unauthorized changes within embedded systems. Its approach focuses on the instructions a device uses to perform its functions. Crytica says the technology can provide deterministic evidence when those instructions change. That signal could help security teams identify compromises with greater confidence. Inside the device. Crytica’s technology uses a probe that occupies less than 100 kilobytes inside a protected device. The lightweight software runs without disrupting normal operations. The probe monitors the device’s instruction set for unauthorized modifications. It can also identify changes involving static data, including configuration files. That distinction matters because many cybersecurity tools observe devices externally. They analyze network traffic, communications, vulnerabilities, and behavior to identify suspicious activity. Those methods can reveal important clues. They cannot always establish whether the device itself still operates from trusted instructions. Crytica calls its internal monitoring technology iNSiM, short for Instruction Set Integrity Monitoring. The system can detect changes quickly and generate alerts for security teams. See All. Faster detection. The technology feeds into Crytica’s Rapid Detection, Alert, and Isolation system, known as RDAi. The system aims to give security operations centers a higher-confidence signal. That signal could complement existing security platforms instead of forcing organizations to replace them. Crytica says its technology can work alongside SOC, SIEM, XDR, and AI-assisted security systems. That integration could become increasingly important as cyberattacks accelerate. IBM reported a 56 percent year-over-year increase in AI-driven attacks in its 2026 breach study. The same report found that half of organizations with security operations centers have deployed AI agents. Automated systems now make decisions and respond to threats at increasingly high speeds. Security teams therefore need reliable information to feed those automated workflows. A compromised device could undermine those decisions if its own operating state remains uncertain. Higher stakes. The stakes rise considerably when attackers target operational technology. Embedded devices can influence infrastructure that supports essential services and physical processes. Healthcare systems also depend on connected devices that must remain reliable. National security applications face similar concerns, especially where compromised equipment could affect mission readiness. Crytica is pursuing deployments across commercial, utility and federal environments. It also works with security vendors, device manufacturers and systems integrators. CEO C. Kerry Nemovicher said effective detection ultimately needs visibility inside devices. He described the company’s probe as a small software agent designed for that purpose. Executive Chairman C. Lloyd Mahaffey said partnerships around deterministic detection are also emerging. Crytica expects to announce additional technology integrations and collaborations in the coming weeks. The broader idea is straightforward: external monitoring can identify suspicious behavior. Internal integrity monitoring could determine whether the device itself has changed. For defenders protecting critical systems, that difference could provide another layer of confidence when every second matters.

The author argues that AI-designed biology is a grave threat. Researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute used generative AI models to produce 16 novel bacteriophages, complete functional viral genomes that infect and kill bacteria in the laboratory. The BBC reports this is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI, and the researchers say the creations pose no threat to people. The author calls this view dangerously naive and describes the work as a bioweapon prototype. He argues that AI lets one person do work that once required government laboratories and billions in funding, that the technique cannot be undiscovered, and that the same models could be pointed at human proteins. He cites DARPA programs announced in July 2025 that aim to turn indirect machine readouts of purported "unknown biothreat" samples into digital protein sequences, calling this an AI bioweapons pipeline built in plain sight. The author then rejects mainstream virology, claiming that no institution has ever isolated virus particles from an infected individual, citing Drs. Thomas Cowan and Andrew Kaufman. He asserts that what are called viruses are really proteins and protein fragments, and he floats the idea, drawn from modernity.news, that the COVID-19 spike protein may have been the human endogenous retroviral protein HERV-K rather than a viral product. He concludes that AI-designed viruses are really novel toxic proteins, and that the same system that promoted gain-of-function research, which he says Dr. Anthony Fauci was caught promoting in a 2012 video, will market such toxins as vaccines, gene therapies or drugs. He claims the spike protein enters cell nuclei and suppresses DNA repair, and he says researchers are unwitting pawns of a profit-driven system pushing a depopulation agenda. He further argues that AI hallucinates in text and images, so it will also hallucinate protein structures, and that a single missed mutation could turn a benign protein into a deadly toxin. He says assurances that no harmful proteins were made are not reassuring and that there is no kill switch. As a defense, he recommends natural nutrients, including astaxanthin, phycocyanin from spirulina, sulforaphane and vitamin C, along with reducing inflammation, neutralizing pathogens and using strong antioxidants. He suggests vitamin C in doses of up to 1,000 milligrams per hour during waking hours, plus magnesium. He urges trust in the immune system and natural medicine rather than the CDC, WHO or Big Pharma. He announces a free course on nutritional strategies for genetic defense and repair, said to protect against bioweapons and post-nuclear radioisotope fallout. The author, Mike Adams, is editor of NaturalNews.com and lab science director of CWC Labs, an ISO 17025 accredited laboratory.

Two malicious LiteLLM releases, versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8, were live on PyPI on March 24 from 10:39 UTC for about 40 minutes before PyPI quarantined them. They carried credential-stealing code designed to harvest environment variables, SSH keys, cloud credentials, Kubernetes tokens and database passwords, then encrypt the data and send it to models.litellm[.]cloud, an attacker-controlled domain. Unit 42 recorded the payload reading model API keys such as OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Version 1.82.8 included litellm_init.pth, which Python runs at interpreter startup, so it executed even if LiteLLM was never imported. LiteLLM tells users to treat any install that day up to 16:00 UTC as suspect, and notes that an unpinned transitive dependency, such as one pulled in by an agent framework, could deliver the package unnoticed. Neither version now appears in PyPI's release history; 1.82.6 and 1.83.0 remain available. CloudSEK says a dataset of roughly 434,000 captured files, obtained from confidential intelligence sources, maps potential exposure to more than 2,500 organizations. It stresses this is not a victim count. The files are loot and logs it assessed as belonging to the campaign, and the figure counts files and exfiltration events, not verified unique jobs. CloudSEK published a searchable public lookup rated High or Medium confidence. High confidence requires the organization's own domain to appear in captured CI runner identity signals; repository namespaces alone support only Medium. Entries include NVIDIA, Cisco, Deloitte, Volkswagen, FedEx, Siemens and X Corp, but inclusion does not show stolen credentials were used. Attribution uses two independent checks, and the final verdict takes the lower confidence level. CloudSEK declined to discuss pre-publication notifications or disputes. The incident belongs to the wider TeamPCP campaign (tracked by Google as UNC6780) linked to Aqua Security's Trivy scanner. On March 19, attackers who retained access after an incomplete credential rotation force-pushed malicious commits to 76 of 77 trivy-action tags and all seven setup-trivy tags, and published a malicious Trivy 0.69.4. The compromise is CVE-2026-33634, added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on March 26 and now listing LiteLLM 1.82.7 through 1.82.8. How the releases reached PyPI is disputed. CloudSEK said the poisoned build published them; LiteLLM said a direct PyPI upload bypassed its CI/CD workflow; Unit 42 described attackers targeting PyPI publishing tokens after the Trivy breach. CloudSEK says these are different stages of one chain, and PyPA's advisory describes a token exposed through the compromised Trivy dependency and used to upload both versions. BerriAI had not responded. The FBI's July 2 advisory (FLASH-20260702-01) warned that actors will likely weaponize exfiltrated credentials long after the compromise, and told organizations to rotate CI/CD secrets, publishing tokens and cloud credentials. Long-lived secrets remain usable unless rotated, so the FBI and Aqua urge moving to temporary tokens. Confirmed downstream impacts include unauthorized access to Checkmarx's GitHub repositories, activity at Mercor that it contained, and a European Commission AWS account compromise, assessed by CERT-EU, with about 91.7 GB of compressed data exfiltrated. Organizations should check for the two LiteLLM versions during the March 24 window of 10:39 to 16:00 UTC, rotate any secrets those systems could access, and search GitHub organizations for repositories named tpcp-docs or docs-tpcp. Because the malware used a tpcp-docs- prefix and uploaded data as a release asset tagged data-, exact-name searches can miss them.

Quick Take. - Validator release v2026.1.1 closes two receipt flaws that could let a receipt be accepted without required approvals. - Juiceberg estimated roughly 4 billion ONE were minted and 2.8 billion reached exchanges; Harmony has not confirmed it. - The size of the excess supply, funds exchanges can freeze, and any rollback remain unresolved. Harmony, the layer-1 blockchain network, has released an emergency validator patch that it says prevents further unauthorized minting of ONE, its native token. The project said it will address tokens already created in a later update, leaving their number and ultimate treatment unresolved. Harmony told validators to install v2026.1.1 on Aug. 12. The notice confirms that minting occurred but does not disclose the amount. Onchain researcher Juiceberg estimated that roughly 4 billion ONE, equal to about 26% of the supply figure used in the post, had been minted without authorization. Juiceberg also estimated that 2.8 billion ONE had reached exchanges. Harmony has not independently confirmed those figures. How the patch blocks more minting. Harmony's published code changes address two weaknesses in cross-shard receipts, which carry transaction results between parts of the network. One flaw allowed an empty signer record and a mathematically neutral aggregate signature to pass a quorum check. The verifier counted the full committee instead of the validators represented in the signer record, allowing a receipt to be accepted without the required approvals. The second flaw affected how the network recorded that a receipt had already been spent. Some proof fields were not bound to the signed block header, so changing those fields could make a previously processed receipt appear new. The destination could then be credited again without a corresponding debit from the source. The signed v2026.1.1 release changes the quorum calculation and ties the spent marker to authenticated header data, closing both paths described in the patch. Harmony also paused bridge.harmony.one during the response, although its notice did not identify the bridge as the exploited component. The project published four implicated wallet addresses and asked exchanges to block and freeze traceable funds, without naming the venues or disclosing how much had been frozen. Harmony's initial response said rollback options were under consideration. The project has not announced that a rollback will occur or specified the point from which transactions could be reversed. The incident differs technically from the June 2022 Horizon bridge exploit, which involved compromised multisig control and about $100 million in stolen assets. The current patch instead addresses receipt verification and replay at the protocol level. Harmony says further minting is now blocked. The remaining risk centers on the size and location of the ONE already created, how much exchanges can freeze, and whether the network will attempt a rollback to remove the excess supply. Harmony is +3.15% over the past 24 hours and currently sits at rank #857 by market cap.

With UF move-in set for Aug. 15-16, students and experts offered advice for new residents. Jack Mondel, a 20-year-old data science junior who lived in Jennings Hall as a freshman, said the dorm experience is what you make of it. His biggest misconception was that friendships would come immediately; even though he picked Jennings for its "social dorm" reputation, he had to "ignite the social activity." He met people by finding others with shared interests, and he met one of his best friends, who lived in the same hall, at a fraternity pre-rush event. He urged students to break routines and explore campus, and said that while he stayed friends with a couple of people from his first weeks, that often isn't the case, so students should treat early friendships as a baseline. Zoey Tabor, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering junior, and her roommate, 20-year-old mechanical engineering junior Alessandra de Simone, remember their freshman dorm year fondly and are entering their third year living together. Tabor credited open communication and urged new students moving in with a stranger to keep an open mind rather than being close-minded about who they befriend. She said there is real value in living on campus the first year. Sydney Kollas, a 23-year-old New York City performer and former resident assistant in the Cypress area who served two years as an RA, advised students, especially those in online classes, to use "third spaces" for work instead of isolating in the dorm. For breaks, she recommended campus events such as GatorNights (formerly GatorDays) at the Reitz Union on Friday nights, and sporting events, which are a low-pressure way to meet people since you're just watching a game. Having had a difficult freshman year, she advised allowing time to adjust and avoiding comparisons with others. Dr. Nick Comeau, a licensed psychologist at Sage Wellness in Gainesville, agreed that comparison doesn't build self-esteem and said students should instead compare themselves to their own benchmark. He noted that leaving home and becoming self-sufficient can be jarring, and offered the acronym "END stress": exercise, nutrition and dive in. He suggested choosing exercise exciting enough to do consistently; it aids adrenal gland function and lowers stress, which may make shy students more open to new things. It can also improve thyroid function, lifting mood and energy, and grow neurotrophic factor in the brain, aiding learning and memory. For nutrition, he recommended minimizing processed foods, whether by cooking in the dorm kitchen or using campus dining, and prioritizing complex carbohydrates and healthy proteins, which break down into amino acids that become neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin. "Dive in" means overcoming challenges during the transition; exposure therapy is among the most effective coping methods. For an introvert that might mean attending an event and meeting people, while an extrovert might spend time alone. Comeau said that as long as you are alive, you can always make a new choice and redefine who you are.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) has teamed up with Colorado-based Quantinuum to bring the latter’s most advanced quantum computer, Helios, to its cloud infrastructure. Under this multi-year agreement, Oracle customers will have access to a hybrid compute infrastructure consisting of high-performance computing (HPC), graphics processing units (GPUs), and quantum computing. Regarded as the next frontier of computing, quantum computers are fundamentally different from the silicon-based computers used widely for daily and supercomputing applications. Instead of using binary bits that can store either 0 or 1 as information, quantum computers use quantum bits or qubits, which can store multiple values between 0 and 1, thereby exponentially increasing their computing capacity. Multiple areas of research, such as drug development, energy, logistics, and financial modeling, have reached the limits of classical computing and could benefit from advances in quantum computing. While research continues building commercial-scale quantum computers, OCI has teamed up with Quantinuum to offer quantum computing services via its cloud infrastructure. Quantinuum’s Helios. At a time when policymakers are worried about the increased demand for energy to fulfill anticipated usage of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, quantum computing also comes in with the promise of a lower energy demand. While quantum computers typically require ultracold temperatures to operate, Quantinuum’s Helios quantum computer has an energy consumption far lower than supercomputers in operation today. Launched in November 2025, Helios is Quantinuum’s third-generation quantum computer built using 98 trapped-ion physical qubits that operate as 48 logical qubits. See All. With Helios, Quantinuum has achieved an average two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.921 percent, superseding the 99.9 percent benchmark that the industry currently follows. Even though Quantinuum is a full-stack operator and lets organizations procure and run quantum computers onsite, this partnership with Oracle allows customers to access their quantum computer through a secure cloud. Hybrid compute. Since quantum computing is still in its early stages, the Quantinuum-OCI partnership is working to explore how a hybrid quantum-AI infrastructure could help enterprises and research institutes solve computationally intensive challenges without switching to entirely new systems of computation. “We believe the next phase of enterprise computing will be shaped by bringing quantum, AI, and high-performance computing together,” said Dr. Rajeeb Hazra, President and CEO of Quantinuum. “Deploying Helios inside OCI gives Quantinuum and Oracle an opportunity to create a unique, deeply integrated environment for hybrid workloads, explore enterprise use cases with customers, and accelerate commercial adoption.” As Helios operates on-site with OCI’s infrastructure, it will integrate seamlessly with existing compute, networking, storage, identity and data services that OCI’s customers use with the same access control. The quantum service will help developers build, test and refine quantum-classical applications using Quantinuum’s open-source hybrid-programming frameworks. “AI has changed what organizations can imagine, and we believe quantum computing can expand what they’re able to solve,” added Mahesh Thiagarajan, Executive Vice President of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, in the press release. “By bringing Quantinuum’s Helios to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, we want to give developers a practical and secure way to explore how quantum computing could complement their existing AI and HPC workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure while improving compute efficiency and energy use.” OCI plans to preview this quantum service in the coming few months.

Aviation's next major efficiency leap is expected to come from fundamental aerodynamic change rather than incremental updates, and Airbus is betting on longer, highly slender wings for its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. Against the backdrop of the Farnborough International Airshow 2026, manufacturers face pressure to cut fuel burn sharply while managing large order backlogs. Aerodynamics has emerged as one of the biggest levers for future designs. Wingspan on narrowbodies is traditionally limited by airport gate dimensions, ground infrastructure and ICAO wingspan limits, as the Boeing 777X's folding wingtips illustrate. Yet longer spans offer a large payoff in reduced induced drag and fuel use. Research from Técnico Lisboa shows that a higher aspect ratio reduces induced drag and wingtip vortices, but it also raises the structural bending moment at the wing root, threatening structural integrity unless weight penalties can be avoided. Airbus has built full-scale ground demonstrators to test advanced manufacturing and assembly technologies. At Farnborough it launched the latest phase of its Wing of Tomorrow programme, shifting from ground structures to live flight testing. Over three years, engineers will build and evaluate full-scale wing extensions, each several meters long, on an A321neo flight-test aircraft operating out of Toulouse. The extensions replicate a folding wing in its fully extended position and carry sensors capturing telemetry on pressure distribution, structural flexing and dynamic response, including under gusts and high-speed cruise. The aim is to safely push past conventional design limits, refine computer models, and confirm that weight savings do not compromise stability or control. Sue Partridge, Head of the Wing of Tomorrow Programme, stressed alignment with partners and certification authorities, saying Airbus is already in dialogue with EASA about requirements. She said the programme explores more than one option because "you don't necessarily know what's going to be the best option," and works closely with suppliers to avoid locking into suboptimal solutions. Traditional aluminum would need heavy reinforcement for such slender wings, offsetting fuel savings, so advanced carbon fiber composites are needed. These allow aeroelastic tailoring: specific fiber orientations let the wingtip twist passively under load, known as wash-out, shedding peak gust loads and reducing stress at the wing root. Producing these geometries relies on techniques such as automated dry fiber placement and large-scale resin infusion. The key test is whether they can move from laboratory experiments to consistent, high-volume production. Airbus is anchoring development in UK facilities, mainly Filton and Broughton, including the Wing Technology Development Centre, where engineers assemble full-scale structures and evaluate more than 100 manufacturing and assembly technologies, including advanced tooling and single-shot resin infusion, on spans of 17 meters (55.8 feet) and beyond. Standardizing automated processes and refining tolerances early is meant to reduce risk before serial production. Engaging regulators like EASA early establishes compliance pathways ahead of any program launch. For airlines, high-aspect-ratio wings promise a lasting structural advantage that complements future propulsion advances, affecting range and payload economics as environmental targets tighten. Whether debuting on a clean-sheet design or an evolutionary derivative, the groundwork suggests future single-aisle flight will be defined by much greater aerodynamic efficiency.

This installment of the VICE column RATED AND SLATED, which describes itself as "terminally online so you don't have to be," opens by joking that its writer is glad not to be a White House journalist. He mocks the beat's sacrifices, including inhaling Donald Trump's "recycled hamburger breath" on Air Force One. He adds that when a credible threat of an Iranian missile being fired at the plane was detected, Trump supposedly swapped flights by hiding in a catering truck. He says he'll stick to dank memes and AI videos, since "brainrot" seems to be the only thing the U.S. and Iran can agree on. Among the "rated" items, Yung Lean's cover of Robyn's "Robotboy" is praised: he sounds both younger and older than ever, and Robyn describes it as him "singing this lullaby to the person he once was." The writer likens it to childhood schoolyard rhymes and says Yung Lean has kept hold of his innocence and sounds like he's "in your corner." Also rated is a meme, "MARIO 64: WAR ON TERROR," which jokes that Super Mario, not Sonic, hunted down and executed Osama bin Laden after 9/11. A photo of Brad Pitt apparently drinking again after seven years sober is imagined as him bowling with friends, claiming to drink "in a more restrained manner." A short video about Jimi Hendrix, "The Will to Power(chord)," is mocked as an algorithm that serves Sydney Sweeney in swimwear alongside "Purple Haze." A viral post about living to 122 is joked about via Jeanne Calment, the chain-smoking Frenchwoman who reached that age. The "slated" items begin with Chet Hanks's cover of Nirvana's "Something in the Way," which the writer says sounds like Limp Bizkit bassist Sam Rivers (RIP) playing Nirvana, a sign that "something has gone very badly wrong." He also jokes about a "Cindy workout" that turns out to be a dungeon session with a dominatrix personal trainer. Next is a joke about Kendrick Lamar's 2024 diss track "Not Like Us" becoming a sorority rush anthem, with the "they" being only Canadians, including Drake. A post captioned "How Yeat sounds when ur not 15 anymore" is riffed on as a confusion between the American rapper Yeat and the Irish poet W. B. Yeats, with "Things fall apart" as the shared sentiment. The column ends with a kid who has finished Finnegans Wake and is rapping about it, with a couplet rhyming "cuck" with Joyce's famous 100-letter thunderword, and a suggestion that the James Joyce estate look into how LLMs are being trained.

Summary. - Twitch auto-enrolled streamers in a default "Training for Generative AI" toggle letting Amazon train on streams. - Disable it at Settings > Security & Privacy > Training for Generative AI on the Twitch website. - Disabling stops Amazon training but not AutoMod, recommendations or sponsorship AI; users are protesting. If you're a content creator and you regularly stream to Twitch, the service has just automatically enrolled you in a new feature. This feature allows Amazon to train its models on your content, and as you might imagine, a lot of streamers are not happy with the change. Fortunately, disabling this feature is quick and easy, although the fact that it wasn't opt-out by default has users a little worried. Twitch is enrolling streamers into AI training automatically. You can turn it off, though. In a new update to the Twitch website and announced in a post on the Twitch Support X feed, the company has added a new toggle in the user settings titled "Training for Generative AI." It's enabled by default, and while it's on, it permits Twitch to use your channel content "to train generative AI content models at Amazon." If you don't want this to happen, you can disable it by following these steps: - Head over to the Twitch website. - Click on your user icon, then click Settings. - Click on Security and Privacy. - Scroll down to the Privacy section. - Click the toggle for Training for Generative AI. Twitch notes that while this does stop Amazon from training off your channel's content, it doesn't prevent all AI processes from affecting your channel. Some examples of AI processes that will still influence your Twitch stream include real-time sponsorship campaigns, cultivating user stream recommendations, and powering the automatic Twitch chat moderation system AutoMod. The user reception to this feature has been seemingly overwhelmingly negative. Users are taking to social media to protest the change, and a new thread titled "Make all AI features optional, and opt-out by default" has been created on the Twitch User Voice website where people can air their displeasure. Said thread has received 13,486 votes at the time of writing, and continues to climb.

VIRGINIA BEACH — A data center company that connects subsea cables with on-land internet service providers will buy 9 acres in Corporate Landing Business Park to expand its existing services. The Development Authority on Tuesday agreed to sell the land off Dam Neck Road to Globalinx for $1.8 million. Globalinx currently operates a cable landing station on 12 acres in the business park where domestic and international internet carriers can connect to three subsea cables that land in Virginia Beach. The company is expanding its existing colocation services in phases. Phase 2 — a $34.5 million investment — is underway on its existing site and will support up to four cable landings and is expected to be completed by the end of 2027, according to the city. The land purchase is for Globalinx’ third phase of expansion, a $65 million investment to include a new 85,000-square-foot facility across from its existing site. It’s expected to create 40 new full-time jobs. Globalinx has commitments on three new cables over the next several years, company President Gregg Twitt has said. The companies behind them have not been disclosed. Unlike hyperscale data centers that provide cloud computing, colocation data centers do not require high levels of electrical power and water to operate. Globalinx will require a capacity of 25 megawatts, which is available at the business park, said Ihsane Mouak, business development coordinator for the city’s economic development department. The new building will be used for additional cable landings and will serve as a carrier-neutral colocation and interconnecting space. It’s unclear how many cable landings the new building would be able to support. The sale requires a 180-day due diligence period and construction must begin within three years of closing, Mouak said. Three major subsea cable systems currently land in Virginia Beach. They include MAREA, which links the United States and Spain and is owned by Microsoft, Meta and Telxius; BRUSA, which connects Brazil and Puerto Rico and is owned by Telxius; and Dunant, a cable connecting the United States and France, owned by Google. In May, the Development Authority approved an $800,000 economic development incentive grant for the company’s Phase 2 expansion. Corporate Landing Business Park was established in 1990 on 325 acres and is owned by the Development Authority. It’s home to a variety of major regional corporate offices including Geico, Groundworks and Lockheed Martin. Stacy Parker, 757-222-5125,.

The US is testing a new way to spot drones without building a separate detection network. A new system uses existing 5G infrastructure to detect, track, and monitor unmanned aircraft. Lockheed Martin and its partners demonstrated the technology near Miami in July. The test showed how commercial wireless infrastructure could support drone detection across busy American environments. The system, called NetSense Airspace Awareness-as-a-Service, analyzes radio-frequency disturbances around cellular networks. It can then identify drone activity and maintain a track as the aircraft moves. The approach could give airports, hospitals, power plants, stadiums and government facilities another layer of airspace protection. It could also help agencies monitor drone activity around sensitive locations. 5G becomes drone sensor. NetSense combines several commercial technologies to turn cellular signals into useful sensing data. Verizon provided the 5G network spectrum used during the demonstration. ODC supplied AI-native radio access network software for the test. NVIDIA’s AI Aerial platform analyzed radio-frequency signals in real time. Keysight Technologies also contributed its RF simulation technology. Lockheed Martin’s systems then processed the resulting data to identify and track the drone. NVIDIA executive Ronnie Vasishta said the technology brings AI-powered sensing closer to the network edge. That allows RF disturbances to receive rapid analysis and supports faster alerts. See All. The system does not require changes to existing cellular radio deployments. That detail could make large-scale deployment easier for infrastructure operators. Engineers can also expand the system as new technologies emerge. Its open architecture allows additional sensors and interceptors to connect with existing systems. Tracking drones in real time. During the Miami demonstration, NetSense detected a drone and alerted operators to its presence. The system then maintained track custody as the aircraft continued its flight. That capability matters as drones become cheaper and easier to acquire. A growing number of commercial and consumer drones now operate near populated areas. Traditional counter-drone systems can require dedicated sensors and specialized hardware. NetSense takes a different engineering route by using infrastructure already deployed across cities. Lockheed Martin says its approach can also complement future 6G sensing networks. The system currently works with 5G spectrum while providing a path toward broader cellular integration. Verizon’s Anil Guntupali said existing 5G signals can provide useful sensing data when paired with intelligent software. That concept could turn communications networks into security tools without replacing their core infrastructure. The company plans to offer NetSense through a subscription model. The service will connect with customers’ existing security operations rather than require an entirely separate command structure. Commercial counter-drone systems. Pilot deployments are planned for the second half of 2026 and early 2027. Lockheed Martin expects broader commercial availability in 2027. Initial customers will include organizations with urgent airspace security requirements. Critical infrastructure operators could become major users as drone activity increases around sensitive sites. The technology could eventually give US cities another tool for monitoring low-altitude airspace. More importantly, it shows how ordinary communications infrastructure could gain a second role. A cellular network built to connect phones could also help security teams understand what is flying nearby. That shift could make drone awareness more scalable without rebuilding America’s existing wireless infrastructure.

IBM Just Made A Huge Fusion Energy Breakthrough Thanks To Quantum Computing. Quantum computing is kicking the doors open on a fusion energy problem that has long challenged scientists. IBM, in partnership with the Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Cleveland Clinic, discovered a new way to model how fusion plants could produce and recover tritium. It's a rare fuel found in several common objects that are radioactive. Tritium is created naturally when cosmic rays reach the upper atmosphere, but supplies are limited as its 12-year half-life results in relatively quick decay. The lack of tritium is a roadblock to having fusion as a power source. But this radioactive isotype of hydrogen can be produced by exposing more commonly available lithium to neutrons. Tritium is notoriously hard to capture and reuse, but a molten salt known as FLiBe (fluorine, lithium, and beryllium) can surround the fusion reaction like a blanket, helping with this process. Scientists need to know which recipe for doing so is the most efficient, but calculations on this scale are too challenging for classical computers. The solution is to use classical computers for simpler modeling and let IBM's quantum hardware determine the nine specific molecular configurations of this material. It helped them model how the molten salt behaves with and without tritium. IBM calls it the first-known instance of fusion-material computations on quantum computers. How quantum computing helps solve fusion's biggest problem. Nuclear fusion is nuclear fission's friendlier cousin. Instead of splitting atoms, fusion combines them, much like the sun. The process doesn't produce chain reactions, and it creates shorter-lived radioactive waste. Fusion has a lower risk of meltdown and a smaller environmental footprint than fission. Yet the potential is enormous, which is why this quantum computing breakthrough is important. Fusion is incredibly hard to control. The process can be hotter than the sun, and a working plant has to absorb fusion neutrons, create tritium, and recapture that tritium as fuel under these conditions. That's where IBM's quantum computing comes in. The models help scientists calculate how strongly tritium binds to the molten salt, a key test for whether a future fusion plant could recover enough fuel to keep running. This difficultly is why there are currently no commercial fusion plants in operation. The U.S. Department of Energy has a roadmap to build them, however, it will only happen with more breakthroughs in fuel production and reactor design. IBM might be the first to commercialize quantum computing, but will have to invest billions to do so. The breakthroughs aren't limited to energy. In May 2026, IBM announced scientists used quantum computing to model how drug-like molecules attach to proteins in water, similar to reactions that would happen inside the human body. It could give pharmaceutical developers a better way to predict which molecules are worth testing before they begin lab work.

ASX shareholder plans to sue former directors over failed blockchain project. ASX’s failed blockchain-based CHESS overhaul faces renewed governance scrutiny after the exchange admitted misleading the market. An Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) shareholder plans to seek Federal Court permission to sue former ASX officers and directors over alleged breaches of duty connected to its failed blockchain-based clearing and settlement overhaul. On Wednesday, ASX said Rosherville Pty Ltd had notified the exchange that it proposes to apply for leave to commence a statutory derivative action under sections 236 and 237 of Australia’s Corporations Act. If approved, Rosherville would bring the proceedings on ASX’s behalf. The exchange said there were no allegations against ASX itself. It did not identify the former officials targeted, describe their alleged breaches in detail or disclose the remedies Rosherville intends to seek, while the court has not considered whether the proposed case can proceed. The proposed lawsuit could test whether shareholders can hold former ASX leaders accountable for overseeing one of Australia’s costliest financial-technology failures. Failed CHESS overhaul draws regulatory action. ASX began exploring a replacement for its Clearing House Electronic Subregister System, or CHESS, in 2016 and selected a distributed-ledger system developed with New York-based Digital Asset. In December 2017, ASX was expected to become the first securities exchange to use blockchain for its core services. The intended launch was repeatedly postponed. In November 2022, ASX paused the project after an Accenture review found significant problems with its design and ability to meet the exchange’s requirements. In May 2023, ASX had formally abandoned blockchain for the replacement and would consider more conventional technology. Related: Australia orders Cryptolink Bitcoin ATMs offline over ‘basic reporting’ failures. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) sued ASX in August 2024, alleging it lacked a reasonable basis for telling the market in February 2022 that the project was “progressing well” and on track for an April 2023 launch. At the time, ASIC called the episode a collective failure by ASX’s board and senior executives. In June 2026, ASX admitted to misleading conduct linked to the blockchain replacement project. On July 3, the Federal Court ordered the company to pay a $14.4 million penalty and $2.1 million toward ASIC’s costs, closing the regulator’s case weeks before Rosherville notified the exchange of its proposed action against former officials.
