Estonia is to get its first large-scale artificial intelligence computing centre later this year after Nebius, the Nasdaq-listed cloud company, agreed to install 22 megawatts of capacity at a data centre near Tallinn. The installation at Greenergy Data Centers in Hüüru, Harju County, will be Nebius’s first AI infrastructure deployment in the Baltic states. The companies say it will be the region’s largest AI factory when its first 22MW phase begins operating before the end of 2026. Despite the industrial label, an AI factory does not manufacture physical products. It is a data centre built around clusters of powerful processors, high-speed networks and cooling systems that provide the computing capacity needed to train and run artificial intelligence models. The project forms part of a €50 million expansion of the Hüüru data centre. MCF Group Estonia, the company behind Greenergy, appointed the Finnish company Caverion as the main contractor last month. The work will add 22MW of IT power and cooling, increasing the campus’s total capacity to 31.5MW. It is expected to be completed in the autumn. Estonia sets its sights on becoming an AI hub. Nebius will become the first international AI cloud company to deploy its infrastructure at Greenergy. Its computing capacity will be offered to researchers, start-ups and larger companies developing and operating AI systems. AI systems rely on data centres filled with high-performance servers that provide the computing power needed to train and run models. Photo by Getty Images on Unsplash. Tom Blackwell, Nebius’s chief communications officer, said Estonia was a “natural choice” because of its engineering talent, digital economy and start-up culture. He said the company intended to work with the Estonian government, universities and industry to improve AI skills and make advanced computing infrastructure more widely available. Kert Evert, the chief executive of Greenergy Data Centers, said securing Nebius as a customer showed that Estonia could compete for large international technology investments. “Their decision to choose Greenergy is a strong recognition of our team’s work,” he said. “This is a start.” Martin Salo, a co-founder of Tensor Estate, which recently became a shareholder in Greenergy, described the installation as the first phase of a broader development intended to establish Estonia as a centre for international AI infrastructure. Tensor Estate co-founder Martin Salo inside a data hall at Greenergy Data Centers in Hüüru. Photo by Raigo Pajula. Finland, Sweden and Norway have so far attracted most of northern Europe’s biggest AI data centres, helped by relatively inexpensive electricity, a growing supply of renewable energy and a cold climate that reduces cooling costs. The Hüüru project brings Estonia into a market dominated until now by its Nordic neighbours. Nebius accelerates its European expansion. Nebius already operates a 75MW facility at Mäntsälä in Finland and is building much larger AI factories in Lappeenranta, Finland, and Béthune, France. It also has deployments in Britain, Spain and Iceland. The Amsterdam-based company emerged from the former Dutch parent of Yandex in 2024 after it sold its Russian businesses and severed its ties with the country. Its customers include Microsoft and Meta. Nebius reported second-quarter revenue of $582.3 million on Wednesday, an increase of 454 per cent from a year earlier, although it recorded a net loss of $190.4 million from continuing operations. The announcement did not disclose the value of Nebius’s contract, the number or type of processors to be installed or how many permanent jobs the project is expected to create.

During the "MapleStory Vibe Camp," a global game jam held June 8–29 by Nexon's blockchain subsidiary NEXPACE and the AI game creation platform Verse8, 693 games were made in three weeks. Five were picked for the top-scoring "The Campfire" category, including "Say Cheese, Yeti!", made by one person in four days. Creator Jung Yu-jin is not a developer. She studied visual design, has worked in disability support and game QA, and now creates cognitive and leisure content for children and seniors with dementia. Lack of coding skill had always stalled her ideas at the planning or concept-video stage, and a prototype once died when a collaborating developer dropped out. Vibe Coding let her finish a project alone for the first time. She built it during maternity leave, with a baby of eight months. By day she kept screens away, organizing rules and priorities in a notebook and queuing prompts to run while she watched the child. Implementation and graphics happened from 10 p.m. to 2 or 3 a.m., four to five hours a day, often interrupted by night wakings. She saw a "make a game without coding" banner four days before the deadline and dived in with a plan originally meant for a hackathon, condensing ten minigame ideas into one. The concept came from an offline MapleStory event, where non-gamers started simple games without explanation, and from people photographing giant character statues. The result is a time-attack party game in which you control Pepe riding a Yeti's back and move to a camera zone to be photographed, scoring by closeness to the center. She filled gaps in the original "Yeti's Secret" rather than altering it, answering "Why does the Yeti run?" with "because it wants to be captured in a beautiful photo." Rounds were cut from 15 photos to 10 after playtesting. She cut interaction gimmicks and varied poses and expressions for time. Her workflow started with the UI layout, then the core loop, tested in small steps. Her mistake was adding multiplayer last despite its importance. Prompts improved once she stated her deadline and abilities and asked the AI only to review her plan for gaps and risks. Character movement, physics and skills worked quickly; the UI needed dozens of iterations, since she had to type coordinates and redo a mobile layout. Because each map object took a prompt, she built her own drag-and-drop map editor, exporting positions as JSON into the game, which let her finish three maps. Official IP assets, effects and sounds were decisive; she composited Pepe onto the Yeti's running frames in Photoshop. After distributing via Verse8's one-button link, feedback led to a shutter countdown display, a 10-second countdown instead of 7, a smaller collision box, and a double jump after reviewers said the map was too high. Online PVP never worked properly, and she reported it as a bug. She described isolation during pregnancy and childcare and doubting whether she could still make things. The project, plus studying alongside a streamer's live broadcasts, helped her recover. She advises others to try something small they wanted to do, since going out aimlessly did not help her. Her plans include a photo-sharing board, rankings, poses and expressions, possible Season 2 entry, and a new solo-friendly, replayable project. She found promotion as hard as development, and said development went from longing before she tried it to curiosity after.

As summer ends, interns face the question of whether they will get a return offer. The job market feels more competitive than usual, and AI adds uncertainty about what companies want, but much of the advice for proving yourself early in a career hasn't changed. Former interns from companies like Google and Tinder who turned internships into full-time offers repeatedly named four lessons. First, show eagerness to learn. Curiosity remains a key trait executives look for. Former Google intern Victoria Rozanska said continuous learning and openness to feedback were critical to her success. Ryan Stewart, who interned at Tinder and later became a full-time brand manager, was initially nervous about approaching senior leaders but found that leading with curiosity made people receptive. Asking questions is also part of learning the job. Kevin Gutierrez, a recent Columbia University graduate who interned at AWS and was later offered a full-time position, said interns should gain a deep understanding of their assigned projects, which makes the work easier. Second, build relationships. Nancy Qi, who spent three summers at Google before receiving a full-time offer, ate lunch with colleagues daily, which created "team chemistry" and motivated her. Interns should also connect beyond their immediate team; Stewart scheduled one-on-one meetings with senior directors to learn about the business. Even if you don't stay at the company, such connections make an internship less intimidating and build your network. Former Google intern Tawfiq Mohammad said it's good to network with people farther along in their careers. Third, take initiative. Speaking up can be intimidating for the least experienced person in the room, but that is more reason to use your voice. Former Tinder intern Taylor Wong said her Gen Z perspective became an asset because colleagues wanted to hear from that demographic, and she urged interns to "lean into that superpower." Interns should also own their projects; Mohammad advised trying to own a project "from A to Z." Eric Brandon Kam, who received a Tinder offer, said he shared his own perspective on how to engineer projects to prioritize both user outcome and long-term code health rather than just implementing tickets. Fourth, keep track of your work and wins, preparing before the return-offer conversation. Lydia Lam, who completed three Google internships before joining full time, recommended "producing a lot of artifacts," such as designs and projects, to demonstrate skills and impact. Qi wrote weekly notes on what she was stuck on and accomplished, then included screenshots and links to them in her end-of-summer reflection, showing effort and her problem-solving process. Stewart went further: he spent his internship identifying gaps in the business and pitched his own full-time role at the end, reasoning that the worst answer was "no" and he had nothing to lose.

Amazon's e-commerce business is redesigning its cloud setup as power and data center capacity grow scarcer, according to internal planning documents obtained by Business Insider. The multiyear effort, known internally as "Region Flex," aims to reduce the concentration of Amazon's online retail operations in a handful of large AWS regions and run systems across more locations at a smaller scale. Plans include shrinking the e-commerce footprint in major AWS hubs such as Northern Virginia and Dublin, Ireland. The AI boom has triggered an industrywide scramble for power and computing capacity. Amazon says it added more capacity globally than any other company last year, yet CEO Andy Jassy said last month that AWS still can't build capacity fast enough to meet demand. Region Flex may not have started because of power constraints, but the documents show they have become a driving force. One planning document from last year said online retail teams were moving infrastructure out of Dublin "to mitigate expansion risk due to AWS power constraints." A grocery team document said Region Flex was required to meet "projected capacity requirements in each region." The logistics organization described it as dividing its service architecture footprint so it could run in more AWS regions at a smaller scale, closer to customers. Amazon's most senior leaders are tracking the initiative. The grocery business called it an "S-Team goal," with more than 100 software migrations planned, and the documents say it also improves resilience during AWS disruptions. Industry conditions are tight: CBRE reported that vacancy rates in North America's largest data center markets fell to a record 1.4% at the end of 2025, pushing data centers into smaller markets where power can be secured faster. In October, Amazon said it had added more than 3.8 gigawatts of data center capacity over the prior year, doubling its cloud scale since 2022, and expects to roughly double its power capacity again by the end of 2027. Dublin is a key focus. Ireland became one of Europe's biggest data center markets, straining its electricity system. An internal plan from last year called for cutting the e-commerce operation's Dublin footprint by 40% through migrations and deprecations in 2025, and contemplated leaving Dublin fully by the end of 2026 and the Northern Virginia and Oregon regions by 2029. Workloads are being spread across regions including Frankfurt and Zaragoza, Spain. This can cost more. One document said some services moving from Dublin to those regions could see infrastructure costs rise 10% to 15% because distribution reduces hosting efficiency, and Amazon estimated $90 million in one-time Region Flex spending in 2025. Capacity limits persist as well: constraints in Zaragoza meant the organization planned to move only 65% of its remaining infrastructure costs there, leaving 35% in Dublin. An Amazon spokesperson confirmed Region Flex but said internal documents don't always reflect current plans and called some timelines and details "not accurate." The spokesperson said evolving infrastructure is nothing new and that using more regions gives the retail business flexibility to meet demand, improve reliability, manage costs and bring services closer to customers. Jassy called power the "single biggest constraint" last year and said demand will keep outstripping supply. "Even at that amount, we will still not have enough capacity to meet all the demand we have in 2026," he said, expecting the same in 2027.

Video game streaming giant Twitch has introduced a setting that allows users to opt out of Amazon using their channel content to train generative AI models, more than two years after a company executive publicly confirmed the practice. Ars Technica reports that Twitch announced the AI opt out option on Wednesday through an updated support page. The streaming platform, which Amazon acquired in 2014, confirmed that user content may be used to train what it calls Amazon’s “generative AI content models” unless users take action to opt out. The support page specifies the types of content covered by the policy. Users who do not opt out agree that their “streams, VODs, clips, stream chats, and pictures and text on your channel [may] be used in future training of a model developed by Amazon whose purpose is to generate or synthesize text, audio, images, or video.” How to Opt Out. - Navigate to the security section of Twitch settings by clicking here. You may be required to sign in to your account. - Scroll down to “Training for Generative AI” and disable the feature. - Confirm the change by navigating to another section of setting and returning to security. Your screen should look like the screenshot below. Twitch’s support page explains what permitting the training entails: “When you allow training, that means that your content may be used for future Gen AI model improvements. An example of what happens when you allow your content to be used for training a Gen AI content model is that your audio might help refine models that create speech to text, which would help improve captions at Twitch but would also help improve captions across Amazon.” Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has faced critcism from users for not spreading the announcement via his own platform. The new opt-out option arrives well after Amazon’s use of Twitch content for AI training became public knowledge. Twitch users are automatically enrolled in the training program and appear to have been for at least a couple of years. At a 2024 event hosted by the news publication The Information, Twitch’s chief monetization officer at the time, Mike Minton, was asked whether Amazon uses Twitch to train AI models. He replied, “Yeah, for sure.” He added: “I mean, I think obviously within the bounds of user trust within the bounds of privacy regulations, which vary all around the world, but of course we have a role to play in that.” The structure of the new control matters to how it will function in practice. Because enrollment is automatic, every Twitch user who does not visit the security settings page and change the default will continue to have their content available for training. Opt-in-by-default arrangements tend to preserve the status quo, since many users never review or adjust account settings. That design, combined with the length of time the training appears to have occurred without a clear way to decline it, may leave some users doubtful about Amazon’s approach to user-generated content. The company now offers a formal mechanism for withholding consent going forward, but the policy does not address content already used to train models before the opt-out became available. Lucas Nolan is a reporter for Breitbart News covering issues of AI, free speech, and online censorship.

Internal records obtained by WIRED through Freedom of Information Act requests to CBP's Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) and the DHS Office of Inspector General show that, from 2009 through 2022, US Customs and Border Protection employees and contractors were accused of abusing sensitive government databases for non-work reasons. The hundreds of allegations include looking up romantic interests, monitoring family members, exposing personal information and, in some cases, giving intelligence to suspected smugglers or drug-trafficking organizations. Examples include a CBP officer who allegedly used databases to contact a flight attendant, an officer accused of using trusted-traveler applications to ask people out, employees accused of providing border-crossing data to someone in a "heated divorce," and a DHS employee who allegedly used ad-tech-derived location data to track coworkers' phones, apparently the first known internal abuse case involving DHS use of such data. Laura Rivera of Just Futures Law said CBP has a long history of impunity and that data abuse is another aspect of it. Of almost 300 data-related entries WIRED identified, 138 were referred to CBP management, 78 were assigned to OPR criminal investigators, and 43 were "Information Only" with no OPR investigation. Smaller numbers fell into other categories, and CBP withheld 21 cases citing active law-enforcement proceedings. Ninety-nine entries involved alleged breaches or unauthorized disclosures and 48 involved improper queries; many breaches occurred around 2020, when pandemic remote work led employees to email files to personal accounts. At least six entries describe employees querying themselves. Former OPR head Daniel Altman said self-queries are a warning sign of future corruption, as employees may test whether searches are monitored or whether they are under investigation. Other cases: in 2010 a customs officer allegedly pulled data on an Air New Zealand flight attendant to contact them; in 2017 an officer faced an OPR investigation for allegedly harassing an airline employee, and another was accused of querying neighbors; in 2022 an employee allegedly obtained an ex-husband's leave schedule to harass him. More serious were a 2016 OPR investigation into an employee allegedly giving database information to a drug-trafficking organization and a 2021 accusation that a Border Patrol agent advised smugglers which border lane to use. Most resolutions were withheld or blank, so it is unclear how often allegations were substantiated or discipline imposed. Altman attributed missing fields to data-entry problems in the case management system. A CBP spokesperson said the agency takes misconduct seriously and that appropriate investigatory, corrective, and disciplinary action is taken. The records come as DHS has built one of the world's largest surveillance systems, including the Enforcement Integrated Database, TECS, the Central Index System, SENTRI, Palantir's Investigative Case Management system and FALCON, and Thomson Reuters' CLEAR. Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app released in May 2025, has been reported used against people engaged in protest. CBP also uses mobile-extraction tools from Cellebrite, Grayshift, and Magnet Forensics. Commercially purchased location data lets government avoid warrants; a 2023 DHS inspector general report found CBP, ICE, and the Secret Service bought it without fully complying with privacy rules. Rivera also cited license plate readers and a Flock Safety scandal in which local officers' camera access assisted ICE and CBP. WIRED found ICE and CBP spent about $515 million on products from firms like Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Palantir, and Cellebrite has taken more than $56 million in federal contracts this year.

Synergy Network Announces Aegis, a Post-Quantum Cryptographic Framework for Its Layer-1 Blockchain. By building key rotation, credential revocation, and cryptographic migration into the network from launch, Synergy says Aegis can adapt to new post-quantum standards without disrupting apps. Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA, August 13th, 2026,. Synergy Network, a Layer-1 blockchain project, has announced Aegis, a cryptographic authority framework built to secure the network against future quantum computing threats. Aegis is designed to manage core security functions including post-quantum identities, signature schemes, key establishment, key rotation, credential revocation, and cryptographic migration. The framework is built directly into Synergy's base architecture rather than added as a later upgrade. According to the project, this approach allows the network to change cryptographic methods, rotate keys, revoke compromised credentials, and migrate to new standards without disrupting applications built on the network. Architecture Overview. Synergy Network separates its core functions across distinct systems. Consensus determines the canonical network history. Aegis, as the cryptographic authority layer, manages identities and signatures. A protected transaction processing layer is designed to reduce information advantages before execution. Execution environments govern what applications are permitted to do. Cross-chain systems manage evidence and settlement involving external networks. The project states that this separation of responsibilities is intended to distribute security functions across multiple systems rather than relying on a single mechanism. Each component operates independently, so an issue in one system does not directly compromise the function of another. Aegis Capabilities. Aegis is designed to handle a defined set of cryptographic operations across the network's lifecycle. These include issuing post-quantum identities for network participants, managing signature schemes used to authorize transactions, and establishing keys used in validator and application communication. The framework also includes processes for key rotation on a scheduled or triggered basis, revocation of credentials found to be compromised, and migration paths for moving accounts and applications to updated cryptographic standards as they become available. Synergy states that these functions are intended to operate without requiring users to manually update wallets or applications each time an underlying cryptographic standard changes. Industry Context. Cryptographic infrastructure across the blockchain industry has largely been built on algorithms designed before large-scale quantum computing was a practical consideration. Migrating existing networks to new cryptographic standards after deployment typically requires coordination among validators, application developers, and wallet providers. Synergy Network states that its architecture was designed to reduce the scope of that coordination problem by building migration and key rotation processes into the network from launch, rather than treating them as a later addition. Background. Blockchain networks rely on cryptographic proofs to verify transaction authorization and account control. Unlike centralized systems, which can reset credentials or update login infrastructure with limited disruption, blockchain assets typically remain tied to the same cryptographic keys for extended periods. Synergy Network states that Aegis was developed to address this structural characteristic by building cryptographic adaptability into the network from launch. About SNRG. SNRG is the native coin of the Synergy Network ecosystem. It is used for network transactions, validator participation, staking, and governance. SNRG also supports decentralized application activity, smart contract execution, liquidity infrastructure, coin launches on the network, and cross-chain operations between Synergy and external blockchains. About Synergy Network. Synergy Network is a Layer-1 blockchain built around a post-quantum security architecture. The network's design incorporates cryptographic agility, consensus, protected transaction processing, execution environments, and cross-chain infrastructure as separate, coordinated systems, with the goal of supporting long-term cryptographic durability as computing capabilities advance. More information about Synergy Network is available at synergy-network.io. Synergy Network Team.

Surprise, surprise: CBP officers are misusing surveillance tech. Agents reportedly used electronic databases to spy on family members and even provide intelligence to drug traffickers. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents have reportedly misused electronic databases to spy on family members, try to get dates and even provide intelligence to suspected drug traffickers, according to freedom of information (FOIA) files seen by Wired. Officers allegedly abused databases that can draw from sources like license plate readers, facial recognition and smartphone searches to violate the privacy of numerous individuals. The FOIA files, ranging from 2009 to 20222, show a number of troubling incidents. A CBP officer is alleged to have used a government database to contact a flight attendant, and another was accused of using data from trusted-traveler applications to ask people out. One employee provided border-crossing data to someone involved in a divorce, and another abused internal policies by tracking coworkers cellphones with ad-tech-derived location data. Of 300 incidents tracked by Wired, 138 were referred to CBP management and 78 assigned to criminal investigators, while 43 others weren't investigated. Many of the claims were handled internally or put under the category of minor misconduct, but 21 were withheld due to potential law-enforcement proceedings that suggest criminal misconduct were involved. The report is noteworthy because the DHS has more access to private citizens' data than ever before and has built one of the largest surveillance systems in the world, Wired noted. Its sources include records on immigration arrests, border screening records, naturalization applications and the SENTRI trusted-traveler program. The agency also has access to Palantir's ICM and FALCON systems, along with the DHS Mobile Fortify facial-recognition app deployed on agents phones. CBP told Wired that it takes misconduct allegations seriously and works to "uphold the rule of law and hold ourselves accountable... [and takes] appropriate investigatory, corrective, and disciplinary action."

The world’s largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown, which boasts an impressive 106-foot wingspan, has just completed its maiden flight in the US, at just USD five worth of electricity. Developed by Heart Aerospace, the X1 demonstrator lifted off from Plattsburgh International Airport in New York on Wednesday, August 12. The piloted aircraft remained in the skies for about 27 minutes and made it to a 1,100-foot altitude above ground level (AGL). According to the Swedish aerospace company, the aircraft has a wingspan of 106 feet (32 meters). It’s additionally 76 feet (23 meters) long and has a takeoff weight exceeding 25,000 lbs (11,340 kilograms). It reportedly delivered more than one megawatt (MW) of power during the flight. The electricity it used for the entire mission cost no more than five dollars. “With the first flight of X1, Heart Aerospace has demonstrated electric flight at the scale of a commercial airliner,” Anders Forslund, Heart Aerospace founder and CEO, pointed out. The five-dollar flight. The debut flight was carried out under an FAA Special Airworthiness Certificate in the Experimental Category (SAC-EC). The test profile included taxi, takeoff, climb, maneuvering, as well as landing. Forslund said that they designed the X1 to show that electric propulsion can work in an aircraft that is large enough for commercial airline operations. The plane is a demonstrator representative of Heart’s ES-30 production aircraft, that is currently being developed. See All. The ES-30 is envisioned as a conventional fixed-wing and hybrid-electric regional airliner. It will be able to carry up to 30 passengers and is targeted to enter service in 2031. The company is currently developing the first pre-production ES-30 at its pilot manufacturing plant in Los Angeles. Flight testing is scheduled to begin in 2028. The United Airlines, Air Canada, and JSX have already made commitments for the aircraft. “Electric commercial aircraft have the potential to fundamentally reshape airline economics and, ultimately, lower the cost of air travel for passengers,” Forslund said. “This is at the heart of our vision for abundant air travel, with electrification enabling more affordable, frequent, and cleaner air service to and from airports closer to home.” Cheaper regional flights. Research suggests that hydrogen and electric propulsion are the best options for making aviation more sustainable. Electric propulsion has been found to greatly reduce water vapor and nitrogen oxide emissions, which are linked to increased radiative forcing. It can also cut noise around airports and inside aircraft. Forslund expects the ES-30 to slash aircraft operating costs by more than 40 percent in comparison with legacy regional aircraft. The savings are set to come from lower energy costs, simpler maintenance, and greater aircraft reliability. For its maiden journey, the X1 relied solely on battery power. It used around USD five worth of electricity. For comparison, global jet fuel prices averaged USD 3.5 per gallon during the first week of August. This represents a 63-percent increase from 2025. Benn Stabler, Heart Aerospace’s CTO, said that the X1 gave the firm the ability to design, build, test, operate, and continuously refine commercial aircraft. “We are carrying that full-stack capability directly into the ES-30, our first production aircraft and the foundation of a broader technology platform for electric airliners,” Stabler concluded in a press release.

Meta is launching an optional Scam Alert feature on WhatsApp that uses on-device machine learning to flag suspicious messages. Earlier this year, Meta also launched scam detection for device linking requests on WhatsApp. The new Scam Alert feature, which is rolling out in a limited beta, shows users a warning if a chat seems like a scam: Meta adds AI screening to detect WhatsApp scams. An AI model on your phone can try to determine if you’re getting scammed. If the model identifies a message as a likely scam attempt, the user sees a warning in the chat, which is not visible to the other person. From there, the user can decide what to do: block, report, or continue the conversation. If they decide that a warning is incorrectly flagged, the user can mark the chat as trusted, in which case the warning is removed and Scam Alert will not flag that chat again. If a user marks that they trust a chat, they can also opt in to share the last 5 messages received with WhatsApp to help improve the feature’s accuracy. With more than 3 billion users, WhatsApp is among the largest areas of scam activity, like wire transfers and pig butchering scams. The FTC said victims reported losing $425 million to scams via WhatsApp alone, out of more than $2.1 billion lost to social media scams in 2025. Meta says “no message content leaves the user device for classification” when its scam detection feature is turned on and nothing is “auto-reported to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else.” Users can also turn off Scam Alert at any time.

The author likes repurposing old hardware for a home lab, but Android phones have become harder to use. Modern apps cause problems on rooted devices, and the custom ROM scene has dried up for no-name brands. Leaving root aside, some tools let FOSS services run on smartphones; as long as containers needing privileged ports are avoided, most of the author's self-hosted stack can run on an old phone. The author first used Termux, which they were already hooked on from emulating PC games on Android with Mobox. PRoot lets Termux run Linux flavors, and simple CLI tools like BentoPDF.sh ran fine in Debian and Fedora PRoot environments. Most tools in LinuxServer's PRoot apps repository worked out of the box, and a couple of repos allowed running Nextcloud and other services directly on Termux. However, Docker or Podman containers are not feasible on Termux without rooting, which prevented deploying most of the application stack. The author chose not to root their old Poco M6 Pro (4G variant). The phone has MediaTek's proprietary source code and limited kernel releases, so none of the custom ROMs available are actively maintained. Since the Shizuku + Canta combo already removes bloatware, the former main reason for rooting, there is no reason to risk bricking a phone that still works. Podroid fills the container gap. Rather than PRoot, it runs a full virtual machine built on Alpine Linux that already ships with Docker, Podman, and LXCs, so no runtime configuration is needed. Deployment uses a menu-based interface. To reach web UIs, the author had to run podroid-forward add android_port vm_port or add port mappings in Settings. The main limitation is that Podroid does not support network mapping for system ports, so Pi-hole and other services needing ports under 1024 won't work. Podroid offers several conveniences. Allocated resources other than storage can be changed through Settings toggles. USB passthrough lets old USB adapters be paired with containers in the VM. It supports SSH access and sharing the phone's Downloads folder with the virtual guests. A backup facility exports container images and data to the phone so tools can be redeployed if experiments break the VM, and an X11 desktop avoids configuring many packages for GUI-heavy apps. On performance, the author first allocated 2GB RAM and 4 CPU cores to the Alpine VM, then raised RAM to 4GB to be safe. This runs BentoPDF (the web UI-based app), ConvertX, n8n, BeaverHabits, and nearly a dozen other apps without issues. The author concedes Podroid cannot replace a dedicated home server for every project. Pi-hole and other apps needing privileged ports are one example, as are Raspberry Pi projects that need GPIO pins for sensor modules. For simple FOSS containers used in everyday tasks, though, the Podman and Docker containers on the phone-powered Podroid instance are reliable.

Crypto group backs Custodia in Supreme Court battle over Fed access. The Blockchain Association argues the Fed should not have broad discretion to deny eligible state-chartered banks direct access to its payment system. The Blockchain Association urged the US Supreme Court to hear Custodia Bank’s challenge to the Federal Reserve’s denial of its application for a master account, which would give the crypto-focused bank direct access to the Fed’s payment system. In an amicus brief filed Wednesday, the industry group argued that federal law requires the central bank to make its payment services available to eligible nonmember banks and that the Fed should not have broad discretion to deny access. The association said the appeals court’s decision effectively gives the Fed veto power over state-chartered banks by allowing it to withhold services needed to operate independently. It also linked Custodia’s case to alleged crypto debanking under “Operation Choke Point 2.0,” arguing that federal regulators discouraged banks from serving the digital asset industry. Custodia, a Wyoming-chartered bank focused on digital assets, applied for a Fed master account in 2020, seeking direct access to the central bank’s payment services without relying on an intermediary bank. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City denied Custodia’s application in 2023, and the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals later ruled that the regional Fed bank had discretion to reject its request. In March, the appeals court voted 7-3 against rehearing the case, leaving the Supreme Court as Custodia’s only remaining avenue for review. The Blockchain Association said the Tenth Circuit interpreted the Fed’s authority too broadly, potentially allowing it to deny payment-system access to eligible state-chartered banks serving the crypto industry. Blockchain Association backs Custodia’s Supreme Court petition. Source: US Supreme Court filing. Crypto companies push deeper into US banking. Custodia’s challenge comes as other crypto companies are gaining greater access to the US banking system, including federal charters and, in one case, direct access to Federal Reserve payment rails. In March, Kraken Financial became the first crypto banking unit to receive a limited-purpose master account from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, giving it direct access to Fedwire. The approval contrasts with Custodia’s rejection by the same regional Fed bank in 2023. In April, Coinbase received conditional approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to establish a national trust company, bringing its custody business under federal oversight without allowing it to take retail deposits or operate as a commercial bank. Circle received final OCC approval for its national trust bank in July, while Kraken parent Payward applied for its own national trust company charter the following month. The OCC also conditionally approved national trust bank applications from Ripple, BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets and Paxos in December. The trend has drawn resistance from traditional banking groups. The Independent Community Bankers of America opposed Coinbase’s approval in April, arguing that crypto companies are seeking the benefits of bank charters without being subject to the full regulatory framework applied to traditional banks. In brief. - The Blockchain Association filed an amicus brief supporting Custodia Bank’s petition for Supreme Court review. - Custodia is challenging a ruling that upheld the Fed’s denial of its master account application. - The group says the case could shape how much power federal regulators have over state-chartered banks. The Blockchain Association is urging the Supreme Court to take up Custodia Bank’s fight with the Federal Reserve, arguing the central bank should not have the broad power to deny payment system access to eligible state-chartered banks. In the amicus brief filed on Wednesday supporting Custodia’s petition, the crypto trade group said a lower court ruling in favor of the Fed gives federal regulators a quiet way to cut lawful businesses out of the banking system. "The decision ratifies the Fed’s misuse of its payment services to further an impermissible policy goal—debanking the digital-asset industry,” the Blockchain Association wrote. An amicus brief is a legal filing from someone who is not a party to a case but wants to give the court additional arguments or context. Here, the Blockchain Association is supporting Custodia’s request that the Supreme Court review the dispute. At issue is Custodia’s bid for a Federal Reserve “master account.” Custodia is a so-called crypto bank based in Wyoming, offering services including digital-asset custody, payments and settlement infrastructure, and dollar-backed stablecoin-related products to institutional clients. It has spent years seeking a master account, which would allow it to settle payments directly with the central bank. In October, an appeals panel ruled that eligibility alone did not entitle Custodia to an account. In December, the bank asked the full Tenth Circuit to rehear the case. The Blockchain Association argues the Fed’s denial threatens the dual banking system, where both state and federal authorities can charter banks. If the ruling stands, the association says, federal regulators could override state banking decisions by denying access to the payments system. “Whether federal regulators, based on their own discretionary whims, can intrude on state prerogatives and debank lawful businesses is a question of exceptional importance with broad consequences for the national economy,” they wrote. The brief said Custodia’s fight is the latest phase of Operation Choke Point 2.0, invoking the Obama and Biden-era program critics said pressured banks to cut ties with unfavorable industries. “In a well-documented campaign termed Operation Choke Point 2.0, the federal government under the prior administration ‘used vague rules, excessive discretion, informal guidance, and aggressive enforcement actions to pressure banks away from serving digital asset clients’ and engaging with digital assets,” the brief said. While the Supreme Court has not agreed to hear the case, for now, the brief asks the justices to decide how much control the Fed should have over access to the U.S. payments system.

Drone delivery is now allowed in some places, with companies like Wing and Zipline bringing hot meals in under 10 minutes. Drones are faster and usually more efficient than sending a car and driver to deliver a single item. The technology was supposed to be common years ago; Jeff Bezos told "60 Minutes" he expected Amazon to be sending out drone deliveries by 2017, yet most people still don't have it. Adam Thierer, author of "Permissionless Innovation," blames "confusing regulations." The Federal Aviation Administration says drones may not fly "beyond visual line of sight" without special authorization. To fly farther, a company needs airline-level certification: the FAA must inspect its facilities, review operating and maintenance procedures, and certify it as an air carrier. Thierer says even a company with Amazon's size and resources finds it hard to get these limited permits. Because permission is so difficult to obtain, only eight companies now do drone deliveries. Some people don't want drones delivering near them. Some worry about privacy and cameras "spying"; Amazon says its drones use cameras and other sensors to navigate, sense and avoid obstacles. A bigger problem is noise, though companies like Wing say they are making drones quieter. Thierer notes that people have grown used to delivery trucks in their driveways, which would once have seemed strange, and that a drone descending from high above could be quieter than a truck. New technologies often seem intrusive at first, as cars and trains did; when trains were introduced, some people believed women's bodies were not designed to go 50 miles an hour. Thierer expects people to freak out a little about drones, then get used to them and bring them into their lives. President Donald Trump signed an executive order, more than a year ago, telling the FAA to fast-track drone deliveries by allowing flights beyond line of sight. The FAA did not respond for months and has now offered only a proposed change, with no clear date for when, or if, it will take effect. Still, there is some movement and experimentation. Thierer warns that if America slows down, the Chinese will "step on the gas," having allowed a vibrant drone marketplace to develop despite being communists. The author, John Stossel, praises Amazon, DoorDash Air, Wing, Zipline, DEXA and other drone delivery companies for taking risks to advance the technology.

CBP Workers Reportedly Used Government Databases To Track Exes and Romantic Interests. The documents were acquired through Freedom of Information Act requests to CBP and the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General, and cover more than a decade of allegations. U.S. Customs and Border Protection employees and contractors have been accused of using powerful government databases to look up romantic interests, former partners, neighbors, and coworkers, while other cases involved allegations that sensitive information was passed to suspected smugglers and drug traffickers. The documents were acquired by Wired through Freedom of Information Act requests to CBP's Office of Professional Responsibility and the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General, and cover more than a decade of allegations, from 2009 through 2022. The outlet identified nearly 300 data-related entries. Of those, 138 were referred to CBP management for review, and 78 were assigned to criminal investigators with the Office of Professional Responsibility. Another 43 were categorized as "Information Only," meaning OPR did not open its own investigation. The allegations range from personal snooping to potentially serious corruption. In one 2010 case, a customs officer allegedly searched for information about an Air New Zealand flight attendant and then used the information to contact the person. Another officer was investigated in 2017 after allegedly misusing government databases to harass an airline employee. Other employees allegedly searched for information about neighbors and former spouses. In a 2022 case, an employee was accused of using a CBP database to obtain an ex-husband's leave schedule as part of an alleged harassment campaign. Trusted-traveler information was also allegedly exploited. According to the records, an officer was accused in 2013 of accessing SENTRI applications, which contain personal and travel information from prescreened travelers, to ask people out. The records do not establish that every allegation was substantiated. Many cases were closed without publicly available information explaining their outcomes, and resolution fields were frequently blank or withheld. CBP told Wired that privacy laws restrict what it can disclose about individual cases, but said allegations of misconduct are investigated and can result in corrective or disciplinary action. Some allegations went far beyond personal curiosity. In 2016, investigators examined an accusation that a CBP employee was providing database information to a drug-trafficking organization. In another case from 2021, a Border Patrol agent was accused of running database searches to tell smugglers which lane they should use at the border. WIRED also identified 99 entries involving alleged breaches or unauthorized disclosures and 48 explicitly involving improper database queries. At least six cases involved employees searching for themselves, something former OPR chief Daniel Altman told the publication investigators viewed as a possible warning sign because self-searches have surfaced in corruption cases. CBP and other immigration authorities can draw on systems containing travel records, immigration files, fingerprints, watch lists, and other personal information. Their tools have expanded to include facial recognition, license-plate information, mobile-device extraction technology and commercially acquired location data. A separate 2023 DHS inspector general investigation found that CBP, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Secret Service had purchased and used commercial telemetry data without fully complying with department privacy policies or establishing adequate policies governing its use. One internal case involved a DHS employee who allegedly used private software to track the locations of several coworkers' cell phones, apparently marking the first publicly reported internal abuse case involving DHS personnel and commercially obtained mobile location data.

Companies such as Microsoft, Meta and Amazon Web Services are pouring money into expanding AI data centers nationally, but the buildout carries environmental costs: fossil fuels used for power and heavy strain on the electric grid. Politicians and community organizers are pushing back, and a coalition of states has placed moratoriums on AI data centers. Tom's Guide interviewed Balaji Tammabattula, an AI infrastructure engineering expert and COO of BaRupOn, about the backlash. Tammabattula says the backlash was inevitable because the industry focused on how quickly compute could be built, not on what was needed to support it. When a data center demands hundreds of megawatts of electricity, water and infrastructure, residents rightly ask what it means for them. He argues communities are not simply resistant to development; they want to understand the tradeoffs, such as effects on electricity rates, competition for water, emergency services, roads and opportunities for their children. He describes his own project, LAMP in Texas, as a different approach. It is developing dedicated behind-the-meter power generation so the campus does not depend on existing community grid capacity. It plans large-scale rainwater harvesting, with the site potentially capturing more than 500 million gallons, along with a fire station and support for local emergency response, plus STEM education and skills development for local young people. The guiding question, he says, should be what infrastructure developers can build and leave behind, not what resources they can take. Tammabattula views moratoriums and permitting pauses as a signal to change the development model rather than opposition to technology. They should force the industry to build better projects, not simply find easier places to build. He defines "Responsible Compute" practically: a developer that consumes enormous power should help create it, one that uses water needs a responsible water strategy, one that changes demands on local infrastructure and emergency services should invest in them, and one bringing billions of dollars of technology should create pathways for residents to share in the economic opportunity. It is not a certification or slogan, he says, but the idea that AI infrastructure should strengthen the place where it is built. On trust, he says it comes not from press releases but from specific answers about power sources, water sources, emergency response, local infrastructure and opportunities for residents, given early. Listening matters, since community concerns can reveal things that should have been in the plan, and engagement should help shape a project rather than follow its design. On electricity demand, he says the assumption that every new gigawatt of compute can become demand on the existing grid cannot continue. Developers must become part of the energy solution, and energy and data-center development will increasingly converge. Policymakers should create regulatory pathways that recognize and accelerate projects that bring their own generation, transmission or other infrastructure. If the US keeps prioritizing speed over responsibility, he warns, more fights over resources will bring more moratoriums, permitting delays and political opposition. He sees speed and responsibility as complementary: building power, water strategy, community infrastructure and local talent alongside compute lets America keep scaling AI without hitting a wall, and could become a competitive advantage.

Hot on the heels of a confirmed WhatsApp scam attack campaign that doesn’t require your password to access your account, Meta has announced it is starting to roll out new protections for WhatsApp users by way of an optional Scam Alert feature powered by an on-device machine learning model. “The feature complements end-to-end encryption while enabling a user-controlled, optional scam alert when the model believes there’s a likely scam,” Meta said in an August 12 engineering team announcement. Scam Alert is currently being rolled out in a limited Beta, and Meta has confirmed it is working with the WhatsApp bug bounty community to stress-test the feature. There is no word yet on when the feature might become available to a wider audience, or on how users can sign up for the limited Beta test program. Here’s what we do know. How The New WhatsApp Scam Attack Feature Works. Scam protections are something that most communications platforms are working hard to implement in the face of continuing threats. Google recently announced “fake call detection” that verifies the legitimacy of the call as long as both parties are using Phone by Google, and already has an AI-powered scam detection feature for Android users. This employs AI to provide real-time warnings and analyze calls and messages, but the conversations themselves remain private, as the AI processing is all done right there on the device itself. Now Meta is taking a similar route with its Scam Alert functionality for WhatsApp users. “No message content leaves the device for classification or is auto-reported to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else,” the engineering team stated. This is thanks to it being relatively simple in terms of such models, small enough to run on any device without any server-side components being required. The Scam Alert is entirely optional, but once enabled, it downloads the machine learning model to the device. From there, it “runs inferences to classify whether incoming messages from non-contacts match known scam patterns.” These patterns are those the AI has trained on using scams that users have reported to WhatsApp. Meta said that the probabilistic classification is based on conversational structure and linguistic signals, and that no content needs to be automatically reported to anyone for the feature to be effective. If triggered, Scam Alert issues, erm, an alert. This warning is not visible to the sender, and the user can opt to block, report or continue. “If they decide that a warning is incorrectly flagged,” Meta said, “the user can mark the chat as trusted, in which case the warning is removed, and Scam Alert will not flag that chat again.” Scam Alert is another slice in what is known as the Swiss Cheese security model. This defense-in-depth approach works by layering slices of Swiss cheese on top of each other. The holes are random in position and size, so the more layers there are, the harder it becomes for a threat to find its way through the stack. Other layers already in place for WhatsApp users include a recent security tools update that can alert users to potential device linking code attacks, as well as the optional Strict Account Settings configuration that automatically silences unknown calls, blocks attachments from unknown users and prevents link previews.

The Blockchain Association filed an amicus brief on Wednesday urging the US Supreme Court to hear Custodia Bank’s challenge to the Federal Reserve’s denial of a master account, arguing that federal law requires the Fed to make its payment services available to eligible nonmember depository institutions and that regional Reserve Banks should not have broad discretion to refuse. Custodia, a Wyoming-chartered special purpose depository institution, applied for a master account in 2020. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City rejected the application in 2023, and the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals later ruled the regional Fed bank had discretion to deny the request — the ruling Custodia is now asking the Supreme Court to review. A master account would let Custodia settle payments directly with the central bank rather than routing through an intermediary bank, along with access to Fedwire and, depending on account type, interest on reserves held at the Fed. The Blockchain Association’s brief frames the stakes beyond Custodia specifically: allowing the appeals court’s ruling to stand, the group argues, would give the Fed effectively unchecked power to exclude any lawful industry from the payment system through administrative discretion rather than a defined legal standard. The Kansas City Fed is due to respond to Custodia’s petition by September 11. The case is harder to frame as a simple story of crypto being locked out of the banking system, because another Wyoming-chartered crypto bank has already gotten through the same door. Blockhead reported in March that Kraken Financial secured its own Fed master account, becoming the first crypto-native institution in US history to hold one — a “skinny” account that excludes interest on reserves but still grants direct Fedwire settlement access. Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi framed the approval as the convergence of crypto infrastructure and sovereign financial rails; Custodia, notably, congratulated Kraken publicly on the approval while noting it would continue pursuing its own master account in parallel with expanding bank partnerships. That divergence is the actual legal question at the heart of Custodia’s petition: if one similarly chartered, similarly regulated crypto bank can get a master account and another can’t, is that a legitimate exercise of case-by-case Fed discretion, or evidence the discretion itself has no real legal limit and is being applied inconsistently. The Blockchain Association’s brief is explicit that it isn’t arguing for special treatment — it wants the Court to clarify the boundary of Fed discretion under the Monetary Control Act for any eligible institution, crypto or not. That framing matters because Custodia’s case is now proceeding alongside a broader shift Blockhead has tracked all year: Circle, Ripple, BitGo, Fidelity Digital Assets, and Paxos have all secured conditional trust or banking approvals of varying kinds, without needing a master account specifically. A Supreme Court ruling that narrows the Fed’s discretion would matter less for how many firms are already operating inside the banking system than for how predictable that path becomes for the next one — replacing a process each firm currently has to litigate or negotiate individually with a clearer legal standard everyone can plan around.

LG Teams With NVIDIA For AI Factory Transformation And GR00T Humanoid. LG has announced a major strategic collaboration with NVIDIA focused on industrial automation and advanced robotics. The partnership centers around two core initiatives: accelerating AI-driven factory transformation and developing next-generation bipedal robotics powered by NVIDIA's Isaac GR00T open reasoning humanoid foundation platform. The two tech giants signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) at NVIDIA's headquarters. As part of the agreement, LG will validate LG CLOiD wheel-based robots at its washing machine manufacturing line in Tennessee, as well as build AI factory reference sites using NVIDIA's DSX and Vera Rubin hardware, and tap NVIDIA's DRIVE Hyperion tech to develop a next-gen AI-defined vehicle platform. NVIDIA and LG are expanding their collaboration to accelerate the next wave of physical AI. Building on years of work together, @JensenHuang and LG Group Chairman Kwang-mo Koo are advancing joint efforts across AI factories, robotics, and autonomous vehicles — combining LG’s… pic.twitter.com/8aPC2VfhSS "The defining opportunity of physical AI is to give every machine the ability to understand the real world, reason and act safely alongside people—reshaping everyday life from the home and factory floor to the road," said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. "Building on years of collaboration, LG and NVIDIA are combining LG's leadership in product engineering and manufacturing with NVIDIA technology to accelerate the next era of robots, AI factories and autonomous vehicles." In the robotics sector, LG is actively developing a next-generation bipedal humanoid robot built with NVIDIA Isaac GR00T, which serves as an open reasoning humanoid foundation model. The bipedal machine will rely on NVIDIA Jetson Thor for onboard computing, advanced reasoning, and control, while incorporating NVIDIA Halos for Robotics to maintain robust system safety. It will also integrate "One LG" hardware capabilities across LG's various segments, utilizing actuators from LG Electronics, sensors from LG Innotek, and high-performance batteries from LG Energy Solution. If all goes to plan, LG will unveil its humanoid robot in the first quarter of 2027. Before the anticipated debut, LG plans to deploy its wheel-based CLOiD robots directly onto the washing machine manufacturing line at the aforementioned Tennessee site. Beyond robotics, LG is utilizing the NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform with plans to build an AI factory reference site powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin hardware in the first half of 2027. This will pave the way for the construction of an 80-megawatt LG AI Factory in Cheonan, South Korea, slated for completion by the first half of 2028. The expansive partnership also extends into the automotive sector. LG intends to develop a high-performance computing platform for next-generation AI-defined vehicles (AIDVs) built upon the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion platform.

Apple will release iOS 27 in September; it is currently in public beta. Alongside a focus on refinement and bug fixes, it brings many features, including a new context-aware, generative-AI Siri. Apple Intelligence powers many additions. Wallpaper "Extend" generates image content around a photo's edges to fill the Lock Screen, and also appears in Photos. Safari automatically groups open tabs into topics (enabled via Tab View) and can notify you when a watched webpage changes with "Notify Me." It can also generate extensions from a plain-language prompt. Reminders and Calendar accept natural-language input and fill in dates, times, people and locations. Shortcuts can be built by describing what you want. Passwords can use Safari to automatically update weak or compromised passwords. Flyover in Maps gets sharper, more realistic imagery for select cities, and a U.S.-only Local Lists section surfaces trending places. Photos adds Reframe, which changes a photo's perspective using spatial data plus AI fill, star ratings and keywords, a frame-grab from video, and slideshows from any album. Image Playground gets a new model on Private Cloud Compute that produces photo-realistic images for the first time, with a hidden SynthID watermark and photo-based editing. The Home app gives written summaries of HomeKit Secure Video motion alerts, but only with an iCloud+ plan of at least 2TB ($9.99/month). Siri-related changes include a new Camera "Siri" mode using Visual Intelligence to identify plants, animals, food (with calories) and more, or add flyer dates to Calendar, translate text and split bills. The Siri app can be switched to ChatGPT, though conversation context doesn't carry over. The iPhone 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max and iPhone Air get a more powerful on-device model enabling voice customization of Siri's expressiveness and pace. Accessibility gains Live Recognition, which describes surroundings and answers questions using the camera. Call Context shows relevant details, such as a reservation number from Mail, during business calls; it runs on device and doesn't analyze call audio. Other changes: Messages lets you reply inline to Android (green bubble) messages and draw sketches. Wallet passes get a Poster Generic layout with up to two quick actions, and a new Insights feature tracks spending via Connected Accounts, with broader support in the U.K. than the U.S. The Lock Screen gains a compact clock option, and a Liquid Glass opacity slider (Settings ➝ Appearance ➝ Liquid Glass) lets you make it clearer or more opaque. Compatible AirPods with the H2 chip (AirPods Pro 2, Pro 3, AirPods 4, AirPods Max 2) get a custom equalizer. Alarms and timers can have their own volume, though wake-up alarms and others with their own volume control aren't overridden. Find My supports custom location-sharing durations or an exact expiry date, and you can pause sharing silently until day's end. FaceTime gains Dual Capture, using front and back cameras at once on iPhone 17 models and iPhone Air.

The U.S. Army is moving to put autonomous ground vehicles into one of the most dangerous parts of the battlefield, selecting six companies to develop production-ready prototypes for missions that currently require soldiers to drive into exposed areas. The Infantry Last Tactical Mile (ILTM) initiative focuses on the stretch between rear support areas and the forward line of own troops (FLOT), where getting ammunition, equipment and supplies forward, or bringing casualties back, can expose personnel to enemy fire. The six selected companies are Maren-Go, Overland AI, Forterra, Hendrick’s Motorsports, American Rheinmetall and HDT. Each is expected to provide four prototype vehicles for Army testing, according to Breaking Defense, citing an Army spokesperson. Rather than simply building another remotely controlled vehicle, the Army wants systems capable of beyond-line-of-sight autonomous operation. The vehicles are intended to conduct logistical resupply, casualty evacuation and network-extension missions, potentially allowing troops to perform critical battlefield tasks without putting additional drivers or medics directly in harm’s way. The “last tactical mile” The concept borrows from a familiar logistics problem. Moving supplies from a large rear-area distribution point to a forward unit can be relatively straightforward until the final few miles. Those roads and trails are often where vehicles become vulnerable to artillery, drones, mines, and small arms fire. See All. That makes the ILTM concept less about replacing conventional trucks and more about removing humans from particularly hazardous portions of the supply chain. The Army says the selected systems will need to support manned close-combat formations while operating autonomously beyond the operator’s direct line of sight. The approach also reflects a quickly occurring shift in military robotics. Autonomy is increasingly being treated as a means of changing how existing vehicles are used rather than simply as a new type of weapon. Six companies, different approaches. The Army has not publicly disclosed the vehicles that all six companies will submit, but some candidates are already known. According to Breaking Defense, American Rheinmetall is expected to provide its Mission Master SP-H, an unmanned tracked vehicle designed for autonomous logistics and other missions. Overland AI will provide its ULTRA platform, an autonomous off-road vehicle derived from Polaris’ RZR platform and equipped with Overland’s autonomy technology. Forterra has previously unveiled MESA, a logistics and casualty-evacuation vehicle based on the Polaris Ranger XD 1500. It combines Forterra’s AutoDrive autonomous driving system with its Vektor communications technology, which is designed to operate in low-bandwidth environments. The other three participants, Maren-Go, Hendrick’s Motorsports and HDT, have not publicly disclosed their intended ILTM vehicles. The variety is significant. Instead of committing immediately to a single vehicle architecture, the Army is effectively subjecting multiple approaches to the same test regime and allowing battlefield performance to determine which ones deserve further investment. From prototypes to soldiers. The selections are not yet a production order for an autonomous Army fleet. The companies are expected to receive formal prototype agreements in the coming weeks, followed by technical demonstrations and evaluations. Each vendor is expected to deliver four vehicles, after which the Army will assess how the systems perform under operationally relevant conditions. The decisive stage is planned for early 2027, when an Army unit will conduct an Operational Assessment. Feedback from soldiers will then help determine which platforms should move toward production. That testing will be particularly important because autonomy in a controlled demonstration is very different from autonomy in a battlefield environment. A useful system must navigate difficult terrain, maintain communications, operate when satellite or other links are disrupted, and respond appropriately when its route or mission changes. The Army’s objective is therefore not simply to create a vehicle that can drive itself. It is looking for a system that can keep logistics moving and evacuate casualties when sending a human crew into the same area would be unnecessarily dangerous. If the ILTM program succeeds, autonomous ground vehicles could become another layer of the Army’s battlefield logistics network, taking on some of the most exposed jobs while allowing soldiers to concentrate on the missions that still require human judgment.

AI is moving beyond experimentation into increasingly autonomous and consequential applications. TCS and Google Cloud opened a Mexico City center with more than 3,000 AI agents, while Meta entered the AI coding-agent market with Muse Code, signaling a push toward AI systems that directly execute software development tasks. At the same time, researchers demonstrated AI-designed viral genomes capable of functioning in living cells, underscoring how rapidly AI capabilities are expanding across commercial and scientific domains. Ready? This is your Week in AI, Cloud & Data! TCS, Google Cloud Open AI Center in Mexico City. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Google Cloud have opened a Gemini Experience Center in Mexico City with more than 3,000 AI agents, adding a new platform for companies seeking to move AI applications from experimentation into business operations. Meta Launches Muse Code to Challenge OpenAI, Anthropic. Meta Platforms launched Muse Code, its first AI coding agent, entering a market already dominated by Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. The terminal-based tool, now available as a public beta for macOS and Linux, plans software changes, writes code, and validates the results across large repositories. The release signals Meta’s push to generate direct revenue from its AI models beyond its advertising business. AI Designs First Fully Functional Synthetic Viruses. Scientists at Stanford University and the Arc Institute report that AI has, for the first time, designed complete viral genomes that function in living cells. In a study published in the journal Science on Aug. 6, 2026, researchers used the genome language models Evo 1 and Evo 2 to generate nearly 700,000 candidate bacteriophage genomes, of which 16 proved capable of infecting and destroying antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli. AI, Cybersecurity Anchor Mexico’s 2026 Tech Spending. Mexican companies plan to direct US$776 million toward AI software and services and US$1.48 billion toward cybersecurity during 2026, according to the consultancy IDC. The figures place both categories among the fastest-growing segments of the country’s technology market, even as a shortage of specialized talent and uneven connectivity limit how broadly companies can put the new tools to use.
