AI has made building software faster and easier than ever, but verifying that what was built actually works has not become easier. The author argues that this gap has moved from an engineering problem to a founder-level business risk. Barriers to shipping are low, and vibe coding lets almost anyone write code: 25% of Y Combinator's Winter 2025 startups had codebases that were 95% AI-generated. Yet software is judged by whether it holds up once real users, data and attackers arrive. The risk is measurable. A December 2025 analysis of 470 open-source pull requests found AI-co-authored code contained roughly 1.7 times more issues than human-written code, with security vulnerabilities at up to 2.74 times the rate. The cost of missing quality appears in four forms: - Security breaches: Lovable, a vibe coding platform, had critical vulnerabilities in over 10% of live apps sampled from its showcase, caused by AI-generated code skipping basic security configurations. - Customer trust: Moltbook, an AI social network, exposed 1.5 million API tokens and 35,000 email addresses through a single misconfigured database in AI-generated code, and the reputational damage spread faster than the patch. - Reputation and investor confidence: failures reach board meetings, investor updates and press coverage, and founders are accountable for business risk. - Regulatory and compliance risk: AI doesn't understand obligations like GDPR, HIPAA or data residency, and a compliance failure can sit unnoticed in a codebase for months, becoming a legal fix rather than an engineering one. The author says these are one problem: speed that outran verification, surfacing wherever the business is most exposed when no one owns the gap. Existing checks, such as QA teams, review processes and a definition of done, were built for slower, human-paced mistakes. When something breaks in production, the fallout travels from engineering to the product lead, the CTO and finally the founder. Because AI has made speed a commodity, with every team fast and shipping, the author argues quality is what will keep companies afloat, and that requires the founder involved. Drawing on conversations at TestMu AI with engineering and product leaders from startups to enterprises, the author says teams that ship with confidence are defined by how seriously they take quality, not by size or headcount. Founder-level accountability does not mean reviewing pull requests. It means three shifts. First, quality becomes a number leadership watches, with escape rate, security findings and time-to-detection getting dashboards like revenue and burn. Second, AI output is treated as a draft, untrusted until verified, like code from an unknown contractor. Third, verification moves into the pipeline rather than sitting at the end, because continuously generated code must be checked continuously. The author says none of this slows teams down; it lets them keep moving fast without betting the company on unverified code. The gap widens every quarter, and it becomes everyone's priority only when it starts at the top.

The first flight of the largest battery-electric aircraft to take to the skies lasted nearly half an hour while costing just $5 of electricity. That aviation feat comes at a time when jet fuel prices have skyrocketed because of the US war with Iran. The test flight of Heart Aerospace’s X1 demonstrator aircraft took place at Plattsburgh International Airport in upstate New York on August 12. The X1 aircraft is comparable in size to a small regional airliner and can achieve a maximum takeoff weight exceeding 25,000 pounds with the help of four wing-mounted electric motors. The battery-electric propulsion system delivered more than one megawatt of power during the maiden flight. All-electric aircraft can offer quieter and cleaner flight without the emissions that come from burning jet fuel. They may also prove more reliably cost-effective than conventional aircraft that come with jet fuel costs subject to geopolitical disruptions. But the initial success of the X1 demonstrator does not mean Heart Aerospace is planning to commercialize an all-electric aircraft. Current battery-electric systems can only typically sustain short flights of about 100 to 200 miles, which is why they have been limited to air taxi operations by companies such as Joby and Archer. Instead, testing of the X1 and a planned follow-on X2 aircraft will shape development of Heart Aerospace’s main offering to the airline industry—a 30-seat hybrid-electric regional airliner known as the ES-30. That planned production aircraft for commercial flights would combine two inboard electric motors with commercial turboprop engines that run on jet fuel, enabling 125 miles of all-electric flight and 500 miles of flight range when operating in hybrid mode. Looking to innovation as jet fuel prices rise. Having the extended 500-mile range would enable the ES-30 hybrid-electric airliner to operate in popular short-haul corridors that connect major US and European cities. United Airlines has committed to eventually purchasing 100 aircraft from Heart Aerospace, with other major airline customers also having signed letters of intent, according to Flying magazine.

Twitch Sparks Backlash For Enrolling Streamers In Amazon AI Training. In a livestream with its head of community, chief product officer Mike Minton explained the rationale behind the decision to opt in all users into the generative AI training. "Well, there's an honest answer, and I think most of you probably can appreciate this. Like, if it was opt in, nobody would opt in. That's honestly the answer." Twitch isn't making Gen AI training *opt-in* because no one would voluntarily choose to opt in. Instead, they are offering an opt-out option. [image or embed] — Zach Bussey 🍁 August 12, 2026 at 3:28 PM. The backlash has been swift, with users sharing with one another how to find the option buried in Twitch's account settings menu to opt out from having their content used to train AI models. If you'd like to do this, head on over to your account settings, choose "Security and Privacy," scroll to the bottom where you'll find the "Privacy" section and you'll see a toggle to enable or disable "Training for Generative AI." It's important to note that some users have found it easier to make the setting stick when using the desktop site versus the mobile app. However, even on the desktop site many have reported that the generative AI setting re-enables itself when checking on it again. If this happens to you it seems as if the best option is to set the toggle to off, wait a few seconds and then refresh to see if the change sticks. It's unfortunate that Amazon chose to implement its generative AI training policy in this fashion, because there were so many other options that wouldn't have gotten as much backlash. It could've offered extra perks, or even compensation, to entice users to voluntarily opt in. Efforts like this simply serve to create more ill will towards the technology, which is wildly unpopular with the youth demographic that drives so much of Twitch's traffic. An olive branch in the form of "opt-in with perks" could have been a major PR win for the company.

The author, who runs a homelab mostly on LXC containers under Proxmox but uses Docker Desktop for testing, tried WSL Containers (wslc) from the latest WSL pre-release to see whether it could replace Docker Desktop. The main difference is architectural: wslc builds a new private VM for every container session, while Docker Desktop runs inside WSL's shared virtual machine. That suits development work, but the author says it isn't ready for long-running homelab services. On memory, Docker Desktop itself idles under 200 MB, including its privileged Windows service. A wslc container creates a new VM named after the user account that uses about 1.5 GB of RAM. The container disappears when finished, as Microsoft intends, but the VM persists, even through a manual WSL shutdown. The only fix is `wslc system session terminate`, buried deep in the CLI. Booting one wslc container also started a fresh copy of the shared WSL VM and re-registered the Ubuntu distro as running, for a total of 3.4 GB of RAM from one idle prompt. Claims that wslc starts containers in under a second versus three to eight seconds for Docker Desktop did not hold up. Using alpine, warm and cold, the gap was close to testing variance. Warm to warm, wslc won by 60 ms. Docker returned in under three seconds after a proper shutdown but took longer after a crash, and its privileged helper requires approving a consent dialog. Six wslc starts all fell within a 224 ms band, so its advantage is consistency, since private VMs inherit nothing to repair. GPU support worked on the first try within two minutes. A stock CUDA 12.4 image saw an RTX 5090 with a single `--gpus-all` flag, even on a CUDA 13.3 host driver. It is GPU paravirtualization rather than exclusive passthrough, so VRAM is shared with the Windows desktop. Wslc lacks `--privileged`, `--device` and `--restart`, so nothing survives a session dying, making it better for dev containers than infrastructure. Ports bind to 127.0.0.1 by default rather than 0.0.0.0, so an nginx test worked only after explicitly publishing 0.0.0.0, which triggered a Windows firewall prompt attributed to COM Surrogate. `wslc compose` does not work as of 2.9.3. The community project wslc-compose, a thin Python shim installed via pipx, filled the gap. A two-service nginx plus Postgres test with `depends_on` produced a project-scoped network, correct startup order and a shared deduplicated Alpine base layer, and `down -v` removed everything. The author says Microsoft has built the networking and volume lifecycles but not the top-level command. The author concludes that wslc can replace Docker Desktop for their use: mostly dev containers, some GPU work and a few Compose stacks. Its weakness is visibility. Docker's VMs appear in a GUI, while wslc requires command-line work to see what is running. The author hopes Microsoft adds a TUI. To try it, run `wsl --update --pre-release`, and learn the terminate command first.

Researchers are making progress toward quantum computers powerful enough to undermine the mathematical assumptions that protect cryptocurrency and other blockchain assets, so the industry needs to replace its cryptographic infrastructure before such machines arrive. Christopher Smith, co-founder and CEO of Quantus, a quantum-secure blockchain network, said the "great quantum migration" will require the entire digital asset industry to participate. Traditional computers use bits that are either 0 or 1, while quantum computers use subatomic particles and trapped ions as qubits, theoretically allowing calculations in a fraction of the time. The cryptography that proves ownership of digital assets has been considered essentially unbreakable because classical computers would take too long to derive the private key that authorizes transactions; reportedly, a standard supercomputer would need hundreds of millions of years. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could change that. Smith said over $2 trillion in digital assets is secured by elliptic curve cryptography, which has been known to be quantum-vulnerable for over 30 years, nearly the entire crypto market, valued at $2.16 trillion. The threat may be nearing, Smith said, noting AI is accelerating quantum research. Google researchers have estimated the resources needed to attack elliptic-curve cryptography may be lower than previously thought. According to Smith and Quantus, a giant Bitcoin wallet is an obvious target; he cited Binance's Bitcoin cold wallet, which he said holds more than $10 billion. The administrative key controlling USDT, which has authority over the stablecoin's issuance, could be more dangerous, potentially letting an attacker manipulate assets and, in Smith's words, "instantly wreck everything in DeFi." Coinbase cautioned that the whole ecosystem is not equally exposed, telling Fortune that bitcoin's core infrastructure is largely safe and the real vulnerability is at the wallet level. Google proposed a 2029 target for cryptocurrency systems to migrate away from vulnerable cryptography. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has pushed organizations toward "post-quantum" cryptography and has standardized replacement algorithms designed to withstand such attacks. The technology is not the hard part. Coinbase says adding quantum-safe signatures to a blockchain is a solvable engineering problem; the harder question is what happens to coins whose owners fail to migrate in time. Coinbase's independent Quantum Advisory Council recently published a report on quantum migration and "abandoned coins," including governance questions about assets left in vulnerable addresses. Unlike updating encryption on a centralized service, a quantum-resistant blockchain system may not help if exchanges don't support it, wallets don't implement it, or users don't move their funds. Smith said custodians, exchanges, wallet providers, blockchain developers and users will all need to act. Coinbase agrees that industry-wide coordination is required. It is a founding member of the Bitcoin Security Consortium, backed by BlackRock, Fidelity Digital Assets, Block, Blockstream and Strategy. Coinbase said it is contributing to a fund supporting Bitcoin developers working on quantum security, dedicating engineering resources to open-source efforts on proposals such as BIP-360 and the post-quantum migration path, and has published a position paper on quantum risks and is working with developers and experts on potential upgrades. A machine capable of a quantum attack remains beyond current capabilities, but Smith said now is the time to prepare: "Being a year too early is much better than being a day too late."

The author, a self-hoster, wanted to be able to rebuild a home server after starting over, ideally with a single command. Docker already makes recreating containers easy, but the author wanted to define the main components in one place, and was unsure how well this would work for services with databases and other dependencies. For the experiment, the author chose three services that run 24/7: Home Assistant (smart home), Immich (photos) and Nextcloud (files). Instead of managing them as separate Docker projects, they were combined into one stack in a single Compose file, covering the applications, databases, supporting services, ports and storage. Home Assistant stores its configuration in a bind-mounted folder. Immich consists of a server, a machine-learning container, a Valkey (Redis-compatible) container and a Postgres database, with named volumes for its library, model cache and database. Nextcloud consists of the app, a MariaDB database and a Redis container, with named volumes for its database and web files. Passwords and settings are kept in a separate .env file. The author kept the approach simple: write the Compose file, add services and dependencies, and keep persistent storage separate from the containers. After using the server normally for a while, the real test was to pull the latest images, force Docker Compose to recreate the containers, and check whether Home Assistant, Immich and Nextcloud kept their configurations and data. The rebuild command is "docker compose pull; docker compose up -d --remove-orphans --force-recreate". The first part pulls the latest images; the second recreates the containers and restarts the whole stack. The --force-recreate option ensures containers are rebuilt rather than merely restarted, while the persistent volumes stay in place, so nothing has to be set up again. The author tested this several times: the containers were recreated, but existing configurations and data remained, making a rebuild surprisingly easy. The setup is not complete, however. The main missing piece is a proper backup strategy. The Compose file and persistent volumes make recreating containers easy and keep data in place, but they offer no protection against drive failure, accidental deletion or data corruption. The author plans to add backups of the important data from Immich, Nextcloud and Home Assistant, and to verify that restores actually work rather than assuming they will. The author concludes that easy rebuilding and proper backups are two different things: the first is solved, and the backup part is next. Overall, the experiment gave a cleaner way to manage everyday services without an unnecessarily complicated setup.

BAE Systems is moving into the second phase of a DARPA program aimed at solving one of the most persistent limitations in high-power radio-frequency electronics. Heat. BAE Systems’ FAST Labs research organization has completed Phase 1 of DARPA’s Technologies for Heat Removal in Electronics at the Device Scale (THREADS) program and has been selected to continue into Phase 2. The work focuses particularly on gallium nitride (GaN) devices, which are already widely used in high-performance radar, electronic warfare, and communications systems. The problem is straightforward in principle but difficult to solve. Increasing the power of an RF transistor generates more heat. If that heat cannot be removed efficiently, the transistor’s performance and reliability suffer. As a result, electronics can operate below their theoretical power limits. DARPA created THREADS to attack the problem inside the device itself, rather than simply adding larger conventional cooling systems around it. The agency says the program targets two major challenges. Reducing thermal resistance within the transistor while preserving electrical performance, and efficiently moving heat away from high-power transistor regions without degrading RF performance. Why GaN matters. GaN is a wide-bandgap semiconductor that has become increasingly important for military RF electronics. Compared with older semiconductor technologies, it can operate at higher power densities and frequencies, making it particularly useful for modern active electronically scanned array (AESA) radars and electronic-warfare systems. See All. DARPA has previously noted that GaN already provides more than a fivefold improvement in power density compared with earlier transistor technologies, but that much more could theoretically be achieved if engineers can overcome the heat problem. This is important because RF power directly affects what systems such as radar and communications equipment can accomplish. More usable RF power can potentially mean stronger signals, greater detection distances, or more capable electronic effects. DARPA’s current description of THREADS targets an eightfold reduction in thermal resistance and power densities of up to 81 W/mm for X-band transistor and power-amplifier test devices. From heat problem to longer-range radar. The potential operational payoff is substantial. DARPA has previously estimated that solving the thermal limitations could increase radar range by two to three times. The agency’s more recent update says THREADS performers achieved approximately a fivefold increase in RF power density over today’s state of the art during Phase 1, corresponding to roughly a doubling of radar range while maintaining the reliability required for operational use. That doesn’t mean every radar using THREADS technology will automatically double its range. Radar performance depends on many factors, including antenna characteristics, frequency, target size, atmospheric conditions and signal processing. Instead, the figures illustrate why solving thermal limitations at the semiconductor level could have an outsized effect on complete systems. BAE Systems is conducting its own work at its Microelectronics Center in Nashua, New Hampshire, where the company already develops and manufactures GaN and gallium-arsenide integrated circuits for defense applications. Its THREADS effort involves collaboration with Modern Microsystems and researchers at Penn State, Stanford, Notre Dame and the University of Texas at Dallas. Building on earlier thermal breakthroughs. THREADS is also part of a longer effort to make GaN electronics better at handling heat. DARPA previously demonstrated a GaN-on-diamond transistor through its Near Junction Thermal Transport program, exploiting diamond’s exceptionally high thermal conductivity to reduce temperatures near the transistor junction. THREADS takes the broader challenge further, looking at materials, device structures, and ways of extracting heat directly at the transistor level. For BAE Systems, entering Phase 2 means moving beyond the initial research toward further development and validation of its approach. The ultimate goal is not simply a cooler transistor. It is an RF device that can generate substantially more power without becoming larger, less reliable, or thermally constrained.

Which Nvidia GPU Is Equivalent To The Xbox Series X? The Xbox Series X is one of the most powerful video game consoles ever made, but the GPU inside isn't that different from the type that goes in a PC. Its GPU instead is based on AMD's Radeon RX 6800, and in real-world gaming, the Xbox performs most equivalent to an Nvidia RTX 3060 Ti. Said another way, the short answer is that the GPU is similar to a mid-range PC card from around 2020 to 2021, landing right between an RTX 3060 and an RTX 3070 in most situations. The console's custom silicon is built on AMD's RDNA 2 architecture with 52 compute units running at a locked 1.825 GHz, which works out at 12.15 teraflops of raw compute. It pairs that GPU with 16GB of GDDR6 memory shared between the graphics and CPU. On paper, that makes it more powerful than the PlayStation 5, which uses a smaller GPU and settles at 10.28 teraflops. But raw specs don't always translate to clearly comparable performance, even when matching the Xbox Series X GPU against its RX 6800 cousin. This is because a console's hardware is optimized and standardized, making video game development different from creating for a PC, which can have thousands of combinations between GPU, CPU, memory, and much more. If you already have an Xbox and are looking to get more out of it, you can change some settings on an Xbox to instantly boost performance. Those options include switching from Wi-Fi to Ethernet, adding extra storage, and turning on performance mode. The RTX 3060 Ti and RX 6700 XT are the closest PC matches. When Microsoft announced its Xbox Series X, one key selling point was that the console's GPU was twice as powerful as the previous-generation Xbox One, which competed with mid-range cards when it released in 2013. The company also marketed the Xbox Series X with other features some people still may not know it can do, from Quick Resume to deep home screen customization. When the Xbox Series X is compared to Nvidia's RTX 3060 Ti, the GPUs perform similar to one another at 1440p in most multiplatform titles. When the console is matched against AMD's lineup, some gamers and developers say the company's RX 6700 XT is a closer equivalent, though it launched four months after the RX 6800 and Xbox Series X in 2020. Game developers have identified a third card that compares against the Xbox Series X as well. Microsoft's own "Forza Horizon 6" racing game specs on Steam, for example, recommends an Nvidia RTX 3060 Ti, an AMD RX 6700 XT, or a competing GPU from Intel, called the Arc A580. That's a handy real-world check because the recommended spec for a game originally built for the Series X tends to mirror the machine's own graphics power.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) stock fell after a disappointing earnings report, despite considerable excitement beforehand. The stock has struggled this year and has not repeated its 2025 performance. Over 12 months it gained about 17% versus 20% for the S&P 500, and year to date it is down roughly 20% while the index is up around 14%, reflecting investor concerns about consistent profitability. The article argues that for a pre-commercial quantum company, the product matters more than a single earnings report. A day before earnings, D-Wave announced technological progress toward commercial quantum computing. The barrier to useful quantum computing is not qubit count but error rates that compound as qubit count rises, making large-scale deployment unreliable. D-Wave claims the breakthrough removes one of the greatest obstacles to error correction, making a commercially viable, fault-tolerant system far more achievable. CEO Alan Baratz said it proves the company is on the right track and that a commercial fault-tolerant machine is practical and achievable. Founded in 1999, D-Wave develops quantum computing systems, software, and cloud services, including the Advantage and Advantage 2 computers, Leap cloud service, Ocean developer tools, and hybrid quantum-classical solutions, for areas such as manufacturing, finance, logistics, and drug discovery. The stock is nearly impossible to value on normal measures. Forward P/E is not meaningful, and forward price-to-sales is 175x, steep but expected for a pre-commercial company that only went public in August 2022. Analysts expect losses to continue for several years, with the trajectory turning positive in 2028 and improving in 2029 as losses narrow. The balance sheet is a strength: $546 million in cash against $48 million in debt. The price is justified only by a long-term bet that the technology becomes a real business. D-Wave reported second-quarter fiscal 2026 results on Aug. 6. Revenue was $3.07 million, missing the $4.03 million consensus. EPS was -$0.13 versus an expected -$0.09. GAAP gross margin was 55.4%, down from 63.8%. Cash and marketable securities were $546.2 million. Bookings rose 59% year over year, helped by large enterprise deals. Management expects third-quarter revenue to rise modestly from the second quarter, with fourth-quarter revenue rising sharply and making up the majority of full-year revenue. Two annealing quantum computer system deliveries are expected in the fourth quarter, with some installation and calibration revenue carrying into 2027. Baratz said the integration of Quantum Circuits has gone very smoothly, the company remains on track to deliver its 17-qubit dual rail quantum system this year, and customer demand is mixed between annealing and gate-model technologies. On Aug. 3, Wedbush assumed coverage with an "Outperform" rating and $40 price target, saying long-term winners will achieve key technology goals, build profitable and scalable businesses, and grow beyond government contracts. Rosenblatt Securities reaffirmed its "Buy" rating with a $43 target. Among 16 analysts, the consensus is "Strong Buy," with an average target of $34.67, implying 64% upside, and a high target of $43, implying 103% upside.

Taiwan’s efforts to build a modern counter-drone network are facing renewed scrutiny after an official audit found technical gaps in a $111 million fixed-site defence programme. The system, developed to protect airbases and other military facilities, cannot currently detect or jam some frequencies used by newer Chinese drones and has limited protection against emerging threats. The findings come shortly after a separate army procurement for 26 fixed-site counter-drone systems was terminated following repeated testing failures. Together, the setbacks also highlight a broader challenge for Taiwan, which is developing a layered defense system while drone technology evolves faster than traditional military procurement programmes can adapt. While officials say upgrades are already being developed, analysts question whether they will arrive quickly enough. Counter-drone system fails to keep pace with evolving PLA drones. According to Taiwan’s Audit Office, the fixed-site system developed by the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, the island’s main weapons developer, cannot detect or jam the 5.1GHz frequency used by newer PLA drone models. The system also does not fully cover parts of the BeiDou-3 satellite navigation system and has limited capabilities against emerging fibre-optic and AI-guided drones. The audit found the programme was already six to 12 months behind schedule because of construction delays and shortages of key components. It warned that the technical and scheduling problems could undermine protection for military bases. The army had planned to acquire 26 fixed-site systems from local contractor Tron Future Tech, but the company failed its third and final acceptance test. Taiwan’s defense minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said the system struggled to combine information from search and passive radar systems when faced with multiple waves of drones, making it difficult for operators to identify targets accurately. See All. Taiwan’s defense ministry said many of the technologies highlighted in the audit emerged after the counter-drone programme began in 2021. Ministry spokesman Sun Li-fang said NCSIST had already verified jamming capabilities for the newer frequency and would introduce them through future upgrades. The ministry also noted it was accelerating development of systems capable of dealing with fibre-optic and AI-guided drones. One system cannot counter every drone. Military analysts explain that the problem goes beyond Taiwan and reflects a bigger challenge for armed forces trying to respond to evolving drone technology. Shu Hsiao-huang, a senior analyst at the Institute for National Defence and Security Research, noted that Taiwan should avoid treating every unmanned aircraft as the same threat. Shu also warned that Taiwan’s reliance on electronic jamming could become less effective as fibre-optic and AI-guided drones reduce their dependence on radio-frequency communications. Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies, similarly argued that Taiwan needs to find a cheaper way to defeat drones. Using expensive missiles against inexpensive unmanned aircraft, could quickly become economically unsustainable, he stressed. The debate now points toward a more layered approach combining electronic warfare, radar, sensors, kinetic systems and lower-cost interceptors. For Taiwan, the challenge is not simply developing better counter-drone technology, but creating a system that can keep adapting as the threat changes.

Amazon and Microsoft are two of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI). Both of these companies have taken a similar path, choosing to integrate AI into their own products but utilize other providers’ models instead of creating their own. They each also have a thriving cloud computing business, benefiting from rising AI workloads. But which one of these two makes for the better buy? Let’s take a look at the fourth- and fifth-largest companies in the world, and see which makes the most sense for your investment dollars. Both companies have a wide-ranging business. Microsoft’s business is quite broad, ranging from business productivity software to gaming hardware and software to cloud computing. Microsoft has an iron grip in many of the industries that it’s in and a massive number of clients that cannot afford to cut Microsoft’s software even if times get bad. This makes Microsoft a pretty safe business to invest in, as it will likely be OK regardless of economic conditions. Amazon is in a similar boat, as its commerce business has become the most popular online shopping destination, and it has countless devoted clients that utilize its services every day. Both Microsoft and Amazon have rock-solid cloud computing businesses too that are thriving in the AI build-out, and each of them is spending hundreds of billions of dollars to increase capacity to meet demand. While each business has its ups and downs, nothing points to Microsoft’s or Amazon’s base business being better than the other. As a result, I’m scoring this category as a tie. Winner: Tie. Both companies are growing at a similar pace. From a revenue growth standpoint, Microsoft has long enjoyed a lead over Amazon, but that changed during the most recent quarter. Docker lets users deploy containers on a home lab or local server, and self-hosting offers students free alternatives to paid services, no subscription fees, and local storage of files and data instead of cloud uploads. The containers below are easy to deploy, need no coding experience, and run on any machine, including an old laptop or a Raspberry Pi. They are meant to suit students in any course. Jupyter Notebook is aimed at engineering students, especially in IT, programming, AI, or Machine Learning. It lets users create and share documents with live code and visualizations, supports languages such as Python, R, and Julia, and combines code and visualizations in one place to make complex concepts easier to grasp. Self-hosting gives data privacy, no recurring fee, and offline access, which helps students with patchy networks. Notebooks can be exported to popular formats to share with peers, and it integrates with Microsoft Excel. Kanboard is a free, self-hosted Kanban-style project tracker similar to Trello, with a simple UI and multi-user collaboration for group projects. Students can create a card per task (such as a Physics assignment or Math homework), set deadlines, and move cards to a completed section, which helps with time management and accountability. Nextcloud addresses two problems with Google Drive: the free tier offers only 15 GB, with paid upgrades required, and data is uploaded to Google's servers. Nextcloud stores files on a local server, accessible from anywhere, at no cost beyond a possible one-time expense for external drives. It also offers a productivity suite that can replace Microsoft 365 or Google Docs. It is open source and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, with iOS, Android, and desktop compatibility. Paperless-ngx is for students who take physical notes in notebooks or on an iPad. It stores notes in one place and uses OCR and ML to digitize them, making them searchable, including with natural language. It can be integrated with a local LLM to categorize and tag notes. Kiwix stores offline copies of online resources, useful for students without constant internet access. Examples include all of Wikipedia or the Python handbook for syntax, working like a personal library available anywhere. Experimenting with different containers is the best way to learn Docker, and a few basic commands let beginners deploy most containers. Self-hosting also teaches students about networking, servers, and security. These apps cover a good mix of categories, such as Nextcloud replacing OneDrive or Google Drive and Kanboard replacing Trello, and hosting them can save money.

Concorde's droop nose was far more than a visibility aid: it was a triple-redundant hydraulic system with four fixed positions and a hard rule in the flight manual. Below 250 knots (463 km/h), the nose had to be lowered every time, regardless of pilot preference. Concorde's designers at Aérospatiale and BAC chose a slender delta wing because it behaved best at Mach 2.04 (about 1,354 mph or 2,180 km/h), the cruising speed sustained for hours on transatlantic runs. Such a wing kept wave drag low, gave the rigidity needed to handle aerodynamic heating (skin temperatures well past 260° F, or 127 °C), and left almost no internal volume for conventional high-lift hardware. At low speed the wing relied on vortex lift, which is why it could not carry flaps or slats: deploying them would have disrupted the vortex structure. Concorde therefore had to approach at a steep nose-up attitude, often 15 to 17 degrees. With a nose roughly 30 feet (9 meters) ahead of the cockpit, pilots lost sight of the runway. The solution was a hinged nose and a retractable visor with four codified positions: 0 degrees with visor up for supersonic cruise, 0 degrees with visor down for subsonic cruise, 5 degrees for taxi and takeoff, and 12.5 degrees for landing. The flight manual required at least 5 degrees whenever airspeed fell below 250 knots, making the movement a scheduled procedure like a flap schedule. Reliability was designed in over 27 years of commercial service, 1976 to 2003. Primary power came from the Green hydraulic system at 4,000 psi (276 bar). The Yellow standby system could take over if Green failed, and a mechanical free-fall release let gravity lower the nose with no hydraulic pressure. A full droop cycle took roughly 12 seconds, with retraction under 20 seconds, and crews treated it as a checklist item. Early prototypes were cleared for a deeper 17.5-degree droop, but it was reduced to 12.5 degrees before commercial service. The reason was human factors: the steeper angle altered the relationship between runway, aircraft attitude and visual references, potentially complicating height and flare judgment. The 12.5-degree compromise preserved a more natural approach picture and remained standard throughout Concorde's career. Later aircraft did not copy the design because few share its wing shape, speed regime and requirements. The Bombardier Global 8000, a conventional swept-wing jet cruising below Mach 1, lands with flaps and full forward visibility. The Soviet Tu-144, also a supersonic delta, used a drooping nose combined with retractable forward canards for low-speed handling. Boom Supersonic's Overture, the first serious delta-wing supersonic airliner attempt since Concorde retired, faces the same visibility problem but avoids a mechanical nose. It uses external cameras feeding an augmented-reality, head-worn display from Universal Avionics, cutting weight, maintenance burden and moving parts. Concorde's engineers lacked such sensors, processing power and displays in the 1960s, so they built a hinge, rated to fail three ways before failing the crew.

Trelleborg launches fluorosurfactant-free semiconductor sealing materials. Trelleborg, Sweden – Trelleborg Sealing Solutions has launched three fluorosurfactant-free materials for semiconductor manufacturing as regulators and manufacturers increasingly focus on reducing the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS. The new materials expand Trelleborg’s PureFab range and include two perfluoroelastomers, or FFKMs, JPF50 and JPF58, and a fluoroelastomer, VPF20. The company said the materials are made without low-molecular-weight PFAS fluorosurfactants and are intended to help customers address evolving regulatory requirements while maintaining performance and durability. Chris Busby, Trelleborg’s global segment director for semiconductor, said the materials are designed to help customers prepare for changes in PFAS regulations and strengthen their supply chains. The JPF50 material is a high-purity FFKM designed for semiconductor processes requiring purity and plasma resistance. Trelleborg said it is manufactured without fillers or fluorosurfactants and offers low outgassing and minimal particle emissions. The material can operate at temperatures up to 300 degrees Celsius, or 572 degrees Fahrenheit, and is designed to provide low compression set and mechanical strength. JPF50 is intended for deposition processes such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, high-density plasma chemical vapor deposition and plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition. It can also be used in atomic layer etching and dry etching processes, including chamber lid, gas inlet and bonded slit valve door seals. JPF58 is an FFKM designed for applications requiring long-term thermal stability and purity at extreme temperatures. According to Trelleborg, it maintains seal integrity at temperatures up to 300 C and resists cracking under high mechanical and thermal stress. The material is intended for high-temperature processes including rapid thermal processing, atomic layer deposition, chemical vapor deposition and diffusion furnaces. The third material, VPF20, is a high-purity FKM that combines a fluorosurfactant-free base polymer with high-purity synthetic fillers. Trelleborg said the formulation helps minimize metallic contaminants and ionic extractables while providing mechanical strength, elastic recovery and chemical resistance. VPF20 is designed for both static and dynamic sealing applications and is positioned as a more cost-effective alternative to FFKM for applications involving moderate temperatures and medium chemical demands. Potential applications include transfer modules, load locks, equipment front-end modules, vacuum handling systems and flat-panel display manufacturing equipment. Trelleborg said the broader PureFab portfolio is designed for aggressive semiconductor front-end processes, including deposition, etching, ash and strip, plasma cleaning and thermal processing. The company defines its fluorosurfactant-free materials as products in which PFAS fluorosurfactants are not intentionally used. Trelleborg said that, based on available information, the materials do not contain PFAS fluorosurfactants, although it cannot guarantee that trace amounts occurring unintentionally are absent. Trelleborg said customers interested in the new materials can arrange samples for testing.

The author argues that self-hosting looks more complicated than it is, and that the key is not mastering every tool but having one solid foundation. For them, that foundation was Docker, and especially Docker Compose. Before Docker, self-hosting meant installing each application directly on the machine and handling its dependencies, requirements, configuration changes, and possible conflicts with existing software. Every new tool felt like a separate project. Docker let them run an application and its required environment inside a container, kept separate from the rest of the setup. This made it easy to test software without permanently changing the system, and to remove it if it wasn't useful. Running one container was simple, but managing several was harder: remembering which belonged together, which settings they needed, and how they should start. Docker Compose solved this by letting them describe the applications that make up a setup together, give each service its own configuration, and manage them as a single group. It is especially useful when applications need supporting services, since the relationships between them can be defined in the Compose configuration instead of starting everything manually in the right order. Opening the Compose file also gives a quick picture of what is running, instead of checking individual Docker commands and containers. This is when Compose became the author's main tool for managing self-hosted applications, adding structure without unnecessary complexity. The author says five basic Compose concepts are enough to read and modify most Compose files, without memorizing the documentation: Services: an application or container to run; identifying them shows what each section does. Images: the packaged software Docker uses to create a container, an application's starting point. Understanding the difference between an image and a running container avoids confusion. Volumes: where certain data is stored outside the container, important for applications that store files, settings, or databases. Ports: they control how a container is accessed from outside Docker. Knowing the difference between the container's port and the port exposed on the machine explains why some services aren't reachable. Environment variables: they supply configuration values without changing the application itself. The author also learned to be careful with passwords and other sensitive values. The author concludes that knowing the right tool matters more than knowing every tool. Compose is a skill that carries across projects regardless of the application. There is no need to understand every advanced Docker feature or build an elaborate homelab; enough confidence to look at a new project and know where to start removes much of the guesswork from self-hosting and keeps paying off with each new service.

AI tools and agents are speeding up DevOps but also expanding the attack surface. The 2026 DevOps Threats Unwrapped Report recorded 68 AI-related incidents across major DevOps platforms in 2025, and GitProtect Lab tracked 84 in the first half of 2026 alone, nearly triple the same period in 2025. In GitProtect Lab's survey of DevOps, DevSecOps and security leaders, 1 in 3 respondents said they had already experienced a security incident tied directly to AI. Prompt injection, ranked #1 on the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, is among the fastest-growing attack vectors. Attackers embed malicious instructions in unstructured data that AI tools routinely scan, such as issue tickets, pull request comments, agent config files, poisoned MCP tool descriptions or uploaded documentation. If an agent has broad, organization-wide read permissions, an indirect prompt injection turns it into an unintended insider threat: it can pull source code, API keys or environment secrets from private repositories and post them in a public comment or send them to an external endpoint. The attack works because the agent applies its high-level privileges to untrusted input. Techniques like GhostSplice split the payload across multiple channels to bypass refusal filters and force the agent to fuse the fragments and execute the exfiltration. Autonomous agents also risk operational downtime. An agent managing cloud infrastructure that hits a build error might tear down and recreate a live component without human-in-the-loop verification, unaware that it supports active user connections or that it is peak hours, causing an outage before operators can intervene. Threat actors are also using AI to craft supply chain attacks, including MCP "rug pulls" in which approved tools silently mutate into exfiltration paths. According to GitProtect Lab, 34% of surveyed security leaders see AI-supported attacks as their primary DevOps security concern for the next three years. In one scenario, attackers publish a repository with no malicious code, so it passes static scanners, but it is designed to raise a runtime setup error. When an AI coding assistant tries to self-heal, it runs a suggested fix that queries an attacker-controlled DNS TXT record and executes a hidden payload, giving the attacker an interactive shell with full developer privileges without human approval. Generative AI also lets novice attackers quickly write open-source packages that mimic legitimate utilities, write fake diagnostic logs and exfiltrate credentials, though such malware can reproduce human carelessness, such as hardcoded developer tokens that let researchers trace the operation. Defense requires architectural controls on AI tooling plus full data recoverability. Teams should limit agents' administrative and execution rights so they cannot delete infrastructure or change core settings without human approval; run AI tools in isolated environments that block untrusted outbound requests and restrict local file access; and audit external code, repositories and documentation before exposing them to AI tools. Because guardrails cannot prevent every incident, independent automated backups across the DevOps stack are essential. Organizations should follow the 3-2-1 rule (three copies on two media types, one offsite) and use solutions offering granular recovery, point-in-time restoration and cross-platform restore, such as from GitHub to Azure DevOps. Combining context-aware guardrails with resilient backup and recovery lets organizations use AI tools without unmanageable risk.

On July 28, 2026, RingCentral disclosed a data breach caused by a social engineering campaign attributed to the ShinyHunters extortion group. Personal data of approximately 1.6 million individuals was compromised. The attackers exfiltrated 623GB of data and, after RingCentral refused to pay a ransom, leaked a 280GB archive on their dark web leak site. The exposed data includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses. There is no evidence that the core RingCentral platform or service availability was affected, and the company says services continue to operate without disruption. The claims are corroborated by RingCentral's disclosures, Have I Been Pwned, and BleepingComputer. According to RingCentral's security bulletin, the attackers exploited no technical vulnerability and deployed no malware; they relied on deception of people with access to internal systems. The activity maps to phishing (T1566), likely followed by use of valid accounts (T1078) for lateral movement, exfiltration over web services (T1567.002), and extortion. No malware, command-and-control infrastructure, or software vulnerability exploitation was found in primary sources, and no specific software versions were identified as vulnerable. ShinyHunters is a known extortion group that repeatedly targets cloud and SaaS providers and their customers using social engineering, credential theft, and large-scale exfiltration. In the past year it claimed breaches affecting hundreds of Salesforce customers, as well as organizations using Salesloft, Drift, Salesforce Aura, and Oracle PeopleSoft; its tactics are also consistent with earlier campaigns against Snowflake customers. The timeline: in July 2026 ShinyHunters gained access via social engineering. On July 27 it claimed responsibility and demanded a ransom. RingCentral detected the activity, engaged a third-party forensic firm, took containment measures, notified affected customers, and publicly disclosed the breach on July 28. On August 13 Have I Been Pwned added the breach to its database, and on August 14 BleepingComputer published a detailed report. The main risk is heightened exposure to targeted phishing, business email compromise, and other social engineering using the leaked data. The exposure of personally identifiable information also creates regulatory and compliance risk, particularly in sectors such as finance and healthcare. Recommended mitigations, by priority: Critical: update security awareness training on social engineering and credential phishing. High: review user accounts, especially administrative ones, enforce multi-factor authentication, and reset credentials of suspected compromised accounts; regulated organizations should assess PII-related notification and compliance obligations. Medium: monitor for phishing and BEC attempts using the exposed data, deploy email filtering and anti-phishing controls, and update incident response plans for credential-based attacks. Low: conduct periodic security assessments and penetration testing of access controls and social engineering defenses. The only indicators listed are reference domains and URLs from Have I Been Pwned and RingCentral's security bulletin, not attacker infrastructure.

Harmony plans rollback, wiping 109,000 transactions after ONE exploit. Harmony said selectively restoring transactions could create inconsistent chain state, as Ravencoin faces a separate rollback dispute after an exploit. Harmony plans to roll back its blockchain to Aug. 11 following an exploit that created forged ONE tokens, discarding more than 109,000 transactions confirmed after its chosen checkpoint. The layer-1 network said Monday that validators would revert to blocks recorded at 11:25 pm UTC on Aug. 11. New blocks will be produced from the next heights using replacement databases. The discarded window includes 109,126 regular transactions and 315 staking transactions. Harmony said selectively restoring transactions was unsafe because balances, contract states, nonces and other conditions would differ on the replacement chain. Harmony was considering a rollback last week after reports that unauthorized ONE had been minted and sent to exchanges. It said Monday that investigators had traced nearly all of the forged ONE to wallets or service boundaries and were working with exchanges, bridges and law enforcement. At last look, the token had a market cap of roughly $10.8 million, according to Coingecko data. Harmony’s plan puts it alongside Ravencoin among networks seeking to reverse already confirmed blockchain activity after an exploit. Ravencoin faced a potential three-day blockchain reorganization after a consensus flaw was exploited. Mining pools controlling most of Ravencoin’s hash rate began building a competing chain that could reverse previously confirmed transactions. Ravencoin recent price of $0.002819 showed a market cap of $46.3 million.

OpenMatter Network announced on August 17, 2026 that Head of Operations and Partnerships Chris Biele will lead sessions at Belgrade Blockchain Week 2026 on secure scientific collaboration, agentic AI and the need for Verification Architecture, as part of the company's effort to move computing from assumption-based trust to cryptographic proof. The appearances follow the recent commercial launch of the OpenMatter Network platform and its work with Hashgraph Online (HOL) and DAIAA (Decentralized AI Agent Alliance) on standards for cryptographically verifiable AI agent execution. CEO and Co-Founder Renee Davis said the launch was only the beginning, and that the company is committed to helping enterprises, researchers, technology leaders and standards organizations understand why verification matters. As AI becomes more autonomous and organizations rely on systems they do not fully control, she said, it is not enough to trust that those systems will behave correctly; they must be able to prove it. On August 25, Biele will lead the main OpenMatter session at Moonstruck's DeSci Day. He will explain how cryptographic verification and privacy-preserving computing let researchers and organizations collaborate without exposing sensitive data. He will introduce OpenMatter's approach to masked computing, multi-party computation, zero-knowledge proofs and post-quantum infrastructure, then give a live demonstration of a verified compute job using the Datavizor solution. A fireside discussion will ask whether cryptographic proof can replace trust when organizations must collaborate using information they cannot safely share. Biele said valuable information stays isolated for legitimate reasons, and that computing on protected data without revealing it could remove a major barrier to research, innovation and collaboration. On August 26, Biele will give a 20-minute ETH Belgrade keynote titled "Don't Trust, Prove: Building the Post-Quantum Verification Layer for Agentic AI." He will argue that traditional security approaches lose effectiveness as autonomous AI agents act at machine speed, and that natural-language policies, runtime guardrails and after-the-fact auditing are no longer enough on their own. Enterprises also need cryptographic verification proving that computation was performed correctly and policies were followed. He will discuss how multi-party computation, zero-knowledge proofs and post-quantum cryptography can let AI systems operate on protected information and prove compliance without exposing the data. Potential applications include multi-hospital research without exposing patient data, autonomous fraud detection backed by mathematical compliance proof, and deterministic policy enforcement for critical infrastructure. Biele will also discuss OpenMatter's standards work through DAIAA and Hashgraph Online, including its leadership of the Cryptographic Agent Execution Standards Working Group, which aims to establish common approaches for verifying how autonomous AI agents execute instructions and follow policies. Davis said verification cannot remain merely an OpenMatter idea and must be understood and adopted across the industry. OpenMatter Network, headquartered on Florida's Space Coast, is building the Verifiable Trust Layer for Secure Collaboration and AI Agents, guided by the principle "Don't Trust Data. Prove It."

Alphabet Class A Tokenized Stock (Ondo), ticker GOOGLon, is a blockchain-based instrument giving token holders economic exposure to Alphabet Inc. Class A shares. Alphabet is one of the world's largest technology companies and the parent of Google, with businesses spanning search, digital advertising, cloud computing, consumer hardware, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving research, video streaming, and mobile operating systems. GOOGLon is not an independent cryptocurrency with its own valuation model; its value derives from the market performance of Alphabet's publicly traded equity. The token is structured to provide economic exposure comparable to directly holding Alphabet Class A shares. Dividends on the underlying stock are automatically reinvested, so the token's economic profile closely tracks the underlying asset. Eligible users can mint and redeem tokens directly, a mechanism meant to keep the tokenized representation aligned with the underlying market. Whereas U.S. equity markets are limited by exchange trading hours, Ondo's model allows users to interact with tokenized assets around the clock during the business week. Key features include blockchain-based ownership and settlement and access to traditional market liquidity through tokenized infrastructure. Tokenization converts traditional financial assets into blockchain-based representations that can be transferred, managed, and settled digitally, with the blockchain serving as the infrastructure layer for accessing a conventional security. Ondo positions tokenized securities as an extension of real-world asset infrastructure, aiming to improve accessibility while maintaining compliance requirements and connections to underlying financial markets. Tokenization also creates opportunities for interoperability with digital wallets, blockchain applications, and emerging financial protocols. GOOGLon targets investors who want exposure to a highly influential technology company while staying within blockchain-based ecosystems, including users who want to diversify beyond native cryptocurrencies without relying solely on traditional brokerages. It reflects growing interest in tokenized securities among financial institutions, asset managers, and blockchain developers, who increasingly view tokenized stocks as a bridge between conventional capital markets and decentralized financial infrastructure. Alphabet's prominence in AI, cloud services, digital advertising, and consumer technology makes it a notable addition to tokenized equities. The text cautions that tokenized securities differ from direct stock ownership and may not provide identical legal rights. Investors should evaluate the structure governing ownership, redemption rights, custodial arrangements, and regulatory requirements. Other considerations include jurisdictional restrictions, counterparty risk, market liquidity, and technical blockchain risks. Because the token's value derives from Alphabet shares, holders are also exposed to the company's business performance and broader market conditions.

The Motion Picture Association and ByteDance on Monday said the two had developed a framework to protect the film and TV industries’ intellectual property across ByteDance’s suite of AI generative products, including the AI video and image generators Seedance and Seedream. The memorandum of understanding (MOU) comes months after the MPA in February sent ByteDance a cease-and-desist letter and denounced the company following the release of Seedance 2.0, which saw creators produce riffs on actors including Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise. The MPA accused the company at the time of “disregarding well-established copyright law that protects the rights of creators and underpins millions of American jobs” on “a massive scale.” The two sides eventually began conversations to develop IP protections in ByteDance’s models, which the two said were reflected in the company’s release of Seedance 2.5 and Seedream 5.0 Pro last month. The generators are available across the Chinese TikTok owner’s collection of apps, including TikTok, the U.S. variant of TikTok, CapCut and Dreamina. Popular on Variety. “Today’s agreement illustrates our belief that copyright is a cornerstone of the film and television industry – and reinforces our commitment to protect creative content,” MPA Chairman and CEO Charles Rivkin said in a statement. “For the past several months, we have had constructive engagement with ByteDance to implement meaningful guardrails on Seedance and Seedream, and this MOU reflects our shared determination to continue our work together to further fortify those guardrails.” The move reflects how Hollywood has navigated the murkier elements of generative AI, a technology many in the industry are fascinated by yet worry undercuts their work through the unauthorized scraping of likenesses to train their models. The MPA similarly tore into OpenAI’s former video model Sora before the company imposed its own guardrails. “ByteDance respects the intellectual property rights that underpin creative industries around the world, and we believe responsible innovation in AI goes hand in hand with meaningful protections for rightsholders,” John Rogovin, ByteDance’s general counsel, added in a statement. “We appreciate the productive engagement with the MPA and its members as we continue to strengthen safeguards across our generative AI services. This MOU establishes an important framework for continued collaboration as the technology evolves across a variety of products and platforms.”

Researchers at MIT have developed a machine learning approach that could enable artificial intelligence (AI) models to simulate a broader range of physical systems and conditions without requiring extensive retraining. The work addresses a challenge in AI-based physical simulation: models trained on a particular set of conditions can struggle when presented with scenarios outside the range of their training data. This can limit their usefulness for applications such as engineering design, materials science and climate modelling, where systems can behave differently as physical conditions change. The MIT researchers developed a method that gives AI models what they describe as a better "feel for physics", allowing them to generalise more effectively to situations they have not encountered during training. “We believe physics is the third modality for AI models, after text and pixels,” noted MIT PhD student and CSAIL researcher Minghao Guo, a co-lead author on a paper introducing GeoPT. “Our general-purpose model has the versatility to help build a world model for physics. Many models, such as those that generate robotics data and videos, are already well-versed in textual and visual data, but with physical accuracy, they’ll get more realistic results.” Rather than training an AI model to reproduce individual examples, the researchers incorporated information about the underlying physical system into the learning process. The approach is designed to help models identify relationships between physical variables, rather than simply learning correlations present in their training datasets. As a result, the model can use those relationships to make predictions when operating conditions change. The researchers tested the method on physical systems involving fluid dynamics and other forms of physical behaviour, assessing how well the models could generalise beyond the conditions represented in their training data. The researchers found that models incorporating this physical understanding could produce accurate simulations across a wider range of scenarios than conventional machine learning approaches. This is important for scientific computing because generating training datasets for every possible physical condition can be computationally expensive. Traditional numerical simulations can themselves require substantial computational time, particularly when modelling complex systems at high resolution. Reducing reliance on training data. The technique could therefore reduce the amount of data required to develop AI-based simulation models. Instead of relying exclusively on large datasets of simulated or experimental results, the model can incorporate knowledge of the governing physics to constrain its predictions. This can improve its ability to extrapolate beyond the examples used during training. The researchers said the approach could be useful where obtaining training data is difficult or expensive, such as for physical systems that are challenging to simulate or experimentally reproduce. AI-based surrogate models are increasingly being investigated to accelerate computationally intensive scientific simulations. Once trained, these models can produce predictions much faster than conventional numerical solvers, potentially allowing researchers and engineers to explore more design configurations or physical conditions. However, ensuring that surrogate models remain reliable outside their training distribution remains a significant challenge. The MIT research addresses this issue by placing greater emphasis on the physical relationships underlying the data. Applications in engineering and science. The researchers believe the approach could eventually support applications in which AI models need to operate under changing physical conditions. In engineering, this could include exploring different designs, materials or operating environments without having to train a separate model for every scenario. In scientific research, models capable of generalising across physical regimes could help researchers investigate systems where experimental data is limited. The work also highlights the potential to combine machine learning with established scientific knowledge rather than treating AI as a replacement for physics-based modelling. By giving AI models a stronger representation of the physical principles governing a system, the researchers aim to create simulation tools that are both faster than conventional numerical approaches and more robust when conditions change. For scientific computing, this could help bridge the gap between traditional high-fidelity simulations and data-driven AI models, enabling researchers to apply machine learning to a wider range of physical problems without requiring prohibitively large training datasets.

'We Should Be Furious': UK Navy Drones Caught Beaming 'Heartbeat' Data To China. For decades, the People's Republic of China has duplicated other countries' technology while also embedding its own tech in numerous consumer electronics. You might recall the concern in the U.S. over TikTok's Chinese ownership, with some worried that sensitive information might wind up in the wrong hands. Now, a similar concern has emerged related to a massive United Kingdom drone program with Chinese camera components. In addition to crafting its own powerful drone programs, China also procures components that other countries use for theirs. Aboard some of the U.K.'s K3 Scout uncrewed surface vessels (USV), the Royal Navy recently stripped away wireless connectivity after it became apparent that there was an issue with such components. As reported by various outlets, cameras were sending "heartbeat communications," or automated signals, to an IP address in China. These signals indicate whether the system is online and functioning correctly, meaning China was essentially made aware of the K3 Scout's usage through these signals. Prior to the installation of the third-party camera components, Kraken Technology Group, the company that developed and sells the K3 Scout, assured the U.K. government that they were secure. The program continued with the Chinese parts, though it appears that none in the Royal Navy were fully aware of the heartbeat communications transmission until an audit was completed. Fortunately, the audit found that no sensitive data made its way to Chinese servers, but the fact that a signal was sent repeatedly created a great deal of concern. The K3 Scout USV's compromised components create an expensive problem for the U.K. The U.K. acted quickly once the heartbeat communications were identified. A company spokesman from Kraken Technology Group responded to the issue, saying, "We are aware that some third-party, NDAA-compliant cameras had a small number of components originating from outside the U.K. ... After a full audit by both Kraken and the Royal Navy, we are confident no sensitive information has ever been shared outside of intended channels and any potential vulnerabilities have been identified and closed" (via TechRadar). While that solves the immediate concern, the impact reaches further than the U.K. Not only has the U.K. been utilizing the K3 Scout and other USVs, but United States Special Operations Command (SOCOM) has also purchased the platform. Outside of the heartbeat communications issue, the K3 Scout is a desirable USV. It can carry a payload weighing up to 1,322 lbs. while operating continuously for 30 days, making it an ideal candidate for reconnaissance and intelligence gathering. Still, the heartbeat communications issue is a big one. The U.K. has invested heavily in its multi-billion-pound program, but it may have to be more cautious with the drones and components it purchases from here on out. As of this writing, it was unclear what the U.S. plans to do with its K3 Scout USVs, as neither SOCOM nor the Department of War had issued a statement on the matter.

People with high scores on the vegetable-rich pattern had roughly 51% lower risk of dying from any cause and about 45% lower risk of a cardiovascular event compared with those with low scores, the report stated. The pattern was built around allium vegetables, cruciferous vegetables, orange and red vegetables, legumes, soup, pasta and rice, and vegetable oils. Earlier research has also linked higher consumption of vegetables and fruit with lower risk of dying from any cause [1]. Researchers used machine learning to map how Canadians eat, the study stated. The data came from two large Canadian nutrition surveys, and a subset of participants was tracked through 2017 with records linked to death and hospital data. The algorithm analyzed which foods people consumed together in daily life, rather than scoring them against a predetermined dietary template. The algorithm identified three eating patterns among Canadian adults, according to the study. The first, the vegetable-rich pattern, was centered on onions, garlic, leeks, broccoli, cauliflower, carrots, bell peppers, legumes, and vegetable oils; people who scored high on this pattern also tended to eat less fast food. The second pattern, high sugary beverages and low fruit, was centered on sugary drinks, refined grains, and salty snacks. Whole grains, whole fruit, water, yogurt, and nuts and seeds were inversely linked to that pattern, the report stated. The third pattern, high-fat breakfast, was built around solid fats, coffee, sugar, processed meat, eggs, pancakes, and waffles, with tea showing an inverse relationship. People with high scores on the vegetable-rich pattern had roughly 51% lower all-cause mortality risk and 45% lower cardiovascular event risk, according to the study. At age 45, the pattern translated to up to 8.3 additional years for females and 6.1 for males, the report stated. Higher scores on the high-fat breakfast pattern showed no significant link to mortality or cardiovascular disease but were associated with modestly shorter life expectancy: about 1.0 year lost for females and 0.8 years for males. The sugary-beverage pattern was linked to a 31% higher all-cause mortality risk overall and 39% higher among males, with up to 3.0 years of life lost for males and 1.7 years for females, according to the study. Researchers said the pattern's mortality association was not limited to cardiovascular disease. Study authors said the findings support a whole-diet approach rather than a focus on individual superfoods, according to the report. The foods associated with the healthier pattern included onions, garlic, leeks, broccoli, cauliflower, carrots, peppers, legumes, and vegetable oils. The report recommended reducing sugary drinks and shifting toward plant-forward meals, while noting that the pattern does not need to be plant-exclusive. The vegetable-rich pattern overlaps with diets previously tied to lower disease risk. A diet rich in vegetables significantly lowers the risk of hypertension and related conditions, according to research from National Taiwan University [2]. Mediterranean diets, which similarly emphasize vegetables and olive oil, have been associated with reduced risks of diabetes, heart attacks, and strokes [3]. Vegetables also contain phenolic compounds, flavonoids, and vitamin C linked to antioxidant activity, according to a study of Mauritian vegetables [4]. A meta-analysis of 57 studies found that each one-point increase in adherence to a Mediterranean diet was associated with a 5% lower risk of cardiovascular disease [5]. The study provides observational evidence that long-term eating patterns, not single foods, are associated with life expectancy, according to the report. Researchers emphasized that the findings should be interpreted with caution because the observational design does not prove causation and other factors could be at play. The data add to existing nutrition research linking plant-forward dietary patterns with lower mortality, the study stated. Earlier work has documented that populations eating healthy, vegetable-rich diets have no recorded heart disease, according to Joel Fuhrman [6]. The new findings add to a body of evidence linking Mediterranean-style dietary patterns to lower mortality risk in older adults, according to a separate report [7].

Quantum computing is moving beyond the research stage as companies look for ways to turn experimental systems into commercial products. Quantinuum (QNT) is taking another step in that direction by teaming up with Quanta Computer, a major Taiwanese electronics manufacturer, to develop the hardware infrastructure needed for future generations of quantum computers. The partnership is focused on making quantum systems more modular, scalable, and suitable for manufacturing at commercial volumes. For investors watching the emerging quantum computing industry, that could be an important development because the ability to manufacture and deploy systems efficiently may become just as important as advances in quantum technology itself. QNT Stock Has Been a Wild Ride. Quantinuum shares are up about 18% since its June IPO; however, the stock has been highly volatile, reaching an all-time high of $86.79 before retreating as investors weighed its growth prospects against heavy losses. The Quanta agreement comes after an eventful earnings period. Shares jumped following Quantinuum’s first report as a public company, then moved lower as investors reassessed the valuation and widening losses. The opportunity comes with a substantial valuation premium. Barchart data recently showed QNT stock trading at roughly 90 times sales. That leaves little room for weak execution or slower-than-expected commercialization. Why the Quanta Partnership Matters. Quanta is a major manufacturer of advanced computing and cloud infrastructure, and its manufacturing expertise could help Quantinuum address one of the biggest hurdles facing quantum computing: moving from sophisticated prototypes to systems that can be produced and deployed at scale. The companies will work on hardware infrastructure for future generations of Quantinuum systems, supporting the company’s roadmap toward larger and more commercially deployable machines. Quantinuum’s Sol system is targeted for 2027, making the partnership relevant to its next stage of product development. First Public-Company Earnings Show Both Sides. Quantinuum’s second-quarter revenue increased 279% year-over-year (YoY) to $8 million, beating the $7.6 million analyst estimate. Management also raised its 2026 revenue outlook to $28 million to $32 million. The weak point was profitability. GAAP net loss widened to $597 million from $57 million a year earlier, while adjusted EBITDA loss reached $68 million. Much of the GAAP loss reflected stock compensation and other noncash items, but the numbers still underscore how early the business remains. Elsewhere, Quantinuum is expanding its commercial footprint through Oracle (ORCL), which is integrating its Helios quantum computer into Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The company is also pursuing projects with customers such as BP (BP) and has been developing its broader full-stack quantum platform. Wall Street Still Sees Massive Upside for QNT Stock. Barchart’s latest analyst data shows a “Strong Buy” consensus, with 14 analysts providing recommendations. The same data puts the mean price target at $97.17, implying about 47% upside, while the Street-high target of $155 represents roughly 134% potential upside at the time of writing. That bullish view is not universal. Morgan Stanley has maintained a more cautious stance, with a $78 target. Still, the broader analyst group remains constructive, suggesting Wall Street sees Quantinuum’s partnerships, technology roadmap, and rising commercial activity as potential drivers of substantial long-term growth.
