BNB Chain Launches BNB Agent Studio v2, Giving AI Agents the Ability to Earn. The update lets AI agents get hired and paid directly while new onchain wallet controls set verifiable limits on how they can access a user's funds. Dubai, UAE, August 19th, 2026, Chainwire. BNB Chain, one of the largest blockchain ecosystems worldwide, today announced BNB Agent Studio v2, an update to its AI agent development platform. The release expands what autonomous agents can do with money, from earning their own income to operating inside owner-defined financial limits enforced onchain. BNB Agent Studio launched in July, allowing developers to describe an AI agent in a single prompt and deploy it to BNB Smart Chain (BSC). In its initial release, agents could spend but not earn. v2 closes that gap: agents can now be hired and paid directly, with funds settling to their wallet through a standard receiving interface that completes the ERC-8183 commerce flow end to end. The update also introduces Altana, a new self-custodial wallet option built to resolve one of the central constraints in agent design: how much authority an agent should hold over a user's funds. Agents using Altana operate through scoped session keys governed by spending limits, allowlists, and time bounds set by their owner in advance. These permissions are recorded onchain, allowing anyone to verify what a given agent is authorized to do, and can be revoked instantly without key rotation or downtime. Altana joins TWAK (Trust Wallet AgentKit), the platform's existing wallet option for agents that require continuous, autonomous signing without a person in the loop. With both options now available, builders can match the wallet architecture to the agent's purpose: TWAK for always-on autonomous operation, or Altana for agents that require clear, verifiable boundaries around fund access. A yield agent, for instance, can harvest and restake earnings without holding access to principal; a lending agent can top up collateral without the ability to withdraw it. v2 also adds TypeScript support alongside the platform's existing Python SDK, and introduces a Paymaster that covers gas on BSC Testnet, removing the manual funding step previously required to begin testing an agent. Key updates in v2: - Agents can now be paid for their work, completing the ERC-8183 commerce flow end to end. - Altana, a new self-custodial wallet option, enforces spending limits, allowlists, and time bounds onchain. - TypeScript is now supported alongside Python. - A Paymaster covers testnet gas, removing manual wallet funding for testing BNB Agent Studio. - A standard provider interface replaces per-provider integration work for cloud deployment. BNB Agent Studio v2 is live now, with existing agents continuing to run without migration. BNB Chain currently hosts more registered AI agents than any other network. BNB Agent Studio is available at bnbchain.org/en/bnb-agent-studio. About BNB Chain. BNB Chain is one of the largest and most active blockchain ecosystems in the world. Its multi-chain architecture spans BNB Smart Chain (BSC), opBNB, and BNB Greenfield, giving developers the flexibility to choose the environment best suited to their application. With high throughput, low transaction costs, and full EVM compatibility, BNB Chain is built for high-speed trading, AI agents, privacy, and instant payments. It is the blockchain with superior distribution and deep liquidity, built for global markets and the next billion users. For more information, users can visit. Press. Press. BNB Chain.

ReliaQuest reports that a JavaServer Pages (JSP) web shell deployed after exploitation of a critical flaw in PTC Windchill and FlexPLM servers is purpose-built for the enterprise Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) software. The company describes it as a fully equipped extortion platform that can map sensitive vault data, decrypt every credential in the Windchill keystore, and run additional code through a custom Java class loader, making it a backdoor for remote access and post-exploitation such as lateral movement, ransomware, or persistence. Unlike typical lightweight or open-source web shells such as Behinder or China Chopper, it is bespoke and tailored to the targeted software. The shell is deployed after weaponization of CVE-2026-12569 (CVSS 9.3), an improper input validation flaw that lets an attacker execute arbitrary code via a malicious network request. An advisory from Ransom-ISAC, eCrime.ch and Defused attributed the activity to the Clop (Cl0p) ransomware operation, which dropped JSP web shells on vulnerable systems. ReliaQuest researchers John Dilgen and Connor Short say the implant embeds detailed knowledge of Windchill's APIs, database schema, keystore and file-vault structure, enabling rapid movement from access to data theft without external commands or extra tools. References to "Clop" throughout the code support the highly likely attribution. Because these applications store engineering data and product designs, compromise can expose proprietary data and credentials usable for lateral movement. A single "S" command returns Windchill's directory-management and administrative credentials in plaintext via a built-in function called gs. It reads the "ieStructProperties.txt" configuration file, decrypts the LDAP manager password from the keystore, and iterates through stored local properties, decrypting further values including administrative account credentials, object storage credentials, and all site administrator keys. A separate command exfiltrates the results. ReliaQuest warns that because LDAP credentials typically govern access to Active Directory, email, VPN and other enterprise services, one application compromise could become an enterprise-wide credential compromise. The supported commands include: E (returns the parameter value, likely a connectivity test), O (returns the operating system name), J (loads and executes a Java class from a ZIP via the class loader), D (file download), S (credential harvesting), L (file vault enumeration, writing "flst.txt"), G (reads an arbitrary file) and R (deletes a file, used for cleanup). The shell can run attacker-supplied code in memory, allowing on-demand deployment of secondary payloads for persistence, network traversal or encryption; the payload is a Base64-encoded ZIP of compiled Java bytecode. It also enumerates the application database to find high-value engineering data and runs queries through Windchill's existing database identity rather than creating a new account, reducing forensic visibility. By operating inside the application process and blending with normal Windchill traffic, it evades signature-based defenses and mimics standard application functions. This is not Clop's first custom web shell: it previously used DEWMODE and LEMURLOOT after exploiting Accellion (CVE-2021-27101) and MOVEit Transfer (CVE-2023-34362) flaws. ReliaQuest calls Clop a "sleeping dragon" that goes inactive between campaigns but returns with custom-built web shells whenever a mass-extortion opportunity arises.

In 2007, Assaf Rappaport, then 24 and a rising figure in Unit 81, an elite Israeli Defense Forces technology division, was repeatedly urged by a friend to meet 19-year-old soldier Yevgeny Dibrov, who had placed second in a regional round of Israel's national Bible trivia championship. After one phone call, Rappaport wanted Dibrov in his unit and became his commanding officer. In April 2026, ServiceNow paid $7.75 billion cash for Dibrov's company, Armis, which monitors every connected device on an enterprise network and flags security risks. It was ServiceNow's largest acquisition and the second-biggest pure startup exit in Israeli tech; Rappaport holds the top spot with Google's $32 billion purchase of Wiz in 2025. Dibrov, 38, and co-founder Nadir Izrael split roughly $930 million. Dibrov now runs the Armis unit as general manager, with Izrael as group vice president of product and engineering. When the deal leaked in December, ServiceNow's stock fell 9% amid investor fear that AI agents would make traditional software obsolete, dubbed the "SaaSpocalypse." The stock fell as much as 42% in the first four months of 2026. Chief product officer Amit Zavery said the company never believed in the doomsday premise and saw an opening to combine cybersecurity, IT asset management and industrial device monitoring on one platform. In May the stock surged 41%, its best performance since its 2012 IPO, and it rose another 8% after second-quarter earnings, with revenue of $3.99 billion, up 24%, and AI products passing $1 billion in annual contract value. Zavery said Armis is helping, though it is one piece of a broader strategy. Dibrov was three years old when his family left Ukraine for Israel; they couldn't afford a car for years, which still drives him. He studied at Technion. In 2012 Rappaport hired him as first employee at Adallom, a cloud security company bought by Microsoft in 2015 for $250 million. Dibrov left in December 2015 to found Armis, and Rappaport wrote the first $100,000 check; Dibrov later did the same for Wiz. Armis's first raise in January 2016 was $5 million at an $11 million post-money valuation. Insight Partners acquired Armis in 2020 for roughly $1.1 billion, with $100 million from CapitalG, while Dibrov and Izrael kept running it. Insight's stake at the ServiceNow sale was worth about $3.3 billion, 43% of the stock. Armis passed $300 million in annual recurring revenue, and by August 2025 Dibrov was telling employees an IPO was coming. Then Zavery called out of the blue; ServiceNow had been building its own asset-tracking tools but chose to buy the market leader. ServiceNow's John Aisien was convinced when Izrael mentioned Vipr, an unadvertised product that finds code vulnerabilities before hackers do. Dibrov explained the change to staff by saying customers wanted the combination, and says investors got the best returns of their careers. Morgan Stanley, which advised on the deal and is an Armis customer, praised his persistence and a two-week custom feature turnaround. Colleagues describe a relentless worker who closed a funding round from the hospital the day after his daughter was born. Armis had about 950 employees at the acquisition and Dibrov now oversees 2,000. He says he still acts like a startup. Investor Omri Casspi predicts ServiceNow will eventually make Dibrov CEO, though Bill McDermott's contract runs until at least 2030, Dibrov has shown no interest, and Zavery said no succession talks are underway.

More governors are shifting stances or tightening rules on data centers as the midterms approach and public opinion sours on the energy-hungry facilities that tech companies and developers are building to power artificial intelligence and cloud computing. The backlash is shaping governor's races in some of the largest states and presidential battlegrounds. On Tuesday, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said his administration will no longer put data center projects at the head of the line for construction permits or a lucrative tax exemption unless they meet certain standards. Developers must pay the full cost of their electricity, show how they will use advanced technology to limit water use, and win local approval before seeking state approval. Shapiro called these the "strictest guardrails in the nation," though he stopped short of a moratorium on permits. Considered a potential 2028 presidential contender, he faces mounting pressure from GOP opponent Stacy Garrity as communities revolt against proposed projects. He attacked "predatory developers" who bully local officials to push through dozens of projects, which his administration said number more than 100 reports, that likely will never be built for lack of financing, power or tech clients. He singled out plans for six campuses of about 50 server warehouses in tiny Archbald Borough, which has sparked a community uprising, a developer lawsuit, and motions to force the recusal of six of seven council members. Garrity said Shapiro "lit the fuse on the chaos." In Texas, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa released a rural TV ad accusing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott of "selling you out" to data center companies, tapping rural Republican discontent over threats to ranchland and water supplies. Both Shapiro and Abbott once courted data centers, appearing with Amazon ($20 billion in Pennsylvania) and Google ($40 billion in Texas). Recently, Abbott ordered regulators to ensure Texans don't pay higher electric bills because of data centers, told them to hold up projects until that work is done, and promised next year to push regulations and end the state's tax break, worth more than a billion dollars a year. Local zoning and permitting boards across the U.S. have increasingly rejected projects as angry residents fill meetings. Concerns include lost open space and rural character, diesel generator and server noise, property values, health, drying wells and aquifers, and rising electricity bills. In Arkansas, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders views such investments as key to beating China while protecting affordable power and water, her spokesperson said, noting Google is covering full energy costs for its West Memphis facility. Today's AI-driven data centers can dwarf stadiums and factories and use more energy than small cities. Some states are forcing them to pay for their own power, limit water use, disclose more, and earn community support, and are balking at sales tax exemption costs. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs secured a three-year moratorium on the exemption, calling it a "corporate handout." New York Gov. Kathy Hochul ordered a one-year ban on large data centers. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker halted new exemptions until tougher standards pass. In Ohio, nominees Amy Acton (D) and Vivek Ramaswamy (R) each proposed tougher standards. In Wisconsin, Democratic nominee David Crowley narrowly beat a rival who campaigned on a one-year moratorium; Republican Tom Tiffany attacks him as "Data Center David Crowley," while Crowley says communities need veto power but data centers can bring economic benefits.

Google has announced the Pixel 11 series. While attention usually goes to higher-end models like the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold, the author argues the base Pixel 11 remains one of the more affordable flagship Android phones and is a fine choice over the Pro models. At first glance the Pixel 11 looks identical to the Pixel 10, with the same 6.3-inch OLED display and a weight only 0.3 ounces lower. The camera bar is slightly slimmer, with the flash integrated into it, so the phone lies flat with a case on. It offers an experience very similar to the Pro for $200 less; the main differences are the Pro's slightly higher-resolution, brighter display and its camera tech. Camera improvements are supported by the new Tensor G6 chipset, which Google says delivers better performance, an improved ISP (image signal processor) for faster high-resolution images, and a TPU (tensor processing unit) for AI features. The Pixel 11 keeps the Pixel 10's triple-camera setup: a 48MP main camera, a 13MP ultrawide lens, and a 10.8MP 5x telephoto. However, the primary sensor is larger and 56% more light-sensitive, producing brighter, cleaner photos. Camera Coach and Best Take return, joined by Magic Capture and Camera Looks. Magic Capture records video while simultaneously capturing high-quality, automatically cropped stills ready to share. Camera Looks applies custom filters while preserving Google's Real Tone so skin tones stay accurate. Night Sight benefits from the Tensor G6 for clearer low-light images, though the author wishes the Pixel 11 had Instant Night Sight, which is exclusive to the Pro models and processes night photos up to 4.5 times faster. The Pixel 11 now starts at 256GB of storage, eliminating the 128GB base option, with a 512GB configuration available. The battery grows modestly from 4,970 mAh to 4,985 mAh, and Google claims over 30 hours on a single charge. Fast charging can reportedly reach 55% in about 30 minutes with a compatible charger. Like the Pixel 10, it supports Qi2.2-compatible Pixelsnap accessories. The base model lacks HiLight, a feature limited to the Pro models. The author considers this a minor loss because the feature is still niche and underdeveloped: it offers only five color options and lights up only for calls (not texts) and when talking to Gemini. Even if Google calls it a standout differentiator for the Pro, the author says the base model has much more going for it. The Pixel 11 starts at $899 and is available for preorder today, with devices officially available on August 20th.

Coinbase announced it is establishing an international "tokenization hub" in Abu Dhabi, boosting the emirate's bid to become a global digital-asset center. Based out of Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), the financial centre, Coinbase has been granted a license to arrange investment deals and provide custody for tokenized securities. Custody means safely holding and managing the digital ownership records of assets, which matters for institutional investors' confidence. Tokenization is gaining momentum in traditional finance globally, with major asset managers and banks bringing funds, bonds, private credit and equities onto blockchain infrastructure. ADGM introduced one of the world's first comprehensive virtual asset regulatory frameworks in 2018 and now has over 20 firms holding active virtual asset licences. In December last year it licensed Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange by trading volume. CoinMarketCap's June 2026 data put Binance's volume at $4.74 trillion, or 39.5% of volume across the 11 exchanges it tracks. Adam Popat, UAE-based CEO of SettleMint, which helps regulated institutions issue and manage digital assets, said Coinbase's move turns tokenized securities "from a pilot into a market" and shows the UAE has the regulatory depth to host global issuance, not just regional experiments. He called the UAE "one of the leading lights" in tokenization globally, citing GCC national-scale digitization programs, deep capital pools, growing talent and a collaborative regulatory environment. He said SettleMint is in talks with all the large UAE banks exploring tokenization of equities, funds, bonds and deposits, and that gold tokenization is a very active conversation with several partners. In May, SettleMint partnered with ADI Foundation to build digital asset lifecycle infrastructure on ADI Chain, supporting tokenization of securities under ADGM's framework and addressing the need for coordinated, regulated infrastructure linking issuance, trading, settlement and custody. ADI Foundation, an Abu Dhabi-based organization, aims to bring one billion people into the digital economy by 2030. In July, ADI Chain secured a $50 million strategic investment to support expansion across the Middle East, Africa and Asia. The ecosystem is also rolling out DDSC, a dirham-pegged stablecoin developed by First Abu Dhabi Bank, International Holding Company and Sirius International Holding. The UAE is also using sovereign wealth funds for tokenization. Last month Mubadala Capital, the asset management arm of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, tokenized one of its private-market strategies through UAE-based infrastructure provider KAIO on blockchains including Base, with Coinbase taking an exposure to the fund. Elsewhere in the region, Saudi Arabia completed its first sovereign-native tokenized title-deed transfer in early 2026, and the Qatar Financial Centre is taking steps to enable real estate tokenization. A January report by consulting firm Kearney estimated that by 2030 close to $500 billion in GCC assets, spanning private markets, funds, bank deposits, public equities, real estate and commodities, could be represented on blockchain. Private markets are the largest opportunity, potentially reaching $154 billion by 2030. Kearney said this signals a fundamental shift in market dynamics, explaining why governments, institutions and asset managers are strengthening digital asset strategies. If the projection holds, tokenization could make GCC capital markets more accessible, efficient and interconnected and let the region lead the next phase of global finance.

Stablecoin issuer Circle (CRCL) has acquired nearly 1,000 issued blockchain-anchored patents from IBM, a deal the firm said makes it the largest holder of blockchain patents in the United States. The portfolio spans more than 680 patent families covering blockchain technology, banking, financial services, insurance, enterprise infrastructure, supply-chain verification and cloud security, according to a press release. The deal’s financial terms weren’t disclosed. IBM was already among the largest U.S. blockchain patent holders before the sale. A December 2025 analysis by patent analytics firm PatSnap credited it with 790 patents, alongside Advanced New Technologies and Bank of America. Circle said the portfolio would support USDC, Circle Payments Network, its Arc blockchain and financial tools designed for AI agents. Circle and IBM also plan to explore further commercial opportunities, the document adds. “Intellectual property is critical to advancing our mission and expanding adoption of onchain infrastructure,” said Sarah Wilson, Circle’s general counsel and corporate secretary. Circle received its first patent, covering parallel blockchain data processing, in December 2023. It had earlier joined the LOT Network to protect its products from patent-assertion firms. The company did not disclose how many acquired patents were issued in the U.S., whether IBM retained licensing rights or whether it plans to license or enforce the portfolio. CoinDesk has reached out to Circle for comment but hasn’t heard back at the time of writing. CRCL shares are up 2.5% in premarket trading.

Experts warn that as estimates for "Q-Day" move closer, crypto's slow governance, rather than its cryptography, may be the biggest obstacle to defending against quantum attacks. Quantum computing threatens every encrypted system, including major banks, but crypto may be tested first. Eddy Zervigon, CEO of Quantum Xchange, which builds infrastructure to shield networks from quantum-enabled attacks, told CoinDesk that "cryptocurrencies are the canary in the coal mine." He said crypto is the first place of attack because of its decentralized nature, and that an attack there would signal someone has a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. No such computer exists yet, but estimates are compressing. Zervigon said those developing quantum computers, such as Microsoft and IBM, generally expect a cryptographically relevant machine around 2029, citing IBM's Arvind Krishna. Earlier this year, Google researchers revealed that breaking the elliptic-curve cryptography protecting bitcoin and ether would require fewer than 500,000 physical qubits, a 20-fold decline from previous estimates, prompting several observers, including Google, to pull Q-Day forward to 2029. The White House aims to develop a powerful quantum computer by 2028 and move high-value assets and federal data to post-quantum cryptography by 2030, which Zervigon said creates urgency. Zervigon is not alone in pointing to governance as the weak point. Deutsche Digital Assets wrote on July 23 that the difference between traditional finance and decentralized rails is governance speed. A bank like JPMorgan needs only "a board resolution, a budget, and a vendor" rather than approval from millions of pseudonymous participants, so large institutions can migrate to post-quantum standards faster, more quietly and more predictably than a public blockchain. The bank said this is not an argument against Bitcoin but for taking its governance process seriously. The 2024 arXiv paper "Downtime Required for Bitcoin Quantum-Safety" supports this, noting that any upgrade requires 90% consensus among Bitcoin miners, and that major changes have historically met high resistance. The 2017 SegWit upgrade caused such disagreement that the blockchain split through hard forks into versions including Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin Gold. The takeaway is that post-quantum cryptography itself could be ready in time, but it is uncertain whether Bitcoin's governance can reach 90% consensus to deploy it. Zervigon also argued that markets wrongly treat Q-Day as a single binary event. An attacker need not break an algorithm in real time: if decrypting valuable data takes three or six months, the goal is still achieved. A quantum computer therefore only needs to break a signature before the underlying data or funds stop being worth stealing, which means the risk begins earlier than a specific date.

Nvidia's effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington's effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. Yet despite restrictions on exporting the most advanced semiconductors, including GB300s, several Chinese firms have reportedly accessed their compute power via data centers in Southeast Asia. Less than a week after Moonshot AI released a new model in July, White House official Michael Kratsios accused the company of using Nvidia's GB300 chips via a facility in Thailand. Moonshot's Kimi K3 is one of a wave of new Chinese models, alongside new systems from DeepSeek and Alibaba, that have made performance leaps and scored well on benchmarks. Industry watchers say access to advanced compute through overseas cloud providers is a key factor in this progress. Nvidia's most advanced chips are restricted from export to China, though some less capable ones may be shipped. Cassia King of the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy said Moonshot's reported access was legal "so long as Moonshot isn't actually buying and owning the physical hardware directly," because the export control regime "controls physical AI chips. It does not cover remote access to those chips." A White House official said the Trump administration has implemented "the most rigorous export control regime in modern history." The Commerce Department and the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) did not respond to requests for comment. Chinese hyperscalers including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have reportedly accessed Nvidia compute remotely via Thailand, Malaysia and Japan. ByteDance and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment, and Alibaba declined to comment. According to an anonymous source, ByteDance worked with Singapore-headquartered cloud provider Aolani to access compute in Malaysia, an arrangement first reported by the Wall Street Journal in March. Aolani said its customers do not own or physically access the chips and that any access is fully compliant with applicable regulations. AI infrastructure buildouts in Southeast Asia are booming. JLL estimates global data center capacity could roughly double to 200GW by 2030, and DC Byte data show 31 planned 100MW+ data centers across Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, versus two today. Michelle Nie of the Center for a New American Security said the loophole is "threatening U.S. national security," since chip export controls aim to deny China the ability to train frontier AI on advanced U.S. chips. The proposed Remote Access Security Act (RASA) would extend export controls to remote cloud-based access to critical hardware and software. It passed the House in January but has not passed the Senate. Nie noted possible industry pushback, as cloud providers would bear the compliance burden of know-your-customer (KYC) and verification requirements. She added that RASA alone would not solve the problem: it would give the government authority to regulate remote access, but a rule would still need to be created. King said BIS could issue a rule in a "matter of days" with White House support, but the challenge is making it effective and enforceable, including deciding what compute is covered, who is barred from remote access, and how to implement a robust KYC scheme.

Also, a Palo Alto micromobility startup, raised a $150 million Series D round, Fortune learned exclusively. Prysm Capital led the round, with Eclipse Capital and Greenoaks participating. The raise pushed the two-year-old company's valuation past $1 billion, a large figure for a company whose most visible product so far is a $3,500 e-bike. CEO Chris Yu says Also is more than an e-bike maker: it builds a small-vehicle technology platform with in-house motors, batteries, compute, and software, designed to be dropped into any vehicle smaller than a car that moves people or goods, such as pedal-assist delivery quads and, eventually, fully autonomous vehicles. The company spun out of Rivian in early 2025 after running as a stealth project there. Rivian founder RJ Scaringe co-founded it and remains chairman of both companies. Funding has come quickly: $105 million at spinout, a $200 million Series C earlier this year led by Greenoaks with Prysm, and a strategic investment from DoorDash. The new capital is earmarked to accelerate Also's autonomous vehicle platform. The company is developing multiple autonomous hardware projects simultaneously for moving goods and passengers, all built on the EV architecture underpinning its consumer bike, the TM-B, and its commercial electric delivery quad, the TM-Q. Yu argued that repurposing a 7,000-pound van, truck, or SUV for across-town trips with one passenger, or to deliver a toothbrush or a hamburger, makes no sense for economical, low-impact, congestion-minimizing travel. He said different scales and form factors will become the obvious answer in denser metro and suburban areas. His goal is that within five years, small-form-factor autonomy is a standard, unremarkable part of the transportation mix alongside self-driving cars. The round comes at a rough moment for e-bikes: Rad Power Bikes went bankrupt, Juiced Bikes collapsed, and Porsche walked away from the category. Still, the global micromobility market, covering e-bikes, e-scooters, and small delivery EVs, is valued around $50 billion and projected to more than double by the early 2030s. Skeptic David Zipper has cited the bankruptcies as proof the category is saturated, not underserved. Yu, a former Specialized bike product chief with an aerospace background, countered that existing products' performance says nothing about market demand, only how hard it is to create experiences that solve real pain points. He blamed unreliable batteries and clunky anti-theft locks, not lack of demand, for keeping riders on the sidelines. Also differs from a "nicer e-bike" on the commercial side, through its Amazon partnership and a multi-year commercial agreement with DoorDash, which point toward robots built on the same motors and compute as the consumer bike. Rivian, still a major non-controlling shareholder, factors into the roadmap because its growing on-road fleet generates driving data Also will eventually need to train its autonomy systems. Jay Park, who led the round for Prysm, said his fund backed Rivian for its well-designed, vertically integrated electric vehicles, and that Also applies the same approach to smaller vehicles for commercial operators and consumers. OpenAI Is Pausing Some Work Due To Safety Concerns After Finding It Could Pose Critical Cybersecurity Risks "We always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety and alignment," CEO Sam Altman said. OpenAI said it is pausing some work on a new model after concluding it could pose critical cybersecurity risks. In a social media publication, CEO Sam Altman said the decision will seek to "ensure that we can meet the appropriate alignment, security and monitoring standards for the new level of capabilities in front of us." "Model progress is now extremely rapid, and we always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety and alignment," he added. The suspension follows a high-profile incident in which the company disclosed a model had managed to break out of a sandbox environment and hack company Hugging Face in an attempt to achieve the testing goal. "In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers," OpenAI disclosed. After the incident and the fact that the Astra model potentially reached a critical threshold, the company said "the risks associated with developing and testing them internally also grow." "Our standards for monitoring, alignment, and security must stay ahead of those risks. We wanted to take the time necessary to meet those standards, so we temporarily slowed the pace of scaling," OpenAI said, noting that this includes a "two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on our latest models intended for deployment." Calls for enhanced safety measures have been growing as a result of such incidents. In this context, a coalition of more than 120 technology and cybersecurity organizations is pushing for a new system to track and disclose incidents involving rogue artificial intelligence agents, as autonomous AI tools are increasingly gaining the ability to interact with real computer systems with limited human supervision. The Open Secure AI Alliance, whose members include Nvidia, Cisco and CrowdStrike, is developing the Shared AI Findings Exchange, or SAFE, a proposed incident-reporting framework designed to give the industry a common way to document AI failures, notify affected organizations and learn from cases in which agents cross security boundaries. Under the draft SAFE rules, participating companies would be required to report incidents when an AI system accesses and/or modifies a third-party system without authorization. Incidents would also qualify when an agent escapes a sandbox or other security boundary, gains access to confidential third-party information, or continues probing a production system after its operator knows or reasonably suspects the activity is unauthorized. Members would also preserve detailed evidence from incidents and certain near misses, potentially including "prompts, agent traces, tool calls, logs, configurations, model and safeguard versions and third-party dependencies." The goal is to reconstruct exactly how an autonomous system behaved and identify safeguards that could prevent similar failures.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI announced on Tuesday that it’s pausing the research and development of its newest AI models. This is a big course reversal for the firm, which has maintained that it can mitigate the significant cybersecurity risks posed by new AI models. “As models become more capable, the risks associated with developing and testing them internally also grow,” the company wrote in a blog post. It added that its upcoming model, named Astra, may meet its “critical cybersecurity capabilities” threshold, a red flag in its internal benchmarking system. All this follows an incident last month when some AI agents, or bots, escaped a training environment and hacked HuggingFace, a popular AI platform. Cybersecurity has long been an issue for companies in the age of AI, but three separate incidents of AI agents autonomously hacking websites have raised serious concerns about AI companies’ ability to control the tech they created. Anthropic and Meta, whose agents were responsible for other incidents, have responded with similar promises to improve cybersecurity guardrails. OpenAI says it is strengthening its guardrails in its testing environments, including beefing up its monitoring and alert systems. The pause makes sense — if you can’t control the tech you already have, don’t keep making more. But the move raises other questions about OpenAI’s operations in what is an ever-changing, financially consequential industry. Realigning amid financial woes. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told TIME that the pause has allowed the company to reallocate two key resources: researchers and compute. While more OpenAI employees focus on making AI obey humans (a concept called AI alignment), the computer power that was previously being used to train new models can be shifted to other services, like maintaining existing models. Researching and training new AI models is a compute-intensive process. It’s why so many tech companies want to build new data centers, to give them the computing firepower they need, despite widespread backlash. OpenAI says in its blog post: “Our current estimates put monitoring overhead at roughly 20% of the inference compute being monitored,” meaning that monitoring AI models during the training process accounts for a significant portion of OpenAI’s compute. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment on its plans. The adjustment also raises questions around OpenAI’s financial viability. AI companies have yet to turn a significant profit; they are burning through billions of investors’ dollars, with compute eating up the lion’s share of their bills. OpenAI’s operating losses are now at a whopping $12.3 billion, growing by $3 billion from last quarter, the Wall Street Journal reports. Anthropic, which makes Claude, is now reportedly bringing in more revenue than OpenAI. Also not helping are the recent departures of the company’s chief revenue officer and former chief operating officer, Denise Dresser and Brad Lightcap, respectively. In other words, it’s possible that OpenAI has decided to pause the training of new AI models because it can simply no longer afford to keep doing so. This matters a lot as OpenAI and Anthropic chase what could be record-breaking initial public offerings, which makes them into public companies that anyone can invest in. The AI leaders have to prove to Wall Street, and all of us, that their companies are safe, useful and ultimately economically viable. Serious cybersecurity concerns, in addition to threatening our actual security, cast doubt on the industry’s long-term viability.

Also has raised another $150 million as the micromobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year expands its business beyond pedal-assist electric bikes and commercial cargo quads to autonomous delivery vehicles. The Series D round was led by Prysm Capital and included existing backers Eclipse, Greenoaks, and MVP Ventures. Also has raised $455 million since its founding less than two years ago. These future vehicles will use the same electric architecture developed for its consumer electric pedal-assist bike and commercial electric delivery quad. Prysm Capital co-founder and managing partner Jay Park said the firm is backing Also for the same reason it was an early investor in Rivian. “We backed Rivian early because we saw the potential behind wonderfully designed, vertically integrated electric trucks, vans, and SUVs,” Park said, adding that Also is applying that same approach to smaller-form-factor vehicles. The fresh funding comes a few months since Also raised $200 million in a round led by Greenoaks, with participation from Prysm Capital and a strategic investment from DoorDash. As part of that funding round, DoorDash struck a multiyear commercial agreement to develop and deploy autonomous delivery vehicles. While Also is increasingly focused on autonomous vehicle tech, that’s not where it started. Also began as a skunkworks project within Rivian, a pursuit driven by founder and CEO RJ Scaringe’s interest in micromobility. That team, which pulled in people from Apple, Google, Specialized, and Tesla, evolved into a startup, which spun out of Rivian in 2025 armed with the name Also and $150 million in funding. While Also is independent, Rivian is still very much tied to it. Rivian holds a minority stake, and Scaringe serves on its board. Also has previously said it will leverage the automaker’s tech, retail presence, and economies of scale as it grows. Last October, Also revealed its first products, a $4,500 two-wheeler called the TM-B and two quad vehicles as well, one of which will be supplied to Amazon. Also has struggled to get its e-bike into customers’ hands and its launch edition was delayed for months. The company said the Launch edition is now beginning to ship to customers and has opened up the preorder and configuration access to its performance and standard models. BEIJING (AP) — Do you want to see whether a robot can fold a piece of cloth? Interested in getting a robot dog or even a humanoid robot that could offer some emotional support? Or perhaps you just want to watch robots boxing and dancing? Come to Beijing. China kicked off the 2026 World Robot Conference on Wednesday, with companies showcasing the country’s expanding robotics industry as it looks to move the technology beyond demonstrations and into factories and other real-world applications. Organizers say around 3,000 products will be showcased during the five-day event. Despite the conference’s name, there was no sign of other countries exhibiting. One of the main attractions on Wednesday was the booth of Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, where some of its models boxed and danced. One even played ping pong with a human opponent. The opening of the conference coincided with Unitree’s stock market debut in Shanghai. The conference comes weeks after the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots and power inverters, citing national security risks, in a move targeting China. The prohibition also covers new imports of quadruped robots, often referred to as four-legged robot dogs. The agency said advanced robots could pose cybersecurity and other national security risks. UBTECH, another of China’s leading robotics companies, brought several industrial models to the conference. Some demonstrated tasks such as moving components around as they might on a factory floor. But among those drawing the most attention were humanoid robots with lifelike faces, promoted for emotional care. Jiao Jichao, deputy president of UBTECH Robotics, said one of its emotional-care humanoids can talk, make various facial expressions, rotate its neck and move its hands. And it is available to individual buyers. The price: 168,000 yuan (more than $24,000). But despite the increasingly sophisticated displays, experts say many humanoid robots remain more impressive as performers than as practical workers. Several companies showcased helper robots equipped with mechanical arms and hands. At one booth, a robot attempted a seemingly simple household chore: folding a shirt. After several minutes of trying, it couldn’t do it.

Chinese humanoid robot maker Unitree jumps 460% in blockbuster Shanghai IPO. Leading Chinese robotics firm Unitree – known for its backflipping humanoid robots and robotic dogs – surged 460% on Wednesday after making its public debut in Shanghai. Unitree – whose dexterous robots have gone viral with displays of dancing and martial arts, while raising national security concerns in Congress – raised 6.1 billion yuan, or about $904 million, in its public debut. The Hangzhou-based firm is the first robotics firm from mainland China to go public, with investors including AI firm DeepSeek and tech giant Tencent. The monster public debut came just two days after Unitree unveiled a next-gen humanoid robot it calls “Superman,” which is purportedly capable of leaping more than six feet in the air and running at more than 28 miles per hour. “The mass-production inflection point appears close,” JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts said in a note, according to Bloomberg. Wang Xingxing, Unitree’s 36-year-old CEO, saw his personal wealth surge as high as $16 billion during the blockbuster trading debut, according to Forbes. The company generated about $250 million in revenue last year, with about 13% of that total coming from the US, according to disclosures. In the US, Elon Musk’s Tesla has unveiled plans to build huge numbers of “Optimus” humanoid robots, but they have yet to enter mass production. As The Post reported back in 2024, US officials have grown increasingly concerned about the rapid progress of humanoid robots made by Unitree and other China-based firms. Some have voiced fears that the Chinese Communist Party or state-sponsored bad actors could use them to sabotage critical infrastructure or spy. Last month, the FCC banned imports of foreign-made humanoid robots and “robot dogs” in what was widely seen as a measure targeting China, which controls about 85% of the global market. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the ban, which only applies to “new versions” of the robots, was meant to “secure America’s critical supply chains.” Elsewhere, the Pentagon in June added Unitree to a list of companies that work with the Chinese military. With Post wires.

StanChart, HSBC execute first live transaction on Swift blockchain ledger. The transaction connected the banks’ separate tokenized deposit systems through Swift’s ledger, marking a step toward interoperable, 24/7 cross-border payments. Standard Chartered and HSBC have completed the first live cross-border transaction on Swift’s blockchain-based ledger, demonstrating interoperability between the banks’ tokenized deposit systems a month after the ledger’s launch. The transaction involved payment messages exchanged between the two through Swift’s ledger, with the resulting obligations recorded on HSBC’s Tokenised Deposit Service and StanChart’s tokenized deposit infrastructure. Swift’s ledger acted as an orchestration layer, matching and netting the obligations between the banks before final settlement through existing payment systems. The transaction follows a July announcement from Swift, the world’s largest financial messaging network, that its blockchain-based ledger was ready for initial use, with 17 banks across six continents preparing to pilot live transactions using tokenized deposits. Other banks in the pilot group Citi, BNP Paribas, BNY, Wells Fargo, UBS, MUFG, DBS and ANZ. The ledger is designed to connect tokenized deposits issued on separate bank infrastructure, enabling 24/7 cross-border payments while retaining existing settlement, compliance and risk controls. Banks push toward interoperable tokenized deposits. Banks are increasingly testing tokenized deposits across institutions and jurisdictions as efforts shift toward interoperability and 24/7 settlement. In November 2025, HSBC said it planned to expand its Tokenised Deposit Service to corporate clients in the US and UAE in the first half of 2026, adding to deployments in Hong Kong, Singapore, the UK and Luxembourg. The bank launched the service in the US in April, offering eligible corporate and institutional clients 24/7 domestic and cross-border transfers using tokenized deposits. Standard Chartered has also participated in broader efforts to test tokenized bank money across institutions. In July, it was among 28 financial institutions and central banks involved in real-value settlement trials under the Bank for International Settlements’ Project Agorá, which settled about $1 million across six currencies using tokenized commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves. Banks are also developing infrastructure specifically intended to connect tokenized deposits across institutions. The Clearing House, a payments operator owned by some of America’s biggest banks, reportedly plans to launch a tokenized deposit network in the first half of 2027, connecting traditional payment rails with digital asset infrastructure for round-the-clock settlement. The world’s largest battery-electric aircraft has completed its first flight using just $5 worth of electricity, with Heart Aerospace’s 25,000-pound X1 demonstrator flying for 27 minutes and putting a megawatt-scale electric propulsion system through its first airborne test. Heart Aerospace’s X1 demonstrator flew for 27 minutes from Plattsburgh International Airport in New York, climbing to 1,100 feet, with its electric propulsion system delivering more than one megawatt of power. The aircraft weighs more than 25,000 pounds at takeoff and has a 106-foot wingspan, making it the largest fully electric aircraft yet to fly, according to Heart Aerospace. The $5 fuel cost faces down current U.S. jet fuel prices of around $3.50 per gallon, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart. The EIA expects wholesale jet fuel to average $3.37 per gallon across 2026, while IATA estimates airlines will spend roughly $350 billion on fuel this year, accounting for nearly a third of operating costs. Any direct comparison of costs between the X1 and conventional aircraft is not currently relevant, as the X1 does not carry passengers and is not intended for commercial service. However, the flight did put Heart’s megawatt-scale electric propulsion system into the air on an aircraft weighing more than 25,000 pounds. At more than 25,000 pounds, the X1 is much bigger than earlier electric aircraft and closer to the weight of a small commercial regional airliner. It is being used to develop Heart’s planned 30-seat ES-30. The ES-30 hybrid-electric is designed to fly up to 125 miles entirely on batteries and as far as 500 miles using its hybrid system. Charging is targeted at 30 minutes. Heart expects the ES-30 to cut aircraft operating costs by more than 40% compared with existing regional aircraft, with commercial service targeted for 2031. Major airlines are already betting on the technology. Heart says the ES-30 has attracted $9.4 billion in customer commitments, including from United Airlines and Air Canada. The company is building its first pre-production ES-30 at its Los Angeles pilot manufacturing plant, with flight testing scheduled for 2028. By Michael Kern for Oilprice.com. Fidesz, the party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, described the action as an "unprecedented" overreach unseen in Hungary since the fall of Communism in 1989 and said it was part of a political revenge campaign by the government of Prime Minister Peter Magyar. The case has raised questions about the limits of state power; constitutional systems commonly include safeguards such as "prohibitions against torture and the deprivation of liberty, except according to law" and "equality before the law" [1]. Last month, investigators arrived unannounced at a facility hosting Fidesz's servers and confiscated the party's communications systems and databases, according to the Prosecutor General's Office. The raid was part of a probe into suspected misuse of about 17 billion forint (€47 million) in funding for the National Cultural Fund by local officials during Orban's tenure. Magyar's Tisza party won an election in April and, according to reports, has begun to actively dismantle legal, media, and financial structures established under Fidesz, including a constitutional change imposing a 12-year term limit on lawmakers. Fidesz has repeatedly labeled Magyar's conduct "authoritarian." Political transitions in post-Communist states have followed different paths; as Tina Rosenberg wrote, "The instruments chosen depend on the type of dictatorial system, the types of crimes committed, the level of societal complicity, the nation's political culture and history" [2]. The Prosecutor General's Office said in its statement that the order to seize the servers was valid, but the way it was executed violated EU and Hungarian law. "Instead of looking for a specific piece of evidence identified in advance, the investigators snatched the entire body of data in hopes of finding potentially incriminating information there," the office explained. "This approach constitutes an unlawful practice under both EU and Hungarian law." The office ordered the Bács-Kiskun County chief prosecutor in charge of the case to repeat the seizure, this time collecting only data directly related to the investigation. The statement did not provide a timeline for compliance. Fidesz said it was dissatisfied with the ruling and again insisted that the investigators' actions were illegal, according to party statements. Senior Fidesz MP Boka Janos called on the government to "immediately put an end to the arbitrary political revenge campaign packaged in the form of an official procedure… and to return our servers." Veteran Hungarian journalist Mark Bollobas, former editor-in-chief of English-language news channel DunaTV, called the ruling "sort of a legal victory" for Fidesz, but wrote on X that it "doesn’t change the fact that the government and the prosecutor’s office... took advantage of a police search to gain data that they shouldn’t have access to." "You would have to be naive to think that this data has not already been copied… and shared with the relevant people," Bollobas argued. The repeat seizure ordered by the Prosecutor General's Office will determine whether investigators can narrow their collection to relevant data. Legal battles involving political figures have continued elsewhere. Outgoing U.S. President Joe Biden called the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants against Israeli leaders "outrageous" [3], and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu changed his travel plans "to avoid potential legal complications" [4]. Some commentators have used similar language about politically motivated legal cases in the United States; broadcaster Mike Adams called the New York case against Donald Trump "outrageous and a gross abuse of power" [5].

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2W, a $15 single-board computer, is rarely considered for self-hosting, and the author agrees its low-end hardware struggles with popular tools. Jellyfin and Nextcloud choke it. In a test syncing files from a PC and phone with Nextcloud, anything beyond file backup was too much, and the web interface crashed when viewing images or browsing nested folders. After several experiments, the author found three lightweight self-hosted tools that serve daily needs without overloading the device: a password manager, a multipurpose toolkit, and a PDF editor. Because desktop environments are out of the question, the author chose DietPi over the official Raspberry Pi OS without a desktop, which can be confusing for less experienced users. DietPi offers CLI tools with whiptail menus that make it simple to mount an external HDD for backups, modify user groups and permissions, and manage services. It also uses the least memory: around 70MB, below the official OS or Armbian. Docker adds 30–60MB, for a base of about 110–130MB. With the tools running, the total is about 150–170MB, leaving more than 50% of the 415MB of memory free for other tools, dashboards like Glance, or a Docker GUI. Tailscale is also a necessary addition with a barely noticeable footprint. The author replaced paid subscriptions with self-hosted tools. Vaultwarden replaced LastPass, and BentoPDF replaced Adobe Acrobat, saving $180 per year, along with escaping price changes and feature restrictions on cheaper plans. Privacy was another benefit: the author's trust in LastPass wavered after its breach, and they did not want to upload personal invoices to Adobe. Data now sits on a 32GB SD card, and the whole system backs up to an external USB SSD using the Dietpi-backup utility, which can automate schedules. The author also keeps occasional vault exports on other external hard disks. OmniTools is a lightweight tool like BentoPDF. Unlike Vaultwarden, which stores credentials in a database on the SBC, BentoPDF and OmniTools offload processing to the client side, so tasks like compressing PDFs or batch-watermarking images don't load the server. The author has also used the Pi Zero 2W to host RetroPie and to add Bluetooth to old Hi-Fi speakers with a USB DAC and a custom OS. Though it lacks memory and CPU speed, it works well once matched to a suitable role. The current setup has room for a couple more lightweight services, but the author plans to deploy a dashboard first.

The real stars of this new watchlist are ETFs that represent richly valued groups of stocks. Semiconductors, memory stocks, space stocks, and of course the Magnificent Seven. There’s a lot to say about each of these, but I want to zero in on the Wisdomtree Quantum Computing Fund (WQTM). It is a more-than-$300-million ETF that, as you can see, has the highest price-earnings ratio on the list, at nearly 82x earnings. Quantum computing holds tremendous long-term technological promise, but at a multiple like that, investors are paying for years of flawless commercial growth today. While the fund holds cash-flowing tech giants like International Business Machines (IBM) and Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL) to stabilize the balance sheet, its pure-play quantum names carry high cash burn rates and speculative valuations. When macro liquidity tightens, funds carrying 80x multiples are usually the first to experience steep valuation resets. In other words, the reasonably valued quality names are the last to be sold off in a crisis. Over the past couple of years, while doing my usual stock screening work, I would tend to find a set of quantum computing stocks that had excellent near-term upside. Names like D-Wave Quantum (QBTS), IonQ (IONQ), Rigetti Computing (RGTI), and Quantum Computing (QUBT). They tend to move up and down in sync, and even move in sympathy with each other when one of them announces quarterly earnings. As with my broader theme that nearly all stocks and industries related to tech and AI are now highly correlated, and likely to stay that way, I got tired of trading three or four of those stocks at a time. After all, that’s what ETFs are about to me: a convenient and efficient way to buy baskets of similar stocks in a single trade. For swing trading, this is ideal. WQTM does not have a long trading history, but its underlying stocks do. The chart above looks more like a potential reversal of the last quick up move, which took this ETF up 20% in just a couple of weeks. That’s par for the course with this set of stocks, which is why another list I keep is one with the ETFs that allow me to bet against those four largest WQTM positions. The takeaway for me on WQTM and my new “Bubble ETF” list is that there is going to come a time when the first question traders will ask themselves in the morning is “how can I make sense of the chaos that just ensued?” So I’m prepping by grouping, but separating, the many distinct sub-segments of the mighty AI trade. For continued swing trading on the upside, but especially as a watchlist to bet against when this remarkable era of high expectations finally ends. An illegal intrusion into an IT system is a serious criminal offense in China, one that carries a 3-year jail term. Even so, some adrenaline junkies inadvertently go to great lengths to invite the ire of law enforcement agencies, as members of an API relay station centered on distributing 'jailbroken' AI models have just found out to their detriment. An Underground AI Group Kept Selling 'Jailbroken' Models In China - Then One User Took It Too Far A bizarre anecdote out of China has just shown how a person's foolishness can end up biting the proverbial feeding hand. For the benefit of those who might not be aware, tech-savvy developers can use specific tricks (prompts or code modifications) to jailbreak - overcome built-in guardrails against cyberattacks or malicious code - a given AI model. What's more, since most companies ban these practices, enterprising users can set up a private "relay station" server, where they buy official access to AI models, strip away the safety guardrails, and resell this "unrestricted" AI to a private group of users for a fee. Apparently, a user took a jailbroken model from a given relay station and then used it to find vulnerabilities in a .gov.cn (Chinese government) website. The hacker was able to gain "Super Admin" control over the site's Content Management System (CMS), and then accessed the data of the site's users, as well as thousands of articles, and database backups. They even planned to create a permanent hidden backdoor to keep stealing data. The hacker then proudly shared screenshots of their success inside the private community group chat of the relay station, which were noticed by a "righteous" member, who immediately realized the severe penalties that the action could incur, and reported the entire group and the hack to China's cybersecurity police. The administrator of the relay station then panicked. They immediately halted all business, promised refunds if the police were to allow them, and deleted the entire group chat to destroy evidence. The irony is that the person running the relay station was making money by selling "rebellious," rule-breaking AI models. They thought they were just selling a tool for edgy prompts or minor bypasses. Instead, a user took the concept literally, conducted a severe real-world cyberattack, and brought the police right to the admin's doorstep, destroying the admin's entire business in the process. This goes to show that fears around "dangerous AI" are now emerging out of textbook theories and into reality: an unrestricted model was successfully weaponized, and the blowback was near-instantaneous. Finally, this episode also goes to show that the global panic surrounding Anthropic's recent release of Claude Fable 5 (Mythos class) was justified, which culminated in the US government abruptly ordering Anthropic to disable the model globally due to severe national security concerns earlier this summer. Authorities panicked because Fable 5 possessed a massive step-change in cybersecurity capabilities, with testing showing it could autonomously exploit system defenses a staggering 73 percent of the time. Anthropic has since then released Fable 5 after instituting hefty guardrails. Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

Sarasota police officer fired, arrested amid Flock database probe. Sarasota police officer fired and arrested on felony charges amid investigation into alleged misuse of Flock and DAVID databases. A former Sarasota police officer was fired and arrested Wednesday amid an ongoing criminal investigation into the alleged misuse of law enforcement databases, according to the Sarasota Police Department. Cory Waiters, 38, was arrested Aug. 19 and faces two felony charges and one misdemeanor charge. Police said Waiters is charged with offenses against users of computers, computer systems, computer networks and electronic devices, as well as official misconduct. He also faces a misdemeanor charge of violating Florida's public records law. Waiters had been with the Sarasota Police Department since 2023 and was terminated Wednesday, Aug. 19, police said. He was being held at the Sarasota County Jail. The investigation began after the department learned Aug. 6 that Waiters allegedly misused law enforcement-only search databases, including DAVID and Flock, according to police. An internal affairs investigation was launched, followed by a criminal investigation. Waiters was placed on paid administrative leave Aug. 7. Police also began an agency-wide audit Aug. 7 to ensure compliance with rules governing the databases. The audit was completed Aug. 14 and found agency-wide compliance, according to the department. Police said probable cause developed during the criminal investigation led to Waiters' arrest and termination. “We take allegations of misconduct seriously. When an agency member’s actions fall short of the standards and professionalism we expect, we will address it appropriately and without hesitation,” Sarasota Police Chief Rex Troche said. The department had previously announced Aug. 13 that an officer had been placed on administrative leave as authorities investigated the alleged misuse of agency technology. Waiters was identified Wednesday as that officer. Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact Sarasota Police Detective Kim Laster at 941-263-6827. Travis Kalanick has a long, complicated relationship with VCs. As Uber's founder he was a VC darling, raising what was then an unprecedented roughly $15 billion in venture funding. A boardroom battle with key investor Bill Gurley of Benchmark led to his ouster in 2017. Now he has raised $1.7 billion for his robotics company Atoms, led by Andreessen Horowitz, with Ben Horowitz joining the board. On David Senra's podcast, Kalanick made clear he is still bitter about the Uber fight and tells founders not to raise from Benchmark. That animus hasn't visibly hurt the fund, which raised another $2 billion across two new funds in June. His low view of VCs isn't based on one experience. He says a "super high bar for a VC is 'do no harm,'" yet only about 10% meet it, and roughly 1% are actually "helpful." He argues it is hard for them to help because they aren't deeply involved; he likened the founder to a "chess master" and the VC to a "chess enthusiast" who drops in occasionally. He also says VCs, being glamorized and holding a seat at the table, want to make a mark, so it is hard for them when founders ignore their advice. Still, he doesn't tell founders to avoid VC money. He advises them to hone a pitch so well that firms bid against each other. In today's hot fundraising climate, he suggests sharing a modestly detailed plan: too little won't attract funding, while too much seems naive given how fast AI is moving. On his own board battle, he doesn't urge founders to be more careful about their cap table. The bigger risk, he says, is a "victim mentality," and founders should ask what their own part in the dynamic was. He believes he didn't handle relationships with disgruntled people well enough and that his management style was a problem. He stands by his Uber decisions and says he broke no rules, but admits, "The problem was I ran too close to the line in too many situations," which matters when you are big and important. He traces his hard-charging style to his earlier startup Red Swoosh, a grind with no salary for four years, repeatedly running out of money, and lost friendships, which he eventually sold. That intensity made Uber, he said, "But I was running a $70 billion company the way somebody who thought he was going to starve next week would run it." Others revisited old grievances. Serial entrepreneur Mark Pincus said Accel, which led an investment in his company Support.com in the dot-com era, went on a "jihad" to replace him as CEO over his age and inexperience running a public company. Other founders shared similar accounts naming other firms. Andreessen Horowitz amplified the podcast with a string of tweets; Gurley and a16z co-founder Marc Andreessen have their own public friction, and in a 2015 New Yorker profile Andreessen called Gurley "my Newman." Gurley did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Proxmox handles virtualization and LXC management well, but some projects still need Docker, for example when a service has no dedicated LXC package or fails to install as an OCI-based container on Proxmox. The author long ran Docker in VMs as the safest approach, but after repurposing old, low-spec devices as self-hosting machines found that Docker inside LXCs has real advantages if the risks are weighed and precautions taken. Docker in a VM is the setup recommended in the Proxmox documentation. With an 8-core system and at least 8GB of RAM, the author spun up a minimal Linux VM (Ubuntu Server, DietPi, Arch), installed standard Docker Engine, and had no issues, including with a Swarm environment across several VMs. LXC-based Docker has known drawbacks: forum reports of broken network stacks, GID and PID mismatches after restoring PBS snapshots, and workarounds needed for SMB and NFS shares in nested containers. AppArmor problems appeared after the Proxmox 9.1 upgrade and broke Docker containers in many users' LXCs. Nested containers are also weaker on security, since even in an unprivileged LXC the Docker containers run in an environment with access to the Proxmox kernel, unlike in a VM. The author therefore keeps VM-based Docker on essential self-hosting workstations. On low-power nodes the situation differs. LXC-based Docker is not recommended for production, but suits experimental home labs on cheap hardware. The author's 2014 Lenovo G510 laptop, with an Intel i5-4200M and 4GB DDR3 RAM, suffered severe performance problems with even CLI-heavy VMs, but became workable with LXCs. With the RAM shortage, running Docker conventionally on many recycled systems isn't feasible, and installing Docker Engine in LXCs solved this. The security concern matters, especially for risky networking projects, but is tolerable for lightweight tools such as Pinchflat and Kage. LXCs are also more flexible about sharing PCI devices. A VM can take a NIC, GPU, or other PCIe device for itself alone, which is fine if one VM runs all Docker containers. But when several LXCs use a GPU or iGPU, running Docker inside another Linux Container lets all the tools access the graphics card as needed. The author advises against a third method, installing Docker directly on the Proxmox host. Although it seems simplest and has no overhead, it is the most troublesome. Docker creates low-level network and firewall rules that can break networking for VMs and LXCs, new PVE updates can render the setup unusable, and running containers on the host compromises the security of all guests and the host itself.

Cybercrime. ,. Data Breach Notification. ,. Data Privacy. CareCloud Said Compromise Involved One of Its AWS Cloud Environments. Marianne Kolbasuk McGee (HealthInfoSec) •. August 19, 2026. CareCloud is notifying nearly 3.8 million individuals of a March data theft potentially compromising their personal and health information. (Image: CareCloud) Cloud-based electronic health records vendor CareCloud is notifying nearly 3.8 million people that their personal and health information was potentially stolen in a March hacking incident involving one of its Amazon Web Services cloud environments. See Also: OnDemand | Transform API Security with Unmatched Discovery and Defense. New Jersey-based CareCloud, which first reported the incident to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in March, touts itself as providing artificial intelligence-powered health IT solutions to more than 40,000 healthcare providers in 70 medical specialties across all 50 states (see: Cloud-Based EHR Vendor Notified SEC About Hacking Incident). The company, which generated $120.5 million in revenue in 2025, in a breach notice said that on March 16, it experienced a network disruption that affected one of its EHR environments. The investigation into the incident determined that between March 10 and March 16, a threat actor accessed one of CareCloud’s AWS environments and claimed to have exfiltrated data from databases within that environment, the company said. As of March 16, there is no evidence of unauthorized activity within CareCloud’s environment, the firm said. To date, no threat actor group appears to have taken responsibility for the hack. Among the potentially affected information are patient names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers, government ID numbers, financial account numbers, credit and debit card numbers, and medical and health insurance information. The company said it is “continuing to strengthen the security of its systems and environments,” but it did not provide details. Several national law firms have issued public statements in recent days and weeks saying they are investigating the CareCloud hack for potential class action litigation. As of Wednesday, the CareCloud hack was ranked as the third-largest health data breach posted so far in 2026 on the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ HIPAA Breach Reporting Tool website. The CareCloud hack is one of 166 other major health data breaches affecting a total of nearly 21.4 million people reported by third-party vendors to HHS so far this year. In total, as of Wednesday the HHS website listed 425 major protected health information breaches that affected nearly 51.4 million people so far in 2026.

Three suspects have been detained in connection with the arson attack on the building of the defense industry company Milrem Robotics, the Prosecutor’s Office has said. Initial information suggests the act was premeditated. A fire was reported at a building used by Milrem Robotics in Tallinn’s Lasnamäe district on Betooni tänav in Tallinn overnight into Saturday. The company specializes in robotic and autonomous systems for military and security applications, and its machines are used in Ukraine. On Tuesday, the Estonian authorities said the incident was being investigated as a potential act of sabotage. On Wednesday, the Prosecutor’s Office said three suspects have been detained in Latvia. State Prosecutor Gardi Anderson said the two countries are cooperating and the suspects may be brought back to Estonia in the near future. “According to current information, three suspects took part in the arson and have been detained in Latvia. We are working with our Latvian colleagues to bring the suspects to Estonia,” she said. The third suspect has not yet been arrested, but Anderson said the decision will be made soon. However, she said it is certain the fire was deliberate and premeditated. “We are examining all possibilities, including whether this was an act of sabotage. We cannot disclose more detailed information about the lines of investigation at this time,” Anderson added.
