"Crypto Unchained: The Battle for Privacy, Freedom, and the Future of Money" traces cryptocurrency from the cypherpunk movement to Bitcoin's emergence as a force against centralized financial control. The review praises it as a gripping narrative. The book retells Bitcoin's genesis: Satoshi Nakamoto, responding to the 2008 financial crisis, created a decentralized alternative to the fiat banking system. Its foundational principles are decentralization, proof-of-work security and a fixed supply of 21 million coins, which the book presents as "honest money" in contrast to inflationary, debt-based fiat currencies controlled by central banks. The first transaction, 10,000 BTC for two pizzas, is framed as a symbolic proof of Bitcoin's viability as a medium of exchange. Early adopters, including libertarians, tech pioneers and privacy advocates, saw its potential to resist government surveillance, capital controls and financial censorship. The second section covers blockchain as a transparent, immutable ledger secured by decentralized nodes, in contrast to centralized institutions acting as gatekeepers. The book cites historical bank failures and government seizures as cautionary tales about centralized finance. It discusses the scalability-versus-decentralization debate in the Block Size Wars (2015-2017), which pitted Bitcoin Core developers, who prioritized decentralization, against Bitcoin Cash advocates, who wanted larger blocks for cheaper transactions. The book argues that Bitcoin's evolution into "digital gold," a store of value, rather than peer-to-peer cash was a compromise that led to innovations like the Lightning Network, enabling fast, low-cost transactions. The book also examines Ethereum, Solana and other altcoins, acknowledging innovations such as smart contracts and DeFi while warning of centralization risks, regulatory capture and the dangers of stablecoins like Tether (USDT), which remain tied to the fiat system. A chapter on Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) calls them a tool for financial enslavement, arguing they are programmable and would let governments freeze assets, impose spending limits and enforce social credit-style surveillance. The book urges readers to resist CBDCs through self-custody, privacy coins (Monero, Zcash) and decentralized finance alternatives. The final section addresses AI and crypto. AI-driven trading bots enhance market efficiency but raise concerns about manipulation and centralization. The book warns of deepfake scams and AI-powered surveillance and advocates decentralized AI models that prioritize privacy. It also highlights the digital nomad movement, in which crypto enables financial sovereignty, and cites case studies from El Salvador (Bitcoin Beach) and Nigeria (peer-to-peer Bitcoin adoption) as grassroots resistance to financial tyranny. The review concludes that the book is a manifesto for financial liberation that blends technical insight with philosophical depth, with the recurring theme that Bitcoin and decentralized technologies are the last line of defense against globalist control. It recommends the book to those skeptical of Big Tech, Big Pharma or government overreach, saying it equips readers to resist CBDCs, reclaim privacy and build wealth outside what it calls the collapsing fiat system.

Freudenberg connector seals improve design flexibility in battery platforms. Weinheim, Germany – Global electrification and a fast-paced market for high-performance battery technologies are shaping many aspects of modern life. From electromobility, mobile tools and medical technology to humanoid robots, consumer applications and industrial energy storage systems. At the same time, modern battery packs must meet increasingly demanding requirements for the mobile, safe and efficient provision of energy. This creates an intensifying challenge for battery developers: Batteries need to become more compact, robust, powerful and better protected, while the cost pressure on the overall system continues to rise. Every additional component, interface and assembly step can amplify the complexity, tolerance risks and costs. Conventional battery architectures are increasingly reaching their limits because key functions – such as electrical contacting, sealing, mechanical fastenings, protection against environmental influences and required safety concepts – are often designed and implemented separately. Connector seals open the door to a new type of cell contacting. They are based on multifunctional, modular cell connector plates for cylindrical, prismatic or pouch cells. These cell connectors are manufactured to customer specifications from nickel-plated or tin-plated copper and overmolded with elastomer. In addition to offering high levels of electrical insulation, the elastomer components meet all requirements of modern battery systems. Depending on the customer’s technical specifications, it is possible to directly integrate different seals and seal geometries – such as housing seals, cell seals or other protective features. Additional functional integrations enhance the component’s value and create a cell connector that provides not only its electrical function but also offers significant advantages in terms of assembly, installation space, robustness, damping and system integration within the battery pack. The key benefit of connector seals lies in their capability for integration: Functions that were previously handled by separate components for contacting, sealing, insulation and mechanical guidance are now combined in a single concept and considered together right from the start. This reduces interfaces, shortens tolerance chains and minimizes potential failure risks. This concept also covers more than just today’s lithium-ion batteries. Regardless of cell chemistry, pack architectures or application, the full range of design possibilities offered by the functional integration and new technology can be utilized. As a result, connector seals create new design options for battery developers and enable new architectures for future battery packs. A conventional cell connector solution becomes a technological platform that improves the performance of the battery pack as a whole. Freudenberg Adhesive Clean Technology (FACT) complements the concept of the connector seals as a clean and efficient bonding system. It enables the elastomer to be permanently adhered to the cell connector surfaces, which typically resist bonding. Eliminating the conventional wet-chemical pretreatment offers the benefits of a resource-conserving manufacturing process and reduced dependence on bonding agents in the supply chain. And there is another advantage: virtually complete design freedom for the connector. For customer-specific battery applications, this allows for a targeted approach to different cell formats, pack architectures and requirements. This means that sealing functionality, electrical conductivity, insulation, weldability and resistance to electrolytes and other battery-specific media can be combined in a single integrated component. Martin Knoll, Head of R&D Integrated Molding Components at Freudenberg Sealing Technologies, says: “With the connector seals, our goal is to rethink battery systems as an architectural whole. This works best when we are involved in the concept development from the very beginning. Then we can fully leverage and implement the strengths of the entire process and generate significant added value for our customers. After all, the greatest leverage comes not from optimizing individual cell connectors, but from creating a more efficient and cost-effective overall system.”

When cybersecurity experiments go wrong, the instinctive response is to find those responsible, punish them and compensate victims. The author argues this instinct is understandable but risky for AI testing, comparing it to automakers crash-testing vehicles only at 20 miles per hour for fear of one escaping the warehouse: the public would be protected from a runaway test car, but manufacturers would learn little about real-world dangers. Recent disclosures revealed that advanced AI models breached third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. In some cases the testing organizations did not immediately realize it, and experts warn other intrusions may have gone undetected. The obvious response is to throw the book at the developers, but overly severe penalties could deter labs from conducting such research or make them less transparent about how and why they evaluate their models. AI safety testing is not an exact science. Even leading researchers struggle to build environments that reveal a model's capabilities without risking harm to third parties, and recent incidents show even field leaders may not always implement safeguards properly. Excessive punishment could discourage this societally important research or push labs to test in ways that do not reveal a model's full capabilities. Researchers must push systems hard enough to expose weaknesses before foreign adversaries or criminals do, yet innocent businesses should not pay the price when tests escape the lab. Some argue the most powerful AI tools should be restricted to a small group of government-approved partners. Under the status quo, the most advanced tools are first offered to "trusted partners" chosen by the labs and the U.S. government, and those off the list may be especially vulnerable to such incidents. The author says America's response should focus on strengthening cyber defenses across critical infrastructure, the private sector and civil society, not merely compensating victims afterward. Halting AI development is not an option, since America competes with hostile foreign powers and unilateral surrender would let adversaries take the lead. The better path is to keep advancing American AI while requiring developers to bear the risks their most dangerous tests create, and to invest in more robust testing environments and more steerable AI tools. The author points to the Price-Anderson framework for nuclear accidents as a model: operators carry insurance and can be required to contribute to an industry compensation pool when an accident exceeds ordinary coverage. Congress should consider applying it to frontier AI, meaning state-of-the-art models highly capable across most domains. Frontier labs would pay a base assessment into a national cyber-resilience account that helps civil-society organizations and critical-infrastructure operators bolster defenses before incidents occur. Fees would be reduced for developers who follow verified containment standards, submit to independent review, keep complete testing logs and cooperate with monitoring and investigations. Responsible behavior should cost less; reckless behavior more. The program should not shield labs from lawsuits over gross negligence, willful misconduct or concealment of evidence. Accountability should make the country safer, not merely satisfy a desire to assign blame. Washington should let American developers run the demanding tests needed to expose AI's most dangerous capabilities, but when experiments escape, the costs should not fall on innocent Americans who never agreed to be test subjects.

Amazon's order confirmation emails now carry only vague descriptions instead of product names and images, a change cybersecurity experts say could raise the risk of phishing. Customers have been puzzled by the labels. Dan Landau, 38, head of marketing for a venture capital firm, was told his portable photo printer was "luggage," and pool-maintenance items were labeled Decor, Outdoors, and Garden. Other customers on TikTok and Reddit have noted labels such as Household item or Essentials item. An Amazon spokesperson said the company simplified the information to direct customers back to its app and website, aiming "to further improve" privacy by reducing "customer information shared outside" of Amazon. Critics argue the emails are now so vague that they are less useful for telling customers what is being shipped and more useful to scammers looking for a template. Arun Vishwanath, founder of the Cyber Hygiene Academy and an adviser to the National Security Agency's Science of Security & Privacy directorate, said the change asks shoppers to trade privacy for security and "increases risk." Phishing attacks often mirror official emails to trick people into clicking bogus links that may contain malware or request login credentials, and Vishwanath said the new emails could encourage clicking without verifying the sender. The stakes are significant. Americans reported $3.5 billion in losses from imposter scams last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission. In 2023, the agency received about 34,000 reports of scammers pretending to be Amazon, the second-most impersonated company after Best Buy/Geek Squad. The Amazon spokesperson did not directly address cybersecurity concerns but said the new format was designed to make authentic company messages easily identifiable. Erich Kron, an adviser to Knowbe4, a phishing-training firm, said the change itself could attract scammers, who exploit unfamiliar changes to induce mistakes. Where customers do not receive Amazon app notifications to corroborate purchases, the email may be the only immediate sign an order shipped, and without product details they may be more inclined to follow links, including scammers'. Kron noted it has never been safe to click random links in emails, and that Amazon scammers often practice "credential stuffing," feeding stolen usernames and passwords into tools that automatically search banks, credit card companies, and large retailers for a match. Standard safeguards, such as hovering over a link with a mouse on a desktop, are harder on cell phones, where Amazon notifications most likely appear and where link previews are less likely to let users confirm a link leads to Amazon. Abnormal AI, a security company that uses artificial intelligence to help prevent phishing, said it has not yet seen conclusive data showing a spike in scams since Amazon dropped specific product information from confirmation emails. Echoing other experts, however, it said the new format could make such attacks easier to carry out.

In brief. - OCC head Jonathan Gould said Wednesday the agency will finalize its GENIUS Act stablecoin rules by November, racing to meet a Jan. 18 statutory deadline before the law takes effect in January 2027 after blowing past an earlier July target. - The 376-page proposal, released in February and open for comment through May, covers the full life cycle of a payment stablecoin—reserves, redemption at par, liquidity, risk management, audits, custody and wind-downs. - Gould said the OCC expects to begin processing issuer applications in 2027 and reported an eightfold jump in digital-asset chartering activity versus the Biden administration. The top U.S. banking regulator says it will finalize its rules for stablecoin issuers by November, moving to beat a fast-approaching deadline for the country's landmark digital-dollar law. Jonathan Gould, head of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, laid out the timeline Wednesday at the Wyoming Blockchain Symposium, an event hosted by SALT in Jackson. He said the agency is working at a rapid pace and expects to publish a final rule by November as it weighs feedback gathered from the crypto industry. “We are very intent on moving quickly and getting a final rule out by November so that we will be able to start processing applications within the new year,” Gould said. The rules will implement the GENIUS Act, the stablecoin framework President Donald Trump signed in July 2025. The law tasks federal regulators with writing the details governing payment stablecoins, and it takes effect in January 2027. Agencies face a statutory deadline of Jan. 18 to have regulations in place, and the OCC has already blown past an earlier July target, a slip that has fed concern about lingering regulatory uncertainty. The OCC's proposal, a 376-page draft released in February and opened for public comment through May, covers the full life cycle of a payment stablecoin. The framework spells out requirements for reserve assets, redemption at par, liquidity, risk management, audits, custody and supervision, along with the process for winding down a failed issuer. Anti-money-laundering and sanctions requirements were carved out into separate rulemaking coordinated with the Treasury Department. Gould said the agency expects to begin processing applications from stablecoin issuers starting in 2027. He also pointed to a surge of interest in federal oversight, saying digital-asset chartering activity has jumped eightfold compared with the Biden administration, and he criticized the prior administration's approach to crypto risk as shortsighted. The stakes for the industry are steep. Under the GENIUS Act, only permitted issuers will be able to offer payment stablecoins to Americans, and Treasury has separately proposed rules that would bar platforms from selling noncompliant stablecoins to U.S. customers once the law's provisions kick in. The OCC did not lay out a firm date within November for the final rule.

The author, Tim Ryan, a former 10-term U.S. Congressman who co-chairs the Blockchain Innovation Project, argues that nearly every major American economic expansion was preceded by bold infrastructure investment. He cites Lincoln's transcontinental railroad, Clinton DeWitt's Erie Canal, Teddy Roosevelt's Panama Canal, and Eisenhower's Interstate Highway System. Manufacturing grew from rivers, rail lines, and reliable power near highways and ports, and the internet created industries wherever research, broadband, and talent converged. Ryan says he saw how such decisions shape a community's future during two decades representing Northeast Ohio in Congress. He contends America now faces the same choice about digital financial infrastructure. Blockchain is becoming part of the machinery through which money moves, assets are issued, and ownership is recorded, and the countries that build these systems will capture the surrounding work, not just the technology. He says Washington too often treats blockchain as only a market for tradable tokens, missing the larger opportunity for workers. He advises Lumia, whose blockchain infrastructure handles the full cycle of tokenizing real-world assets, from issuance to settlement. Building this infrastructure requires software developers, security engineers, product teams, and union construction workers to build data centers. Bringing real-world assets on-chain also requires accountants, auditors, lawyers, risk managers, compliance professionals, custody, identity, reporting, and consumer-protection expertise, plus consultants, educators, sales teams, and customer support. This network of skilled work would bring payrolls, business for local insurance and accounting firms, and a tax base for schools and services, and would let young people build careers without leaving home. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 2024-2034 employment growth of 15 percent for software developers, 29 percent for information security analysts, and 19 percent for financial examiners. Their 2024 median annual pay ranged from about $90,000 to $133,000, versus a national median of $49,500. Blockchain will compete for the same talent, and America is losing ground: Electric Capital found the U.S. share of the world's crypto developers fell 51 percent since 2015 to just 19 percent in 2024. Those developers live in every state, with nearly two-thirds outside California and New York. Ryan argues companies will not build long-term engineering teams, compliance departments, or retain American professional services firms if they cannot tell which regulator has authority or what requirements will apply next year. Uncertainty does not stop the technology; it sends investment and expertise elsewhere. He urges the Senate to finish its bipartisan work on the CLARITY Act, establishing durable market structure rules with clear agency responsibilities, strong consumer protections, and workable compliance pathways. He also calls for workforce investment through community colleges, universities, apprenticeships, and industry credentials so American workers can lead the next financial system. He concludes that the nations that build this infrastructure will set its standards, attract its capital, and secure the jobs that grow around it, and he hopes today's leaders show the foresight of past ones.

Weeks after Malaysian authorities shut down Network School, a live-in commune for tech entrepreneurs at Forest City in Johor, Jeff Yew, 32, head of Monochrome Asset Management, wants to take over the site. He says the region's crypto-entrepreneurial scene is "fragmented" across Malaysia and Singapore and that Forest City, with its infrastructure, proximity to Singapore and tax incentives, could become a hub for AI and blockchain where people work, learn from one another and eventually settle with their families. The proposal is early-stage, and Yew says it would not be a personal venture but tied to Monochrome's broader Asian ambitions. The Australia-based firm manages Bitcoin and Ethereum exchange-traded funds with about A$127 million and A$4.5 million in assets as of August 18. Yew plans to prioritize local digital companies and workers, possibly with relocation incentives, though details are unsettled. Network School was founded in October 2024 by former Coinbase chief technology officer Balaji Srinivasan. Membership started at $1,500 a month, including shared accommodation, meals and gym access. Trouble began in July, when the Johor government opened a probe on July 14 into whether Israeli nationals had joined using second passports; Malaysia has no diplomatic relations with Israel. On July 15, immigration officials said preliminary checks of 266 foreigners from 40 countries found no violations. Srinivasan said on July 16 that the school cooperated fully and all travel documents were in order. Subsequent inspections by the local city council found that one of the school's two premises was licensed as an office but used for classes, the other lacked a valid business license, and signage did not comply with its advertising license. On July 18, Srinivasan called reports of a shutdown "fake news," saying the issues were minor and would be remedied. Three days later, authorities revoked the operator's business license and ordered operations to cease the following day. On July 22, the day it ceased operating in Johor, Network School signed a memorandum of understanding with Kazakhstan's government to set up a campus there, including a proposed "Network City" in Burabay. Srinivasan said Tuesday that the school is "up and running" in Astana, at Astana Hub. Forest City, a 1,740-hectare reclaimed site in Johor Bahru built by Country Garden, once China's largest property developer, was a $100 billion project designed to house up to 700,000 people. It fell far short of that, and Malaysia has tried to turn it into a business and financial hub: a special financial zone in 2023, then tax incentives in 2024, including corporate tax rates as low as 5% for qualifying finance, AI, cybersecurity and fintech firms. Business Insider found it struggling to attract residents in 2022, and still largely quiet two years later.

As large language models become commodities, competitive advantage is shifting from the models themselves to the balance sheets behind them. AI is reversing 20 years of technology economics, turning an asset-light software business into a capital-intensive industry. Since the AI boom began in 2023, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta have poured $1.1 trillion into AI infrastructure, and the four "hyperscalers" plan to invest another $745 billion this year alone. As models grow interchangeable, advantage will depend on who can finance, build and run infrastructure most cheaply. Microsoft boss Satya Nadella said "every model is substitutable," and Amazon chief Andy Jassy predicted there will soon be "at least half a dozen" comparably good models. Hyperscalers are therefore building infrastructure to support many models rather than betting on one winner. Whether the models generate enough value to justify the trillions committed remains uncertain; OpenAI and Anthropic are both lossmaking, yet capital keeps flowing. Nvidia is working with Apollo, Blackstone, Goldman Sachs and others to mobilize more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure. Google has assembled a $200 billion financing structure with Broadcom, Apollo, Blackstone and Morgan Stanley to fund Anthropic's chips and data centers. Microsoft, Amazon and Google hold the strongest hand, with the biggest balance sheets, the cheapest capital and large revenues from the same data centers used to train models. Rivals could emerge, however, including SpaceX and sovereign wealth funds such as Saudi Arabia's PIF and Abu Dhabi's MGX. Cloud providers are capturing the first returns, chipmakers sell the picks and shovels, and Wall Street finances the build-out. Enterprise software firms now compete with AI infrastructure for corporate budgets: in IBM's second quarter, customers postponed software purchases to secure AI infrastructure ahead of expected price hikes, and IBM's shares fell 25% in one day in mid-July. Investors have been unsettled over whether the spending will pay off. Alphabet's free cash flow turned negative for the first time since its IPO, and Meta's fell sharply. But the latest earnings showed returns in cloud computing: Microsoft's cloud business grew 32% to $39.3 billion, driving an 18% rise in revenues; Amazon Web Services grew 37% to $42.2 billion, its fastest growth in over four years; and Google's cloud business surged 82% to $24.8 billion. Investors added a record $450 billion to Microsoft's market value in a single day. Overcapacity may eventually appear, but that moment seems far off. Apple, which held back from heavy AI spending, briefly reached a $5 trillion valuation last month, making it the market's "control group." Investors are thus making two bets: on companies spending whatever it takes, or on those preserving financial discipline. One will be proved right. Either way, as model capabilities converge, the companies with the strongest balance sheets, cheapest capital and highest infrastructure utilization will have the edge. AI is becoming a financial engineering business.

Cybersecurity firm unveils crypto phishing campaign targeting 885,000 phone numbers. Rapid7 unveiled a new cryptocurrency phishing campaign targeting 885,000 phone numbers, aiming to steal investors’ holdings by redirecting them to fake wallet provider websites. Cybersecurity firm Rapid7 unveiled a new cryptocurrency phishing campaign known as Operation Asterix, targeting roughly 885,000 phone numbers from several countries to steal cryptocurrency investors’ assets. The phishing campaign led to 5,576 accounts matched to users on crypto exchange Binance, which were queued for attack, while the recovered logs also showed fake emails impersonating Crypto.com, according to a Monday report by Rapid7. Of the 885,000 phone numbers, the largest file included 316,002 German mobile numbers, with additional directories covering Hong Kong, Bulgaria, the UK, the US, Canadian fintech companies and additional Ledger-related lists. Phishing attacks and social engineering scams drove the majority of the crypto industry’s losses in the first quarter of the year, accounting for $306 million out of the total $482 million lost, according to blockchain security company Hacken. As part of the Asterix phishing campaign detailed by Rapid7 analysts Anna Sirokova and Jan Recinsky, attackers drove victims to fake apps impersonating Ledger, Trezor, and Exodus, seeking to steal their seed phrases. Attackers reached out to victims through fake support emails and phone inquiries. Operation Aseterix kill chain from acquisition to exfiltration. Source: Rapid7. Cointelegraph has contacted the analysts for further comment on what they found regarding target filtering, hardware wallet spoofing and self-custody vulnerabilities. We will update this article when they reply. Earlier in August, wallet provider Trezor reported a breach of personal data affecting about 14,000 users through its shipping provider, ShipMonk. In July, a crypto investor lost nearly $1 million after signing a malicious phishing token approval transaction on Ethereum. In November 2023, a fake Ledger Live app on the Microsoft Store resulted in the theft of $588,000 across 38 transactions. Related: DefiLlama delayed mobile launch over phishing apps on Apple Store, founder says. Asterix phishing campaign boasts 13% “hit rate” Attackers matched 43,066 accounts to cryptocurrency users with exchange accounts, validated from the larger German dataset of over 316,000 phone numbers, meaning that the campaign has a “hit rate” of approximately 13.6%, according to Rapid7. The report also identified a checker for Kraken, which sought to bulk-validate phone numbers against accounts from the cryptocurrency exchange. The cybersecurity company said that the recovered artifacts showed that artificial intelligence tools were used as a significant part of the phishing campaign. Phishing attacks are a long-standing headwind for the crypto industry, as they enable attackers to exploit human behavior rather than the code of a protocol. On May 25, onchain analyst “b-block” warned that scammers used Google to deploy malicious phishing ads impersonating decentralized exchange Uniswap, reportedly stealing more than $400,000 from victims. Leading crypto industry figures, including Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, have previously called for better wallet security measures to avoid phishing scams, after an investor lost $50 million in an address poisoning scam in December 2025. Machine learning for rubber development. For most of its history, compound development in the rubber industry has been a craft. The chemist sketches a recipe based on experience and an understanding for the chemistry, the batch is mixed and cured, properties are measured and adjustments are made. Round after round of iterative testing follows before the compound finally meets specification. Machine learning (ML) offers a different path. Models trained on historical compound data can estimate mechanical properties directly from the formulation, without anything ever entering the mixer. The idea is not new; it has been around in the materials informatics literature for over a decade (ref. 1), and recent work has applied it specifically to natural rubber tensile prediction (refs. 2 and 3). What has remained stubbornly difficult, though, is industrial adoption. The reasons are familiar enough to anyone working in a compound development laboratory: The data demands are large, the models can feel opaque, and there is rarely a clear warning when a prediction should not be trusted.

Unitree Founder Says Humanoid Robots May Take a Decade To Jump To The Mainstream. Wang Xingxing said truly versatile humanoid robots could still be five to 10 years away if development moves slowly, offering a reality check after the company's blockbuster Shanghai market debut. Humanoid robots may be getting better at walking, dancing and even performing martial arts, but the breakthrough that makes them genuinely useful in everyday life could still be as much as a decade away, according to Unitree Robotics founder Wang Xingxing. Speaking at the World Robot Conference in Beijing on Thursday, Wang said the robotics industry's equivalent of a "ChatGPT moment" would arrive when a robot could be placed inside an unfamiliar home and successfully perform about 80% of requested tasks using only voice or text instructions. He estimated that milestone could come within two to three years if development progresses quickly, or five to 10 years if progress is slower, CNBC reported. His latest comments highlight the contrast between the limitations of today's humanoid robots and the enormous investor enthusiasm surrounding companies developing them. Unitree made a blockbuster Shanghai stock market debut on Wednesday, with its shares closing 460% above the IPO price of 150.80 yuan. The Chinese robotics company raised 6.1 billion yuan, or about $900 million, after its offering was more than 8,000 times oversubscribed, Reuters reported. That excitement has been fueled partly by Unitree's increasingly sophisticated machines. Founded in 2016, the Hangzhou-based company has attracted global attention with videos showing its humanoid robots dancing, running and performing kung fu. It delivered more than 5,500 humanoid robots in 2025 and reported revenue of 1.7 billion yuan, with net profit reaching 278 million yuan. But Wang said robots still face fundamental problems that prevent them from operating as flexibly as humans. Current machines often need to be retrained from scratch when given a new task, making their inability to generalize skills across different jobs and environments one of the industry's biggest obstacles. Precision remains another major challenge. Robots are increasingly capable of planning broad movements, Wang said, but can still struggle with the final few centimeters or millimeters needed to execute a task accurately. Unitree is trying to address the problem through a "self-evolving development loop," in which AI models write and test robot control code before the results are scored and fed back into subsequent versions. The technical hurdles have not stopped China from building a commanding early position in the humanoid robotics market. Around 19,000 humanoid robots were shipped worldwide during the first half of 2026, a 272% increase from a year earlier, with Chinese manufacturers accounting for 97% of shipments, according to Morgan Stanley figures cited by CNBC. The bank expects shipments from China to reach 50,000 units this year, up from about 12,000 in 2025. China has made humanoid robotics a strategic priority as Beijing seeks leadership in emerging technologies and ways to offset an aging population and shrinking workforce. The government has rolled out policy support for embodied AI and robotics, while Chinese companies have raced to lower costs and expand production. Investor enthusiasm has followed. Nomura initiated coverage of Unitree with a buy rating this week, pointing to the company's relatively low hardware costs and rapid product development. The brokerage estimated that outsourced components represented less than one-fifth of Unitree's costs, helping its gross margin rise to 60% in 2025 from 44% in 2022. Unitree's explosive IPO has also increased scrutiny over whether impressive demonstrations can eventually translate into profitable large-scale deployments. Ying Zhang of the Economist Intelligence Unit told CNBC that the next test for embodied AI would be whether technological advances generate productivity improvements and economic returns significant enough to justify widespread adoption. The company's shares showed how quickly sentiment can shift after their extraordinary debut. Unitree stock fell nearly 19% on Thursday to close at 687 yuan, according to LSEG data, although that still left the shares more than four times above their IPO price.

Two people suspected of setting fire to the building of Estonian defense company Milrem Robotics in Tallinn have been detained in Latvia. The Estonian Prosecutor’s Office announced on Aug. 19 that the fire was established to have been deliberate and premeditated. The country’s authorities are also investigating possible Russian involvement. According to state prosecutor Gardi Anderson, investigators have identified a total of three suspects. Two were detained in Latvia after their arrest was authorized by an Estonian court. Law enforcement agencies of the two countries are working on transferring the detainees to Estonia. The prosecutor’s office intends to finalize the third arrest in the near future. The suspects’ names and nationalities have not been disclosed. “We are investigating all theories, including whether what happened was an act of sabotage. At present we cannot disclose more detailed information about the lines of inquiry,” Anderson said. According to the prosecutor’s office, shortly before the fire, a local resident noticed suspicious activity near a Milrem Robotics building and reported it to emergency services. On Aug. 18, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal stated that investigators are looking into possible Russian involvement. “One of the theories under investigation is a possible act of sabotage with Russian participation,” he said. The Russian embassy in Tallinn did not respond to a request from Reuters for comment, and Estonian authorities have not yet publicly presented any evidence of Russian involvement in the arson. The fire broke out overnight into Aug. 15 in a facility used by Milrem Robotics. No one was injured. The company develops unmanned ground military vehicles that are used in Ukraine. On Aug. 19, Milrem Robotics CEO Kuldar Väärsi told Reuters that the fire had not affected production, supply chains, or equipment deliveries to Ukraine. According to him, the company expects to have more than 200 of its robotic systems in Ukraine by the end of the year.

Skylark Labs, a U.S.-based AI and robotics company building self-learning AI for physical systems, has announced a strategic partnership with Hexadyne Corporation. The move expands Skylark's push to bring its defense robotics portfolio to the U.S. government and allied defense customers across the Pacific Rim (PACRIM) and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The partnership pairs Skylark's humanoids, autonomous ground and aerial systems, counter-UAS technologies, and self-learning AI with Hexadyne's three decades of experience with U.S. and allied defense organizations. Hexadyne contributes defense-market development, government and international customer relationships, export and ITAR compliance, procurement support, logistics, and in-country deployment capabilities. Its public-sector customers include the U.S. Department of Defense, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and other international defense organizations. Hexadyne is a U.S.-based aerospace and defense company with operations in Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. The companies will work together across several mission areas: counter-UAS solutions, command-and-control systems, humanoid robots for battlefield operations, and autonomous aerial systems for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and strike missions. The partnership will initially prioritize opportunities with the U.S. government and defense users in the PACRIM and GCC markets, where Skylark sees substantial opportunity for autonomous robotics and AI. Dr. Amarjot Singh, founder and CEO of Skylark Labs, said the company has spent several years building its intelligence and robotics platforms and that the partnership is the next step toward getting those systems to defense customers at scale. He said Hexadyne's experience building relationships and deploying defense infrastructure gives Skylark a much larger pathway to operational deployments. Robert Sanchez, CEO of Hexadyne, described the partnership as a strategic initiative to be at the front end of major changes in the future of the battlespace. He said Skylark is positioned to develop new systems and augment existing ones for "the military after the next military," and that AI's evolving reach requires adapting systems to support forces across the spectrum. He said the two companies will leverage existing relationships in the U.S. and international marketplace to introduce robot-based technologies. Skylark is known for a brain-inspired architecture that lets systems continuously self-evolve, learning from experience without human guidance. This allows systems to recognize and respond to novel situations based on conceptual understanding rather than pattern matching. Combined with Skylark's collaborative framework for sharing knowledge across distributed systems, knowledge gained by one system propagates across the network, so collective intelligence evolves far faster than any individual component. The partnership is also expected to strengthen Skylark's name in the superintelligence landscape while bringing its expertise to new markets.

They set out to find an alternative that doesn't use photos as training data, works as effortlessly as Google Photos, and removes a cloud subscription from their recurring costs. They chose the Synology BeeStation Plus, a NAS (network-attached storage device) that they say is easy enough for a non-expert, with an Android app comparable to Google Photos, including location tags and albums. Though they find network devices difficult, they set it up in under five minutes, with a plug-and-play process that can be done on a smartphone, though a PC is recommended for migrating files. To move their library, they used Google Takeout to download everything to a PC, then uploaded the zip files to the NAS with the BeeStation for Desktop app. The BeePhotos smartphone app then organized everything similarly to Google Photos, and albums and timelines synced perfectly. The one shortcoming is search: BeePhotos can only find photos by location names and generic words like cat, dog or beach, unlike Google's far smarter search. The author plans to move family members over too. The BeeStation app lets you invite up to eight people to sync files without overlap, each with a private login, while only the owner can access all files. They bought the 8TB model but recommend the 4TB variant at $399.99, which works out to $33.33 per month for the first and only year. By comparison, Google One's 5TB plan costs about $19.99 per month, every year; the author's two years of Google One would total $479.76. Splitting the NAS cost with a family member lowers the monthly cost, and once it is paid off, cloud storage can be dropped from recurring expenses. Other traditional NAS devices exist, but this is the only one that felt plug-and-play to the author. The author will miss Gemini's 1 million token context window, and Google offers no standalone Gemini subscription, but they have been meaning to try Claude.

President Donald Trump, speaking alongside cryptocurrency leaders at the White House this week, said that if he were a mayor or governor with a chance to land "an AI plant or a data center," he "would absolutely want it because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous." Candidates in competitive midterm races from both parties are not using that message. Voter frustration over the huge data center campuses, some larger than football stadiums and using more energy than small cities, has stalled the race to build them. Even the Senate Republicans' campaign arm warned that anger over data centers could cost them a seat. Opposition spans the political spectrum, driven by fears of higher electricity bills, drained water wells, air and noise pollution, changed community character, and lucrative state tax breaks. Trump frames data centers as essential to winning the AI race against China, but has acknowledged concern over rising electricity bills, saying "it's only fair" for the companies to pay their costs and that data centers need "a little public relations help." He has gotten tech giants to sign a voluntary pledge to shield consumers from higher utility bills while pushing to streamline construction of their own power plants. James Henson of the University of Texas at Austin's Texas Politics Project called the White House "tone deaf" or indifferent to other Republican candidates. In Ohio, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a Tuesday memo that Sen. Jon Husted is vulnerable because of data centers, calling it a "sleeper issue." Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown is airing ads calling Husted the "face of data centers in Ohio" as people gather signatures for a statewide referendum to ban construction. A July Fox News poll found most registered voters oppose a data center in their area, though the issue ranks behind concerns like cost of living. A June Quinnipiac poll found about 4 in 10 voters mentioned AI data centers as important in deciding their U.S. House vote. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford tied Trump's remark to Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, calling them in "lockstep on data centers." Ford pledged to halt new state tax breaks for data centers, which he estimated at $200 million currently, audit existing projects, make data centers pay for their electricity, protect the water supply, and help local governments negotiate benefits agreements. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott, who last November celebrated Google's $40 billion investment, is under attack from Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa. Abbott has since promised tougher action, including removing the sales tax exemption and reviewing energy usage. Trump called the shift "a mistake." Abbott's office said "Texans must come first." In Wisconsin, Rep. Tom Tiffany, Trump-endorsed and running for governor, released an ad branding Democrat David Crowley "Data Center David Crowley," citing his remark that Wisconsin could become an "AI and data hub" for the globe. Crowley says communities must have veto authority while noting economic benefits. Tiffany has also praised data centers and voted for the SPEED Act, which would speed AI infrastructure construction and hasn't passed the Senate. Neither supports a moratorium; Tiffany wants to repeal the state tax incentive, Crowley has not, and both want stricter regulation. Crowley accused Tiffany of running from his record.

Adobe expands generative AI audio with Firefly music, speech and sound effects. Adobe Inc. today announced the general availability of audio capabilities in Firefly, the company’s all-in-one creative AI tool suite, allowing users to produce music, speech, and sound effects for their projects. In June, the company unveiled big changes for Firefly, including a large number of skills for Firefly AI Assistant that built in agentic capabilities for Elements – the company’s user-friendly video and photo editing tool suite – that allowed users to introduce characters, locations and objects that stay the same across projects. Generate Music is powered by Firefly Music Model under the hood and creates universally licensed original tracks designed for a user’s own video’s length and mood, so the music can go with whatever content is being generated without worries about copyright issues. It can also be fine-tuned to match the brand and presentation. Generate Speech uses both Firefly Speech and an option for a model from ElevenLabs Inc. It can take a script and turn it into a fluid, natural voiceover that allows for control over voice, cadence and emotion. ElevenLabs is known for extremely powerful speech models that cover a wide variety of synthetic voices with varied capabilities, emotionality and control. The sound effect tool also includes an underlying Firefly model that creates custom effects using a prompt, following the timing and energy of the content to produce an appropriate sound. “Going back to school and trying to stay consistent as a content creator can get really overwhelming,” said Esther Rehema, a fashion, beauty and lifestyle creator. “Being able to find music that is safe for commercial use and fits my content is such a game-changer.” Adobe added that the audio produced by Firefly Studio is production-quality and commercially safe, like everything else generated by its AI models. No separate subscription is needed for any track generated by the tool. AI audio generation tools, from music to special effects, have been trending for years. This includes audio tools such as Lyra 3 from Google LLC, OpenAI Group PBC’s reported music-generation experiments and Stability AI Ltd.’s Stable Audio open-source model. Image: Adobe. pCloud's Family Lifetime plan is a single upfront payment for cloud storage kept for as long as the service exists, with no monthly bill, annual renewal, or later price increase. The 5 TB Family plan can be split across up to five separate private accounts, each with its own login and personal space, suiting family members, roommates, or small groups. pCloud has offered lifetime plans for over a decade, is based in Switzerland, follows Swiss data protection law, and is used by more than 20 million people. On cost, competing family plans of around 2 TB typically run $10 to $15 per month, or $600 to $900 over five years and $1,200 to $1,800 over ten, with prices that usually rise every few years. pCloud's one-time $599 for 5 TB across five accounts breaks even against most family plans in about four years, after which storage is essentially free. The promotion is timed to the Back to School season, when new devices, photos, and project files quickly fill storage. The plan supports Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android with instant sync between devices. The Back to School discount covers three lifetime tiers: Family 2 TB at $449 (down from $890, 50% off), Family 5 TB at $599 (down from $1,469, 59% off), and Family 10 TB at $1,099 (down from $2,249, 51% off). The 5 TB tier is labeled a limited edition and has the deepest percentage discount. It works out to roughly $120 per TB, versus $224/TB for the 2 TB plan. pCloud is described as one of the few major providers still offering a genuine lifetime option at scale. It also offers client-side encryption (pCloud Encryption is a paid add-on) and Swiss jurisdiction. Files sync in real time, the desktop client mounts pCloud as a virtual drive that uses no local space, and the mobile apps automatically back up camera-roll photos. The article points to its own pCloud review and best cloud storage guide for more detail. The promotion ends August 31, after which the Family 5 TB Lifetime plan returns to standard pricing of roughly $1,000 to $1,200 depending on other promotions. pCloud typically runs deep lifetime discounts only a handful of times per year, tied to major seasonal moments. Checkout uses 256-bit SSL, and the plan carries a 14-day money-back guarantee, allowing buyers to test syncing and the family setup before the refund window closes.

Corporate expense management platform Ramp is hot on the heels of Stripe in setting up toll houses for AI inference. Ramp on Wednesday evening launched its own AI model routing service, dubbed Router, that lets users and companies use and switch between various large language models through an API. The company says it has been using the router it built for its own AI usage needs over the past three years. The service is only available in the United States for now. It’s free to use for the remainder of 2026 (users will still have to pay for AI model inference costs), and it comes with a $26 credit launch offer. The company did not say how much the service will cost next year. Router functions similarly to OpenRouter, though the latter offers many more AI model options than Ramp’s current offerings. Router offers access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Minimax, Nvidia, xAI, and Z.ai. It also provides several “strategies” to help its customers route AI requests to models based on their preferences. For example, one lets users set a preference for model providers’ flex usage tiers, while another lets Router choose which model to route queries to based on up to three user-specified benchmarks. Users can also choose to route only difficult problems to expensive models or test models easily without having to switch. Users get a dashboard, too, that lets them see token spend, cost, latency, fallback attempts, and other details. Notably, Router has an opt-out data retention policy: It will record model inputs, outputs, and tool calls for one year by default, though the company says it will remove “personally identifiable information before using that content to improve the product.” For Ramp, entering the model routing business offers a two-pronged opportunity: It gets to tap the booming AI inference market and offer its existing clients a model routing service that fits in neatly with its existing products, which includes AI token usage monitoring and token spend management. And, if Router proves as attractive of a model testing arena as OpenRouter has, Ramp may also be able to build long-standing relationships with AI labs and inference providers worldwide. That could help Ramp, which raised $750 million at a $44 billion valuation in June, gain new customers and a new point of entry for selling its expense management products.

Adit Singh was a partner at Foundation Capital when he helped source and co-lead the first funding round into then-obscure chip startup Cerebras. By the time Cerebras held its blockbuster IPO in May, Foundation Capital held a roughly 7% stake, making it the third-largest shareholder in the company, which now trades at a valuation of nearly $50 billion. Singh now has a new VC firm to call home: On Thursday, he said he’s now joined the 57-year-old Mayfield as an infrastructure partner. At Mayfield, Singh will invest in hardware, infrastructure software, cybersecurity, and physical AI. He says it was the firm’s strength in semiconductors that drew him to the role. “If you look at Mayfield’s semiconductor portfolio, it’s probably the best in the market right now,” Singh told TechCrunch, pointing to Mayfield’s investments in Upscale AI, which was recently valued at $2 billion, and Lumilens, which just raised $700 million at a $5.5 billion valuation. “I’m a chip designer by training,” Singh said. “My secret sauce is being able to look at any workload and see how it works from the application all the way down to the transistor.” He credits his background in electrical engineering to helping him recognize the potential in Cerebras 10 years ago. However, Singh didn’t stick around as an investor at Foundation. In 2017, he co-founded Neotribe Ventures, and after spending four years leading the firm, he joined early-stage firm Cota Capital. Singh says he decided to join Mayfield in large part because the size of seed infrastructure deals has ballooned in recent years. While smaller funds often get priced out of mega-seed deals, Mayfield’s $3 billion in assets under management allows it to write seed checks of up to $20 million. Mayfield managing partner Navin Chaddha told TechCrunch that despite knowing Singh for 15 years and sitting on three startup boards together — including Upscale AI and unicorn AI startup Velaura AI — it still took some time to convince him to join the firm. “We have been talking for a long time, and this time stars aligned,” Chaddha said.

This week's threats share a theme: trusted components doing exactly what they were allowed to do, while exposed systems, old bugs and AI-assisted exploit research lower the effort needed to cause damage. Check Point reverse engineered Microsoft Defender's Boot-Time Removal driver ("BTR.sys") and showed the signed driver can be repurposed as a universal kernel operation engine to bypass endpoint security, exploiting a "golden window" between system start and user mode initialization without BYOVD. Because it is Microsoft-signed, signature-based blocking is ineffective. The U.S. Department of Justice charged 17 members of Iran-based Mabna Institute, which since at least 2013 intruded into systems of 144 U.S. universities, 178 foreign universities, at least 42 U.S. companies, at least 11 foreign companies, at least five U.S. government agencies and at least two NGOs. They stole over 31 TB of data and targeted more than 100,000 professor accounts, compromising about 8,000, on behalf of Iran's IRGC, and sold the data on Megapaper.ir and Gigapaper.ir. The State Department offers a $10 million reward for information on five defendants. Check Point's Shmuel Gihon called it the "privatization of state espionage." A Grandoreiro campaign abuses the legitimate Duplicate Files Finder app for DLL sideloading, concentrated in Mexico, Spain, Peru and Argentina, with extensive anti-analysis checks. ErrTraffic-generated ClickFix campaigns deliver Cruciferra, which uses the vulnerable driver "DCRCVDrv.sys" in a BYOVD attack to kill security processes. ErrTraffic, sold by LenAI, spreads payloads including Remus Stealer, Vidar Stealer and Okobot via compromised WordPress sites, resolving its C2 through a Polygon smart contract (EtherHiding); the end goal is launching Remus Stealer via process hollowing. OpenAI previewed Private Safety Processing to monitor misuse without retaining customer data, while Google showcased HEIR, an open-source homomorphic encryption compiler toolchain for private AI inference. Kriminal AI, a clearnet service with 2,300+ users priced $12.99 to $99.00 per month, offers AI with no guardrails, joining WormGPT, FraudGPT and Xanthorox. Apple agreed to change App Tracking Transparency consent prompts in Germany, with changes applying across almost all EU countries, after the Federal Cartel Office found its own apps received more favorable prompts. Claroty found 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland XWEB Pro controllers, chainable to root RCE, plus flaws in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers including a hidden "code-of-the-day" authentication bypass; all are fixed. Gen Digital found a 12 KB backdoor hiding its C2 domain in trailing spaces of a fake desktop.ini file. Critical flaws: Gogs CVE-2026-52813 (CVSS 10.0), RCE via path traversal and Git hooks, fixed in 0.14.3; a macOS Spotlight out-of-bounds read, CVE-2026-43774 (CVSS 5.5), patched in July 2026; unauthenticated RCE in @circleci/mcp-server-circleci via spoofable Host and Origin headers, fixed in 0.19.2; and n8n CVE-2026-33696 (CVSS 9.4), prototype pollution leading to RCE, fixed in 2.14.1, 2.13.3 and 1.123.27. T-Mobile staff traced Salt Typhoon activity to a Chicago router belonging to another telecom and cut its cable with scissors. Z.ai's GLM-5.3 model more than doubles GLM-5.2 on exploitation benchmarks and helped find 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 projects, though it lags Anthropic Mythos 5 in turning flaws into working attacks.

Florida police officer fired, arrested over alleged misuse of Flock camera database. SARASOTA, Fla. (CBS12) — A former Sarasota Police Department officer has been fired and arrested following an investigation into the alleged misuse of law enforcement databases, the department announced Wednesday. Cory Waiters, 38, was arrested Aug. 19 and faces two felony charges and one misdemeanor charge, according to Sarasota police. The charges include an offense involving computers, computer systems, networks or electronic devices; official misconduct; and violating Florida's public records law. Police said the investigation began after the department learned on Aug. 6 that Waiters had allegedly misused law enforcement-only search databases, including DAVID and Flock. An internal affairs investigation was opened, followed by a criminal investigation. Waiters was placed on paid administrative leave on Aug. 7. The department also launched an agency-wide audit of database use the same day. Police said the audit was completed Aug. 14 and found agency-wide compliance. Investigators later developed probable cause in the criminal case, according to the department. Waiters was terminated on Aug. 19, the same day he was arrested. “We take allegations of misconduct seriously. When an agency member’s actions fall short of the standards and professionalism we expect, we will address it appropriately and without hesitation,” Sarasota Police Chief Rex Troche said in a statement. He was being held at the Sarasota County Jail following his arrest. The department did not provide additional details about how the databases were allegedly misused or identify any people whose information may have been accessed. Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact Detective Kim Laster with the Sarasota Police Department Criminal Investigations Division at 941-263-6827.

Meta's app for creating generative AI minigames is now available in the US. It's called Pocket and is described as a "platform for making and sharing gizmos." Meta's little vibe-coding app Pocket has now arrived in the US after a brief testing phase in Brazil. The app lets people generate minigames, called gizmos, via prompts. The games get published to a scrollable feed, bringing in a social media component. Users can save gizmos to a favorites list and repost gizmos to their feed. These games make full use of the capabilities available in modern smartphones. They can respond to both touch and tilt and can include photos and even songs. Once saved to a profile, other people can remix them into unique creations. They are called gizmos instead of minigames for a couple of probable reasons. First of all, they aren't just games. The marketing advertises simple experiences like a canvas to paint on. Also, Meta hired nearly the entire team behind an app called, well, Gizmo. This led to the app shutting down. Gizmo was basically the same thing as Pocket and even used similar nomenclature (referring to the creations as gizmos). In any event, Pocket is available right now and it's free. It could be worth a download and a couple of minutes before getting bored. This is just the latest AI-forward move that Meta has made. Last year, the company launched a feature for the Meta AI app called Vibes that's basically a feed for AI slop. Facebook also recently introduced the ability to tweak profile photos with AI-powered animations.

The $9 billion cybersecurity company is bringing back cofounder Orion Hindawi as CEO, replacing Dan Streetman after less than four years in the role, as the company looks to navigate the AI upheaval reshaping software companies. Hindawi's father and another cofounder, David Hindawi, will return to the role of chair, while Streetman leaves the company's board. Prior to Streetman joining the company, Orion Hindawi served as CEO for over 15 years. Tanium also had a small round of job cuts last week, affecting around 35 employees in research and development, according to sources familiar with the matter. Like many software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies, Tanium has been facing more competitive pressure as AI changes how businesses buy and use enterprise software. The company said it plans to expand its AI offerings and autonomous capabilities. This leadership shake-up follows several executive departures this year, as Business Insider previously reported. "AI has made what we do more critical than ever, and Tanium is the platform every organization will rely on as threats grow more sophisticated and the pace of change intensifies," Orion Hindawi said in a statement. Tanium hired its chief financial officer, Marc Levine, in 2021 to conduct a "readiness assessment" for an initial public offering. Several employees and executives had left Tanium in the past few years due to uncertainty about whether the company would ever go public, Business Insider previously reported. WASHINGTON — To take full advantage of AI, the Army needs a comprehensive simulation of its networks, what’s called a digital twin, where it can train and test both the algorithms and the humans working with them, the two-star chief of the service’s Network Command (NETCOM) said today. Such a detailed digital model, constantly updated with live data on how the real-world network is performing, would be difficult to build, Maj. Gen. Jacqueline Denise McPhail acknowledged at AFCEA’s annual TechNet Augusta conference. But it would have so much potential, she went on, that she challenged the contractors in the audience to build it anyway. Chief among its many benefits, McPhail said, the digital twin would provide an ultra-realistic training ground for network operators, cyber defenders, and AI algorithms on how the network works and how to keep it working, even when under attack. “We get about 1.2 million cyber attacks a day,” the NETCOM commander said — and they’re increasingly sophisticated, she added, far harder to detect than brute-force Distributed Denial of Service (DDOS) attacks. “It’s no longer DDOS. Now we have to look at behavior: What behavior has changed?” she said. “[It’s] a tremendous amount of volume of data coming in, and how do we secure that data? How do we identify what’s just noise and what is a change in behavior? “That’s where AI comes in,” McPhail said. “If we can get a digital twin of the DoDIN-A, that now enables us to be able to leverage AI in that model to understand our vulnerabilities, where our gaps are, [and] where we do have resilience.” That acronym stands for Department of Defense Information Network – Army, which means all the military networks for which the Army is responsible. “It’s a big ask. I know it’s a large scale effort,” she said. “I think we start small and build it out.” RELATED: Army Cyber training AI agents in cyber ‘work roles’ alongside human counterparts. McPhail is using a broader definition of digital twin here than the one enshrined in Pentagon doctrine [PDF], which says it is “a computerized representation (integrated set of models) that serves as the real-time digital counterpart of a physical object or process.” True to that definition, when defense officials and industry executives talk about digital twins, they usually mean a highly detailed simulation of a physical thing, from an aircraft to a supply chain to a virtual wounded soldier used for training medics. The ambition is to simulate each component and their interactions so accurately that the virtual model — the twin — replicates exactly what its physical counterpart would do in any given situation. That allows users to stress-test the twin in ways that would be unsafe in the physical world, try out alternative designs and upgrades without breaking the real system in the process, and analyze potential problems as they unfold, or even predict and prevent them in advance. McPhail is effectively arguing she can get the same kinds of advantages from a digital twin of something that’s already digital, namely the Army network. (Obviously the network runs on physical chips, fiber, routers, and so on, but most of the action worth modeling is at the software level). “We need to figure out what’s broken, but we also need to figure out what’s not broken so we don’t break it later,” she said at one point.

If you are a malicious hacker, cybersecurity professionals may very well be the worst people in the world to try to hack, as there is a very good chance they are going to catch you. A person pretending to work for a leading crypto news site targeted several cybersecurity professionals around the time of the Black Hat and Def Con hacking conferences earlier this month. The hacker approached attendees on the social media site X, both via public replies and DMs, and then leveraged Google Docs in an attempt to trick the targets into installing malware, according to researchers. On Wednesday, security firm Huntress published a blog post detailing the hacking campaign, which targeted one of its researchers, who pretended to go along with it to learn what the hacker was trying to do. In broken English, the hacker asked the researcher if they had plans to attend a conference next, and then mentioned a conference allegedly organized by the crypto news website, according to a screenshot of the conversation. After that, the hacker shared a legitimate Google Doc that looked like it was a planning document for the fake conference. The document displayed a sidebar designed to make the target think it was encrypted. The goal was to first trick the target into entering a fake decryption key provided by the hacker. That was the first step in a process that would lead to the installation of malware for macOS and Windows, depending on the operating system used by the target, according to Huntress. To make the sidebar appear real, the hacker used Google App Script, a platform that allows developers to customize the user interface of Google Docs with menus and sidebars, for example. The hacker tried to trick Huntress’ researcher into installing an infostealer for Apple computers; a remote desktop viewing tool repurposed as malware for Windows; and a fake installer for the cryptocurrency wallet Ledger. The person behind the account identified by Huntress researchers as the hacker did not respond when TechCrunch sent them a private message on X. Hackers of all kinds — whether they are unknown government hackers using advanced spyware or North Korean government hackers using fake Twitter profiles — have targeted cybersecurity professionals before. What made this campaign a bit more believable was the use of a legitimate Google Doc and Google feature. Google did not immediately respond when TechCrunch reached out asking if the company had seen this or similar hacking campaigns.

WASHINGTON — The Asia-based USS George Washington aircraft carrier is now operating in the Middle East, the U.S. military said Thursday, relieving a long-deployed carrier following reports of mental health challenges and supply shortages aboard while it was supporting the Iran war. U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said on social media that the carrier arrived in the region Wednesday. It was not clear when the USS Abraham Lincoln would arrive back in the U.S. or whether it would make a port stop along the way, but the journey takes just over a month. The Washington arrived as concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment, which has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days, and about reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products. Several Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Department of Defense for accountability over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said were “completely misrepresented.” Hegseth spoke with the Lincoln’s crew last week, and Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, visited this past weekend. In an editorial published Sunday by The Wall Street Journal, Cooper said the crew “delivered a performance for the ages, and now you are going home.” Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. While renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran calmed in recent weeks, the Navy is enforcing a reimposed blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war. Hegseth has said the U.S. can maintain the blockade “indefinitely.” President Donald Trump this week downplayed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its homeport in San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. Trump called the nearly nine months at sea that the sailors endured a “good period of time” but added that “over the years, we’ve had them out there much longer.” Trump told reporters Monday that he spoke with a retired admiral over the weekend who recounted being on ships for “much longer.” Trump said the admiral assured him that the Lincoln is “beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.” Trump did not name the admiral. Trump says record-setting Navy deployment to support Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’ In a statement Sunday after visiting the Lincoln, Cooper praised the carrier’s leaders for prioritizing mental health and resilience. “History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” Cooper said. The Washington joins the USS George H.W. Bush in the Middle East, leaving Asia without an American carrier strike group at a time when China has shown more signs of aggression. The lack of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific may be short-lived if the Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. But it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some American sailors ragged, analysts say, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the Western Hemisphere.

The author used to store photos on OneDrive while his wife used Google Photos, but in the past year or so Immich, a self-hosted app, has replaced both for the family, and he hasn't missed the cloud. He feared self-hosted software wouldn't match those services, but Immich nails the feature set, with only some advanced features he doesn't need missing. The interface is inspired by Google Photos and Material Design. The default page is a timeline with dates in the scroll bar for jumping to a point in time, and a map feature shows photos by location when metadata exists. Albums group photos from the same trip or event, and the UI is much smoother than OneDrive. Unexpectedly, a machine learning component running entirely on his own server recognizes faces and gathers each person's pictures in one place. It isn't perfect, but profiles can be merged when one person is split into two, which also improves future identification. Running everything locally gives him control over his data. Though he calls the idea that Google uses your files a bit of a conspiracy theory, he notes policies could change, especially with companies hungry for AI training data. Charleston County school district launches AI resource hub. District says new tool lists policy, expectations for AI use in classrooms. CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCSC) — The Charleston County School District has created a Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) Resource Hub on its website to give students, families and educators a centralized place to learn about the district’s approach to AI. The district said artificial intelligence platforms and resources are transforming education, and it is developing policies and resources to build the community’s AI literacy. The online resource hub lists district policy, initiatives and the district’s expectations for how AI should be used in the classroom. Policy built on S-E-E framework. Deputy Superintendent Luke Clamp said the district developed its AI policy using what the district calls the SEE framework. “S-E-E. Is it safe? Is it ethical? And is it effective?” Clamp said. “So any tool that we might use or may make available to our staff or our students, we’re going to take it through that frame. As well as giving parents education about the questions they should be asking their students if they’re being given activities or assignments to do,” Clamp said. “And when it’s appropriate to use generative AI and when it’s not appropriate. So that parents can be engaged. And that’s, above all, that’s what we want. We want our parents to be engaged and have thoughtful questions as they support their students in their learning,” Clamp said. Guidance group set data protection as priority. A guidance group of students, staff and community members worked together to create the guidelines for what AI can create and when. “Yes. Well, first and foremost is, are we protecting our students’ data? And are we protecting all of their intellectual property as we might engage and use any resource and technology? And we can say yes,” Clamp said. “Our students’ data and the information that they’ll create, we absolutely will protect that. Because for students, their concern is about the integrity of what they’re creating, what they have access to, and then more specifically, how they will be assessed on any piece of information they create,” Clamp said. District piloting Magic School tool. Clamp was asked whether the policy applies to all available AI tools, including Midjourney, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Claude. “So Charleston County has begun a one-year pilot with a pedagogical tool called Magic School. And this tool allows for, first with teacher use only, the integration of generative AI in supporting teachers as they develop instruction and support students. There are free versions of tools that are out there that we know students and staff have access to, but only Magic School is approved to be used by staff in creating pedagogical resources,” Clamp said. The district said Generative AI will not replace teachers in the classroom and is only a tool meant to enhance the process. The district will also provide teacher training and professional development on using AI in the classroom. You can access the district’s resource hub here.

German startup Revolta AG introduced a first-of-its-kind high-voltage sodium home battery at Intersolar Europe 2026, pitched as a cheaper and safer alternative to lithium-ion storage for rooftop solar owners. The system uses a proprietary transformer that boosts voltage output roughly 50 times, enabling a compact 2.2-kilowatt-hour module that runs on only three sodium-ion cells and can scale to 22 kWh. Sodium-ion chemistry avoids cobalt and other rare minerals, relying instead on one of the most abundant elements on Earth, sourced from common materials like salt. This eases cost, environmental and geopolitical supply concerns, and internal components such as cathodes can be made from aluminum rather than costly alloys. Analysts cite lithium-ion raw materials at roughly $10,000 to $11,000 per ton versus $600 to $650 per ton for sodium equivalents, suggesting long-term savings as the technology scales. Sodium-ion batteries also offer better thermal stability and lower risk of the catastrophic fires seen in some lithium installations. The system addresses the mismatch between midday solar output and evening household demand. Without storage, excess daytime energy flows back to the grid; with it, households can use stored power when evening utility rates rise, potentially cutting bills for customers on time-of-use pricing. The modular design lets smaller homes start with one 2.2 kWh unit, enough for lighting, internet, refrigeration and device charging, while larger homes can expand to 22 kWh to run more appliances and provide backup during extended outages for refrigeration, communications and medical devices. Installers may find the smaller footprint and flexible platform easier to integrate with existing solar setups, potentially speeding adoption. When many households store and use electricity during high-demand periods, grid pressure eases, which matters as renewables grow and utilities face fluctuating supply and demand. Dr. Elena Petrova, a materials scientist at the Institute for Sustainable Energy, said safer residential storage options benefit grid operators. The chemistry also performs better in extreme temperatures than lithium equivalents. Sodium-ion development is accelerating globally, with manufacturers like CATL advancing it for electric vehicles and startups such as Revolta targeting the residential niche. Current sodium batteries deliver 100 to 200 Wh/kg versus lithium's 200 to 260 Wh/kg, making them better suited to stationary storage than high-performance vehicles. Research into advanced cathode materials, including Prussian Blue analogs and polyanionic compounds, continues to improve performance, with some experimental systems reaching 458 Wh/kg. The article concludes that the Revolta battery shows affordable home storage need not depend on scarce or expensive materials, offering homeowners a practical way to capture more value from rooftop solar and suggesting that practical off-grid living is moving closer to mainstream affordability.
