Nearly 200 activists in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" (MAHA) movement are criticizing President Donald Trump's promotion of coal to fuel artificial intelligence data centers, according to a letter sent Friday and first obtained by The Associated Press. Signed by at least two former staffers from Kennedy's 2024 presidential campaign, it marks the first major MAHA mobilization over fossil fuels and the latest rift between the activists and the Trump administration over environmental policy. Addressed to Trump, Kennedy and other Cabinet officials, the letter laments a 2025 executive order aimed at boosting coal to power data centers, citing pollution concerns, and asks the administration to consider renewable options such as solar and geothermal energy. It says American AI leadership "should not come at the cost of a more toxic burden for American children." It also asks for transparent review of data center location and power sourcing decisions and for respect for existing environmental review requirements in permitting. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers responded that greenhouse gas emissions dropped to a 30-year low during Trump's first term and that Trump "was given a mandate to roll back the radical climate policies that are burning a hole through taxpayers' wallets." The agencies receiving the letter did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Prominent figures behind the letter include Zen Honeycutt, a former Kennedy campaign staffer and founder of Moms Across America, and Charles Eisenstein, a former Kennedy campaign speechwriter. Honeycutt said she asked the Kennedy-aligned PAC MAHA Action to sign on but received no reply. She said she researched coal ash's impact on communities after Trump's order and was disturbed by what she found, and that she is also concerned about data centers' land use and effects on nearby residents. "We vote for those who put health and safety first," she said. The letter may not reflect all MAHA activists' views, but the criticism, coming less than three months before November's midterms, could challenge Republicans seeking to win over this voting bloc. Kennedy has made policy changes catering to the movement, including trying to scale back childhood vaccine recommendations, seeking to remove artificial dyes from food, and encouraging diets free of ultraprocessed foods. But many in the movement, which Trump credits with helping him win back the White House, are frustrated by the administration's embrace of pesticides such as glyphosate and its deregulatory environmental agenda. Some say they will vote on issues over party this fall. Trump has embraced what he calls "big, beautiful coal" despite environmentalists' outcry over greenhouse gases and toxic chemicals from coal plants. His administration has moved to reverse tighter Biden-era greenhouse gas standards; such emissions can harm children's brain development and increase adult heart attack rates. Trump is also a vocal data center advocate, framing them as necessary to beat China in the AI race and citing the jobs and tax revenue they bring. Data centers have become a political flashpoint this election year, with voters across the spectrum criticizing them for raising electricity bills, draining water supplies and causing air and noise pollution.

Taipei, Aug. 22 (CNA) With Taiwan’s gross domestic product (GDP) per capita forecast to approach US$50,000 in 2027 amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, how to ensure a more balanced distribution of income generated by the AI-driven economy is becoming a concern, according to an economist. Although Taiwan’s GDP per capita is rising rapidly, the benefits of strong exports driven by robust global demand for AI-related products have been concentrated in the information and communications technology (ICT) sector, raising concerns about a “K-shaped” economic recovery. K-shaped growth refers to a divergence in the performance of different sectors, with some moving higher while others decline, creating a pattern resembling the arms of the letter “K.” Taiwan’s GDP per capita topped US$10,000 for the first time in 1992 after two decades of economic development. It reached US$20,000 in 2011 and surpassed US$30,000 in 2021. It is expected to rise further to around US$45,000 in 2026 and nearly US$50,000 in 2027. More funding for social welfare. Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明), president of the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER), is among the economists concerned about unbalanced economic development, as Taiwan’s GDP is forecast to grow 6.04 percent in 2027 after an estimated 11.05 percent expansion in 2026. GDP per capita is forecast to reach US$49,874 next year, according to the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS). In a recent interview with CNA, Lien said the government should allocate more funds to social welfare programs, including labor insurance, civil servant insurance and national health insurance, to strengthen their financial foundations. Injecting public funds into social welfare programs could improve wealth distribution and create long-term benefits for social equality and economic stability, Lien said. “Fund allocations to social welfare will be a long-term task,” Lien said. “Although such efforts are unlikely to produce immediate effects, they are a must.” Earlier this week, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) announced that his administration will include NT$235.7 billion (US$7.40 billion) in its proposed 2027 central government budget to fund a universal NT$10,000 cash handout so “the AI dividend can be shared by all.” Lien said the cash handout could be an effective way to put some of those benefits directly into people’s pockets, but strengthening social welfare would be a better approach to providing greater support for low-income families. Low-income people find it difficult to share in the benefits of AI development, which has been a major driver of Taiwan’s economic growth, Lien said. Taiwan’s GDP per capita growth not an overnight phenomenon. Tsai Yu-tai (蔡鈺泰), head of the DGBAS’s Department of Statistics, said the rapid growth in Taiwan’s GDP per capita did not happen within just one or two years. Amid trade tensions between the United States and China in 2018, the government encouraged Taiwanese investors in China to return to Taiwan and relocate their investments in higher-value-added products, including electronics and communications equipment, machinery and metal products, Tsai said. Manufacturers in Taiwan then took advantage of the COVID-19 pandemic and the surge in AI demand to meet global demand, helping boost the country’s income, Tsai added. However, Tsai cautioned that fluctuations in the value of the Taiwan dollar against the U.S. dollar could affect GDP per capita calculations. If the Taiwan dollar depreciates against the U.S. dollar, GDP per capita measured in U.S. dollars will fall, and vice versa, he said. According to Tsai, the GDP per capita for 2027 was estimated based on an exchange of around NT$32.35.

In a "Front Page Authority" podcast conversation, photographer and artist Ron Agam and Baltimore Sun co-owner David Smith discussed creativity, discipline, technology and the human need to create. Agam is the son of Yaacov Agam, a pioneer of kinetic art. Smith, a businessman and entrepreneur, also does photography, woodworking and furniture making. Smith said art is about creation: making something, standing back to admire it, and ideally giving it to someone who likes it. Agam recalled realizing around age 11 or 12 how respected his father was. In Paris, President Georges Pompidou invited Yaacov Agam to the Élysée Palace and asked him to rethink part of the presidential apartments, which became the Salon Agam. Both men were drawn to photography by watching an image appear in a darkroom, Agam at age 6 and Smith at 15. Agam resisted painting, comparing it to a physicist whose father is Einstein, until a serious personal crisis and depression at 52 led him to paint for months without intending to sell anything. Smith built black-and-white and color labs at home, then abandoned film in 2001 after using an early Fuji digital camera in Africa. He said film teaches discipline, forcing thought before the shutter, while digital lets one shoot 8,000 photographs and keep three. Agam is fascinated by faces. His photographs of people at Jerusalem's Western Wall became his first major public photography exhibition in New York, which coincided with Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis's funeral nearby and the death of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, drawing attention to his photographs of Hasidic Jews. Madonna acquired many of them, and she and Mayor Rudy Giuliani contributed to a book of his photography. In November 2008, during the financial collapse, his exhibition of 6-foot flower photographs made devastated visitors smile, which he said shows art's power. Carrying a famous surname made finding his own signature difficult; his three-dimensional lenticular works became his own language. He values movement because, as his father said, change is life's most constant element, and kinetic art makes viewers participants. Agam traced his activism to age 10 in Paris, when a woman shouted an antisemitic slur at him after he won a roller-skating competition. On technology, Smith said everyone can now make images, so the barrier is no longer making something but making something meaningful. Agam described a CNC machine in Carrara, Italy, replicating a Michelangelo sculpture in about a week. On artificial intelligence, Smith said humans still direct and iterate; Agam agreed but was more cautious, warning that an uncontrolled machine could control us and raising questions about employment, medicine, education and thought. Smith concluded that creators of all kinds understand each other. Agam recalled his father asking whether people were coming to his museum, and said art begins in one mind and can affect people for generations.

The Swift space observatory has been in operation since 2004. It specializes in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most energetic electromagnetic explosions known in the universe. Its original mission was supposed to last just two years. More than two decades later, it continues to explore some of the most violent phenomena in the cosmos. Now it is nearing the end of its life. Swift doesn’t have a propulsion system capable of significantly raising its orbit. Although it is hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface, there are still atmospheric particles at that altitude that exert a small but constant drag on the satellite. With each orbit around Earth, it loses a tiny amount of energy and, little by little, altitude as well. If this process continues without intervention it will eventually reenter the atmosphere. NASA knew that Swift had limited time left. Some models had indicated that the observatory could remain in orbit until the 2030s, but increased solar activity during 2024 changed those projections. Energy from the sun heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Estimates eventually placed its likely reentry before the end of 2026. Faced with the rapid deterioration of Swift’s orbit, NASA decided to attempt a rescue maneuver straight out of a movie. The plan was simple in concept but astonishingly complex to execute. A robotic mission would catch up to Swift, capture it with mechanical arms, and use its own thrusters to raise the observatory to a safer orbit, where it could continue operating. To do this, NASA turned to the company Katalyst Space Technologies and its LINK spacecraft. LINK was launched into space on July 3, 2026. However, problems arose soon after. The spacecraft suffered failures in its attitude control system, which is responsible for keeping it properly oriented and stable in space. For weeks, engineers worked to regain control. On Wednesday, NASA canceled the rescue mission. In a statement, agency administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the decision was due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system. LINK will no longer capture Swift or raise its orbit. The spacecraft will continue to approach the observatory to conduct demonstrations of rendezvous, navigation, and close-proximity operations. The agency hopes to use this attempt to gather information that can be applied to future missions aimed at repairing, relocating, or extending the lifespan of satellites in orbit. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said in a press release. The agency had warned from the outset that this was a high-risk mission. Swift was not built to be captured or repaired in orbit, while LINK was developed and launched against the clock in response to the observatory’s rapid descent. “NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” Isaacman noted. Without an intervention to raise its orbit, Swift will continue to lose altitude until it reaches the denser layers of the atmosphere. During reentry, much of the observatory will be destroyed by intense heating and aerodynamic forces. It is still too early to determine exactly when and where this will occur. For now, NASA estimates that Swift will likely reenter the atmosphere before the end of the year. This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

BEIJING (AP) — Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including beating Usain Bolt’s 100-meter sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, the organizer said. The five-day games, now in its second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the U.S. heats up, with 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and soccer. The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week as Beijing held the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. China makes the majority of the world’s humanoid robots. The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from the country. Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations. At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination. At a 100-meter sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid. Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second. Still, experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research — at least for now — and it will still take time to achieve mass real-world deployment. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities. Humanoid robots are “evolving rapidly,” said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. “At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.” “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing,” said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator. Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said that he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer.” This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war. ____. Chan Ho-him reported from Hong Kong. Olivia Zhang and Liu Zheng contributed to this report from Beijing.

When it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) and software-as-a-service (SaaS) stocks, investors have generally taken a cautious approach. Between AI disintermediation, vibe coding, and the potential shift to more consumption-based business models, investors have identified several risks that could impact the industry. However, not all SaaS companies are alike, and it is more likely that software companies will play a critical role in the future of AI. One of the big reasons for this is that they are model-agnostic. If AI models shift in leadership or move more to commoditization, organizations don’t want to be tied to a single model. At the same time, software is often deeply embedded within organizations and has important compliance and security guardrails in place, making this a strong option for AI to be deployed. Against that backdrop, let’s look at three SaaS stocks with big upside from AI. Palantir Technologies. When it comes to benefiting from AI, no SaaS company has been better at it than Palantir Technologies. It has taken its roots as a data-gathering and analytics company for the U.S. government and created one of the most important AI platforms on the planet. In simple terms, its AI platform essentially acts as an AI operating system that significantly decreases potentially harmful AI hallucinations and makes AI more useful to organizations in the real world. The strength of the platform can be seen in the company’s surging revenue growth and remarkable net dollar retention, which came in at 157% in Q2. While the stock is not cheap, Palantir has the potential to grow to become one of the largest companies in the world. AIP can be used to help solve problems across various departments and industries, making its growth runway just enormous. Microsoft. Among megacap tech stocks, Microsoft has been one of the most underappreciated. The company remains the 800-pound gorilla of enterprise software, and its Microsoft 365 suite of productivity tools remains deeply entrenched within enterprises. Big organizations tend to be cautious about new technologies like AI, so they’ve been turning to a trusted leader like Microsoft to help them incorporate AI into their workflows. This is leading to strong adoption of Microsoft’s AI assistant, Copilot, and is helping drive strong growth in its enterprise software segment. This should remain a strong growth driver for the company. At the same time, Microsoft’s cloud computing unit, Azure, has been growing rapidly and has one of the largest backlogs in the space. The company is also just starting to place greater emphasis on developing its own custom AI chips and foundational AI models, which should help improve margins over time. Throw in a 27% stake in OpenAI, and this is a SaaS stock with a lot of potential AI upside. GitLab. Turning to a much smaller SaaS company, GitLab has all the ingredients to see its stock surge higher. The stock is cheap, trading at an attractive price-to-sales multiple of just 5.5 times based on fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) analyst estimates, amid investor concerns about the impact of AI on its DevSecOps (development, security, and operations) platform. However, GitLab looks much more likely to be an AI winner than a loser. AI is driving more software development, not less, and all of it still needs to be done in a secure environment. Meanwhile, commentary from Microsoft, which owns code repository GitHub, and JFrog, which provides software supply chain solutions in the DevSecOps sector, point to strength in the sector. The Porsche 911 GT3, the track-focused variant below the GT3 RS, is quicker on a track than the lighter, mid-engined 718 Cayman GT4 because of power, chassis hardware and aerodynamics. The PDK-equipped GT3 uses a 4.0-liter naturally aspirated flat-six making 502 horsepower and 331 pound-feet of torque, with a curb weight of 3,278 pounds. The Cayman GT4 has a 4.0-liter flat-six with 414 horsepower and 309 pound-feet, at around 3,276 pounds, so the GT3 has 88 more horsepower and 22 more pound-feet. The GT3 also has a double-wishbone front suspension from the 911 RSR race car, while the GT4's 718 platform keeps MacPherson struts at both axles. The GT3 has standard rear-axle steering, which turns the rear wheels opposite the fronts at low speed to sharpen turn-in and in the same direction at higher speeds for stability. Top Gear reports 849 pounds of downforce at 124 mph for the GT3 in its most aggressive setting, thanks to a redesigned front diffuser, spoiler lip, underbody air guides and rear wing. The GT4 makes 268 pounds at top speed with a less aggressive package. The GT3's standard front brakes are 408 millimeters versus 380 for the GT4; both can have the same PCCB carbon ceramics. In acceleration, the GT3 reaches 60 mph in 2.7 to 3.3 seconds and covers the quarter mile in roughly 10.9 to 11.5 seconds. The GT4 takes 3.3 to 4.4 seconds to 60 mph and 11.6 to 11.8 seconds for the quarter mile. At the 12.9-mile Nürburgring, the 992.2 GT3 lapped in 6:56 versus the GT4's best of 7:32; small per-corner advantages in tires and mechanical grip compound over such a long lap. Although the GT4's mid-engine layout helps agility, the GT3's rear-engine placement aids exit from slower corners, and its aerodynamics let it carry more speed and stay stable through mid- and high-speed corners. The Cayman is now discontinued, and the last GT4 is one generation older than the current GT3. The article argues the GT4 is not simply a "poor man's GT3." The 2022 GT3, which the author reviewed and rated 10 out of 10, started at $162,450, while the GT4 launched at $100,550, a gap of about $62,000. Since Porsche ended 718 production in October 2025, used GT4s have traded above their original sticker: Classic.com puts the average sale price at $125,654, and one 2022 car sold for $181,000 in July 2026, nearly double its original MSRP. The GT4 also places its mass between the axles rather than behind the rear wheels, giving a different balance and character unrelated to outright pace, which is why some drivers choose it deliberately rather than as a compromise.

The article argues that Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) remains the gold standard among AI semiconductor stocks and is still a buy, but predicts that Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) can outperform it over the next three years. Nvidia dominates chips for AI model training, since most early foundational AI code was written with its CUDA software platform and optimized for its GPUs, creating a wide moat. It is also a large player in data center networking, which has helped it become a complete AI infrastructure provider offering end-to-end rack-scale solutions. It has built its own custom Arm-based CPUs, which should help as agentic AI drives servers to contain more CPUs. For inference, it has positioned itself through its "acquisition" of Groq and its language processing units (LPUs), which use a small amount of SRAM and are strung together to cut latency. In inference systems, Nvidia will pair GPUs for the compute-heavy pre-fill phase with LPUs for the low-latency decode phase. Its fiscal first-quarter revenue rose 85% to $81.6 billion and adjusted EPS rose 140% to $1.87. The stock trades at a forward P/E of about 24.5 times fiscal 2027 analyst estimates, which the author considers attractive. However, given its size and the law of large numbers, the author expects AMD to do better. AMD is set to be a serious competitor in inference, the faster-growing market and one expected to become much larger. Bloomberg Intelligence projects inference growing at a 32% compound annual rate through 2032 and becoming nearly double the size of the training market, with annual spending of $1.3 billion. Inference is less technically demanding than training, and AMD has improved its ROCm software stack in recent years. Because inference is generally more memory-bound than compute-constrained, AMD's chiplet design, which can be packaged with more memory and works as part of a whole system, reduces latency. AMD made two acquisitions for this market. MEXT optimizes memory by offloading rarely used data from DRAM to underused flash and using predictive AI to move it back before it is needed. Taalas, an inference chip start-up, hardwires AI models directly onto chips, which is less flexible but a cheap, fast inference option. AMD has also partnered with Cerebras on a disaggregated inference system: AMD's Helios handles pre-fill, while Cerebras' ultrafast but expensive solution handles decode. AMD also sees a large opportunity in agentic AI. It is a leader in server CPUs and has been steadily taking share from Intel. As the GPU-to-CPU ratio shifts from 8:1 for training to 1:1 for agentic AI, AMD sees this becoming a $220 billion market in the next few years. As a much smaller company than Nvidia, AMD has room for explosive growth. With big deals in place and revenue growth about to take off, the author concludes the stock can outperform Nvidia over the next three years. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include AMD in its latest list of 10 best stocks to buy. The author, Geoffrey Seiler, holds a position in AMD.

Chinese humanoid robots smash human records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games The five-day games, now in its second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the U.S. heats up, with 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place including running, table tennis and soccer. (AP Video: Olivia Zhang and Liu Zheng) BEIJING (AP) — Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including beating Usain Bolt’s 100-meter sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, the organizer said. The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week as Beijing held the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. China makes the majority of the world’s humanoid robots. The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from the country. Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations. At Saturday’s opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination. At a 100-meter sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Both robots were from Beijing-based X-Humanoid. Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second. Still, experts say humanoid robots are still mostly used for demonstrations, performances and research — at least for now — and it will still take time to achieve mass real-world deployment. Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities. Humanoid robots are “evolving rapidly,” said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident. “At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.” “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing,” said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator. Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said that he was hoping to see “the best robots China currently has to offer.” This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war. ____. Chan Ho-him reported from Hong Kong. Olivia Zhang and Liu Zheng contributed to this report from Beijing.

The Federal Reserve's Jackson Hole symposium and Nvidia's earnings will be the focus of markets in the week ahead, Reuters reported. Investors will sift for clues from these events on whether the artificial intelligence-led stock market rally would be able to sustain itself amid uncertainty over growth and interest rates, according to the news outlet's report. The US Treasury Department's efforts to calm markets provided only a brief relief, with yields rebounding on Thursday. Panasonic Avionics Corporation provides in-flight entertainment and connectivity (IFEC) systems across a large global fleet serving hundreds of airlines and billions of passengers annually. Diagnosing the root cause of passenger-experience issues across thousands of unique deployment configurations required manual correlation of logs, metrics, and ticketing data, which could take hours and demanded deep institutional knowledge. Working with AWS and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, which provided architectural guidance, Panasonic built an agentic AI system using Amazon Bedrock, Amazon SageMaker, and AWS Glue to reduce diagnosis time while maintaining accuracy. The challenge: although Panasonic's AWS-based data lake stores large volumes of fleet operational data, each configuration generates unique log patterns, complicating fleet-wide assessment. Manual correlation extended analysis cycles. Detection relied mainly on ticket generation and manual review, affecting Mean Time to Detect (MTTD), while heavy investigative effort lengthened Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR). Repetitive tasks, the need for deep system familiarity, and engineer time spent on diagnostics reduced bandwidth for innovation and reliability work. The goal was proactive health monitoring and fleet-wide pattern recognition without losing diagnostic rigor. The architecture is a multi-agent workflow with three layers: a Trend Analyzer that identifies anomalies from key performance indicators and degradation metrics; parallel Diagnostic Agents for correlation analysis, system checks, and log pattern matching; and a large language model (LLM) Summarizer that produces diagnostic reports with root cause analysis and recommended actions. It operates in five phases. 1. Ingest and normalize: Raw fleet data is transformed into standardized service metrics and stored in an Amazon S3 lakehouse using Apache Iceberg, via AWS Glue and Amazon EMR. A domain ontology normalizes terminology across fleet variants and links metrics with configuration metadata and ticketing information. 2. Detect: The Trend Analyzer continuously evaluates KPIs, service-level adherence, and degradation, using fleet-wide relationship modeling to find patterns invisible in single deployments, shifting from reactive to proactive detection. 3. Diagnose: Parallel agents investigate simultaneously. The Correlation Analyzer determines whether an issue is isolated or systemic; System Checks validates metadata and service status against ticketing workflows; the Log Analyzer matches logs against known failure modes. Amazon SageMaker orchestrates them using LangGraph, with the Strands Agents SDK providing agent implementation. In internal testing, this cut investigation from hours to minutes. 4. Contextualize: Past incidents and resolutions are stored as vectors in Amazon RDS with pgvector, enabling semantic search for similar patterns even when symptoms differ. 5. Recommend and act: Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock synthesizes findings into structured reports with root cause hypotheses, impact analysis, and prioritized remediation. Critical findings automatically trigger alerts and routing to engineering teams. Recommendations are grounded in retrieved data, validated against deterministic business rules, and supported by evidence; human engineers approve remediation for significant incidents, and decisions remain traceable for auditability. Lessons from reaching production: Panasonic validated accuracy early against ground truth data, exceeding requirements. It designed modular, transparent agents with human-in-the-loop review, allowing independent updates. It limited LLM use to summarization and error reasoning, using tuned parameters for deterministic outputs. The system went live only when automated actions aligned with expert assessment, and it now generates daily diagnostic reports covering the active fleet. Results: manual analysis effort fell significantly, and both MTTD and MTTR improved. In targeted use cases, the system showed 20–40 percent improvements in operational efficiency. Support teams reported reduced repetitive investigative burden, and engineering capacity for independent diagnostics increased. Actual results may vary with data, operational context, and configuration.

Quick Take. - Blockchain Association and CCI sued Illinois over a 0.2% digital asset tax set to begin Jan. 1, 2027. - The levy is based on covered customer digital-asset activity by value, not gains or broker service fees. - Filing the complaint did not pause the law; courts must still decide whether to block enforcement. Illinois’s 0.2% digital asset tax, scheduled to start Jan. 1, 2027, now faces another industry complaint as brokers prepare for a levy tied to the value of customer assets rather than their gains or service fees. Blockchain Association and the Crypto Council for Innovation said they filed the complaint on Aug. 21 in the Circuit Court of the Seventh Judicial Circuit in Sangamon County. The filing came one month after The Digital Chamber announced a separate Sangamon County challenge. The new complaint names Illinois Department of Revenue Director David Harris, Attorney General Kwame Raoul and Sangamon County State’s Attorney John Milhiser in their official capacities. The plaintiffs seek a declaration that the Digital Asset Tax Act is invalid, plus preliminary and permanent injunctions blocking implementation and enforcement. Their seven counts allege preemption under the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act, violations of the Commerce Clause and federal and state due process protections, and breaches of Illinois constitutional rules on tax uniformity, delegation and the legislative process. Those are allegations, not judicial findings. The two complaints have different captions and defendant lineups. Neither group’s public materials report a joint schedule or court order coordinating, joining or consolidating them. The version of the Blockchain Association and CCI complaint posted by the plaintiffs also leaves its case-number field blank. What the January deadline means for brokers. The enacted statute taxes an Illinois customer’s receipt of covered digital asset business activity at 0.2% of the value of the asset involved. A broker making or effectuating the sale must collect the tax. Covered activity includes a single occurrence of exchanging, transferring or storing a digital asset as part of a business or on behalf of a customer who agreed to receive those services. The rule does not make every direct self-custody transfer a broker-collected event; the taxable transaction requires activity supplied by a digital asset broker for valuable consideration. For a remote broker headquartered outside Illinois, the collection nexus applies when gross receipts from covered digital asset business activity sales to Illinois customers reach at least $100,000 over the preceding 12 months. Illinois requires the test quarterly. Once the threshold is met, the broker is treated as maintaining a place of business in the state and must collect, remit and file returns for one year. Registration requirements are addressed separately. If an Illinois customer purchases taxable digital asset business activity and the broker does not charge the tax, the customer must remit it by the 20th day of the following month in the form prescribed by the Department of Revenue. The new plaintiffs have asked for relief that could stop enforcement, but filing the complaint did not itself suspend the Act. Their public materials report no injunction or court timetable. Unless a court enters relief or the law changes, Jan. 1 remains the operative compliance date.

I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans,” she said. “But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look.” “These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing,” said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator. The author argues that using generative AI "slop" to sell cameras makes no sense, citing two companies that published such content over one weekend. The first is Xtra, which posted an AI-generated Instagram video using animals to promote its Muse gimbal camera. The Muse is essentially the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 under different branding, and it is now outdated given the Muse 2 and the Pocket 4. Xtra is also in a dispute with the FCC over whether its gimbal camera is original or really the Pocket 4 in disguise. The author says the commercial undercuts the reason anyone would buy such a camera: to make something real with it. This was not unexpected. Before the launch of the Muse 2 Pro, which has been indefinitely delayed, Xtra supplied a press packet of "sample videos" presumably shot on the camera, and many were clearly AI-made, with no disclosure. The same folder contained more than 20 clips of genuine Muse 2 Pro footage, so the company evidently had real material but padded the gallery with slop. The author says it would be easy and inexpensive to show the real product in a real person's hands. One possible explanation is that sentiment toward generative AI is less negative in Asia, especially China, than in the United States, Canada or Europe. The author notes that DJI did the same thing last month. The second example is more confusing: a Ricoh GR Europe blog post about night photography that appears fully AI-generated. Proof is hard, but the text shows hallmarks of AI copy, there is no byline, and there are no photo credits, which the author finds suspicious since a real person would want credit. Four AI image detectors (DeepAi.org, SightEngine, ZeroGPT and WasItAI) each flagged the images as "likely AI generated" with more than 95% confidence. The author acknowledges these methods are not foolproof. The article's thumbnail also shows a man holding the Ricoh GR to his eye, though that camera has no viewfinder. The author emailed Ricoh contacts for comment but does not expect a reply until Monday, and those contacts are not in the division that published the post. If Ricoh GR Europe can prove the post was not AI, the author says they would retract and apologize. Even so, the question arising at all suggests the marketing team did not do due diligence to avoid its content being mistaken for AI. The author concludes they do not understand why companies selling creative tools would think fake AI visuals will entice buyers. People who buy cameras want to see what the cameras can really do, and a dog lamenting its inability to use a phone or a vapid night-photography guide filled with fake street photos does not sell these products. An update on 8/23 added another AI example from the Ricoh GR Europe article.

The Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger aircraft, has four engines but thrust reversers only on the two inboard engines (numbers 2 and 3). Airbus departed deliberately from the convention of four-engine airliners such as the Boeing 747, after aerodynamic, structural and operational analysis. Reverse thrust is supplementary: airliners rely mainly on wheel brakes, spoilers and anti-skid systems, while reversers reduce brake wear and help on contaminated runways. The main reason is the aircraft's size. With a wingspan of 79.75 meters and a maximum take-off weight of more than 575 tonnes, the A380 fits Code F airport standards, which specify a 60-meter runway width. Many airports were built to Code E standards, with 45-meter runways, and airports such as London Heathrow and Frankfurt spent hundreds of millions of pounds upgrading. Even on compliant runways, engines 1 and 4 sit much closer to the runway edge, sometimes only a few meters from the pavement edge, near grass, gravel or other unpaved surfaces. This raises the risk of foreign object damage (FOD). Debris ingested by high-bypass turbofans can damage fan blades, compressors and the engine core, and objects thrown up by reverse thrust can also strike the wings, landing gear or fuselage. When reversers deploy, blocker doors redirect fan airflow forward, and that airflow spreads across the runway surface and lifts loose material. The closer an engine is to the edge, the more likely it is to disturb unpaved surfaces. Restricting reversers to engines 2 and 3 keeps the strongest reverse airflow over the paved center, lowering engine wear and maintenance issues. There are structural benefits too. A reverser includes actuators, blocker doors, hydraulics, electronic controls, locks, structural reinforcement and nacelle modifications, and each large-engine system weighs roughly 500 kilograms or more. Omitting two saves about one tonne, only 0.17% of maximum take-off weight, but because the outboard engines are farthest from the fuselage, the weight acts through a long lever arm and increases wing bending moments and loads. Less weight also reduces fuel burn over thousands of long-haul flights, and fewer moving parts lowers inspection, maintenance and lifecycle costs. Reverse thrust is also not required to stop safely. Certification rules do not rely on it for dry-runway landing-distance compliance; manufacturers must show an aircraft can stop using wheel brakes, spoilers and tire friction alone, even if all reversers fail to deploy. After touchdown, the A380's spoilers destroy lift and put nearly the full weight on the landing gear, letting the carbon brakes, managed by anti-skid systems, deliver maximum braking. The two inboard reversers act as an added safety margin, helping on wet, snow-covered or contaminated runways, lowering brake temperatures and reducing the risk of aquaplaning. On dry runways, the stopping-distance difference between two reversers and four would be relatively small. Airbus concluded that the extra braking from four reversers would be outweighed by added weight, maintenance demands and greater FOD risk to the outboard engines. This fits a wider design philosophy: for example, mathematical optimization of fuselage panels and other components saved more than 700 kg. Every system was weighed against its benefit, delivering the greatest operational value with the simplest effective solution.

GPUs that power AI computation are expected to become commodities traded on benchmark and futures markets, like crude oil or electricity, and AI service pricing is projected to shift from flat monthly subscriptions to dynamic pricing that moves in real time with supply and demand. According to a BCG report titled "Is AI Compute Power Becoming a Commodity?" published on the 23rd, the global AI compute market will grow from $360 billion last year to about $2.3 trillion by 2030. AI compute covers GPU chips, their usage fees, and tokens billed to end users. The flat-rate era is ending. AI developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI previously charged enterprise customers flat monthly fees and, when servers hit capacity, throttled speeds or blocked usage rather than raising prices. Citing intensifying compute shortages, Anthropic switched in April to usage-based billing: a $20 monthly base fee per seat plus API usage charges. OpenAI moved Codex from flat message-based billing to token-based usage billing. Experts see dynamic pricing as the next stage, similar to wholesale electricity prices. The market is currently opaque. Published and actual transaction prices diverge, most contracts are undisclosed discounts, reservations and enterprise deals, and the same GPU can show price differences of up to 41% on the same day depending on the index used. Volatility is severe: Nvidia H100 hourly rental rates peaked near $8 in early 2024, fell to $1.96 by the end of last year, then rebounded to $2.64 in April. BCG calls for a liquid, transparent market, citing crude oil, where price reporting agencies standardized actual transaction data so Brent and WTI became global benchmarks. However, BCG expects AI compute to resemble efficient regional electricity markets rather than a single global price, because computation must occur where data resides, making cross-regional arbitrage difficult. Transparency could surface what BCG calls "dark value," latent value from supply-demand inefficiencies. BCG estimates full commoditization could unlock up to $140 billion annually: up to $17 billion in AI chips, $34 billion in compute rental, and $46 billion in end-user tokens. Companies that manage costs amid price volatility could gain competitive advantage. Lee Joong-hoon of BCG Korea said South Korea benefits from AI infrastructure demand such as HBM and power equipment but also buys global AI models and compute at high prices, so corporate AI competitiveness will depend on maximizing cost-effectiveness. He advised improving efficiency for general tasks like summarization, investing boldly where AI can redesign work processes, and continuously monitoring models, pricing and quality to avoid vendor lock-in and switch flexibly. Separately, South Korea's stock market shows weak investor sentiment despite rebounds in large semiconductor stocks. The KOSPI's average daily turnover rate from the start of the month through the 21st was 0.56%, the lowest since August last year's 0.50% and less than one-third of March's 1.74% yearly high. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix average daily volumes (24.91 million and 4.69 million shares) fell about 22% and 30% from the prior month. Analyst Kim Hyun-sung of Sangsangin Securities said household funds are shifting from domestic to overseas markets and retail investors feel fatigue after sharp swings, so sentiment will be hard to strengthen for now.

Apple is cutting more than 200 jobs as the tech giant sharpens its focus on AI and updates its Siri digital assistant. Roughly 100 of the eliminated positions are tied to the Vision Pro team. Another 100 hit groups working on Siri and the Intelligent Systems Experience team, the division focused on bringing generative AI features into Apple devices. This software reshuffle comes as Apple eliminates legacy engineering roles to clear room for specialists who can rebuild Siri on an entirely new generative AI architecture. Apple confirmed the cuts, saying it was “looking to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users.” “While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also impact a limited number of existing roles,” the company said. Siri has lagged behind OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Gemini for years, particularly when it comes to remembering what users were talking about and handling follow-up questions naturally. Siri has historically responded with a basic web link instead of actually answering the question. The company’s revamped “Siri AI” in the public beta of iOS 18 has narrowed the functional gap by focusing on integration across its ecosystem. Meanwhile, Vision Pro has become one of Apple’s biggest commercial disappointments. The headset features industry-leading micro-OLED displays and precise eye-tracking, but consumers haven’t embraced it. Apple never released official sales figures, but estimated global sales fell to just 45,000 units in the final quarter of 2025. In response, Apple is trimming its Vision Pro operations while shifting resources toward newer AI efforts and devices. The company is also dealing with higher production costs as an AI-driven memory shortage pushes up expenses. Apple raised prices on its Macs and iPads earlier this summer and recently introduced a leasing plan covering its major hardware products as it looks to bring in more customers while offsetting those costs.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-PA), one of the more centrist Democrats on Capitol Hill, took to social media on Saturday to underscore his stance on data centers after Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA) signed an executive order restricting their development in Pennsylvania on Tuesday. “AI supremacy and energy dominance underpins our national security,” Fetterman said on X in reaction to an article about the artificial intelligence race between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party. “China continues to fuel and benefit from our overreaction. I reject the political pandering and hyperbole over data centers or AI doomsdaying.” Debates about data center construction have intensified in recent weeks and months, prompting lawmakers to publicly clarify or alter their positions on the controversial infrastructure used to power artificial intelligence models. Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX) called for an audit of new developments on Aug. 3rd after Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-NY) signed the first one-year, statewide moratorium on data center development in July. Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers also told Detroit News this week he supports a one-year data center moratorium, while Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-WI), the Republican nominee for governor in Wisconsin, has called his opponent David Crowley “Data Center David Crowley.” Fetterman has consistently pushed back against such data center and broader AI doomerism throughout the summer, as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have been forced to take a policy position on an issue that’s both new and subject to shifting public opinion. He said “China wins” in reaction to Hochul’s announcement, and “this must not happen” after Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) sent a letter to CEOs of AI companies calling for a pause in further industry development. “America must lead in the development of AI, otherwise we live under China’s rules,” he said in reaction to Sanders’ policy proposal, who introduced a bill alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) in March that would enact a data center moratorium “until Congress passes comprehensive AI legislation that ensures the safety and prosperity of the American people.” JOSH SHAPIRO SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDER RESTRICTING DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT IN PENNSYLVANIA. President Donald Trump defended data center construction on Friday, citing local job creation and tax benefits. “If you pick the right location, and it’s going to be not every location is perfect for it, but if you pick the right location, what it means for a community is jobs and lots of money and lower taxes,” he said. Trump also touted his ratepayer protection pledge while speaking to reporters, which requires that major technology companies that build data centers will “build, bring, or buy all of the energy needed for building and operating data centers” to “protect American consumers from price hikes due to data center energy and infrastructure requirements.”

Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg released a 6,500-word manifesto detailing how the company will make agentic artificial intelligence (AI) a mainstream resource. “Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about,” Zuckerberg said in his open letter. Superintelligence can revolutionize industries and give consumers access to more valuable tools, but what about investors? Here’s how the company’s efforts to double down on its AI buildout will affect shareholders. Superintelligence can diversify Meta Platforms’ revenue. It’s no secret that Meta Platforms makes almost all of its revenue from online advertising. It represented 97.6% of total revenue in the second quarter, with “Other revenue” and Reality Labs making up the remaining sliver. Meta Platforms has been trying to diversify beyond online advertising for several years. Other tech rivals like Amazon and Alphabet have diversified into multiple industries, with online advertising still playing a key role. Meta Platforms fumbled with the metaverse, and subscription revenue hasn’t been moving the needle much. AI agents can initiate the revenue diversification Meta Platforms has been seeking for years. A push into neocloud services, which Zuckerberg floated earlier this year, can also aid the company in unlocking new income streams. This development can make the company less reliant on advertising, which is still a fast-growing segment. The stock only trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 20, which is a low valuation just for the online advertising component. Any meaningful commercial progress with the superintelligence buildout can trigger a big rally, especially if online advertising revenue growth rates remain elevated. Meta Platforms is still losing a lot of money on AI. Meta Platforms is still doing fine. Revenue jumped by 28% year over year in the second quarter. Operating income dipped by 8% year over year, but it may be a small price to pay if diversification efforts pay off. “If” is the big problem here. The Metaverse debacle was a few years ago, but high capital expenditures without the payoff can bring that memory back. Reality Labs produced a $4.6 billion operating loss in the second quarter, while online advertising operating income slightly decreased year-over-year. Although Meta Platforms doesn’t face many competitors in the AI landscape, a few hyperscalers can quickly secure a large portion of the market. For instance, Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet control more than 60% of the cloud computing market. Oracle, the fourth-largest cloud provider, only has a 4% market share. A similar setup with AI agents that doesn’t include Meta Platforms at or near the top can make it harder to justify increased spending. Big investments in AI are necessary for the company to keep up with other tech leaders and finally diversify beyond online advertising. Meta Platforms is correctly acting upon this opportunity, but it must translate this spending into commercial success while pivoting back to positive operating income growth rates to reignite the stock.

The article compares Quantum Computing and Red Cat, two high-growth, unprofitable technology companies, to decide which better suits an investor seeking next-generation innovation. Quantum Computing makes integrated photonics and quantum optics products, including thin-film lithium niobate chips, for markets such as cybersecurity and aerospace. Government contracts accounted for roughly 70% to 80% of revenue as of mid-2026, a customer concentration that adds risk. For the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue was $682,000, up 82.8% year over year, with a net loss of $18.7 million, an improvement on the prior period. As of December 2025, its debt-to-equity ratio was zero and its current ratio was 102.4x, but free cash flow was negative $37 million. Its risks include long-term financial viability, a continuous need for capital to fund quantum computer research, execution risk in scaling chip fabrication where defects could hurt competitiveness, and competition from giants such as IBM. Red Cat provides tactical drone and robotic solutions for defense and national security, with a focus on government projects such as the U.S. Army's Short Range Reconnaissance program. In fiscal 2025, revenue was $40.7 million, up 459.8%, with a net loss of $72.1 million and a net margin of -177%. Its debt-to-equity ratio was 0.1x and its current ratio 15.3x, but free cash flow was negative $95.8 million. Its risks include heavy dependence on U.S. government defense contracts, exposing it to budget cycles and policy changes; regulatory burdens such as FAA flight rules and Department of Defense cybersecurity requirements; and reliance on third-party suppliers for critical components, which could cause delays if supply chains are disrupted. On valuation, Red Cat has a significantly lower price-to-sales ratio, suggesting it is more reasonably priced. Neither has a forward P/E, since neither is expected to be profitable soon. The author notes both firms post strong sales growth but have not reached profitability, common among fast-growing tech companies; the question is whether they can sustain rapid expansion. Quantum Computing operates in a nascent field without widespread commercial adoption, making revenue unpredictable, as one large sale can swing income. It earned $5.6 million in the second quarter versus $61,000 a year earlier. Red Cat's military drone focus is paying off amid rising defense spending: second-quarter sales were $20.2 million, up 527% year over year, and it forecast 2026 full-year revenue of $150 million to $180 million, far above 2025's $40.7 million. The author would buy Red Cat, citing its strong sales in a sector rapidly adopting military drones. Quantum Computing's technology remains early in commercial adoption, making it hard to know whether the stock will pay off long term.

Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100-meter sprint world record in humanoid bot games. A humanoid robot has beaten Usain Bolt's 100-meter sprint record at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, China on Saturday. The robot, made by Beijing-based X-Humanoid, was able to run the 109 yards in 9.39 seconds, beating the 2009 record of 9.58 seconds set by the Jamaican athlete. At the end of the 100-meter dash, the robots slammed into a cushion and fell to the ground in order to stop, footage from the event showed, before being carried out in stretchers. A separate robot made by the same company was able to beat the human record in the standing high jump. The humanoid reached 2.88 meters, surpassing the 2.45 meters set by Cuba's Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Other robots were not so successful, with some tripping, falling and smashing into pieces during competitions or even catching fire. Both records were set on the opening day of the Olympics-like event which sees more than 2,000 humanoid robots participating, according to the organizers. The event is in its second year and aims to demonstrate China's rapid progress in the development of advanced robotics, with competitions in sports such as running, table tennis and soccer. At Saturday's opening of the robot games, the organizer and robot makers said that Chinese humanoid robots defeated human world records, as hundreds of humanoid robots marched in formation onto the field in a massive display of synchronized coordination. Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots. The FCC cited national security reasons in a move that targeted China. The Pentagon recently also added Unitree, one of China's leading humanoid robot makers, to its list of companies that it deemed have ties with the Chinese military. Beijing has hit back at the accusations. China currently leads in the production of humanoid robots, with some manufacturers there saying they have thousands of orders from both government and private businesses. However, some experts say this technology is still mostly used for demonstrations and performances and will take some time to achieve mass real-world deployment.

Archer Aviation Inc. (ACHR), an electric aircraft developer focused on urban air mobility, disclosed a notable insider sale after Chief Strategy Officer Eric Lentell sold 100,000 shares on August 20 for $6.31 each, bringing in about $631,000. Fitting such a mechanism into a smartphone requires far more engineering tolerance than a fixed aperture, since it must stay aligned through temperature changes, drops and repeated use within a module no thicker than the current camera bump. The article suggests Apple's work on the iPhone Air's camera module shows it is capable of this. Industry experts expect a renewed focus on product surprise and artificial intelligence strategy.

The $3,200 LiDAR-based Dreame A3 AWD Pro, tested for about a week in its middle 3500 model (rated for more than three-quarters of an acre), is a capable but compromised robot mower. Its navigation needs no satellite signal, and its all-wheel drive handles lumpy yards and steep inclines. But it is more prone to carving bald spots and wheel ruts than the cheaper Segway Navimow X430, and unless you have a very big lawn, its price is hard to justify. Because it doesn't depend on satellites, setup is easier than with competitors like the X430: the dock can go anywhere, and no RTK beacon is needed. Automatic mapping worked better than on other mowers, covering the biggest open space in the reviewer's cluttered backyard; the rest had to be mapped manually. Early Bluetooth problems made manual driving lurchy, though the connection later stabilized to about 20 feet. The Dreame Home app shows an overhead map and a 3D point-cloud view of the yard. Navigation was about as good as the X430's. The A3 runs over slightly taller plants the Segway avoids, which meant mowing over daylilies and getting snagged on the same wire garden fence that troubled the X430, but adjusting map boundaries fixed the problem spots, even at night. Grass-trimming was excellent: after two or three passes, most of the lawn had an even trim. The mower is designed to mulch short grass, not cut overgrown yards, and a string trimmer is still needed for edges. Battery was never an issue; on roughly 2,400 square feet it had about 65% charge left. It was more cautious than the X430 around obstacles, leaving a strip beside raised garden beds unmowed, yet it reached a backyard corner the X430 couldn't and fit through a tight gate. Its tank-like turning and low center of gravity let it climb a short, steep hill easily. However, turning on uneven ground pushed its rear wheels sideways and left ruts, and repeated 360-degree spins at its dock created a bald patch, likely worsened by a rainy week of frequent runs. Extra features include a security patrol mode that detects people and announces, "You are in a robot-guarded area; please proceed with caution," plus live video, photos, and patrol routes. Captured images are encrypted and stored on a German cloud server for 30 days, and Dreame says it cannot access them. The mower can mow shapes like hearts or stars, but the checkerboard pattern feature didn't work, and Dreame is still looking into it. Dreame offers a 30-day return policy. Owners of small yards should skip it: the Roborock RockNeo Q110H or an on-sale Segway Navimow i2 LiDAR cost almost $2,000 less and mow almost as well on flatter lawns. Steep lawns might suit the non-Pro Dreame A3 AWD models, from $2,000, which are more compact with a range of at least a quarter of an acre. For a very large lawn, the A3 AWD Pro 3500 is a last resort if the X430 can't keep a satellite connection; the X430 is $700 cheaper, less likely to create bald patches, and covers more ground (a full acre in 15 hours versus 0.87 acres). Dreame often discounts heavily, and the 3500 was already $2,700.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second. After smashing into the wall, the robots were placed on a stretcher, unlike Bolt, who was able to jog a lap to celebrate human achievement in 2009. ROBOTS BEAT HUMANS IN HALF MARATHON. The World Humanoid Robot Games, in its second year, features more than 2,000 robots in 51 events and 1,000 competitions like running, table tennis and soccer. The five-day event highlights China's rapid progress in robotics amid a heated tech race with the U.S. The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week Beijing was holding the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war. "I welcome these Executive Branch national security determinations, and I am pleased that the FCC has now added foreign produced advanced robotics and power inverters to the FCC’s Covered List," FCC Chair Brendan Carr wrote in a statement last month. Anthropic is adding watermarks to text generated by its AI so that writing produced by AI can be identified. The update is not driven by market demand or innovation but by the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, whose strict rules prohibit various conduct and impose many new requirements on AI deemed high-risk. The rules for "high-risk" AI went into effect this month. Prohibited AI uses include "deploying subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques to distort behavior and impair informed decision-making, causing significant harm," and inferring emotions in workplaces or educational institutions, except for medical or safety reasons. The most severe penalties are fines of up to 7% of global revenue. The law is sure to make the EU a tougher place for American AI companies to do business, but its impact will be global: Anthropic is rolling out watermarks in all countries, noting the change relates to the law's transparency requirements. Anthropic is adopting a method developed and already used by Google. It works through how the AI model chooses specific words and word fragments. Anthropic has a key involving two lists of words, and the generated text must include enough words from one list to be statistically significant. The method has limitations: it does not work well on shorter passages and reveals only the "likelihood" of AI authorship. According to Anthropic, because the watermark is part of the text, it travels with the text when copied and pasted and may persist through some editing. It will be applied at the model level, so it will be present regardless of which Claude product or surface produces the text. If it works well, readers should not notice it, and it does not change the meaning, quality or readability of Claude's responses. Theoretically, watermarks could help identify AI-generated text anywhere. However, the move is likely to raise concerns about Anthropic's power over users' text output and what it means for intellectual property. Anthropic's adoption of watermarks is expected to ignite more pushback from the Trump administration, which worries about thwarting tech innovation and harming U.S. tech giants. President Trump said last month that the administration will conduct a formal review to retaliate against the EU's "discriminatory" digital practices, stemming from another EU digital law that has led to huge fines against U.S. tech giants. The growing backlash will also focus more attention on Google's use of text watermarks for its AI model Gemini. As the EU's AI Act gradually comes into full force and American AI giants work to comply, the U.S. relationship with Europe is only set to become more tense.

In brief. - ACE Robotics Chairman Wang Xiaogang predicts embodied AI could reach its “ChatGPT moment” by the end of 2027. - A shortage of real-world training data remains a major obstacle, with ACE aiming to collect tens of millions of hours within two years. - The Chinese startup plans to deploy its technology in 1,000 stores over the next year and eventually pursue an IPO. Humanoid robots can walk, dance, and box, but getting them to perform useful work in the unpredictable physical world reliably remains one of artificial intelligence’s biggest challenges. ACE Robotics Chairman Wang Xiaogang believes advances in AI models and real-world training data could soon give robots the intelligence needed to move beyond demonstrations and into commercial use, according to a report by Reuters. “We expect to reach the ‘ChatGPT moment’ for embodied intelligence by the end of next year, driven by world models and environmental data capture,” Wang told Reuters. Founded in July 2025, ACE Robotics is a Chinese startup developing AI models for humanoid robots. Backed by Ant Group and SenseTime, it raised more than $100 million in the first half of 2026 and, according to Reuters, plans to pursue an IPO “as early as permitted.” While large language models such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek have spread rapidly, robots still struggle to perform a wide range of tasks in unfamiliar environments, and a lack of training data remains a major obstacle. Embodied AI enables robots and other physical agents to perceive their environment, reason about it, and convert decisions into actions through sensors and actuators. At the same time, world models help AI understand how the physical world works by learning how objects and environments behave. For robots, that means anticipating what might happen when they move, pick something up, or interact with their surroundings before taking an action. “Over the past few years, the entire industry has accumulated data of roughly 100,000 hours, which is far from enough to train embodied foundation models,” Wang said. Researchers elsewhere are experimenting with similar approaches. In October, researchers unveiled HumanoidExo, a wearable exoskeleton that captures human movements to train humanoid robots. Other companies are developing their own AI models for robots. In January, Boston Dynamics unveiled the production version of its Atlas humanoid, saying advances in AI helped bring the robot closer to commercial deployment. In June, Alibaba introduced its Qwen-Robot Suite, a set of AI models designed to help robots navigate, perform physical tasks, and simulate real-world environments.

China’s humanoid robots have shown they can run quicker than the fastest humans. Now comes the real test: Can they also handle packaging and warehouse operations while reliably performing precision tasks like connecting cables designed to evaluate their ability to work like humans in less flashy jobs? The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games, which began Saturday in Beijing, combine events modeled on human sports with those designed to test the robots in simulated factories, restaurants and offices and in emergency situations. The games, heavily promoted in Chinese state media, feature 51 events, including 30 sports competitions and 21 scenario-based contests. More than 40% require robots to operate fully autonomously, according to Huawei, a tech partner of the games. On Saturday, two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt’s 9.58-second world record in the 100-meter sprint. That was a sharp improvement from 2025, when the winning robot’s time was more than 20 seconds. Braking was an issue, as the machines slammed into a thick mat that organizers placed several feet after the finish line. Humanoid robot beats Usain Bolt's 100-meter record. Another humanoid, the same model as the 100-meter champion, ran 400 meters in 39.7 seconds, faster than South African Wayde van Niekerk’s world record of 43.03 seconds. “The intensity is higher than last year, which places significant demands on the robot’s battery management and thermal dissipation capabilities,” said spectator and robotics investor Xu Qiaosheng. “It holds huge significance for the development of China’s industrial sector.” Robots will compete in tug-of-war and weightlifting, while tai chi and pitch-pot — in which contestants throw arrow-like sticks into a narrow-necked vase — will give traditional Chinese sports a futuristic twist. Beyond the spectacle, the more revealing tests could come when robots encounter the small imperfections of the physical world: a cable at the wrong angle, an object just out of reach, a shifting package or a missed step. That tests whether robots can identify objects, accurately position their hands and bodies, apply controlled force and recover from errors without human intervention. Lumos Robotics Chief Executive Yu Chao said the games could help improve hardware and provide a showcase for the industry. But Yu said the longer-term value will depend on real-world problem solving. “Only when it can work in those end scenarios does it have real value,” Yu said. “Simply running and jumping does not improve efficiency.” In addition to more familiar events drawn from human sports, robots will compete in EV charging, restaurant work, emergency incident handling and hand-dexterity contests. There are also industrial assembly and material loading events. A cable connection challenge is a test of vision, mechanical alignment and force control. Beijing-based robotics startup Galbot said it would stage an autonomous humanoid tennis match, with robots attempting singles and doubles play, including ball tracking, serving and returning shots. For Hua Rong, chief marketing officer at robotics firm Zeroth, the real test will come after the demonstrations end. “The competition will be whether, after the product is sold, it can really solve users’ problems,” she said.

Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Education Secretary Linda McMahon discussed the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the K-12 classroom. After citing examples where AI has shown success, including the Alpha School in Austin, TX, CNN host Dana Bash asked whether parents should be able to decide whether their children are taught by AI. According to McMahon, parents should have the option to choose something different. “[T]hat’s what going to be one of my questions — which is, do you believe parents should be able to opt out of using AI as a teaching tool if they so choose?” Bash asked. McMahon replied, “I certainly think that parents should be very much involved in their children’s education. If they’re going and they’re involved and they are looking to see what is happening with their child, I think it’s up to the school to be able to show, OK, this is what we hope to accomplish, this is how we believe this is going to be helpful to your child in particular, and let us show you the outcome.” “And if the parent is not seeing that outcome, the parent has every right to go in and say, ‘No, I want something different for my child,'” she added.
