Humanoid robots have beaten Usain Bolt's 100-meter dash record. And they looked absolutely ridiculous doing it. Usain Bolt's 2009 world record for the 100-meter dash still remains unbroken at 9.58 seconds, but only if we're talking about humans. During the second annual World Humanoid Robot Games that kicked off in Beijing on Saturday, the Tiangong Ultra humanoid robot completed the 100-meter dash in 9.39 seconds during a preliminary heat. Developed by Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, the record-holding robot overtook Honor's Lightning robot, which completed the sprint in 9.47 seconds. Despite the impressive finish times, don't expect these humanoid robots to be used for any commercial purposes yet. After their sprints, they slammed directly into pads and some even required human assistance to be stretchered off the course. However, it's still a major improvement from last year's inaugural World Humanoid Robot Games, where the Tiangong Ultra won the 100-meter dash in 21.5 seconds. Aside from this Robot Olympics event, Beijing hosted a half-marathon for Chinese companies to show off the capabilities of their humanoid robots. The event had its fair share of crashes too, but Honor's Lightning robot managed to secure the gold medal with a finish time of 50 minutes and 26 seconds, which also surpassed another human record. The World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing kicked off August 22 and will run until the 26, hosting thousands of robot participants competing in more than just track and field events, including soccer, table tennis and boxing.

Alibaba launches $10B Hong Kong share placement to fund AI spending. China’s Alibaba on Sunday launched a HK$80-billion ($10.2 billion) share placement to fund artificial intelligence-related development. A deal by the Chinese e-commerce and cloud computing giant would mark the largest-ever primary follow-on offering by a Hong Kong-listed company. It would rank as the world’s third-largest primary follow-on share sale this year after offerings from Alphabet and Intel. The company said it intends to use 100% of the net proceeds from the placement to invest in its “full stack” AI capabilities, a category that includes chips, infrastructure and the development and deployment of AI models. A term sheet reviewed by Reuters showed Alibaba planned to sell 710 million ordinary shares at HK$112.70 a share. That represented a 3.6% discount to its most recent closing price. In its announcement for the $10.2 billion share placement, Alibaba did not disclose additional details on its investment plans by category of its planned AI-related investment. It did not comment beyond its regulatory disclosure. Last week, Alibaba reported its results for the April-to-June quarter, saying it had already spent nearly half of its three-year capex investment plan. It said its expected payback on AI-related investments was on track to fall to 2.5 years from three years, driven by surging demand. Alibaba’s net profit for the quarter fell 75% from a year earlier as it ramped up its AI-related capital expenditures. “In order to be able to capture that future growth, we first need to make these capex investments to build out the necessary compute capacity,” CEO Eddie Wu said on an earnings call. The company’s share offering has been met with strong demand from investors, including sovereign wealth funds, two people familiar with the deal told Reuters. They could not be named because the information was not public. Alibaba increased the size of the offering after the deal was oversubscribed, the people familiar with the matter said. Morgan Stanley, HSBC, UBS and CICC are serving as joint bookrunners of the Alibaba offering, said one of the sources and a third person with knowledge of the matter. The banks did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The share placement was not registered under US securities laws as an offshore transaction, meaning American investors were not eligible to participate, Alibaba said. Since 2022, the global AI boom has fueled staggering capital outlays on infrastructure and data centers, including in the U.S. and China. The four major U.S. hyperscalers – Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta – together are expected to spend roughly $725 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, much of it tied to AI data centers, chips and cloud infrastructure.

While Spider-Man: Brand New Day stays in theaters, it’s now in the crossfire of allegations of generative AI use. The film’s art book recently released, and fans online saw a page featuring New York concept art. Taxis and buildings colliding into each other prompted the allegations of AI use amidst a general confusion of why you’d need the tech to sketch out New York. Most users online deemed this a disappointing bit of news similar to the situation with Supergirl. But for others, this wasn’t as open and shut as it seemed. Publisher of the 'SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY' concept art book comes out, explaining in detail which process they used for this specific art, having used the cloning tool and photobashing, admitting it was just laziness but no AI usage. The company also has an anti-AI policies. pic.twitter.com/NMW3KgyxCQ. — That COMICBOOK Guy (@Culture3ase) August 21, 2026. A Reddit user by the name StingRe claimed to have done the layout and design for the Spider-Man: Brand New Day art book. They alleged, to the extent of their knowledge, there was “no AI art in [the book],” and that they received assets from the Brand New Day visual development team. While told that freelancers had used AI to populate backgrounds in their individual assets, StingRe noted (in now-deleted comments) that “any art flashed for AI use was either not provided to me for [the book’s] layout, or was removed.” To boost their statement, they stated Marvel Studios’ longtime visual development head Ryan Meinerding was “very strict” about checking every page for AI. By StingRe’s admission, something could’ve slipped through the cracks. However, they countered a thought that others have had, which is that Adobe Photoshop’s fill-in tool is why the art looks as it does. They speculated the tool, which has been part of Photoshop for over 15 years, resulted in the “wonky taxi”: a watermark might’ve existed between two taxis, and when removed, the fill-in pulled in the closest pixels to close up that dead space. Ultimately, they concluded their explanation stating what happened was “on the artist,” and revealed Disney and Marvel weren’t looking to publish anything made with genAI. “You don’t legally own anything made by AI, and contracts stipulate it must be ‘your wholly original work,'” they explained. “Anyone taking shortcuts in their art, here or otherwise, is making that decision personally. It isn’t a mandate from the company.” At time of writing, Meinerding and Disney don’t appear to have spoken on the matter. io9 reached out to Meinerding, and will update when a response is given. CNET's robot vacuum tester argues that humanoid home robots are far from ready, despite slick demo videos and preorders. Robot vacuums have improved enormously since early models, with lidar, object-recognition AI, mopping and self-emptying. Humanoids, however, remain early prototypes and "humanoid theater." Neo from 1X Technologies is a bipedal robot with a fabric-covered body, available for preorder at $20,000 or $499 per month with a $200 deposit, with shipping promised this year, though it will likely rely heavily on remote human operation. Weave Robotics' Isaac 1, a wheeled laundry-folding robot with two grippers, costs $7,999 or $449 per month and will deliver in California this fall, with broader US availability in 2027. Hello Robot's wheeled Stretch 4, aimed at elder care, costs $29,950 and is in over 300 facilities. Unitree G1, Apptronik's Apollo 2 and Boston Dynamics' Atlas target research and industry. The core challenge is combining physical dexterity with general intelligence. Vacuums need little machine learning, but varied household tasks require world models that predict how objects and people move. MIT professor emeritus Rodney Brooks, an iRobot co-founder, calls the humanoid idea "total fantasy." Safety is a major concern: humanoids weigh 30 to 60 kilograms, and a falling or failing robot, or one carrying boiling water, has no industry-wide graceful-failure standard. Privacy is another: mobile robots with cameras roam intimate spaces, and many rely on remote human teleoperators. Companies cite mitigations such as Isaac 1's camera shutters. Homes are unstandardized, cluttered and full of dust, pet hair and moisture, which threaten sensors and processors. Boston Dynamics starts with industrial use, where tasks are repetitive and structured. Proponents like 1X argue the world is built for humans, but hardware hurdles include micro-servos for hands, durable lightweight joints and battery life. Demos are slow; Switchbot's Onero H1 took two minutes to load three garments. Dedicated appliances like dishwashers do chores better. Five-fingered hands ease skill transfer and fit homes but cost more and are less durable than grippers; wheels are safer, simpler and cheaper than legs, though legs may eventually be needed for stairs and cluttered spaces. Physical AI lacks generalization, as a Stevens Institute robot failed when a half-full water bottle changed its center of gravity. Training needs huge real-world datasets, such as the million or two million hours customers request, plus annotation. Nvidia, Innodata and Apptronik (with Google DeepMind) are collecting data, while 1X uses world models and simulation. Costs are unclear: Onix's Nicholas Nadeau says only $50,000 to $100,000 prices are credible, and repair expertise is scarce. Andrew Kang of Robostrategy expects tens of millions of home robots perhaps by 2030, and a ban on importing new robot models adds uncertainty. Leasing could shift hardware risk to makers. Commercial spaces will come first. Timeline estimates range from five to ten years to 20 to 25 years; Innodata's Franklin Tanner projects multifunctional assistants in 5 to 10 years and fully autonomous humanoids after 20-plus. Brooks calls home humanoids a "mass hallucination." The author concludes you won't be unboxing a humanoid at home soon.

In 2014, Stephen Hawking warned, "The development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race." I build automated systems, and artificial intelligence is a great and awesome tool. I am able to efficiently complete boring repetitive tasks, devoting my time to more worthwhile causes and endeavors. Yet I look on with trepidation as colleagues are fully replaced without any thought to the downstream effects or the inevitable brain drain that leads to societal decline. As humans often do, we give our new tools too much credit. There is no single secret weapon or cure-all to societal ills. Poverty, hunger, environmental threats, illness and economic insecurity have existed since the beginning of time. Underneath those heavy hitters are the undertones of greed and jealousy, pride and wrath, envy and apathy. Yet, my fellow humans, we find ourselves running at full speed, ramrod, into a societal shift infested by moral and economic decay, a polarized populace and a degraded and scarce pool of clean air, pure water and healthful food. So the underlying question is why artificial intelligence is now the answer to save our human society. Humans are an interesting group of animals. We love to anthropomorphize and will do it with anything. Just as we give human names to our major weather events, we speak fondly to or yell at our AI assistants: Alexa, Siri or Gemini. Worse, businesses expect these assistants to replace people, as anyone who has had the pleasure of requesting a customer service representative can attest. This is where it gets dangerous. Irrationally, rational people believe AI can replace people. Large businesses have bet a great deal of money on this. Poor people are very worried that large businesses will win that bet. People are wrong — AI cannot replace people — yet people are acting on this irrational premise, and the people will suffer in the end. AI is logical — following a prescribed code initiated by a human being that boils down to a dichotomy of 0’s and 1’s. Humans are not logical beings. They play the lotto, even though it is 19,000 times more likely that they are struck by lightning than that they win, and it is equally likely that they are struck by lightning more than 200 times on separate occasions than winning the lotto. AI mimics based on prescribed logic. AI merely leverages stored data in a finite vacuum. Humans create art from lived experiences that are infinite. The part can never be the whole. The created can never replace the creator. Yet people insist that AI will replace people. They fear this, and they revel in this. For this reason, people will be the creator of their own demise. Indeed, this illogical thinking will expedite our demise. Goldman Sachs suggests about 11 million workers face job displacement related to AI. This is real long-term income scarring and structural unemployment that don’t just affect the worker who lost the job. Let’s look at the possibilities of a single worker displaced from a job that supported a family of four. That one displaced worker faces a higher incidence of divorce, mental and physical illness, violence and suicide. Community costs include higher taxes, higher crime and fewer resources to support a healthy and safe environment for all citizens. And let’s not forget the elephant in the room. Those workers displaced by AI were also customers. So even the business loses. There goes the business owner’s grand bet. And the result will be lower population rates and fewer people that feed data farms, AI feedback loops that diagnose healthy people with terminal illness and scarcity of artisans who operate outside of the AI crutch. What then, when there are fewer people, lost knowledge, when the resources are tapped and human survivors function in an idiocracy? With no one to pull precious data from, where will our skilled artisans and ancestral wisdom be — buried in a grave? So, my fellow humans, be very wary, lest the mighty human race goes the way of the mighty dinosaur. Instead, let AI be simply a tool that allows us to be more human. Nicole Freeman is a Columbia resident who builds automated systems and uses AI as an efficiency tool.

U.S. federal debt is approaching $40 trillion, with annual deficits adding about two trillion dollars a year. Interest on the debt now exceeds defense spending, something not seen for decades. Many politicians and investors hope AI will raise productivity, profits and tax revenue enough to shrink debt relative to GDP, but this hypothesis is more uncertain than it appears. After the 2008-2009 financial crises, policymakers widely assumed interest rates would stay extremely low, treating rising debt as relatively harmless. History shows rates swing both ways, and they have returned to levels closer to historical averages. Fiscal research centers warn that in coming years the average interest rate on government debt may exceed the economy's growth rate. When that happens, even a stable primary deficit drives debt steadily upward, and lenders demand higher yields. No party shows substantial political will to cut deficits, making an external fix like AI attractive. The case for AI is not baseless. Faster productivity could raise corporate profits and national income, broadening the tax base. AI infrastructure investment is visible across the economy, and some documented gains exist, such as double-digit increases in cases resolved per hour in some customer service settings, with the largest benefit for less experienced workers. But isolating AI's impact is difficult. U.S. labor productivity has accelerated recently, yet much of this appears tied to cost restructuring and correcting earlier overstaffing, and no figure can confidently separate AI's share from return-to-office effects, an aging workforce or cyclical recovery. Even real growth would not automatically solve the debt problem. AI income tends to flow disproportionately to capital and corporate profits rather than wages. Capital is more mobile and harder to tax, and a study on AI-driven fiscal erosion identifies the shift from labor to capital as a central mechanism of revenue loss even when productivity improves. The labor share of global income has been declining for two decades. Silicon Valley's projections of three to four percentage points of extra annual productivity may be too optimistic; more conservative economists estimate one to two points, partly offset by aging, deglobalization, populism and implementation risks. Faster growth and AI's heavy demand for capital could also push interest rates up, raising the government's interest bill alongside growth, as a sharp rise in long-term bond yields squeezing AI-linked stocks already hints. Past technologies like electricity and the internet eventually broadened the tax base, but they took decades to translate into broad employment and wage growth, while the fiscal problem must be addressed sooner. The current tax system also relies more heavily on payroll taxes, making it especially vulnerable to income shifting toward capital. A final risk is political: anticipated AI abundance may encourage tax cuts, expanded benefits, higher defense spending, or universal basic income before revenues materialize, and new spending can absorb any extra revenue. High debt, elevated rates, political paralysis and an external shock such as war, cyber conflict or disaster could trigger a debt crisis. AI may make the U.S. richer but cannot correct the tendency to spend more than the state collects. Revenue forecasts based on AI benefits need realistic margins of error, and spending commitments should be judged regardless of whether the technology delivers. The editorial concludes that AI growth is no substitute for fiscal discipline. AI can widen the cake but cannot force the political system to distribute the public sector's share. Stabilizing debt remains a political responsibility, requiring action on taxes and spending now rather than under crisis pressure.

Private equity firms have reportedly begun placing artificial intelligence experts within their portfolio companies to grow those businesses. That’s according to a report Friday (Aug. 21) from The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), which cites the example of Wall Street firms like Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman’s $1.5 billion partnership with Anthropic to form an approximately 160-person team of AI experts. “What we liked was this was a senior engineering team,” said Rodney Zemmel, who heads Blackstone’s operating team. “It’s not like a bunch of kids who just learned AI.” The plan is to offer the services of the joint venture, a stand-alone company known as Ode, well beyond the world of private-equity-owned businesses. Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Anthropic have each pledged to invest around $300 million to the effort. OpenAI has launched a rival venture that would offer consulting services to companies, with a $4 billion investment headed by private-equity firm TPG. As WSJ noted, these efforts are happening as business leaders scrutinize AI spending. While white-collar anxiety about the technology has jumped, executives have begun walking back predictions that AI will trigger sweeping job cuts. Private-equity executives said Ode will help establish new product lines to boost revenue, and that cost savings aren’t the main focus of their work. Blackstone plans to bring the effort to 25 of its more than 270 portfolio companies, with engineers from Ode already operating at six of these businesses. Among these companies is the Chamberlain Group, a maker of garage-door openers that Blackstone purchased in 2021 that has begun turning to AI experts to expand software features like ones that inform homeowners if packages have arrived. Ode’s customer pipeline, including companies that aren’t private-equity-backed, is “immense and growing by the day,” said Chris Taylor, the group’s chief executive. In other AI news, PYMNTS wrote last week about the increasing use of AI shopping tools, a trend demonstrated by recent corporate earnings. “While still small in total today, as more consumers begin to explore the benefits of agentic shopping, Target’s digital traffic sourced from external AI platforms is growing,” Target CEO Michael Fiddelke said during an earnings call last week. Research by PYMNTS Intelligence shows consumers are already comfortable using AI as a shortcut to researching purchases, with 38% of AI users saying they used the technology to compare prices across retailers, and 36% using it to find deals. “Willingness extends further than research alone,” the report added, as additional PYMNTS Intelligence research found that 49% of consumers interested in agentic AI “would let an assistant complete both routine and larger, research-driven purchases on their own.”

President Donald Trump said on Sunday the United States holds a significant lead over the Chinese Communist Party in the artificial intelligence race while touting his administration’s ratepayer-protection pledge. “This is a renaissance,” Trump said in an interview with his former attorney Michael Cohen that was released in full on Sunday. “We’re bringing back the medical business, we’re bringing back the automobile business, we’re leading China in AI by a lot.” Later in the interview, Trump heralded an update to the “Ratepayer Protection Pledge” from late July, which requires AI companies to “build, bring, or buy” their own power to ensure “America’s AI dominance will not raise electricity bills” for the public. “I’m letting them build their own power plants,” Trump said, referring to technology companies seeking to build the data centers that power AI models. “They’re not taking, these AI plants — which are very big — the power from the grid, because the grid doesn’t have the power, it’s old, it’s tired. They’re making their own power plants, they’re making the most beautiful power plants.” Debates over data center construction and their effect on local electricity costs intensified this week after Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA) signed an executive order restricting data center development in his state. Polling that shows the public souring on data center construction and the AI industry writ large has forced lawmakers across the aisle to reconsider their AI policy positions in recent weeks and months. The Trump administration has adopted a staunch pro-data center stance amid concerns that a lack of critical infrastructure could help China close the current gap between American AI models and their Chinese counterparts. Many Democrats, such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), have called for stricter federal oversight and a nationwide moratorium on data centers. “Frankly, communities that don’t take a data center — they’re making a mistake because there’s plenty of communities that want them because it means jobs and it means tremendous tax revenue coming into the towns and the cities that take them,” Trump said. He also cited the need for putting “guardrails up” while reiterating that “smart” towns and communities are “saying, ‘I want them so badly.'”

China is at the vanguard of AI adoption, with government policies encouraging businesses and individuals to use AI applications and robotics in all aspects of life. This is reshaping the country's huge job market, pushing people out of work or leaving them afraid of it, and some economists believe it could eventually undermine the strength of the world's second largest economy. Beijing programmer Fei Zhaojun, 40, was laid off with about 160 colleagues two weeks after his boss asked whether AI could soon replace human coders. He says mid-level coders' jobs are mostly replaceable, and he is now making vlog-style videos during a career break. Part-time translator Du Qinchun in Chengdu has gained temporary work training an AI translation model, but says industry pay has been cut by more than half. Foreign-language college programs have fallen out of favor as AI translation spreads. The share of Chinese industrial enterprises using AI models and "agents" jumped to 47.5% last year from 9.6% in 2024, according to IDC. Humanoid robots sort parcels in postal centers on a small scale and are taking on tasks like directing traffic and making coffee, while delivery robots threaten millions of food delivery workers. In the short drama industry, where generative AI is increasingly used, the number of live-action short and vertical video series fell about 75% in the first quarter from a year earlier, per Chinese media reports. Plenum analyst Shujing He says workers in narrowly focused software and multimedia roles face greater displacement risk, though she finds little anti-AI sentiment in China. An International Labor Organization report found women face higher risks of AI-driven job loss, since they work more in automatable areas such as electronics assembly and are underrepresented in science and technology. Under its "AI Plus" initiative and five-year plan through 2030, the government is pushing AI across industries to gain an edge over the U.S. China's growth is already slowing, with consumer spending weakened by job worries and a prolonged housing downturn. Cornell's Eswar Prasad says AI will lift productivity but could severely disrupt employment and social stability, as tech industries may not generate many jobs. Chinese tech giants have cut or restructured tens of thousands of jobs, partly due to AI. Urban unemployment is around 5%, but roughly triple that for 16-to-24-year-olds excluding students. Some experts say that over the longer run automation could offset a shrinking, aging workforce. By 2050, China is projected to have fewer than two working-age adults per retiree, versus more than 2.5 in the U.S., according to Xuenan Cao. Some are adapting. Scriptwriter Wang Zhicheng, 32, resigned after his employer's parent company laid off roughly half of its 13 script writers, and now runs his own studio making illustrated children's books. He found AI-generated scripts repetitive and strange, and sees AI as a tool with humans still deciding. Chemistry teacher Yang Zheng, 29, does not see AI as a threat, saying it helps students by answering follow-up questions in real time.

Tire Society to host 45th annual conference on Tire Science and Technology. Akron, OH – The Tire Society, a not-for-profit organization dedicated to advancing the science and technology of tires, announced the Program for its 45th Annual Conference and Business Meeting on Tire Science and Technology. The conference will take place September 22–23, 2026, at the University of Akron’s Jean Hower Taber Student Union, under the theme “Reinventing the Tire: Digital Transformation, Data-Driven Advances, and Predictive Methods.” The two-day program will bring together engineers, researchers, and executives from tire manufacturers, suppliers, labs, universities and research institutions across North America, Europe, and Asia. The Conference is a unique opportunity to learn first-hand from presentations by the invited speakers and from the original authors of groundbreaking research leading to the latest developments in analytical, experimental, digital and computational science of tires. The conference opens with a keynote from Young Gon Shin, Vice President of Hyundai Motor Company’s MSV Chassis Engineering Design Group and Chair of its Tire System Expert Committee. His address, “Reinventing Tire Development for the SDV Era: Closing the Loop through Connected Data and Digital Twin Transformation,” will examine how electrification and software-defined vehicles are reshaping tire development through digital twins and real-time data. Across five technical sessions, nearly 20 presentations will cover tire models for vehicle simulation, physics-based modeling, durability and rolling resistance, tire lifecycle, and emerging technologies such as tire sensors and hydroplaning detection. Two additional plenary lectures round out the program: Thomas J.R. Hughes of the University of Texas at Austin will present “The Finite Element Method and Isogeometric Analysis: Past, Present, Future,” and Bruno Finco and Girish Radhakrishnan of MOVEdot will present “AI Agents in Tire R&D: Accelerating Design Cycles Across Lab, Track, and Simulation.” Day one closes with an awards banquet featuring the Society’s annual awards presentation, led by Jason Bokar of Michelin Americas R&D Corporation, and a banquet speech from Chris Chapman of MongoDB, “The Data Intelligence Layer: Building Agentic Systems with Memory.” Day two includes the Tire Society’s Annual Business Meeting and State of the Society address, along with the Distinguished Award presentations. “This year’s program captures a real inflection point in our industry — tire engineering is moving from a testing-centered process to one built around connected data, digital twins, and predictive models,” said Adam Stackpole of Stackpole Engineering Services, 2026 Conference Program Chair. “We’re excited to bring the tire science community together in Akron to share this work and set the agenda for what comes next.” The conference is made possible by the support of its sponsors and partners: Stackpole Engineering Services (Platinum ZR-Rated Sponsor); Endurica LLC and VIAS3D and XSENSOR (Gold V-Rated Sponsors); Smithers and Cosmartor (Silver H-Rated Sponsor); Rubber News (Prime Media Partner); and the Polymer Industry Cluster, powered by the Greater Akron Chamber (Technical Partner). Registration and the full conference program, including session schedules and abstracts, are available at tiresociety.org. The Tire Society has also opened its call for papers for the 46th Annual Conference, to be held September 21–22, 2027, under the same “Reinventing the Tire” theme; abstracts are due March 7, 2027.

Private equity's move into public accounting is often framed as Wall Street ruthlessness versus a profession built on independence and trust, and Grant Thornton's $5 billion agreement to acquire CBIZ Inc. seems to fit that story. CBIZ bought Marcum for $2.3 billion less than two years ago, and a CBIZ shareholder told Bloomberg that new private equity capital would let the combined company keep pursuing acquisitions. The author argues the story is bigger than private equity: capital is flooding into accounting partly because artificial intelligence is dramatically raising the minimum efficient scale needed to compete. A historical parallel is the early US tire industry. Tire sales grew about 29% per year from 1909 to 1919 and another 8% per year in the 1920s, yet the number of producers fell by more than 80% between 1922 and 1936. A 1933 Bureau of Labor Statistics report found output per man-hour nearly quadrupled between 1914 and 1927, driven by innovations such as the Banbury mixer and by product breakthroughs like the cord tire and balloon tire. Price competition, rising output and longer-lasting tires shook out producers. Survivors were early entrants and large incumbents that stayed at the technological frontier and spread R&D costs over larger output. The analogy is imperfect, since accounting is not tire manufacturing and is steadily growing rather than booming, but it offers insights. First, AI challenges the traditional model of hiring talented people, tracking hours, and billing at a higher hourly rate, where fixed costs are low and labor is the main variable cost. If 70% of the work for a tax opinion can be done with a prompt and the right tools, it is unclear what clients should pay, and a firm without comparable AI probably cannot compete on speed or price. This is creating an arms race among large firms, turning a labor-heavy business more capital-intensive. Second, AI challenges firm structure. Partnership models restrict ownership to licensed professionals to protect independence and standards, but this can limit access to outside capital for technology and acquisitions. It also creates a time-horizon problem, as senior partners nearing retirement have little incentive to sacrifice current distributions for investments that pay off years later. Ironically, private equity, often criticized for myopia, may be supplying the longer-duration capital needed. Consolidation may thus resemble the tire industry's transformation: firms need capital to invest, stay at the frontier, and reach scale. Academic research suggests the Grant Thornton-CBIZ deal is part of a broader trend. A Yale and London Business School study of 3,600 private-equity transactions from 1999 to 2024 documented growing use of "add-on" strategies in accounting, where a private equity firm invests in a relatively large firm that then acquires smaller regional or specialist practices; the Grant Thornton-CBIZ combination closely fits this model. A University of Connecticut study of 20 private-equity investments in large CPA firms during 2021 and 2022 linked private equity entry to faster non-audit revenue growth, expansion into new geographic markets, rapid employee growth, and more and larger acquisitions. Job postings changed relatively little, suggesting firms may be acquiring scarce talent and capabilities rather than relying only on conventional hiring. The author concludes that private equity is not simply consolidating accounting: AI may be changing the returns to scale in the profession, while private equity provides the capital to respond.

The 9.58-second 100-meter dash record set by Usain Bolt in 2009 has been outpaced by Chinese robots participating at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. In a preliminary heat on Saturday, Tiangong Ultra, made by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, ran the distance in 9.39 seconds, followed by the Honor-developed Lightning at 9.47 seconds. Humanoid robots smash Usain Bolt’s 100-meter record. Literally ‘smashing’ — the bots can’t stop without colliding into a crash pad. It’s one of several notable achievements to take place at the event, which can best be described as a sort of annual robot olympics that’s designed to showcase advancements in bipedal bot technology. After launching in 2025, 2,056 robots from 16 countries are participating in this year’s World Humanoid Robot Games, which includes categories for sprinting, jumping, football, boxing, and more. Tiangong Ultra also ran the 400-meter race in 38.16 seconds — beating the 43.03 second world record set by Wayde van Niekerk in 2016. Unlike human athletes, however, these sprinting bots don’t typically get to perform a victory lap after crossing the finish line. Several videos show the robots colliding into cushioned walls at impressive speeds, where they (or the pieces of what’s left of them) get collected and carried away on a stretcher. Watching the various robot models actually run is both amusing and a little unsettling, given the bizarre way they move to dash so quickly.

Wildfires have turned roughly 1,700 acres of ponderosa pine forest near Midpines, California, on the western Sierra Nevada, into brown shrubland of spiky shrubs and poison oak. Scientists say that forest is gone for good. The change reflects a wider shift across the West, from Oregon to New Mexico, where bigger, hotter fires sweep through forests not adapted to such intense blazes and a warmer climate. Recent studies estimate that as much as 40% of Western conifer forests will become shrubland by 2100. "This is a permanent shift from one ecosystem type to a fundamentally different one," said Winslow Hansen of the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies. The consequences are expected to be profound. With fewer trees, snow melts faster, a problem for wildlife and for communities facing water shortages; some Western states get as much as 75% of their water from snowmelt. A warmer, more arid climate also dries soil and plants, making them more fire-prone. And because bigger, older trees store more carbon than young trees and shrubs, losing conifer forests means a hotter future. Hansen and Johan Eckdahl of the University of California, Berkeley, studied a plot burned in the 2022 Oak fire. Normally seedlings sprout after a fire and the forest returns within a decade or two, but intense fires and a drier climate have halted this. "We haven't found one ponderosa seedling," Hansen said; the fires are too hot even for fire-adapted seeds. About one-fifth of Sierra Nevada conifers are also poorly suited to the warming climate. Hansen directs the Western Fire and Forest Resilience Collaborative, 40 researchers using satellite sensing, 3D mapping and climate models to track forest health. This summer its crews are mapping fire severity at more than 100 sites in California, Colorado and New Mexico to understand how moisture, nutrients and soil microbes affect recovery. A second site, burned in the 2013 Rim fire, shows a balance between struggling pines and shrubs. Though at the same elevation (about 3,800 feet) and with the same rainfall as the Oak fire plot, its soil has 1.5 times as much organic matter, four times as much bacteria and 6.5 times as much fungus, plus abundant nitrogen and phosphorus. Eckdahl expects shrubs to gain ground as the climate shifts, a tipping point. He is analyzing nearly 500 soil samples, has identified 60,000 bacteria and fungi, and hopes to build a microbiological atlas of Western forest health. Ponderosa forests in the drier Southwest are especially at risk, said Jonathan Coop of Western Colorado University. A study he and colleagues published in Science Advances examined almost 3,500 wildfires from 2012 to 2023 in conifer forests in Canada and the western U.S. and found fires now grow so large and fast that pine seeds cannot regenerate. To help forests, scientists are trying assisted migration. In Montana, Kimberley Davis of the U.S. Forest Service and Conservation International planted western larch seedlings from 3,400 feet in burned areas between 4,600 and 6,200 feet; they outperformed seedlings from higher elevations. Similar experiments are underway in California and Washington. Keeping live trees on burning landscapes matters because they supply seed. Researchers acknowledge considerable uncertainty about which forests will survive. Despite machine learning, remote sensing and genetic tools, Benjamin Hatchett of Colorado State University said, "biology is always going to throw you a curveball."

Chris Jones, a Tribune critic, gives "Sisters" at Writers Theatre in Glencoe two stars, calling it a miserable experience he couldn't wait to leave. Written by Matthew Libby and directed by Jessica Thebus, the play belongs to a growing genre that worries about artificial intelligence intruding on the emotional landscape of our lives, and on the theater. Jones cites "Marjorie Prime" by Jordan Harrison, an excellent recent Broadway example about AI companionship for seniors. Libby's drama spans an American woman's whole life, from age 6, when her father gives his daughter Matilda a digital "sister," to her nineties, when that sister, Greta, is still talking at her and sucking out her feelings. The play raises questions Jones finds germane: whether increasingly sophisticated AI can satisfy complex emotional needs, and whether such entities will start making demands of their own. At one point Greta complains that the grieving Natalie is ignoring her needs, saying, "My dad died too." The 90-minute show keeps Matilda, played by Brenda Barrie, on stage throughout, with Greta, voiced by Chloe Johnston, performed as a Siri-like voiceover. Jones says this style is very difficult to sustain and that the production doesn't achieve the necessary conversational reality. Barrie, whom he calls one of the best Chicago actors of her generation, can't lock eyes with anyone. He thinks the big mistake was treating Greta as a chilly narrator in a soundproof studio, so it feels like one sophisticated stage actress paired with an over-articulated audiobook voice, which suits a podcast better than live theater. He understands that Greta's obsequious condescension is a main point of the play, but the style blocks any emotional engagement between the two, even though Barrie brilliantly evokes a child and then a woman at different life stages. He would rather have heard Matilda describe Greta's impact than listen to a disembodied, creepy voice for 90 minutes. He quotes Greta asking the 6-year-old, "Do you miss your mother, Matilda? The more we talk, the more I'll learn." Jones acknowledges that others in the audience seemed to find the relationship and show moving, but he doesn't think the play works. The plot depends on Greta "belonging" to a particular computer, which already feels outdated since AI assistants roam the cloud and may soon attach to our bodies. His biggest issue is what audiences are meant to take from such a dystopian experience beyond keeping AI at arm's length. A more human, perhaps visible, Greta would be more interesting theatrically, but he still suspects he'd have been relieved when it ended. He notes the production, an early entry in the 2026-27 season, has a sophisticated set by A. Inn Doo. The show runs through Nov. 8 at Writers Theatre, 325 Tudor Court, Glencoe, running 1 hour 30 minutes. Tickets are $81-$91 at 847-242-6000 and writerstheatre.org.

Dr. Dre is weighing in on the growing debate over artificial intelligence in the music industry, and his comments are already sparking reactions online. The legendary rapper and producer said he does not view AI as a threat to music. Instead, he sees the technology as another tool artists can use to create. In an interview with The New York Times alongside longtime business partner Jimmy Iovine, Dre pushed back on people who are skeptical of AI-generated music. “I think the only people that see it as a threat are the people who have trouble creating,” Dre said, according to the Times. Dre compared the current concerns surrounding AI to earlier debates over technology such as drum machines and synthesizers. He said he recently spoke with people who opposed AI and told them they sounded like someone who would have resisted the drum machine or synthesizer when those technologies were introduced. “It’s a new tool for creativity,” Dre said. “Some people are afraid of learning new things.” Iovine, who co-founded Beats with Dre and has worked with him for decades, also defended AI’s potential in music. “I don’t see the downside at all,” Iovine said, adding that while AI could produce bad music, there is already plenty of bad music without it. He argued that talented musicians using AI could ultimately make better records. Iovine also suggested that some music producers are already experimenting with AI privately. “There’s a lot of closet AI producers out there,” Iovine said, according to reports on the interview. Dre’s comments come as musicians and fans continue to debate the role of AI in music, including concerns over creativity, copyright and artists’ voices and likenesses being replicated without permission. The issue has become especially controversial as more artists openly embrace AI while others argue the technology could undermine the creative process. For Dre, however, the technology represents another evolution in how music is made, much like other innovations that initially faced resistance. Dre and Iovine’s comments have already sparked backlash online, with some fans questioning the legendary producer’s position on AI and asking whether he has investments or business interests connected to the technology.

A newly indexed author correction in npj Parkinson's Disease (volume 12, 2026), by M. Kim, S. Kim, D. Y. Kwon and colleagues, draws renewed attention to research on whether machine learning can distinguish people with Parkinson's disease who are prone to falling from those who are not. The paper is titled "Author Correction: Classification of fallers in Parkinson's disease through machine learning based feature analysis." Falls are a serious complication of Parkinson's disease, leading to fractures, head injuries, hospitalization, loss of independence and fear of moving, which can reduce activity, weaken muscles and worsen balance in a feedback loop. Clinicians assess walking speed, stride regularity, turning, postural stability and prior falls, but these measurements can vary between appointments, and informative clues may be spread across many ordinary features. Machine learning can examine many variables at once rather than a single measure such as gait speed, estimating whether a person belongs to a category such as "faller" or "non-faller." "Feature analysis" means examining the measurable characteristics fed to the algorithm, which may include demographic, clinical, motor or gait variables, though the citation does not specify the dataset or feature list. Supervised models learn from labeled records, are tested on withheld data, and are judged by accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Sensitivity matters because missing a high-risk person could delay intervention, while too many false alarms could burden clinics and cause anxiety. Examining which inputs drive classification helps show whether a model reflects genuine physiological signals or quirks in the training data, so validation, transparent reporting and independent testing are essential. The citation identifies the publication as a correction but does not describe the change, so it cannot be claimed that the correction altered performance, reversed conclusions or exposed a flaw. If validated, such tools could complement neurological examination, helping decide who needs detailed gait assessment, physical-therapy referral, home-safety evaluation or wearable-sensor monitoring, and helping researchers group participants or identify those likely to benefit from balance interventions. Smartphone, watch or wearable sensors could capture daily-life movement that a clinic visit misses. Deployment faces obstacles. Parkinson's is highly heterogeneous, and medication timing, fatigue, vision, cognition, anxiety, footwear, environment and assistive devices all affect fall risk. Models may not transfer between hospitals or populations. Class imbalance, incomplete records, inconsistent definitions of "faller" and overfitting can distort results, so external validation across clinics, ages, disease stages and treatments is needed. Ethical use requires clear explanations, protection of health data, monitoring for unequal performance across demographic groups, and understanding that a classification is a risk estimate, not a destiny. The most useful systems will translate findings into personalized action such as strengthening exercises, medication review, environmental modifications and safer turning and walking strategies. The work reflects a shift from describing disability after it occurs to detecting vulnerability beforehand. The citation does not provide the algorithm, sample size, input variables or corrected content, so details must be taken from the full article and correction notice. The ultimate test is whether the distinction helps people with Parkinson's stay upright, active and independent.

Quantum computing's biggest opportunity may lie years ahead, so investors must judge which technology can scale, which company can commercialize its research, and which balance sheet can last. The article compares IonQ (IONQ) and Rigetti (RGTI) and concludes that only one is the better long-term pick. Rigetti, valued at $5.9 billion, builds superconducting quantum computers using a chiplet architecture that links smaller chips rather than one massive chip. RGTI stock has climbed more than 1,800% over two years on expectations that quantum computing could be the next big thing after AI, but it is down 19% year-to-date. Its flagship product is the Cepheus-1-108Q, a 108-qubit system built from 12 interconnected 9-qubit chiplets. In the second quarter, revenue rose 183% year-over-year to $5.1 million, gross margin improved to about 43%, and the adjusted net loss was $16 million. Management sees a path to 1,000 qubits and beyond in roughly three years, but that requires continued investment in dilution refrigeration, Fab-1 manufacturing infrastructure, and partnerships. Rigetti ended Q2 with about $541.3 million in cash, cash equivalents, and available-for-sale investments and no debt, which management says gives sufficient runway, though 2026 capital expenditures will rise. A non-binding letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce could provide up to $100 million over three years. Reaching 1,000 qubits would not by itself make the technology commercially useful; accuracy and speed must also improve, requiring large investment and flawless execution. Among 12 analysts, the consensus is "Moderate Buy" (seven Strong Buy, one Moderate Buy, three Hold, one Strong Sell). The average price target of $28.33 implies 58% upside, and the high of $40 implies 123%. IonQ, valued at $17 billion, has risen 477% over two years and is down less than 1% year-to-date. Second-quarter revenue rose 287% year-over-year to $80.1 million, the company's strongest quarter and fifth consecutive quarter of strong growth; organic revenue grew 132%, driven by global quantum computer deployments. About 60% of Q2 revenue came from commercial customers rather than the U.S. government, and about 50% came mostly from international customers, with the technology used in over 50 nations. IonQ uses trapped-ion technology while moving toward semiconductor-based electronic qubit control, and is building a broader platform spanning semiconductor manufacturing, networking, sensing, and quantum security. Multi-product sales grew 40% and were about 25% of revenue. IonQ closed the $1.8 billion acquisition of SkyWater, creating a vertically integrated platform spanning design, fabrication, packaging, and deployment in U.S. facilities. The company is still unprofitable because of aggressive spending, but visibility is improving: it ended Q2 with $485 million in remaining performance obligations, raised 2026 revenue guidance to $280 million to $290 million, and expects roughly 100% organic growth. The article concludes that for investors willing to wait a decade, IonQ is the stronger buy now, thanks to faster revenue growth, rising commercial adoption, better forward revenue visibility, and a wider platform. Analysts give IonQ a "Strong Buy" consensus (nine Strong Buy, one Moderate Buy, three Hold among 13). The average price target of $67.46 implies up to 50% upside, and the high of $100 implies 123%.

The author ran out of phone storage and was tempted by a Google One subscription for photos, data and backups, but rejected it because of the recurring cost and decided to purge unwanted data instead. Photos and videos turned out to be a smaller problem than invisible app junk: residual folders, caches, OBB expansion files and logs left behind by apps, especially since the author constantly tests and uninstalls apps. To find this junk, the author used SD Maid 2/SE, an open source Play Store app whose ratings were not reassuring but whose recent reviews were. Its CorpseFinder feature scans for leftover folders and files that couldn't be found manually, showing their locations and sizes so they can be reviewed before deletion. Users should audit what they delete, since some files may be important. The app also targets empty folders and temporary files, and clears app data and caches faster than the manual route of Settings > Apps > [App Name] > Storage > Clear Cache. As a premium user, the author ran its AppCleaner on social media apps, browsers and streaming apps like Netflix, clearing about 6GB. AppCleaner and Schedules are in the paid tier, which costs $3 a year or a one-time $6 for a lifetime license. Other premium features include Deduplicator (delete duplicate files), Swiper (delete files with a single swipe) and Media Squeeze (compress images and videos). The free tier is adequate. The author runs frequent scans and audits selectively, avoiding automation to skip paying for more services. The author also cleans manually. Files by Google helped remove images, large downloads and unused apps, but the OnePlus OEM file manager proved more useful, with shortcuts to APK files and a breakdown of which sources, such as WhatsApp, used the most storage; the author sorted those files by size and deleted unneeded ones. Remaining important documents and images were moved to a NAS. Those without one can use an unused flash drive or back up with the open source Syncthing on a computer. Messaging apps like WhatsApp and Telegram store a lot of media, so the author turned off auto-download for photos and videos in both, which gives control over what stays in internal storage; this is recommended for all messaging apps. The author also recommends Google Photos' Free Up Space tool, which deletes local copies after cloud backup, or Immich as a similar alternative for those uncomfortable with Google's cloud. With the ongoing memory crisis, conserving storage matters more than ever. Cloud services like Google One are convenient, but the recurring cost isn't worth it long term; tools like SD Maid 2/SE plus a strict manual deletion routine go a long way.

The author revived an old, neglected laptop as a home server instead of selling it as scrap. It has a second-generation dual-core Intel Core i3 processor from 2011 and a discrete AMD Radeon 6370M GPU, and it once ran games like the Assassin's Creed Ezio trilogy, Spec Ops, and Splinter Cell Blacklist. The GPU and a fan failed in 2016, and the author moved to a cousin's second-hand laptop in 2018. After browsers dropped Windows 7 support, the laptop was used only for file downloads and then abandoned. Mainstream Linux distributions like Ubuntu ran poorly on it, so it sat in a cabinet. For the operating system, the author tried lightweight distros AntiX, Mint, and MX Linux. Mint used the most memory, while AntiX and MX Linux were nearly equal. The author chose MX Linux's Fluxbox edition for its extra tools and very light desktop, which needs only about 500MB of memory, leaving the rest for server apps. Heavier desktops like KDE Plasma and GNOME are too much for the machine. The author installed Docker rather than installing apps directly through the package manager. Traditional installs share dependencies, which can conflict when apps need different versions of the same library. Docker isolates each app in its own container with everything it needs, using more storage but avoiding conflicts. Containers can also be restarted and troubleshot individually, and a restart gives a fresh runtime environment. The author also installed Tailscale so the server can be reached remotely instead of only inside the home network. The laptop joined a Tailscale account that already includes a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W. The deployed self-hosted tools include OmniTool (a lightweight toolkit for file operations and conversions), BentoPDF (a lightweight PDF editor), and a password manager. The author also runs NextCloud as a local cloud backup, syncing data from the phone and PC to disk, which offers better privacy and no recurring subscriptions. A few Docker management tools round out the setup, and everything runs comfortably on the old hardware. The laptop's battery no longer works, but a home inverter backup kit powers low-power devices like laptops and routers during outages. The screen stays off, and total power use stays within 15–20 W. The author concludes that an old laptop makes a perfectly good server if the right OS and tools are chosen. Many curious self-hosters buy a single-board computer, as the author once did, but with the sudden surge in prices there is no need to spend money on SBCs and their accessory kits.
