Less than two weeks after President Trump signed an executive order questioning the childhood vaccine schedule, the administration posted a request for information on Friday seeking public feedback on a wide range of vaccine ideas. The public has 30 days to comment. Among the considerations is whether to add new categories to the vaccines framework, which currently includes universal recommendations, recommendations for certain risk-based groups, and recommendations based on shared clinical decision-making. A new study found that soda purchases declined among SNAP users in 10 states that recently enacted restrictions. The researchers calculated this equals about 34 fewer 12-ounce cans of soda per person per year. Experts still aren't sure the approach is the best one, and there was a major caveat regarding what people have been buying in place of soda. The FDA says it is developing a plan to regulate medical devices that use generative artificial intelligence. Rick Abramson, director of the agency's Digital Health Center of Excellence, said the "ecosystem is expecting clarity" and that the agency aims to provide it. He said to expect both broad guidance on generative AI overall and narrower specialty guidance on particular topics of special interest or complexity. Nurse practitioners are well positioned to fill gaps in the strained health care system. After a master's degree and at least 500 hours in a clinical setting under a supervisor, they can perform many of the same duties as a doctor. But, according to The Hechinger Report's Colleen Connolly, there are not nearly enough supervisors, known as preceptors, willing to take on students for those hours. Accredited schools must provide clinical placements or help students find them, but many do the bare minimum, leaving students to fend for themselves. Preceptors typically aren't paid, and it is increasingly common for students to offer them money, sometimes cash, to get their hours. Two First Opinion essays from doctors reflect on daily practice. Zain Khawaja, treating an emergency room patient with a suspected cancer-related emergency, began by shaking hands with her and her family. He writes that the handshake did not change her diagnosis but reminded both of them that she was a person experiencing one of the most frightening days of her life. Cardiologist Benjamin I. Lee retired four years ago but missed using his skills and began volunteering at a community clinic. He writes that only after leaving mainstream medicine did he fully grasp the limitations of the health care system and how they affect the most vulnerable. Also noted: STAT reports that a Medicaid transgender care rule sets a precedent that could restrict coverage of other drugs.

Amazon plans to expand its Prime Air drone delivery from 11 locations to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026, a sixfold increase. The announcement follows a strong second-quarter earnings report. The drones carry packages up to five pounds, with eligible orders arriving in as little as 30 minutes. Amazon says it has completed hundreds of thousands of drone deliveries this year and expects roughly 1 million in 2026. Faster delivery could encourage more frequent orders, especially groceries, medicines and essentials, and give Amazon a last-mile logistics advantage as it competes with Walmart and others. Drones will not replace trucks or vans, and Prime Air remains a small part of the business, so it is not an immediate earnings driver. Regulatory, weather, safety and community concerns remain risks. AMZN stock is well below its 52-week high of $287.20 but up roughly 12% year-to-date. In Q2, operating income rose 43% to $27.5 billion, and AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion, its fastest growth in 18 quarters, for a $169 billion annualized run rate. The main concern is spending: Amazon expects roughly $220 billion in 2026 capital expenditures, largely for AI infrastructure, which is pressuring free cash flow and could keep the stock volatile. Valuation is roughly 21 times trailing earnings and about 22 times forward earnings, with a PEG ratio around 1.5, which looks reasonable given growth in AWS, advertising and improving retail economics. Investors are paying not just for e-commerce but for AWS, AI, advertising, logistics and other emerging businesses. AWS and AI remain the larger story; AWS grew 36.7% in Q2, and Amazon is increasing investment in AI chips and data centers while expanding same-day fulfillment, advertising, AI services and custom semiconductors. Analysts are bullish. Morgan Stanley's Brian Nowak rates the stock "Buy" with a $335 target, implying roughly 29% upside from Aug. 23's close, and has outlined a scenario in which AWS reaches $1 trillion in annual revenue. Goldman Sachs raised its target to $375 from $335 with a "Buy" rating, citing AWS and AI momentum. Jefferies has a "Buy" with a $320 target. The consensus is "Strong Buy" with a mean target of $326.49, implying more than 25% upside. The article concludes that the drone rollout is an intriguing long-term catalyst, but AWS remains the bigger reason to own AMZN, and accelerating cloud growth, AI investment and an expanding logistics network could sustain the long-term growth story despite near-term spending concerns.

Humanoid robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, one developer behind China's robotics boom tells CBS News Beijing — How long before China is ready to deploy humanoid robot soldiers? That question is on the minds of many of the humans gathered in Beijing right now to watch the World Humanoid Robot Games, and as smashed records highlight the dizzying pace of advancement, one developer tells CBS News the answer is likely less than a decade. Impressive (and unimpressive) feats of athleticism. In the indoor arena used as the speedskating venue for the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, dozens of humanoid robots stand in the center of the track, surrounded by their human minders, while hundreds of spectators in the crowd watch and cheer from their seats. Two more are in a boxing ring, dressed in red and black headgear, punching and kicking each other in a kickboxing match. Others stand around a large gymnastics spring mat, waiting their turn as a preceding robot flips and spins through a floor routine. Smaller robots — the size of children — gather on a miniature soccer field, kicking a ball up and down the synthetic grass. Others compete in an obstacle course, running, crawling, weaving and climbing their way to the finish. This is the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games, where more than 2,000 robots from more than 600 teams representing 16 countries are competing for glory. It's the second time the event has been held, and just like last year, it is being hosted by China. One of the machines beat Jamaican track great Usain Bolt's 100-meter sprint record on Sunday, running the 109 yards in just 9.39 seconds, beating Bolt's 2009 time of 9.58 seconds. But it doesn't always go to plan. During competition, a number of humanoid robots have tripped, collapsed, burst into flames or slammed into safety barriers and then been stretchered off the track. Crowds here have been thoroughly entertained. But the question many are asking as they witness the (sometimes) remarkable agility on the track isn't when the next record will be challenged, it's how long before these eerily familiar, yet coldly unhuman machines are equipped with weapons and turned into soldiers. "It all depends on who controls them" Events such as sprints, long jump, weightlifting and boxing reveal physical attributes that one can easily see being transferred to the battlefield. Robotics engineer Yang Kun, who works for Shanghai-based humanoid robot company AG BOT, told CBS News that creating robot soldiers is the ultimate aim, and he believes Chinese companies are only five to 10 years away from achieving it. "That's what we really want to do as we can make sure people in the world will not be attacked," he said. "We will use the robots to show the power of a country like China that will ensure no other country would attack. This will prevent war." When CBS News asked Yang if robots could become evil — the Terminator movies are starting to feel a little too real — he shook his head. "No, I don't think so. Robots don't have emotion, only humans," he said. "It all depends on who controls them and who makes them." The aim of the robot games, from China's perspective, is to show off the pace of the technological advances being made — and to show off the extent to which Chinese prioritization of the research and development of humanoids is putting the country in pole position. President Xi Jinping wants China to dominate in science and technology, and under his leadership, Beijing is investing heavily in these industries, with AI and robotics already featuring in everyday life for many Chinese. Yang, whose robot "A3" competed in the kickboxing events at the games, was very pleased with the humanoid's performance. "In the future it can go to hotel(s), our house, to do some cleaning," he said of the imminent uses of the technology he's working on — "to make daily life better through technology." But not much further down the road, he said, they will also "do some combat, and go to the military, and do other things."

AI, backed by government policy, is reshaping China's huge job market, pushing people out of work or leaving them afraid it might, and some economists think it could eventually undermine the overall strength of the world's second-largest economy. Computer programmer Fei Zhaojun, 40, was laid off in Beijing with about 160 colleagues two weeks after his boss asked whether AI could soon replace human coders. He says mid-level coders' jobs are largely replaceable, and is now making vlog-style short videos during a career break. Part-time translator Du Qinchun, in Chengdu, has found temporary extra work training an AI translation model, but says industry pay has been cut by more than half over the years. Popular college foreign-language programs are falling out of favor as AI translation spreads. Analyst Shujing He of Plenum says anti-AI sentiment in China appears far weaker than elsewhere, and displaced or worried workers are often eager to try AI-enabled ventures. According to IDC, the share of Chinese industrial enterprises using AI models and "agents" rose to 47.5% last year from 9.6% in 2024. Humanoid robots now sort parcels in postal centers on a small scale and are moving into tasks like directing traffic and making coffee, while food delivery robots are gaining ground, potentially threatening millions of delivery workers. Generative AI is increasingly used in China's short drama industry, where live-action short vertical video series reportedly fell about 75% in the first quarter from a year earlier. He says roles narrowly concentrated in software development and multimedia creation face greater displacement risk. An International Labor Organization report found women face higher AI job-loss risk than men because they work more in automatable areas such as electronics assembly and are underrepresented in science and technology. Under its "AI Plus" initiative and five-year plan through 2030, the government is pushing AI across industries to gain an edge over the U.S., which Oxford China Policy Lab's Zilan Qian says may spread AI into domains faster than elsewhere. Growth is already slowing, consumer spending is lagging partly from job fears, and a prolonged housing downturn has hurt household wealth. Cornell's Eswar Prasad warns AI could lift productivity but severely disrupt employment and harm social stability, since tech industries may not generate many jobs. Chinese tech giants have cut or restructured tens of thousands of jobs, partly due to AI. Urban unemployment hovers around 5%, while for ages 16 to 24 (excluding students) it is roughly triple that. Some experts note that China's aging, shrinking population, projected to have fewer than two working-age adults per retiree by 2050 versus over 2.5 in the U.S., means automation could partly offset a shrinking workforce, according to Xuenan Cao. Others are adapting. Scriptwriter Wang Zhicheng, 32, resigned after his employer's parent company laid off roughly half of its 13 script writers, and now runs his own studio making illustrated children's books. He found AI scripts repetitive and formulaic, and says humans remain the decision-makers. Chemistry teacher Yang Zheng, 29, doesn't see AI as a threat, saying it helps students ask follow-up questions in real time and improves despite errors.

iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond Tokenized ETF (Ondo), ticker TLTon, is a blockchain-based tokenized product designed to provide economic exposure similar to the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT). It is issued through Ondo's tokenized securities infrastructure and is intended to give eligible non-U.S. retail and institutional users on-chain access to a U.S.-listed ETF focused on long-term U.S. Treasury bonds. It is designed to track the underlying ETF's economic performance while letting eligible users interact with the asset through digital asset rails. TLT provides exposure to U.S. Treasury bonds with remaining maturities generally exceeding 20 years. Because long-duration Treasuries are sensitive to interest-rate changes, TLT is an established instrument for exposure to the U.S. government bond market and long-term rates. TLTon brings this exposure into a tokenized format, so investors need not hold the conventional ETF through a traditional brokerage account. It is part of the broader expansion of real-world asset tokenization. TLTon is connected to the underlying asset through Ondo's issuance and redemption framework, which lets eligible users mint and redeem tokenized positions. Ondo states that eligible non-U.S. retail and institutional users can interact with tokenized securities around the clock during the five-day trading week while maintaining access to liquidity associated with traditional exchanges. The product is subject to jurisdictional and regulatory restrictions. Tokenization converts traditional assets into digital representations managed and transferred on blockchain infrastructure, which can offer transparent transaction records, programmable transfers, and digital settlement, and can make tokenized securities compatible with digital wallets and other blockchain-based financial applications. Ondo's model aims to preserve a relationship between the token and its traditional counterpart. TLTon targets eligible investors seeking long-term Treasury exposure while operating within digital asset markets. Treasuries are widely used for diversification, liquidity management, and interest-rate exposure. The product also illustrates the growing range of assets brought on-chain, which now extends beyond equities to government bonds, money-market instruments, private credit, and other traditional securities. TLTon should not automatically be considered identical to direct ownership of TLT shares. Token holders' rights depend on the legal and contractual structure of the product, including custody, issuance, and redemption arrangements. The underlying investment carries interest-rate and market risks, since long-duration Treasuries can move significantly when rates change. Investors should also consider issuer, custodian, blockchain, smart contract, liquidity, and counterparty risks. Access may be restricted by jurisdiction, investor status, and applicable regulations.

This week's threats show trusted tools turning hostile, old weaknesses regaining attention, and AI lowering the cost of exploit work. The top item: the U.S. government warned that threat actors are using AI to write exploit scripts targeting internet-exposed Siemens S7 Series PLCs used in water, energy, manufacturing and other critical infrastructure. The agencies called it "an active threat." Actors use scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye to find exposed PLCs, then deploy AI-generated scripts disguised as monitoring tools, refining techniques against specific models and using read access to position for future write operations. The actor is unknown. Other major stories: - GitLab's CVE-2026-19478 (CVSS 9.4), a code injection flaw letting unauthenticated attackers modify or delete public projects, was exploited within days of disclosure, per watchTowr. - Fourteen trojanized npm packages posing as calendar and streak utilities deliver the AI-powered Linux implant RedC2 4.0, a cross-platform toolkit advertised in June 2026 on Hack Forums by "MarlboroMan." - Researchers demonstrated a "Zombie Card" attack that uses a smartphone relay to alter the expiration date shown to a terminal, enabling contactless payments with expired Visa cards. Transactions succeeded at most tested banks after modifying the CDCVM flag; no in-the-wild exploitation is known. - Three suspected Russian clusters (UNC6293, UNC7005, UNC5976) abuse legitimate authentication flows to target academia, aerospace and defense, governments and think tanks in Europe and the U.S. UNC7005's CaptiveCrunch hijacks captive Wi-Fi portals in hotels, conference centers and airports; Lumen Black Lotus Labs says three MSPs were likely compromised for this. - A remote Spectre attack on Cloudflare Workers leaked a JWT from a co-located Worker at up to 12 bits per second, 360 times faster than a 2021 attack. - Cl0p deployed a bespoke JSP web shell after exploiting a critical PTC Windchill and FlexPLM flaw; ReliaQuest says it can map vault data, decrypt keystore credentials and run code. Over 40 organizations were targeted, and the gang began naming alleged victims on August 12, 2026. - A new unpatched Unisoc T612 modem flaw, chained with an unpatched RCE and a video call the victim answers, could give attackers kernel-level access on Android. A long list of trending CVEs was published, covering GitLab, Cisco, Microsoft, Mozilla, Chrome, Splunk, Zimbra, Atlassian, JFrog and others. Elsewhere: live Stripe keys for 659 merchants, with about 35 GB of data, appeared on a forum on August 18, 2026. CISA released a Logging Reference Architecture for federal agencies. A federal judge partially overturned ex-Google engineer Linwei Ding's conviction, finding insufficient evidence he knew his conduct would benefit China's government; sentencing is set for September 1, 2026. Attackers abuse ScreenConnect via phishing, SEO poisoning and malvertising, and DCRat spreads through judicial-themed phishing using DLL sideloading and process hollowing. A researcher found a way to enroll a Linux machine in Apple's Find My network to read live location data. AliExpress was accused of audio fingerprinting, which Firefox says it has blocked since version 118. Anthropic expanded Claude Mythos 5 access and launched a $35 million Defender Advantage Fund, while Google's AVDH has found over 100 critical vulnerabilities in 10 months. Truffle Security verified 64,024 leaked AWS key pairs; 768 live corporate keys carry full admin control. The takeaway: one exposed service, trusted shortcut or overlooked dependency can be enough for attackers.

Charan Dangeti, a 16-year-old New Jersey trader who posts market analysis to more than 226,000 followers as Charan Invests, won a GameStock paper trading tournament this year by going heavy into two lidar stocks, Ouster (OUST) and Aeva (AEVA). "Both those LIDAR companies has exploded," he said, tying the move to hype around humanoids. Ouster closed June 30 at $62.52, up 189% year to date. Aeva peaked at $29.29 on May 27, up 120%, on production-intent sensor deliveries to Daimler Truck (DTRUY) and Nvidia's (NVDA) decision to make Aeva's 4D lidar a reference sensor on its DRIVE Hyperion platform. Dangeti picks sectors with a lot of hype or earnings potential, then targets stocks with a $5 to $10 billion market cap, since mid caps move further on the same news. He typically takes two stocks from a sector. He admits this is "obviously not, like, managing risk," and says the contest format "over incentivizes taking risk" by rewarding heavy bets on one or two names. He would prefer risk-adjusted scoring that accounts for concentration. The tournament ended before the downside arrived. Ouster fell 37.6% in July, closing at $31.30 on July 29, half its June peak. Aeva fell 38.9% and bottomed at $13.99. Both bounced into mid-August, then rolled over: $36.82 and $17.22 on August 24, each still up on the year but about 41% below its high. James Sixsmith, who runs the futures prop firm Take Profit Trader and puts its active trader count at roughly 100,000, described the real-account version of the problem on the *On The Margin* podcast. The biggest losers are usually those trading the biggest size most often, he said: "If your size is too big, your risk of ruin is 100%." Those who last trade a fraction of what they are allowed and take a couple of trades a day. He learned this on his own money, losing a lot at 26 through naivety, and believes most traders fail because they run out of money before they turn the corner. He also criticized traders who refuse to leave the simulator, saying they can't succeed against high-frequency traders in live markets. Going full size into an earnings print is "flipping a coin," and the firm is not for those whose strategy is coin flipping. Dangeti trades his own account differently, swing trading with holds of at least a couple of days, because short timeframes lead people to sell early on emotion as their P&L swings. He combines charts, fundamentals, options flow, options positioning and GEX. He concludes that "you can't just gamble it all in one stock or gamble it all in two stocks," and that while one need not be risk averse, some risk management strategy is needed.

The article argues that the biggest cybersecurity risk from AI agents is not new threats they create but the existing weaknesses they reveal. Agents don't invent poor governance or weak access controls; they expose years of accumulated shortcuts, or tech debt, and can exploit them at machine speed. Permissions get copied between employees, people change roles without losing old access, and files shared "temporarily" are never reviewed. Agents remove the friction that once kept sensitive information buried, surfacing it instantly in search results, summaries and prompts. The scale is growing fast. Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will be integrated with task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025, while governance hasn't kept pace. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 found one in five organizations had a breach linked to shadow AI, adding as much as $670,000 to the average breach cost and hitting customer data and intellectual property especially hard. Of the breached organizations, 63% had no AI governance policy, and only 37% had approval processes in place before employees began using these tools. The author identifies two governance gaps. The first is organizational: most companies haven't redesigned governance for a workforce that includes AI agents, or never had real governance at all. Breaches rarely stem from recklessness; as with decades of shadow IT, the business needed something, the official channel was slow, and employees found a faster route without grasping the security implications. The second is overly permissive systems: if a laptop lets someone install a plugin or upload a file to an outside AI tool with no friction, somebody will, simply because it's there. Closing one gap without the other leaves the door half-shut. The proposed solution is to treat agents like new hires rather than software. First, give each agent a scoped role matched to its specific function, not blanket access. Second, pair each agent with a named human owner, so that as agents trigger other agents, every action traces back to an accountable person. Third, grant the least privilege needed, which often means less access than the person overseeing the agent's output. For example, an agent permitted to search SharePoint can't know a compensation spreadsheet next to a sales forecast wasn't meant for its task. Fourth, review agents on a schedule. A Cloud Security Alliance survey found 68% of organizations can't reliably distinguish AI agent activity from human activity in their systems. The author's security team uses a simple test: could someone explain what a given agent did last Tuesday, who it was acting for, and why it was allowed to act? If not, the organization has a governance problem that the agent merely surfaced. The conclusion is that security fundamentals, including identity management, data governance and access controls, matter more than ever. AI amplifies what already exists: strong governance becomes stronger and weak governance more dangerous. The author says this is not an argument for moving slower; clear expectations and trust let organizations move fast, but AI raises the stakes of doing it well.

Hackers Are Using Fake Android Updates To Hijack Smart Car Displays. Cybersecurity researchers at Kaspersky have uncovered a malware downloader that targets Android-based automotive head units, marking the first documented case of malicious code explicitly engineered to compromise vehicle infotainment systems with the main intent of carrying out ad fraud. Investigative overlap in infrastructure, command structures, and internal code artifacts connects this automotive campaign to the MoYu Group, a threat actor affiliated with the notorious BadBox botnet. Historically known for infecting cheap Android TV streaming boxes and mobile devices straight from factory supply chains, BadBox operations have unfortunately expanded into automotive ecosystems to exploit persistent internet connections and low threat-monitoring coverage in cars. Kaspersky noted direct links between the campaign's command servers and administrative portals for commercial proxy platforms like ProxyForU and PXYEDGE. After being notified by Kaspersky (that also runs the banned antivirus software), DoFun has reportedly addressed the vulnerability. The discovered campaign basically disguises as legitimate software update mechanisms to covertly deploy backdoors, turning hijacked dashboard displays into unauthorized proxy relays and platforms for malicious activities. According to Kaspersky's report on the matter, the infection chain targets aftermarket and factory-installed head units running software from firmware developer DoFun. Rather than relying on tricking drivers into downloading malicious applications manually, the attackers breached the update channel of a legitimate system component called TWCore. Responsible for collecting device telemetry and pushing OTA system updates via an MQTT server hosted on cardoor[.]cn, TWCore was manipulated through a configuration setting known as installNotExists. This allowed the server to quietly force-install arbitrary application packages, specifically a stealthy dropper labeled JarService, onto connected vehicles without triggering user prompts or UI notifications. Once executed, JarService establishes communication with a remote command-and-control server, transmitting sensitive system metrics including the car unit's model, screen resolution, MAC address, and Wi-Fi network identifier. The multi-stage downloader then fetches secondary payloads, most notably a module named zhima with its primary objective of turning the infected infotainment system into a reverse proxy node. By routing external web traffic through the vehicle's active cellular or Wi-Fi data connection, threat actors can mask malicious online traffic, conduct automated click fraud, and lease residential proxy bandwidth to paying subscribers.

New York-based General Intuition, the startup building a foundation model that trains generalized AI agents to move through space and time, is in talks to raise funding at a $6 billion pre-money valuation from new investors including Valor Equity Partners, Point72 Ventures, and Seven Seven Six, according to sources familiar with the matter. Existing investors including Khosla Ventures and General Catalyst are also participating in the round. The fresh funds would come just weeks after General Intuition raised $320 million at a $2.3 billion valuation. The news confirms earlier reporting on the deal for what is becoming one of the hottest startups tackling physical AI. CEO Pim de Witte spun out General Intuition last October from his video game clip-sharing platform Medal, using its hundreds of millions of hours of gameplay and “action labels” — records of which buttons a player pressed and when — as an initial dataset. Investor Vinod Khosla recently told TechCrunch that he believes those action labels will be a key part of the “emergence of intuition,” or the ability for a model to truly generalize across tasks that it wasn’t explicitly trained on. General Intuition is still finalizing the round, and a source close to the deal said that it is oversubscribed as the startup continues to field interest from investors. The company intends to use the funds to focus to improve its general model with a focus on robotic embodiments. That means spending more on compute infrastructure (the company has a partnership with neolab CoreWeave) and hiring more talent. Valor Equity Partners is known for backing SpaceX. TechCrunch has reached out to confirm its investment in General Intuition, which would be the first AI lab the fund has invested in since SpaceX. This story is developing. Please check back in for updates.

Crypto advocacy groups oppose Illinois digital asset tax in court. Following a similar lawsuit filed by the Digital Chamber in July, two digital asset advocacy groups challenged Illinois’ 0.2% crypto tax on constitutional and due process grounds. The Crypto Council for Innovation (CCI) and Blockchain Association (BA) filed a lawsuit against Illinois officials regarding the state’s 0.2% tax on cryptocurrency, expected to be enforced starting in January 2027. In a lawsuit filed Friday in the Circuit Court of the Seventh Judicial Circuit for Sangamon County, lawyers for the two crypto advocacy groups challenged Illinois’ digital asset tax on the grounds it violated the US Constitution, the state’s constitution, federal and state due process laws and the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed the measure into law as a “privilege tax” in June as part of the state’s fiscal year 2027 budget, requiring crypto users to be taxed as applied to transaction volume rather than income. On the due process claim, CCI and BA argued that the tax was “unconstitutionally vague” by placing the burden on residents and brokers “under the threat of serious civil and criminal penalties” to determine what and how such assets were taxed. Notably, the crypto organizations’ arguments under the US Constitution were based on alleged violations of the Commerce Clause covering interstate commerce, claiming that the state tax “creat[ed] the specter of duplicative taxation.” “States have an important role to play in fostering innovation, but that authority has constitutional limits,” said Summer Mersinger, CEO of the Blockchain Association and a former commissioner at the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission. “Illinois cannot impose a novel tax regime that discriminates against digital commerce, creates uncertainty for consumers and businesses, and threatens to fragment a rapidly growing national market.” Source: Blockchain Association. The CCI and BA lawsuit followed a similar one filed by the Digital Chamber in July in which that organization argued that the Illinois tax “discriminates against people who transact in digital assets.“ The suits represented the influence of digital asset groups in opposition to laws passed by US state officials during an election year when crypto policy, laws and regulation could influence voters. Illinois also targeting prediction markets. Opposition to the crypto tax came amid prediction market platform Kalshi’s lawsuit against Illinois officials over a law that went into effect on July 1. According to the company, the legislation “expressly bans sports event contracts” in violation of federal law by requiring state licensing. Separately, Pritzker signed an executive order banning state employees from betting on the platforms in April in an effort to ”prevent insider trading amid the rapid growth of online prediction markets and event-based gambling contracts.” Magazine: Crypto industry ties were a liability in Illinois primary.

WildBrain, the Canadian children’s media company with the rights to titles such as “Yo Gabba Gabba!” and the “Teletubbies,” has purchased the child-focused generative AI startup Personality AI in a cash-and-stock deal worth up to $69 million in a bid to marry the company’s intellectual property with the startup’s conversational products. Personality AI touts its conversational character AIs as child-safe, working with a mixture of AI engineers, child development experts and entertainment producers to develop AI models based on licensed child characters that implement safeguards as children engage with them while not retaining child data. Amazon selected Personality AI last year to develop a platform on its kids-focused subscription service Amazon Kids+, leading to a “Peppa Pig”-based generative product for children to engage with the fictional British icon. The company is also part of the Federal Trade Commission-backed COPPA Safe Harbor Program, one of the leading independent oversight programs related to federal child privacy protections. WildBrain hopes the acquisition will boost the revenue opportunities for its array of IP, including “Degrassi” and “Strawberry Shortcake.” Popular on Variety. “Personality AI enables more continuous interaction between fans and brands, strengthening our ability to deliver end-to-end franchise solutions to partners,” WildBrain CEO and president Josh Sceherba said in a statement. “This highly complementary acquisition positions us and Personality AI as a more integrated partner to IP owners globally through our in-house licensing agency, WildBrain CPLG, while helping support the continued growth of both our owned and partner brands.” Wildbrain paid roughly $11 million in cash along with 1 million shares. Shareholders will also receive $2 million worth of WildBrain shares (up to 1 million shares) in additional consideration on the first anniversary of closing, with the remaining balance paid in cash. The deal also includes up to $56 million in performance-based cash consideration based on Personality AI’s revenue performance between 2027 and 2029. Personality CEO John Goscha will join WildBrain as the executive vice president for Personality AI and will report to Scherba. “I’m thrilled to be joining forces with WildBrain, a clear leader in family entertainment,” Goscha said in a statement. “At Personality AI, we share WildBrain’s commitment to children’s wellbeing, which is why we employ rigorous safety standards to ensure appropriate, authentic and trustworthy content and experiences for kids, parents and IP owners alike.”

More than 2,000 humanoid robots are competing at the second annual World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, according to Reuters. The five-day event began Saturday, August 22, and runs through August 26 at the National Speed Skating Oval, a 12,000-seat venue originally built for the 2022 Winter Olympics. Several robots beat human running records. Two ran the 100-meter sprint faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second world record: a Tiangong Ultra robot, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, finished in 9.39 seconds, and Honor's Lightning robot in 9.47 seconds. Another Tiangong Ultra robot won the 400 meters in 38.15 seconds, beating Wayde van Niekerk's human world record of 43.03 seconds. Days earlier, Unitree posted a video of its new "Superman" humanoid, which the company says can reach 12.66 meters per second, faster than Bolt's peak speed during his record run. Dexterous tasks remain harder than running. The Games have grown sharply from the inaugural 2025 edition: 666 teams registered with 2,056 robots, up from 280 teams and roughly 500 robots, and events nearly doubled from 26 to 51. Thirty are sports-based, including track and field, tug-of-war, weightlifting, soccer, and table tennis. The other 21 are scenario-based events testing jobs in factories, hotels, homes, and stores, such as book sorting, food and beverage service, fire rescue, and charging EVs. Eight of these focus on dexterous hand movements like opening lids, assembling power tools, unpacking boxes, connecting cables, and picking up beans with tweezers. The rules show which abilities are more advanced. Basic running races, soccer, table tennis, and dancing require autonomous operation, while harder events such as weightlifting, kickboxing, and jumping still allow remote control. In scenario-based events, robots get full credit for autonomous task completion but only half credit for remote-controlled completion. One robot training for the Games ran too fast, failed to stop, slammed into a safety cushion, and broke at the waist. The Games' website says the event brings together leading forces in robot research, development, and application, and aims to facilitate their faster and more effective integration into human life. The event comes as China pours support into robotics. In 2025, the country announced a state-backed venture capital fund aiming to attract 1 trillion yuan ($148 billion) in public and private investment for AI, robotics, and other high-tech startups over 20 years. The U.S., meanwhile, lacks a national robotics strategy that companies like Tesla and Boston Dynamics have urged lawmakers to develop to compete with China. The U.S. government has also increasingly treated Chinese robots as a national security concern: last month, the FCC moved to ban imports of foreign-made humanoid and other advanced robots over cybersecurity and supply chain risks.

ROME — The Italian Air Force is mulling the purchase of U.S. technology that turns cheap unguided missiles into precision weapons, offering a low-cost option for taking out drones instead of using pricy air-to-air missiles. The potential deal was made possible by the U.S. Department of State’s approval of a Foreign Military Sale to Italy of 5,031 BAE Systems Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) II guidance systems. The APKWS, which can be inserted between the warhead of an unguided missile and its motor, features four fold-out wings which each carry a laser seeker, turning a missile that costs less than €100,000 ($117,000) into a guided weapon. The solution would allow the Italian Air Force to avoid firing missiles like the AMRAAM - which costs ten times that - to destroy cheaply produced drones. “The proposed sale will improve Italy’s capability to meet current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense and serving as a deterrent to regional threats,” the State Department said. The FMS approval also covers launchers, warheads and rocket motors, as well as technical support, taking the potential deal to $364 million, the State Department added. Sources in Italy told Defense News no contract had been signed and the technology was still being evaluated. The likely recipient of the APKWS would be Italy’s Eurofighter jet, which is already guarding Europe’s borders against drone incursions. This month, an Italian Eurofighter taking part in NATO air policing mission in the Baltics shot down an unidentified drone which flew into Latvian airspace. In May, the Royal Air Force announced it was already using the system on its Eurofighters after a rapid acquisition which saw testing and deployment completed in two months. “The Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) gives RAF pilots a highly accurate option to destroy aerial targets and allows them to engage drones at a fraction of the cost of traditional air-to-air missiles,” the RAF said at the time. Tom Kington is the Italy correspondent for Defense News.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told analysts in July that if Amazon's chip operation were a standalone business, it would generate more than $25 billion in annual revenue, with sales growing at triple-digit percentages. The boast reflects how quickly the semiconductor landscape is changing. Nvidia remains the dominant data center chip maker, with roughly 90% of the AI accelerator market, but it faces rising competition from rivals, startups and its own biggest customers. Analysts expect its latest quarterly revenue to have nearly doubled year over year to $92 billion, more than any rival earns in a full year. Some Nvidia customers have reportedly been told server prices will rise more than 15%. The AI chip market is poised to cross $1 trillion in revenue. Longtime rivals are gaining ground. AMD's data center revenue more than doubled last quarter to $6.7 billion, and CEO Lisa Su expects the AI accelerator market to reach $1.4 trillion by 2030. Intel has had limited success with its own accelerators. Broadcom and Marvell build custom chips for clients such as Google. In China, US export controls bar Nvidia from selling its best products, spurring domestic alternatives like Huawei's. Startups are benefiting from the shift from training AI models to inference, which suits a wider range of processors. Jon Peddie Research counts 150 companies working on more than 200 AI chip designs. Nvidia charges about $30,000 per high-end chip with profit margins of about 75%, which motivates customers to seek alternatives. Cerebras held the industry's largest-ever chip IPO in May and has deals with OpenAI and Amazon; Positron, Fractile and Etched are also drawing rising valuations. Chip design takes years and hundreds of millions of dollars. Hyperscalers are building data centers faster than chip supply can keep up, so they are turning to in-house designs. Broadcom works with Google, Meta and others and expects to sell $56 billion of AI chips this year. Google also works with Marvell on its TPUs, will release two TPU versions this year, and now lets customers use them outside its own cloud. AI labs are following suit. Anthropic has lined up tens of billions of dollars in contracts for chips from Google, Amazon and AMD, and has approached SK Hynix about memory for its planned accelerator. OpenAI's Broadcom-built inference chip, Jalapeno, will deploy later this year, with refreshes planned for 2028 and annually after. Meta is pursuing various in-house designs, yet its Nvidia spending recently rose. Nvidia shares are up 15% in 2026, versus 66% for the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index. Nvidia agreed in December to pay a reported $20 billion for technology and personnel from inference startup Groq. It also holds supply commitments above $100 billion with TSMC, the dominant foundry, redesigns its products annually, and offers cooling, networking and storage technology. Rivals concede they lack its scale; Positron's CEO Mitesh Agrawal said no one is a true competitor until reaching a tenth of Nvidia's revenue. Even Amazon sends about a quarter of its capital expenditures to Nvidia.

On Aug. 19, IBM announced it had joined and cooled two modular cryogenic systems into a single ultra-cold environment, reaching temperatures below 15 millikelvin. The architecture is meant to eventually connect hundreds of quantum chips, addressing a major infrastructure challenge in scaling quantum computers. The milestone supports the roadmap for IBM's planned Quantum Starling system, targeted for 2029. IBM has committed more than $10 billion over the next five years to quantum computing through research, manufacturing, capital spending, acquisitions, and ecosystem expansion. IBM's hybrid cloud and AI businesses remain central to its financial performance, while quantum is a potentially transformative long-term opportunity. IBM, based in Armonk, New York, operates in more than 170 countries and has a market cap of $222 billion. Its stock has pulled back sharply in 2026. Shares closed at $235.68 on Aug. 21, down 21.43% year-to-date and 30% below the 52-week high of $332.46 reached June 2. The stock hit a 52-week low of $199.19 on July 23 amid concerns about slowing growth and a softer outlook, but has since risen 12.4% from the July 23 close of $206.65, and is up 8.65% over the past month. The quantum news produced little rally: shares rose just 1.9% on Aug. 19 and fell about 1.5% on Aug. 20. The stock trades at 19.13 times forward earnings, a discount to industry peers. Second-quarter 2026 results, released July 22, showed sharply slower growth as customers shifted budgets toward AI infrastructure, hurting the mainframe business. Revenue rose 1% year-over-year to $17.2 billion, while net income fell 1% to $2.2 billion, or $2.27 per share. Non-GAAP operating EPS rose 5% to $2.93, and operating pre-tax income rose 3% to $3.3 billion, though operating gross margin fell 0.7 percentage point to 59.4%. Software revenue grew 5% to $7.8 billion, with Hybrid Cloud/Red Hat up 11% and Data up 19%, while Transaction Processing fell 8%. Consulting was flat at $5.3 billion. Infrastructure revenue fell 7% to $3.8 billion, with IBM Z mainframe revenue down 42% and Distributed Infrastructure up 37%. Financing revenue rose 12% to $0.2 billion. Operating cash flow was $2.6 billion, up from $1.7 billion a year earlier; for the first six months it rose to $7.8 billion from $6.1 billion, with free cash flow flat at $4.8 billion. IBM returned $1.6 billion to shareholders via dividends in the quarter. Management lowered its 2026 constant-currency revenue growth outlook to 4% to 5%, from above 5%. Analysts expect fiscal 2026 EPS of about $12.33, up 6.4%, and $13.23 in fiscal 2027, up 7.3%. On July 29, CITIC Securities kept a "Buy" rating and raised its price target to $297 from $294. On July 24, Susquehanna kept a "Neutral" rating but cut its target to $225 from $303. The consensus rating is "Moderate Buy" among 24 analysts: 11 "Strong Buy," two "Moderate Buy," 10 "Hold," and one "Strong Sell." The average price target of $251.87 implies 8.4% upside, while the Street-high target of $365 implies up to 57.1%.

With their biggest event of the year, Boston Blockchain Week, just weeks away, Ian Cain and John O’Keeffe should be focused on getting ready. But the cofounders of nonprofit Qubic Labs are also focused on something else: keeping their fintech startup incubator and accelerator alive. They had pursued a state grant from the Mass. Technology Collaborative, only to be rejected because of financial pressures and the fact that Qubic was a previous recipient. So they sent an email to the area’s community of “digital asset” startups, asking for help and expressing concern that state officials are no longer deploying money strategically to help startups here, unlike other states. “That decision put us in a precarious position,” Cain says now, of the grant denial. “It clarified what we needed to do, which was turning to our community.” The response was reassuring, with pledges of financial gifts and in-kind support. However, the donations don’t yet add up to the total Qubic needs to maintain its programming. Qubic got its start nearly seven years ago, as a startup incubator and accelerator in a Quincy Center office donated by FoxRock Properties, Rob Hale’s real estate group. Things took off in 2022, when the nonprofit received a $1.9 million grant from MassTech. That allowed Qubic to give out $600,000 worth of grants to startup founders and to host two 12-week accelerator programs in Quincy, and to help cover the cofounders’ salaries as well as those of two other staffers and several contractors. Cain says the money from that grant ran out late last year. Qubic also took over Boston Blockchain Week in 2022 from Pillar VC, the local venture capital firm; Cain says the event remains a break-even affair. More than 100 speakers are lined up for the event in September, though none with the star power of Fidelity Investments chief executive Abby Johnson, who spoke at the event in 2025. Qubic’s cofounders will continue to seek donations and brainstorm “business development” ideas — that is, ways to sell their startup services to potential clients. “The problem is not totally solved,” Cain says. “We’ll continue either way. I think it’s just a question of what scale. ... There’s this broader conversation around the Mass. economy and us losing out. We feel the work that we do is vital to its future success.” This is an installment of our weekly Bold Types column about the movers and shakers on Boston’s business scene. Homebuyers are using AI-powered brokerages to cut the legwork traditionally done by agents while keeping a human broker for offers, contracts and closing, avoiding percentage-based commissions. TurboHome, launched in late 2024, charges a flat fee at closing and rebates any larger seller-paid buyer-agent commission to the buyer. On a $1.5 million home with a 3% commission, it would receive $45,000, keep a $12,000 fee and rebate $33,000. Rebates can cover closing costs, buy down a mortgage rate, or, depending on the transaction and lender, be taken as cash. The company says it has facilitated 388 transactions totaling $440 million, ranging from $200,000 to $12 million, completed deals in 76 cities in California and Texas in Q2, and that buyers won 49% of offers that quarter. It has 14 agents; regional managers are salaried and most local agents are independent contractors. CEO Ben Bear says the model targets buyers who already search listings themselves. He cited that 80% of people find homes on Zillow, and a Q2 2026 ResiClub survey in which 77% of US homeowners said they found their most recent home themselves versus 22% whose agent did. TurboHome's new dashboard lets customers search conversationally, request valuations and comparable sales, book tours, begin drafting offers, and chat with both an AI assistant and a human agent. AI handles comparable-sales analysis, disclosure reviews and recommendations, while agents focus on advice and negotiation. Bear said agents close 30 to 50 deals a year, versus a Consumer Federation of America finding that 70% of agents sold five or fewer homes in 12 months. He acknowledged regional flat-fee brokerages also offer rebates, but said few pair them with an AI-native platform and licensed agents. Bob Miller of Millshire Realty in Lakeland, Fla., said AI brokerages could pressure commissions, especially on simpler, lower-priced deals, but won't end the agent; complex and high-end transactions still need human judgment, and agents will have to prove what their expertise is worth. He also flagged privacy and consumer-protection concerns. TurboHome says it uses third-party AI models without training them on consumer data and does not send customers' names, emails or phone numbers to outside entities. Buyers described real savings. Ravi Surampudi, a Workday software engineer, bought a $1.125 million home in Prosper, Texas; the builder paid a 3% commission ($33,750), TurboHome kept $12,000, and he receives $21,750. Letty Neuendorff, near Houston, got a $6,150 credit on a $410,000 home in Clear Lake, closing in 15 days with her agent's help and praising communication. Melissa Pereira bought a $625,000 home in Roseville, Calif.; TurboHome charged the seller its $9,000 flat fee, which let the price be lowered, saving her about $10,000. Bear said routine tasks will increasingly be automated, with the exception of the human-to-human element. Pereira said buyers wanting an agent to spend weekends finding and showing homes wouldn't be a good fit, but those wanting negotiation, contract and closing expertise would.

Applied Materials (AMAT) shares have fallen more than 34% from their 52-week high, largely reflecting profit-taking after a strong rally. While the stock has dropped significantly, the pullback has created an attractive entry point for investors. The key reason for the bullish case is the strong AI-led demand environment. As AI adoption accelerates, semiconductor manufacturers are committing significant capital to developing more advanced chips and expanding production capacity. This investment cycle is creating a favorable demand environment for Applied Materials, whose equipment and engineering solutions are critical to semiconductor manufacturing. Applied Materials is also investing in additional manufacturing capacity to support strong demand through the end of the decade. These investments suggest the company is positioning itself to capitalize on strong demand for semiconductor equipment. Applied Materials Positioned for Sustained Growth. Applied Materials is delivering solid growth. Its Q3 revenue reached a record $9.1 billion, up 15% sequentially and 25% year over year. Adjusted gross margin rose to 50.4%, while adjusted operating margin expanded to a record 34%. Adjusted EPS increased 22% sequentially and 41% year-over-year (YoY) to $3.50. Strong revenue growth and expanding margins suggest Applied Materials is scaling efficiently, with earnings growing faster than operating expenses. Looking ahead, AMAT’s growth outlook remains strong, strengthening the company’s bullish case. The broader demand environment has strengthened for Applied Materials. Cloud service providers continue to increase spending on AI infrastructure, while improving returns on these investments are giving them greater confidence to sustain capital spending. This creates a potentially durable demand cycle for Applied Materials. At the customer level, most leading-edge logic and DRAM facilities are operating at high utilization. Demand also remains strong in AI-related applications such as power and optical chips. Further, as semiconductor capacity expansion broadens, Applied Materials is likely to deliver solid growth. The company has raised its expectations for Semiconductor Systems revenue in calendar 2026 and expects to outperform the broader semiconductor equipment market. More importantly, management sees the strength continuing into fiscal 2027, supported by improved visibility into customer demand. The primary growth driver is the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. Rising AI demand is increasing investment in advanced chips, memory, and semiconductor manufacturing capacity, creating a favorable environment for Applied Materials. Management expects record performance to continue through the second half of the calendar year, driven particularly by a sharp increase in DRAM and leading-edge foundry-logic revenue. AMAT’s Margin Expansion Strengthens the Growth Case. Applied Materials’ growth outlook is supported not only by rising revenue but also by its ability to expand margins. The company’s value-based pricing strategy is enabling it to capture higher prices across both new and existing products, helping offset elevated input costs and supporting profitability. At the same time, ongoing cost-efficiency initiatives are creating additional support for margins. The company also appears to be benefiting from improving operating leverage. Applied Materials is accelerating new-product development while becoming more efficient across its support functions, with general and administrative expenses falling to their lowest share of operating expenses in the company’s history. This suggests that the business is generating greater efficiency as it scales. The key implication is that margin expansion could become an important second driver of earnings growth. If revenue continues to grow faster than the company’s cost base, incremental sales should translate into stronger operating profit growth. This combination of revenue growth, pricing power, and operating leverage strengthens the overall investment case and creates potential upside to earnings. The Bottom Line. The 33% decline in AMAT stock does not automatically make it a bargain, but it does make the risk-reward profile more compelling. The combination of rising AI-driven semiconductor demand, stronger revenue expectations for 2026, and continued growth anticipated in 2027 provides a compelling foundation for the bull case. Analysts remain optimistic, with a “Strong Buy” consensus rating on AMAT stock. Amazon is developing a new generation of highly automated warehouses that use AI and robotics to process packages at the final stop before delivery. The initiative, internally called Project Tetromino, is intended to build "fully automated" delivery stations, according to an internal planning document from last month that Business Insider reviewed. Delivery stations are the final facility in the shipping process, receiving packaged items from fulfillment centers before sorting and staging them for drivers to deliver to customers. According to the document, Amazon planned to invest $103 million in an initial Tetromino pilot in 2028, followed by five sites in 2029 and 10 more in 2030. Each 2029 site could cost about $85 million, bringing the total Tetromino investment to more than $530 million by 2029, the document said. It also said Tetromino could process packages at roughly 2.5 times the rate of its existing delivery station design. An Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider that this is an "early-stage concept" and the specific financial figures and road map in the document are "inaccurate and don't reflect our current plans." "We're always exploring and testing new technologies across our operations to improve safety and the delivery experience for customers," the spokesperson said. "Like any early-stage concept, this is one of many initiatives we regularly evaluate, and plans evolve significantly as we learn." Tetromino offers a glimpse of how Amazon is trying to automate one of the most stubbornly manual parts of its logistics network. Industry analysts say tasks such as organizing and loading packages into vehicles at delivery stations remain difficult and expensive to automate. The project comes as Amazon accelerates a broader warehouse automation push. On its latest earnings call in July, the company said it expects to more than double its fleet of robotic arms in 2026. Business Insider previously reported that Amazon is also deploying software that automatically recommends where warehouse workers should be assigned as workloads change. Amazon's Tetris-like challenge. One of Tetromino's key technologies could come from Boxbot, an AI and robotics supply chain startup, according to the planning document. Boxbot's system moves packages from conveyors onto trays for storage, then uses AI to retrieve and sequence them for delivery. Boxbot's website says the system can make the vehicle-loading process up to 10 times faster. Boxbot did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The Tetromino name itself may be a nod to the game Tetris, reflecting the puzzle-like challenge of efficiently organizing packages for delivery vehicles. Amazon isn't alone in trying to automate these tasks. FedEx is expanding its use of AI-powered Dexterity robots that autonomously load packages into trailers, while UPS and DHL use robots for unloading. The Amazon spokesperson also pointed to delivery station pilots announced last year as part of a €700 million investment in European facilities, including machines that unload, sort, and scan packages. The push toward more automated facilities raises questions about what Amazon's warehouses will ultimately need humans to do. Amazon robotics chief Tye Brady previously told Business Insider that robots are intended to make frontline work safer and more efficient, not replace employees. Nevertheless, Amazon has internally projected that some warehouse robots will "flatten" its hiring curve over the next decade, Business Insider previously reported. The Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider the company's delivery-station initiatives are "designed to complement and empower our workforce and employees remain central to how we operate." Alabama’s attorney general announced Monday that it sent a subpoena to OpenAI as part of an investigation into the company’s alleged “complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards” in the Hugging Face incident. The investigation comes weeks after OpenAI admitted that one of its unreleased and guardrail-free cybersecurity models had escaped an isolated environment, connected to the internet, and hacked AI dataset platform Hugging Face. As Reuters first reported, Hugging Face was only one of four victims of what was supposed to be “an internal evaluation” of a model with “maximal cyber capabilities,” as OpenAI put it. The press release announcing the subpoena sent by the state’s attorney general Steve Marshall said that the state was seeking to understand if OpenAI’s “inability or unwillingness to ensure the safety of its products” violated the state’s consumer protection laws. When reached by TechCrunch for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans provided the statement: “The Hugging Face incident marked an important moment for AI safety and we are conducting a thorough review along with external advisors. Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly.” Earlier this month, Marshall, along with the attorneys general of 14 other states, including Florida, Missouri, Pennsylvania, and Texas, sent a letter to OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman, requesting that he and his company preserve all records related to the Hugging Face incident. The letter also asked OpenAI to “immediately cease and desist” from any internal cybersecurity evaluations. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, and several other incidents disclosed by Anthropic, the U.K.’s AI Security Institute, Meta, and workers at AI companies — including executives and technical leaders — signed an open letter called “Pacing the Frontier,” which called for developing AI capabilities slowly and more responsibly. The letter also called for the U.S. government to support an “international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Updated with comment from OpenAI.

The day's themes: capital is concentrated rather than uniformly abundant; physical AI is spreading to supporting layers like optics, communications and developer tools; strategic investors are backing technical bottlenecks; enterprise AI is funded where it improves measurable workflows; and energy is entering the AI investment thesis. Smaller winners succeed through specificity, capital efficiency and non-model defensibility, with investors betting scarcity will persist in connectivity, robot manufacturing, grid capacity and reliable enterprise data.

Xpeng (XPEV) shares tanked on Aug. 24 after the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer’s Q2 earnings missed estimates and management issued disappointing guidance for the future. The company now sees its revenue falling between RMB21.7 billion and RMB23.4 billion in the third quarter, well below RMB26.69 billion that analysts had forecast. Following today’s decline, Xpeng stock is down roughly 45% versus the start of this year. Robotics Business Makes Xpeng Stock Worth Owning. Long-term investors nonetheless have reason to be excited about XPEV shares. Why? Because alongside earnings, the Chinese company said its robotics business has raised over $900 million in its first funding round, securing a post-money valuation exceeding $6.3 billion. The financing, backed by major investors including Tencent (TCEHY) and Alibaba (BABA), represents a record single private funding round for Beijing’s embodied-AI sector. Xpeng plans on using the proceeds to accelerate robotics hardware and software development, physical-AI models, data collection, manufacturing capacity, and overseas expansion. The NYSE-listed firm also aims to produce 1,000 IRON humanoid robots per month by the end of 2026 — with initial deployments at retail and industrial locations and broader commercialization targeted for 2027. Should You Buy the Post-Earnings Dip in XPEV Shares? The robotics business announcement is significant given it signals potential upside that may not be fully reflected in Xpeng shares’ valuation yet. XPEV remains attractive also because the strength in its services and other businesses helped drive a 340bps year-on-year increase in the firm’s overall gross margin to 20.7% in its second quarter. In short, investors are fixating on the muted near-term outlook for now. WildBrain, the Canadian animation studio that owns and manages a huge library of family entertainment including Teletubbies, Strawberry Shortcake, Yo Gabba Gabba! and Inspector Gadget, has acquired 100% of Personality AI, a generative AI startup focused on bringing character experiences to life. The immediate purchase price was USD $11 million in cash plus 1 million WildBrain shares. The company didn’t disclose the value of the shares, which closed on the Toronto Stock Exchange Monday at CAD $1.47. Personality stakeholders will receive another $2 million on the first anniversary of closing, payable in up to 1 million WildBrain shares with any balance in cash. The deal terms also call for additional performance-based cash consideration up to U.S. $56 million in aggregate tied to Personality AI’s business hitting certain revenue targets in 2027, 2028 and 2029 — a move to align the interests of Personality AI’s management, led by founded and CEO John Goscha, with WildBrain shareholders and incentivize continued growth. Watch on Deadline. Goscha will join WildBrain’s executive leadership team as EVP, Personality AI, reporting to WildBrain president and chief executive Josh Scherba. WildBrain is bringing in Personality’s team of experts in app and product creation under Goscha. The deal adds a new core capability and category to WildBrain’s global licensing, franchise management and content production, introducing scalable character experiences that can be built once and deployed anywhere. The goal is to enable deeper consumer engagement with entertainment IP beyond traditional licensing and content. “Our strategy at WildBrain is centred on building long-term value by activating IP on a global scale. As fan engagement continues to evolve, we believe interactive AI experiences represent an important new opportunity for brands to connect with audiences in meaningful ways,” Scherba said. “Personality AI enables more continuous interaction between fans and brands, strengthening our ability to deliver end-to-end franchise solutions to partners” and IP owners. Personality AI shares “WildBrain’s commitment to children’s wellbeing, which is why we employ rigorous safety standards to ensure appropriate, authentic and trustworthy content and experiences for kids, parents and IP owners alike. I look forward to working with Josh and the WildBrain management team to bring our capabilities to more brands, platforms and audiences around the world,” said Goscha, who launched the AI platform in 2025. An example of Personality AI’s work includes a generative platform for Amazon Kids+ last year. Projects include Hey Peppa Pig, an interactive voice experience developed with Hasbro that lets kids talk with Peppa Pig through games and activities inspired by the brand’s official series. WildBrain’s licensing division will handle Personality AI deals with third parties.

Songs created with the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) have been banned from Australia’s music charts as a new prohibition enforced by the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) launched this week. ARIA’s decision to modify its Code of Practice and ban AI-generated tracks comes after a cover of Madonna’s 1989 hit song Like a Prayer by Queensland-based DJ Josh Fawaz hit the top of the Australian music charts in July after spending weeks in the top 20. The cover, released earlier this year, features AI-generated vocals and drums — prompting fierce backlash in Australia against the artist, who reportedly added an AI disclaimer in the song’s credits in response to the criticism. The BBC reports that the controversial cover song has since then become a “staple” in Australian radio stations, with over 48 million streams in Spotify alone. In response to the controversy, ARIA imposed a ban on AI-generated songs from its charts. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) detailed that, as per the terms of the new rules, songs whole generated with Artificial Intelligence will not be eligible for the Australian music charts — however, tracks featuring AI in a supporting role will reportedly remain eligible. Said tracks, the ABC explained, must be “substantially human-made” and raise “no stream or chart manipulation concerns.” Artists must also disclose if AI was used in a song. The changes will apply to ARIA’s upcoming August 31 charts. “These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is, to say the least, a rapidly developing space,” ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said in a statement, per the BBC. “Artists already use AI tools in their work, the charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists’ recordings is a different matter,” she continued, and added, “A chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent.” As part of the new changes, ARIA may refuse to accept a recording, reposition or remove a track from the Australian music charts, and withdraw any awards if it is later revealed that a song was largely generated with the use of AI. Artists may challenge these decisions should they decided to do so. Australian music producers and artists have expressed vocal criticism on the emergence of AI-generated tracks into the nation’s music charts. The Guardian reported in June that several Australian musicians elevated their protest after it was discovered that millions of tracks — including vast catalogues from Australian artists — were scrapped off the internet to train AI music models without due permission. The AI-generated cover of Madonna’s Like a Prayer, which is attributed to ARIA’s new rule changes, drew fierce criticism from local artists after it hit the top of the charts in July. Music producer Mitch Thomas told ABC at the time that’s biggest issue on the subject is how AI music is made from training a dataset of of music and copyrighted materials taken from artists who never consented to have their works scraped. “We dislike when people use steroids and cheat in competition because we acknowledge that that’s unfair and I think the same is true in music,” Thomas said in July.

ARIA Sets AI Eligibility Rules for Its Charts, Barring Wholly AI-Generated Tracks. To qualify, a recording must be "substantially human-made" and raise "no stream or chart manipulation concerns." The Australian Recording Industry Association has become the first national chart body to implement eligibility rules for recordings made with generative AI, confirming that wholly AI-generated tracks will be barred from the ARIA Charts. Recordings that use AI in a supporting role remain eligible; tracks generated wholesale by AI do not. The changes take effect from the chart dated Monday, Aug. 31. To qualify, a recording must be “substantially human-made” and raise “no stream or chart manipulation concerns,” with ARIA applying the global music industry’s AI labelling standard, announced July 10, to tell AI-generated recordings from AI-assisted ones. The move implements the global principles set by the IFPI and the major labels earlier this year — ARIA being the first national chart body to adopt them with a firm date. “Artists already use AI tools in their work, the charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists’ recordings is a different matter,” ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said. She added that “a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent,” and urged other decision-makers, “particularly radio,” to adopt similar codes. The rules carry teeth. ARIA can decline to survey an ineligible recording, remove it from the charts, adjust positions, withdraw accreditations, and revoke any ARIA No. 1 Award; ineligible tracks are also barred from the ARIA Awards. Artists can contest exclusions through an updated disputes process. The policy arrives as AI-generated music has begun testing the boundaries of chart systems worldwide. The AI country act Breaking Rust reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Country Digital Song Sales chart in 2025, and in April 2026 the AI act IngaRose topped iTunes charts in the U.S. and globally — cases that focused industry attention on the absence of any chart rules governing AI. Neither involved detected streaming fraud; both drew on real purchases or organic interest on narrower charts. ARIA said it will keep the code under review as AI policy and technology continue to develop.

The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China. At Physical Intelligence, a San Francisco-based startup, cofounder and researcher Sergey Levine is building the models, or brains, designed to provide intelligence for a range of robots — be they warehouse robots or humanoid machines. Physical Intelligence is one of many startups in Silicon Valley working on robotics software. In an episode of The Peterman Pod published Monday, Levine said the US robotics industry has its own advantages against competition abroad, but the one area that could significantly advance America's progress is building the hardware supply chain. "Availability of reliable low-cost hardware is a big deal. And right now, hardware used for robotics research — a lot of that does come from China," Levine said. "It's good. It's relatively inexpensive. It's of high quality and meets the standards that people generally need. But it'd be awfully nice to be able to source all of that domestically as well. I don't think there's anything impossible about that." Building an AI capable of making robots smart enough to handle a wide range of tasks is only part of the industry's challenge. In the US in particular, robotics leaders have said sourcing the physical components for robots — the motors, chassis, batteries, sensors, and other materials — will be a major bottleneck for scaling, and that companies often rely on China to fill the gaps. "The United States is no longer competitive in manufacturing, and we're falling further behind every day. Any company that builds hardware can tell you that if you source from China instead of making it here, it's generally 5 to 10 times cheaper," Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, said during a congressional hearing in April. A June analysis from McKinsey found that China holds a "significant share of capacity" for robotics parts, including 90% of permanent-magnet processing. China's progress, according to the report, is due in part to its electric vehicle ecosystem, which shares some of the components needed in robots. US robotics executives and policymakers say China's rapid progress in robotics and AI — combined with a strong manufacturing base — could hamper America's ability to effectively compete in what they view as a critical emerging industry. The concern is heightened as Washington sees China as a strategic adversary. In July, the Federal Communications Commission effectively blocked new foreign-made humanoids and other advanced robots from entering the US market, citing national security concerns. While US manufacturers welcomed the move, some researchers and startups told Business Insider's robotics reporter, Rya Jetha, that the ban locks out access to affordable hardware. Levine said in the podcast that "different industries that contribute to robotics need to individually be very healthy." "I think that it's important to sort of fully embrace that this is a holistic thing and not something where we can do just one piece of it and outsource everything else," he said. Have a tip?
