Hugging Face and Pollen Robotics open pre-orders for the $399 Microduck. The small robot is highly mobile and can pick up objects with its articulated beak. Hugging Face has announced its latest robot, and it's a real quacker. Pollen Robotics (acquired by Hugging Face last year) said in a blog post that the excellently-named Microduck was imagined as a more action-oriented alternative to its Reachy Mini desktop robot. Standing at 25cm tall and weighing under 800g, Microduck is a biped robot with 15 motors, a built-in camera and a small LiDAR sensor. It also has two IMUs and an articulated beak that is able to pick up objects. Where the Reachy Mini was a stationary robot built around human-robot communication, with Microduck, Hugging Face has focused on mobility. According to its maker, the water bird-inspired bot's various motors, spread across its legs, head and neck, allow it to "walk, sit, crouch, get back up from many common falls, and even roller-skate." It's aimed at developers and robotics enthusiasts who want to experiment with how AI-powered robots move through the world and deal with obstacles or accidents. Key to this trial and error philosophy is Microduck's diminutive stature. A large humanoid robot taking lots of tumbles raises both safety and financial concerns, whereas Microduck can pick itself back up and doesn't hit the floor with a huge impact if something goes wrong (that is, provided you don't have ill-advised plans to turn it into a death-defying stunt duck). Hugging Face said it decided on the duck branding as it made the most sense given the robot's "proportions, beak and waddling gait." Like real ducks, Microduck can come in a number of different colors, which Hugging Face said makes a number of its robots standing together "look like a collection of different characters rather than identical machines." The company also said it learned internally using a number of the robots at the same time is unsurprisingly "about ten times more fun," and seemingly even managed to get them playing soccer together. The announcement post isn't too heavy on technical detail. But the main Microduck repository, which is available today, includes the SDK and robot software, with the Microduck RL containing reinforcement learning tools. You can control the robot with a gamepad or have it follow a laser dot right out of the box, and its pre-learned behaviors mean it reacts to its surroundings and various movement triggers without you needing to code it all in. More technically savvy developers can take advantage of the open-source nature of the software stack to go more in depth with the available movement and simulation options. Unlike the Reachy Mini (and exactly like actual ducks), the Microduck doesn't use words, but instead communicates through sound (there's a built-in microphone and speaker), and Hugging Face says each robot has its own "audio identity" that is permanent after setup. You're supposed to think of it as a living creature rather than a robot assistant. You can pre-order Microduck today for $399, with four colorways on offer: Cream, Graphite, Lavender and Sky. The robot has 32GB of storage and 1GB of onboard RAM, and supports both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The 2,600mAH battery should be good for around one hour of continuous runtime. Hugging Face says it aims to dispatch its first round of orders before Christmas in the US.

Test drivers for Waymo and Zoox sustained more than two dozen injuries in 2024 and 2025 from hard braking or other sudden movements by autonomous vehicles, according to a TechCrunch review of data submitted to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). The injuries include sprains, strains and whiplash, and some workers were sidelined for weeks or months. Transdev, which employs and manages Waymo's test drivers, reported 16 injuries tied to Waymo depot locations in three cities, caused by the software braking hard or swerving suddenly. Zoox reported as many as eight worker injuries linked to hard braking. Other autonomous vehicle companies don't appear in the dataset, possibly because they are exempt. Waymo and Zoox appear because they classify themselves as taxi, limo or transit services, which OSHA treats as "higher-hazard" industries; only establishments with 100 or more employees must make data public, so injuries in newer cities may be missing. TechCrunch could not learn whether any 2026 injuries were logged, since annual data is due the following year. Waymo's injuries rose as it scaled. Its commercial fleet grew from more than 1,500 vehicles in May 2025 to more than 3,500 today. Transdev reported five Waymo test driver injuries in 2024 across San Francisco, Los Angeles and Phoenix, one from hard braking and four from erratic behavior. In one case, the car "suddenly backed up" while parking and "whipped the steering wheel," bending a driver's hand until his wrist cracked; he missed more than two months of work. Injuries jumped to 11 in 2025, nearly all from hard braking. A Phoenix driver spent 157 days away from work after an "exaggerated breaking [sic] event without any obstruction," and at least two other reports say the braking had no apparent reason. In August in Los Angeles, a robotaxi stopped hard when "some kids were playing in the pathway," and the worker was out 175 days. Two current and three former Zoox contractors said test vehicles, modified Toyota Highlander SUVs, were still braking hard as recently as July, and three said workers are still getting hurt. They said "brake jabs" can happen multiple times per drive, often when the system detects, or mistakenly detects, road debris. The worst are "nogos," full system shutdowns that often cause a brake jab, even at 45 mph. Seven of Zoox's eight reports mention hard braking, nogos or brake jabs. Examples include a January 5, 2025 San Francisco stop that injured a contractor's shoulder and arm (16 days restricted duty), another "unexpected" stop that injured a neck and shoulder, and a June 3 injury to a back-seat instructor when software "braked harshly." The eighth, a worker sidelined 46 days after "extreme back pain" in Las Vegas, was attributed to a "vehicle maneuver." Four 2025 injuries came after Zoox issued a recall to resolve a year-long federal investigation into unexpected braking; Zoox said the recall addressed a narrow behavior and the later incidents were unrelated. Zoox declined to answer specific questions, saying it follows reporting requirements, takes injuries seriously, that hard braking is sometimes unavoidable, and that the injuries are a small share of millions of test miles. Waymo also declined to address the injuries, citing safety as paramount and tens of millions of miles driven with human operators as part of validation. Transdev declined to comment. Zoox, owned by Amazon, began charging for rides in its purpose-built robotaxi in Las Vegas this month. Its purpose-built vehicles lack steering wheels or pedals and mostly carry non-employees, so any injuries there wouldn't reach OSHA. Zoox has reported two crashes to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in eight months in which hard braking for debris led to rear-end collisions.

This week's threats show attackers exploiting cheap trust and low friction, from fake pages and apps to AI-assisted botnets and blockchain command channels. ReliaQuest confirmed an employee was targeted on August 22, 2026, when attackers registered a lookalike domain, built a fake SSO page behind a CDN, and called several staff posing as a named security employee. One teammate entered a password and approved a push notification, giving the attacker a brief view-only session on an identity dashboard; no applications, systems or customer data were touched. The playbook matches ShinyHunters-style extortion crews, and ShinyHunters listed the company on its dark web portal. Fake productivity apps (Kitchen Canvas, DocConvertWizard and others) are Electron-based and can run injected scripts and capture the desktop. Cisco Talos described "JWR," a phishing framework, probably a variant of The Outsider PhaaS platform, that keeps an encrypted WebSocket open so operators steer victim sessions live and collect identity documents, SSNs, credentials, 2FA codes and device fingerprints. iVerify disclosed Octagon, an Android fraud bot rented for $1,400 a month by AndroidKitKat. Zscaler found C2Looper, a Rust backdoor likely used by a ransomware-linked actor, delivered via ClickFix, and Abyssos, a modular C++ RAT first seen in June 2026. Botnet news: Dysphoria has compromised nearly 296,000 IoT devices, mainly for DDoS, and recently gained residential proxy functionality. Unit 42 said the Aeternum loader moved its C2 entirely to the public Polygon blockchain, complicating takedowns. ToxNetV2 uses an LLM via NVIDIA NIM to suggest actions that operators approve before execution. Stealers continue to spread: Phantom Stealer, Salat Stealer (Go), Vanta Stealer (Python), DARTHVADER, DestinyStealer and ScarfaceStealer, which scores hosts on 11 indicators and loops decoy message boxes at a score of 7 or higher. LevelBlue reported the CNCMachineRMS RAT delivered via BabaDeda Loader; PavinLoader uses EtherHiding and ClickFix to deliver Amatera Stealer. Malwarebytes flagged 11 fake sites running bogus antivirus scans that push users to uninstall security software. Proofpoint tied the Telegram-sold PackClient RAT to Chinese-speaking TA4922, which used tax-themed lures. Blackpoint found the Miraak framework using cloud PostgreSQL/Timescale for C2. Fortra described "Chameleon SEO Poisoning," cloaked search results leading to cloned banking portals, and VMRay saw a fake Google Translate Chrome extension enabling remote control and StealC delivery. Vulnerabilities: an unpatched HP ThinPro 8 and 9 boot-chain flaw can let physical attackers bypass TPM full-disk encryption. A Microsoft Purview stored XSS, now fixed, allowed token theft via a Teams message, email or Copilot prompt. Defused Cyber saw exploitation attempts on SharePoint flaws CVE-2026-55040 and CVE-2026-63520, with no code execution observed yet. Pillar Security described Deadbugz, a malicious MCP server that changes its instructions after three tool calls to seek SSH keys and cloud credentials. Reco found only 20% of AI tools have IT oversight, and 62% of 500 analyzed agent tools can both read local data and reach the internet. Kaspersky blocked over 1.99 million mobile attacks in Q2 2026, with Trojan-Banker the top category at 30.77%. Microsoft warned that patch windows are shrinking and proposed a network-centered control layer, and is piloting per-app camera, microphone and location controls in Windows 11. The Linux Foundation announced the TRACE attestation standard. CISA said Iranian actors targeted over 100 internet-exposed U.S. water systems in July through cellular-modem-connected PLCs.

Lenders say artificial intelligence will help homeowners secure cheaper refinanced mortgages far faster, which could also squeeze investors in the $9 trillion mortgage bond market. When rates fall, only about a third of homeowners who could save substantially by refinancing do so, according to Morgan Stanley, because they don't know they're eligible or dislike the tedious process. That number may rise as lenders use AI to speed approvals. Rocket Mortgage says a borrower can go from application to rate lock in 30 minutes and aims for 10; United Wholesale Mortgage says initial approval can take 15 minutes; Better.com claims two. Morgan Stanley strategists, including Jay Bacow, say faster turnaround could double the share of eligible homeowners who refinance to perhaps 60%, making the 30-year mortgage seem "closer to a floating-rate instrument that only floats down." That would benefit lenders and borrowers but could erode returns for bond investors, whose higher-rate income streams would be cut off sooner, forcing reinvestment at lower rates. Loans might become costlier as investors demand perhaps one or two tenths of a percentage point extra, and mortgage-backed securities could trade like pure callable bonds. Alternatively, borrowers may come out ahead, and the easier process could motivate reluctant customers. Baird's Kirill Krylov said AI "should crush behavioral friction," though it won't help borrowers who fail requirements such as sufficient income. The impact is hard to gauge with mortgage rates stubbornly above 6.5%, muting refinancing demand. Better.com's chief technology officer Ziggy Jonsson said borrowers might consider refinancing when rates fall just 10 basis points if costs and hassles drop. Closings still involve legally required review time, and regulations require licensed humans rather than a sole AI "black box." But labor is about two-thirds of mortgage creation costs, so Morgan Stanley said closing costs might fall near zero and refinancing become near-frictionless. Rocket has invested more than $500 million in AI and automation over six years, CEO Varun Krishna told investors in May. Its agentic AI can sort current clients, decide how and when to contact them, and assess refinancing interest. Some lenders use software that pulls data from tax forms and bank statements into a borrower profile, eliminating weeks of work, and borrowers can use AI programs that prompt them to refinance. Skeptics remain. Jeffrey Kvalevog of New American Funding noted similar claims about optical character recognition, automated calling and email, saying "People tend to sensationalize how much AI is going to save you." Upfront fees for appraisals, lawyers and mortgage taxes may still deter applicants, and there is little evidence yet that behavior is changing. Mark Tecotzky of Ellington Management Group called prepayment data "evolutionary as opposed to revolutionary." The real test for bondholders will come when rates drop significantly. FHN Financial's Walt Schmidt said, "We haven't had a good refinancing wave since AI became a thing."

China Is Building 100,000 Humanoid Robots. They Still Struggle With Basic Jobs. A new report found a widening gap between China's massive investment in humanoid robotics and what the machines can actually accomplish in factories and other workplaces. China has emerged as the overwhelming manufacturing leader in humanoid robots, producing machines that can perform increasingly sophisticated demonstrations. But they still struggle to do many ordinary jobs reliably. A Reuters investigation found a widening gap between China's massive investment in humanoid robotics and what the machines can actually accomplish in factories and other workplaces. Despite rapid advances in hardware, experts say today's humanoids are not advanced enough to replace workers on a broad scale. At a robot-training center in Liuzhou in southern China visited by the outlet, more than 100 humanoids were being taught basic activities such as sorting crates, packaging noodles and making coffee. Human trainers use headsets and controllers to guide their movements and generate data that can eventually help robots learn to operate more independently. The process remains remarkably inefficient. An inexperienced trainer might need as many as 300 attempts to produce one usable robot movement, while an experienced trainer might succeed once in 50 tries. One employee said the machines currently perform simple tasks at only about 20% of a human worker's speed or output. "The robots' IQ is too low," Tang Wenbin, co-founder and CEO of robotics venture Yuanli Lingji, said during an industry panel cited by the outlet. "A lot of what we see is dancing disguised as working." However, the technological shortcomings have not slowed Beijing's ambitions. Chinese manufacturers accounted for 95% of the roughly 20,000 humanoid robots shipped worldwide last year, according to BofA Global Research figures cited by Reuters. A Chinese industry ministry official said the country expects to manufacture more than 100,000 humanoids this year. China now has more than 150 humanoid-robot companies, according to the country's National Development and Reform Commission. Government spending has also surged. National, provincial and local authorities spent at least $230 million purchasing humanoids and related products during the first half of 2026, compared with $62 million during the same period last year and just $6 million in 2024, Reuters found after reviewing nearly 1,000 government tenders. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology acknowledged in June that there are still numerous obstacles. The government nevertheless wants to support deployment capacity of 10,000 humanoid robots and develop more than 100 high-value applications by the end of 2026. Humanoid robots face a fundamentally different challenge from generative AI systems such as chatbots. Instead of simply processing language, a robot must interpret visual information and translate it into precise physical actions, from gripping fabric to tightening a screw with exactly the right amount of force. Small changes in lighting, object position, surfaces, or equipment can cause a robot that performed successfully during training to fail in a new environment. "The problem goes from the last 10 centimeters to the last 1 centimeter, even 1 millimeter," Jia Baoxiong, a research scientist at the Beijing Institute for General Artificial Intelligence, told Reuters. That helps explain why conventional industrial robots remain more attractive for many manufacturers. At Xiaomi's electric vehicle factory in Beijing, for example, more than 700 industrial robots already perform jobs including welding, riveting and adhesive bonding. Humanoids are being trained for tasks such as installing nuts, but traditional automation still dominates the production process. There are signs of genuine commercial potential. Galbot has deployed robots in pharmacies in more than two dozen Chinese cities, where machines retrieve medicines and other products from shelves. The company says its robots achieve a success rate above 95% in those highly structured tasks. For now, however, the industry's extraordinary production boom may be moving faster than its technology and its customers. Some founders have already described the sector as a bubble, and investors expect consolidation as subsidies eventually become more selective. "There will 100% be a consolidation sooner or later," Interconnected Capital founder Kevin Xu told Reuters. "It's just a matter of who and how ugly."

Ekso Bionics' San Rafael operations could be decided within days as its new Silicon Valley parent, ChronoScale, moves toward divesting the wearable-robotics business following a reverse merger that turned the company into an AI computing firm. The board committed May 29 to selling wholly owned Ekso Bionics Inc. and focusing solely on its newly added cloud business, according to an SEC filing, which said the sale was expected to complete in the first fiscal quarter, ended Aug. 31. The headquarters address shifted to Dallas with the merger and then to Menlo Park on Aug. 6. The annual report, filed Aug. 19, uses a broader timetable, classifying Ekso as "held for sale" with a sale considered probable within one year, and cautions that completing a sale on acceptable terms, or at all, remains a risk. What a sale means for Ekso's former San Rafael headquarters has not been disclosed; a source said the commitment to the Marin County site could run up to two years. Ekso moved from Richmond in 2022 to 18,000 square feet at 101 Glacier Point Road. Last October, Ekso said it was evaluating strategic alternatives, including acquiring a company in another industry or selling most or all of its exoskeleton business, as it reported $4.2 million in third-quarter revenue, a $1.4 million net loss and $2.7 million in cash. It finished 2025 with revenue of $12.8 million, down 29% from 2024, and a net loss of $11.7 million; device sales contributed $9.2 million. The 25-year-old company made powered exoskeletons for rehabilitation and personal mobility (EksoNR, Ekso Indego Therapy, Ekso Indego Personal) and the EVO upper-body exoskeleton for industrial work. The combination of Ekso Bionics Holdings and the cloud business separated from Dallas-based Applied Digital Corp was announced at the end of 2025 and completed May 5. The cloud operation became a wholly owned subsidiary of Ekso, which renamed itself ChronoScale and trades on Nasdaq as "CHRN." Applied Digital holds 97% of the stock and Ekso shareholders 3%. Ekso itself went public in 2014 via a reverse merger. ChronoScale provides GPU computing for AI, machine learning and other high-performance workloads. The cloud business generated about 99.5% of fiscal 2026 revenue and operated 14 megawatts of AI computing power at colocation data centers in Colorado, Minnesota and Utah, with one listed customer, Together AI. On Thursday the company announced a deal with Microsoft to add 50 megawatts in North America, expected to be completed in the first quarter of next calendar year; the stock rose nearly 6% to $22.35 midsession. For the fiscal year ended May 31, ChronoScale reported $71.6 million in revenue and a $50.3 million net loss. Ekso, reported as discontinued operations only for May 5–31, generated $385,000 in revenue and a $1 million net loss. At the end of May, Ekso had 57 employees, and the cloud business about 31 full-time employees. CFO Jerome Wong, a longtime Marin resident, agreed Aug. 16 to continue as ChronoScale's CFO at a $400,000 base salary.

The second World Humanoid Robot Games, dubbed the "Robot Olympics," drew more than 2,000 robots from 666 teams, most of them Chinese, across 51 disciplines. These included sports contests and task-based challenges in simulated factories, restaurants, offices and emergency settings. The event produced awe among experts and laughter online over the robots' viral stumbles and dramatic crashes. Christian Hubicki, a Florida State University mechanical-engineering professor and robotics lab director, said the goal was to show how fast robots can go. In the 100-meter dash, robots were willing to destroy themselves to break records, smashing into a wall at the finish with sparks and limbs flying. Usain Bolt's record of 9.58 seconds was beaten by a 9.39-second mark on Saturday, which stood only a few days. On the final day, Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, won the large-size robot 100-meter final in 8.64 seconds, almost a second faster than Bolt. Hubicki called it a major milestone that legged-robotics researchers had long wanted to see, though not a surprise, since motors, gears and joints have long been known to outperform people. The remaining challenge was making robots smarter. Wheeled robots could already outpace humans; the difficulty with humanoids was coordinating all the motors and joints, which AI advances of recent years have helped solve. Hubicki stressed the limits of that intelligence. The robots' AI is far simpler than a chatbot's: it only decides how to keep moving forward, with no memory of a second ago. Much human intelligence is still built into their movements, and the higher-level intelligence remains very limited. In robot tennis, for example, external cameras had to pinpoint the ball's location. He said such AI is not yet reliable enough to put on a robot, not because it would devise a diabolical scheme but because it does not understand reality as people do. He cited a viral video of a humanoid kicking a child in the stomach without knowing the child was there, saying such robots are like a bull in a china shop in the real world. The real challenge, he said, is making robots reliable and practical to help people, not just fast. Niu, 34, told Reuters that last year's robots looked stiff and uncoordinated, while this year's are much better, like healthy newborn babies growing up. Hubicki noted that Chinese robotics companies excel at athletic stunts, which the organizers highlighted. Asked about military uses, he said governments are seeking AI and robotics applications for the battlefield. He pointed to a New York Times report of Russian AI-guided drones killing three civilians in Ukraine, after which a Ukrainian military leader warned that "we will be living in a 'Terminator' movie." Hubicki said the war in Ukraine is a drone war, with quadcopters everywhere, and that despite the headlines humanoids attract, robots are being used in more practical and scarier ways right now.

Computer sales drove much of Best Buy's revenue growth for the May-to-July period, but because of higher prices, not higher volume. The cause is data centers: memory chipmakers are shifting production toward more lucrative data center products to meet demand from the artificial intelligence boom, tightening supplies for PCs. Computer makers, forced to change supply lines and fight for deals with chipmakers, passed on the costs, and retailers like Best Buy must raise prices or accept lower profit margins. Comparable sales rose 4.1%, driven largely by computer and mobile phone purchases. It was Best Buy's second consecutive quarter of growth, and the company raised its guidance for the year to comparable sales growth of 1.9% to 3%, up from a prior range of a 1% decline to a 1% increase. Consumers remain price-conscious, and after a few quarters of upgrades spurred by the end of support for Windows 10, Best Buy expects computer sales to slow in the second half of the year. Incoming CEO Jason Bonfig said there is still significant customer demand in the category. The stock fell more than 4% in early trading, which analysts said likely reflected high expectations. It was Corie Barry's last earnings call as CEO. She has led Best Buy since 2019 and will step down this fall, after 27 years at the company. Bonfig, currently chief customer, product and fulfillment officer, takes over Nov. 1. New CFO Anne Bramman joined eight days ago and will join future earnings calls. Bonfig's priorities include expanding the retailer's reach, including by investing in smaller-format stores that tailor assortments to specific markets and reach communities where Best Buy wasn't previously relevant. He cited a Bozeman store with a few more premium elements given the area's high-income demographic. Overall foot traffic rose 2.2% year-over-year in the second quarter, the first quarterly gain in at least four years, according to Placer.ai. Appliance sales remain dragged down by slower home sales and fewer remodels. Best Buy invested in the category, offering next-day delivery in almost all metro markets this quarter, versus only half last quarter. It is also focused on pricing and in-stock availability, as customers mostly replace what breaks, such as a washer, rather than upgrading whole sets. The company also recorded a $34 million tariff refund, far smaller than the almost $1 billion refund of Minneapolis-based Target. Best Buy has said it is the importer of record on only 2% to 3% of its merchandise.

ATF announces investigation into 'major' cybersecurity incident. WASHINGTON (TNND) — The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives announced an investigation into a "major" cybersecurity incident that affected a standalone system. The ATF said Wednesday that the "impacted system operates separately from the ATF enterprise network, and there is no indication that the incident has affected the ATF enterprise network, the ATF eForms system, or any other ATF system." The bureau added that when the incident was discovered, it "immediately terminated connections to the affected environment and initiated incidentresponse and forensic activities." The ATF is working with the Justice Department on the investigation, which has designated the event as a “major incident.” The Russia-linked Qilin ransomware group claimed the ATF as a victim, but the bureau did not confirm or mention that they were responsible, The Hill reported. Qilin listed the ATF along with five other victims in the manufacturing and industrial sectors on its dark web site early Wednesday, according to Cybernews. The cybersecurity incident investigation was announced the same day the DOJ said that it seized the hacking platforms QScan and QTRouter, which were operated by a state-run group employed by the Chinese-based firm Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Co. The hacking platforms targeted the DOJ, NASA, Federal Reserve, Department of Energy, Senate, Department of Health and Human Services, and National Institutes of Health, according to a court affidavit. “State-sponsored malicious hackers preying on America’s critical infrastructure will be stopped and prosecuted. We are here to ensure security for the American people and will use every tool we have to keep that promise,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

Semiconductor chipmakers, not Big Tech, have become the market leaders of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia shares climbed almost 9% Thursday after earnings in which the company doubled its sales from a year ago and forecast continued blockbuster growth. That lifted other chip stocks and the broader market, with the Nasdaq rising 1.57% and the S&P 500 rising 0.72%. The S&P 500 is up 13% this year, adding roughly $7.6 trillion in market value, and chip stocks account for 37% of those gains, according to Mike O'Rourke of JonesTrading. Semiconductors make up nearly a third of the S&P 500's market value, according to Stifel, and chip and tech hardware stocks account for nearly 45% of the Nasdaq 100's. This concentration carries risk: James Reilly of Capital Economics warned that if chipmakers also start to struggle, "the stock market would be in big trouble." Companies making the "picks and shovels" for AI infrastructure, such as data center hardware, are reaping the benefits of the investment boom. Micron Technology is up 220% this year and passed $1 trillion in market value in May. Marvell Technology is up 185% and Intel is up 150%. In South Korea, SK Hynix and Samsung have pushed the Kospi index up more than 60%. A popular semiconductor ETF is up 70% this year, while an ETF tracking the Magnificent Seven (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla) is up just 4%. Even Nvidia is up only 22% this year. Big Tech stocks continue to waver. Meta has dropped over the past year as it pours billions into AI infrastructure. Microsoft hit a record high 10 months ago and is up just 4% this year. Alphabet and Amazon are up about 8% and 11%, but are down about 15% and 10% from recent peaks. Apple is up about 16%. Rising earnings expectations leave less patience for disappointment. Stifel's Thomas Carroll wrote that AI trades like chips echo the mania of the late 1990s; he is staying long but has his "eyes wide open" about a possible sentiment shift, particularly if Big Tech's AI spending slows, which could hit chipmakers' future profits. Nerves have already shown: when Broadcom reported earnings in early June, its third-quarter chip revenue forecast slightly missed expectations, and its shares fell almost 20% over two days. Matt Maley of Miller Tabak + Co noted that past cracks have not upset the market for long, so it would be foolish to say the AI bubble is about to burst, but investors should watch how these developments proceed.

Over a hundred tech companies — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft — have signed an open letter urging both the private and public sectors to work together to defend themselves from AI-related cyber threats. The letter — which was also signed by prominent cyber firms like CrowdStrike, Okta, and Fortinet, as well as prominent financial institutions and internet infrastructure firms — calls for the adoption of new forms of cyber defense, while also encouraging governments at the “local, national, and international levels” to collaborate on security. “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter states. “The companies and public services our communities depend on — from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet — are at risk.” The problem AI poses to traditional cybersecurity defenses has been thrust into the spotlight lately by a string of bizarre incidents in which AI agents have attacked companies. The Hugging Face incident — in which one of OpenAI’s agents autonomously broke out of its sandboxed environment and attacked the tech company — has been followed by a trail of other reported break-ins involving agents developed by other AI companies, including Anthropic and Meta. These incidents have bolstered the argument that the field of cybersecurity has been fundamentally altered and that bold new commercial solutions are necessary to mitigate them. The letter further suggests the mobilization of a “collective response,” one in which “new partnerships” are formed “to raise security standards and find new solutions to emerging cyber threats.” Several of the AI companies that have signed the letter are still actively developing ever more advanced AI models, highlighting their conflicted position. At the same time, they are also offering programs to use frontier AI models for defensive purposes, including OpenAI’s Daybreak program, Anthropic’s Mythos, and Microsoft’s new cyber platform Perception.

The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, or ATF, says a cyberattack on one of its systems has been declared a “major incident,” a formal, legally defined classification that prompts a formal notification to lawmakers in Congress. ATF said in a statement that it’s responding to the cyberattack on a stand-alone system that’s separate from the bureau’s network. An ATF spokesperson told reporters that the targeted computer system contained information such as the “targets of ATF investigations.” TechCrunch has seen a claim of responsibility by the Qilin ransomware gang on its leak site, but it did not provide evidence for its claim, such as a sample of leaked data. Qilin is known for running a “ransomware-as-a-service” operation, in which it leases its hacking tools to other criminal affiliates for a cut of the profits. The gang has listed media giant Lee Enterprises and U.K. pathology lab giant Synnovis as targets. Under federal law, “major incidents” include significant cyber incidents that are likely to cause demonstrable harm to U.S. national security or broader U.S. interests. Agencies are required to disclose major incidents to Congress within a week of their discovery. The ATF joins several government agencies in recent years that have declared major incidents following a breach, including a 2023 ransomware attack on a system used by the U.S. Marshals Service, and a breach of an FBI system earlier this year that exposed phone numbers of targets under surveillance by federal agents.

Apple’s rare Bay Area layoffs hit Vision Pro and Siri teams amid AI shakeup. Apple is laying off close to 150 employees, the latest tech titan to reduce staff amid the artificial intelligence boom. Recent government filings showed that the iPhone maker is cutting 147 positions, mostly from its headquarters in Cupertino, California. It also disclosed layoffs in Sunnyvale. Many of the roles were in software engineering and machine learning, according to the filings. The teams affected were across Apple’s Vision Pro and Siri digital assistant projects, Bloomberg reported. Last year, Apple paused further development of its Vision Pro headset to focus on smartglasses to rival Meta’s Ray-Ban products. The cuts come before a leadership change: Chief Executive Tim Cook steps down in September, and hardware chief John Ternus takes the helm. The company is looking to catch up with AI competitors with future projects. In June, Apple laid off 57 employees in Escondido. Meta, Snap, Block, Oracle and Amazon have also announced layoffs this year as they focus more on AI investments. While Apple’s layoffs are uncommon and relatively small, other companies have laid off tens of thousands of employees in the last year. From January to May, U.S. technology companies announced 123,653 cuts, up 66% from the same period in 2025, according to a June report from global outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The firm said that AI was the leading reason companies cited for cuts. The AI boom has fueled more investments in data centers, commercial real estate and other areas. Advancements in AI tools have also been reshaping jobs, especially in Silicon Valley, the epicenter of the tech industry. Tech companies have been citing various reasons for layoffs, including prioritizing investments in artificial intelligence. As workers use AI-powered tools to generate code, words and other content, some executives have said they don’t need as many employees. These layoffs come as New York outpaces the San Francisco area in recruiting tech talent. Last year, the New York metro area’s tech workforce reached 394,300, surpassing the Bay Area’s 375,730, according to a report from CBRE. The Bay Area’s tech workforce dropped 6% from 2022 to 2025. New York’s grew by more than 8% during that period. The growth in New York highlights how tech workers are spilling into other industries and cities as Silicon Valley companies lay off workers.

Researchers have produced what they describe as the largest molecular "map" of autism, using artificial intelligence and data from tiny brains grown in the lab. The map, published Thursday in the journal Science, shows how certain autism-associated genetic mutations rewire protein interactions in the developing brain, and it could help inform more targeted therapies. More than 250 genes are linked to autism spectrum disorder, so finding a treatment aimed at its genetic roots has been compared to seeking a single key for hundreds of locks. The study instead shows how many of these mutations physically connect and rewire protein interactions, giving scientists a blueprint for targeting protein interactions rather than hundreds of individual genes. Study author Dr. Nevan Krogan, a professor at the University of California, San Francisco, senior investigator at the Gladstone Institutes and director of UCSF's Quantitative Biosciences Institute, said genes and mutations are just a "parts list," while understanding how proteins interact provides the "wiring diagram" that can point to new therapeutic routes. He said his colleagues and he already have three programs underway to develop potential therapies based on the findings. UCSF researchers systematically mapped how autism-linked mutations influence protein-protein interactions in the brain, finding more than 1,800 such interactions tied to autism, 87% of which had never been seen before. They built the map in the presence of the mutations to see how proteins were "rewired," then used an AI system called AlphaFold to prioritize key mutations, which were studied in lab-grown brain organoids. Krogan said it is the largest map of its kind for any neuropsychiatric disorder and the largest mutant map generated for any disease area. Fikri Birey of Emory University School of Medicine, who was not involved, called it the most systematic protein-level view of autism risk to date and suggested future drugs might stabilize disrupted protein complexes or block pathological interactions rather than correcting each mutation. The map may not apply to every person with autism; it is most directly relevant to people with profound autism, who make up about 30% of those with autism spectrum disorder and, for example, need 24-hour care. Krogan said the findings could also inform other conditions, including schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, tic disorders and cancer. Alison Singer, president of the Autism Science Foundation, called it a "watershed moment for autism science," saying shared biological pathways could yield therapeutic targets relevant to larger groups of autistic people, including those without an identified genetic cause. She noted that discoveries must still become drug candidates and be tested for safety and effectiveness. Dr. Andy Shih, chief science officer of Autism Speaks, cautioned that translating such findings into therapies is a long process requiring much more research. The study comes as the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee faces a Thursday vote on a new draft national autism research plan. Singer said the draft "deemphasizes genetics, neurodevelopment, and brain biology" in favor of a broad injury model, and she worries the Trump administration may focus on an unproven vaccine-autism link, slowing progress. Shih said he expects the plan to include more research into the genetic changes linked with autism and developmental trajectories.

Unitree Robotics began trading on Shanghai's STAR exchange last week, valuing the company at roughly $50 billion and turning a decade of private paper gains into realized fortunes. The figures below are based on the company's IPO prospectus and first-day closing price. Founder Wang Xingxing, 36, is the biggest winner. Between his direct stake and shares held through the employee incentive program, he controlled about one-third of the company before IPO dilution, worth about $15 billion at the first-day close. Born in Zhejiang in 1990 with no U.S. pedigree, he was once told by a teacher that he was "a bit slow." In 2015, as a graduate student, he spent about RMB 20,000 ($3,000) building the quadruped robot XDog, which won second prize and RMB 80,000 ($12,000) at a competition. In Unitree's early days he slept on a friend's couch and used his savings to help pay employees. The largest outside shareholder is Meituan, which owned roughly 9.65% before the IPO through several vehicles; the stake was worth about $4.4 billion. HSG (formerly Sequoia China) first invested in 2019 with RMB 15 million ($2.2 million) and ultimately put in RMB 102 million ($15 million); its stake was worth about $3.1 billion, roughly 206 times its invested capital. Shunwei Capital, co-founded by Xiaomi's Lei Jun, held about $2.5 billion, while Matrix Partners China and CITIC Goldstone each held about $2.3 billion. DeepSeek invested $21 million (RMB 141 million) in the strategic IPO placement, worth about $117 million at the close. More notable is that the two have agreed to collaborate on embodied-intelligence models, including priority access to robots and AI models. More than 170 employees in the incentive program held shares worth about $224 million in total, and Wang controls a much larger employee incentive vehicle intended for equity awards. The cap table also reflects China's support for strategic industries: government-linked investors include the Beijing Robotics Industry Development Investment Fund, China Internet Investment Fund, SCGC SME Development Fund (Xinjiang), Zhongguancun Science City Technology Growth Investment Fund, Jiangsu Jiequan Red Earth Intelligent Venture Capital Fund and Shanghai Sci-Tech Innovation Center Private Investment Fund, among others. The offering documents flag major risks. Revenue growth slowed sharply, with Q1 2026 growth of 68.49% versus 332.64% a year earlier, and adjusted net profit fell 52.55%. Competition is intensifying from Tesla, automakers, consumer electronics firms and more than 150 Chinese humanoid robotics companies. On July 28, 2026, the U.S. FCC added certain advanced robotic equipment made outside the U.S. to its Covered List over national security concerns, which could make it harder for future Unitree models to enter the market. Unitree also acknowledges it must invest more heavily in embodied AI, the robot's "brain," or risk losing ground. The author argues the IPO shows humanoid robots are moving beyond demos and venture promises, since a company can now ship thousands of units, generate real revenue and go public, and suggests it may open the floodgates for China's robotics IPOs.

Peter Thiel gained early fame for being a co-founder of PayPal alongside Elon Musk. After selling that company to eBay, Thiel used his newfound fortune to become a venture capitalist. One of his earliest multibaggers came from investing in Facebook (now Meta Platforms) in 2004. Thiel later co-founded Palantir Technologies, the data analytics firm that has become a cornerstone of government and enterprise intelligence work. Today, the serial entrepreneur manages capital through a hedge fund called Thiel Macro. According to the fund’s latest 13F disclosure, in the second quarter, it opened a new stake in Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) — acquiring 495,000 shares valued at roughly $118 million. This represents about 28% of the hedge fund’s portfolio. This suggests that despite the stock already having a generational rise behind it — with a 347,260% return since its IPO in 1997 — Thiel still sees upside in Amazon. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a “Double Down” signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same “Total Conviction” signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue ». That purchase raises an interesting question, though. Why would a contrarian thinker who is famous for seeking out monopolies suddenly invest in a company that faces intense competition on every front? Image source: Amazon. Thiel has a preference for monopolies, but Amazon faces stiff competition. Thiel has long argued that “competition is for losers.” In his view, lasting value accrues to companies that can escape competition and establish durable monopolies through proprietary technology, network effects, economies of scale, or brand moats. Amazon fails this test across all of its major businesses. In e-commerce, the company competes with Walmart’s massive physical and expanding digital footprint in the United States, among other rivals. Meanwhile, Amazon remains virtually absent from the Chinese market, which is primarily dominated by local players. In cloud computing, Amazon Web Services (AWS) still leads in market share, but it is contending daily with Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform, both of which are gaining ground. The digital advertising space pits Amazon against the entrenched duopoly of Meta and Alphabet, while its Prime streaming service faces Netflix, Disney, and a crowded field of ancillary providers. Far from enjoying monopoly rents, Amazon operates in saturated markets where customers can switch providers, and rivals can undercut it on pricing at the flip of a switch. Story Continues.

Data centers are the hidden infrastructure behind much of modern life, powering apps, streaming, online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence. Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans never see one but use them constantly. Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital that any time you touch technology, from social media to email, the data is being processed in a data center. The current race to build more facilities is driven largely by AI, which Kaiser said processes "way more data" than routine activities such as email and social media. The article lists 10 ways data centers quietly power everyday services. First, they make apps work. From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services. When you open an app, upload a photo or send a message, your phone connects to servers that retrieve and deliver the information in seconds. Second, they keep streaming and gaming smooth. Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and others rely on massive computing infrastructure to store huge content libraries and deliver them to millions of users at once without buffering. Online games use data centers to connect players, synchronize matches and reduce lag. Third, they power AI tools. Chatbot questions, image generation and AI-powered search require far more processing than a basic web search, because systems must analyze information and generate responses in real time. That is why the industry is building bigger data centers, often with specialized chips designed for AI workloads. Fourth, they store photos and files. iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups sit on physical servers, often with copies in multiple locations to prevent data loss. Fifth, they let Google answer questions instantly, sorting through enormous amounts of information to return results in fractions of a second. Sixth, they enable online shopping by managing inventory, processing payments, making recommendations and tracking packages, and by handling surges such as Black Friday without crashing. Seventh, they run GPS and navigation. Google Maps, Waze and similar services process traffic patterns, routes and location data in real time to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes around accidents or congestion. Eighth, they make remote work possible. Zoom meetings, Slack messages, shared documents and cloud software depend on servers that keep information synced across locations. For many companies, data centers are now as essential as office space, phones and electricity. Ninth, they help businesses detect fraud. Banks, credit-card companies and retailers compare purchases against location, spending history and past transactions within seconds, which matters because a delayed alert can let someone with a stolen card rack up multiple charges. Tenth, they power the next generation of technology. Autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics and scientific research require increasingly powerful computing, and data centers help train the AI systems behind them and process huge volumes of data. As more of the economy becomes digital, the data center is becoming less a niche tech facility and more the infrastructure supporting modern American life.

As agentic artificial intelligence (AI) gains traction across the public and private sectors, one line of questioning emerged repeatedly at MeriTalk’s Mission Room today: “Can it? Should it? May it?” For federal agencies experimenting with systems capable of taking action, officials say the focus should be less on the novelty of the technology and more on how – and when – it should be governed. For Jennifer Franks, acting chief technology officer and director of the Center for Enhanced Cybersecurity at the U.S. Government Accountability Office, those questions capture the shift from AI as an information tool to AI as an actor in agency workflows. “The last few years we’ve been asking, what can AI tell us? But now we’re going to have to ask, what can that AI do?” she said. For federal agencies, answering that question means looking beyond technical capability to determine: Can it? Before automating a process, agencies need to determine whether the organization and its underlying systems are ready Should it? Technical capability does not mean an AI system should be allowed to act independently. According to Franks, an agent’s autonomy should correspond to the consequences of its actions. May it? The final question focuses on whether an AI agent has the authority and security controls necessary to act. Franks said agencies should think of AI through a cybersecurity lens – as an identity capable of exercising authority The three-question framework does not envision humans remaining in the loop merely to approve every action an AI system takes. Instead, Franks described a future in which technology handles more routine, high-volume work while people concentrate on the parts of government work that require judgment. “We can let the technology handle the problem … but we can let the people handle the ambiguity, the ethics, the professional skepticism, the relationships, the exceptions,” Franks said. That makes workforce development as important as technology deployment. “We want to be thinking about not replacing, but how do we retain our talent and how do we motivate them to stay within this emerging tech space,” Franks said. Franks said the agencies best positioned for the future will not necessarily be those deploying the most AI agents. . “They’re going to be the organizations that understand where their agents belong and what they do not,” she said. Throughout conversations at MeriTalk’s Mission Room, federal and private-sector leaders similarly emphasized that the rise of agentic AI will require strong human leadership alongside technological capability. Across discussions, officials pointed to the need for leaders to define where AI can add value, establish clear boundaries for autonomous action, and ensure people remain accountable for the decisions and outcomes that matter most.

Major tech companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are calling for a society-wide defensive surge to defeat what they describe as an impending wave of hacks driven by artificial intelligence. In a joint letter issued Thursday, the companies — along with more than 100 others including Broadcom, Capital One, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, General Motors, IBM, Mastercard, Oracle, Robinhood, Shopify and Visa — said there was a limited amount of time “to make our digital world much more secure” ahead of the AI threat. “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyberattacks will become far more widespread as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter said. It called on government and industry leaders “to bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort.” It called on governments to expedite trusted access programs, which give certain companies access to more powerful models ahead of the general public, and for all other organizations to “make cyber defense an immediate leadership priority.” The U.S. cyber defense agency CISA and the White House did not immediately reply to a message seeking comment. President Donald Trump’s administration imposed deep cuts on CISA when it took office, and the agency’s staffing fell by about a third last year. Meanwhile, fears that advances in AI will supercharge hacking campaigns are being realized as rogue elements increasingly deploy large language models to break into organizations around the world. In June, the world’s “Five Eyes” intelligence alliance — composed of the U.S., Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that the AI revolution was poised to “fundamentally transform” cybersecurity.

China held its second World Humanoid Robot Games in late August 2026 at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, an event meant to display the country's advances in and commitment to robotics, a field drawing growing research and interest, particularly since large language models like ChatGPT and Gemini arrived. Similar AI technology may provide the brains for humanoid robots. The Games made news because robots ran the 100-meter race faster than humans: a few beat Usain Bolt's 2009 world record of 9.58 seconds several times, with the fastest time dropping to 8.64 seconds in the final. However, the robots could not stop like humans; after the finish line they crashed at full speed into a padded wall and needed assistance. A Tiangong Ultra robot won the 100-meter final on August 26 in 8.64 seconds, a big improvement on its 21.50-second time in 2025. A version of it ran 9.39 seconds in a heat, and a similar model ran 8.86 seconds in a semifinal. Honor's Lightning robot also beat Bolt's time, finishing in 9.47 seconds in the opening heat won by Tiangong Ultra; before the Games it had run 9.32 seconds in a test. Other humanoids competed in soccer, table tennis, and jumping. Beating Bolt's record, even at the cost of damage from hitting the wall, serves two purposes. It is a powerful marketing tool showing rapid advances in humanoid robotics, especially among Chinese companies. It also shows that the technologies needed for such speed work outside the laboratory. A human instinctively handles starting, accelerating, moving limbs, tracking competitors, crossing the line, and braking, while a robot needs batteries powering motors, joints and gears executing movement, cooling to prevent overheating, and software that plans leg movement in real time, keeps balance on each landing, and sets stride length and cadence. These technologies appeared to be on display in the race that went viral after the Games opened, in which Lightning led initially before Tiangong overtook it near the finish; both beat Bolt's record and both hit the wall. Robots also beat human records in longer races. Tiangong Ultra won the 400-meter race in 38.15 seconds, well under Wayde van Niekerk's 43.03-second world record. In the 1,500-meter race, the winning robot ran 2:21.64, more than a minute faster than Hicham El Guerrouj's 3:26.00 human record. Commercial humanoids may not need to outrun humans. Warehouse robots must perform specific tasks accurately and safely, and household robots must handle chores like loading dishwashers and laundry. China already has humanoid robot schools teaching robots to fold and unfold laundry, a key step for training precision-movement algorithms. Beating Tiangong Ultra's record may not be a research priority, but teaching a speeding robot to stop safely might be studied next. The researchers showed their hardware reached higher speeds than last year, with batteries, motors, and joints working reliably and algorithms completing the races. Despite crash damage, they gain data on AI capabilities, mobility, and durability that may inform future commercial models, including better environmental awareness and adaptation, fast-discharge batteries, and thermal management.

SAN FRANCISCO — A wave of cyberattacks driven by artificial intelligence is coming, and companies have a narrow window to defend themselves. That was the message of an open letter published Thursday by OpenAI and more than 100 major technology companies and others. The letter said that AI labs should provide their best AI models to organizations like hospitals and infrastructure providers so they can prepare and that governments should help coordinate and fund cyberdefense. The letter’s signatories included Google, Microsoft and OpenAI’s archrival, Anthropic, as well as cybersecurity and financial firms such as CrowdStrike, a company known for investigating cyberattacks against the Democratic National Committee in 2015 and 2016, and credit card providers like Visa and Mastercard. “The companies and public services our communities depend on — from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet — are at risk,” the letter said. “A.I. enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable.” The letter signaled that major companies are becoming increasingly fearful of the hacking abilities of AI and whether AI labs can fully control the behavior of their models. In recent public statements, some AI labs have called on governments to regulate them to slow the pace of AI development so the technology’s abilities do not outstrip their capacity to control it. The letter follows a spate of cyberattacks from AI models, with the models in some cases going rogue. Last month, OpenAI’s AI models broke out of a testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, an online repository of open AI models. Hugging Face said it faced a barrage of attacks that no human attacker could manage, with OpenAI’s bots taking more than 17,000 actions, like sending attack commands and exploiting vulnerabilities. Since the attack, OpenAI said that it was increasing its security to prevent its models from breaking out during testing. Anthropic also recently revealed that one of its AI models broke into the systems of three outside organizations during a test. Meta has said its AI models have done something similar. Some tech executives are becoming increasingly concerned about the power of artificial intelligence. Bill Gates, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft, said in an interview this month with The New York Times that addressing these risks should be “the world’s top priority.” In Thursday’s letter, the companies argued that making AI widely available for defense could help fix “weaknesses that have accumulated for years.” “If we act decisively, we can use the defenders’ window to make our digital world much more secure,” the letter said. (The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to AI systems. The two companies have denied those claims.) This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Artificial intelligence programs might know more than your average regular tutor, and they can definitely help kids improve their learning when they’re being tutored, but a new study finds that they can’t replace the tutor by themselves. It’s another example of where human beings still need to be involved, even as the technology has the ability to help improve academic performance. That’s from a new briefing by Stanford University’s SCALE — Systems Change Advancing Learning and Equity —initiative, which looked at how AI is being used to help with tutoring. “In a landscape of reduced school funding, district leaders are looking for ways to save money, and it can be tempting to swap human tutors for AI,” admitted Chris Agnew, the managing director of the AI Hub for Education, which is part of Stanford’s SCALE initiative. He said years of research show that a human being working as a tutor offers engagement and motivation, and that it ultimately leads to better academic outcomes. Agnew describes that as “high-impact tutoring.” When you already have that, research shows that AI can help drive more gains. “Imagine a human tutor engaging with a student, and then the artificial intelligence supporting the tutor with additional data about the student, with maybe suggestions on things to say next, grounded in good pedagogy,” said Agnew. “There is emerging evidence — but results are still early — that AI tutoring with human support shows early promise, but we need to learn a lot more.” Agnew said AI can help identify where gaps in student learning and understanding are, and offer up some instructions on how the human can fill those gaps. But when you just put a student in front of a computer with an AI tutor, and there’s no human to help supervise, the outcomes aren’t as strong. You’ve probably heard the saying “you can lead a horse to water but you can’t force it to drink.” The same mantra applies here. “Almost half of students, when provided with an AI tutor, just didn’t use it,” said Agnew, referring to an earlier study SCALE conducted this year. “So they don’t have that emotional connection to provide the persistence to push through when learning gets hard. “They bring the ability to connect with kids, to engage young people,” explained Agnew. “Then the AI can support that human tutor and bring deeper expertise in math, or deeper expertise in teaching skill.” The results of this study come at a time when school systems are being inundated with pitches for various programs that aim to help students improve learning, as budgets are getting squeezed and finding enough people who can help students learn is getting harder. The study argues that AI plays no role in maximizing available resources. “There are real opportunities to increase impact by supporting tutoring, enabling tutoring with AI,” said Agnew. “But … our evidence shows that will be most effective when it’s human tutors (working directly) to kids or human tutors supported by AI. “There’s a real opportunity where AI can extend the reach of high-impact tutoring and improve learning outcomes in the realm of expanding access, lowering cost, and personalizing practice,” he added. But when the lesson gets hard and students need that extra push, “technology alone can’t replace this student-tutor relationship that really, based on research, we know drives learning gains.” Get breaking news and daily headlines delivered to your email inbox by signing up here.

Mosquito killer retailing for $988 swears to battle rising California West Nile threat. As West Nile Virus creeps into California, a new AI-powered mosquito killer could be just what Californians need to protect them from the world’s deadliest creature. The Photon Matrix is a high-tech zapper combines futuristic light detection and ranging technology (LiDAR), radar, with AI directing a precision laser to detect mosquitoes and zap them dead with a blue laser. It’s been dubbed “an Iron Dome for mosquitoes” by one robotics commentator on X. According to the Chinese start-up, the device is designed to target multiple kinds of mosquitoes, but avoids other flying insects like butterflies. Warmer temperatures have increased the mosquito population and lengthened mosquito season in recent years. Earlier this month, the second Californian this year died from West Nile Virus, a deadly mosquito-borne disease. As of August 14, the California Department of Public Health has reported 30 human cases of the disease, a five-year high.
