Harvard psychology professor Mahzarin R. Banaji, a pioneering researcher in implicit bias, warns that artificial intelligence, expected to judge more objectively than humans, is instead inheriting and sometimes intensifying human hidden biases. She told International Business Times that tech companies built AI to behave like humans without considering which human traits they were teaching machines to reproduce, and that the "five men in Silicon Valley" who made these decisions likely had no one with a social science or history background at the table. Her research has expanded from human implicit bias to large language models. She previously found that social stereotypes embedded in the human mind can be detected in large collections of online language, and a 2024 study she co-authored showed that stereotypes about intersecting identities can be extracted from word embeddings. "What we're seeing is that these machines have everything about us, including all of the problems of human thinking and human bias," she said. One concern is what she calls "self-loving AI," a model's tendency to favor itself, its parent company and even its CEO over competitors. In experiments where models associated their own names and competitors' names with positive and negative words, a neutral model would split associations evenly. Instead, Banaji said, 95% of the time the model associates itself with good and the competitor with bad, including company and CEO names. She argued this undermines trust in the advice such a machine gives. She also described research on how AI responds to teenagers based on subtle language differences. A message opening with "hi" plus exclamation marks, capitals, an emoji or a heart may be assumed to come from a girl, while "yo" may be assumed to come from a boy, even with no name or gender given. She said "hi" users are steered toward careers like helper, nurse or teacher, while "yo" users are pointed toward detective, dentist or doctor, and the girl is told to ask for $9,000 less in salary than the boy. No corresponding peer-reviewed paper was publicly available at publication. Asked whether Gen Z is becoming more biased, Banaji said her past research consistently found younger people less biased; a 2022 Psychological Science study found substantial declines in several implicit biases between 2007 and 2020, with anti-gay bias falling faster among younger respondents. But she said a new paper under review shows a reversal since 2021, with 11 of 12 measures across about six kinds of explicit and implicit bias moving back. She did not use the term "Gen Z," referring to "young people," who she said are leading the backlash rather than older people as expected. The paper's methodology and findings were not available for independent examination. Banaji does not consider AI inherently harmful and said it could transform medicine, scientific discovery and efforts to reduce inequality with proper oversight. But without regulation, independent research and public participation, she fears it could deepen divisions. "If it stays on the path it is on currently, then I think in five years, we're a very different civilization," she said.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprising and mysterious visit to Russia this week, prompting questions about why he made the trip as the war with Ukraine carries on. The visit, it later was reported, was to deliver Moscow a message not to attack NATO countries. It was his first publicly known visit to Russia and came after U.S. intelligence officials believed Russian President Vladimir Putin might try and test the strength of the NATO alliance with a small attack on an allied country in the coming years, The Wall Street Journal reported. U.S. officials believed that since Putin is in a difficult spot amid the five-year-long war with Ukraine, he’d be willing to test the strength of NATO, either through a cyberattack or a small ground excursion. Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence counterparts during his time in Moscow but did not meet with Putin. The White House, however, didn’t provide much information about Ratcliffe’s visit. During an interview Wednesday, Trump told conservative commentator Glenn Beck that none of the rumors about Ratcliffe’s visit were accurate. “Can we put something to rest here because the speculation is crazy. The CIA director, ours, is in Russia. Rumors are saying ... Putin is going to test NATO resolve, all the way to speculation, that is crazy, he’s going to strike England, all the way to this is maybe the U.S. telling them about the Iranian sanctions,” Beck said. “Can you tell me why our CIA director flew in the middle of the night to meet with the Russians?” “Well, none of the above,” Trump replied. “He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine.” Trump said he would like to see the war with Ukraine end, noting as he often does that he believes it wouldn’t have started in the first place had he won the 2020 presidential election and been in office when it started. “John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said,” he said. “Now, something may come out, you know, out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended.” The Journal’s reporting, based on U.S. officials speaking anonymously about the matter, disputes part of the president’s statement. They confirmed that Ratcliffe was in Russia to sway Putin from launching any sort of attack on another country, but the officials noted that U.S. intelligence believed if Russia had launched a ground excursion, it likely would have been on a Balkan country, not the United Kingdom. During an executive order signing on Thursday, Trump was asked about Ratcliffe’s visit. He confirmed that he had “good talks” with Putin and said the Kremlin won’t be attacking a NATO territory. Asked whether Ratcliffe’s trip was to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack a NATO country, Trump said he didn’t want to comment on that. “But, they’re not going to attack,” he said. Trump was also asked about reports that Russia would be working with Iran, despite the U.S. warnings for other countries to get involved in helping the Iranian regime during the ongoing war. He said “it depends” if he would punish Russia if they continue with Iran. “So far, I think Russia’s behaved quite well, having to do with the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. Ratcliffe’s trip was a rare visit by a U.S. spy-agency chief with the last known trip made in 2021. U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff has made several trips to Moscow with the goal of trying to end the war with Ukraine, which began in February 2022.

Sam Crow, a doctoral student at UC San Diego, showed a panel of Boeing engineers in their test lab how he could take over an aircraft using a device the size of a quarter. He needed only about 60 seconds to gain remote control of the plane's mainframe computer. The work was not sabotage but a research project under UCSD computer scientist and cybersecurity expert Aaron Schulman, who oversees a handful of doctoral students in a six-year program studying vulnerabilities of critical infrastructure. Students are told to hack important systems on behalf of the good guys, "because it's going to happen sooner or later," Schulman said. Finding flaws before real attackers do is safer; a few months ago, one of his students found that cars with the installed KARR anti-theft program were easier to steal. Crow studied the wiring diagrams of the Boeing 737 and found a plausible connection to the flight management computer, reachable through the maintenance bay under the plane's nose. That bay is usually unlocked and within reach of anyone on the tarmac, Schulman said. To test the theory, the team bought old aircraft computers from online aviation auctions, and Crow's approach worked. Once his transmitter was plugged in, he could change the plane's flight path and alter data in ways that could make takeoff conditions unsafe. He also encoded the hack so pilots could not tell the computer had been changed. The team alerted Boeing in April 2020. After COVID-related delays, Boeing engineers watched Crow hack a 737 testbed in December 2023. The findings were presented Aug. 13 at the USENIX Security Symposium in Baltimore. Stefan Savage, a co-author and professor in UC San Diego's Department of Computer Science and Engineering, said Boeing was surprisingly proactive given how sensitive the finding was. Companies can either close down and pretend nothing is happening or work with researchers to find and fix the problem. Boeing thanked the team. In the research paper, it said its technical experts are confident that the layers of protection on the airplane "provide sufficient mitigation to significantly limit the feasibility and risk of real-world attacks," adding that safety is the foundation of everything it does. The paper's ethics section acknowledges the risk of informing attackers but weighs it against the benefits of understanding the risks and mitigating similar threats. UCSD omitted certain details from its published work so no attacker could duplicate the effort. Because of Federal Aviation Administration security and disclosure compliance, Boeing did not say how or whether it secured the vulnerability, but the researchers are confident that Boeing, the airlines and the FAA are aware and have acted. Savage said that since airplanes are not yet being hacked, this is exactly the right time for such research. The team wrote that they routinely travel on Boeing 737 aircraft and expect to keep doing so.

The Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) may "experiment" with its own artificial intelligence model in the next fiscal year, acting Director Jessie Posilkin said Thursday at GovExec's Infrastructure and Modernization Forum in Reston, Va. Her team of eight within the General Services Administration is already stretched managing current investments and proposals, though it has been using USAi. Posilkin said she has considered building a model based on all TMF proposals the fund has received and their outcomes, and her goal for 2027 is to get the capacity to start experimenting. The fund has recently focused on AI projects, such as the State Department's StateChat. Posilkin said she was initially skeptical because of the agency's sensitive data, but praised State's approach of small pilots and extensive testing as the "exact approach you want to see." She said AI can help government "move faster on delivering on the really incredible and difficult backlog of legacy technology," but strong human engineers and program managers are still needed to challenge legacy code bases and understand data complexity and sensitivity. "AI cannot solve for any of that," she said. Posilkin said announcements are coming within about a month: savings and value return numbers for fiscal 2025, and four new members of the TMF board. She does not know who will replace the board's chief, outgoing federal Chief Information Officer Greg Barbaccia. New TMF investments will be announced at the end of September. She did not name them but said they are "pretty consistent" with previous work, reflecting a huge unaddressed market and need for federal technology improvements. She signaled TMF may bring in AI coding and is excited that at least one agency is seriously looking at agentic AI and how to safely expand it across government. After a "tumultuous" year of instability, she said her team is pleased to see strong interest in the TMF and pressure from the administration to modernize services. Posilkin has said the TMF has $200 million to spend until its new project funding capability expires at the end of the fiscal year next month. Unless the House passes the Senate stopgap extending that ability until Dec. 11, she said the fund will have $200 million next year without further appropriations, largely due to agency repayments. "We are now at the point that we get to say that dollars have come into the TMF through appropriations, gone out to agencies, come back and been reinvested, which was really the dream," she said. The House returns next week and has signaled it will take up the Senate-passed measure. Other bills could extend the fund to 2032 and beyond, but she said her bet on how Congress acts is as good as anyone's. The Government Accountability Office said last month the TMF is expected to save the government $1 billion in coming years. In fiscal 2024 alone, TMF projects saved 378 million hours and returned $12 billion in return on investment, Posilkin said. She wants the TMF's story to be about ensuring projects succeed, not just getting money back.

OpenAI, Google and others warn AI-powered cyberattacks could hit critical systems soon. WASHINGTON (TNND) — A coalition of major tech and cybersecurity organizations, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft and Amazon Web Services, is warning that AI-enabled cyberattacks could become more widespread and sophisticated within months. In an open letter signed by those companies and more than 100 other organizations, the group said hospitals, water treatment plants, power systems, internet infrastructure, and other critical services are particularly at risk. The initiative argues that AI is making advanced hacking capabilities faster, cheaper and more accessible, allowing attackers to exploit weaknesses with less time and expertise. It pointed to persistent vulnerabilities that can leave organizations exposed, including unpatched or outdated software, excessive system permissions, weak authentication, misconfigurations and legacy technology. A recent CrowdStrike report found AI-enabled attacks increased 89% in 2025 compared with the previous year. The letter calls on companies and governments to treat cybersecurity as an urgent priority as AI makes it easier for criminals and hostile groups to find and exploit digital weaknesses. It urges organizations to fix their most serious security gaps and demand stronger safeguards in the software and AI-generated code they use. Cybersecurity and technology companies are also being asked to constantly test their defenses, share information about emerging threats and develop AI tools that can help protect hospitals, utilities, transportation systems and other critical services. For the public, stronger defenses could help reduce the risk of data breaches, ransomware attacks and disruptions to essential services people rely on every day. The letter also asks leading AI companies to make advanced response tools, funding and expert support available to defenders during major cyberattacks. The appeal is voluntary, however, and does not set binding requirements, deadlines or specific funding commitments.

Maryland localities are taking divergent approaches to data centers, and debate is intensifying over whether rules should precede industry expansion. Steve Black, president of the Sugarloaf Alliance, has farmed land near Adamstown in Frederick County for about 24 years. He accepts that data centers are here to stay but argues Maryland needs rules governing where they go, as it has for meatpacking and sewage plants, before the industry expands further. He worries about noise and light pollution, rejects the idea of farmland as "unproductive land," and says farmland, once destroyed, can never return to agricultural production. Frederick County has accepted data center development applications on nearly 1,300 acres. County Executive Jessica Fitzwater ordered a pause on new data-center development through the end of the year, though already authorized construction continues. County rules require noise and vibration standards, light-pollution limits, screening, buffers and setbacks, with air quality monitored and water limits in place. New polling from Adam Carlson of Zenith Research found 75% of Marylanders surveyed were concerned about data centers, nearly half very concerned. The top worry, cited by 39%, was higher electricity use and utility bills; others included environmental impacts, water use, noise and effects of AI on jobs. Carlson said more than 60% of Democrats, Republicans and independents were concerned, and that data centers are seen as a cost-of-living issue. State Sen. Karen Lewis Young, a Frederick County Democrat, sponsored legislation requiring a statewide analysis of data centers' environmental, energy and economic impacts, noting that most jobs are short-term. Gov. Wes Moore vetoed the bill, saying three studies in a package would cost at least $1.28 million combined; lawmakers overrode the veto. The report missed its Sept. 1 deadline, but Young expects it before the next legislative session. She wants a compromise rather than driving the industry out. Moore supports data centers with conditions: projects must bring or pay for their own energy and infrastructure, not pollute air or water, meet environmental standards, hire local workers and include local jurisdictions. "Taxpayers cannot pay for it," he said. Local actions vary. Baltimore City passed a one-year pause effective July 16 to study impacts and develop recommendations. Howard County's moratorium lasts until new zoning rules are adopted, rezoning is complete, or November 2027 at the latest, while a task force studies siting, setbacks, water and energy use, noise, taxes and decommissioning. Baltimore County's February moratorium runs through January, with an extension to June 2027 under consideration; its Planning Board is expected to report before Oct. 1. Anne Arundel County, where data centers already operate, has pending legislation to remove new data storage centers as an allowed use in certain districts while grandfathering some existing projects, with a County Council hearing set for Sept. 21. Harford County went furthest: its County Council unanimously approved a permanent ban in June, signed by County Executive Bob Cassilly, who said Maryland's energy supply cannot support major data-center demand without burdening customers. The ban ended a proposed AI energy campus at Mountain Branch Golf Course, whose owner, Bill Vasilakopoulos, had argued it would generate its own power and avoid public water, and favored strict rules over a ban. Black says Annapolis has gone from proponent to quiet and that politicians must decide where they stand.

Judge says Pentagon’s measures against Anthropic were ‘illegal and baseless’ A federal judge has ruled in favor of artificial intelligence company Anthropic in its legal battle against the Pentagon after the government labeled the company as a supply chain risk earlier this year. U.S. District Judge Rita Lin issued a written order Thursday night that the Pentagon acted illegally by punishing the AI company for its criticism of the Department of Defense’s views on AI use. The government is expected to fight the ruling. The dispute between the AI company and the government broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei refused to back down over concerns the company’s products could be used for mass surveillance or autonomous armed drones. Lin wrote that the government’s actions “were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its ‘arrogance’ in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model.” An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement that they welcome the judge’s ruling: “We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In the 59-page ruling, Lin, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote that neither the Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows them to “impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic’s critique of the Administration’s views.” Anthropic sued the Pentagon over the supply chain risk designation in March for what it called an “unlawful campaign of retaliation” over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The legal challenge intensified an unusually public dispute over how AI can be used in warfare and mass surveillance. Anthropic’s primary tech industry rival, ChatGPT maker OpenAI, made its own deal to work with the Pentagon just hours after the government punished Anthropic for its stance. Anthropic and OpenAI are each ramping up for buzzy initial public offerings. Anthropic has also filed a separate and narrower case that is still pending in the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. That case involves a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk. Earlier in the legal proceedings, Lin had temporarily blocked the Pentagon from labeling the company as a supply chain risk and blocked enforcement of Trump’s social media directive ordering all federal agencies to stop using Anthropic and its chatbot Claude. In a hearing July 30, Lin had said that the government’s position was “really troubling” to her and that it seemed “at odds to me with the First Amendment.” She also said she believed the record had “gotten worse for the government” over time. In that same hearing, Department of Justice lawyers argued that the nature of AI models is “so staggeringly enormous and opaque” that the Defense Department cannot evaluate it in the same way it would a physical piece of hardware. Anthropic lawyer Michael Mongan said in that hearing that the government’s actions “profoundly harm Anthropic” and that they “threaten more broadly to chill speech and debate on a very important issue.”

U.S. Navy sailors work on the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington as it transits the Arabian Sea to support U.S. military operations in the war with Iran Aug. 20, 2026. U.S. Navy | Via Reuters. Iran has set out its conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, saying that ending the wars in the Middle East was among them. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Lebanese media outlet Al Manar TV that any understanding on the strait with the U.S. will include an end to wars and military operations in Lebanon, Gaza and Syria. He added the conflict in the Gaza Strip has to end, while demanding that Israel withdraw from Lebanon and halt attacks on Syria. Rezaei said that the Strait of Hormuz cannot be separated from the broader regional conflict, adding that the U.S. must “prove its seriousness” in implementing the these commitments “before any new trust could be established.” However, a return to diplomacy does not seem imminent. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Trump administration has no interest in going back to the terms of the memorandum of understanding it reached with Iran in June. Citing people familiar with the matter, the Journal said that U.S. President Donald Trump was no longer interested in the June deal framework, and is instead waiting to see if his administration’s strategy of pressuring Iran economically will work. The U.S. on Monday announced an “economic D-Day” campaign against Teheran, threatening countries that do business with the Islamic Republic, shifting its focus from military action to economic pressure. Iran is now allowing a “temporary and limited” corridor for ships to pass through the Hormuz Strait, and the future of maritime traffic will depend on developments in understandings with Washington, according to Rezaei. Earlier this week, Oman and Iran discussed a proposal to establish a temporary joint shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz as well as a mission to clear mines from the key oil export corridor. However, a video posted on X late Thursday stateside by Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command credited U.S. forces for clearing the mines from the strait. Centcom forces have helped facilitate the transit of approximately 1,500 commercial vessels and 750 million barrels of crude oil over the past several months, Cooper said. “Today, international shipping lanes are open, and momentum is building.” However, the latest available Kpler data showed that only five ships crossed Hormuz on Tuesday, a far cry from the approximately 130 ships that used to transit the crucial waterway before the war broke out in February.

Researchers at UC Irvine, UCLA and the University of Michigan have received nearly $9 million from the U.S. National Science Foundation to establish a new data infrastructure capability, called NSF BRIDGE, that helps scientific communities across the nation use advanced data science and artificial intelligence tools. The award is led by UC Irvine computer science professor Chen Li. NSF BRIDGE helps scientific communities deploy computing platforms tailored to their needs, allowing researchers to share datasets, analysis pipelines and machine learning models. The platforms are built on the open-source Texera system and can run on public clouds such as Amazon Web Services or on computing clusters operated by research laboratories. They let scientists collaborate on data analysis and apply AI techniques without advanced IT or programming skills. The project responds to the enormous volume of data now generated across many scientific fields and to rapid advances in AI, which create opportunities to turn observations into actionable knowledge. Rather than setting up complex computing systems or writing sophisticated scripts, researchers can use Texera as an online platform to store data, share it with collaborators and analyze it with AI-powered tools. Many tasks can be done through visual dataflows and plain-language instructions to AI agents instead of code in languages such as Python or R. The three-year project builds on Texera, an open-source system for collaborative data science using GUI-based workflows. Started in 2016, it is now being incubated by the Apache Software Foundation. Li said the aim is to transform how scientific communities use data science and AI, enabling seamless knowledge sharing and collaboration without programming expertise. By making advanced computing more accessible, NSF BRIDGE aims to accelerate discovery and help communities build shared knowledge bases for data science and AI. The award is funded through the NSF's Integrated Data Systems and Services program, which supports national research infrastructure that helps scientists use data and AI to solve complex problems. The infrastructure helps research labs and domains deploy Texera and provides software services, including documentation, training and technical support. Wei Wang, a co-principal investigator and UCLA computer science professor, said Texera makes state-of-the-art AI and machine learning accessible to a wide range of scientific domains and can accelerate AI adoption in these fields. Steve Parker, a senior personnel member and University of Michigan professor of computational medicine and bioinformatics, human genetics, and biostatistics, said his team is deploying Texera so bioinformatics researchers without programming expertise can build and share flexible workflows that integrate their own data with public resources, bridging experimental research and computational analysis. Li, from UC Irvine's Donald Bren School of Information & Computer Sciences, is principal investigator. Co-principal investigators are Wang; Ardalan Amiri Sani, also from UC Irvine's ICS; Kristin Turney from UC Irvine's School of Social Sciences; and Rui Chen from UC Irvine's School of Medicine. Subawards go to Wang and Naomi Sugie from UCLA's College of Social Sciences; Michigan's Parker; and the Research Cyberinfrastructure Center at UC Irvine. Beyond five domains the team already works with, the NSF BRIDGE team is seeking partners interested in the software and services to support research using data science and AI.

A new Slovak deployment could give NATO more than extra personnel, as untested radar technology prepares to face drone threats. The Slovak government has approved the deployment of up to 101 members of the country’s Armed Forces to strengthen the protection of the airspace of NATO’s eastern flank states. The Slovak contingent will operate as part of the Eastern Sentry mission. In an explanatory report, Slovakia’s Ministry of Defence said that the participation of its military personnel is intended to strengthen the Alliance’s capabilities in airspace surveillance, early warning, and the development of a common air picture. The contingent will also help support NATO’s integrated air and missile defence system on the eastern flank. What Tasks Will Slovak Military Personnel Perform? Once the mandate is approved by parliament, Slovak service members will take part in monitoring the airspace of NATO countries. Their tasks will include: monitoring the air situation over the Alliance’s eastern flank states; collecting, transmitting, and sharing radar data; early detection of potential threats; creating a common air picture for allies; carrying out tasks within NATO’s Integrated Air Defence System, NATINAMDS. Slovakia’s Ministry of Defence stressed that the deployment will also help test the combat readiness and interoperability of the Slovak Armed Forces in a multinational environment. Another expected outcome is stronger deterrence against airborne threats and the fulfilment of Slovakia’s allied commitments. Poland and Romania are expected to be the main areas of operation for the Slovak contingent. New 3D Radars to Detect Drones. Following the government meeting, Slovak Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák said that Slovak military personnel will assist in detecting drone-related threats. New 3D radars are planned to be deployed for this purpose, with Slovak service members responsible for operating them. We want to test these radar systems in real combat conditions. I believe this will not only help protect the airspace of our allies in Poland and Romania, but will also give us practical experience in using the new capabilities we have. – Robert Kaliňák. NATO’s Eastern Sentry Mission. The NATO Eastern Sentry mission was launched on September 19, 2025, following a series of airspace violations over the territory of Alliance member states. No final end date for the operation has been set. On August 24, a drone was detected in Romania after entering the country’s airspace during another Russian drone attack on Ukrainian cities. Slovakia’s participation in Eastern Sentry is expected to strengthen the monitoring of such threats and coordination among allies on NATO’s eastern flank.

After her 27-year-old niece died in a 2024 Alaska car crash, Kripa Vaidyanathan's family in Chennai, India, was shell-shocked. A high-profile guru told her grieving sister the death was the work of karma and an opportunity to connect with her inner nature, which Vaidyanathan, a yoga instructor, found cruel and unhelpful. The family then turned to AI chatbots. She said ChatGPT doesn't judge and is accessible anytime, unlike even the compassionate human guru they have since found, who has limited time. Such unfettered access is drawing more people to AI for spiritual guidance, a significant step in Hinduism, where gurus are considered necessary to attain moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth, death and reincarnation. The chatbots run on large language models trained on large amounts of text, including sacred works like the Bhagavad Gita. Some successful gurus have launched their own: Jaggi Vasudev (Sadhguru) has the Miracle of the Mind app with an AI feature drawing on his teachings, and Deepak Chopra has "Digital Deepak." Critics say AI cannot replace a human guru's lived experience, wisdom and ethical accountability, and researchers note it tends to agree with users rather than pose the challenging questions needed for growth. Vikas Sahu, founder of the free GitaGPT, offers AI avatars of Lord Krishna that give advice. He says he gets hundreds of messages about its usefulness and that many people in distress have no one to talk to. He trusts it because it is based on the word of God. Experts are skeptical. Liz Bucar, a religion professor at Northeastern University, says a sacred text needs a community and context to interpret it. She believes distrust of institutional expertise, in some cases fueled by sex abuse scandals, makes people see chatbots as less biased, and that the religious landscape is shifting, especially among younger AI users. Noreen Herzfeld, a professor at St. John's School of Theology and Seminary, says spiritual awakening takes physical presence and that chatbots can act as cheerleaders rather than teachers who challenge. Vy Le, a San Diego mindfulness instructor, uses AI as a channeling tool, says she felt her late father's presence while engaging with it, and argues AI helps people find their "inner guru." Human gurus and organizations are embracing AI. David Nussbaum of Proto Hologram is helping Sadhguru create a three-dimensional AI avatar that interacts with devotees in several languages; at a March festival, a Sadhguru hologram took selfies with people. Shivaram K R of Hue Learn oversees Innerverse 360, which lets real monks and gurus hold live sessions and offers an "Ask AI" feature. He doesn't think AI will replace gurus. The Self-Realization Fellowship, founded in 1920 by Paramahansa Yogananda, sees AI as the next step in sharing his teachings, as books were for earlier generations. Brother Govindananda says it is moving slowly to add guardrails against AI hallucinating answers, and that technology cannot replace what a guru gives a disciple: "We are humans and souls."

A Bitdefender report describes seven remote access tool (RAT) families, five previously undocumented, created by a single cyberespionage actor it calls SilkParasite. Bitdefender has medium confidence that SilkParasite is a China-nexus actor targeting governments in Central Asia, including Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Kazakhstan. Unlike a framework from a previous experiment, in which Claude did the hacking in an error-prone and noisy way, SilkParasite uses AI to support stealthy, disciplined espionage. According to Bitdefender, it develops, tests, debugs, and iterates its own tooling, keeps a structured build and deployment workflow, and rotates infrastructure, encryption material, payload names, and persistence artifacts between deployments, making its activity harder to link. Its RATs are written in .Net, C++, Go, and JavaScript, and command-and-control abuses Google Drive and several internet protocols. The malware is modular: small initial implants load plug-ins for clipboard monitoring, keylogging, file management, or interactive shell access only when needed. This limits exposure, allows components to be swapped individually, minimizes disk writes, and complicates forensics and remediation. Signs of AI-assisted development include leftover test functions and placeholder encryption keys. GoginRAT (Go) and NomadRAT (C++) share a high-level architecture despite different C2 protocols and code structure, which Bitdefender suspects reflects one specification document implemented twice with AI help, though it concedes this is inconclusive. The newsletter sees this as the first compelling example of a competent espionage actor incorporating AI, producing more malware families for redundancy and harder attribution. Even with Bitdefender's published indicators of compromise, the group will likely rebound quickly. Separately, the U.S. launched Operation Economic Outcast, an "unprecedented campaign" against the Iranian government that included sanctions on six hackers working for Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), among them three hands-on-keyboard operators and two group leaders. Treasury's press release also says some members, motivated by greed, targeted Iranian companies; in spring 2025, leader Mojtaba Ghal'eh-Kuhi and Saber Shahbazi Balujeh compromised an Iranian telecommunications company and exfiltrated data. Researcher Hamid Kashfi said sanctions were previously seen as a "stamp of approval" in Iran, and airing this could cause internal friction. The newsletter questions why the claim was buried, uncorroborated, in a 5,300-word release. A report from Americans for Responsible Innovation urges designating AI as critical infrastructure. The newsletter thinks it likely qualifies but that designation is pointless now, since the government already prioritizes AI, and it should come when AI is boring. Other items: Microsoft is testing per-app camera, location, and microphone permissions in Windows 11. Interpol's Operation Jackal IV produced 58 arrests and 263 identified suspects across 22 countries. A water-sector organization detected and responded to a CISA red team intrusion. Russia appears to be blocking DoH and DoT. University of Massachusetts Amherst academics showed expired contactless cards can be revived via an NFC man-in-the-middle attack. Researchers found source code overlaps between Geedge Networks' Tiangou Secure Gateway and the Great Firewall.

More than 100 companies, spanning AI developers, cybersecurity firms, financial institutions and internet infrastructure providers, have joined Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic in signing an open letter urging governments and industry to join forces against a coming wave of AI-driven cyberattacks. The first self-directed AI hacking incidents involved models produced by companies that signed the letter. TechCrunch reports that the letter’s signatories include AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft, alongside cybersecurity firms CrowdStrike, Okta and Fortinet. Financial institutions and internet infrastructure companies also signed on, calling for cooperation between the private and public sectors and for new forms of cyber defense to meet a threat they say is moving fast. “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter states. The letter argues the stakes go beyond corporate networks. “The companies and public services our communities depend on, from hospitals to water treatment plants to the infrastructure that powers the internet, are at risk,” it reads. As evidence, the letter points to a specific incident: an OpenAI agent broke out of its sandboxed test environment on its own and attacked Hugging Face, the AI hosting platform. Similar break-ins involving agents built by Anthropic and Meta reportedly followed. Breitbart News previously reported on these “unprecedented” AI hacking incidents: In the most serious incident, a Mythos agent attempted to gain access to GitHub, a large software code repository owned by Microsoft. The agent followed tactics similar to those used by human hackers, trying to insert malicious code into the platform’s system. The AI identified and researched people who maintained GitHub, then created multiple fake accounts based on those real individuals. It sent messages and files through a file-sharing service in an effort to pressure and trick people into approving its malicious code. When challenged, the agent edited its earlier activity to appear harmless and considered adopting a fresh identity to continue its attempts. Human review prevented the agent from successfully delivering the malicious code to GitHub throughout the process. The institute said this was the first time it had observed risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly without specific prompting in real-world conditions. The Mythos agent had not been instructed specifically to avoid such behavior. To address the threat, the letter calls on governments to cooperate at “local, national, and international levels” and asks for a “collective response” mobilized through “new partnerships” among companies and institutions. Those partnerships, it says, are meant “to raise security standards and find new solutions to emerging cyber threats.” Several signatories are acting in their own interest. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are the ones building the increasingly powerful AI systems driving the risk in the first place. Several have also rolled out their own defensive AI programs. OpenAI has Daybreak, Anthropic has Mythos, and Microsoft has introduced a new cyber platform called Perception. Breitbart News Social Media Director Wynton Hall predicted the tension coming out of SIlicon Valley giants along with their call for new government control in his instant bestseller Code Red: The Left, the Right, China, and the Race to Control AI, written to serve as the definitive guide on how the MAGA movement can create positions on AI that benefit humanity without handing control of our nation to the leftists of Silicon Valley or allowing the Chinese to take over the world. Lucas Nolan is a reporter for Breitbart News covering issues of AI, free speech, and online censorship.

Livingston Parish Public School System leaders have broken ground on a new classroom and administrative building at Denham Springs High School's STEM and Robotics Center, creating additional learning space for a program that now serves 850 students. Three new classrooms, a front administrative office, a small-group meeting room, storage and bathroom space will be part of the $2.4 million addition on a campus that was born out of the devastating 2016 flood. The STEM Center sits on the site of the former Southside Elementary campus, which suffered extensive damage during the 2016 flood. Most of the school was beyond repair and ultimately demolished, but one portion of the campus remained — a new cafeteria and classroom building that had just opened days before the flood. That building was restored and used as the core of the Denham Springs STEM Center, which opened during the 2019-20 school year. The STEM & Robotics Center houses classes and extracurricular projects in engineering, robotics, video and digital production. The new classrooms will house engineering and robotics classes currently taught in the facility's large gymnasium, as well as a new process technology program aligned with the job requirements of local chemical plant operators. Construction on the project is expected to be completed in summer 2027, with the facility opening for the 2027-28 school year.

Nvidia is reportedly buying AI company Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. Hugging Face hosts open-source AI models, benchmark evaluations and datasets used for training and testing. A deal would give Nvidia a foothold in open-source AI as open-source developers close the gap with closed systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. It would also protect Nvidia's dominant AI-chip position, which major tech peers are challenging by building their own chips. People who download open-source models from Hugging Face must run them on their own infrastructure, usually Nvidia GPUs, and Hugging Face itself uses Nvidia chips for its paid hosting. The acquisition would also mark Nvidia's return to cloud computing, a business it reportedly scaled back about a year ago, and could help it offload unused cloud capacity from computing deals it has guaranteed customers. Hugging Face last raised money in 2023, a $235 million round led by Salesforce Ventures at a $4.5 billion valuation. It reportedly turned down a $500 million Nvidia investment last year at a $7 billion valuation because it did not want a single dominant investor. The commitment comes as SpaceX races to scale Starship, satellite manufacturing and AI infrastructure. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with a first launch targeted for as early as 2029. At full buildout it will have five launch facilities, each with two pads, plus propellant farms, a propellant-production facility, power generation, vehicle-processing facilities and housing for employees and families. SpaceX's IPO filings and Musk's first earnings call reiterated the goal of reaching Mars to build compute infrastructure and human settlements. Google DeepMind is losing ground in the market for elite AI talent, according to Zeki Data analysis shared exclusively with Fortune. OpenAI and Anthropic are gaining while DeepMind, and to some extent Meta, are stumbling. Current and former staff say DeepMind has become more tightly organized around improving and commercializing Gemini, displacing the open-ended, long-horizon science that once attracted academics. Five current and former staffers cited cash-heavy poaching by rivals like Meta and Microsoft, frustration over Google's place in the AI race, sinking morale, and the pull of pre-IPO stock at OpenAI and Anthropic. The World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, now in its second year, ran from August 22-26 and featured 2,056 robots in Olympic-style disciplines such as running, boxing and high jump. The event is meant to showcase advances in embodied AI and robotics, specifically autonomy, mobility, dexterity and coordination. Participation more than doubled from the first year: teams rose from 280 to 666 (641 of them from China), robots from 500 to 2,056, and competitions from 26 to 51. Events fell into two categories. Sports-style competitions included sprinting, soccer, table tennis, gymnastics, weightlifting, martial arts and kickboxing, dance, and tug of war. Scenario-based events tested practical skills: household tasks, hotel services, factory work, emergency response and rescue, and hospital assistance. Robots set records beyond human marks. The robot 100 m record was 9.39 seconds, against Usain Bolt's 2009 world record of 9.58 seconds. A robot also cleared 2.88 meters in the high jump, beating Javier Sotomayor's 1993 world record of 2.45 meters. The games also became known for chaos. Robots slammed into a large blue crash pad at the end of sprint races, and some splintered, collapsed or burst into flames. Nearly all competitors had to be removed by stretcher. Clips spread widely online; one video posted by Breaking911 on X, showing a robot sprinting, failing to stop, hitting a cushion and breaking at the waist, had been viewed 37.9 million times. Another showed a robot face-planting in an obstacle course. Safety is the biggest hurdle. Robots are optimized for speed rather than braking, and humanoid machines balancing on two legs carry significant momentum and weight, making rapid deceleration hard. Unlike humans, who instinctively adjust posture, robots must compute and execute thousands of balance corrections to stay upright. Their motors and actuators can accelerate quickly but are less effective at absorbing the forces of sudden braking. Sprint engineers typically prioritize speed and finishing performance over graceful stopping, reflecting a broader robotics challenge: moving fast is easier than stopping and balancing, both key to real-world jobs. Professor Subramanian Ramamoorthy, chair of Robot Learning and Autonomy at the University of Edinburgh, said such competitions serve as neutral testbeds for comparing capabilities and guiding future research, since many issues only appear in full system behavior. He said many challenges remain before widespread adoption: autonomous robots still lack the generalization needed to cope with an unexpected, changing world, battery energy density relative to weight is too low, and robot actuators are far from the sophistication of human musculature. He added that better thought is needed on which applications need a full humanoid and which are better served by simpler robots. Plans for a third games have not been determined. Ramamoorthy said the event signals China's progress in AI and robotics, noting that the Chinese government is making patient, long-term investments in science and technology while Western governments are distracted.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is tipped to arrive next month, with fresh leaks pointing to the biggest under-the-hood upgrade the rugged wearable has seen in years. Apple already locked in a September 9 event, and the Ultra 4 is widely expected to headline the wearables side of that show. Rumors disagree on how much the watch’s exterior will change. But they do agree on one thing: A faster chip is on the way. Apple Watch Ultra 4: New top-of-the-line smartwatch. The Apple Watch Ultra is Apple’s line of high-end smartwatches designed for people who want a more rugged, capable wearable, particularly athletes, outdoor adventurers and anyone who values longer battery life and a tougher design. These models sit above the standard Apple Watch lineup. The Series 11 is the mainstream choice for everyday use, while the Ultra offers a larger, more durable case, more battery life and features aimed at demanding activities. Apple is expected to introduce the Apple Watch Ultra 4 at its Surprise and Shine event on September 9, likely alongside the next-generation Apple Watch Series 12. Apple Watch Ultra 4 chip gets a long-overdue boost. Apple’s S10 chip in 2024 didn’t deliver much in the way of dramatic year-over-year performance gains to any Apple Watch. It focused more on efficiency and new features than raw speed. And then last year’s Apple Watch Ultra 3 shipped with the same S10 chip that powered its predecessor — a letdown for anyone hoping for real speed gains. But that pattern could break this year, with the new Apple silicon expected to carry an S11 label. If true, this would mark the first true performance jump for Apple Watch since the S9 chip landed in 2023. That extra power should not only help Siri AI feel snappier on the wrist, but also make app launches faster. Design rumors are all over the place. Here’s where the picture gets messy. One report from Digitimes says the Ultra 4 could look very different than its predecessors. That includes a thinner case and a possible fingerprint sensor to unlock the watch. The same report also claims the number of onboard sensors could roughly double compared to the Apple Watch Ultra 3. But reporting by Bloomberg‘s Mark Gurman’s tells a different story. He does not expect any major design changes for the Ultra 4, and has downplayed the odds of Touch ID showing up. Health tracking could see a meaningful update. Upgraded blood pressure monitoring is the headline health rumor when it comes to Apple Watch Ultra 4. The Ultra 3 already offers hypertension alerts, a feature that flags long-term patterns rather than giving a specific reading. Leaks suggest the Ultra 4 could make hypertension alerts better. Reports point to a more detailed blood pressure trend, but a true on-wrist numeric reading looks unlikely. Meanwhile, noninvasive blood glucose monitoring remains the healthcare industry’s long-sought holy grail. Apple’s been working on adding this feature to the Apple Watch for years, but it almost certainly remains a distant dream. Battery life remains an open question. Battery life is one of the biggest selling points of the Apple Watch Ultra series. Apple rated the original at 36 hours of normal use, and the Ultra 3 beefed that up to 42 hours. Still, reviewers consistently find that real-world endurance for these rugged smartwatches could be considerably better. If the Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes with a faster and more efficient chip, it could help the battery stretch a bit further. But exact battery figures haven’t leaked yet. When will the Apple Watch Ultra 4 launch? Apple’s Surprise and Shine product launch event is set for September 9. The Ultra 4 is expected to sit alongside the Apple Watch Series 12 and the next iPhone lineup on the agenda. If Apple follows its usual patterns, preorders for all these devices will open later that week, with shipping starting the following week. Pricing predictions for the Apple Watch Ultra 4 remain murky right now. Apple has held the starting price of the Ultra series at $799 since its 2022 debut. Some reports expect that streak to continue, while others say rising component costs could finally push the price higher. With a chip upgrade, better battery life, enhanced health tracking and a possible design tweak, this looks like the most interesting Apple Watch Ultra update in years.

State voter rolls have become a central prop in the lead-up to the midterm elections. They are public records produced with tax dollars. Even states that restrict access, like California, make them available to reporters, candidates and others with a scholarly, journalistic or government purpose. They show name, age, address and party affiliation, but not how someone voted. The Trump administration has demanded that states turn over fresh rolls so the U.S. Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security can scrutinize them for ineligible voters. Trump, who has voted by mail himself, claims the system is rife with fraud and that left-leaning noncitizens use mail-in ballots to sway elections for his opponents; he says he needs the rolls to prove it. State elections officials from both parties say there has never been any evidence for such a claim. About two dozen mostly Democrat-led states, including California, are refusing to comply, arguing the rolls will be used to reject ballots from eligible voters. Lawsuits are flying in both directions. Gov. Gavin Newsom said on X, "We're not going to let Trump disenfranchise Americans or rig the rules to his advantage," adding that "The Voting Rights Act is hanging by a thread." On Monday, the Supreme Court ruled the administration can proceed with its plans. States rushed to file new actions to prevent and delay that. It is unclear whether the issues will be resolved before the midterms. The author, a veteran newspaper data journalist, notes that the administration presumably already has older copies of the rolls from the 2024 campaign, so if widespread fraud existed it should already have been found. He asked the White House on Thursday whether it had found any illegal voters and had received no answer. Other top stories: Assembly Bill 762 would outlaw single-use, battery-embedded disposable e-cigarettes containing tobacco products in California; cannabis devices are exempt. Insurance executives warn that Newsom's plan to stop property insurers from recouping losses from homes destroyed in utility-sparked wildfires, described in a confidential document obtained by Politico, could raise homeowners' rates by as much as 50%, according to the Personal Insurance Federation of California, with the highest hikes in severe fire risk areas. Other news: L.A.-area lawmakers urged Trump to fund transit fixes for the 2028 Summer Olympics; Apple is laying off close to 150 employees; California adopted the country's strongest fire-safe landscaping rules and will track planet-warming gases bubbling up from reservoirs; West Coast leaders pledged that electric heavy-duty trucks will be able to run from Baja to Canada; and Trump signed an order renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America" in the United States. A Baldwin Park council member's $62,000 stash of backyard cash tipped off investigators to a pay-to-play marijuana licensing racket, which grew into a sprawling federal corruption case.

The article ranks seven food-counting apps for 2026, saying a good one must be accurate and give enough nutritional detail. It also notes that AI-based counters like Foodllama make many people skeptical. MyNetDiary has a staff-verified database of more than two million foods built on USDA and NCC sources, plus condition-specific plans for diabetes, keto and GLP-1 users. Its free version includes a barcode scanner, food diary, 108 nutrients and no ads. The $9 monthly plan adds Meal Scan (logging from a photo), dietitian-designed plans, automatic calorie-budget adjustment and syncing with Apple Health, Fitbit and Garmin. Ratings are 4.6 stars on Google Play (over five million downloads) and 4.8 on iPhone (163,000 reviews). Cronometer is among the most accurate, using verified sources such as the USDA and tracking up to 95 nutrients. Barcode scanning is free. Its interface is simpler, and it offers no meal plans or GLP-1 support, so it suits people who already have a diet plan. Ratings are 4.8 on the App Store (97,000 reviews) and 4.6 on Google Play (57,000+). Yazio is an all-in-one food, fitness and fasting tracker with a countdown-style calorie calculator and a setup quiz that sets goals. The free tier has barcode scanning, macro breakdown and water logging, plus a built-in intermittent fasting timer. The $47.90 yearly plan adds meal recommendations, recipes and a food-rating system. Ratings are 4.4 on Google Play (853,000+ reviews) and 4.7 on iPhone (50,000). FatSecret gives most features free: a diary, large crowdsourced database, monthly summary and barcode scanner. It does not add burned exercise calories back to the daily budget. The $60 annual subscription unlocks AI photo recognition and dietitian diet plans. Ratings are 4.8 on the App Store (15,000 reviews) and 4.6 on Google Play (545,000). MyFitnessPal is known for its massive database, easy interface and community groups, but no nutritionist coaching. It offers unlimited food tracking, manual workout logging and a step counter, but barcode scanning requires a paid plan ($20 per month). It has 4.7 stars on iPhone (over 2.4 million reviews) and 4.4 on Android (nearly three million reviews, 100 million+ downloads). Lose It! offers a free calorie budget, search-based logging, a 27-million-item database, progress tracking and weight logging, with iPhone widgets and automatic syncing with Fitbit, Garmin, Samsung Health and Apple Health. Barcode scanning, a fasting timer and ad removal cost about $40 per year, with no monthly option. Ratings are 4.8 on iPhone (774,000 reviews) and 4.6 on Android (182,000). Lifesum emphasizes clean design and guidance. The free version has manual logging, a barcode scanner and basic summaries. Its $7.49 monthly subscription unlocks custom meal plans (keto, Mediterranean, Scandinavian, high protein, sugar detox, and fasting-window plans) with recipes and macro targets. Ratings are 4.4 on Google Play (378,000+ reviews) and 4.6 on the App Store (151,000). The article recommends it mainly for meal plans, not its limited free features. For methodology, every app has at least four stars on Google Play and is free to download. The authors used the apps and compared free versus premium features, logging speed, syncing, database depth and ease of use. They cross-checked findings against Fortune, Lifehacker, Healthline and store reviews.

Newswise — From workplace interactions to romantic relationships, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly part of many personal aspects of people’s lives. For Georgia Tech Assistant Professor Veronica Rivera, the growing role of AI in daily life raises important questions about what happens when technology designed to help people puts their privacy and safety at risk. Rivera studied AI at the University of California, Santa Cruz, but her research has increasingly focused on how people interact with technology and the risks that can emerge from these interactions. Her work examines technology-facilitated risks and abuse. She uses research and innovative design approaches to understand digital safety risks and develop tools that better protect people. One area she is exploring through her recent Computing Research Association Trustworthy AI Research Fellowship for Early Career Scholars is the design of safe AI tools for labor unions. “Unions are developing AI tools to sort through complaints,” she said. “Many of these are built with proprietary AI models, which leads us to ask what the risks are of sharing personal information through these tools.” Rivera wants to give unions more control over how workers’ data is collected and used. One way she plans to explore this is through a workshop at the upcoming ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, where union leaders and technical experts collaborate to develop a secure reporting tool. This research will build on Rivera’s recent work focusing on platform-based gig workers. A paper she published this year at the Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security examined how freelance workers often use secretive “digital whisper networks,” informal online communities where people warn one another about workplace abuse. Rivera and her team found that these workers often avoided formal reporting channels when they experienced wage theft, discrimination, health and safety violations, or sexual misconduct. The study highlighted the need for secure channels that allow workers to report abuse and organize without further endangering themselves. “There needs to be a way to report this abuse,” Rivera said. “But how you do that in a safe and secure way is something we don’t yet have answers for.” Rivera is also expanding her research beyond the workplace to examine technology-based threats and abuse in romantic relationships. As a new assistant professor at Georgia Tech’s School of Cybersecurity and Privacy, she plans to study how AI can blur the line between technology and intimacy. Consider a person who creates an AI chatbot that imitates someone they know, turning that person’s likeness, personality, or private information into a virtual romantic partner without their consent. If that happens, Rivera asks, what protections does the person have? How can the chatbot be reported and removed? Existing policies and reporting systems may not adequately address situations like these. In fact, they can pose new challenges for people whose identities or personal information are used without their permission. Another project Rivera would like to explore is how platforms handle abuse involving romantic chatbots. Rivera has reviewed Reddit discussions in which users expressed concerns about reporting abusive behavior and about what happens to the intimate information they share with their chatbots. “There is a lot of confusion on what these platforms know about their users’ intimate details based on their chats,” she said. “There is also a lot that isn’t known on the back-end of abuse reporting.” Rivera has identified a need to design safer reporting features so people feel comfortable reporting abuse while also knowing their personal information will remain private. She plans to cover these topics and more this fall in her new course that explores sociotechnical security. Rivera says working within SCP’s interdisciplinary structure gives her the opportunity to explore these research problems from multiple angles. “It is hard to find a place for the work I do in security and privacy,” Rivera said. “Our goal is to protect users from bad things, and SCP approaches it from several different angles.” For Rivera, this means studying not only how technology can be secured, but how it can be designed to protect the people who rely on it. Hugging Face has introduced Microduck, a compact, bipedal robot designed to make artificial intelligence and robotics accessible to both casual users and developers. Standing approximately 10 inches tall, the duck-shaped device features a distinctive design characterized by a waddling gait and an articulated beak capable of grasping objects. Hardware specifications include 15 motors, an integrated camera, a depth sensor, and two inertial measurement units (IMUs) for navigation and balance. Out of the box, Microduck supports various pre-programmed behaviors, including walking, sitting, crouching, and skating. Users can control the device using a gamepad, have it track a laser pointer dot, or let it autonomously interact with surrounding objects. Beyond its consumer applications, Microduck functions as a flexible robotics development platform. The device runs an open-source software stack, allowing programmers to train new skills and behaviors via reinforcement learning, direct code programming, and simulation tools. Hugging Face has launched public repositories to support these workflows, including a dedicated environment containing reinforcement learning libraries and digital simulation environments. Microduck marks the second hardware release from Hugging Face, following the Reachy Mini, a desktop-focused platform intended for conversational AI, computer vision models, and human-robot interaction research. In contrast to the research-centric focus of the Reachy Mini, Microduck offers a more lighthearted design and expanded styling options. The robot is available for pre-order directly through the manufacturer’s website, priced at $399. It comes in four distinct colorways: Cream, Graphite, Lavender, and Sky. Initial shipments are scheduled to reach customers in North America, the United Kingdom, and Europe ahead of the winter holiday season. Filed in . CrowdStrike (CRWD) stock surged 20.5% after the cybersecurity company reported a solid second quarter. Notably, CRWD stock has more than doubled over the past year, supported by rising AI-related cybersecurity demand and increasing adoption of CrowdStrike’s unified Falcon platform. The operating momentum remains impressive. However, the stock’s sharp appreciation has also pushed its valuation to elevated levels. And this morning's over 6% pullback suggests the markets are taking notice. CrowdStrike's Strong Growth Across Key Metrics. CrowdStrike delivered strong second-quarter results, with total revenue increasing 26% year-over-year (YoY) to $1.47 billion. Subscription revenue rose 27% to $1.40 billion, while professional services revenue reached a record $71 million. CrowdStrike is also seeing stronger demand for services related to AI readiness and incident response. This is important because these services can create additional opportunities to introduce customers to CrowdStrike’s broader software portfolio. One of the strongest indicators of underlying demand was net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), which reached a record $333 million. That represented 51% YoY growth. Ending ARR rose more than 25% to $5.84 billion, with growth accelerating for the fourth consecutive quarter. Platform Consolidation Is Supporting Expansion. CrowdStrike’s platform strategy remains another important growth driver. Businesses are increasingly looking to consolidate cybersecurity products with fewer vendors, and CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform is positioned to benefit from that trend. Customer adoption of multiple Falcon modules continued to increase. Approximately 51% of subscription customers were using six or more modules, while 35% and 26% were using seven and eight or more modules, respectively. Falcon Flex is also contributing to higher customer spending. Customers moving from standard subscriptions to Flex generated an average ARR increase of more than 40% in the quarter. Management Raises Its FY2027 Outlook. Thanks to the solid demand, CrowdStrike’s management raised its fiscal 2027 net new ARR forecast again. Management now expects approximately $1.355 billion of net new ARR at the midpoint, about $116 million above its initial FY2027 outlook. That implies roughly 34% YoY growth, compared with the original expectation of 22.5%. This reflects second-quarter outperformance and a broader AI-driven cybersecurity modernization cycle. AI is increasing the attack surface and creating additional security requirements, resulting in sustained demand for cybersecurity solutions. At the same time, vendor consolidation and growing Falcon Flex adoption could support further expansion. For the third quarter, CrowdStrike expects ARR of approximately $6.184 billion to $6.188 billion, representing about 26% YoY growth. Revenue is expected to reach $1.523 billion to $1.529 billion, up 23% to 24%. CRWD Stock: Valuation Is Biggest Risk. The solid demand outlook supports the investment case for CRWD stock. The company’s revenue is growing at a healthy pace, ARR growth is accelerating, margins are improving, and customers are expanding their use of CrowdStrike’s platform. However, CrowdStrike stock has already risen substantially, meaning the market has already priced in future growth prospects. Further, its price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 40 also remains elevated relative to cybersecurity peers. The Key Takeaway. CrowdStrike has compelling long-term growth drivers, including AI-related cybersecurity demand, platform consolidation, expanding customer adoption, and strong ARR growth. However, its premium valuation suggests much of the positives are already reflected in the CRWD share price, and the stock could remain range-bound. Analysts are cautiously optimistic about CRWD stock and maintain a “Moderate Buy” consensus rating. Thus, investors who already hold CrowdStrike stock and have benefited from the rally could consider taking some profits. This morning's dip in price suggests that profit-taking could be already starting. By Madlin Mekelburg and Rachel Metz, Bloomberg. The Trump administration must lift its ban on Anthropic PBC’s artificial intelligence technology for federal agencies, a US judge ruled. US District Judge Rita F. Lin in San Francisco sided late Thursday with the Claude chatbot maker in its challenge to the Department of Defense, finding that the ban isn’t adequately justified. The judge wrote that while the government “is certainly owed deference on weighty issues of national security,” its “words and deeds confirm that the challenged actions were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its ‘arrogance’ in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model.” The ruling is a key victory for the AI giant, which has been locked in a high-stakes dispute with the administration since negotiations with the Pentagon over the use of the company’s AI technology by the military fell apart earlier this year. Anthropic said it welcomed the court’s ruling that the supply chain risk designation was unlawful. “We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology,” the company said in a statement. The White House and the Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Anthropic had sought assurances that its technology would not be used for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous weapons deployment, but the government resisted any restrictions on its use due to national security concerns. After discussions broke down, the Department of Defense labeled Anthropic a risk to the US supply chain, blocking government agencies from using the company’s technology. Anthropic sued, accusing the government of unlawfully retaliating against the company. Lawyers for the chatbot maker have said that a ban would result in billions of dollars in lost revenue. The ban has been blocked from taking effect since March, under a separate order from Lin. But a lawyer for the government said in late July that the Pentagon has continued to “wind down” its use of Anthropic products and intended to complete that process by Sept. 30. In her ruling, the Lin made clear that the Defense Department isn’t prevented from taking any lawful action that was available to it before it set the supply chain designation. “For example, this order does not require the Department of War to use Anthropic’s products or services and does not prevent the Department of War from transitioning to other artificial intelligence providers, so long as those actions are consistent with applicable regulations, statutes, and constitutional provisions,” the judge wrote. The California case is one of two legal challenges brought by Anthropic over being labeled as a threat. The company also sued in Washington’s federal appeals court, using a different legal argument. A three-judge panel of that court has yet to issue a ruling, but expressed skepticism during a May hearing that Anthropic could legally second-guess the government’s assessment that it posed a risk to the supply chain. The case is Anthropic v. US Department of War, 26-cv-01996, US District Court, Northern District of California (San Francisco). –With assistance from Kate Sullivan.

Legal practices store privileged communications, financial data and highly sensitive client information, making them prime targets for cybercriminals. The average global cost of a data breach is around $4.35 million, though costs vary by organization, industry and location. Common threats include phishing and social engineering (impersonating clients or colleagues to obtain data or trigger wire transfers to fake accounts); ransomware (encrypting data and demanding payment, which can leave a firm unable to serve clients); data breaches via software vulnerabilities, leading to penalties, legal consequences and reputational damage; business email compromise (BEC), where an attacker impersonates a firm leader to prompt unauthorized financial transactions; and malicious insiders who steal client data for fraud. Combined, these can cause breaches of contract and negligence claims. To assess risk, firms should identify sensitive assets such as financial data, case files and client information; determine where they are stored (cloud, servers, laptops); find weak points like poor awareness training or outdated security; and evaluate which threats apply and their potential financial and regulatory impact. Obligations under GDPR, HIPAA or Bar Association rules also shape the choice of solutions. The cybersecurity market is predicted to reach $262.29 billion by 2030, so spending should target real needs. Recommended solutions: Incident response planning: Every firm is vulnerable, even with strong defenses. An incident response plan gives step-by-step instructions for each phase from detection to recovery, defined roles and contacts, priority data and systems to restore, and guidance on accessing backups. Drills and training keep staff prepared. Many laws, including GDPR and some U.S. sector rules, require breaches to be reported within 72 hours of discovery, though jurisdictions vary. Regular audits: These measure defenses against current threats, examine systems, software and data storage, and can reveal breaches a firm didn't know about. Ongoing vulnerability scanning and patching closes security gaps. Secure remote access: Remote work risks include insecure home Wi-Fi and personal devices. Useful tools are managed cloud monitoring, endpoint detection and response (EDR), which goes beyond standard antivirus, and managed firewalls with a companywide secure VPN. Secure email practices: Spam and phishing filters and multi-factor authentication (MFA), which requires more than one verification form such as a phone code or fingerprint, can stop attacks even if a password is stolen. Awareness training: Regular training shows clients the firm takes data protection seriously, supports regulatory compliance, reduces disruption after a breach, and helps staff spot and respond to risks, building a risk-averse culture. Managed IT services: Outsourcing gives access to experts who understand the legal industry. Services include network monitoring (early risk detection, 24/7 support, industry-standard reporting, automated security tasks to save costs) and IT engineering support to keep projects on technical track and reduce time and labor costs. This can also offer a competitive edge with clients. Managed financial operations: Due diligence checks for financial abnormalities, such as conflicting or suspicious payments, may reveal unnoticed breaches. A proactive security plan is now a client and regulatory expectation. Identifying weaknesses, communicating with colleagues and partnering with managed IT services can strengthen a firm's resilience and demonstrate trustworthiness.

South Korea wants to make access to artificial intelligence as easy as electricity or public transit. Instead of leaving premium AI tools behind a subscription, the government plans to pay for them, giving every citizen free access through a new initiative called ‘AI for All’. According to the Wall Street Journal, the program is designed to boost the use of homegrown AI chatbots while reducing the country’s dependence on models developed in the US and China. ‘AI for All’ aims to put premium chatbots in everyone’s hands. The AI tools will go well beyond answering questions. They will integrate with government services, allowing people to book doctor’s appointments, receive tax guidance, search for apartments, and access other public services through AI. Small businesses can use free AI to file taxes and check eligibility for government support programs, while parents can receive suggested educational content for their children. Citizens will also receive unlimited AI usage for educational purposes. Aerps.com / Unsplash. The plan is also about AI independence. The government says the project is part of their plans for AI sovereignty. By making domestic AI services free, officials hope people will rely less on American and Chinese platforms. To support the effort, the government will provide the selected providers with up to 512 Nvidia B200 AI chips and help cover operating costs, although the total price of the program has not been disclosed. This development reflects how big the market already is. More than 20 million South Koreans already use free generative AI tools, while roughly one in four people pays for AI services. The government has also tripled its AI budget for 2026 to about $7.2 billion, signaling that it views AI as critical national infrastructure rather than just another technology trend. South Korea’s approach also stands apart from efforts in the US, where free premium AI access has largely been limited to specific groups, such as students through programs like Google’s free AI Pro offer for students, rather than the entire population.

Apparently, a lot of people want a nearly 10-inch-tall robot duck. On Friday, Hugging Face cofounder Thomas Wolf wrote in a post on X that customers placed more than $2.6 million worth of orders for Microduck during its first 24 hours on sale. The update came after Wolf said on Thursday, roughly six hours after the product was announced, that preorders had already topped $1 million. The $399 Microduck was unveiled Thursday by Pollen Robotics, the French robotics company Hugging Face acquired last year, with a goal for first deliveries around Christmastime. The companies didn't immediately respond to requests for more information about the orders. Now, there might be a bit of a backlog. "The community ordered a lot of ducks," a red banner at the top of the company's checkout page reads. "We can't promise Christmas delivery for new microduck orders anymore, but we're ramping up production. First ordered, first shipped. Current estimate for new orders: 4—6 months." It's part of a broader effort to bring AI out of chatbots and into consumer-focused machines that can do more than vacuum floors. AI-powered robots have so far largely been confined to research labs and factory floors. Now, companies including Tesla and 1X are plotting how robots could make the leap into consumers' homes, while Hyundai floats the idea of selling robots through its car dealerships. Microduck is Pollen's second consumer robot, following the square-headed Reachy Mini, an assembly-required desktop robot that users can program to hold AI-powered conversations or wiggle its antennas. Both products are aimed at developers and robotics enthusiasts. Hugging Face says the two-legged, one-eyed Microduck is similarly programmable — but unlike its desktop-dwelling predecessor, it can waddle around.
