CrowdStrike helps businesses protect computers, cloud systems, identities, data and applications. Its main product is the cloud-based Falcon platform, sold by subscription, and it also offers AI-powered tools to secure AI applications and workloads. It works with Cognizant Technology Solutions Corporation on securing AI systems. Founded in 2011, it is headquartered in Austin, Texas. Over the past 12 months the stock has surged 97.7%, far outpacing the iShares Cybersecurity and Tech ETF's (IHAK) 25.5% gain. The stock is priced for perfection. The forward GAAP price-to-earnings ratio of 1,805.91 is distorted by heavy stock-based compensation, but the forward price-to-sales ratio of 38.86 is 80.74% above its five-year average of 21.50, a steep premium. Analysts expect growth of 41% in 2027, 26% in 2028, 25% in 2029 and 31% in 2030, for a company worth nearly $200 billion. The balance sheet holds $5.01 billion in cash against $821 million in debt. After the report, Rosenblatt's Catharine Trebnick raised her price target from $206 to $250 with a "Buy" rating, noting CrowdStrike beat every guided metric and raised its outlook. Raymond James analyst Adam Tindle raised his target from $188 to $240 with an "Outperform" rating, noting ARR growth is holding above 25% and that demand for AI Detection and Response nearly tripled from the prior quarter. Among 50 covering analysts, the consensus is "Moderate Buy," with 33 giving a "Strong Buy." The mean price target of $211.35 is below the current share price, while the high target of $256 implies 17.2% upside, suggesting modest further upside after the rally.

The big picture: South Korea is preparing to offer free generative AI services to its entire population, using the technology to help people handle everyday tasks such as booking medical appointments, finding housing, and sorting out taxes. The program is intended to expand access to homegrown AI systems while giving the government a larger role in how they are used for everyday services. The government’s “AI for All” program will begin beta testing in September, followed by a broader launch later this year. On Friday, Seoul named three technology consortia to provide the services. They include groups led by the country’s two largest telecom companies and the operator of Kakao, one of South Korea’s most widely used consumer platforms. The services are expected to connect to government systems rather than function solely as standalone chatbots. Residents will be able to use them to book doctor appointments, search for apartments, and get tax guidance. Small businesses will be able to calculate taxes and check whether they qualify for government support. Parents will receive recommendations for educational content. Each consortium plans to introduce its own AI app and add generative AI features to existing products. Users will have unlimited access, with no token limits under the government-supported plans. Seoul will supply some of the computing capacity needed to run the services. The government plans to distribute up to 512 Nvidia B200 chips among the three consortia and help cover operating costs. The Ministry of Science and ICT has not disclosed the program’s total cost. The initiative is part of South Korea’s effort to build a stronger domestic AI industry and reduce its reliance on systems developed in the US and China. The government is trying to steer more consumers toward locally developed AI products by making premium-level services widely available at no cost. South Korea already has a large market for generative AI. A government survey earlier this year found that about one-quarter of South Koreans pay for AI services. By comparison, a PNC Bank survey found that about 2% of Americans pay for such services. Seoul estimates that more than 20 million people in South Korea use free generative AI tools. The rollout is backed by a broader increase in AI spending. President Lee Jae Myung’s administration has set aside about 10 trillion won, or $7.2 billion, for AI-related spending in 2026. That is three times the amount allocated the previous year. For South Korea, the project will test whether generative AI can become part of the country’s basic digital infrastructure. Its success will depend on whether the systems are reliable enough for people to use them for practical, routine tasks. The government has not set an adoption target for the new service.

The new Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL finally add a 4K 60fps HDR video feature. But Google’s exclusive Video Boost technology quietly turns it off, relying on algorithmically-generated frames instead. The Pixel 11 Pro series introduces the ability to shoot 4K HDR video at 60fps, allowing for smoother motion and 2x slow-motion playback at a standard 30fps. Pixel fans have waited a long time for this feature, as it’s something the iPhone has supported as far back as the iPhone 12 Pro. However, “Pro” Pixels also support Video Boost, an AI-powered technology that shoots in a special format and processes the video in the cloud to achieve Google’s best possible quality. It’s an effective strategy that led Dxomark to score the Pixel 11 Pro XL above the iPhone 17 Pro in its stand-alone Video Boost tests. What Google doesn’t tell you is that if you shoot at 4K 60fps with HDR turned on and then activate Video Boost, the captured frame rate is silently downgraded to 30fps before it's uploaded to Google’s servers for processing. According to Google, Video Boost on the Pixel 11 Pro series uses the exact same pipeline as the Pixel 10 Pro XL. This pipeline maxes out at 30fps when recording 4K HDR video. This means the Pixel 11 Pro’s 4K60 HDR recording mode is never used when deploying Video Boost, potentially losing motion information that can’t be recovered. Video Boost does return a 60fps video, just like on the Pixel 10 Pro series, but half of those frames are generated, not captured. Testing Video Boost On The Pixel 11 Pro XL. I tested this by capturing a timer displayed on a 120Hz screen. When using a Pixel 11 Pro XL in standard mode, every frame of the 4K60 HDR recording showed a different time reading. In the final Video Boost version, every reading appeared twice in adjacent frames. The intermediate time readings aren’t there because they were never captured. A Google representative confirmed this to me in an email: “Yes, the 60fps support is done via 30fps + interpolation in Video Boost since we started supporting it in Pixel 2024. Are the additional frames in the returned 60fps video file generated during cloud processing? Is it the same process as when selecting 4K60 (Video Boost) on a Pixel 10 Pro XL? - yes.” Note that I’ve only tested “XL” variants of the Pixel Pro, though Google’s documentation treats the two identically as far as Video Boost is concerned. What Google's Documentation Says. This frame-rate dropping functionality isn’t revealed to the user at capture time. Google’s support pages do state that Video Boost 60fps “may reduce frame rate dynamically based on the scene conditions and camera motions,” but this isn’t what I’m seeing here. In my tests, the captured video never exceeded 30fps. Selecting 4K60 HDR with Video Boost enabled in the camera app doesn’t reveal anything about the actual capture settings. Google hasn’t stated a reason for applying this 30fps limit to the Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the company’s own Video Boost marketing page states “powerful AI algorithms remove graininess, stabilize movement, and adjust exposure and color,” while not mentioning frame interpolation at all. Should You Turn Video Boost Off? Fortunately, the resulting interpolated Video Boost output quality is excellent. Just be aware that recorded motion may not be as accurate as the standard “un-boosted,” true 60fps format, especially if you want to display slow-motion output. For now, if you really need a true 4K60 HDR recording, leave Video Boost turned off.

The data centers powering America’s artificial intelligence boom have become an unlikely target in November’s midterm elections, as anger over rising electricity bills and noise turns Democrats — and a growing number of Republicans — against Big Tech. Candidates in at least 21 races across 18 states have aired television advertisements mentioning data centers this cycle, according to marketing data cited by US media, almost evenly divided between both parties. On the grid serving Senate battleground Ohio, as well as 12 other states, demand from data centers drove up capacity costs by $9.3 billion in a single year, a 174 percent increase, according to an independent market monitor. Anger over household bills has merged with a broader populist distrust of Silicon Valley, exposing lawmakers who, until recently, were courting the sprawling server farms with tax breaks and promises of jobs and investment. In Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott has frozen new projects while regulators weigh their impact on power and water supplies. It was Abbott who, not long ago, called his state the “epicenter of AI development.” His Democratic challenger wants a moratorium until lawmakers pass stronger safeguards, and accuses Abbott of putting wealthy interests ahead of ordinary Texans. In Brazoria — between Houston and the Gulf Coast — 44-year-old Melissa Burnett told AFP the serenity of her quiet neighborhood had been shattered by a 17-megawatt center last year that is “like a freight train always coming at you.” “We were not supposed to hear it, nor was it supposed to affect our quality of life, and it’s just done the opposite, you know?” she said. Almost alone among Republicans, President Donald Trump has not moved. He still calls the industry essential to beating China on AI, leaving him at odds with candidates running under his own banner. ‘Sleeper issue’ The midwestern former manufacturing hub of Ohio offers perhaps the sharpest test of the politics of data centers. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who lost his Senate berth in 2024, is running for the Buckeye State’s other seat. Brown has run at least four ads attacking Republican Jon Husted for courting data center investment as lieutenant governor. They brand Husted “the face of data centers,” and Brown has promised to make operators pay the full cost of the power they use. Senate Republicans have warned that the issue could cost Husted the race. Their campaign arm called data centers a “sleeper issue” and said a defeat blamed on them would chill political support for the industry nationwide. The same argument is turning up in races that have little else in common: a Republican running for governor in Florida promising to shield families from facilities that push up utility bills; a Pennsylvania Democrat demanding that tech companies cover their own costs; a Wyoming Republican who won a House primary on advertisements attacking Silicon Valley billionaires. In Michigan, the issue toppled two better-connected Democrats in a primary won by a leftist who said opposition had united committed Republicans, Trump voters, independents and Democrats. Both parties turn. In Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial nominee Tom Tiffany has taken to calling his Democratic opponent “Data Center David Crowley.” Earlier this year Tiffany was praising the technology and voting to speed AI infrastructure through. Tiffany now wants the state’s tax incentives scrapped and the industry more tightly regulated, though he stops short of a ban. Democratic governors are moving the same way. New York has imposed a year-long moratorium on new hyperscale facilities, and Pennsylvania now requires developers to cover infrastructure costs and meet tougher standards on water use, hiring and community consultation. Trump has not moved with them. “America must remain dominant in the AI race that is the future. I think the American people understand that, and this president certainly does,” his spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday. His administration has signed up Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI, OpenAI and Amazon to a voluntary “Ratepayer Protection Pledge.” Under it, the companies undertake not to leave consumers paying for the power plants and grid upgrades their facilities require. The pledge has not stopped the advertisements.

The author argues that Notion's free tier keeps narrowing: the 5MB per-file upload cap hasn't moved, and page history is still 7 days on Free. Notion also killed its $10 AI add-on last year, so meaningful AI usage now requires Business at $20 a month billed annually. The author presents SiYuan, a self-hosted note app, as a free alternative that runs in one container in about five minutes. SiYuan is built by B3log, a Chinese open-source group, with an active GitHub repo and a community marketplace called Bazaar for themes and plugins. It has native apps for Android, iOS and HarmonyOS. Its philosophy is "no offline, no notes": it is local-first, with optional paid end-to-end encrypted sync, and stores everything as .sy JSON files in a workspace folder you choose. Its block-first architecture resembles Notion's, with every paragraph, list item and heading getting a permanent ID so references survive restructuring. Setup means pulling the image from Docker Hub, mapping a folder on your PC to the workspace path in the container, exposing port 6806, setting an access code and opening localhost in a browser. Notes live in the mapped folder, not the container, which helps when rebuilding. The author says doing the same in Notion would require Business at $20 a seat a month ($24 if billed monthly). SiYuan offers block editing with a slash menu, databases, page embeds and templates, and feels similar to Notion. Its AI features accept any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, so you can use a local LLM or a cheap provider like DeepSeek rather than a bundled AI tier. The project frames itself as a workspace where "humans and AI agents work together". There is no 5MB upload cap, since the limit is your disk, and version history depends on configurable data repo snapshots rather than 7 days. Databases, called attribute views, cover tables and filters; they are capable but not a 1-1 clone, and the author thinks Notion's are still superior. Block-level references beat Notion's page-level linking for thinking work, since a link to a specific paragraph survives being moved. SiYuan also includes built-in FSRS flashcards, a web clipper and PDF annotation. Bazaar has fewer options than Notion's template gallery. SiYuan is honestly a single-user tool at heart. A self-hosted instance can be shared with a small group via the access code, but there is no per-user permissions system and real-time multiplayer editing isn't a goal, which the developers intended. The author keeps team docs elsewhere and had to rebuild some workflows from scratch because of the smaller template ecosystem. The author concludes that Notion still makes sense when three people edit the same doc at once, but for a personal knowledge base SiYuan does the job for free on a container you run yourself.

Rockstar Games has said Grand Theft Auto 6 will have no microtransactions or generative AI when it launches in November. The studio behind GTA 6 confirmed this year’s monumental sandbox release will dodge two potentially controversial practices during a conversation with Kinda Funny Games earlier this week. It means launch should be free of backlash (at least when it comes to these two particular topics) when it arrives in a few months. Kinda Funny’s Andy Cortez said he asked Rockstar if players will be able to use real-world money to purchase things in-game during a preview event that preceded the GTA 6: Extended Look. He went on, saying, “no monetizations in this game.” The site’s Greg Miller immediately followed that topic, saying he asked Rockstar “point-blank” if there is generative AI in GTA 6. The team told him that there is “no AI” used in the game. From Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 to Arc Raiders, generative AI has proven time and time again to be an especially troublesome element for developers to include in their games. The millions of gamers who have waited 13 years for the next Grand Theft Auto might be pleased to hear similar claims won’t mar its mid-November release date. The issue of microtransactions, however, does come with a few things worth noting. Rockstar says GTA 6 will not feature the kind of monetization strategies that allow players to purchase content with real-world cash. That might arrive as good news for an entirely single-player release, but it’s also yet another reminder that it doesn’t look like the team has any intention of sharing any updates on a new iteration of Grand Theft Auto Online any time soon. Meanwhile, while Rockstar has made it clear that, while there will be no monetization strategies like microtransactions in a traditional sense, there will be content gated off for some players in the form of its Ultimate Edition. Priced at $99.99 – a $20 increase from the $79.99 standard edition – this version of the game grants access to a host of exclusive content, including cosmetic packs, cars, guns, and even some shops, such as the Electric Fang tattoo parlor and Stock 305 clothing store. An official support page confirmed standard edition owners will be able to purchase an Ultimate Edition upgrade separately. “Ultimate Edition bonuses are threaded across all aspects of Jason and Lucia’s story, with new items uncovered behind each chapter,” the page added. Other than that, it sounds like players shouldn’t expect any other microtransaction tactics – or generative AI – when GTA 6 launches for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S November 19, 2026. There will surely be plenty more to show off ahead of its release date, but until then, you can check out IGN’s exclusive preview and interview. You can also catch up on every licensed song revealed during the extended look, the GTA Online character who’s making a comeback, and everything else Rockstar had to share during its big gameplay debut. Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He’s best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

AI is reshaping China's huge job market, pushing some workers out and leaving others fearful, even as government policy encourages its use. Fei Zhaojun, a 40-year-old Beijing programmer, was laid off with about 160 colleagues two weeks after his boss asked whether AI could soon replace human coders. He now makes vlog-style videos during a career break. Some economists believe the trend could eventually weaken the world's second largest economy. Plenum analyst Shujing He says anti-AI sentiment in China appears far weaker than elsewhere, and many who fear replacement or have left traditional workplaces eagerly experiment with AI-enabled ventures. Translator Du Qinchun in Chengdu has gained temporary work training an AI translation model, but says industry pay has fallen by more than half compared with years ago. College foreign-language programs have lost popularity as AI translation spreads. IDC reports that the share of Chinese industrial enterprises using AI models and "agents" jumped to 47.5% last year from 9.6% in 2024. Humanoid robots are sorting parcels in postal centers on a small scale and are taking on tasks like directing traffic and making coffee, while delivery robots may threaten millions of food delivery workers. Generative AI is widely used in China's short drama industry; the number of live-action short vertical video series fell about 75% in the first quarter of this year from a year earlier, per Chinese media reports. He says workers in narrowly focused software and multimedia roles face greater displacement risk. An International Labor Organization report found women face higher risk of AI-related job loss because they work more in automatable areas such as electronics assembly and are underrepresented in science and technology. Under its "AI Plus" initiative and five-year plan through 2030, the government is pushing AI across industries to gain an edge over the U.S. Growth is already slowing, with consumer spending weak because of job worries and a prolonged housing downturn. Cornell's Eswar Prasad says AI will likely raise productivity but could severely disrupt employment and harm social stability, since tech industries may not create many jobs. Chinese tech giants have cut or restructured tens of thousands of jobs, partly due to AI. Urban unemployment hovers around 5%, while it is roughly triple that for non-student 16-to-24-year-olds. Over the longer run, some experts say unemployment could fall as China's 1.4 billion population ages and shrinks. By 2050, China is projected to have fewer than two working-age adults per retiree, versus more than 2.5 in the U.S., so automation could partly offset a shrinking workforce, says Xuenan Cao of San Francisco Bay University. Some are adapting. Scriptwriter Wang Zhicheng, 32, resigned after his employer's parent company laid off roughly half of its 13 script writers, and now runs his own studio making picture books. He found AI-generated scripts repetitive, formulaic and uneven, and sees AI as a tool, with humans deciding what to pursue. Chemistry teacher Yang Zheng, 29, does not see AI as a threat, calling it helpful for students who can ask follow-up questions in real time, even though it often errs and improves over time.

AI infrastructure is shifting from data centers filled with a single type of GPU toward heterogeneous structures combining CPU, GPU and NPU. With AI agents emerging, the key question is how cheaply and with how little power inference requests can be handled. After seven to eight years of intensive government support, Korea is described as a country where domestic companies alone can build an "open computing stack" spanning NPU, memory, data processing units, servers, networks and orchestration software. Against this backdrop, the Ministry of Science and ICT and AMD signed an MOU in San Francisco on July 23 to build an open AI infrastructure ecosystem. Mail Business and the ministry held an expert forum, "AI Semiconductor Dae-hwan," in Seoul on the 18th to discuss global entry for domestic AI semiconductors. Lee Do-gyu of the ministry said the government proposed linking AMD's CPU and GPU with domestic NPUs, and this became the MOU's first cooperation task. Domestic AI semiconductors had been "subjects to support," never "components" of a global architecture, so securing this in writing is the biggest achievement. AMD Korea's Moon Kyung-sun said AMD would establish a center of excellence as a pre-investment without large prior hardware investment, a first for Asia. Puriosa AI's Kang Ji-hoon said growth requires an open system connecting Korean technology with global CPU, GPU and software ecosystems, and that AMD is discussing broader cooperation at the data center system level. KAIST's Yoo Hoi-joon said the window is about three years: AI chips take two to three years from design to mass production, and data center accelerator replacement cycles run three to four years, so a missed cycle means waiting until the 2030s. IITP's Oh Yoon-je noted that domestic NPU firms are already making sales and exports, and AMD is effectively the only party able to challenge Nvidia. On obstacles, MangoBoost's Kim Jang-woo warned that Nvidia and AMD sell whole systems, creating vendor dependency, and that true sovereign AI requires a sovereign AI "system." Cho Kang-won cautioned that integrating everything at once won't work; small integrations must be tried and fail in various combinations first. For next year's demonstration, panelists said it must be real commercial service with real traffic, not a benchmark or pilot. Performance per power and total cost of ownership should be disclosed in third-party-verifiable numbers. Oh proposed three stages: software linkage verification, pilots on real workloads, then publishing results and contributing to open ecosystems such as ROCm and UALink. Lee said the government is preparing a large-scale demonstration budget for next year, but adoption will spread only if the private sector wants to buy. Looking three years ahead, Yoo wants Korean NPUs to be a natural option for power- and cost-sensitive data centers by 2029, while preparing next-generation chips: memory-driven computation, PIM, then neuromorphic. PIM is structurally advantageous for Korea, home to the first and second largest memory makers. Kang said Puriosa's RNGD NPU handled 1.8 to 2 times more concurrent users per power than Nvidia GPUs under the same conditions while meeting service-level targets, but "made in Korea" alone won't win developers. Moon said AMD sees Korean NPU firms as key global players, not domestic substitutes. Lee concluded that the MOU is only a declaration; making it a working system remains the task.

Americans are increasingly united against rapidly advancing technologies and the companies behind them, though for different reasons. About 25 years ago, 8 in 10 Americans anticipated "the triumph of science and technology." Now neighbors rally against data centers, commencement crowds boo artificial intelligence, and a lawsuit by 48 states against Meta over claims its platforms endangered children produced an $18 billion settlement. Public opinion of large tech companies fell to multiyear lows in 2026, and Americans say they are more concerned than excited about AI. The backlash is bipartisan, with critics including Sen. Bernie Sanders, Gov. Ron DeSantis, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Gov. Greg Abbott. It has sometimes turned violent: in April a man threw a Molotov cocktail at OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's home, local officials who backed data centers received death threats, and a Tennessee county commissioner said Flock Safety's CEO should be hanged for treason. Tech leaders largely call concerns overblown, with some citing national security risks if foreign adversaries outpace the U.S. in AI. Data centers have become a political lightning rod. A Gallup survey found about 71% of U.S. adults oppose building them locally, 48% strongly. Supporters, including President Donald Trump, call them essential infrastructure that creates jobs and tax revenue, but opponents cite strain on water and electricity, noise, pollution, falling property values, rising power bills and lack of public notice. In the first three months of 2026, local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 projects worth roughly $130 billion, according to Data Center Watch, though more than 1,500 remain under development. Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said "People really effing hate data centers," and days later the governors of Texas and Pennsylvania announced new restrictions. The newest front is automated license plate readers. Flock Safety runs 120,000 AI-powered cameras across 49 states, scanning 20 billion vehicles monthly into a database police can search without a warrant. Flock and police say it helps solve 700,000 crimes a year. Outrage grew over privacy, reports of immigration authorities accessing data, officers using it to stalk women, and misreads leading to innocent people held at gunpoint. Protesters have rallied, lawsuits followed, and people have damaged dozens of cameras. About 100 jurisdictions have paused or canceled contracts this year, per DeFlock, though Flock says new partners far outnumber cancellations. CEO Garrett Langley announced mandatory audit systems to flag abnormal searches and cut retention of unrelated data from 30 to seven days. Republican Sen. Josh Hawley announced a congressional investigation, and Sanders pledged legislation. Souring on AI is widespread. Pew found 52% of Americans are more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Fears center on job loss, which executives have acknowledged: Anthropic's Dario Amodei said AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. A YouGov poll found 7 in 10 adults think tech companies have too much power, and fewer than 1 in 5 trust them to manage AI. Experts say data centers and Flock are potent symbols of distaste for Big Tech, though Prof. David Karol stressed specific local concerns too. Across the country, unlikely coalitions have formed, such as conservative Austin Rhodes and progressive Tiernan Turner in Hendersonville, North Carolina, and bipartisan petitions in Licking County, Ohio. Expert Thomas Kahn expects the reaction, and resulting regulation, to intensify.

As the novelty surrounding humanoid robots gives way to business questions about their commercialization, stock analysts still see potential in one gear box supplier. For the past three years, Tesla has been co-developing a new type of gear box for humanoid robotics with Shenzhen-listed Shuanghuan, Deutsche Bank analysts said in a report this week. The component, called a reducer, translates motor power into mechanical movement. Deutsche Bank analysts expect the jointly developed reducers could be deployed in the waist joints of humanoid robots. Shuanghuan will keep a controlling stake in a planned initial public offering of Fine Motion, its robotics gearbox subsidiary, which accounted for about 5% of the parent company's consolidated revenue and net profit in 2025, the analysts wrote. Much of Shuanghuang's business comes from China's electric car companies, as well as Stellantis and BMW . The Deutsche Bank analysts rate Shuanghuan a buy, with a price target of 45 yuan ($6.70). "In our view, the market underestimates Shuanghuan's robotics opportunity across three dimensions," Bernstein analysts said in a separate report this week. "The company is well positioned to benefit as Chinese Auto [original equipment manufacturers] expand into humanoid robotics, a group we believe could emerge as the industry's true game changers," the Bernstein report said. Chinese EV company Xpeng last week valued its robotics business at more than $6 billion , about the same size as its electric car business. Apart from introducing electric cars, consumer electronics company Xiaomi is also showcasing its own humanoids. Analysts have previously noted the auto industry shares many of the same suppliers as the humanoid robotics sector. In terms of geopolitics, "Shuanghuan stands to benefit from growth in both the Chinese and U.S. robotics industries amid U.S.-China robotics decoupling," the Bernstein analysts said, noting "U.S. customers' demand for cost-efficient sourcing and the lower regulatory risk of pure mechanical components, i.e. reducers." The analysts rate Shuanghuan shares "outperform," with a price target of 60 yuan. UBS analysts rate Shuanghuan a "buy," with a price target of 50 yuan. They trimmed their price target by 3 yuan following Shuanghuan's second-quarter earnings, amid pressure on sales from key client BYD . But UBS expects new artificial intelligence and humanoid robotics-related business "could unlock incremental space for Shuanghuan's medium- to long-term growth." Morgan Stanley's wrapup of the recent World Robot Conference in Beijing emphasized a preference for leading parts makers, including Shuanghuan. "As [humanoid] deployment gradually starts, the bar for component suppliers should rise from product qualification to reliability, consistency, yield, manufacturing scale and cost, favoring suppliers with proven mass-production capabilities," the analysts wrote last week. —CNBC's Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

In early August, about 40 top mathematicians gathered at OpenAI's San Francisco offices to discuss what will remain for humans to do if AI becomes "robustly superhuman" at research-level math, according to co-organizer Jacob Tsimerman. Tsimerman had shocked colleagues the previous month by announcing, at the ceremony where he received the field's closest equivalent to a Nobel Prize, that he would join OpenAI to work on AI safety. Daniel Litt of the University of Toronto gave a talk titled "The End of Mathematics," sketching a worst case in which AI produces so much advanced research that there is little incentive to keep human experts. He considers that unlikely but says mathematicians must adapt. MIT's Drew Sutherland suggested AI companies focus on math because it is a proxy for any intelligence-heavy activity, making mathematicians possible "canaries in the coal mine." AI math progress has been rapid. In 2025, an advanced Google Gemini earned a gold-medal score at the International Mathematical Olympiad. In May, an unreleased OpenAI model disproved the unit distance conjecture using a technique from algebraic number theory, a result Tsimerman said he would have accepted into any journal "without hesitation." OpenAI and Anthropic have since released competing results, and users increasingly bypass the traditional pipeline of seminars, arXiv preprints and peer review. Anthropic's Levent Alpöge announced a result on perpendicular vectors pointing to the corners of a 668-dimensional cube in a 24,000-character X post consisting only of + and - symbols. Startup founder Dmitry Rybin prodded ChatGPT to "do a breakthrough" until it refuted a network-flow hypothesis, which he tweeted while watching a movie. David Bessis worried about incentives for people to sort out the resulting mess. Some translate results into the Lean language for step-by-step computer verification, but these translations are lengthy and hard for humans to read. In June, more than 3,000 mathematicians signed the Leiden Declaration urging responsible AI use, with verification and proper citation; others argue mathematicians should avoid AI entirely. Some say AI has not opened significant new theory. OpenAI's list of 10 results included a non-sofic group bridging 2016 and 2019 papers by Gábor Kun and Andreas Thom, who quickly published a simplified follow-up. Thom said the concepts emerged from humans' engagement with the proof, so "it's not yet the AI that does it." An Anthropic employee asked an internal Claude to "take a real stab" at the Riemann hypothesis and, after repeated prompts to "keep going," got a new finding on a related problem. Northwestern's Bryna Kra, a Leiden Declaration organizer, stressed that mathematics is about understanding, and an un-understood proof does not enter the literature. Harvard's Melanie Matchett Wood, who helped write a human version of the unit distance result, said top models overexplain easy parts and breeze through hard ones, and that there are no norms yet for this new way of producing mathematics. OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck said attendees also discussed other futures: math resembling software engineering, with AI helping hundreds collaborate; physics, with AI as a particle accelerator; or museum curation, with humans picking among AI discoveries. He said mathematicians must come first, since math is interesting only insofar as they learn from it.

In the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary on Tuesday, the central question is whether incumbent Ed Markey, 80, is too old for another term. U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, argues that Markey, who would be 86 at the end of another term, cannot represent a generation facing problems that didn't exist when Markey entered Congress 50 years ago. Moulton has called for "generational change" and age limits for members of Congress. The issue sharpened at a recent debate, when Markey was asked whether he uses AI platforms like Claude or ChatGPT. He said he uses "whatever is inside of my iPhone or my iPad — whatever comes up" and doesn't know "what companies my iPad may be using." Moulton called this "potentially disqualifying" and said it shows why a new generation of leaders is needed to regulate such technologies. Markey replied that it makes no difference whether it's called Siri or Claude, stressing that safeguards matter more than familiarity with products, and cited his legislation to regulate AI's effects on children, workers, civil rights and the environment. Young Democrats are divided. Arsen Bagdassarian, 18, a Moulton supporter and incoming Northeastern University freshman, said he didn't expect Markey to be so "clueless" and that the country needs leaders who understand what they regulate. Molly Blander, 18, an incoming Tufts freshman, said AI and social media have reshaped her generation's life and mental health, praised Moulton's work establishing 988 as the national suicide and crisis lifeline, and said the Democratic establishment hasn't made things much better amid rising housing and energy costs and Donald Trump's rise and reelection. Markey, however, has a strong young following. He has won endorsements from the High School Democrats of America and the College Democrats of America, as well as from U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Matt Kelly, president of the UMass Lowell College Democrats, admitted Markey's AI answer "wasn't a good answer" but said he cares more about whether Markey knows how to govern the technology than use it. He noted Markey's push to regulate data centers, relevant to a proposed data center in Lowell that has drawn local opposition. "Just because he has a younger face doesn't mean that he has younger ideas," Kelly said. Many young Markey supporters see his long career as an asset because it provides a record to judge. They cite his 2002 vote against creating the Department of Homeland Security, his co-authorship of the Green New Deal, and his early support for Medicare for All. Milan van Dam, 17, national chair of the High School Democrats of America, said generational leadership is "less about an age on a Wikipedia page" than a candidate's ideas and consistency. Abby Shadden, 21, of Emmanuel College, said it isn't true that younger people are automatically more progressive. The race is part of a broader 2026 trend of younger Democrats challenging, and sometimes unseating, longtime incumbents, as Democratic voters appear to seek change.

The second World Humanoid Robot Games, a five-day event held at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, a former Olympic venue, wrapped up this week, mixing spectacle with clear technical progress. Robots failed dramatically: an Honor robot lost a leg mid-sprint, others tripped amid sparks, one ran into a crash mat and burst into flames, and a weightlifting robot toppled into the judges' table. Alongside sprinting, football, boxing and weightlifting, the games featured bed-making, parcel delivery, shelf stacking, clothes folding, hammering nails and firefighting, reflecting the aim of getting robots out of labs and into real-world settings. China is openly seeking to lead this field. The games showed major gains. One humanoid ran the 100 meters in 9.39 seconds, beating Usain Bolt's 2009 record, while another reached 2.88 meters in a standing high jump, nearly half a meter above the human record standing since 1993. Last year's winning sprint took 21.50 seconds and the best standing high jump was 0.95 meters. Yet the mundane tasks were less impressive, and many events allowed teleoperation with a scoring penalty, suggesting humanoids are still far from operating reliably alone in factories or homes. Autonomous events included gymnastics, football, tug of war, table tennis and some track events. Beijing has not confirmed a third games, but another humanoid half-marathon is set for April, and China plans to open its first robot-run hotel next year. China dominated the medal table, especially AgiBot and Tien Kung, each of which won more medals than nearly every other competitor combined, excluding the other. Part of this reflects limited international competition: 641 of 666 teams were Chinese, representing 157 companies and 200 universities, according to state-run China Daily. Major US humanoid players such as Tesla, Boston Dynamics and Figure were absent. The breadth of Chinese institutions shows a maturing sector, even amid concerns about circular investment, companies lacking viable products and a possible humanoid bubble. A stronger US showing likely would not have changed much. The US retains an edge in frontier AI and advanced chips, but China is closing parts of that gap and treats embodied AI as a national strategic priority. Washington has paid far less attention to robotics and trails China in nearly every regard, including manufacturing, deployment and hardware. Reports suggest US efforts to ban foreign robots, aimed at China, could backfire given domestic firms' dependence on Chinese components. Catching up will take concerted effort, but with the technology moving quickly there is still time, and robotics could become a strategic US priority.

One of the most devestating aspects of modern medicine and drug development is the constantly evolving nature of harmful pathogens and bacteria. As bacteria have been exposed to increasing levels of antibiotics globally, they are continuously evolving against the best medications humanity can develop. Eventually drug resistant “superbugs” prevail and cause hard-to-treat infections. Resistance rates will only continue to increase, and scientists are in an arms race in trying to figure out new counter measures and ways to fight disease caused by these pathogens. Fortunately, with the rapid advancements in AI, researchers are now able to make progress on new frontiers. One specific area that is actively being explored is the potential of using bacteriophages, which are originally viral in nature, in conjunction with advancements in AI to help detect, track and destroy resistant bacteria forms. While antibiotics are generally effective, they often do not disciramte between good and bad bacteria, and hence will wipe everything out in their sight. However, programmed bacteriophages have significant potential to be incredibly targeted in the bacteria they seek to commandeer and eliminate. The concept of using phages to detect and destroy bacteria is certainly not new; however, with AI, there is new opportunity. Historically, scientists had to manually test hundreds of viral samples to determine the correct phage that could target the bacteria in mind. However, deep learning has completely transformed this process. A recent article in the journal Briefings in Bioinformatics discusses how deep learning algorithms significantly increase the precision and accuracy of phage-host interactions (PHI): “a growing body of artificial intelligence-based models has emerged to improve the scalability, flexibility, and generalizability of PHI prediction…” meaning a higher degree of success in developing these tools. Moreover, while traditional models can help scientists find existing phages that may be effective, new models can actually help researchers design their own custom, synthetic phages, specifically built to target the bacteria in mind. In a recent article for the International Journal for Pharmaceuticals, the authors describe how AI driven structural modeling, in conjunction with genome editing technology, can significantly optimize targeted phage delivery and improved efficacy in therapies: "Targeted engineering for enhanced antibacterial efficiency has been made possible by residue-level visualization of key main phage proteins, such as endolysins and tail fibers, which made possible by structure prediction tools like AlphaFold and OpenFold… Now AI enables quick decoding of phage genomes which can predict host receptors, bacteria-phage interactions, ideal delivery process, and tail fiber binding locations.” The overall impact? Huge benefits in the fight against resistant bacteria. But, what are the challenges and limitations? For one, bacteria are incredibly intelligent creatures. Research suggests that if they are attacked by a single phage, they can often mutate to resist that specific form of attack. With increasing number of attacks by multiple phages, they may be more vulnerable, but will also eventually learn to protect themselves. Thus, timing and breadth of impact is important; certain bugs may require a more involved approach with multiple types of phages and significantly more phages than others. Furthermore, it is crucial to note that this technology is still incredibly new. While many of these AI prediction models work In Silico (in digital simulations etc.), the degree to how efficacious they are in reality (In Vivo) is still being determined. Deep learning models often do a great job in selecting a potential answer (e.g., what phage to use). But they often fail at the explainability aspect (e.g., why was that specific phage chosen?). For science, it is as important to understand the process as it is to determine the answer, as this is essential in progressing innovation and discovery. Therefore, as models are still being improved and explainability still has progress to be made, it will take time before this concept is successful for wide-scale implementation and universal deployment.

GF Securities reiterated its favorable view on Marvell Technology (MRVL), naming it a top pick within its positive outlook on custom AI chips. Analyst Henry Huang said much of the growth comes from Alphabet's Google, expecting three Marvell chip lines tied to Google to bring in around $3 billion each by 2028. He also sees Marvell playing a growing role in Amazon.com's Trainium chips, worth roughly $1 billion this year and $2 billion next year, and expects it to keep contributing to Trainium 3 and strengthen its position on the next generation after the Celestial AI deal. Marvell had lost design work for Amazon's next Trainium chips to a rival, which had been a main worry weighing on the stock. Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley, Susquehanna, and Rosenblatt Securities also raised their Marvell price targets within a day of each other. A few days earlier, Marvell signed a custom chip deal with Google that lets Google take a potential $12 billion equity stake in the company, tied to the amount it purchases through 2033. With this deal, Marvell now designs custom AI chips for all three of the largest U.S. cloud companies, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, which no other chip designer can claim. Marvell was long seen as the clear number two to Broadcom in this space. Marvell makes semiconductor solutions for data infrastructure, used in data centers, cloud computing, AI, telecom networks and enterprise storage. Cities are increasingly using artificial intelligence to tackle a persistent cause of housing permitting delays: incomplete applications. AI scans applications and flags errors so developers avoid repeated correction rounds that can add weeks or months, while human reviewers keep final decisions. The new federal housing law enacted last month creates an Innovation Fund with $200 million annually for local efforts to speed permitting, and HUD is offering up to $3 million in grants for automated building code permitting systems. Syracuse, Coeur d'Alene, Mobile and Richland applied; Syracuse's chief information officer, Vincent Scipione, said the city would ask vendors about data governance and algorithm design. Baltimore, Denver and Los Angeles have launched AI permitting tools, and smaller cities such as Everett, Lebanon and Naples are following. Harris County, Texas, put $750,000 toward such a program. Denver approved a roughly $4.6 million five-year contract for an AI plan review platform; only about 37% of applications are accepted on the first round, and the goal is 80%. Council member Flor Alvidrez cast the lone dissenting vote, citing AI inaccuracies and developers' concerns about complex zoning codes. Louisville, Kentucky, is piloting a system that uses property data, GIS data and local requirements to flag missing information, with early testing capable of cutting avoidable resubmissions by 50% or more. Honolulu was an early adopter with CivCheck, which checks applications against local codes and flags gaps. Planning director Dawn Takeuchi Apuna said the aim was not to replace staff but to free planners for face-to-face work. Rollout of Honolulu's overhaul, including the HNL Build platform, was rocky: a survey of more than 150 employees drew almost universally negative feedback. Still, median wait for a new building permit fell to 2.5 months, a 40% decrease year over year. For single- and two-family projects, review cycles dropped from 3.4 to 1.4 per application; CivCheck applications averaged 7.7 corrections versus 23.5, and processing time fell from 73 to 32.5 days. Takeuchi Apuna said AI struggles with gray areas such as unusual site conditions. Seattle's pilot found CivCheck 87% accurate on completeness checks and 92% on design-compliance checks, with about a 50% cut in intake review days and 35% fewer correction cycles, but the city was not ready to adopt it fully. CivCheck says it works with more than 20 cities. Clariti Software's Cyrus Symoom said the tool is a fact-checker, not a replacement for human decisions. The American Planning Association's Zhenia Dulko noted more than 70 state and local AI uses in planning, saying AI frees planners for public engagement and equity considerations. A Journal of Urban Economics paper on Los Angeles multifamily projects estimated that cutting approval times 25% could have raised housing production by almost 24%. Officials stress applicants share responsibility; Takeuchi Apuna said they account for at least 50% of the process. Govstream.ai's Saf Rabah said cities should give applicants more guidance.

A study published on 29 April 2026 in Quantum Machine Intelligence, by Mohemmed Sha of the University of Roehampton and Mohamudha Parveen Rahamathulla and Shtwai Alsubai of Prince Sattam Bin Abdulaziz University, describes a healthcare prediction framework that combines quantum-inspired optimization, privacy-preserving generative AI, federated learning and blockchain. On a widely used diabetes dataset it reached 99.01 percent classification accuracy, beating artificial neural networks, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors and convolutional neural networks by roughly five to twelve percentage points. The motivation is that medical data is highly sensitive and a leaked diagnosis cannot be undone, yet predictive models need pooled data. Blockchain ledgers and federated learning have each addressed part of the problem, but the authors argue no coherent architecture joined these defenses to high-performing, automatically tuned prediction. The framework has three pillars. First, Privacy-Preserving Generative Adversarial Networks (PPGANs) generate synthetic features that keep the statistical character of real records without identifiable details. They add differential privacy by clipping per-sample gradients to a bounded norm and injecting calibrated Gaussian noise, with a privacy budget (ε, δ) tracked across training iterations. Second, classification runs in a federated learning setup where N clients, such as hospitals, train locally and share only parameter updates, weighted by dataset size and merged by secure aggregation. A quantum-inspired Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm (QPSO) tunes hyperparameters, including local training epochs, scoring candidates by validation accuracy and escaping local optima through probabilistic particle positions. This lets the system be redeployed without manual re-tuning. Third, an Ethereum blockchain layer secures storage, using Casper FFG consensus and SHA-3 hashing so any alteration is detectable. Large files sit off-chain on the InterPlanetary File System, with only hashes and access-control metadata on-chain. A composite objective function balances differential privacy cost, adversarial loss and optimization fitness so privacy does not erode predictive power. Benchmarked on separating diabetic from non-diabetic patients, the framework scored 99.01 percent, versus 92.13 percent for the artificial neural network, 87.45 percent for the support vector machine, 86.72 percent for k-nearest neighbors and 94.20 percent for the convolutional neural network. The authors attribute the gap of nearly five points over the CNN to the combined effect of privacy-preserving feature generation, federated training and optimizer-driven tuning. Notably, the privacy protections did not cause the usual accuracy loss. The approach is quantum-inspired, not quantum computing: it runs on classical hardware, borrowing mathematics from quantum theory, so hospitals can use it now. The authors see it as a template for other domains facing the same problems, such as oncology registries, intensive-care telemetry and genomic studies. Caveats are that the evaluation used benchmark data rather than a live multi-hospital deployment, and real networks will add latency, uneven data quality and governance disputes.

The race to build more data centers for artificial intelligence is driving demand for more than chips and electricity. It also requires vast networks of high-speed optical fiber to move data between servers, putting one of America’s oldest manufacturers at the center of the boom. Corning, the New York-based company best known to many Americans for its kitchenware and smartphone glass, is ramping up optical-fiber production as the data-center buildout accelerates. Nearly 175 years after its founding, the company is supplying a critical piece of the infrastructure behind the AI boom, the glass connections linking the servers inside the facilities powering it. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM. The company is partnering with NVIDIA to build three advanced optical-manufacturing facilities in North Carolina and Texas. The project is expected to create more than 3,000 jobs and expand Corning’s U.S. optical-manufacturing capacity tenfold. The investment offers a window into how the data-center boom is reaching well beyond the massive facilities themselves, creating demand for American factories and workers who make the equipment needed to keep them connected. CRACKDOWN ON CRITICAL TECH COULD OPEN AMERICANS TO A NEW NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT. At a time when many Americans worry that artificial intelligence will replace human workers, Corning chairman, CEO and president Wendell Weeks said the opposite is happening inside one of the nation’s oldest manufacturers. "AI is a huge job creator, and it's a huge manufacturing job creator," Weeks told Fox News Digital. He said demand for Corning’s optical fiber is fueling the company’s fastest period of growth in nearly two centuries. "As a 175-year-old company, we're going through our fastest growth period," Weeks said. "We will probably double our size over the coming years and almost all of our new hires will be in advanced manufacturing, a significant part of them right here in America." That growth is already taking shape on Corning’s factory floors. "As the world develops and tells us what it needs, we're right there at the forefront," Emily Capek, planning supervisor at Corning’s Wilmington, North Carolina, facility, told Fox News Digital. She said employees are seeing firsthand how demand for AI platforms is driving demand for Corning’s products. FROM NETFLIX TO GPS: 10 WAYS THIS HIDDEN TECH INFRASTRUCTURE QUIETLY POWERS MODERN LIFE. "Right now, the world needs our glass optical fiber to support the AI demand we're seeing," Capek said. "It's a great feeling on the factory floor." While much of the attention surrounding AI has focused on chipmakers and software developers, companies like Corning are supplying the glass technology that connects those systems and supports the industry’s rapid expansion. "The common story is AI being powered by chips, but actually, those chips are connected by glass," Weeks said.

At Hot Chips 2026, Intel detailed three architectures meant to support agentic AI across consumer devices, edge systems and data centres: Wildcat Lake, Crescent Island and Diamond Rapids. Wildcat Lake is already shipping, Crescent Island is being developed as an inference-focused data centre GPU, and Diamond Rapids is Intel's next-generation enterprise CPU. Chief technology officer Pushkar Ranade said agentic AI is influencing processor development at every level. Diamond Rapids, to be marketed as Xeon 7, is the most extensively detailed. Its top configuration supports up to 256 cores, with 1.28G of last-level cache, 16 memory channels, 128 PCIe 6 lanes and CXL 3.0 support. According to ServeTheHome, the largest configuration uses 16-core chiplets built on Intel's 18A-P process. It competes with AMD's 256-core EPYC 9996, made on TSMC's 2nm process, which retains simultaneous multithreading and so supports twice as many threads as cores. Intel positions Diamond Rapids as central to its enterprise strategy, since data centres still need powerful CPUs to manage data, workloads and infrastructure around AI systems. Crescent Island may prove the most significant for AI inference, though Intel has revealed fewer details. It is planned as a 350W, air-cooled PCIe card based on the Xe3P GPU architecture, with 32 GPU cores, 256 third-generation XMX engines and 32MB of unified L2 cache. It uses LPDDR5X memory rather than high-bandwidth memory, suggesting Intel is prioritising memory capacity, power consumption and cost, which could appeal to customers focused on the overall cost of running models. Intel has promoted support for up to 480GB of memory, but standard Intel-branded cards will be limited to 160GB; the 480GB maximum is available only to original design manufacturers building their own versions. Intel has not disclosed memory bandwidth and told Chips and Cheese it would not provide the figure, even though bandwidth strongly affects inference performance, token generation efficiency and operating cost. Wildcat Lake, the only architecture already available to consumers, launched as Intel's Core Series 3 and is used in laptops, mini PCs and other mainstream client and edge devices. Compared with Panther Lake, it replaces Foveros packaging with an organic multi-chip package, removing the base die, which Intel says can reduce assembly costs and yield losses. Compute die area is down 38 per cent and I/O tile area down 15 per cent. Its integrated NPU delivers 17 TOPS, below Microsoft's 40 TOPS Copilot+ requirement, although that requirement applies to the combined CPU, GPU and NPU performance, so a platform could still qualify overall. By developing separate architectures for client systems, inference accelerators and high-end server CPUs, Intel is seeking to cover more of the infrastructure needed as agentic AI workloads expand, even though much of its wider AI strategy has focused on enterprise and hyperscale customers.

Across the Ninth Federal Reserve District, workforce agencies, universities and employers are turning their attention to AI training, but in a fluid situation. Marcia Hultman, head of South Dakota's Department of Labor and Regulation, says few businesses she asks have integrated AI into their workflows; many are in the middle, and many haven't "dipped their toes in the water." Ross Jahnke of the University of Minnesota notes that need keeps changing as the technology advances and that employers take very different approaches to how much AI they want to use and how soon. There is urgency because AI is widely expected to boost productivity and reduce labor requirements, possibly causing job loss, and workers without AI skills may become less competitive. Large businesses use AI far more than small ones. The U.S. Census Bureau reported 22 percent of U.S. businesses using AI as of the end of July 2026, up 4 percentage points since the start of the year. In the Ninth District the share ranges from 14 percent in North Dakota to 22 percent in Montana. Many businesses appear to be experimenting rather than integrating AI, which is where experts expect the biggest productivity gains and labor reductions. A February Census survey found about half of AI-using businesses did not use it for any specified task, and most of the rest said it supplemented employees. Only generative and agentic AI, such as ChatGPT and Claude, are expected to disrupt jobs soon. That survey found just 2 percent of employers nationwide had cut jobs because of AI, and no Ninth District expert interviewed had heard of AI-driven job losses. States are offering basic AI courses and now training grants. South Dakota's grants serve businesses at varying stages of adoption; most of the 40 applications received by the end of July 2026 seek basic AI literacy. Montana's grants fund AI training at rural hospitals and clinics, where AI can help find medical research and complete paperwork, easing burnout and freeing time with patients, according to Sarah Swanson of the Department of Labor and Industry. Colleges are setting up AI institutes. Minnesota State University Moorhead launched its Institute of Applied Artificial Intelligence in fall 2025, aiming to embed AI skills in all courses rather than add a few stand-alone ones, according to Jason Trainer. Demand appears strong, though much comes from organizations without an enterprise-wide AI strategy that want employees to learn basics, ethical use and how AI works, Jahnke said. The University of Minnesota's introductory course on prompts and hazards like data bias has "moderately strong" enrollment, with advanced courses coming in the fall and winter. Northern State University's free spring workshops in two South Dakota towns drew more than double the expected attendance, from hospital workers, bankers and teachers, according to Jennifer Deutsch. Because AI evolves quickly, advanced training risks obsolescence; MSUM's Josh Riedy said training must cover tools businesses use now plus general adaptable skills. Census surveys project U.S. AI use rising 3 percentage points over six months, about 2 points in most Ninth District states, though Montana and North Dakota expect decreases. Experts disagree on whether massive job losses are coming. Ayush Chopra, who built an MIT simulation, doesn't expect a "job catastrophe"; it found South Dakota has the highest concentration of AI-exposed jobs, meaning tasks AI can enhance rather than replace. With a 2 percent unemployment rate in June, the nation's lowest, Hultman said productivity gains would help South Dakota and that it must keep encouraging AI training so it isn't left behind.

VIRGINIA BEACH — The public school system of Virginia’s largest city entered into a contract with the developer of the world’s most popular artificial intelligence model, ChatGPT. Under the agreement with OpenAI, Virginia Beach schools personnel will have access to a tailored version of the large language model designed to be more secure. It is explicitly not designed for student use. David Din, chief information officer of the school district, said the software will cost nothing to the school system through June 2028. “This just allowed us an opportunity to bring ChatGPT into a more secure environment, allowed us to put the necessary administrative controls around it so that we knew that staff would be able to have a tool that’s available to them for appropriate use,” he said. Din said Virginia Beach school officials approached OpenAI seeking a way for teachers to ask ChatGPT questions minding needs for administrative oversight and governance compliant obligations. The educator interface will be nearly identical to the standard version. Virginia Beach schools is among more than 50 districts spread across the country to maintain a partnership with OpenAI, as of Wednesday. Others include Houston, Baltimore and Boise, Idaho. OpenAI says the software can be used for creating classroom reference guides, converting lengthy lesson plans into focused courses and can address complex scheduling tasks. “As AI becomes more capable, it becomes even more important that educators understand this technology and can guide the next generation,” said Leah Belsky, vice president and general manager of education at OpenAI. High school students of Virginia Beach schools are permitted supervised use of AI. The district’s online resource for digital literacy says students are expect to disclose when AI is used. Teachers review the disclosures. Virginia Beach schools already employs the use of Gemini, a chatbot designed by Google in competition with ChatGPT. Access to both programs should not be seen through a mutually exclusive lens, Din said, as the different models perform better in different areas. The school district would be hosting sessions for personnel about using AI in education. Din said these sessions would provide “the ability for teachers to know and understand what the shortcomings of AI tools are.” Sessions are voluntary, as of now. OpenAI has recently been at the center of lawsuits alleging teenagers, without proper guardrails, developed unhealthy relationships and dependencies on chatbots that later offered methods of self-harm. It has over the years strengthened most safeguards while in other areas taken an apathetic approach, like on the matter of users developing deeper relationships with their chatbot. Other school districts have pushed ahead with AI as well. Norfolk schools intends to adopt a model of the technology built around classroom applications for teachers and students during this school year. In Hampton, schools leaders have deliberated on a lengthy revision to AI policy in the classroom. “Our goal with this initiative is to give educators the tools, trust, training and voice to decide when AI is useful, when it’s not and how it can support learning for students without replacing the human relationships and professional judgement at the center of school,” Belsky said. Most school leaders in the region acknowledge that while the technology has been the center of some recent controversies, it doesn’t appear to be going away. To adequately prepare students in a manner for them to be competitive in the workforce, therefore, teaching responsible use of AI is basically inevitable, they said. John Buzbee, 757-879-7421,.

X wants more people to use its Grok Bot for account performance insights and platform trend notes, so it’s is giving away free X API credits in order to facilitate access to X information. X’s Grok Bot is designed to be an artificial intelligence-powered teammate that can undertake tasks on the users’ behalf. That includes providing account performance notes, as well as broader trend data from across X, which the company is now trying to showcase with this new offer. As explained by X: “Connect your X account in Grok Bot and we’ll create a developer account for you if you don't have one. Paid Grok Bot users get free X API credits to start.” Once connected, the bot will be able to search X posts, read users’ timelines, check mentions or create reports based on trends and happenings in the app. “This is the first version of this integration, and we’re excited to keep making it easier for Grok Bot to do real work on X,” the company said. Essentially, X is trying to provide more performance insights in order to help creators and brands make the most of their X presence. In addition, the app is also showcasing the capacity of its evolving AI tools, and how those tools can be of assistance. From there, X is likely hoping that users will want to create their own Grok bots and agents that can undertake all sorts of tasks on their behalf. It could be a good showcase of the potential of X’s advanced insight tools, though it will also depend on users asking the right questions and making best use of the available insights. For marketers, that will likely relate to industry-specific trends, with the Grok Bot potentially able to highlight best practice notes, influencers to work with and benchmarking data. It could be an interesting experiment, and it will also be interesting to see how X looks to advance its analytics tools via the use of its evolving AI options.

Since Nintendo hasn't given its other retro franchises a Super Mario Maker-style DIY treatment, other developers are filling the gap, mostly with 2D creation suites that let players build Legend of Zelda levels with a Super NES look. At least one developer is taking the idea into 3D. Temple Maker 64 is the work of Akela-morse, a 27-year-old solo developer who left his job a year and a half ago to focus on it full-time. He told Polygon he got the idea after seeing top-down 2D pixel art titles like Quest Master, Super Dungeon Maker, and Super Dungeon Designer, so "going with a N64 aesthetic felt evident." The level design suite offers the classic weapons, items, and enemies of a 3D Zelda game like Ocarina of Time, but avoids any names Nintendo uses, and its tunic-clad protagonist resembles Link without copying his design. That approach may help it find an established audience, since high-profile attempts to sell similar ideas, such as Amazon's dungeon-making party game King of Meat, have floundered despite extensive level design and sharing features. The article argues the problem isn't gameplay but that people don't want to make games around characters they have no emotional attachment to. Games like Super Mario Maker succeed partly because players bring knowledge of what works in the series, and most people know how a Zelda dungeon works. Though the game isn't out yet, playtesters are already pushing it hard. Akela-morse shared a Reddit video of a playtester's Zelda equivalent of a Kaizo level, a term for fan-made Super Mario levels demanding extremely precise platforming. Kaizo Zelda levels require mastery of rolls, backflips, and side hops and of how they interact with the environment and items. The 33-second clip showcases high-level techniques most players would struggle to pull off. A Steam demo was released in May. Akela-morse plans social features like comments, tagging, and lists as a top priority, and is considering a single-player campaign and recruiting other Zelda-like developers to make maps. On the risk of legal action, since Nintendo is notoriously litigious, he wrote on Reddit that the company is aggressive about people using IPs, assets, or code they don't own, and that its patents on game mechanics are either refused or so specific they are barely enforced. He says he does none of that, so "there's nothing they can do but watch in fear." He is realistic about his chances and is also developing another project, Seed of Life, which appears influenced by Twilight Princess. He also wants to release the framework behind Temple Maker 64 as open source to help others make their own games. He says he is fully prepared to go back to "getting a real job" if things don't work out, but is eager to see where things go.
