Responding to Timothy Garton Ash's argument that serious AI risks demand international action, Dr Simon Nieder says "AI Hiroshima" may be the wrong picture. Hiroshima was not technology going rogue: humans designed, authorised and dropped the bomb, and it worked as intended. Many of AI's gravest harms could likewise occur without a dramatic "AI takes over" moment, for instance AI helping design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions, such as more autonomy here or one safeguard removed there, so that by the time danger is obvious the key decisions have been made. He argues international agreement could begin without consensus on superintelligence or extinction odds, by agreeing that some doors AI should never open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious starting points. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what, and share serious failures and near-misses internationally. Dr Anthony Harris, responding to Prof Jonathan Michie, notes that the Serbelloni group, led by Donald Michie (then at Edinburgh University), was weighing AI's social dangers as early as 1972. AI itself is not new, with roots in Frank Rosenblatt's 1957 perceptron, the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and Alan Turing; what is new is the hardware and software infrastructure driving it at terrifying speed. The 1973 Lighthill report brought an AI winter in the UK and shifted the field's centre of gravity across the Atlantic, with consequences still felt. Donald Michie, who had worked with Turing at Bletchley Park, argued against the cuts in the televised Lighthill debate without success; a quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, was "Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness." Harris, a computer scientist and humanities scholar, argues for reviving a "Serbelloni debate" involving both the sciences and the humanities. David Kyler, responding to Miles Brundage's article on regulating AI, says it failed to mention an international effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. That effort builds on an address at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as it spreads in weaponry and public surveillance. Kyler argues that a fragmented approach would make timely, internationally negotiated and effective controls much harder, since AI, corporate agendas, national defence and economic goals, and energy-intensive datacentres are interlocked systemically and cannot be resolved by disjointed incrementalism, especially as innovation accelerates. He warns that fragmented efforts would divert attention and cause crucial delays, while risks include malicious human use and deceptive activity by renegade algorithms, examples of which are already alarming. He adds that well-justified bipartisan opposition to datacentres is diverting political attention needed to control AI and to impose bans or moratoriums until reliable safeguards exist, like treating a symptom instead of the disease. A multifaceted strategy is possible, and the sooner guardrails are set, the fewer datacentre harms will occur. Like climate change, AI threats are inherently global, so an international approach is essential.

During the Second World War, the Allies, particularly the US and UK, massively outproduced the Axis powers, particularly Germany, in bombers and transport aircraft. The war accelerated aircraft development as countries sought to defeat each other and sustain operations worldwide. Five of the largest military aircraft produced were as follows. The German Messerschmitt Me 323 Gigant, with a wingspan of 181 feet and a max take-off weight of 94,799 lbs, is regarded as the largest land-based transport aircraft flown in the war. It was a powered variant of the Me 321 military glider, which was built for Operation Sea Lion, the planned invasion of Great Britain. Germany built 213 Giants (including 15 converted from Me 321 gliders). Because Germany lost the Battle of Britain, the invasion never happened, but the Me 323 served in the Invasion of Crete, the Invasion of the Soviet Union, and the North African campaign, carrying around 100 fully-equipped troops or military vehicles. The Boeing B-29 Superfortress (wingspan 141 feet, max take-off weight 133,500 lbs) was the most successful of the large aircraft. It succeeded the B-17 Flying Fortress and arrived late in the war, so it was mostly used against Japan, where it carried out much of the fire-bombing and dropped the two nuclear bombs that ended the war. It served in the Korean War and was retired in 1960. Two, including 'Doc', still fly. At $3 billion, it was the war's most expensive military project, costing more than the $1.9 billion Manhattan Project. Its innovations included an analog-computer-controlled fire-control system, a pressurized cabin, and dual-wheeled tricycle landing gear. The Douglas XB-19 (wingspan 212 feet, max take-off weight 162,000 lbs) was an experimental four-engined heavy bomber slightly bigger than the B-29 and the largest bomber built for the US Army Air Force until the Convair B-36. It was obsolete before completion. Plans to convert it into a cargo aircraft were never completed; it last flew on August 17, 1946 and was scrapped in 1949. The Hughes H-4 Hercules, the 'Spruce Goose' (wingspan 319 feet, empty weight 250,000 lbs), remains the largest flying boat ever built and one of the largest aircraft ever flown. It was a prototype strategic airlift flying boat meant to carry men and equipment across the Atlantic above German U-boats, under a 1942 contract from the US Department of War. Wartime restrictions on aluminum meant it was made almost entirely of birch. By the time it was ready the U-boat problem had passed; it flew only once, briefly, on November 2, 1947, and was then canceled. It is now on display at the Evergreen Museum. The Blohm & Voss BV 238 (max take-off weight 220,462 lbs) was the heaviest aircraft ever built when it first flew in 1944 and the largest produced by the Axis powers. A flying boat intended as a slow, heavily armored and armed bomber to demonstrate German technological superiority, it weighed as much as two B-29s and had a range of over 6,000 miles. It was never successful: only one prototype was produced, with two more incomplete, and the prototype was strafed by the Allies and partially sank near Lübeck.

Minnesota man invents AI-powered machine to kill weeds. EDINA, Minn. (FOX 9) - A Minnesota inventor has built a weed-killing machine that uses artificial intelligence, robotics, and steam — no chemicals required. AI-powered weed killer uses steam, not chemicals. What we know: Mark Boysen modified a lawn mower into the device, which uses AI to identify weeds, distinguish them from surrounding plants, and then hit them with a targeted burst of steam. "We're able to detect weeds with A.I., distinguish the difference between a weed and what's not a weed, and we hit it with a burst of steam, and it kills — just 100% water — and it kills the weed in about 20 minutes," Boysen said. The backstory: Boysen has since secured a patent for the invention and submitted it to the Minnesota Cup competition last summer. He also won the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency's Green Sustainability Award. His company, NAWARE, has now developed a smaller version of the machine, which Boysen believes will be more commercially viable for everyday homeowners looking to keep their yards chemical-free. He asked that the full design of the newer machine not be shown on camera yet, saying it is not ready for its public debut. How the steam weed killer works. Dig deeper: Demonstrations in his yard show that repeated steam applications cause weeds to die off within about 20 minutes. "These will be dead in about 20 minutes. You smell it — it'll smell like spinach — and that's the weeds cooking. Basically breaking down the cellular structure," Boysen said. A version of the invention is already operating at a winery in Arizona. Boysen also gave a talk about his sustainability efforts at the Minnesota State Fair. What they're saying: Before founding NAWARE, Boysen spent 12 years as a product coach, working with a wide range of companies. "I was teaching companies and enterprises all the way up to Fortune Four, from startups to Fortune [500], and teaching them how to basically build products. And I was like, hey, maybe I got to listen to my own playbook here, and now's the time to develop something," he said. Neighbor Ryan Finnefrock, who has two young children, said the chemical-free approach matters to him personally. "I got two young kids, right, a four-year-old and a seven-month-old. So what we do know, there's a lot of products out there that do the job, and they're very effective, but are they the best for kids and stuff? We don't know, right," Finnefrock said. "We know that steam is not going to hurt anything. So that's incredible that he thought of that idea and has grown it." Boysen said demand for the product is already outpacing what he can deliver. "We've got more demand than we can keep up with, honestly. It really comes down to how quick can I develop the product out of it," he said. For more information, visit the Naware website.

ONE Store announced on August 31 that it has officially launched its app marketplace 'ONE Store Global' and D2C (direct-to-consumer) payment platform 'ONE shop' across 122 countries worldwide. 'ONE Store Global' began service in 122 countries, including North America, Latin America, and Asia. It secured over 1,000 titles at launch, including AI and blockchain-based games in its lineup. Developers can launch games simultaneously across target countries using a single global build. 'AI Games', a service showcasing games created with AI, is also scheduled to launch in the global market in September. It features games made by creators using AI, which users can run directly on 'ONE Store Global' without downloading a separate app. ONE Store plans to expand this service globally after initiating it in Korea in August. Launched alongside it, 'ONE shop' is a D2C channel that integrates ONE Store's ONE Web Shop and NEXUS's CROSS Shop. Adding the US, Japan, Taiwan, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines to its existing service region of Korea, it operates in a total of 7 countries. A sales commission of 5% excluding PG fees is applied to developers. Developers can adopt 'ONE shop' without developing a separate build by leveraging existing ONE Store in-app purchase integration specifications. A site builder feature is also provided, allowing developers to directly customize product display formats, banner orders, background colors, images, and more on their sales pages. NEXUS CEO Jang Hyun-guk said, "Starting from Korea, ONE Store has launched the world's first AI and blockchain game platform across 122 countries," adding, "We will ensure that innovations occurring in AI and blockchain translate directly into game content and platforms". ONE Store plans to expand its service countries, regional support for 'ONE shop', and content lineup in the future. Sort by: Comments :0.

The European Central Bank is preparing to issue a tokenized euro directly on blockchain infrastructure, a step that could change how institutional securities are settled across the eurozone while leaving room for private stablecoins in payments and trading. Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel outlined the strategy at the Jackson Hole symposium. The plan targets wholesale money used by banks and financial institutions, not consumers, and is distinct from the separate digital euro initiative aimed at the general public. Schnabel said tokenized markets need a settlement asset that only a central bank can create, describing it as a programmable reserve issued directly by the ECB. She argued that stablecoin issuers cannot expand money supply during market panic as a central bank can, citing the 1907 US banking panic and the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, which created an elastic public backstop. She nonetheless did not predict the demise of private tokens, saying stablecoins should complement central bank money, particularly for liquidity provision, wallet transfers, remittances and access to decentralized markets. The near-term vehicle is Pontes, a Eurosystem project due to go live in September. It will connect market distributed ledger technology platforms with TARGET Services, the eurozone's real-time gross settlement infrastructure, enabling atomic settlement in which transactions either complete fully or not at all. At launch, legal finality will remain within T2, the existing RTGS system. Participants can choose between settling with cash tokens on a Eurosystem ledger or completing the cash leg in T2, with Hash-Link technology synchronizing delivery-versus-payment. Later upgrades will add smart contracts, continuous operations and full on-chain finality, potentially supporting programmable repo operations and automated collateral calls. A pilot between May and November 2024 involved 64 institutions across nine jurisdictions, settling nearly €1.6 billion in central bank money across 58 use cases. The article notes Europe's dependence on foreign blockchain liquidity. DeFiLlama puts total stablecoin supply at roughly $304.6 billion as of late August 2026, with dollar-denominated tokens dominant and euro-pegged tokens below $1 billion. A tokenized euro could appeal to institutional platforms wanting to cut counterparty and operational risk through a direct claim on the central bank, compared with tokens carrying issuer, custody and redemption risks, though tokenized deposits offer similar programmability. The Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation lets compliant stablecoin issuers keep operating payment services in the EU, and Schnabel's positioning suggests private tokens will retain roles where portability, open access and cross-platform reach matter more than settlement finality. A parallel project, Appia, will determine the final architecture for the ECB's digital solutions by 2028, weighing a single unified ledger, a central bank ledger linked to private blockchains, or multiple interoperable ledgers, with tradeoffs among liquidity, resilience, governance, competition and technological concentration. France's Lise platform, described as Europe's first licensed fully tokenized financial exchange, shows how public infrastructure can open markets to smaller enterprises. Settlement in ECB-issued digital money could narrow stablecoin demand for tokenized bonds, funds, equities and repo transactions, but not erase uses where stablecoin flexibility and decentralized reach remain valuable. On the ECB's current trajectory, the two will operate as separate but complementary layers of Europe's digital financial infrastructure.

Yokohama Rubber develops proprietary generative AI system. Hiratsuka, Japan—The Yokohama Rubber Co., Ltd., announces that it has developed and begun full-scale operation in August 2026 of a proprietary generative AI system utilizing RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), which searches various technical documents accumulated internally and presents responses based on their contents. This new system contributes to further accelerating and enhancing tire development by providing rapid and accurate access to technical information necessary for decision-making during the tire development process, including material development. Yokohama Rubber developed this new system to expand the practical environment of its proprietary HAICoLab AI utilization framework, which was established in October 2020. Yokohama Rubber has previously developed AI systems that predict a rubber compound’s physical properties and tire characteristics, generate new rubber compounds, and support mold design, and the Company is increasingly using data to create material and tire designs. Meanwhile, the technical knowledge (domain knowledge) that developers need to make decisions during the tire development process can be found in a vast array of technical documents that include regulatory documents, procedure manuals, technical reports, and case studies. Creating a system that can quickly search this vast collection of data and provide information appropriate to development objectives and circumstances has been a challenge. A framework for “collaboration between humans and AI” that drives a virtuous cycle of innovation in products, processes, and services alongside human growth through a process that starts with enhancing AI by using data and knowledge accumulated in the company, the formulation of hypotheses by humans using metacognition, and development staff interpret and judge the results using the enhanced AI. Expertise and knowledge in a specific field or industry. Yokohama Rubber development staff using this new system input questions tailored to the development’s objectives and situation, and the generative AI searches for the most relevant information from internal technical documents and provides responses based on that content. Yokohama Rubber development staff also created a mechanism in which an implemented AI agent grasps the intent of the staff’s questions and enhances the accuracy of its response by autonomously repeating the process of planning searches, retrieving information, and evaluating the results. Additionally, with the system displaying links to the original documents that serve as the basis for responses, development staff can verify the basis and appropriateness of those responses and use them in interpretation and decision-making. This has added a new mechanism that uses domain knowledge accumulated in technical documents with AI, thereby expanding the tire development environment based on HAICoLab. Along with the development of these AI systems, Yokohama Rubber is training DX staff capable of using HAICoLab. Yokohama Rubber will continue its efforts to enhance the new system’s capabilities and use data and knowledge accumulated internally to develop innovative products, processes, and services.

Ethereum's validator activation queue held 2.059 million ETH at 12:37 UTC on Aug. 30, meaning a deposit joining the back of the line faces a wait of about 35 days and 18 hours. The backlog comes as more than 42 million ETH, nearly 35% of supply, is already staked; both figures are record highs. Only 96 ETH was waiting in the exit queue. Staked ETH has risen from about 36 million, nearly 30% of supply, in January. The imbalance shows demand for staking capacity exceeds Ethereum's ability to activate deposits, even though the queue has fallen from more than 4 million ETH earlier this year. ETH waiting for activation earns no consensus rewards. At current staking rates, the backlog represents roughly 141 to 148 ETH of delayed consensus rewards per day, about $348,000 to $366,000 at an ETH price near $2,466. This is delayed reward opportunity, not a realized loss, since deposits nearer the front activate sooner. Ethereum deliberately limits how fast stake can enter and leave the validator set to avoid abrupt changes to network security. Under the Electra consensus rules, activations and exits are each capped at 256 ETH per epoch; with epochs of about 6.4 minutes, that is roughly 57,600 ETH per day per side. When deposits arrive faster than this, the queue grows. Beaconcha.in counted 29,668 pending deposit requests, but this is not the number of new validators. Electra allows compounding validators to hold an effective balance of up to 2,048 ETH while keeping the 32 ETH minimum, and top-ups to existing validators use the same activation lane as deposits for new validators. The backlog therefore mixes potential new stake with balance additions by existing operators, and does not show that investors recently bought 2.06 million ETH or that all of it is fresh institutional demand. The queue has been shrinking. A Morgan Stanley Ethereum Trust filing recorded about 3.64 million ETH waiting and a 63-day delay on May 18, while Lido, the dominant liquid staking provider, said the queue exceeded 4 million ETH in January before falling to 2.9 million at the end of June. The current level still imposes roughly a five-week delay. The Morgan Stanley filing states that ETH allocated for staking does not accrue rewards while awaiting activation. Ethereum's staking page showed an annual reward rate around 2.5%, while a queue tracker put it near 2.63%. A 32 ETH deposit joining at the back would forgo roughly 0.078 to 0.082 ETH in potential consensus rewards over the 35.75-day wait, worth about $193 to $203. These figures assume unchanged rates and prices and exclude execution-layer rewards, maximal extractable value, provider fees and compounding. Who bears the delay depends on the product. A solo validator waits without rewards directly, while an exchange, fund or liquid-staking provider can spread the cost across a pool, absorb it or pass it to users. Lido said in its first-half report that foregone rewards made some stVault deposits unattractive. With more than 42 million ETH staked and another 2.06 million waiting, the immediate constraint is not investors leaving but how quickly Ethereum can process those trying to get in.

BOSTON -- The 2026 midterms have brought a number of generational challenges like the one Massachusetts Senate challenger Seth Moulton is waging against incumbent Ed Markey, with younger Democrats taking on -- and in some cases unseating -- longtime incumbents. There are signs that Democratic voters, especially, are looking for change, and some young voters argue older politicians can't truly understand a world transformed by artificial intelligence, rising housing costs and student debt. When asked in a recent debate whether he uses AI platforms like Claude or ChatGPT in his work, Markey, 80, seemed unclear on the topic. He responded that he uses "whatever is inside of my iPhone or my iPad -- whatever comes up" and added that he doesn't know "what companies my iPad may be using." For Arsen Bagdassarian, an 18-year-old supporter of Markey's rival, 47-year-old U.S. Rep. Moulton, the answer reinforced a concern that has become central to Moulton's campaign to unseat the incumbent in Tuesday's party primary: that Markey, who would be 86 at the end of another term, is too old to represent a generation confronting problems that didn't exist when Markey entered Congress 50 years ago. "To be frank, I didn't expect him to be as clueless as he really was on that topic," said Bagdassarian, an incoming freshman at Boston's Northeastern University. Artificial intelligence is "a major concern," he said, and the country needs leaders "who understand what they're being asked to regulate." But that hasn't been the case for all young people voting for the Senate nominee in a heavily Democratic state where the primary often decides who wins office. Markey has a strong following of young supporters, some of whom say that the internal party debate is more over policy than age. He's won the endorsement of the High School Democrats of America and the College Democrats of America, as well as the backing of popular progressives such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Among those younger supporters is Matt Kelly, president of the UMass Lowell College Democrats. Kelly doesn't dispute that Markey stumbled when asked about his use of AI, saying, "I'll admit it wasn't a good answer." But Kelly said he cares less about whether Markey knows how to use the latest technology than whether he understands how to govern it. Moulton's relative youth, Kelly said, doesn't necessarily make his views more representative of young voters. Many of Markey's younger supporters turn Moulton's argument about the senator's 50-year political career on its head. To them, longevity provides a record they can judge -- one that shows whether politicians held the same positions before they became popular with younger voters. Abby Shadden, a 21-year-old Emmanuel College student, pointed to Markey's co-authorship of the Green New Deal and his early support for Medicare for All. "There is this idea that younger people are just automatically more progressive when, in this case, it is very much not true," she said. For some of Moulton's young supporters, the argument is about more than the candidates' ages. Molly Blander, an 18-year-old incoming Tufts University freshman, pointed to artificial intelligence and social media as technologies that have reshaped life for her generation -- including its mental health. She cited Moulton's work to establish 988 as the national suicide and crisis lifeline as an example of the kind of response she wants to see. "In my lifetime, I haven't seen the Democratic Party and the Democratic establishment really make things much better," she said. "And so I feel like the status quo and the establishment that we have now just isn't working." Information for this article was contributed by Michael Casey of The Associated Press.

Cronos switched off its entire blockchain on Sunday to contain an exploit at Tectonic, the network's largest lending protocol, freezing every position on the chain. Cronos said it had "identified an exploit" and, a day later, confirmed the chain was still down while it investigated with support from security teams across the industry. Crypto.com CEO Kris Marszalek said the exchange and app were operating normally and customer funds were safe, and promised a postmortem. Tectonic told depositors not to interact with the protocol until it confirmed doing so was safe. Tectonic lets users deposit crypto for others to borrow against collateral. It was the first such protocol on Cronos and holds close to half of all capital in the network's DeFi apps; the next-biggest lender, Mimas Finance, holds about $30,000, per DefiLlama. Onchain researcher Weilin Li called it a "Mango-market style pump-and-borrow price manipulation attack," referring to the $100 million Mango Markets exploit of October 2022. He said TONIC's price surged 100-fold within 20 minutes before the attacker borrowed against it. The root cause, in his account, was that Tectonic gave its own governance token a 20% collateral factor despite thin liquidity of about $1.34 million. He first put the haul at $66 million, then about $75 million after finding another attacker-controlled address holding $8 million. PeckShield estimated about $74 million. A separate analysis measuring gross outflow from the pools put the total moved at about $119.5 million. Shortly before the incident Tectonic held about $121.7 million in deposits and $82.7 million in active loans, per DefiLlama. By Monday that had fallen to roughly $3 million, a 97.5% drop over 30 days. The halt worked in containment terms: only about $6 million of proceeds reached Ethereum before block production stopped, leaving roughly $60 million immobilised on the frozen chain. Li suggested part of it was parked in a decentralized exchange pool to avoid blacklisting. DefiLlama data fits this: the largest Cronos decentralized exchange gained close to $61 million in deposits over 24 hours, while chain-wide DeFi holdings fell 22%. The shutdown was feasible because Cronos runs a capped validator set of 100, but it also stopped open loans, trades, payouts and automated positions for users unconnected to Tectonic. Li called it the third Mango-style attack in recent weeks, after one on Moonwell, where manipulation of the illiquid MAMO token cost an estimated $8.7 million, and one on a Pendle reUSD market that triggered roughly $36 million in liquidations on August 25. It is not Tectonic's first breach. DefiLlama records two earlier protocol logic failures, one in February 2024 costing $250,000 and another in November 2024. It classifies Sunday's attack as oracle manipulation via spot price manipulation, with a $75 million loss. Neither Cronos nor Tectonic has given a restart timeline, confirmed a final figure, or said whether depositors will be made whole.

Researchers have developed a method for putting numerical error limits on quantum simulations, showing how much confidence to place in their results. As quantum simulators become powerful enough to tackle problems beyond the reach of conventional computers, verifying their accuracy becomes difficult. When classical calculations are still possible, the two approaches can be compared directly, but beyond that point another way to verify results is needed. The work was led by Tristan Kraft of the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller of the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information at the Austrian Academy of Sciences, together with Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. A team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos tested the approach on an ion-trap quantum simulator with as many as 51 ions, at IQOQI Innsbruck. Quantum simulators are physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems, and are especially useful for complicated many-particle systems that overwhelm classical computers. But real devices are imperfect: interactions may differ from expectations, the environment influences the system, and measurements carry uncertainty. Rather than assuming a simulator behaves as intended, the researchers use experimental measurements to determine how it actually operates. From this data they determine the relevant interactions and key influences from fluctuations and noise, then calculate how uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results. The simulator thus provides not just a single value but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy. The method was first tested on ten ions, a system small enough to be calculated on a conventional computer, allowing the resulting model and its predicted error bounds to be checked against independent measurements. The approach was then extended to a chain of 51 ions, showing the strategy works for substantially larger systems. The next target is two-dimensional quantum systems. Zoller explains this is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as particle numbers grow, which also makes independent verification increasingly complex and experimentally determined error limits all the more important. The researchers are adapting the method for the newest generation of two-dimensional simulators, which offer greater precision and can handle more particles. In the longer term, the approach could offer a way to measure quantum advantage quantitatively. Instead of judging a quantum simulator only by whether it is faster or larger than a classical computer, researchers could also compare how reliably each system solves the same problem. As Zoller puts it, what is also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error. Performance may thus depend not only on system size or speed but also on whether a difficult problem can be solved with independently quantifiable accuracy. The study, "Bounded-Error Quantum Simulation via Hamiltonian and Lindbladian Learning," was published in Physical Review X on 13 August 2026. Funding came from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, and BMW, among others.

The Airbus A330 and A350 share a manufacturer and role but represent two technological generations: the A330 reflects the mature fly-by-wire technology of the 1990s, while the A350 reflects the digital, composite-era innovations of the 2010s. Pilots often describe moving between them as going from a refined classic to a state-of-the-art successor. Airbus deliberately built in commonality. The two aircraft share a type rating, so pilots certified on one can transition to the other with about eight days of differences training, according to Airbus. Across the Airbus lineup, from the A320 family to the A380, pilots use side-stick controllers, flight envelope protection and similar flight management systems, and follow the "dark cockpit" concept, where panels stay unlit until a warning or abnormal condition occurs. Many pilots see the A350 as an evolutionary step, though its technology represents a major leap. The A330 entered service in 1994 and became one of the world's most widely used widebodies. Its original A330-200 and A330-300 (CEO, Current Engine Option) variants were developed alongside the quadjet A340. The cockpit has six primary display screens, side-sticks and the ECAM system, favoring reliability and clarity over advanced graphics. Pilots describe its handling as stable, predictable and somewhat heavy, which many appreciate on approaches and in turbulence. The A330neo (A330-800 and A330-900) arrived in the late 2010s with Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines, sharklet wings and updated avionics. Its cockpit borrows A350 features such as improved displays and system integration, narrowing the technology gap. The A350, introduced in 2015 to compete with the Boeing 787 and 777, is more than half carbon-fiber composite, giving greater range, lower fuel burn and better aerodynamic efficiency. Its flight deck has six large, interchangeable 15-inch LCD displays that improve situational awareness. Tools include Brake-to-Vacate, which selects the optimal runway exit; the Airport Navigation Function with taxi maps; and integrated electronic checklists. Airbus designed the cockpit with airline pilots' input, and pilot feedback cited by Simple Flying points to better ergonomics, visibility and workload management, reducing fatigue on ultra-long-haul flights. Differences are most obvious in flight. The A350's new wing has a higher aspect ratio, greater span and more flexibility, improving climb performance and cruise efficiency. Pilots report it feels smoother in turbulence, reaches cruise levels faster and handles more responsively in pitch and roll, while the A330's older wing gives a heavier control feel. In avionics, the A350 uses Integrated Modular Avionics that centralize systems, enabling predictive maintenance and diagnostics, better flight management calculations and integrated checklists. The A330's older architecture requires more manual crew oversight. A head-up display, fitted to both the A350 and A330neo, projects flight data into the pilot's view during takeoff and landing. Overall, the A330 is stable and dependable, while the A350 feels more agile, automated and advanced. Because of shared fly-by-wire logic, control laws and procedures, pilots can move between the two with relative ease.

Fighter jets have existed since the closing months of World War II. Five generations have followed, with a sixth expected to begin with the F-47, which won't be completed until the mid-2030s. A 4.5th generation also exists, improving on fourth-generation designs without matching fifth-generation capabilities. First generation: The Messerschmitt Me 262, the first operational jet fighter, flew over 500 mph and was first used in combat on July 25, 1944, over Munich. Germany built over 1,400, but only around 300 saw combat because of infrastructure destruction. Its two Junkers Jumo 004 engines gave a 540 mph maximum speed, versus 437 mph for the P-51D Mustang. The Soviet MiG-15, introduced in 1949, was built with swept wings and a Klimov VK-1 engine producing 6,000 lbs of thrust, reaching 668 mph. More than 13,000 were made, and some still serve in North Korea. Second generation: Guns proved ineffective at supersonic speeds, and fighters became multirole. The Lockheed F-104 Starfighter, nicknamed "the missile with a man in it," was the first aircraft capable of sustained Mach 2 flight, reaching 1,320 mph with afterburner via its General Electric J79 engine, and it used AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles. The MiG-21 is the most-produced supersonic jet ever, with over 10,000 built; India used it until September 2025. It had a delta wing and adjustable shock cone, reaching 1,300 mph, and its maneuverability initially exceeded that of the gunless F-4 Phantom II in Vietnam. Third generation: The F-4 Phantom II, with 5,195 built, was the most-produced U.S. supersonic aircraft. Later versions added a 20 mm M61 Vulcan cannon and advanced radar, and with AIM-7 Sparrow and AIM-9 missiles it achieved air superiority. All five fighter aces of Vietnam flew it. The Saab 37 Viggen (1971, retired 2007, 330 built) was the first production aircraft with canards and the only jet to lock its targeting system onto an SR-71 Blackbird. Fourth generation: This generation brought composites, fly-by-wire, supermaneuverability and stealth. The Dassault Rafale (2001) has a canard delta design, digital fly-by-wire and two Snecma M88 engines reaching Mach 1.8. It performs many mission types; over 530 have been ordered, and the 300th was built in October 2025. The Eurofighter Typhoon (operational 2003) is a swing-role aircraft with quadruplex fly-by-wire and two Eurojet EJ200 engines giving 40,000 lbs. of thrust and Mach 2, with 13 hardpoints. 4.5th generation: The Boeing F-15EX Eagle II, in U.S. use since 2024, has a strengthened airframe, new radar and avionics, and two F110-GE-129 engines. It carries 12 AIM-120 missiles or up to 29,500 lbs. of ordnance, reaches Mach 2.5, and has a service life over 20,000 hours. Russia's Sukhoi Su-35S (2008) can supercruise using two Saturn AL-41F1S engines, reaches Mach 2.25 with afterburners, and has 12 hardpoints. Fifth generation: The Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor (2005) was the first fifth-generation fighter; only 200 were built, flown solely by the USAF. Considered the world's best air-to-air fighter, it has two F119-PW-100 engines (35,000 lbs. thrust), thrust-vectoring nozzles and supercruise, and should serve into the 2030s. The F-35 Lightning II is the dominant strike fighter of the USAF, USN and USMC and is flown by other nations. Variants include the conventional F-35A, the short-takeoff/vertical-landing F-35B and the carrier-capable F-35C. It features near-complete instrument automation and a see-through floor view via a $400,000 helmet, making it the most advanced fighter to date.

Students will embark on a new school year next week, with NYC public schools reopening on Sept. 10. But with just 10 days to go, the city’s Department of Education (DOE) has yet to address one major classroom issue that has many parents and educators greatly concerned: the use of artificial intelligence (AI). In the 2025-26 school year, the DOE implemented an AI policy that many critics found to be lacking in addressing the technology’s most important impacts on a child’s education. The DOE policy used a “traffic light framework that spelled out various uses of AI and their risk levels,” as Chalkbeat reported. It left out guidance for how students should use AI, prohibited teachers from using it for assessments and grading, but allowed its use by teachers to create their day-to-day lesson plans. Parents and educators revolted, and the DOE, guided by Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels, implemented a pause on the plan. They set a new deadline for creating and introducing a modified AI policy, but that deadline came and went without any new guidelines in place. With the clock rapidly ticking toward the start of the new school year, parents, teachers and education advocates at the city’s Panel for Educational Policy (PEP) Aug. 26 meeting demanded action. Some wanted the DOE to bar AI’s usage outright, fearing the impact on the students’ critical thinking and psychological development. Those concerns are not without merit; a study published by the American Psychological Association on July 1 found that adult workers who had used generative AI in researching and finding answers to their questions also “engaged in less critical thinking when they used it to complete work tasks.” Those tasks included brainstorming new ideas, “learning about new topics, and getting guidance when making a decision.” While that study focused on AI’s psychological impacts on adults, it serves as a cautionary tale in the education of our children. If schools and educators use AI without proper regulation, it will instill in students a tendency to lean more on AI than their own minds. That will have a devastating impact on their ability to learn and think for themselves, and make important decisions in their lives. AI is a tool much like a computer or a calculator. Schools have regulated the use of computers and calculators in day-to-day instruction to ensure that children use their brains and develop critical thinking, reading comprehension, creativity, problem-solving, and other vital cognitive skills that the world needs to formulate new ideas and solutions to challenges we face every day. Because it is a tool, AI must be regulated by NYC public and private schools alike to prevent over-reliance upon it, and deterioration of cognitive skills for current and future generations. The DOE needs to listen to parents and educators and roll out as soon as possible a responsible plan for AI usage in the classroom that informs teachers and students of the best practices for using this incredible tool without undermining the quality of education provided.

Adobe offers free AI tools to 27 million Saudis in $4 billion Humain deal. Adobe is making one of its biggest AI distribution bets yet, offering more than 27 million people in Saudi Arabia a year of free access to its generative AI tools as part of an expanded partnership valued at more than $4 billion. The software giant announced the initiative Monday at LEAP 2026, saying eligible Saudi citizens and residents aged 13 and older will receive 12 months of free access to Adobe Firefly Standard and premium features from Adobe Express. The offer is expected to begin rolling out by the end of 2026. The deal, which was announced on Monday, brings Adobe deeper into Saudi Arabia’s AI ambitions through a partnership with the country’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and Humain, the AI company backed by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. At the center of the partnership is something more ambitious than giving away software. Adobe and Humain are preparing to launch a jointly developed image-generation model built using Adobe Firefly Foundry and tuned to Saudi culture. Adobe says it will be the first image-generation model jointly developed with Firefly Foundry, with imagery informed by Saudi cultural context, visual references and creative needs. “AI should understand the context in which it operates,” Humain CEO Tareq Amin said. “Our partnership with Adobe combines Adobe’s creative technology with HUMAIN’s regional intelligence to bring greater cultural relevance to image generation. We are building it locally but designing it to compete and scale globally.” That localization push addresses a persistent challenge for generative AI systems trained on enormous datasets that may poorly represent languages, cultures and visual conventions outside their dominant training material. Adobe has taken another step on the language side, launching Modern Standard Arabic right-to-left support for Adobe Express globally across desktop, web and iOS. The update includes Arabic typography, text editing, interface controls and a collection of templates tuned to Saudi culture. Adobe’s $4 billion Saudi bet goes beyond free AI. For Adobe, putting Firefly and Express in front of more than 27 million potential users could serve another purpose: customer acquisition at a scale few conventional marketing campaigns could match. Adobe remains one of the biggest names in creative software, but generative AI has opened the door to a growing field of AI-native design and content tools. Giving millions of people access to Firefly creates an opportunity to build familiarity with Adobe’s AI ecosystem before those users settle into competing platforms. The $4 billion figure represents Adobe’s stated value of the free-access commitment, not a $4 billion cash investment in Humain. Adobe is also extending the program into Saudi Arabia’s startup ecosystem. Beginning in early 2027, eligible startups and early-stage entrepreneurs participating in MCIT’s Center of Digital Entrepreneurship (CODE) and The Garage will receive one year of free access to select Adobe creative tools, training and expertise. The expanded agreement builds on a partnership Adobe and Humain announced at the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum in November 2025, Reuters reported. The companies previously laid out plans to develop AI models and applications for more than 400 million Arabic speakers. Humain has emerged as a central piece of Saudi Arabia’s bid to become a global AI hub, backed by the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund and striking agreements with major technology companies across models, chips and infrastructure. Adobe’s latest move adds a consumer- and startup-facing dimension to that strategy. Instead of AI investment remaining largely inside data centers and corporate contracts, millions of people could get direct access to the resulting technology. For Adobe, that creates an unusually large real-world test: give much of a country access to your AI tools for a year, build around its language and culture, and see how many users stay after the free period ends.

This week's threats mostly arrived through things already trusted: shipped devices, familiar prompts, support tools, valid access, and systems meant to protect the network. ZeroBEC detailed an email-bombing campaign hitting 10 users with about 3,000 messages daily, followed by Teams contact from fake help desk staff; a local-admin victim granted Quick Assist access, enabling Xray-core deployment, credential theft via a fake Windows update prompt, and NTLM relay attempts. ZeroBEC's CEO confirmed the same actor hit two victims, with overlap to Aurora ransomware. A rogue installer posing as adware led to ValleyRAT, linked to Silver Fox; Kaspersky saw it over 100,000 times, affecting 1,500+ users mainly in China and India. Brazil's ANPD fined ByteDance 153.8 million reais ($29.81 million) for processing teenagers' data without legal basis. Unit 42 found only 12 of 405 AI-integrated malware samples reached production, and behavioral detection still catches them. India's I4C warned of fake pornography apps spreading a banking trojan. The lesson: ask what trusted systems can also do, who else can reach them, and whether their evidence can be trusted.

The author uses an old, cheap Poco M6 Pro smartphone and Podroid to run Docker containers, and has spent a couple of days testing various environments with surprisingly decent results. Although dedicated x86 servers already run dozens of containerized utilities in the home lab, and Tailscale provides remote access to them, there are times when certain quality-of-life tools on those rigs are unreachable. The phone lets the author carry essential tools on the move without relying solely on the servers. IT-Tools offers developer-centric utilities that suit mobile tasks. Its updated arsenal includes syntax converters, Crontab generators and WYSIWYG editors, plus a basic auth generator, password strength analyser and OTP code generator for creating and checking passwords. A percentage calculator and chronometer help with benchmarks, while website link and Wi-Fi QR code generators make sharing links and passwords easy. The dev tools also help fix broken YAML/JSON syntax when only a laptop and smartphone are available. It also includes an emoji picker and ASCII art generator. Omni-Tools is a more generalized toolkit for tedious everyday chores. For text, it can add pull quotes, shift characters, censor words and extract email addresses. For images, it can annotate, apply watermarks and remove backgrounds. For video, it can crop clips, change playback and add audio tracks. It also has an image-to-GIF converter, Discord timestamp generator and weekday calculator. None of these are game-changers, but they spare the author from sketchy cloud apps for niche tasks. ConvertX is a self-hosted file converter that avoids the forced watermarks, long queues and ads of mobile and cloud converters. It supports nearly every format the author uses, including text files, images, ebooks, videos, 3D models and phone contacts. BentoPDF replaced limited, ad-laden or privacy-invasive PDF editors. The author uses it to decrypt, compress, deskew, rasterize, extract and sign documents directly on the phone, and it also supports metadata manipulation, document flattening, timestamping and other advanced utilities. Conventional data-archival containers can also run on a smartphone. The author sticks to simple Docker environments to avoid maintaining duplicate instances of archival apps on both phone and home server. Users less deep into home labbing could turn a phone into an all-in-one self-hosting workstation, since Jellyfin, Nextcloud, Calibre-web and similar services work well on most smartphones, including outdated ones. The only trouble comes from utilities that rely on system ports, which cannot be assigned to containers on unrooted phones.

President Donald Trump criticized the rising wave of anti-data center sentiment, clashing with his administration’s aggressive efforts to build out the domestic artificial intelligence sector. Trump has placed a concerted focus on making the U.S. the global leader in AI, but voters have steadily voiced concerns about building the data centers needed to power the technology over concerns that they will raise utility prices in the areas where they are constructed. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president wrote on Truth Social Monday morning. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” Trump added that “China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement” and “can’t believe” that voters have made the topic a top issue ahead of the November midterm elections. The president’s comments go significantly further than past comments he’s made regarding the national data center buildout, even as 2026 Republican candidates look to thread the needle between supporting the president’s platform and addressing voters’ affordability concerns. Earlier in August, Trump said he “absolutely” would look to build a data center in his community if he were a state or local politician, while acknowledging that AI companies could “use a little public relations help.” Trump also said recently that he didn’t care if Republican candidates split with him on the issue. “If a Republican’s against the data center, that’s OK with me,” Trump told reporters before a campaign stop in South Carolina earlier this month.

Nvidia Corp. had another astounding quarter, beating revenue expectations. The announcement came alongside an expanded collaboration with Cisco Systems Inc. on AI infrastructure, a reported $12.9 billion deal to acquire Hugging Face and another investment in Perplexity. John Furrier of theCUBE Research said the AI build-out phase has moved to "execution and control," with "tokens equal profit," and that the story is bigger than GPUs, with AI factories, networking, inference, agents, robotics, software economics, security and political backlash all converging. On theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante analyzed Nvidia's role in the AI ecosystem, the impact of Anthropic PBC's Claude Mythos on cybersecurity, and why fears of a "SaaSpocalypse" have been overblown. The Cisco partnership combines Nvidia's accelerated computing and Spectrum-X architecture with Cisco networking and enterprise operations to build rack-scale AI factories. Vellante said it creates a bridge from general-purpose enterprise IT infrastructure, which holds trillions of dollars in installed value, to accelerated computing and CUDA, making Cisco "exceedingly relevant again." The deal reflects a shift from networking that connects computers to networking that creates the computer by orchestrating thousands of GPUs. Furrier said it is evidence that rack-scale AI is moving toward enterprises, which can plug into sovereign clouds and neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nscale, or into Amazon. He predicted distributed computing, including data centers in hospitals with smaller racks of around 30 kilowatts. On software, Salesforce Inc. crushed earnings expectations and its stock rose almost 23% Thursday. Furrier said the simplistic SaaSpocalypse narrative is dead: infrastructure demand remains extraordinary, and incumbent software firms are showing AI can expand rather than destroy their business, though bad software will die and software must become AI native. Frontier model vendors need data that software companies can provide, and both analysts described a "system of intelligence" organizing the emerging AI enterprise. Vellante expects frontier models to acquire or partner with companies like Salesforce, possibly through a "Trojan horse strategy" aimed at taking their alpha, though he noted Benioff and Ellison are "no fools." He sees this as a first step toward simplification of AI. In security, Anthropic's Claude Mythos sent shock waves through security operations by showing how quickly advanced AI can find and exploit vulnerabilities. That created a tailwind for CrowdStrike Holdings Inc., which delivered $333 million in net new ARR, $45 million above the high end of guidance. Vellante said theCUBE had predicted CrowdStrike would hold and gain territory, helped by its Falcon Flex push for new logos and by the timing of the Microsoft event, which aided firms consolidating security vendors. He cited data from Qualitate supporting the view of Mythos as an inflection point. Furrier called Mythos a "ChatGPT moment" for security and "a call to arms," saying cybersecurity is less healthy than assumed because cracking one spot gives access, and agents, "like drones everywhere," could go off the rails.

Sony & Warner Sue Anthropic in Latest AI Music Lawsuit: ‘Illegally Harvested to Fuel Claude’ In the newest case over AI music training, the two music giants claim Claude was "built on copyright theft," ranging from iconic Christmas songs to Taylor Swift hits. The publishing units of Sony Music and Warner Music Group have filed a new copyright lawsuit against Anthropic, claiming the artificial intelligence giant “illegally harvested” more than 20,000 of their songs to train its models. The case, which follows a similar lawsuit by Universal Music Group, BMG and Round Hill, claims Anthropic stole thousands of songs to “fuel Claude,” including “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Mariah Carey‘s “All I Want for Christmas is You,” and Taylor Swift’s “Paper Rings.” “[Publishers] bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history,” lawyers Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music write in a Friday (Aug. 28) complaint obtained by Billboard. The new action comes after similar music lawsuits against Anthropic, an AI behemoth targeting a $2 trillion valuation — first by Universal Music Group and Concord, then more recently by BMG and by Round Hill Music. Major music firms have also brought such litigation against Suno, the leading music-specific AI firm. In the new case, attorneys for Sony and Warner’s publishing units say they “recognize the potential of ethical AI technology,” but that “even the most revolutionary of technologies must develop within the bounds of the law, and Anthropic’s Claude models are no different.” “These acts… inflict immense harm on music publishers and the songwriters they proudly represent,” the music companies write. The lawsuit also names Anthropic founder and CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann as defendants. In a statement to Billboard, a spokesperson for Anthropic said: “This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts. Training generative AI models is a transformative fair use — as the court held in [a previous case] — and we will defend ourselves robustly.” AI firms feed millions of works into models to “train” them to create new ones. Dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country over that process, claiming it infringes copyrights en masse. AI companies say training is instead a legal form of copyright “fair use” that fuels innovation. That crucial argument is largely undecided, with billions in damages and licenses hanging in the balance. Like other recent AI cases, Friday’s lawsuit claims Anthropic not only infringed copyrights by using the songs, but also in how it acquired them in the first place. That’s become a crucial element of such cases after a judge ruled last year that even if AI training is legal, using pirated materials to do it is not. “In blatant violation of copyright law, defendants have unlawfully acquired troves of music publishers’ musical compositions,” Sony and Warner write, citing a “brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale.” In that earlier case, Anthropic ended up paying a whopping $1.5 billion settlement after the judge’s piracy ruling. Sony and Warner cited that case as evidence of Anthropic’s wrongdoing — and said more legal action was clearly still needed. “Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” the music companies write. “And $1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering $2-trillion-dollar valuation.”

Once hailed by politicians in both parties as economic engines and job-producing boons, Democratic candidates and increasingly more Republicans have turned sharply against the facilities in their messaging as the public backlash intensifies over their enormous size, staggering energy consumption, noise and lack of direct benefits to the surrounding neighborhoods. Trump’s outspoken backing of data centers is at odds with several Republicans on the midterm campaign trail including Texas Senate Republican nominee Ken Paxton, who endorsed Gov. Greg Abbott’s moratorium on new data centers, and Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee of governor in Wisconsin, who has attacked his Democratic opponent, David Crowley, over data centers. Data centers, which house networks and services for digital information and services, are proving to be the rare issue that cuts through party lines. A Gallup poll conducted in March found 71% of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their areas ‒ including 75% of Democratic voters, 63% of Republican voters and 74% of independents. Yet Trump, who is aligned politically with several tech industry CEOs, has remained a booster of data centers in the face of widespread opposition, arguing the facilities are critical for the United States to compete with China in AI innovation. Trump has called Abbott’s freeze on data centers in Texas “a mistake.” To address one concern of critics, Trump has said he wants data centers to build their own dedicated power stations, which is part of a Ratepayer Protection Pledge that several tech companies and governors signed after the president introduced it this year. However, the industry-friendly pledge is not binding and does not mandate any actions.

Instagram is revising its artificial intelligence transparency labels for accounts to better align with user expectations around AI disclosures. The change is designed to ensure that people know when they’re engaging with non-human entities in the app. In order to address potential confusion, Instagram is renaming its “AI creator” account labels, which were added in May, to “AI generated profile” labels instead. The update will also include a description noting that the images posted by the account may feature AI-generated characters. That will make it easier for IG users to see whether a profile is run by a human, or is just posting AI-generated content. As explained by Instagram: “As generative AI becomes a bigger part of how people create, we’ve heard that people don’t like seeing a profile that seems human, only to find out later that the person featured is AI-generated. They want to know when a profile features an AI-generated person.” In other words, Instagram wants to ensure that fewer people are being duped by AI-generated characters in the app. In addition, Instagram said that it will limit the reach of profiles that feature an AI-generated person but do not add this label. The update reflects a growing backlash against AI-generated content and the intrusion of AI bots. This has always seemed likely to be a problem, since a key trait of social media is the social element. Social platforms were built on enabling people to share their thoughts and ideas with other actual humans, and were not designed as a place to review the latest outputs from machines. In some ways, AI tools are redefining the concept of what social actually means in this sense, since more people are now socializing with AI bots. But on social media platforms at least, there has been significant pushback against the influx of AI bots. The fact that Meta has had to take a step back on this front may also be a blow for the company’s larger AI push. In late 2024, reports emerged that Meta was planning to unleash a range of AI bot personas in its apps, which would interact and engage as if they were human-run accounts. That concept was designed to drive more human activity in its apps, with the idea being that people would get more replies to their posts and more post likes, and would subsequently feel like they were being seen and heard more. Meta didn’t share additional information on this plan, but it doesn’t appear that the company moved ahead with it, amid broader criticism of AI content and profiles on other apps. That leads to this update. Meta is now looking to tag AI-generated accounts more clearly and reduce the reach of AI bot profiles that don’t disclose themselves as such. It seems like a positive step, which should provide more clarity around AI-generated content, while also giving users more insight into who and what they’re engaging with.

The author runs a bare-metal Debian homelab on a repurposed 8-year-old Dell Latitude 7480 (Core i5-6300U, 2 cores/4 threads, 12GB RAM, 256GB storage). Starting with Portainer and Jellyfin, it has grown to more than 20 stacks, none with explicit CPU or RAM limits. The server never crashed, but it felt sluggish from time to time, with unpredictable morning resource spikes. The hardware wasn't the issue: 12GB is enough for the actual workload, but there is not enough guaranteed headroom when workloads overlap. Five stacks (Omada, Pulse, Jellyfin, Immich and Stirling) alone consumed more than 5GB of memory, and each treated the full 12GB as its own, grabbing whatever was available under load. Before upgrading hardware, the author decided to experiment with container limits. The hard part was that publishers state minimum requirements but no upper limits. Jellyfin idles at around 800 MB of memory and about 0.02% CPU, but with a couple of streams and one or two transcoding sessions on the integrated GPU (there is no dedicated GPU), its CPU can peak at 100% and its RAM can climb to a couple of GB, disrupting other services for minutes. CPU and memory limits behave differently: a container hitting its memory ceiling is OOM-killed, while one hitting a CPU ceiling is throttled. Lacking perfect numbers, the author used Beszel to review a week of actual usage, deciding which containers needed limits and which were already stable. Steady services like AdGuard Home, NetAlertX and Ntfy got about 20% extra headroom, and job-based workloads like Jellyfin and Stirling PDF got about 50%. These figures come from practical experience, not Docker documentation, and depend on hardware and workload. Portainer and Postgres were left unlimited, because limiting them, especially a database's memory, could cause failures such as during a write operation. The aim was to trade peak performance for reliability: downloads, transcodes and machine learning jobs can wait, but DNS queries, database writes and management services need room. After a week there were no dramatic benchmark gains, but the unusual spikes disappeared and the graphs became flat and, in the author's view, pleasantly boring. Peak loads from qBittorrent, Jellyfin or Immich Machine Learning now hit their ceilings and wait instead of taking other containers' resources, so jobs take longer but this is an acceptable trade-off. Some containers needed more than limits: Stirling PDF failed with a 1024 MB memory limit, so the author switched from the full image to the ultra-lite version, which was sufficient anyway. The author stresses that limits are not equivalent to new hardware and won't fix broken containers, bad network configuration or database issues; they only stop one container from overloading shared resources. The server needed a boundary, not a redesign or expensive upgrade, and reliability means preventing a couple of services from deciding the server's fate.

China laid out conditions for artificial intelligence talks with the U.S., striking a strident tone ahead of a much-anticipated meeting while accusing American AI company Anthropic PBC of bad behavior. A Sunday post on Yuyuantantian, a social media account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, said the US must prove its AI companies are subject to the same safety, disclosure and audit rules before any “substantive” discussions with China can take place. “A clear distinction must be drawn between genuine security threats and mere technological competition,” said the post, published by an account frequently used to signal official policy thinking. “This line must be drawn jointly by all participating parties,” it added. Officials from the U.S. and China are expected to hold talks on AI before Xi Jinping’s state visit to the U.S. on Sept. 24 for a summit with Donald Trump. No date has been announced for that AI dialogue and Chinese officials last month were still seeking clarity on the agenda, in part to decide who to send, Bloomberg previously reported. Tensions are mounting around the AI race between the world’s biggest economies. Underscoring that point, Yuyuantantian singled out Anthropic’s Claude for criticism, accusing that model of overstepping user data boundaries, engaging in covert monitoring and transmitting website domains without authorization. “The problem is that America’s own frontier models have already developed in a distorted direction,” Yuyuantantian’s post said. “This means the negotiation is not simply a technical dialogue from the start, but a continuation of all the earlier problems: the US is trying to turn the ‘safety boundaries’ it has drawn into the default rules for the entire world.” The U.S. government should be guarding security boundaries around AI, yet it has “repeatedly retreated” from doing so, according to the post titled “Anthropic Has Contracted the American Disease.” Anthropic and the U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside U.S. office hours. The Yuyuantantian post said the US approach to AI reflects a broader effort to contain China’s technological rise. “The ‘control’ proposed by the US is, in essence, an attempt to make China accept an order partly defined by American companies,” it added. Chinese officials are growing anxious that Anthropic’s Mythos could be wielded against their country, Bloomberg previously reported. They see the potential for models like Mythos to be used as an offensive weapon, and question why Anthropic is denying China access to the systems for normal purposes, people familiar said. Anthropic blocked its services from Chinese-controlled companies last year, citing US national security concerns. But that does not seem to have effectively stopped Chinese companies from using its products. The firm, along with OpenAI and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, has expressed concern about its models being used in China. Anthropic has also accused Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. of “illicitly” accessing Claude using thousands of fraudulent accounts, an allegation the Chinese tech giant has not responded to.

Crypto.com-promoted Tectonic forces Cronos to halt, rewind. The Crypto.com-supported Cronos blockchain had to halt and rewind its history this week to stop an ongoing theft due to the Tectonic protocol that Crypto.com had spent months promoting. Tectonic warned users to pause using its protocol altogether. PeckShield first estimated the value of compromised funds at approximately $74 million. Crypto.com supplied one of the largest retail onramps for Tectonic, this newly compromised protocol that nearly drained tens of millions of dollars from Cronos’ DeFi ecosystem. As fear about the hack has spread, Cronos’ CRO token has lost 6% of its value over the past 24 hours. Kris Marszalek’s Crypto.com exchange proudly offered TONIC purchases through more than 20 fiat currencies. Crypto.com advertised TONIC-denominated Visa card spending at 80 million merchants. It listed TONIC for trading on its main exchange, advertised staking returns of up to 100% per annum, and promoted staking rewards within its Crypto.com DeFi Wallet. Crypto.com’s Earn program guide provided step-by-step instructions for TONIC staking, including mentioning its ‘automatic compounding’ of ‘earnings.’ Crypto.com’s DeFi Wallet even simplified TONIC staking with one-click access with no lock-up periods. Tectonic’s oracle page lists only two data sources for the USD price of TONIC, VVS Finance and — you guessed it — Crypto.com. Crypto.com’s Cronos blockchain halts, erases history. After Tectonic suffered an exploit on Sunday, the Crypto.com-supported Cronos blockchain stopped producing blocks. Validators erased some of the blockchain’s history by reverting to the pre-exploit state and then resuming block production. Tectonic’s litepaper talked up its connections to Crypto.com and identified Particle B as its incubator, which was renamed Cronos Labs. Crypto.com’s $500 million investment arm is a “strategic partner to Cronos Labs.” Researcher Weilin Li described the TONIC exploit as a Mango Markets-style price manipulation hack that allowed the thief to withdraw real collateral from DeFi lending protocols using an artificially inflated price of TONIC. Although Crypto.com’s Cronos EVM blockchain describes itself as ‘permissionless,’ its official FAQ says its 33 validators serve by invitation only. Applications to become a validator are also closed. Total value locked (TVL) on Cronos DeFi protocols has fallen 92% since 2022. This controversy is certainly not the first in Crypto.com history. In 2021, Cronos ‘permanently’ burned 70 billion CRO tokens to boost scarcity and hype the price of its token. However, in March 2025 it pushed through a community vote — using its own majority validator control and despite heavy opposition — to re-mint those 70 billion tokens into a ‘Cronos Strategic Reserve’ that restored supply to 100 billion as a de facto benefit to Crypto.com. Crypto.com effectively controlled the Cronos Strategic Reserve in practice, because the exchange and its affiliated validators held majority power governing the Cronos chain, which administered the reserve’s terms.
