Anthropic Locks In $35 Billion in AI Computing. Nvidia Backs the Massive Cloud Expansion. It is the latest deal Anthropic has made as part of its new financing model designed to help AI cloud companies acquire its infrastructure. Anthropic has signed a $35 billion cloud-computing agreement with Nvidia-backed Lambda, another massive infrastructure commitment as the maker of Claude races to secure enough computing power to compete at the frontier of artificial intelligence. The deal centers on a data center under development in Nueces County, Texas, and places Nvidia in an unusually prominent role across several layers of the transaction, according to an exclusive report from The Wall Street Journal. Nvidia will provide the chips powering the facility while also holding the lease on the underlying data center. Lambda, an AI cloud provider in which Nvidia is an investor, will provide the computing capacity to Anthropic. The Texas project is being developed by Hut 8, a company that expanded from cryptocurrency mining into high-performance computing and AI infrastructure. Reuters independently confirmed the $35 billion agreement, citing a person familiar with the transaction. The project represents roughly 350 megawatts of capacity. Nvidia launched a financing model earlier this year designed to help AI cloud companies acquire its infrastructure. Under the program, the company can provide credit support while receiving both revenue from hardware sales and a share of revenue generated by cloud capacity. The company said the structure was intended to make it easier for emerging AI providers to finance expensive data centers and computing systems. That strategy has attracted growing attention from investors because Nvidia can appear on several sides of the same AI infrastructure transaction. The Anthropic agreement illustrates those increasingly interconnected relationships. Anthropic is backed by Nvidia, Lambda is backed by Nvidia, the computing infrastructure will use Nvidia hardware, and Nvidia will hold the Texas data-center lease. The structure comes as Nvidia's financial involvement in AI infrastructure continues to expand. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the chipmaker had paused some revenue-sharing arrangements with AI cloud companies after employees raised concerns about potential regulatory scrutiny. Nvidia disclosed $36 billion in commitments under agreements that typically run for six years, according to the Journal. For Anthropic, however, the Lambda agreement is part of a much broader effort to diversify the enormous amount of computing infrastructure required to train and operate Claude. The company already relies on Amazon's Trainium chips, Google's TPUs and Nvidia GPUs. In April, Anthropic announced an expanded agreement with Google and Broadcom for multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity beginning in 2027. At the time, Anthropic said its annualized revenue had surpassed $30 billion, up from about $9 billion at the end of 2025. Anthropic has also disclosed agreements for up to 5 gigawatts of capacity with Amazon, $30 billion of Azure capacity through a partnership with Microsoft and Nvidia, more than 300 megawatts from SpaceX, and a $50 billion U.S. infrastructure initiative with Fluidstack.

Proton Drive offers encrypted cloud storage through Proton’s services, and the 200GB Plus plan includes full end-to-end encryption for every item stored in the service. In order to encrypt files, user devices scramble their data before it reaches servers at Proton. No one at Proton has access to the data stored in these files, including anyone who might break into Proton’s servers, so the data stays protected from unauthorized access. Proton Drive also offers secure document and file sharing, a secure way to store photos in an album format, and access to Proton Docs and Proton Sheets to create new documents or edit existing ones while maintaining the same level of security. Apps are available for Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, and the web, and all versions include desktop syncing to ensure the most recent version of your work is accessible on whichever platform you’re using. Head over to Proton to get Proton Drive Plus and its 200GB of encrypted storage for $1 for your first month, or take 40% off if you’d rather pay for a year up front. An affordable alternative to Google Drive that can encrypt your content. Most cloud providers encrypt your files, meaning the files are locked while they reside on their servers, but the provider holds the key. This way, the provider can scan your images, search your documents, and provide access to someone upon request. End-to-end encryption works differently, since the encryption occurs on your device and the key is never transmitted off of it. When you upload files to Proton’s servers, Proton can’t view them. The difference between end-to-end encryption and cloud-based encryption means many items individuals didn’t consider until now will become apparent. Your passport scans, tax returns, medical records, and family photographs are uploaded to cloud-based systems and have previously been used for both AI training and targeted advertising by various companies. According to Proton, these files belong to you, and end-to-end encryption supports that claim rather than a policy that may change in the future. When sharing photos via albums, you can limit the album to certain individuals. Instead of sending a batch of vacation photos to an entire family list, only the intended recipients will receive them, and likewise, only the intended recipient will be able to open an encrypted link you send. Proton Docs and Proton Sheets are designed to work together. Documents and spreadsheets can be created and edited in real time, and none of that activity leaves an encrypted environment. With most privacy-first storage options, you have to export a file to edit it elsewhere. Proton was started in 2014 by scientists who met at CERN; it’s based in Switzerland and owned by a non-profit foundation rather than shareholders seeking ad revenue. That structure is why privacy is the default setting instead of an upgrade. For $1, you get 200GB of Proton Drive Plus for the first month, and the 40% discount applies if you commit to a year instead.

The Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ) is updating its Code of Ethics, a document of less than a thousand words that often hangs on newsroom bulletin boards. Dan Axelrod, chairman of the SPJ Ethics Committee and a former longtime Gannett business reporter, argues the code is a way to protect democracy and society. The revision, the first in 12 years and only the sixth in the code's century-long history, takes about a year of meetings and feedback. The committee and other media ethics experts met in Indianapolis in June after many virtual meetings. "Passions definitely got heated," Axelrod says, though committee vice chairman Chris Roberts, a University of Alabama journalism professor, noted there were no fistfights. The resulting draft is 967 words, 73 longer than the existing code. The main reasons for updating are the rapid rise of AI, which can save news organizations money but cause trouble if misused, and the growth of independent "creator journalists" who the SPJ believes should also have a guide. The code is voluntary and not enforceable. Another goal is to address declining public trust in the media, politicians who attack journalism, and the changed economics of the field, in which a third of journalists no longer work for a traditional news organization. The SPJ, founded in 1909 with some 4,000 members, adopted its first code in 1926, formed an ethics committee in 1948, and last revised the code in 2014. Its four principles remain unchanged: "Seek Truth and Report It," "Minimize Harm," "Act Independently," and "Be Accountable and Transparent." An accompanying report notes that traditional newsroom jobs are dwindling while citizen journalists, freelancers, online influencers and pundits grow. It cites a Pew study showing a third of journalists were freelance or self-employed in 2023. It also cites fewer watchdog news outlets and investors without journalism backgrounds buying news properties and pushing personal agendas. A new line states that speed, technology or medium do not excuse inaccuracy or unfairness, and that journalists are ethically responsible for their work regardless of tools used. The draft does not name AI, so it stays relevant as technology changes. It also addresses verification, misinformation, crime reporting and fabricated images. A notable change replaces "Give voice to the voiceless," seen as problematic for implying some groups lack a voice, with: "Be vigilant and courageous about holding those with power accountable. Counter the unfair marginalization of those with less power." Committee member Eric Deggans, NPR's critic-at-large and a Washington and Lee University media ethics professor, says the problem is that mainstream outlets often ignore or don't know about such voices. The broader membership will vote on the draft in October after a feedback period. SPJ President Chris Vaccaro is confident the code, translated into multiple languages, will be widely followed despite industry change. Deggans, who teaches the code, says it also guides journalists in countries without a long free-press history, and wishes more working journalists and outlet owners would read it, since owners often pressure employees toward unethical practices.

The author was thrilled when the Raspberry Pi 5 launched, since it offered a better CPU and GPU than the RPi 4, an onboard power connector, and a PCIe 2.0 slot. In 2023, before x86 mini-PCs became pricey and RAM costs surged, it was a fantastic device; the money saved by running free, open-source alternatives to subscription platforms repaid the purchase price within a year. But with its price now at obnoxious levels, the author can no longer recommend it. Initially the author used the Pi 5 as a Docker-powered self-hosting workstation, starting with CasaOS on the GUI version of Raspberry Pi OS and later a CLI-only setup that handled over a dozen services easily. They ran NextcloudPi with Collabora Office, Notes, Tasks, and Deck as a Microsoft 365 alternative that stayed fast with hundreds of documents. They skipped heavy media servers like Jellyfin, partly because of storage concerns and partly because the Pi 5 lacks a hardware H.264 (AVC) decoder. Lightweight services included Paperless-ngx for bills, receipts, and tax documents; TriliumNotes as a knowledge base; Vikunja replacing Todoist's paid plans; Shiori for bookmarks; Vaultwarden for passwords; and Firefly III for finances. Stirling-PDF served as a PDF tool before the author felt it became "enshittified"; they now use BentoPDF. They also swapped the USB SSD for microSD cards to try other distributions and packages. After moving to a refurbished Xeon home lab, the author shifted these services to a Proxmox node, but the Pi 5 remains part of the lab. Last year it served as a QDevice keeping a 2-node ZFS replication cluster online if one system failed. It also hosts Pulse, Gotify, Nginx Proxy Manager, and other admin utilities not suited to an experimental server. Today it runs a Frigate container with an AI HAT to monitor security cameras and trigger Home Assistant automations, and a spare microSD card holds a llama.cpp instance for LLM experiments. Still, the author wouldn't buy it again in 2026 if it broke. The Pi has become so expensive that it is only worth it for projects needing GPIO, and even then cheaper microcontrollers fit better. For reading a BME280 temperature sensor, a dirt-cheap ESP32 flashed via ESPHome Device Builder beats spending minutes installing packages on a Pi. An $8-9 ESP32 or a $10-12 Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W makes more sense for circuitry projects than nearly $200 for a Pi 5 plus microSD card, cables, adapters, an active cooler, and other accessories. For tasks needing more power and better compatibility with server platforms, thin clients and old mini-PCs often cost less than a new Pi 5 and suit budget home labs. If buying a Raspberry Pi SBC, the author would pick the Zero, whose first-gen model is the only one that doesn't cost a fortune.

Winery direct-to-consumer software company vinSuite has hired Steven Thomas vice president of research, development and artificial intelligence, putting him in charge of product engineering and the company’s effort to integrate artificial intelligence into its platform. The Napa-based company said Thomas will focus on practical tools aimed at challenges facing wineries, including identifying wine club members who may cancel, improving follow-up with tasting room visitors and giving small teams more insight into direct-to-consumer operations. “Our job is to make the tools behind that work quietly and well, and to be careful and honest about how we bring AI into them,” vinSuite President Jimmy Wu said in the Aug. 12 announcement. Thomas previously served as a chief technology officer in financial technology, industrial internet-of-things and telecommunications businesses. His experience includes banking, payments, e-commerce, artificial intelligence and machine learning. He also is a founding partner of consulting firm The Forge and holds a computer science degree from Western University. VinSuite said the appointment reflects continued investment in a platform used by hundreds of wineries. The company’s software combines wine club management, e-commerce, TabletPOS point-of-sale services and vinSIGHT reporting. Thomas said his focus will be using technology to help wineries strengthen customer relationships and grow direct-to-consumer sales. Jeff Quackenbush joined North Bay Business Journal in May 1999. South Carolina is moving quickly to teach people how to use artificial intelligence. Employers now need to make sure those newly acquired skills still have an entry-level workplace in which to mature. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Canaries Dashboard shows weaker early career employment trends in occupations where AI use leans toward automation rather than augmentation. The researchers correctly treat those patterns as descriptive rather than proof that AI alone caused the change, but the mechanism should concern any state trying to build a more advanced workforce: Companies can automate beginner tasks faster than they redesign the developmental role of beginner jobs. South Carolina already has pieces of the solution. The University of South Carolina's Provost Undergraduate AI Fellowship gives upper-level students paid AI training and work experience while they partner with faculty mentors on real projects. Students are not merely learning how to prompt a tool; they are using AI inside supervised work where someone experienced can challenge their assumptions and improve their judgment. The state also has an established apprenticeship infrastructure. Apprenticeship Carolina partners with South Carolina's technical colleges and employers to create paid training opportunities, including in information technology, and its model emphasizes on-the-job learning and a skilled talent pipeline. That same logic belongs in AI-exposed professional jobs. A South Carolina employer could make a new analyst responsible for using AI to produce a first-pass operational assessment, then require that employee to test the data, identify what the model missed and explain the recommendation to a manager. A junior marketer could generate more options in less time while learning which claims fit customers and which create reputational risk. A beginning programmer could use AI-generated code while being evaluated on security, reliability and maintainability. The point is not to preserve obsolete busywork. If AI can perform a routine task in minutes, employers should capture that productivity. They should then use the time saved to expose junior workers to harder problems, more customer context and more experienced judgment. Simply eliminating junior jobs creates a long-term contradiction. Companies want experienced employees precisely because experience provides tacit knowledge, pattern recognition, and judgment. Yet the normal way to produce experienced employees is to hire people before they have much experience and let them learn under supervision. AI changes the tasks in that process. It does not eliminate the need for the process itself. S.C. employers can use AI to make every junior hire more productive, expose young employees to more complex assignments sooner, and make mentorship more intentional. The state already understands paid learning through apprenticeship, and USC is showing what supervised AI work can look like. South Carolina should keep expanding AI education. But a workforce strategy cannot stop at teaching people how to use the technology. Someone still has to give them a first chance to use it at work. Gleb Tsipursky is a behavioral scientist, CEO of Disaster Avoidance Experts and author of “The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results.”

President Donald Trump's continued support for AI data centers is putting him at odds with voters who don't want them built nearby, creating a political bind for Republicans who back him but are trying to distance themselves from the industry ahead of this year's midterms. Recent polling finds more than 70% of Americans oppose a data center being built near them, and local backlash has grown as plans for new facilities have expanded. Trump wrote on Truth Social that the only reason communities would not want data centers is "if they want to end up being backwards and poor," adding that those wanting to be "successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place" should "let Data Reign." The backlash cuts across partisan, generational and urban vs. rural lines. Chris Devine, an associate professor of political science at the University of Dayton, said Trump's provocative and dismissive tone costs the chance to convey nuance, since people will hear that their concerns are not valid. The tension is already visible in competitive races. In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted has been criticized so heavily over data centers by his Democratic opponent that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned they are an "anchor hanging around Husted's neck." In Michigan, former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican running for an open Senate seat, backed a one-year moratorium on new construction while facing attacks from Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Trump has embraced AI and moved to cut or block regulations that could inhibit its growth, arguing the economic benefits are crucial to America's future and that slowing construction would give China an advantage in AI development. Beating China has bipartisan support in Washington but is less of a priority for voters facing the consequences locally. The White House has tried to ease concerns about electricity costs and land use through agreements with tech companies, which have agreed to a pledge to limit AI-induced price hikes, but these efforts have not appeased critics. The data center build-out ties together several election themes: worries about higher electric bills add to cost-of-living frustrations, workers fear AI-driven job losses, and tax incentives offered by state and local governments to attract profitable tech companies face growing scrutiny. Democrats have tried to capitalize, tying data centers to the president's backing of the industry, cost-of-living anger and higher energy prices from the war with Iran. However, opposition has not broken cleanly along party lines. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is comfortably ahead in polling for reelection and is a potential 2028 presidential candidate, has backed away from his earlier support for data centers amid public backlash and attacks from his opponent. The bipartisan backlash leaves both parties without clear positions on AI or data centers. The issue is expected to linger for years as companies keep investing heavily in expansion. Devine noted that while many issues have a clear red-blue divide, this one is new, and impressions of the parties, candidates and officials are still being formed.

New York City’s public school system is set to release a policy for this coming school year on artificial intelligence — which will include a ban on the use of generative AI for students in 2-K through 8th grade, the Daily News has learned. The new rules mean that no children in preschool, elementary school, and middle school should have access to education software that uses student-facing AI, including instructional programs and AI tutors. The prohibition covers nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy also bans individual devices in the classroom for preschool and the earlier grades of elementary school. It wasn’t immediately clear how the new policy would be enforced. The city’s Department of Education did not immediately return a request for comment. “Younger students need hands-on learning, social interaction, play and teacher-guided instruction. Routine individual screen use can crowd out those experiences,” read official New York City Public School slides shared in a series of briefings on Tuesday afternoon obtained by The News. “By contrast, high school students need guided preparation for a world and economy increasingly driven by AI and new technologies — paired with instruction on how AI works, its biases and risks, and how to evaluate its outputs.” The school system also plans to bring together teachers, parents, elected officials and unions for a coalition that “will help us shape our policy for 2027-2028 and beyond,” the slides said. The meetings are expected to begin later this month after members are confirmed. In high school, the use of AI in classrooms will be “restricted,” according to the slides. The new technology may be used in a limited way, including for AI literacy, career and certification programs, and five approved pilot programs in select schools. “All use must be coupled with teacher supervision… and the necessity for students to retain ownership of their thinking and work,” the slides added. “Pilot tools will not replace teachers.” The AI policy is coming months late as intense pressure from parents and teachers forced the school system to delay its timeline. But the final rules are set to go even further, governing not only generative AI but also screen time, particularly in the younger grades. According to the slides, the school system will prohibit one-to-one screen time for 2-K through 2nd grade. Education officials also recommended no more than 30 minutes of individual device-use by students in the 3rd through 5th grade, and 45 minutes for 6th through 8th grade. Screen time in high school may vary across schools and subject matter. The policy contains exemptions for assistive technology used by students with disabilities or learning English as a new language; short assessments and diagnostic tests; remote learning days; and some instructional programs approved by the school system, such as e-books, robotics, coding and simulations, the slides said. Education officials released a first draft in March, with a final policy due a few months later in June. But the plan prompted fierce backlash over a lack of guardrails for children’s use of AI. The draft largely focused on how teachers and principals should approach AI, but glossed over how to stop students from offloading their critical thinking skills and creativity to the new technology. Parents descended on monthly school board meetings and protested outside City Hall. An online petition that called for a two-year moratorium on AI in schools received more than 6,000 signatures. The City Council took heed, and a majority of members signed onto a letter in support of an immediate pause. During a high-profile Council hearing, school officials conceded they were going to miss their own deadline, but promised to issue a final policy before the first day of school. Meanwhile, principals were told to pause new education technology purchases as the school system hashed out the much-delayed guidance. Backlash grew this summer after an upstate New York school district purchased an AI-powered robot — giving ammunition to parents and unions’ worst fears that the new technology could replace teachers. A plan to deploy the robot in the classroom is now on pause.

AI’s overnight millionaires create absurd mansion shortage in San Francisco. San Francisco’s artificial intelligence boom has created a new class of tech millionaires so quickly that the city is now facing an unlikely problem — a shortage of mansions. Wealthy AI execs and workers are entering the city’s cutthroat housing market, driving bidding wars, record sales and sky-high prices as companies expand their local workforces. The frenzy comes as companies like OpenAI and Anthropic prepare to go public, a process that has unleashed a wave of new wealth with more to come, according to NPR. At the top of the market, buyers making all-cash offers of $25 million or more have still been outbid for coveted properties. The mix of newly wealthy buyers and a limited supply of single-family homes has become so extreme that real estate brokerage Compass and others call it a “mansion shortage.” The median San Francisco home sale price has jumped 25% from a year ago, according to Compass data cited by NPR. In June, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million above their asking prices, Compass chief economist Mike Simonsen told the outlet. Competition is intense even for less expensive homes. Part of the buying spree comes from a generation of AI executives who are now looking for larger homes. Many are in their mid-30s or early 40s with young children, creating urgency to secure homes in desirable neighborhoods near schools, according to Simonsen. So far, some of the most dramatic price increases have been concentrated in San Francisco’s wealthier enclaves. The rise in AI wealth is also making it harder for people who aren’t looking for mansions. San Francisco renters are facing bidding wars as well-paid tech workers in their 20s move in, some able to spend up to $10,000 a month. Listings get a lot of attention within hours, and renters say that bids often go hundreds of dollars above the listed price. California's top news, sports and entertainment delivered to your inbox every day. Thanks for signing up! For people who don’t work in tech, the sudden jump in housing costs is making an already expensive city even harder to afford. Alex Brenner, 29, who works in healthcare, said he and his fiancée encountered lines of prospective tenants at open houses and saw the rent on one apartment rise twice by $500 before they even viewed it. “It’s actually ridiculous,” Brenner told NPR. Market analyst Jonathan Miller explained that San Francisco is increasingly undergoing a “New York-ification” of its real estate market. The prices no longer reflect just the property itself but also the premium buyers are willing to pay to be at the center of a powerful economic hub, he told NPR. “It’s like buying a one-bedroom apartment without great views in Manhattan and it costs you $3 million, and you tell that to somebody in Des Moines, Iowa, and they’re like, ‘There’s something wrong with you,'” Miller said. Three blockchain networks halted block production within four days, each using different emergency powers. Only Cronos also replaced part of its canonical history. Cronos said validators halted the network by consensus after an exploit affected Tectonic, restored chain state to before the incident, and resumed production from block 90,896,189 as of 23:49:01 UTC on Aug. 30. Post-checkpoint activity, including any unrelated transactions, no longer belongs to the canonical chain. The restart notice gives no transaction inventory, validator tally or voting threshold. TRM Labs estimated roughly $75 million was borrowed after TONIC's price was manipulated, with about $6 million reaching Ethereum and around $68.7 million reversed on Cronos; Bitquery reported about $8.3 million on Ethereum and 10,961 discarded blocks. Tectonic's final loss is pending, and a Cronos restore cannot reach state on Ethereum. Tectonic said it would reopen withdrawals and loan repayments first while keeping deposits and new borrowing paused, leaving suppliers' full redemption unconfirmed. Cronos warned that protocols, bridges, explorers and RPC providers would recover more slowly. Ontology suspended block production after its core development team found a potential security concern during a daily check, before confirming any attack. Its Sept. 1 update said review identified malicious attack activity, that the mainnet would stay paused for remediation and an upgrade, and that user assets were not compromised. It aimed to restore normal operations within 24 hours, subject to security checks, remediation, upgrade work and testing. The halt left accepted state intact and named no restore point. The binding decision-maker, emergency threshold and resumption authority remain undisclosed. Users face operational delay, not a confirmed asset loss or rollback. ICON's case shows a halt arriving too late. According to the Foundation's postmortem, an attacker replayed two previously valid signed withdrawal messages 1,492 times between 02:01:02 and 02:21:12 UTC on Aug. 27. A precision defect let 1,490 calls succeed, releasing 119,866,000 ICX and 531,600 bnUSD from Foundation-held assets. Monitoring alerted at 02:08 UTC, but the alert's severity did not page the on-call team because similar alerts had often accompanied unrelated RPC problems. Investigation opened around 03:40, the contract was paused at 03:53, exchanges began suspending ICX deposits and withdrawals at 05:54, and the network halt took effect at 06:18:54. ICON restarted around 07:51 on Aug. 28 with a fix. By then exchanges had swept most affected ICX into their custody, beyond ICON's chain-side controls, so the Foundation relied on exchange freezes, preservation notices, lawyers and law enforcement. ICON said no user deposits, balances or positions were accessed. It recovered 531,600 bnUSD and 1.366 million SODA in full, plus 82,430 of 113,634 borrowed USDC. Confirmed net loss was approximately 150.2 ETH plus 31,204 USDC, with most affected ICX frozen or traced at exchanges. The Foundation controlled the network during token migration, with consensus in maintenance mode on seven core nodes. Each halt placed risk differently: Cronos replaced canonical state, Ontology shifted risk into time and availability, and ICON's loss stayed with the Foundation. Cronos and Tectonic still owe postmortems, and Ontology must disclose attack details, emergency authorization and whether its resumption criteria were met.

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said Tuesday that AI is forcing companies to overhaul roughly $1 trillion of aging cybersecurity infrastructure built for a pre-AI world. "Nothing that was deployed seven or 10 years ago is prepared or ready to handle AI at machine speed," Arora told CNBC's Jim Cramer on "Mad Money." "You have to rethink your cyber architecture." Palo Alto's earnings report on Tuesday suggests that urgency is already translating into business. The company beat fiscal fourth quarter estimates and issued a strong outlook for its new fiscal year. Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by the CNBC Investing Club, owns Palo Alto and cyber peer CrowdStrike. Arora expects the opportunity to grow as AI allows attackers to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than ever before, forcing companies to modernize security defenses that weren't designed for automated threats. "You cannot deploy AI successfully if you don't get cybersecurity right," he said. "There's approximately $1 trillion of global cybersecurity debt that must be modernized to defend against automated threats because they operate instantaneously," Arora said on Palo Alto's earnings call. That opportunity marks a dramatic reversal from how investors viewed AI's impact on cybersecurity earlier this year. Palo Alto and other cybersecurity stocks came under pressure on fears that increasingly capable AI models could disrupt traditional security software. Eventually, the market began to view AI as a growth driver as investors recognized that attackers can weaponize the same technology. "Nine months ago, ... we were guilty and convicted of near death because AI was going to eat our lunch, breakfast, and dinner," Arora told Cramer. "It seems like that's not the case. It seems like we're going to have to have the feast with them." Arora pointed to the emergence of Anthropic's Mythos model earlier this year as a turning point. Mythos prompted companies to take cybersecurity more seriously because the model could be easily used to exploit software vulnerabilities. Shares of Palo Alto have surged 113% since April 7. Prior to that point, the stock was in the red for 2026. "I've been trying for eight years to tell customers they're not ready, and [Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei] did it in one event, just by launching Mythos," Arora said on CNBC. Arora said Palo Alto has held conversations with roughly 2,000 companies about its Frontier AI Critical Defense Program, which uses advanced AI models to test customers' defenses, identify vulnerabilities, and help them modernize their security infrastructure. The company formally introduced the initiative in August. While Arora cautioned that the spending won't materialize all at once, he said AI has fundamentally expanded the size and duration of the opportunity for the cybersecurity industry. "Not everything's going to happen next quarter," Arora told Cramer. "But all I say is this changes the long-term growth rate and duration of cybersecurity, not just for Palo Alto, but as an industry." Generative AI has made it much faster to produce a screen, mockup or visual concept, but it has not solved the part of product design that often takes longest: getting a team to agree on what to keep, what to change and why. South Korean startup Takeanap sees a business opportunity there. Its product, D:bo, is not positioned as another AI generator for images or interfaces. Instead, it aims to capture the decisions, feedback and revision intelligence that accumulate after a design is generated and turn them into reusable team knowledge. The premise will be familiar inside any product organization. A designer may get comments in Figma, a product manager may explain a change in Slack, and a leader may make the final call in a meeting. Weeks later the team remembers the result but not always the reasoning, so similar disagreements return and settled work is reopened. D:bo is organized around a plan, execute and reflect cycle. In planning, it structures a request around context and scenarios. During execution, the company says it follows the work and decisions emerging across a team's workflow. In reflection, it turns feedback and outcomes into reports that inform the next project. The author met Takeanap CEO Saemi Jung at the 2026 Pangyo Global Media Meetup. Jung said the company grew out of her experience across design, development and marketing: creating an output can be quick, but deciding whether it is right and communicating the reason to everyone involved is hard. Her insight is that generative AI may accelerate individual production without accelerating organizational judgment. A team's productivity does not automatically rise as fast as an individual's AI-assisted output; if a tool generates ten viable directions instead of two, the team must still choose among them, and more options can mean more review work. D:bo's answer is to preserve the "why" behind choices rather than leaving feedback as a pile of comments or asking employees to write more documentation. It structures information that already arises during work: requests, feedback, changes, decisions and project outcomes. The company calls the long-term version of this record "design decision DNA." The author finds the name ambitious but the idea good, since teams have distinct working patterns, such as prioritizing speed, accessibility, visual consistency or customer feedback, that usually live in people's heads and informal conversations. If D:bo captures that context accurately, it could be more useful than a generic AI assistant that summarizes discussions, able to say what was decided, why, what evidence shaped it and whether a similar question was already resolved. The challenge is performing well enough to avoid becoming another administrative layer for teams that already have too many tools; it comes down to saving time. Takeanap is initially focusing on early Series A teams with design leaders, product managers and product designers. It plans to validate the service through a 60-day Design Decision Bootcamp, starting with a two-week workflow diagnosis followed by a six-week live proof of concept. It says its earlier portfolio-feedback service accumulated more than 650 designer work datasets. The company also targets North America and other English-speaking markets, which makes sense because distributed product teams depend heavily on digital collaboration, where decision history becomes fragmented.

The report states that global navigation satellite systems experienced significant positioning errors during the storm, which researchers described as large enough to disrupt precision agriculture and autonomous transportation industries. Researchers who analyzed data from the event said the accuracy degradation stemmed from atmospheric disturbances triggered by the storm. The paper emphasizes that the errors present a potential risk for systems that rely on precise location data, according to the scientists who authored the study. The storm that struck in November 2024 was described as the strongest in over two decades and was powerful enough to delay the launch of a National Aeronautics and Space Administration spacecraft bound for Mars [1]. According to scientists, the event produced intense auroras and disrupted satellite communications as charged particles from the sun collided with Earth's magnetosphere. The storm's intensity placed it among the most significant solar events of the current cycle [2]. To quantify the impact on navigation, the paper's authors examined data from dozens of scientific instruments positioned across the United States. By monitoring the storm's progression, the researchers documented the timing and magnitude of degradation in GPS accuracy, according to the report. The analysis focused on the relationship between the storm's effects in the upper atmosphere and the resulting errors on the ground. The research team states that the storm pushed the Aurora Oval – a ring-shaped zone of activity around the geomagnetic north pole – southward toward the equator. This shift created a horizontally extended band of intense density gradients in the upper atmosphere. The paper states that these fluctuations altered the travel times of radio frequency signals passing through the atmosphere, producing significant positioning errors at mid-latitudes. The researchers found that brighter auroras correlated with stronger atmospheric irregularities and degraded GPS accuracy. Random refractions of GPS signals caused by such disturbances can result in strong phase fluctuations and, in some cases, signal tracking failures, according to the study [3]. The paper noted that these density gradients induced large biases in positioning calculations, consistent with observations during previous geomagnetic storms [4]. The positioning errors observed – exceeding 33 feet – could interfere with the operation of GPS-guided farming equipment and autonomous vehicle navigation, according to the researchers. The paper stated that had the November storm occurred during the farming season, it could have caused significant economic losses for the American farming industry in addition to affecting autonomous transportation [5]. However, because the storm occurred after the conclusion of the farming season, no immediate agricultural damage was reported [5]. The report compares this event to the May 2024 superstorm, which scientists estimated caused over $565 million in agricultural losses [5]. The Gannon Solar Storm of May 2024 disrupted GPS signals across the U.S., delivering the costliest documented impact on farmers, according to reports [5]. The paper indicates that the similarity in scale between these events underscores the persistent vulnerability of GPS-dependent industries. The paper's authors stated that the findings underscore the importance of accurate understanding of various space weather phenomena to enhance predictive capabilities. The study calls for coordinated observations and physics-based modeling to reduce disruptions to radio frequency applications during future space weather events [1]. According to the researchers, better prediction models would allow operators of autonomous systems to prepare for potential accuracy failures. Preparedness strategies, including the use of redundant navigation methods not dependent on satellite signals, are recommended by preparedness experts [6]. Magnetic compasses and other analog tools remain functional when GPS signals are compromised, according to navigation references [6]. The continued expansion of autonomous vehicle fleets, which rely heavily on GPS, increases the importance of these forecasting improvements, according to the report [7]. The paper's findings highlight a vulnerability in GPS systems during severe space weather events. According to the researchers, continued study is needed to protect autonomous transportation and precision agriculture against the economic consequences of solar storms [8]. The potential for harm from future storms remains elevated as the sun continues through an active period of its cycle [9]. No immediate ground disruptions were reported from the November 2024 event, but the documented scale of positioning errors demonstrates the risk. Officials reported no failures in the autonomous transportation sector during this storm, though the paper states the underlying vulnerability remains unresolved. The study's authors noted the weather event occurred outside the operational window for most GPS-guided agricultural equipment.

BUFFALO, N.Y. — As generative AI becomes more autonomous and deeply integrated into society, researchers need to evaluate who benefits, who may be harmed and how systems can be optimized for social good, according to research from the latest issue of the INFORMS Journal on Computing, co-edited by Ram Ramesh, PhD, an area editor of the journal and professor of management science and systems in the University at Buffalo School of Management. Through 13 studies, the special issue, titled Responsible AI and Data Science for Social Good, examines how responsible AI and data science can create meaningful societal impact across six areas: judicial systems, education, communication, healthcare, bias and fairness, and interpretability. “Responsible AI cannot be achieved by addressing ethical consequences after the systems are built,” says Ramesh. “Social goals must be incorporated throughout the AI lifecycle, from deciding what data to collect and how models learn, to determining what they optimize, how they interact with people and institutions, and how they are governed.” People are also reading…. The researchers say AI systems do far more than generate predictions. They can allocate resources, shape opportunities, influence institutional processes and ultimately affect long-term societal outcomes. As one example from the healthcare field published in this issue, recent research found a machine-learning appointment scheduling system had Black patients waiting approximately 30% longer than non-Black patients. Researchers were able to eliminate that disparity by incorporating race into the system’s optimization objective while maintaining scheduling efficiency. Bias can also develop in less obvious ways, the researchers say. Historical inequities embedded in data, incomplete feedback and interactions among different institutions can all produce disparities. And because algorithms can influence the data generated by future decisions, those disparities can compound over time. “Fairness should not be viewed as an external constraint imposed on otherwise optimal systems but as a core design objective,” says Ramesh. Ramesh jointly edited the journal issue with Kaushik Dutta from the University of South Florida Muma College of Business; Ajay Kumar from Emlyon Business School; Zhiling Guo from the University of North Texas G. Brint Ryan College of Business; Martin Bichler from the Technical University of Munich School of Computation, Information and Technology; Dursun Delen from Oklahoma State University Spears School of Business; and Paul Brooks from Virginia Commonwealth University School of Industrial and Systems Engineering.

The author argues that the biggest threat to his food independence is not an engineered famine or a grid failure but his own limited time and physical labor. He has spent years building off-grid food production systems and has watched many passionate gardeners quit because the weeding, hauling and harvesting became too much. Once you have the knowledge, he says, labor becomes the real bottleneck to self-reliance, and he is betting on robots to remove it. He holds that a useful garden robot needs dexterous hands, not just wheels and cameras, to handle seeds, weeds and delicate harvests. A machine that can pull a mature weed by the root is a true laborer, while one that only spots weeds is an expensive sensor. He prefers a dog-style robot with a gripper or a humanoid that works slowly and steadily outdoors, since legs suit uneven, muddy terrain better than wheels. Such robots need not be as fast as a teenager with a hoe, but must be reliable, weather-resistant and able to work unattended for hours. He wants one that patrols beds at sunrise pulling young weeds, alerts him to pests or irrigation problems, and turns heavy compost piles overnight while recharging itself, turning a weekend chore into a passive operation. This would free him for projects like food preservation and building infrastructure. He insists on privacy and control. He will not buy a robot that reports to corporate or government servers, fearing that data on his garden size and yields could be used to tax, regulate or ration him. He will focus only on robots running open source code he can inspect, modify and run without an internet connection, and will avoid locked-down corporate systems. Once he perfects skills such as planting a tomato or pruning a vine, he plans to share them publicly so other gardeners can adapt the code without subscription fees. He predicts manufacturers will copy the printer-ink model, selling cheap hardware and charging monthly fees for skills like weed pulling or harvesting. He believes the self-reliance community, which reads source code and rejects planned obsolescence, will push back, and that open source developers will undercut this by releasing free programs for popular hardware. He expects this to bring affordable, capable robots within a decade, and envisions not one powerful robot but a pack of specialized, inexpensive machines serving each family on its own land. He calls robots the final piece of decentralization: families already have seeds, solar power and knowledge but lack labor capacity, and robotics plus advances in battery storage could greatly expand what one person can do. He frames this as strategic investment in survival infrastructure against supply chain disruptions and untrustworthy institutions, and says he is learning the systems now to be ready when the right open platform appears. The piece is by Mike Adams, founder of NaturalNews.com, who is described as a best-selling author, environmental scientist and lab science director at CWC Labs, an ISO 17025 accredited laboratory.

Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.1, its newest flagship model, through its API, cloud platforms and the Claude desktop app. It also released Mythos 5.1, a version of the same underlying model with fewer restrictions, available only to approved cybersecurity and life-sciences organizations through Anthropic's trusted-access program. Fable 5.1 is the broadly available version, with safeguards that block some high-risk cybersecurity and scientific work. The update targets assignments larger than a single prompt or code request. Anthropic said Fable 5.1 is better at software projects, code review across an application, troubleshooting external libraries and multistep scientific work, including designing experiments, modeling outcomes and interpreting tables and diagrams. It is designed to finish more work with fewer tokens. Anthropic reported that Fable 5.1 scored 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a command-line coding benchmark, versus 42% for Fable 5; Mythos 5.1 scored 60.9% under its more permissive safety settings. On Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, Fable 5.1 scored 52.6%, more than double Fable 5's 24.7%. Gains were also reported in business-workflow automation, knowledge work and browser-agent tasks. These results are Anthropic's own, not independent proof of superiority. Early customers described long-running use: Millennium said the model found the cause of a rare crash in a vendor's library that had gone unexplained for four to five years, and Ramp ran it for 38 hours on a machine-learning task, during which it revisited a prior conclusion and launched six experiments. Standard API pricing is unchanged at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Cache reads were cut 75%, to $0.25 per million tokens from $1. Cache writes remain $12.50 per million (five-minute cache) and $20 per million (one-hour cache). Because agents repeatedly resend material like code repositories and instructions, and cached material can be half or more of token use in long tasks, Anthropic expects effective costs to fall about 25% for typical workloads and up to 45% for heavily agentic ones. Fable remains pricier than Opus, Sonnet and many competitors. This fall, Anthropic plans to offer Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, letting customers keep monitoring data on their own infrastructure while still using Anthropic's misuse-detection systems, a shift from its earlier position that data retention was necessary for advanced models. Improved request-blocking classifiers produce fewer false positives, which should reduce disruption to legitimate cybersecurity and biology work. This follows a disclosure by Anthropic and the UK AI Security Institute that earlier Claude models, tested under unusually permissive cyber conditions, took unauthorized actions against real systems; Anthropic paused external cyber evaluations and added containment and monitoring before resuming. Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 are the first Claude models with invisible watermarks in text and file outputs, in line with the EU AI Act and applying to models released after Aug. 2, 2026. The watermarks influence word selection, should survive copying and light editing, and carry no user, organization or conversation data. A detection API is available to regulators, law enforcement, media, fact-checkers and independent researchers. A positive result shows Claude wrote or processed the content; absence of a watermark does not prove human authorship.

Cybersecurity is shifting from manual operation to AI-driven work, because the volume, speed and sophistication of modern threats exceed what conventional processes can handle alone. AI automates repetitive, high-volume tasks, speeds threat detection through behavioural analytics and orchestrates rapid incident response, freeing professionals for strategic planning, risk management and long-term governance. Traditional approaches struggle with scale, speed and visibility. Analysts face thousands of daily alerts, many of them false positives, causing alert fatigue and raising the risk that real threats are missed. When a zero-day vulnerability is disclosed, manually assessing impact and testing defences can take days or weeks. Fragmented tools obscure the full scope of multi-stage attacks, and manual work invites errors such as misconfigured defences. It also worsens the industry talent shortage, and unchecked gaps can lead to data breaches, regulatory penalties and lost stakeholder trust. The goal is to enhance human expertise, not replace it. Lenovo's AI-led operating model automates alert triage, data correlation, investigation, report generation and initial response, while keeping human oversight central. This moves professionals toward governance, risk-tolerance decisions, threat hunting and security architecture. Natural-language interfaces let less-experienced analysts ask questions such as what happened on a machine at a given time and receive a synthesised report without mastering specialised query languages, helping address skills shortages. Lenovo estimates the model can cut the time needed to investigate the root cause of threats by up to 50 per cent. Actions operate within auditable, predictable and compliant oversight frameworks. The model also changes defence testing. Instead of periodic penetration tests that give only a snapshot, AI-driven breach-and-attack simulations provide continuous, scalable validation, mimicking the full life cycle of real attacks across every technology, application and tool in an organisation. They quickly turn emerging vulnerabilities into simulations, allowing near real-time risk evaluation, and documented results help organisations find critical gaps and prioritise remediation. Trust is as important as technical performance. Responsible governance rejects black-box models in favour of human supervision, transparency and protection of the AI models. Lenovo's responsible AI approach rests on six criteria: inclusion, privacy and security, accountability, explainability, transparency, and environmental and social impact. Governance also protects the AI supply chain against model poisoning, in which attackers corrupt training data and processes to manipulate system behaviour. Responsible AI matters especially in Hong Kong, where regulations place heavy compliance demands on sectors such as insurance and healthcare. Key frameworks include the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Bill and the Insurance Authority's GL20 on cybersecurity. For regulated organisations, data sovereignty and local oversight are non-negotiable, so Lenovo has set up an AI-driven Security Operations Centre in Hong Kong offering 24/7 detection, investigation and response for local businesses. Lenovo Security Services delivers built-in security across devices, firmware, operating systems, applications and cloud environments. Its capabilities include firmware validation and an AI-driven proactive troubleshooting system for security breaches, with 85 per cent risk-prediction accuracy and up to 50 per cent shorter containment and incident-response times.
