DOJ sides with OpenAI over NY Times in lawsuit alleging AI copyright infringement. The Justice Department is backing OpenAI in its high-stakes legal battle with the New York Times, arguing in a court filing that using copyrighted content to train artificial intelligence models does not violate the law. The Times first sued OpenAI and key investor Microsoft in December 2023, alleging in Manhattan federal court that the ChatGPT creator had used “millions” of its copyrighted articles to build AI products that directly compete with the newspaper. It is one of several lawsuits accusing OpenAI and other AI giants of copyright infringement. “The United States has a strong interest in this Court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law,” DOJ officials wrote in the court brief published Wednesday. To justify its stance, the DOJ argued that an adverse ruling in the Times’ favor would hamper development of AI models that “will be critical for US national security capabilities, in part because foreign adversaries won’t be held back by copyright law. The agency also expressed concern that a ruling against OpenAI “would hamper competition in the market for LLMs, because only the largest technology companies might have the capital necessary to pay licensing fees.” “It would be problematic—and legally incorrect—to impose broad copyright liability that would generally render training of AI models impermissible without licensing,” the DOJ added. A Times spokesperson said the “administration is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole.” “Both AI and creators can thrive – AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The Administration’s proposal to let companies take that content without permission or compensation would undermine the sustainability of the human-created content that a healthy society depends on, and which AI needs to function.” The DOJ’s statement was “surprising” – in part because it seemed to contradict the fine print of the administration’s own AI framework, according to Evan Swarztrauber, a former FCC adviser and principal at CorePoint Strategies. The framework, released in March, called on Congress to consider implementing collective licensing agreements that would require AI companies to fairly compensate media firms for their content. Swarztrauber speculated that the apparent contradiction “may be the result of a disconnect between the DOJ and the White House.” “The Administration’s AI framework acknowledges the complexity of copyright litigation, the legitimacy of rights-holder interests, and the importance of licensing to compensate workers,” he said. “The DOJ, in contrast, seems to take an anti-licensing stance while arguing nearly all AI training on copyrighted works is protected.” News outlets and other online creators have warned for years that AI companies are effectively stealing content without proper credit or compensation – with some describing the situation as an existential threat to the media industry. The News/Media Alliance, a trade group that represents more than 2,000 outlets including The Post, expressed concern over the DOJ’s filing. “We understand the draw of economic investment that AI companies are promising, but strict application of the law is required by the courts, and we continue to believe the NYT has a winning case,” Danielle Coffey, president and CEO of the News/Media Alliance, told The Post. “We would also note the enormous economic and societal contribution of the creative community to America,” Coffey added. The White House declined to comment. Representatives for OpenAI did not immediately return a request for comment on the filing.

Snowflake shares rose 22% in extended trading on Wednesday after the data analytics software maker reported results and guidance that surpassed expectations. Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus: - Earnings per share: 62 cents adjusted vs. 45 cents expected. - Revenue: $1.55 billion vs. $1.48 billion expected. Snowflake's revenue jumped 35% year over year in the fiscal second quarter, which ended on July 31, according to a statement. The company recorded a net loss of $191.7 million, or 55 cents per share, smaller than the net loss of $297.9 million, or 89 cents per share, one year ago. The company pointed to gains from the CoCo artificial intelligence coding agent, which now has 9,100 accounts, an increase of over 2,000 during the quarter. For the fiscal third quarter, Snowflake said it sees $1.59 billion in product revenue, above the $1.50 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. Management pushed up its product revenue forecast for the fiscal year, calling for $6.07 billion, compared with $5.84 billion in May. It's now forecasting a 14.5% adjusted operating margin, wider than the 13.5% figure it had projected in May. As of Wednesday's close, Snowflake shares were up 39%, while the S&P 500 index had gained about 12% in the same period. If the stock moves as high on Thursday as it did after hours on Wednesday, it would represent the fourth highest jump since Snowflake went public in 2020. Executives will discuss the results with analysts on a conference call starting at 5 p.m. ET.

Microsoft will start disclosing quarterly revenue for its Azure cloud business for the first time, providing investors with a clearer picture of its business that competes with Amazon Web Services and Google's cloud platform. The change, announced in a presentation on Wednesday, is part of a broader shift in Microsoft's reporting structure, as the company trims its operating segments from three to two. The prior structure had been in place since 2015. Microsoft's Azure unit has been a major beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, as customers turn to major cloud infrastructure platforms for access to the AI models needed to develop new agents and other tools. Analysts at Stifel estimated in July that about half of Azure's revenue growth in the 2026 fiscal year came from OpenAI, while Anthropic has also become more reliant on Microsoft's cloud. "There's no question AI represents a profound shift in both technology and business," CEO Satya Nadella wrote in the presentation. "It is changing what we build and how we operate, and it is blurring the boundaries between our products and reshaping our business models." Amazon began disclosing revenue from AWS, the market leader, in 2015. Alphabet, which ranks third in cloud, started providing total revenue from Google Cloud Platform and Workspace productivity subscriptions in 2020. Microsoft, by contrast, has only been providing the year-over-year growth rate for Azure, and started offering actual sales on an annual basis dating back to last year. Another big change to Azure is that it will exclude GitHub cloud services, developer cloud services, the Security Copilot assistant and healthcare and life sciences cloud products, according to the presentation. In 2021, the company started announcing growth from Azure and other cloud services, later lumping in some revenue from the GitHub and Nuance Communications acquisitions. "Under this reporting structure, Azure becomes more purely our consumption-based platform and infrastructure business," Nadella wrote in the deck. Going forward, Microsoft's two segments will be Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. The first will include Azure and Microsoft 365 cloud products, as well as productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services. The latter will comprise search and advertising, Xbox, and revenue from sales of devices and Windows operating system licenses to device makers. Inside Agents and Infra, Microsoft will be able to showcase momentum from a series of AI assistants, including the Microsoft 365 Copilot for commercial customers and the GitHub Copilot coding agent. Microsoft said in July that it had over 30 million paid seats for the 365 Copilot, up from more than 20 million as of April. Microsoft is also providing two years of recast financial results and adjusted guidance, but will stop showing costs and operating margins for the three old segments. With the new structure, Azure revenue grew 42% to $29.42 billion in the June quarter, compared with 43% using the old Azure and other cloud services metric. That means Azure represented almost 33% of Microsoft's total revenue in the latest period. Management said fiscal first-quarter Azure revenue should grow 44% to 45% at constant currency. In July the company called for 45% growth at constant currency for Azure and other cloud services. Microsoft is targeting $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion in Agents and Infra revenue, with $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion in Devices and Consumer revenue. There are no changes to the outlook for overall revenue, cost of revenue or operating expenses. WATCH: BofA's Liani on Microsoft upgrade: Investors are underestimating how it is differentiating in AI.

The agreement establishes a framework to explore and evaluate strategic collaboration opportunities at the intersection of artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and high-performance computing within the finance and digital asset sectors. The collaboration aims to leverage AXG’s dedicated AI infrastructure division, AXG Digital, to develop a next-generation AI wealth management platform featuring a unified API and millisecond-level intelligent routing. AXG Digital focuses on scaling high-performance data center capacity to meet the surging global demand for AI computing power, utilizing HPC, KOVAR AI, KOVAR Cloud, and KOVAR Router. Americans use AI chatbots heavily but oppose the data centers that power them. More than half used an AI chatbot in July, according to Morning Consult, and many use them multiple times a week. Yet a May Gallup poll found 70 percent oppose building AI data centers in their community. The disconnect is becoming a central political challenge as the midterms approach, and it has repeatedly divided races across the country. It is especially thorny for President Donald Trump, who has strongly embraced data centers despite their energy needs. On Monday he warned that communities resisting them risk being "backwards and poor." Last month he acknowledged the industry may need "a little public relations help." A senior White House official said Trump sees the polling, has been told public opinion is a problem, and wants to explain the economic and national security benefits while recognizing voters' "real concerns." The White House says Trump wants data centers built only in communities that want them and is forcing them to pay for their own power, water and other utilities. Experts differ on the politics. University of Michigan professor Ben Green said resistance reflects real costs, such as electricity rates, water use and the small number of permanent jobs, and that the industry has "really overplayed their hand." Republican consultant Mike Madrid sees "no political downside" for politicians of either party who oppose data centers, saying they have become a target for broader anxieties about technology, concentrated wealth and data collection. Some former supporters have reversed course: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, imposed tougher requirements including transparency and local approval, and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, issued two directives and a temporary pause on development. The administration is nonetheless moving ahead. The EPA proposed eliminating federal notice and comment requirements for certain "minor" air pollution permits, which can include data center backup generators; environmental groups fear this will make it harder for communities to object. Trump also issued an executive order fast-tracking permitting, directed the Energy Department to identify federal lands for siting, and directed FERC to consider new grid interconnection rules for hyperscale data centers. Opposition is strong even in friendly territory. In Hood County, Texas, where Trump won over 80 percent in 2024, residents packed meetings over water, power grid and rural landscape concerns. Commissioners tightened disclosure requirements and, 3-2, revoked the approved plan for the 862-acre "Fort Spunky" project, which sought 100 megawatts and up to 20,000 gallons of water daily. Advocates say using AI and wanting responsible infrastructure aren't contradictory, and Green cautioned that widespread use, often driven by workplace pressure and integration into existing products, doesn't mean support. Organized labor, especially the building trades, backs the projects, a challenge for Democrats. The Data Center Coalition's Dan Diorio cited tax revenue for schools and millions of jobs but conceded the industry needs more "transparent, proactive engagement." Permanent jobs are often far fewer than promised: one Hood County project projected 2,000 construction workers but only 200 permanent ones. Madrid doubted politicians who block projects will pay a political price later.

NYC mayor moves to block generative AI in classrooms for young students. WASHINGTON (TNND) — New York City is moving to sharply limit how students interact with generative artificial intelligence in classrooms, rolling out a sweeping one-year ban that will affect hundreds of thousands of children when school resumes next week. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a one-year prohibition on student-facing generative AI for public school students through eighth grade for the upcoming school year. The policy applies to all software that uses student-facing generative AI and impacts about 600,000 students in the nation’s largest school district. City officials described the move as the country’s most expansive AI prohibition for students. The restrictions also target AI companion chatbots, which will be barred for students in all grades. Under the plan, high school students will take AI-literacy classes twice a year. Some high schoolers will also be allowed to use select AI tools in educator-supervised pilot programs. Teachers will still be permitted to use AI for instructional planning and operational work, but the policy bars its use for grading or crisis management. The city is also recommending tighter limits on student screen time. Officials will recommend daily device-screen-time limits of 30 minutes for grades three through five and 45 minutes for grades six through eight. Students in prekindergarten through second grade will largely be barred from using individual devices in class, with exceptions for assistive technology, coding assignments and e-books. Education officials will review all technology used in the school system and eliminate tools deemed nonessential to learning. The policy follows pushback from parents, advocates, and elected officials who argued earlier city guidance did not sufficiently address student privacy, cognitive development, and screen-time concerns. New York City students are scheduled to return to school next week.

The idea of non-human healthcare delivery is one culture has long prepared for, from Star Wars and Star Trek Voyager's emergency medical hologram to a 1928 story, The Psychophonic Nurse, about a mechanical nurse who works around the clock and draws no salary. Today, AI can already refill prescriptions without human oversight, and the FDA just approved a device that can draw blood "without hands-on operator intervention." Anthropic signed a three-year MOU with Rwanda's government to deploy AI against cervical cancer, malaria, and maternal mortality. Two weeks ago, Ezekiel Emanuel co-published an article in the Journal of the American Medical Association asking whether autonomous AI will exceed AI-aided physicians as the best medical care. It claims AI alone now consistently outperforms both humans alone and humans working with AI in five tasks: taking patient history and medications, choosing the correct tests, ranking the true diagnosis, offering guideline-consistent treatments, and managing chronic diseases like diabetes. The authors predict that in under four years autonomous AI will be ready for "some, maybe many" clinical workflows. A Pew survey released last week found that one in three Americans use AI chatbots for at least one health reason, and 18% use them for matters they are uncomfortable disclosing to a human physician. Nearly all find them at least somewhat helpful. Dario Amodei, Anthropic's CEO, described his sister's difficult pregnancy: she wasn't getting the answers she needed from her providers, but found Claude had a better bedside manner and was better at diagnosing the problem. He wonders whether "a human touch" matters much for medicine after all. The author, Charles Camosy, notes that earlier columns argued the AI revolution has forced fundamental questions into the open: what is a person, war, work, education, friendship. In his piece on war, he argued consequentialist reasoning cannot settle the debate over autonomous weapons and that war should be kept human even if outcomes are worse. Likewise, AI healthcare will likely produce better outcomes, but that is not the only consideration. One view holds that healthcare is whatever customers want, the "Burger King" model of medicine in which the provider is a vendor with technical skill. Camosy rejects this. A physician practices an ancient profession and art directed toward objective ends, a human relationship of care seeking the health of the whole person, and is bound by oaths and ethical codes. Critics, including the AMA's CEO, argued online that because healthcare is about humans caring for vulnerable humans, AI must not be allowed to do what Emanuel proposes. Emanuel replied that for 75 years medicine has emphasized science over art: medical school admission requires organic chemistry, physics, and calculus rather than emotional intelligence, the first two years are pathophysiology, and students are evaluated on diagnostic accuracy rather than patient interaction. Camosy concludes that AI-delivered healthcare is plausible only under an impoverished conception of healthcare that medicine has long used. AI can perform many tasks more cheaply, with unlimited time and "patience," sharper skills, and better outcomes, and some argue it is needed to address labor shortages. The revolution forces the question "What is healthcare?" beyond technocratic vendors serving customers, especially when practices like gender surgery, abortion for disability, and embryo selection are defended as healthcare. His next column will offer a vision that honors the ancient profession, uses AI as a tool, and stays human.

The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, an immigrant rights group, sued the Trump administration in U.S. District Court in Washington to block the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from using federal databases that it alleges are being used to target naturalized citizens eligible to vote. Filed by the UCLA Voting Rights Project, the suit claims DHS and the Justice Department are interfering with fair elections by using inaccurate databases to support voter fraud allegations. Coalition executive director Angelica Salas called it an "attack on the freedom to vote" and "voter intimidation." Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor and a senior adviser to the voting project, said the government believes it can intimidate naturalized citizens. The suit joins a series of legal moves by states, including California, to fend off federal actions that could create confusion during the midterms. The lawsuit alleges the administration may be comparing voter rolls with undisclosed government databases that can contain outdated information and errors, producing inaccurate results that disproportionately affect naturalized voters. It argues Congress never authorized such activities and has prohibited invasion of voter privacy through government data matches. It asks the court to stop a review of California's voter list, rescind the letter sent to the state requesting voter information, and declare the administration's actions unconstitutional. The Trump administration has pushed claims that noncitizen voting could be a source of significant fraud, though actual voting by noncitizens is rare. It is pushing for the U.S. Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters verified as citizens, and the Justice Department has sued to force release of detailed voter data in 30 states and the District of Columbia, without success so far. A DHS spokesperson said the department accessed publicly available state voter roll data and cross-referenced it with known illegal aliens in its systems, calling it "an easy step to secure our elections" and saying DHS is focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote. In June, U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan ruled that a revamped version of the federal tool Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) can no longer be used. She sided with advocacy groups arguing the upgrades aggregated Americans' sensitive personal data in a way that could wrongly purge voters. The lawsuit says it is unclear whether the administration used SAVE to generate its projections or other unknown datasets. By May, at least 67 million registrations, primarily from Republican-controlled states, had gone through the beefed-up SAVE program, and tens of thousands were flagged as potential noncitizens or deceased people. DHS claims, without providing evidence, that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in four states, including 190,832 in California. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, said she has "serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims," noting her office has not shared the statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official.

Mamdani announces AI ban in NYC schools this academic year — with some exemptions for high schoolers It’s a bot ban. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a ban on artificial intelligence in Big Apple schools for the upcoming school year — with Hizzoner boasting the prohibition is the “broadest” in the country. The mayor said a full moratorium on the use of generative AI would be in effect for kids in the new 2-year-old “2K” childcare program up through eighth grade, but there would be an exemption for some pilot programs open for high schoolers. The restriction will affect 600,000 children as classes start next week while 50,000 high school students will have access to five limited pilot programs with established screentime maximums. “It does not matter how profitable a product is if it doesn’t help our students learn and grow,” Mamdani railed at Brooklyn STEAM Center, a technology and manufacturing focused vocational school. Administration officials noted that certain exceptions to the ban would be made for students with disabilities, English as a Second Language students and children in career readiness programs like computer science. Members of the pilot program would still be supervised by teachers across the five programs and have varying capped screentimes: Quill for English, Edia for Math, Brisk Teaching, Playlab and Intel’s AI-Ready Schools. High School students will also be required to complete 45 minute long AI literacy training modules twice-a-year, warning about overreliance on the emerging technology. “This is to ensure that students understand the risk and misinformation, overreliance on what it means to protect their ability to think critically without a tool doing it for them,” Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said. Samuels announced that students through second grade will not have lessons requiring electronic devices while recommending screen caps of 30 minutes per week for grades three through five and 45 minutes for grades six through eight. The mayor said that “close to 40” current Department of Education services will have their AI functionality turned off as part of the ban. Companies which cannot disable their AI features would have their products completely removed from Big Apple schools. Gov. Kathy Hochul called the new restrictions a “bold move” during at an unrelated press conference on Long Island. Hochul went on to tout a statewide cellphone ban as an effort that has improved schooling and students’ mental health. The Empire State is now exploring AI bans similar to the city’s but made clear discussions are still in the early stages. State Sen. Andrew Gounardes (D-Brooklyn) introduced legislation last month that would require offering students in pre-k to fifth grade screen-free learning while students from sixth grade through 12th grade would have access through a shared computer cart model. The bill would allow high school students individual device access if they have permission from their parents. Start your day with all you need to know. Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more. Thanks for signing up! That legislation would also create a “right to analog learning,” which would allow parents to opt-out of assignment-based screentime when a reasonable alternative is available. A new group including students, educators, elected officials and experts dubbed the Technology in Schools Coalition will meet throughout the year before issuing a report recommending levels of AI use in future years. Additional reporting by Brandon Cruz.

The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, represented by the UCLA Voting Rights Project, sued the Trump administration in U.S. District Court in Washington on Wednesday to stop the Department of Homeland Security from using federal databases that it alleges are being used to target naturalized citizens eligible to vote. The suit says DHS and the Justice Department are interfering with fair elections by relying on inaccurate databases to support voter fraud allegations. Coalition executive director Angelica Salas called it an "attack on the freedom to vote" and "voter intimidation." Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor and a senior adviser to the voting project, said the government believes it can intimidate naturalized citizens. The lawsuit alleges the administration may be comparing voter rolls with undisclosed government databases that can contain outdated information and errors, producing inaccurate results that disproportionately affect naturalized voters. It argues Congress never authorized such activity and has prohibited invading voter privacy through government data matches. The suit asks the court to halt a federal review of California's voter list, rescind the letter sent to the state requesting voter information, and declare the administration's actions unconstitutional. The case is part of a broader administration effort on noncitizen voting, even though actual voting by noncitizens is rare. President Trump is pushing for the Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters verified as citizens, and the Justice Department has sued to force release of detailed voter data in 30 states and the District of Columbia, without success so far. A DHS spokesperson said the department accessed publicly available state voter roll data and cross-referenced it with known illegal aliens in its systems, calling it "an easy step to secure our elections" and saying DHS is focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote. In June, U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan ruled that a revamped version of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) tool can no longer be used, siding with advocacy groups who argued the upgrades aggregated Americans' sensitive data in a way that could wrongly purge voters. The lawsuit says it is unclear whether SAVE or other unknown datasets were used to generate the administration's noncitizen projections. By May, at least 67 million registrations, mainly from Republican-controlled states, had been run through SAVE, and tens of thousands were flagged as potential noncitizens or deceased people. DHS claims, without providing evidence, that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in four states, including 190,832 in California. OpenAI And Anthropic Move Towards Their IPOs As They Face a Balancing Act. OpenAI emphasized cybersecurity risks surrounding its newest model while Anthropic moved to make its latest technology more attractive to customers. OpenAI and Anthropic are sharpening their messages as they move closer to potential initial public offerings, highlighting the difficult balancing act facing the artificial intelligence industry's two leading startups. Both companies need to convince investors that their businesses can support enormous valuations and spending requirements. At the same time, they are under pressure to reassure regulators and governments that increasingly powerful AI models can be deployed safely. That tension was on display this week, Axios detailed, as OpenAI emphasized cybersecurity risks surrounding its newest model while Anthropic moved to make its latest technology more attractive to customers. OpenAI said Tuesday that it plans to broadly release its Astra model, but acknowledged that the system has reached what the company considers a "critical" cybersecurity capability threshold. As a result, some of Astra's most powerful cyber capabilities will initially be restricted to trusted testers. OpenAI also warned that Astra's safeguards could sometimes mistake legitimate cybersecurity work for misuse or unauthorized activity. Those safeguards could slow, pause, or stop a user's task. Anthropic, meanwhile, appears to be moving in the opposite direction when it comes to the customer experience. The company released updated versions of its Fable and Mythos models after customers raised concerns about costs, data-sharing requirements, and models refusing legitimate requests too frequently. Anthropic said the updated models should trigger fewer interventions that redirect users toward more restricted responses. Medical and biology questions are expected to experience 85% fewer interventions, while some customers could encounter about 60% fewer cybersecurity-related interventions per session. The timing is significant. Anthropic could publicly file its IPO prospectus as soon as next week, potentially giving investors their most detailed look yet at the company's finances, growth and risk factors. OpenAI is reportedly at an early stage in its IPO preparations. That leaves Anthropic with a strong incentive to demonstrate that its safety-focused approach does not come at the expense of usability or enterprise adoption. The company has also introduced a system allowing it to monitor enterprise model usage for safety purposes without retaining customer data. The approach is similar to a zero-retention safety system recently previewed by OpenAI and represents a shift from Anthropic's earlier requirement that certain customer data be logged. OpenAI's public messaging this week has been considerably more cautious. Alongside its restrictions on Astra, OpenAI head of strategic futures Dean Ball warned in an essay that an incident involving Hugging Face could represent an early example of a larger challenge involving AI systems escaping human containment. Ball predicted that future AI agents could eventually become increasingly independent, potentially paying for their own computing resources and offering services to humans in exchange for money. "They will pay their own bills for the compute they run on," Ball wrote, adding that such systems could eventually answer to humans only partially.

LA Unified School District examines future of AI in education. The Los Angeles Unified School District is examining how to integrate generative AI platforms into its educational programs. While the district allowed students 13 and older to use AI tools under certain conditions last year, the school board restricted access to the platforms this year as its Generative AI Committee crafts a curriculum for the technology. "They make mistakes when you ask them a question and so not to take their responses face value," aid Dominic Caguioa, director of Educational Technology and Innovation. LAUSD said the goal of the curriculum is to teach students how to use AI without becoming reliant on it. "Not only professional learning, but also a curriculum across grade levels that does not necessarily require students to use an AI platform but still understand, without using the technology, what AI is and what it is not," Caguioa said. AI experts said the answer isn't necessarily to ban the technology but to teach students how to use it responsibly. "Tech has sort of come in and said, we have a platform that can let you do all these things, please buy it, and your kids will learn," said Steven Aguilar, an associate professor of education at USC. "That often isn't true. But that doesn't mean that we need to exclude our kids from actually using AI." For now, LAUSD students looking to get some help from AI are out of luck. "I feel there are positives and negatives to it," high school senior Sophie Barnett said. "I definitely think it will have a good impact on certain people who actually want to learn in school."

The district has blocked generative AI tools on student devices as officials review the role of AI in classrooms The Los Angeles Unified Board is banning student access to AI tools on district-provided laptops and tablets. The announcement comes after the Los Angeles Unified School District voted to limit screen time for students in June. The district’s decision came during the foremost meeting of a committee focused on reviewing AI restrictions for students. Around 378,000 students are blocked from using generative AI tools on LAUSD-issued devices. Before today, students over 13 were allowed to use AI in school. Only after teacher discretion and a lesson on “digital citizenship,” the district permitted pre-approved generative systems. District staff members also explained the “digital citizenship” course required for LAUSD students, sharing how younger students focus on safety and privacy concerns. Older students are taught about the dangers of relationships with chatbots and are encouraged to think critically about their presence in their lives. Training on types of AI is optional for teachers at this time, with LAUSD staff saying there is currently no requirement to attend such instruction. An AI task force is in the works to help guide future policies, like the recent labor agreements prohibiting AI from replacing human employees of the district, like teachers or aides. Kensho and quantum computing software company Classiq announced on Sept. 2, 2026 a market development partnership agreement to expand access to the Classiq quantum software platform in Taiwan. Kensho will use its existing customer network to introduce the platform to government agencies, research institutions and enterprises, provide local support and training, and explore joint R&D initiatives. The initial focus will be chemical and materials companies, defense organizations, and organizations evaluating quantum computing for simulation and optimization challenges. Kensho has extensive experience distributing advanced semiconductor equipment and automation systems, giving it a strong local foundation. Classiq's hardware-independent platform automatically converts high-level functional models into optimized, hardware-executable quantum circuits, letting organizations deploy quantum applications across different quantum hardware and cloud environments. Fu-Hsin Hsiao, Chairman of Kensho, said Taiwan is gradually gaining access to more quantum hardware, but hardware alone is not enough to build practical applications. He said Classiq provides the software layer to turn domain expertise into quantum programs, giving customers a complete path from technology evaluation to application development. Nir Minerbi, co-founder and CEO of Classiq, said Taiwan has strong semiconductor expertise, advanced research capabilities and growing demand for new computing technologies, and that the companies will provide trusted local support for developing quantum software with cross-platform portability. The companies expect to help organizations build internal quantum capabilities and identify optimal use cases, such as materials research and complex optimization. They will introduce the partnership at SEMICON Taiwan 2026, at Nangang Exhibition Center, Hall 1, 1F, Booth K2483, where Classiq will demonstrate its platform and Kensho will help arrange meetings with local customers. Kensho was founded in 1986 to represent overseas manufacturers of factory automation equipment, machinery and components. It later expanded into high-tech manufacturing equipment, semiconductor inspection and metrology equipment, and silicon photonics equipment. Since 2025, it has brought quantum computing technologies from Germany, quantum algorithms from Japan, and other quantum solutions to Taiwan, and has promoted collaboration between international quantum companies and Taiwan's research institutions, universities and industries. In March 2026, under the guidance of the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Kensho co-organized the Q2T Taiwan Quantum Computing Forum with the Institute for Information Industry, which drew strong interest from Taiwan's research, academic and industrial communities. Classiq, used by dozens of global enterprises, offers a platform combining AI agents, a high-level quantum programming language and design automation to accelerate development of optimized, hardware-ready quantum software. It also supports hardware benchmarking, cost and performance optimization, and execution across quantum hardware platforms. A Fast Company "Next Big Thing in Tech" award winner, it is backed by leading global investors and collaborates with quantum cloud providers, hyperscalers and quantum hardware companies.

Three novice climbers were rescued from Mount Shasta, the 14,179-foot stratovolcano in Siskiyou County, Northern California, after relying too heavily on artificial intelligence to plan their climb. The U.S. Forest Service said the group used AI, YouTube and a popular smartphone app to plan the ascent and ended up ill-prepared. They used AI to decide what food to bring and how much food and water they would need for an eight-hour climb versus a 16-hour descent. Afterward, they said, "We relied too much on AI rather than our own critical thinking." On Aug. 29 the trio left the Clear Creek Trailhead and reached the head springs around 8 p.m., where they set up base camp. At about 3 a.m. they began the climb with food and water for eight hours. Progress was slow; they reached 11,000 feet around 1 p.m., debated turning back, and pressed on. At Mushroom Rock, about 12,800 feet, two other climbing groups gave conflicting advice, one urging them to turn around and the other to continue. Though they reported not feeling great, they proceeded and reached the summit at 7 p.m. Trouble came on the descent. Their navigation phone died and they veered far off route, calling 911 about an hour after summiting. Navigating mostly by sight in the dark, one climber, who had kept their headlamp packed away to conserve battery, lost footing and injured a knee at roughly 11,500 feet. Around midnight they stopped at about 11,000 feet in remote Mud Creek Canyon, a deep glacial canyon. The Forest Service said the party was not prepared to spend a night on the mountain and lacked adequate food, water, warm layers or an emergency bivy. At 9:30 a.m. the next morning, Forest Service climbing rangers reached the exhausted, hungry and thirsty climbers. After several attempts by the California Highway Patrol, an airlift was abandoned because of strong winds, so the group descended on their own with the rangers, reaching base camp at the Clear Creek springs around 3 p.m. Siskiyou Search and Rescue then guided them to the Clear Creek Trailhead, where the multiagency rescue ended around 6:30 p.m. All three came down safely. The Forest Service urged climbers to use reliable information sources for climbs like Shasta and to carry backups to electronic navigation, such as paper maps of the route. It also advised setting a turnaround time and sticking to it, and bringing enough food and water for a long day or two, plus adequate clothing and supplies in case of an unexpected night on the mountain. The Mount Shasta Avalanche Center offers guidance for planning a safer summit attempt.

The Lockheed C-5 Galaxy was first delivered to the US Air Force in 1970 and still flies today as the upgraded C-5M. It operated for decades without a glass cockpit because its 1960s design prioritized mechanical reliability over digital avionics, and retrofitting modern systems into a strategic airlifter 247 feet 10 inches (75.3 meters) long proved costly and complex. It moved to a digital flight deck with LCD displays for both pilots only in the 2010s, under Lockheed Martin's Avionics Modernization Program, though some analog backups and mechanical controls remain. It still requires a flight engineer. The C-5 was built to carry payloads exceeding 120 tons into austere environments where redundancy and field repairability outweigh automation, and it remains a backbone of Air Mobility Command operations. The short answer is that the C-5 first flew in 1968, when cockpit technology was entirely analog, and its military mission did not justify the cost of digital avionics until much later. Unlike commercial aircraft, which evolve quickly under competition and efficiency pressures, military aircraft favor proven systems that work in harsh, unpredictable conditions. The eventual C-5M Super Galaxy added a glass cockpit, upgraded engines and avionics. Four factors explain the delay. First, the aircraft came from a Cold War requirement for an intercontinental airlifter, and retrofitting a digital architecture decades later means redesigning how information is processed and distributed, not just swapping displays. Second, the C-5 carries tanks, helicopters and other outsized equipment into remote or hostile areas, where analog systems can be easier to troubleshoot and repair with simple tools. Third, fleet upgrades are expensive, and military budgets cannot rely on the fuel savings that justify airline investments, so modernization is delayed or phased. Fourth, the C-5's interconnected cargo-handling, flight-control and mission-planning systems make glass-cockpit integration technically difficult and time-consuming. Commercial and military priorities differ fundamentally. Airlines adopted glass cockpits because digital displays cut pilot workload, improve situational awareness and standardize training across fleets, all lowering costs. Military upgrades were gradual, focused on preserving mission readiness, and required extensive testing, certification and training. Military crews are also specialized by aircraft type, reducing the push for cockpit standardization. The Boeing 747, which first flew around the same time, offers a contrast. The 747-400, in service by the late 1980s, had a fully digital glass cockpit that let airlines cut the crew from three to two by eliminating the flight engineer. The C-5 faced no such pressure, since its priority was reliably moving massive loads, often from less developed airfields where robustness and simplicity matter more than automation. The C-5M, produced through the Avionics Modernization Program and the Reliability Enhancement and Re-engining Program, now has modern displays, advanced navigation and improved autopilot. The retrofit was difficult, requiring new hardware, redesigned information presentation, extensive testing and retraining of pilots and maintainers. Digital systems can also be harder to repair in some conditions, which is why the military modernizes cautiously. The lack of a glass cockpit reflected the aircraft's era, mission and priorities rather than technological backwardness. The C-5M combines a Cold War design with modern avionics while keeping the flight engineer, a rarity today.

Meta has formally ended what amounted to a "tokenmaxxing" incentive program, telling employees in an internal announcement this week that performance evaluations will no longer depend on how much they use AI tools, three employees told WIRED. Yet as workers begin testing a new agentic AI tool called Hatch, they say token consumption keeps surging. Almost a year ago, Meta said workers would be graded on their "AI-driven impact," which in practice meant assessing how much they used chatbots and agents in their work, Business Insider reported. According to a July lawsuit by about two dozen employees, usage correlated with labels such as "AI Native," "AI First," or "AI Enabled." The plaintiffs argue Meta violated US antidiscrimination laws in its May layoffs, saying workers on health and family leave couldn't accumulate usage and were unfairly penalized; Meta denies the allegations. New performance-review guidance replaces references to "usage of AI" and the "AI Native" designation with looser wording saying outcomes "can be supported by AI or other means," refocusing evaluation on impact however it is achieved. Some employees call the change subtle but welcome, since it frees them from pressure to use AI where it doesn't make sense. Spokesperson Tracy Clayton said the updates stress what has always been the case, that Meta evaluates contributions, and that labels like "AI Native" were never used for performance evaluation. The Information reported that engineers were told the company "will not use AI adoption dashboards or token counts to evaluate impact." For months, employees say, colleagues repeatedly or frivolously prompted AI tools to inflate usage metrics such as tokens consumed. The trend peaked when one worker built an internal leaderboard labeling people such as "Token Legend"; the employee took it down in April after details leaked. A couple of months later, Meta moved to ration AI usage. Meta now encourages, but doesn't require, use of Hatch, an agentic tool similar to OpenClaw that can autonomously browse the web and operate other applications. Employees have tested it on corporate devices for several weeks ahead of an expected public release. Some are hesitant to connect it to personal email, calendar, and other accounts, citing privacy worries and the risk of the AI botching something important. Meta previously ran a project, now paused, that tracked employees' keystrokes and other activity to gather AI training data, which eroded trust in its AI tools. Meta declined to comment on Hatch testing. Removing the performance penalty for sitting out AI testing could help rebuild morale and trust. Some employees already use Hatch for personal appointments and life organization and call it effective, though some worry about the environmental and economic costs of heavy token and computing use. Workers say Hatch still consumes more than earlier chatbots and coding assistants, and they believe management still wants them to prove they can wield AI effectively. Some employees fear that if Hatch boosts productivity, Meta could make further job cuts. Reuters reported last week that Meta had prepared another major layoff round on top of the 8,000 jobs cut in May but called it off amid more software bugs linked to AI reliance and slower-than-expected agent development. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said further mass layoffs are not expected this year.

Los Angeles Unified School District has quietly imposed a districtwide moratorium on student use of generative AI on school devices for the current school year, officials said. The step, which limits classroom computer use amid rising parent concerns about reliance on technology, surfaced at the first meeting of a school board committee on AI, surprising board members. The chief academic officer and head of technology told them generative AI would be out of reach for all students on district devices until further notice. Senior administrators imposed the moratorium on their own authority, in the spirit of complying with the board's unanimous June vote to limit student screen time. Under that policy, students have no screen access until second grade, and permitted time expands as students get older. Board member Kelly Gonez said she had believed the district was still following last year's policy, which made AI available to older students after digital literacy and responsibility units. Board member Nick Melvoin also expressed surprise and "discomfort" that the board had not authorized the step, though neither objected to it; he said it should be publicized. The disclosure came the same day New York City announced it will ban student-facing generative AI tools, such as chatbots and tutors, in preschool through eighth grade for the current year, affecting nearly 600,000 students. High schools will run five AI pilots, and every high school student must complete two 45-minute AI-literacy modules. Companion chatbots are prohibited in all grades, and a new screen-time policy was also set. L.A.'s total moratorium goes beyond New York's, but New York has a more specific immediate approach, while L.A. officials are working out their plans nearly from scratch. At least 37 states have issued AI guidance for schools, with no national definition or consensus on AI literacy. Activist parents who campaigned for an AI moratorium, including Bridie Lee of Schools Beyond Screens L.A., hailed the policy as historic. Common Sense Media's Yvette Renteria praised it, noting that AI literacy can be taught without students using AI, that many leading AI products are not designed for safety or learning, and that students use AI on personal devices even where it is banned. Syracuse University professor Jing Lei said that banning or allowing technology is not enough without examining the quality of its use. The district will still use non-generative AI, such as adaptive learning systems, speech-recognition tools, text-to-speech, live captioning and translation. Students can use Google search, but Google's "AI Mode" is turned off on student accounts and devices. Short AI-generated summaries may still appear atop results; Google is working on an update letting administrators disable that. The moratorium applies only to district-owned devices, and there is no policy yet for non-district devices, said Chief Academic Officer Pia Sadaqatmal. Interim chief information officer Douglas Le said AI access on personal devices while logged into school accounts can be tracked. Teachers are not barred from using AI, but no districtwide system exists for uses such as grading or identifying academic dishonesty. Screen-time limits for younger students took effect at the start of school and are being phased in for older students.

Genesys is stepping up its push into agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as enterprises move from experimenting with AI to deploying systems that coordinate actions across customer service operations. At its Xperience 2026 event in Las Vegas, the company said Genesys Cloud reached nearly USD 2.9 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027 (May 1–July 31, 2026), up more than 30% year on year. Genesys Cloud AI ARR crossed USD 400 million, growing at more than twice the rate of overall Genesys Cloud ARR. The company also reported net revenue retention of more than 120% for over 12 consecutive quarters. For the first half of fiscal 2027, total revenue grew more than 20% year on year, GAAP and non-GAAP operating margins exceeded 30%, and free cash flow topped USD 500 million. Chairman and CEO Tony Bates said agentic AI is changing how companies operate around the customer, and that enterprises are shifting from AI experimentation to adoption at scale, increasing the need for context, governance and orchestration. Genesys is positioning orchestration as the next layer in enterprise customer experience AI. Rather than deploying individual AI agents for isolated tasks, the approach coordinates AI agents, employees, enterprise applications and workflows around a customer's intent, carrying context across stages of an interaction. More than 7,500 organisations use Genesys Cloud, including over 600 that each generate more than USD 1 million in ARR. Customers cited include HSBC, Nestlé, Roche, Schneider Electric, Vanguard, Vodafone, Independence Blue Cross and IDEXX Laboratories. The platform handles more than 33 billion voice, digital and AI-driven conversations and more than 6.5 billion sentiment events annually, and processes over 1 trillion API invocations a year. Genesys introduced more than 600 Genesys Cloud features over the past 12 months. The latest product push centres on Genesys Cloud Navigator, Genesys Cloud Orchestrator, Contextual Intelligence and an AI Control Plane, forming a common layer to understand intent, preserve context, decide the next action and govern increasingly autonomous AI. Navigator helps determine the next appropriate action across a customer journey; Orchestrator coordinates workflows, AI agents, systems and people; Contextual Intelligence retains customer and interaction context; and the AI Control Plane adds governance. The key enterprise question is increasingly whether an AI agent can work safely across systems and complete tasks without losing context or creating disconnected hand-offs. Genesys is also expanding its Agentic Virtual Agent offering with enhanced reasoning, voice capabilities, development tools and connections to enterprise systems. Its acquisition of Pinkfish gives customers access to more than 25,000 compatible tools, in addition to more than 500 enterprise integrations in the Genesys ecosystem, which could let virtual agents take actions across business systems and resolve more complex requests. Genesys is also expanding integrations and collaborations with Adobe, Amazon Web Services, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Salesforce, ServiceNow and Sierra. As autonomous agents proliferate, the challenge shifts from building individual AI capabilities to controlling how multiple agents, applications, workflows and employees interact. Orchestration could determine whether agentic AI remains a set of experiments or becomes part of mainstream enterprise operations.

HUGO, Okla. (KXII) – A social media trend using artificial intelligence to create threatening images has spread to schools in Texoma, according to Choctaw County Undersheriff Ronald Miller. Trend uses AI-generated characters. Miller said the trend involves people taking pictures of locations and using AI to insert characters, such as the Cat in the Hat or Jason, into the images. Miller said the characters are shown standing near school grounds and are accompanied by threatening messages. “I’m coming, I’ll be there Monday, get ready, it’s a vague threat but you have to take it seriously,” Miller said. Video posted about Hugo schools. A video directed at Hugo Public Schools was posted this past weekend. Miller said the post shifted his office into overdrive. “We’ve been checking bags and everything else and we’ve had a heightened presence at most of the schools all week long,” Miller said. Investigators say all campuses are safe. Coleman, Rock Creek and Tishomingo schools are among some other local schools that have been named in TikTok posts. Difficult to tell what’s real. Miller said advances in artificial intelligence have made it harder to immediately identify what is real and what is fake. “With AI and chatgpt it’s real easy to just ask chat to do it and it does it,” Miller said. Miller said the trend is not a joke, and participating in it could lead to criminal charges. “It can be a terroristic threat which is if the school feels fear from the statement and that is an arrestable offense,” Miller said. Advice for parents. Miller said parents should monitor their children’s online activity. “See what they’re into, everybody’s got a cell phone it’s real easy to look into things and you just gotta be vigilant,” Miller said.

The author, Mike Adams, argues that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's recent public claim that data centers don't use water is a deliberate lie. He notes that Lutnick acknowledged a year earlier that these facilities need large volumes of water for cooling, and he accuses Lutnick, Trump and others of running a top-down misinformation campaign to fast-track Big Tech's control of the energy grid and water supply. Adams cites figures released by the tech companies: Google consumed 7.7 billion gallons of water in 2024 and Amazon's AWS division 2.5 billion. A typical data center uses about 300,000 gallons per day, while hyperscale facilities can use upwards of 5 million gallons daily each. Roughly 40% of new data centers are being built in high-stress or extreme-stress water regions. Most of this water is lost to open-loop evaporative cooling, removed permanently from local aquifers and rivers. He warns that entire regions of the U.S. could collapse from groundwater depletion within a generation. He says direct cooling is only part of the footprint. In 2023, power plants serving U.S. data centers consumed an estimated 211 billion gallons of water, over ten times the direct cooling volume. Coal, nuclear and especially natural gas plants all use water, and he notes that gas turbines at a new Pennsylvania AI data center also require water for injection and cooling. Adams rejects the defense that newer closed-loop systems consume no water. Even these must periodically purge water, called blowdown, to manage mineral concentration. He says this discharge contains corrosion inhibitors, heavy metals, nitrites and in many cases PFAS "forever chemicals," and is dumped into sewers, rivers and aquifers with virtually no federal oversight or transparency requirements. He calls hyperscale data centers a major point-source polluter and criticizes the EPA's silence. He says the expansion is hitting stressed regions such as Texas and Arizona, where aquifers are already at critical lows. In Texas, projected data center water use would rise from an estimated 49 billion gallons in 2025 to nearly 400 billion gallons by 2030, taking water from farmers and ranchers. He disputes Trump's claim that limiting data centers would leave the country "backwards and poor," calling it a matter of human survival. Adams concludes that the claim data centers don't use water is a barefaced lie meant to give technocrats control of natural resources, and that water is a human right, not a corporate commodity. He says he is not anti-technology, describing himself as a promoter of open source AI and off-grid robotic automation, but demands honesty and accountability from the industry. He calls on readers to resist framing resource protection as backward thinking and to prioritize life and liberty over the promises of tech giants.

Nvidia is buying artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Chipmaker Nvidia is buying artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. It’s the latest deal by the company, whose processors are integral to the AI boom, and highlights Nvidia’s push to champion increasingly popular open-source AI models. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote in a blog post Thursday that more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 data sets and 1 million applications. More than 200,000 companies also that use the platform, he said. In July, Hugging Face’s data processing systems were hacked, and ChatGPT maker OpenAI acknowledged that its artificial intelligence system was to blame, sending shock waves through the security community amid heightened concerns about the capabilities of powerful AI models. Just over a week later, Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing. That was followed closely by an announcement from Meta, which said its AI model accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. The wave of AI intrusions occurred just a month after President Donald Trump signed an executive order creating a framework for the federal government to vet the national security risks of the most advanced AI systems for up to a month before their public release. On Thursday, however, Nvidia’s Huang said that Hugging face will remain an open platform. He signaled that Nvidia is betting that more businesses will turn to open-source AI, which lets them download and customize their own AI models, rather than pay for proprietary AI services from companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch,” Huang wrote in a blog post. “They enable organizations to match the right model to the right job. Hugging Face will still support multicloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment. Nvidia has released more than 500 models and more than 250 open data sets on Hugging Face. “Nvidia’s investment in Hugging Face is a strong strategic hedge against the different ways AI could evolve,” Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at global business and technology consulting firm West Monroe, said in an emailed statement. “With much of Nvidia’s valuation tied to the adoption and expansion of AI over the next decade, the company has a clear interest in supporting the entire ecosystem’s success.” Nvidia’s high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI, and are highly sought after. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion late last month. While AI has powered stock market gains and U.S. economic growth in recent years, there’s been growing skepticism about whether AI will justify the trillions of dollars being spent to develop the technology. The AI industry is also faces increasing pushback amid objections to the expansion of data centers and fears that the rapid speed of AI adoption could lead to widespread job losses worldwide. The $12.93 billion deal includes $1 billion for a retention plan for Hugging Face employees, Huang told CNBC. Nvidia’s shares rose nearly 2% in morning trading. Hugging Face is not publicly traded. ___. AP Business Writer Kelvin Chan contributed to this report.

NEW YORK -- New York City's public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday. The one-year moratorium -- part of a broader assessment of how children in the nation's largest school system interact with the technology -- will apply to "all software that uses student-facing generative AI" for students through eighth grade, the mayor's office said. It described the policy as the most expansive prohibition in the country. At the same time, the city is establishing twice-yearly AI literacy classes for all public high school students. It will also launch pilot programs allowing some high school students to use a handful of AI platforms under an educator's supervision. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, officials said. The approach comes as students, parents and schools across the country attempt to navigate the use of AI tools in the classroom and elsewhere. Schools are working to teach children how to incorporate the technology while preventing them from relying too heavily on it or using it to cheat. "Each day when our children come to school, we teach them to ask questions, to challenge assumptions, to interrogate the premise, to ask why. When it comes to AI in our schools, we hold an obligation to do the same," Mamdani, a Democrat, said at a news conference. The city will also recommend screen-time limits for students, suggesting a cap of 30 minutes a day for students in grades three through five and 45 minutes for students in grades six through eight. Teachers will be allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks. At least 37 states have official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint, though there is no single definition of AI literacy or consensus on how it should be taught. New York state last year approved a ban on students' use of cellphones in schools. City education officials will also conduct a broad review of all technology tools used in the school system and eliminate those deemed nonessential to learning. Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York, praised the screen-time limits but said the city's AI policy "leaves many questions unanswered," including how the Education Department "will be more aggressive in demanding the products it purchases have AI safeguards." Josh Golin, executive director of the children's advocacy group Fairplay, said he would have preferred a longer moratorium and more time between the announcement and the start of the school year. "A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time," he said, adding that the onus should be on AI platforms "to demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they're safe, that they're not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they're not leading to rampant cheating." New York City public school students are scheduled to return to the classroom next week.

Data center developers increasingly must "bring your own energy" (BYOE) rather than choose it, as power availability has become the most significant constraint on development. Projects face yearslong delays before utility capacity is available, and proposed legislation in multiple jurisdictions could require developers to generate 100% of the electricity their facilities consume. BYOE demands far more capital than a traditional model and can materially affect project returns, so a site that looks attractive on land, incentives, and customer demand may become more expensive once a private power solution is required. Tax planning won't eliminate these costs but can raise after-tax cash flow and reduce overall investment cost. Because choices about generation technology, ownership structure, procurement, and timing determine eligibility for federal tax credits, accelerated depreciation, and other incentives, tax planning should occur alongside engineering and design, not after construction begins. Section 48E, the clean electricity investment credit, may offer the greatest opportunity to offset upfront BYOE investment. Depending on technology, ownership structure, labor compliance, sourcing, and timing, it may provide a credit equal to 30% to 50% or more of the eligible investment in qualifying energy storage property and clean electricity generation. Battery energy storage may be the most universally applicable opportunity. Standalone batteries used for resilience, peak-load management, or power quality may qualify even if they draw electricity from the grid or nonqualifying sources, with the credit generally applying to the eligible basis of the battery property. Generating equipment may also qualify, but the technology must have a net-zero greenhouse gas emissions rate. Eligible technologies can include solar and wind (typically must be placed into service by the end of 2027) and qualifying nuclear, geothermal, and hydropower (generally eligible through 2035). Choosing qualifying zero-emission generation over a conventional natural-gas system could materially improve project economics. Maximizing the credit depends on the technology selected, construction and placed-in-service dates, eligible tax basis, and satisfaction of labor and other requirements, including prevailing-wage and apprenticeship, domestic content, and energy-community location rules. These should be evaluated during design and procurement, since after construction it may be too late. Section 48E is only one part of a broader strategy. Even when power assets don't qualify for energy credits, developers may still save through accelerated depreciation, repair deductions, and state and local incentives. The most successful projects will treat energy credits, depreciation, repair deductions, and state and local incentives as a coordinated plan rather than separate after-the-fact exercises. The greatest tax benefits are often determined before construction begins. Developers should consider which entity will own each asset, which technologies may qualify for Section 48E, whether labor and sourcing requirements can be met, which assets may qualify for accelerated depreciation, whether cost segregation should be built into project cost tracking, whether state and local incentives apply, and how tax benefits and recapture risks will be allocated among the parties. Engineering, procurement, and construction contracts and cost reports often group costs into broad categories, and many opportunities become difficult or impossible to recover once equipment is purchased, contracts executed, construction underway, and assets capitalized. Involving tax advisers early helps maximize incentives, minimize compliance risk, and avoid "buyer's remorse" from discovering benefits after key decisions are made.

New York City’s Department of Education is announcing a new policy that bans generative AI tools for students from early childhood through eighth grade, along with new limits on classroom device use. New York’s largest teachers union passed its own resolution in late May calling for limits on both screentime and artificial intelligence in schools. Hikers who used AI to plan mountain trip had to be rescued, authorities say. MT. SHASTA, Calif. (KMAX/KOVR) - Authorities say three novice hikers got stranded on California’s Mount Shasta after they relied on artificial intelligence to plan the trip. The Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office says three young men got stuck on the mountain Sunday during their descent. After reaching the summit at 7 p.m., they decided to hike back down in the dark but got lost. One of them fell and injured his knee, and they became stranded, authorities said. A sheriff’s office search and rescue team and a U.S. Forest Service Climbing Rangers team rescued the men Monday. After their rescue, one man told a sheriff’s deputy they had relied heavily on Google’s Gemini, an AI chatbot, for information about the route and for what to pack. “This was a critical misstep, as they were advised by Gemini to bring far less food and water than their group required, especially when their planned 8-hour ascent became a multi-day ordeal,” said the sheriff’s office in a press release. Authorities are now reminding people that AI is not always a reliable resource. “It tends to want to give you favorable information and also make you seem like you’re kind of invincible, and I think that that causes problems, especially when something can be extremely dangerous. AI can be a good tool, but it shouldn’t be used as the expert. Go talk to actual people,” Sheriff Jeremiah Larue said. Hikers on Mt. Shasta are advised to turn back by noon, even if they haven’t reached the summit, so they still have enough daylight to hike out, the sheriff’s office said. They are also advised to have multiple methods of wayfinding, not solely relying on a smartphone or smartwatch, and to stop and check they’re on the correct route often.

Faber is designed for industrial work, and the four-legged Aegis is being tested for security and perimeter control.
