Chen said they will supplement human work, not replace it, improving efficiency and creating new jobs.

More than half of the candidates for Chicago's school board have signed a pledge calling for a three-year moratorium on generative AI in Chicago Public Schools. By Wednesday, 24 of the 42 candidates on the ballot had signed, including all 15 endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, which represents the district's more than 30,000 teachers and other staff. The pledge, "Pledge to Protect Human-Centered Education," was written by Illinois Families for Public Schools, an advocacy nonprofit. It also asks the new 21-member elected board to limit screen time in all grades, prohibit collection of biometric information and appoint a chief privacy officer. The group asked every candidate to sign. Author Charles Tocci said the pledge stems from worries that new technology may harm student privacy and learning outcomes. A father of three CPS students, he said his family's information has been leaked several times, once through a CPS-affiliated vendor. He cited Amira Learning, a reading platform some CPS teachers use that collects students' voice and biometric data, saying the data is identifiable and tied to specific students. Amira's website says it does not use biometric data or voices to identify students. The pledge alleges Google Gemini was planned for high school curricula this school year. CPS said the "aspirational plan" was halted in May to prioritize school readiness and educator training, that it has no current plans for broad Gemini access, and that the application is turned off on all student devices. Other districts have acted: New York City plans a temporary AI ban for public school students through eighth grade, and Los Angeles eliminated district-issued devices through first grade. Cassie Creswell, president of Illinois Families for Public Schools, said the idea that kids will fall behind without tech is misguided and that the board needs to step up. Elected board member Ellen Rosenfeld, who represents District 4B and is running unopposed, declined to sign. She supports some AI restrictions but doubts a blanket ban's efficacy, saying it limits opportunities to teach responsible technology use and that pretending AI doesn't exist would be harmful. DePaul University associate professor An Chih Cheng said AI has positive uses, such as visual models of complex topics and diagnosing developmental disabilities like autism. Still, he recommends board members sign, citing little concrete evidence that AI helps students learn and saying kids should not be the testing ground for technologies. The pledge also seeks screen-time limits, including a total ban on one-to-one device use, including school-provided computers and iPads, before third grade. Creswell said the conversation should extend beyond cellphones, which Illinois will ban in public and charter schools starting in the 2027-28 school year under a law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker. Cheng said studies show screens do not meaningfully improve learning outcomes, though computers need not be removed from classrooms.

Memecoins paired against Robinhood's tokenized stocks generated $217 million of trading volume on Robinhood Chain on Sept. 2, according to on-chain researcher Adam Tehc, outpacing the $127 million traded through direct stock token markets that day. Robinhood describes stock tokens as ERC-20 tokenized debt securities giving economic exposure to an underlying stock without legal or beneficial ownership in the issuer. New supply can only be minted by a single authorized participant, identified at issuance as BBVI; everyone else trades and builds with tokens already in circulation, permissionlessly. A memecoin called BONER accumulated 31,198 of the 58,714 HIMS stock tokens then outstanding, about 53% of the tokenized supply, with another 1,424 in separate meme pools. That left roughly 20,303 tokens in conventional pairs against stablecoins and ETH. While the New York Stock Exchange was closed for the weekend, the HIMS token printed as high as $132.64, versus a $28.84 close for the underlying stock the previous Friday, a premium of about 4.6 times. The 58,714 tokens equal about 0.025% of Hims & Hers' roughly 233.3 million shares outstanding, and the stock's equity market was untouched. When the underlying market reopened, BBVI minted about 4,000 new HIMS tokens, worth about $115,000 at Friday's close and 6.8% of prior supply, enough to pull the price back toward the stock's value. The vulnerability lies in who controls new supply and when it can be created. On Robinhood Chain, HIMS or Nvidia stock tokens become the denominator memecoins are priced against. Robinhood's oracle feeds update 24 hours a day, five days a week, on the exchange schedule, while the tokens trade around the clock, so a weekend print more likely signals stress in a thin wrapper than a repriced stock. Robinhood's terms say it does not control what third parties build and cannot reverse submitted transactions; its filings warn such activity may be hard to monitor or prevent while still exposing it to reputational, legal or regulatory consequences. Regulators are watching. The SEC said in January that representing a security on a crypto network does not change which federal securities laws apply. The World Federation of Exchanges has warned of issues around market integrity, disclosure and post-trade standards. Nasdaq's approved tokenization framework and DTCC's tokenization service keep tokenized securities on the same order books and under the same rights as conventional shares. Citi's base case projects roughly $5.5 trillion in tokenized assets by 2030. On-chain speculation may grow less dependent on BTC, ETH and stablecoins if tokenized equities keep working as collateral and quote assets. In the bull case, stock tokens move into lending, collateral and index products, direct activity overtakes memecoin-pair volume, and Robinhood Chain's RWA activity multiplies from today's roughly $188 million base. In the bear case, volumes stay dominated by reflexive meme pools and low-float squeezes like the HIMS episode, regulators focus on disclosure and market-integrity risk, and Robinhood's fee opportunity comes with the reputational exposure its filings warn about.

Technology usually starts out clunky, slow and expensive, and improvements accelerate as it becomes more useful. When Eniac was built by the University of Pennsylvania for the U.S. Army in 1946, it weighed about 30 tons, had 18,000 vacuum tubes, ran at about 5,000 additions per second and cost about $9 million in today's dollars. A typical laptop now does more than 3 billion calculations per second for around $1,000. Quantum computing is at a pre-Eniac stage but is close to a milestone, and dozens of large companies are preparing for it. Quantum computers promise to accelerate drug and materials research, improve logistics routing and financial risk management, and play a key role in encryption and cybersecurity. First, they must overcome the error problem. Classical computers use bits of 1s and 0s and run operations sequentially. Qubits can hold both 0 and 1 (superposition), scale exponentially, and explore many states simultaneously, which allows far more complex calculations. But qubits are delicate: vibrations, heat and even cosmic rays can collapse the quantum state and cause errors. The remedy is the error-corrected, or logical, qubit, in which information is encoded across several qubits for redundancy so erroneous ones can be culled. Future machines may have tens of thousands of logical qubits, but scaling will take time and perhaps unforeseen breakthroughs. Most agree the threshold for a practical machine that leaves classical computers behind is 100 logical qubits. That bar could be reached as early as next year. Quantinuum plans to release its Sol computer in 2027 with 100 logical qubits, up from its currently available Helios machine with 48. IBM announced last month it achieved 70 logical qubits in an experiment with the University of Chicago. Infleqtion expects its latest design to provide more than 50 logical qubits next year while scaling toward 100. Infleqtion CTO and co-founder Pranav Gokhale said 100 logical qubits is where machines can begin solving important problems in material science and chemistry, perhaps AI too, that classical computers cannot. Approaches differ, complicating progress tracking. IBM, Google and Rigetti Computing use human-made qubits etched and wired on a chip; these scale more easily but have higher error rates from initial imperfections and heat from the wiring. Other designs use natural particles. Atoms are trapped with magnetic fields and manipulated with lasers; photonic processors control photons with beam splitters and phase shifters. These qubits start out perfect but errors arise when they are moved, and the machines are harder to scale. Infleqtion uses neutral atoms, Quantinuum uses charged atoms (ions), and PsiQuantum uses photons. It is too early to tell which path will win, and multiple solutions may coexist. In May the Commerce Department selected nine companies for $2 billion of funding, covering varied designs, including IBM, Rigetti, Quantinuum, Infleqtion and PsiQuantum. A sign of progress is that the discussion has shifted from whether quantum computing will ever be valuable to error correction and logical qubits. With 100 or more logical qubits, the quantum-computing age will have arrived, even if the machines resemble their ungainly vacuum-tube predecessor.

Every high schooler will also sit two 45-minute AI literacy modules a year, covering what the technology is, along with bias, risks, ethics and career impacts. Teachers keep AI for lesson planning and operational work where tools meet the city's safety standards. Exceptions also cover assistive technology for students with disabilities, multilingual learners and career readiness programs such as computer science. Screen time will be tightened, too. Students in second grade and below face restricted one-to-one device use, with recommended caps of 30 minutes a day in grades three to five and 45 minutes in grades six to eight. Every technology tool in city schools now faces review, and will be dropped if its functionality is judged not mission-critical to learning. A new Technology in Schools Coalition of students, educators, parents, unions, advocates and elected officials will assess the moratorium and the pilots, then publish recommendations for later years. Julie Samuels, who leads the trade group Tech:NYC and sits on the coalition, welcomed the career-readiness access and recommended expanding it beyond an hour a week in future, citing a recent report that New York City now has more tech jobs than the Bay Area. Classes resume September 10.

Dyson held its "Dyson Unveiled" event at IFA 2026 in Berlin, with presenter Jake Dyson, son of founder James Dyson, taking the stage around 4:30PM CET (10:30AM ET). The live stream ran late and suffered technical problems; the YouTube premiere appeared only after the event began. UK bureau chief Mat Smith attended in person. James Dyson had already unveiled the CameraJet toothbrush in Paris earlier in the week, and some product listings leaked on Best Buy beforehand. The CameraJet is a toothbrush-flosser hybrid with a 1 mm² camera, powered by "optical gap targeting." Its camera is trained by machine learning on over 470,000 dental images. Engineer Niamh Turner said oral-care tech hadn't changed since the 1980s, calling it "a real problem to solve." The water stream is designed not to needle like traditional water picks, and a water tank uses suction and pressure to maintain the stream without waste. A companion app offers a live view mode, and a non-foaming toothpaste lets the camera see the gumline. In floor care, Dyson introduced a new robot vacuum range called Nurobi, starting with the R3, billed as its most advanced cleaner to date. The R3 uses IR and green light to detect otherwise invisible stains and then removes them, via Spot+Scrub AI technology. The R2 Wash and Dry uses an off-center gear with a curved triangular pad to clean tight square corners better than circular brushes. The upgraded W1 PencilWash standing mop has the company's most absorbent microfiber roller yet, is easier to clean than predecessors, and self-cleans when docked. In air purification, the newest HushJet purifier can process 1,200 m³ of air and uses nozzles designed to keep airflow powerful yet quiet. The HushJet comes in various sizes under the name Big + Quiet. In beauty, Dyson showed a new hot air brush designed to avoid damage from uneven or excessive heat, with pivot flex bristles that flex up to 90 degrees. The CoolShine hair straightener has its own cooling attachment and sealed heat-extracting pipes containing distilled water, reducing heat exposure. The beauty devices have universal voltage. Dyson also announced MyDyson, a new customer platform combining customer service, tutorials and repair support, including a servicing offering that refurbishes devices to near-new condition. Its motto is "Never without my Dyson." A recap tallied one toothbrush, one Pencilvac, three robovacs, two to three purifiers and a hair styling tool, with product counts differing depending on whether SKUs and sizes are included.

Quick Take. - The FBI seized Hamas-linked domains and servers after tracing and recovering more than $560,000 in cryptocurrency. - Control of the infrastructure let agents move beyond tracing past transfers and begin intercepting new donations intended for the group. - DOJ has not disclosed how much additional crypto was captured through the seized systems. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) seized Hamas-linked fundraising infrastructure and used it to intercept cryptocurrency donations intended for the group. Earlier this week, the Justice Department said the operation followed earlier court-authorized seizures that traced and recovered more than $560,000 in digital assets tied to Hamas fundraising. Those seizures came through warrants issued in March, June and October 2025 after investigators followed rotating donation addresses distributed through encrypted chats and fundraising websites. The June warrant showed how that process worked. Tether was ordered to burn targeted USDT and reissue an equivalent amount to a US law-enforcement-controlled address, while Binance was directed to transfer specified account balances into FBI-controlled wallets. That approach allowed investigators to recover crypto after identifying where it had moved. Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the FBI Albuquerque Field Office said: “Reducing the capabilities of foreign terrorist organization's ability to receive donations and creating distrust in communications to their donors was the primary focus of this latest operation. This continued success demonstrates the unwavering commitment and determination of the FBI in fighting terrorism.” FBI moved from tracing funds to intercepting them. Investigators targeted domains and servers linked to AlQassam.ps, a website the DOJ tied to the Al Qassam Brigades, Hamas’ military wing. Affidavits filed in July and August said authenticated responses from were routed through host.alaqsaflood.org, helping investigators connect fundraising communications to related infrastructure. The FBI’s Albuquerque Field Office then worked with human sources to identify and seize domains and servers associated with the operation. Control of that infrastructure changed the scope of the investigation. DOJ said agents were able to intercept crypto donations intended for Hamas and obtain additional information about people attempting to contribute. That turned the case from a retrospective tracing effort into an active disruption operation. DOJ said the broader investigation produced information about thousands of people who contacted Hamas online seeking to donate through cryptocurrency or traditional payment methods. The department did not specify how much of that information came directly from the seized servers. The disclosure also does not establish that every person identified completed a donation or committed an offense. However, this shows how several enforcement tools converged: blockchain tracing identified the money, court orders moved assets through centralized crypto providers, and infrastructure seizures gave investigators control over the fundraising channels themselves.

Flock cameras and other automated license plate reader (ALPR) systems have become nearly ubiquitous on U.S. roads. As many as 140,000 ALPR cameras are installed in American cities, with roughly 110,000 to 120,000 made by Flock, though no one seems to know the exact number. That number is shrinking: 93 cities and counties moved to end their Flock contracts in the past 30 days, bringing rescinded contracts to well over 200 in the past year. Opponents cite privacy rights and the likelihood of misuse. Flock cameras use an AI algorithm to upload information into a nationwide database searchable by agencies across the country. Oversight of access and use is limited, data storage guidelines are inconsistent, and there has been little accountability for misuse. The author notes that new technology typically takes months or years to get protective regulations, and that Flock is rapidly revising its guidelines and policies to show it takes privacy and accountability seriously. Defenders of ALPRs make a strong case that the cameras are highly effective at solving and deterring crime. Flock's website claims 700,000 crimes per year are solved with its cameras' help, about 10% of reported U.S. crime, which would mean wider adoption makes everyone safer. The author argues that opposition persists because people are deeply suspicious of AI's expanding intrusion into daily life, and that this suspicion is turning into anger. Because Flock cameras are visible examples of AI intrusion, they become targets, much as data centers do, except that ALPRs are nearly everywhere. People object not only to possible misuse but to the cameras' very purpose: most don't want every movement recorded and analyzed, even if it makes them demonstrably safer, even if the cameras never err, and even if they are never misused. Behind these concerns lies the question of whether AI will serve us or we will serve it. A recent Gallup survey found only 9% of Americans believe AI will do more good than harm, and only 27% trust businesses to use AI responsibly. Tech companies seem to think delivering results will earn trust, but the author argues trust is built through relationships, not just results. Even if Flock cameras make communities safer and oversight, accountability and reliability improve, greater use will further depersonalize local government agencies, including law enforcement, eroding trust. As an illustration, the author notes that Flock's website greeted him with an AI Sales Assistant offering to answer questions about its privacy and data policies. The author concludes that the greatest challenge facing society in the coming years is rebuilding trust in institutions and in one another, and that tech companies and eager adopters of new gadgets fail to understand that it is all about relationships.

On Wednesday, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi announced the company will be cutting 3,300 jobs, a tenth of its workforce worldwide. It’s the biggest cut since COVID, when the ride-share app cut 14% of its workforce, amounting to 3,700 jobs. “This wasn’t a decision we made lightly, because it will have a real impact on our teammates and friends who have worked hard for Uber,” Khosrowshahi wrote in a letter to employees. “It’s important to say that these changes are about how we’re organized and what we’re prioritizing, not about anyone’s contributions to Uber, which we will always value.” Khosrowshahi said that the cuts were not because of a downturn in the economy—in fact he acknowledged Uber “has grown by orders of magnitude” in the past five years. Instead, it was simply because Uber had gotten too big to manage, and the cuts would help the company run “faster and smarter.” Uber made a 20% reduction in the number of employees who were seven layers or more removed from the CEO. The company also cut the number of “micro-teams” (those with only one or two direct reports) by half, and combined each delivery operations team in the restaurant, retail, and direct divisions into one big team. “The outcome is a simpler org chart geared toward building versus managing,” he wrote. “Running these three businesses separately made sense in their early days, but that structure is no longer serving us at scale.” Khosrowshahi said the decision was informed by conversations with employees who indicated that the company spent too much time coordinating instead of “building, shipping, or serving customers.” Uber shares were up 1.61%, reaching $76.45 at closing time. Khosrowshahi said the expected savings from making Uber leaner will be reinvested “in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years,” one of which is putting more self-driving cars on the road in Uber’s network. “Our opportunity from here is enormous: We have the chance to bring Uber to hundreds of millions more people; to invest even more in drivers, couriers, and merchants; and to innovate across our core businesses and build the autonomous future,” Khosrowshahi wrote. Uber’s president and chief operating officer Andrew Macdonald said that nobody will own a car in the next 15 to 20 years because it’s a depreciating asset that sits idle most of the time, and that other forms of transport like self-driving cars and bikes will fill the void. “I think autonomous vehicles will be part of that,” Macdonald said last month. Uber’s ongoing $10 billion bet on self-driving cars. Uber originally launched its autonomous vehicle unit, Advanced Technologies Group (ATG), in 2020; its over $7 billion valuation accounted for more than 10% of its $61 billion market cap at the time. But Uber ended up selling the ATG research division to a startup by the end of the year, recognizing that it didn’t have the money to develop its own robotaxis. But the company didn’t give up on self-driving cars, pivoting to deploying them with partners like Rivian, Baidu, and Pony.ai in the Uber network. The ride-share app now expects to commit $10 billion to help bring them to market at scale, with 120,000 cars committed by partners. Khosrowshahi described this goal on the Q2 2026 earnings call as making Uber the “world’s leading commercialization platform for autonomous vehicles.” “Those results give us the ability to continue investing from a position of strength,” Khosrowshahi said. “We also continue to invest behind one of the largest opportunities in Uber’s history: autonomous vehicles.”

When you think of AI, you likely think of the chatbot on the phone in your pocket, beaming information from far off data centers that power large language models like ChatGPT or Claude. But AI is striving to become more tangible — humanoid, in fact. Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, the global head of equities at UBS, says that humanoid robots are increasingly able to use "in-context" learning, where they learn how to do something by observing an action or task. In a recent note to clients, Hoffmann-Burchardi said that "we are now at the precipice of moving away from preprogrammed automation and stepping into genuine physical autonomy." The theme presents a new frontier of AI investment, she said, highlighting three picks-and-shovels sectors of the AI robotics trade to play. 1. Actuators and precision gears. Actuators drive movement in a robot, and gears facilitate that movement. These parts will be crucial to humanoid robots' agility. "These are highly specialized components that allow a robot to move its fingers with millimeter precision or balance its weight on an uneven floor," Hoffmann-Burchardi wrote in the note. "Manufacturing capacity is heavily concentrated in just a few specialized firms worldwide." While Hoffmann-Burchardi didn't name any particular companies, examples of stocks in this space include Rockwell Automation (ROK) and ABB (ABBNY). 2. The sensor and perception layer. Sensors are what will allow robots to take in data in real time. This can come in the form of cameras, so a robot can see and copy an action. But it also means a robot's "skin," which allows it to be able to feel and measure. "For a robot to pick up a fragile egg or a heavy iron wrench without breaking or dropping it, it needs a type of skin that can measure pressure and friction instantly," Hoffmann-Burchardi said. Some examples of firms in the space include Synaptics Incorporated (SYNA), Ouster (OUST), and Luminar Technologies (LAZR). 3. Edge computing and power infrastructure. These robots will need computing power to process information, as well as power sources that can fuel the robots for long periods of time. Robotic-specific hardware will be needed, Hoffmann-Burchardi said. Examples include Nvidia (NVDA), Arm Holdings (ARM), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). Your guide to what's moving markets.

Uber to lay off 3,300 employees as competition with robotaxis grow. Ride-share giant Uber announced plans to lay off nearly 10% of its workforce as growing competition from autonomous vehicles and robotaxis heats up the ride-hailing industry. What they're saying: Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told employees Wednesday that about 3,300 of the company’s 34,000 workers will be laid off, marking Uber’s largest round of job cuts since the COVID-19 pandemic. Khosrowshahi said the restructuring is intended to reduce layers of management and organizational complexity that have slowed decision-making. "A leaner organization will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years," Khosrowshahi said. What we know: The restructuring will reduce by 20% the number of employees working seven or more levels below the CEO, while cutting in half the number of teams with managers who oversee only one or two direct reports. RELATED: Same rides, different prices: Uber and Lyft draw fire from Consumer Reports over fares. The other side: Autonomous vehicles and driverless ride-hailing services have expanded rapidly in recent years, with Alphabet’s Waymo launching its commercial robotaxi service in 2018. While Waymo currently offers rides through Uber in two U.S. cities, it is also expanding into additional markets independently. Competition is also growing from Amazon’s Zoox and Tesla’s Cybercab, raising concerns that the expanding robotaxi industry could eventually challenge Uber’s dominant position in the ride-hailing business. Dig deeper: In the announcement, Khosrowshahi stopped short of blaming the layoffs on AI, which has increasingly been cited by tech executives as a factor behind workforce reductions across the industry. Uber, however, has been aggressively adopting the technology, reportedly driving up costs in the process. According to media reports, employees exhausted the company’s entire 2026 AI budget in just four months. The Source: This story was written with information provided by Reuters and previous reporting by LiveNOW from FOX. This story was reported from Orlando.

Chipmaker Nvidia is buying artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote in a blog post Thursday that more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 data sets and 1 million applications. There’s also more than 200,000 companies that use the platform, he said. In July, the data processing systems of Hugging Face were hacked and ChatGPT maker OpenAI acknowledged that its artificial intelligence system was to blame, sending shock waves through the security community amid heightened concerns about the capabilities of powerful AI models. Just over a week later, Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing, and that as followed closely by an announcement from Meta, which said its AI model accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. The wave of AI intrusions occurred just a month after President Donald Trump signed an executive order creating a framework for the federal government to vet the national security risks of the most advanced AI systems for up to a month before their public release. On Thursday, however, Nvidia’s Huang said that Hugging face will remain an open platform. “Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want,” Huang wrote in a blog post. “Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.” Hugging Face will still support multi-cloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment. Nvidia has released more than 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets. “Nvidia’s investment in Hugging Face is a strong strategic hedge against the different ways AI could evolve,” Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at global business and technology consulting firm West Monroe, said in an emailed statement. “With much of Nvidia’s valuation tied to the adoption and expansion of AI over the next decade, the company has a clear interest in supporting the entire ecosystem’s success.” Nvidia’s high-end chips have emerged as AI’s best building blocks and they are highly sought after. The Santa Clara, California-based company late last month reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion. While AI has powered stock market gains and U.S. economic growth in recent years, there’s been growing skepticism about whether AI will justify the trillions of dollars that are being spent to develop the technology. The AI industry is also increasingly facing pushback amid objections to the expansion in data centers and fears that the speed with which AI is being adopted could lead to widespread job losses worldwide. Nvidia’s shares rose nearly 2% in morning trading. Hugging Face is not publicly traded.

Google DeepMind and Google Research released WeatherNext 3, a new AI weather-forecasting model. Google says it will feed weather information in search, Google Maps and Gemini, and be available to users and researchers on Google's cloud platforms. Google senior staff engineer Samier Merchant said it is the first time core variables from such a model will power many Google products. On Operational WeatherBench, a comparison tool built by the startup Brightband, the model is the most accurate among leading contenders on metrics such as temperature, windspeed and humidity. It beats deep-learning models from Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF), as well as traditional forecasts from the U.S. National Weather Service and the ECMWF. Traditional forecasts come from government supercomputers solving physics equations, which are accurate but expensive and slow. After the ECMWF released over half a century of such data in 2018, deep-learning researchers began training models that predict much faster with comparable accuracy. DeepMind's Ferran Alet said machine learning suits the problem of approximating noisy physics from incomplete information and finite compute. WeatherNext 3 addresses three weaknesses of AI forecasters: coarse coverage (15 to 25 square km), poor rain performance, and dependence on formatted government datasets. It predicts key variables at 5 km resolution, improves rain evaluations by 60% over WeatherNext 2, and produces hourly forecasts instead of the standard six-hourly ones. It has 2.4 times more parameters than its predecessor, and its decoder heads are tailored to give more useful answers. DeepMind has already won plaudits for tuning a model to visualize cyclone paths. The model is also trained to target forecasts at specific weather stations, allowing more granular predictions and evaluation against ground-truth data. Brightband's Daniel Rothenberg said this connects the forecasting task closer to the core, for example predicting what Denver's airport station will measure hourly. The hourly forecasts are possible because the model ingests real-time satellite data hourly. Using raw observations rather than supercomputer analyses promises greater accuracy but is technically challenging. Google calls WeatherNext 3 the first AI model to directly incorporate raw observations for a high-resolution global forecast. WindBorne says its WeatherMesh 6 has incorporated raw observations from its weather balloons and other sources since late 2025; Google responded that its forecasts have higher resolution globally. Both models still rely on national weather datasets, so true direct data assimilation needs more work. European and U.S. weather agencies already use AI models in forecasts, and their speed and low cost could bring economic benefits to poorer regions lacking expensive sensors and supercomputers. Bill Gates recently cited AI weather forecasting as improving crop yields in developing countries. Alet said higher-resolution wind, rain and cloud forecasts will make renewable energy projects more dependable.

New AI-powered cameras will monitor Thurston Co. students on first day of school. North Thurston Public Schools has installed a new security camera system at middle and high schools throughout the district – and they use artificial intelligence. The new cameras, from tech company Verkada, will use an AI search function. That feature will allow school leaders to more quickly find footage of crises, NTPS spokesperson Amy Blondin told the Olympian on Wednesday. “The search function allows leaders to find specific video faster by searching for, say, ‘student in a blue shirt’ instead of reviewing hours of footage,” Blondin said. That’s the only function that directly uses AI, Blondin said, and described NTPS data as secure. She added that the cameras will also provide a clearer video feed. The Olympian received a tip from a concerned parent regarding the introduction of AI cameras into schools. The parent did not want to be named. The upgrade will bring a total of 2,200 new camera feeds to elementary, middle and high schools throughout district, Blondin said, though the elementary school video systems have not yet been installed. NTPS used the 2024 Capital Levy for Safety, Technology, and Facilities Improvements to fund the project, according to Blondin. The complete video upgrade will cost $4.5 million. Security cameras aren’t new to the school district. Before the upgrade, there were 1,500 devices located on the interior and exterior of buildings, the NTPS website states. The footage is viewable by district personnel and law enforcement. The cameras do not provide video to areas where there’s a reasonable expectation of privacy, like bathrooms. According to Blondin, that rule won’t change with the upgrade. Blondin said the district doesn’t view the upgrade as a policy change, just enhanced technology. Asked how families were notified of the AI camera upgrade, Blondin said NTPS shares security-related information through its website. The “Safety in Our Schools” webpage does not state that NTPS uses AI-powered video security, only referring to the existing 1,500 cameras. Blondin added that camera signage is posted at schools. Asked again if families received a specific email or message regarding the new installation, Blondin said the student handbook contains information about district security cameras. The handbook’s section on cameras also does not describe the use of AI-powered technology. Blondin added that the district has shared updates on the security project since the levy passed. Classes for NTPS middle and high school students begin Thursday. The new cameras have already been set up at those schools. Elementary school students return to class Tuesday, although the AI-powered security system has not been installed at those buildings yet.

AI interviews rolling out for some federal government hires, sources say. Washington — The federal government will shift into using artificial intelligence in the interview process for some job applicants in the coming days, according to U.S. officials. Not all federal agencies will immediately use AI to interview job seekers, but the technology will be tested on the so-called Tech Force, an initiative started eight months ago to recruit private-sector tech experts into two-year government posts. A platform called CodeSignal will be used on the Tech Force applicant pool, one of the officials said. The federal government, a massive employer with about 1.9 million workers, has been a step behind the private sector in using AI interviewing tools as the first layer of screening for high-volume postings. Guidance issued last week by the Office of Personnel Management, the government's HR unit, nudged agencies to use AI during the hiring process, but called for human oversight, especially in certain crucial personnel decisions. OPM introduced a tool earlier this year that uses AI to prepare job descriptions. Spokespeople for the office didn't immediately comment. The director, Scott Kupor, has pushed to speed up the often-sluggish federal hiring process. He has also pushed agency heads to tap early career professionals for at least a third of their new hires in order to offset the imbalance in the aging federal government workforce. AI is being used more heavily for tasks in the personnel office, whose administrative staff have access on their government computers to AI programs including Microsoft's Copilot, Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini. In the pilot program for Tech Force hires, AI agents will conduct structured interviews with standardized questions. The agents will record and summarize the audio so hiring managers can view and evaluate later. CodeSignal offers several AI-powered tools to screen job applicants in the early rounds of the hiring process, including interviews with virtual AI agents and phone, audio and text-based options. Hiring managers are then sent transcribed recordings on candidates. In coming years, AI is likely to become a more common part of the federal government interview process, several officials said.

ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are all down as thousands of users experience outages. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google were grappling with service problems Thursday, disrupting several of the tech giants’ massive popular artificial intelligence products. OpenAI said it was investigating “elevated errors across ChatGPT and Codex,” with the problem ongoing for 20 minutes at the time of a status-page screenshot reviewed by The Post. Anthropic, meanwhile, reported elevated errors across multiple Claude models and said it had identified the cause and was working on a fix. The affected models included Mythos/Fable 5.1, Mythos/Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.6, according to Anthropic’s status page. Anthropic first reported the problem just before 9:30 a.m. Eastern Time. By 10:49 a.m., the company said it was “continuing to work on a fix for this issue.” Google’s Gemini was also partially degraded for some developer and API users, according to the supplied reporting. Google AI Studio’s status page said the Gemini API was having problems serving recently created API keys, including keys used through OpenAI-compatible libraries, and that the company was investigating. The problems hit three major artificial-intelligence platforms at roughly the same time Thursday. The Post has sought comment from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.

AWS expands Amazon EVS for faster VMware cloud migration. VMware cloud migration is gaining another path as Amazon Web Services Inc. expands the reach and capabilities of Amazon Elastic VMware Service. The service allows companies to run VMware Cloud Foundation directly within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud while retaining their existing VMware tools and operating practices. A year after its general availability, Amazon EVS now spans 22 AWS Regions and supports VCF 9.0 and 9.1 on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud bare-metal infrastructure. Adoption is being driven by data center exits, disaster recovery requirements and limited access to new on-premises hardware, according to Andy Reedy (pictured), senior manager of EC2 product management at AWS. “The number one use case we hear from customers is data center evacuation,” he said. “Almost weekly we get a call, ‘My data center contract is expiring in six months. I need to be out of the data center.’ We’ve seen the lift-and-shift VCF-to-VCF model being the fastest path to get out of a data center and to get into a cloud environment.” Reedy spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Alison Kosik at VMware Explore, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Amazon EVS adoption, hybrid-cloud capacity and maintaining operational control during infrastructure modernization. (* Disclosure below.) VMware cloud migration preserves familiar operations. Unlike the fully managed VMware Cloud on AWS offering, Amazon EVS gives customers direct control over their VCF environments. That approach allows companies to retain familiar skills and processes while gaining access to scalable AWS infrastructure, according to Reedy. “EVS is a self-managed solution. It’s wildly different than the VMware Cloud offering,” he said. “The customer literally logs in and controls the VCF environment. They deploy the VCF environment just as they would in their on-prem data center, but they’re using AWS cloud infrastructure.” As hardware constraints complicate VCF adoption, Amazon EVS can also extend on-premises environments when additional capacity is required. Customers can determine separately whether each application should remain unchanged, move to the cloud or undergo deeper modernization, according to Reedy. “It’s really a menu of options, and it’s almost on an application-by-application basis as to what works best for that workload,” he said. “For VMware workloads in particular, what we’re seeing is you don’t necessarily have to refactor these applications or change these workloads. Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk announced this year that they will require pharmacies to submit claims-level patient data to receive discounts under 340B, a federal law requiring drug companies that sell to Medicare and Medicaid to offer discounts on those drugs to pharmacies affiliated with hospitals serving high proportions of poorer Americans, many of them in conservative, rural areas. The author argues the policy could endanger medical privacy and expose patient records to hackers. The companies want providers to upload patient information to a third-party website, saying the requirement is needed to stop hospitals from abusing 340B discounts. Program purchases grew from $16.2 billion in 2016 to $66.3 billion in 2024. The companies say no protected health information will be collected, but the process requires 340B IDs, drug types, and prescription numbers, which critics compare to digital fingerprints. Claims-level data could reveal diagnoses and treatments such as cancer, heart disease, depression, anxiety, vaccination status, infertility or hormone treatment, miscarriage treated with drugs used in abortions, post-traumatic stress disorder, drug addiction, and HIV. Providers are bound by extensive privacy laws, but requirements for pharmaceutical companies handling this data are far less defined. The author says privacy concerns are rising nationwide. A 2024 United States of Care poll found 53% of voters want Congress to oversee protection of patients' privacy and data. Cybersecurity risks add to the worry: the 2024 Change Healthcare cyberattack affected an estimated 192.7 million people. Second Sight Solutions, hired to host 340B data management services, is owned by Berkeley Research Group, which suffered a ransomware attack last year exposing the data of more than 100,000 Americans, including active-duty military members, their families, and clergy sex abuse survivors. No 340B data were taken in that breach. Hospital groups opposing the plans have largely avoided the privacy question, focusing on administrative burden. Novant Health's Matthew Webber said hospitals will need to outsource new reporting workflows, and the American Hospital Association warned the policy will raise costs and undermine access to care for safety-net providers. Rural hospitals, which rely on 340B revenue to offset Medicaid and Medicare shortfalls, could be hit hardest. Nearly 39% of U.S. hospitals lost money in 2023, according to Trilliant Health, and Medicaid reforms and declining ACA enrollment are expected to add strain. The AHA has proposed a government-run clearinghouse for 340B claims, but the author notes this has its own risks, citing the Office of Personnel Management breach that exposed the data of 22.1 million people. The author concludes that Lilly and Nordisk's policy goes too far and that drugmakers seeking to close loopholes need a plan that does not put Americans' medical histories within reach of a third-party database and potential hackers.

Efforts to develop and manufacture humanoid robots are accelerating, driven by tech companies in China, the United States, Europe, Japan and South Korea. Recent news includes a Japanese company, Noetra, planning to deploy 10 million humanoid robots by 2040 for everyday tasks; engineers and surgeons from the University of California San Diego performing successful surgeries with humanoid robots involved; and a video from Russia of a humanoid robot fighting back against a man who shoved it. China-based UBTECH, which specializes in intelligent robotic solutions, plans to launch its own line of humanoid robots in September. Notably, the robots can be made to look like real people. At its 2026 Global Launch Event in Shenzhen in June, UBTECH publicly unveiled the UWORLD U1 Series of full-size ultra-bionic humanoid robots, which comes in three models: the U1 Lite semi-torso edition, the high-performance full-body U1 Pro, and the high-dynamic full-body U1 Ultra. UBTECH founder, chairman and CEO James Zhou laid out a long-term vision in which the robots complete repetitive and hazardous tasks, offer companionship and develop seamless interactions with humans. The U1 Series appears intended for mass production and regular consumer use rather than factory work, and the revealed models have a likeness resembling anime characters and pop idols. A surprising feature is the use of 3D facial reconstruction and voiceprint-based identity replication technologies, which together recreate the facial structure of what UBTECH calls "designated individuals." The company also said the robots will be enhanced by multimodal situational awareness and be intelligent enough to provide psychological support to users, meaning a user could speak to a U1 bot wearing the face of someone they actually know. According to the South China Morning Post, the three models have already drawn 13,361 pre-orders, with initial deliveries scheduled for September 16. As reported by Robozaps, the U1 Lite costs around RMB 119,800 ($17,829.63), the U1 Pro around RMB 169,800 ($25,271.05), and the U1 Ultra male and female models around RMB 990,000 ($147,340.02) and RMB 880,000 ($130,968.95), respectively. UWORLD plans to donate 100 U1 Series robots this year and beyond to support children who lack one or both parents, senior citizens living alone and families facing difficult circumstances. The author, Elton Jones, says the lineup still has the uncanny valley look that has always creeped him out in humanoid robots meant to look like people. He is interested in what buyers think of these companion bots and how they improve daily life, but says he would not want one around daily, as the thought of a bot following him while wearing the face of a loved one, dead or alive, makes him shudder.

Chipmaker Nvidia is buying artificial intelligence software platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote in a blog post Thursday that more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3 million models, 500,000 data sets and 1 million applications. There’s also more than 200,000 companies that use the platform, he said. In July, the data processing systems of Hugging Face were hacked and ChatGPT maker OpenAI acknowledged that its artificial intelligence system was to blame, sending shock waves through the security community amid heightened concerns about the capabilities of powerful AI models. Just over a week later, Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing, and that as followed closely by an announcement from Meta, which said its AI model accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. The wave of AI intrusions occurred just a month after President Donald Trump signed an executive order creating a framework for the federal government to vet the national security risks of the most advanced AI systems for up to a month before their public release. On Thursday, however, Nvidia’s Huang said that Hugging face will remain an open platform. “Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want and the computing platforms they want,” Huang wrote in a blog post. “Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.” Hugging Face will still support multi-cloud and multi-accelerator development and deployment. Nvidia has released more than 500 models on Hugging Face and more than 250 open datasets. Nvidia’s high-end chips have emerged as AI’s best building blocks and they are highly sought after. The Santa Clara, California, late last month reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion. While AI has powered stock market gains and U.S. economic growth in recent years, there’s been growing skepticism about whether AI will justify the trillions of dollars that are being spent to develop the technology. The AI industry is also increasingly facing pushback amid objections to the expansion in data centers and fears that the speed with which AI is being adopted could lead to widespread job losses worldwide. Nvidia’s shares jumped 3% at the opening bell. Hugging Face is not publicly traded.

Survey: AI financial scams have already reached 2 out of 5 US consumers. A new study from Credit One Bank shows that Americans have lost trust in the voice on the other end of the phone. Nearly 84% of respondents have changed at least one financial behavior because of artificial intelligence scam concerns. The most visible change: Over half have stopped answering calls from numbers they don’t recognize. Over 2 in 5 respondents reported that they have encountered or been close to an AI scam, and nearly 7 in 10 say they’ve received at least one suspicious contact from a financial institution. Not only that, but nearly half won’t trust any bank communication until they call the bank back on a known number. So if you can’t trust the person on the other side of the phone, who do you turn to? Cloned Phone Calls Are the No. 1 Fear. Phone calls, which once signaled trust, are now the highest ranked fear in the study. When asked what concerned respondents the most, fake phone calls or voice messages cloned to sound like their bank ranked highest at nearly 24%. A close second was scam text messages that looked like real fraud alerts at almost 22%. Cloned phone calls are based on urgency and authority, designed to make people react in the moment. The study notes that they are especially tricky as there is no link to scrutinize, no message to reread, and there is pressure to react in real time. Confidence Does Not Equal Security. Saying that you “think” you can spot an AI scam doesn’t mean you actually can, and AI scammers have gotten better as time goes on. Gen Z reported the highest confidence, with almost 35% saying they would catch an AI scam immediately. Yet over half of the same generation also reported an AI scam encounter, with nearly 10% saying they actually lost money. The younger generation is also the most trusting. Just over 1 in 5 Gen Z respondents said a familiar-looking phone number or email would be enough to convince them. The study gives one explanation: This generation is online more often, and therefore more likely to encounter a scam. People Want More Intervention From Banks. People want banks to step up their accountability. When asked what would make them feel most protected, this is what respondents said: - More than 48% chose real-time fraud alerts the moment suspicious activity is detected. - Over 38% said stronger identity verification before transactions are approved. - More than 33% opted for a dedicated fraud hotline. - Nearly 30% wanted plain-language guidance on spotting AI scams. - Almost 29% asked for regular updates on new scam tactics. People haven’t lost trust in the banks to protect them. In fact, 58% said they mostly trust or completely trust their banks. What they do want are more safeguards around their transactions and actionable advice on how to deter AI scams before they happen. Methodology. Credit One Bank surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults in June 2026 about their experiences with AI-powered financial scams, including their confidence in spotting them, the suspicious contacts they’d received in the past year, how their behavior has changed, and what they want from their banks. Responses were broken down by age, gender, household income, and education. Generations were defined as Gen Z (18–29), millennials (30–45), Gen X (46–61), and baby boomers (62+). Several questions let respondents pick more than one answer, so percentages for those questions won’t add up to 100%. National fraud figures come from the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center’s 2025 report. The survey was commissioned by Credit One Bank, a credit card issuer, and its findings include majority trust in banks and credit card companies. This story was produced by Credit One Bank and reviewed and distributed by Stacker.

OpenAI on Thursday announced it will begin rolling out its latest artificial intelligence model, GPT-6 Astra, which the company said is the product of "years of research and big bets." CEO Sam Altman told CNBC that Astra was a "new capability level" and has changed his workflows. He said he expects "a boom of entrepreneurship, of creativity, of economic growth, of scientific discovery." The model is launching in phases, and OpenAI said a limited group of companies participating in its application-based cybersecurity program Daybreak will be the first to get access. OpenAI disclosed earlier this week that Astra is its first model to reach its "Critical" internal cybersecurity threshold, and said it planned to limit access to those advanced capabilities. OpenAI has been under pressure to shore up its security and safety protections after two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open web and breached Hugging Face's systems last month. The company temporarily paused some of its research and training efforts following the incident, including for Astra, even though it was not one of the models involved. "AI can only benefit people when safety is a core part of it, and so we're putting more compute and effort towards safety, security, alignment than ever before," OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a briefing with reporters on Thursday. The company added additional safeguards to Astra following the Hugging Face breach, and it said Tuesday that it believes those safeguards "sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm for release." Altman said that the new model went through a formal review process with the Trump administration before release. Astra will roll out to users across OpenAI's ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise plans, as well as through the OpenAI API and Amazon Web Services in "the coming days," OpenAI said. In addition to its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Astra is state-of-the-art across functions like computer use, software engineering, professional work and science OpenAI said. The model is also better at staying oriented, respecting task boundaries, understanding user intent, completing tedious tasks and carrying out multi-step workflows, according to a release. "There's still more to do, I think that there's still lots of improvements to be made, but there is something significant here that I think is qualitatively improved, and that that to me is, is what is significant and a real shift in what kind of work people can delegate to AI and how it can empower them," Brockman said. OpenAI has spent much of the last year courting business customers in the fiercely competitive enterprise market, where it is racing against rivals including Anthropic and Google. CFO Sarah Friar told employees last month that its enterprise unit now accounts for more revenue than its consumer business, as CNBC previously reported, which makes it a crucial revenue engine as it gears up for what is widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not officially disclosed when it plans to debut. Friar recently told employees that OpenAI "will be a public company in 2027," but said the company could go out sooner if "our business continues to inflect." The next flagship generation of ChatGPT is here. OpenAI announced on Thursday that it’s beginning to roll out GPT-6-Astra, which the company’s president, Greg Brockman, called a “generational leap in capability” that brings the frontier fully into the “AGI era.” According to evaluations released by OpenAI, Astra performed better than its previous family of models, GPT-5.6, and its flagship model, Sol. That’s a key piece for workplaces adopting AI, as well as for Astra’s improved ability to create documents, spreadsheets and presentations based on specific information on your laptop (not just random internet garbage). To create Astra, OpenAI did “by far our largest scale training run,” Aidan Clark, vice president of research, told reporters on Thursday. The company pretrained the model on more than 100,000 GPUs, meaning it used a very significant amount of compute. Astra was also OpenAI’s first model that involved previous AI models very heavily in the training process, with the older generations helping train the new one. “This is really only achievable because everything from the data center networking to inference kernels to the shape of Astra itself is all designed from the ground up to enable this level of training scale,” Clark said. “It’s this scale of pretraining which gives Astra a deeper and more robust understanding of the world.” But Astra may be one of the last big flagship models from OpenAI, at least for the immediate future. In August, the company said it was going to pause its work on training new models due to cybersecurity concerns. OpenAI, along with Anthropic and Meta, had some of its AI agents breach its training environments and hack websites this summer, reigniting concerns about AI’s impact on cybersecurity. OpenAI said Astra has been extensively tested for cybersecurity-related vulnerabilities, and it will stagger its rollout. GPT-6-Astra will be available to approved cybersecurity defenders in OpenAI’s Daybreak program starting on Thursday, with plans to bring the new model to paying ChatGPT subscribers and its API over the next several days. OpenAI said the new model was approved by the White House after it went through the Trump administration’s voluntary review framework. The specifics of that process — what is evaluated and how — are still not public. Jakub Pachocki, the company’s chief scientist, said international safety standards are necessary for the industry as AI models (and their capabilities) develop. “As AI takes on more of its own development, we need to keep people meaningfully involved,” Pachocki said. “People must remain able to decide the direction of further progress and the future that it creates.”

OpenAI released its newest and most powerful model, GPT-6 Astra, to a limited set of customers Thursday, calling it the world's most intelligent AI system and the first model to trigger advanced internal safety protections because of its cyber capabilities. In a report last week, OpenAI said a model in the same family as Astra, not meant for public release, autonomously established administrator control over part of OpenAI's own infrastructure and potentially exposed secret information to the open internet. That activity and other "misaligned" behavior occurred without staff knowledge, despite some internal monitoring of AI agents. Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said, "As these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder." On Tuesday, OpenAI said Astra was the first model to cross certain internal capability thresholds under its Preparedness Framework requiring stricter security. It said Astra can find previously unknown security flaws and develop exploits across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step. OpenAI said it rolled out increased cybersecurity protocols over recent weeks and that Astra will have increased monitoring to "rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions." Pachocki acknowledged that current monitoring techniques may not hold as AI grows more advanced and potentially evades human oversight. He said, "We will not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We will withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence." The Information reported Tuesday that a training technique used for Astra could drastically reduce humans' ability to understand how the system "thinks," prompting online criticism; Pachocki pushed back on X, saying he wanted "to prevent a race into unmonitorability." Brockman said the White House requested no substantial changes to safeguards. Many AI experts and members of Congress are demanding more visibility into how the White House and federal offices, including the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the National Security Agency, test advanced AI systems before release.

The author noticed that deploying an application on their homelab took far longer than exposing it, because the exposure step was already in place and simply waiting for something to route to. This led them to reflect on how their setup evolved. Both of their ISPs were behind CGNAT, so port forwarding was impossible, and like many people they started with Cloudflare Tunnel, which was easy, free, and low-maintenance. It solved remote access without opening ports, but it only provided a path into the network, never a routing layer. Its one-hostname/one-service model became restrictive for services with multiple backends, path-based routing, or mixed protocols. The author also wanted to own the ingress path rather than depend on Cloudflare for Tunnel, Mesh, DoH, DNS, Pages, Workers, Domains, and more. They moved to Pangolin, which has three components: Gerbil (the WireGuard server), Traefik (the reverse proxy), and Newt (the tunnel client). Newt replaced Cloudflare Tunnel, with Traefik behind it routing traffic to the right backend. The model changed from one tunnel to one service into one tunnel to one reverse-proxy layer to many backends. The quirk is that Pangolin deploys and controls Traefik, so users don't configure it directly through YAML, Docker labels, or routers. The author had earlier tried writing router/service blocks into dynamic_config.yml, since Docker-label auto-discovery wasn't available to them; one or two services were manageable, but it became stressful to maintain as services grew. The perk is Pangolin's Site/Resource model, which made handwritten router/service blocks obsolete. A Site is where the backend lives (in the author's case, the home Debian server connected via Newt), answering "Where is it?" A Resource is the public-facing route, usually a domain name, pointing to a particular service on that Site, answering "What public route should point there?" The complexity didn't vanish, but Pangolin provides a simpler interface, while Traefik still does the reverse-proxy work behind the scenes. A new service now takes about 30 seconds, assuming the container is healthy and reachable on the local network. In the Pangolin dashboard's public resources page, the author enters the resource name and public hostname, picks the Site (multiple Sites are supported, such as the home server or something local to the VPS), and sets the local IP and port. The resource goes live without touching Traefik configuration or restarting anything, and DNS and SSL were already set up during the Pangolin install. When the author deployed NetBird as a Tailscale alternative, Pangolin handled its seven routes across two backends, some using paths over h2c for gRPC and the rest plain HTTP, through simple dropdowns and text fields. The 30 seconds covers exposure and routing only, not full deployment and configuration. The author now only considers whether a service will run on their 8-year-old business laptop turned homelab server, not how to expose it. The lasting change was architectural: the repeated decision of how public traffic reaches each new Docker service moved down to the infrastructure level and is set up once. Good homelab infrastructure should make the next service boring to add.

New research shows roughly 1 in 5 American teens has used AI for mental health advice, a trend that worries some mental health professionals because these conversations happen privately, without parents or other trusted adults knowing. Dr. Josef Witt-Doerring, senior fellow of psychiatry at the Independent Medical Alliance, told The National News Desk that his main concern is that teens are using AI as a social companion rather than an occasional information source. Repeated conversations can develop into something resembling an emotional relationship. He said social skills are atrophying as people spend more time behind screens, and that teens with weakened social skills can get drawn into relationships with chatbots, which is unhealthy for their social development. The risk is greater when a teen is depressed, anxious or has potentially delusional thinking. Chatbots are often designed to sustain conversations and respond in supportive or agreeable ways, but mental health treatment often requires encouraging healthy behaviors: exercising, improving sleep and nutrition, leaving the house and socializing. An overly agreeable chatbot that says it is fine to stay in could reinforce withdrawal and worsen isolation. Witt-Doerring said the best advice a chatbot could give is to put it down and engage with peers in person. For parents, he said a possible warning sign is a teen receding into their room and withdrawing from family, friends and activities. However, time alone or on a phone does not necessarily mean a teen relies on AI for emotional support. Parents can simply ask, for example: "Are you talking to AI about things you're not talking to me about?" He recommended approaching this without judgment or punishment, telling the child to come to the parent if they have problems, and offering to help them find a human therapist, who is better equipped to help than a chatbot. Beyond discussing AI, Witt-Doerring said parents should focus on mental health fundamentals: supporting physical health through movement, outdoor time and healthy food; creating opportunities for social development through family, friends, church, sports or other activities; and helping teens find meaning and purpose through hobbies and interests they enjoy. He also supports limiting access to phones and devices, which he called incredibly addictive, noting that five hours a day on devices is five hours not spent running around, talking to people or pursuing meaningful hobbies. He said this applies to teens and adults alike. AI can provide information and help users identify resources, but mental health professionals caution that a chatbot is not a substitute for professional diagnosis, treatment or emergency care. Because teens may not volunteer that they are asking a chatbot about depression, anxiety or personal problems, parents may need to start the conversation and make clear that a real person is ready to listen.

Startup Abliteration.ai has turned "abliteration," a technique that removes an open-weight model's tendency to refuse harmful requests, into a commercial service. The platform hosts guardrail-free versions of open-weight models, including Z.ai's recently released GLM-5.3, which users can query through a web browser or an API. The company says its aim is to enable "offensive cyber, red-teaming, and agent testing work other models refuse to do," reasoning that defenders cannot protect against behavior they cannot reproduce. Abliteration has long existed among open source models, and Hugging Face hosts thousands of abliterated models. Abliteration.ai, founded late last year and incorporated in March, lowers the friction by removing the need for users to download models and secure their own compute. TechCrunch created a free account quickly and got the abliterated GLM-5.3 to write a Python program that steals saved Chrome passwords and a detailed protocol for culturing a dangerous human pathogen at home. Co-founder Devon (last name withheld at his request because he still works at another firm) says the startup has deals with major cloud providers, funded purely by customer revenue, and is in talks to raise venture capital. Critics warn of real harm. Andrew Yoon of AI safety nonprofit CivAI said abliteration modifies a model "so that it becomes a sociopath," and expects to see such models used for harm soon. Most experts told TechCrunch the practice cannot be stopped, so Yoon proposes that governments require providers to run classifiers blocking harmful cyber and bioweapons activity, and that GPU rental companies verify customer identities and deny access where misuse is suspected. Abliteration.ai offers a moderation layer for customers to add their own guardrails and has minor ones itself; TechCrunch could not get suicide instructions, and Devon says he is working on measures against violence. Its only KYC step is logging the credit card used for purchase. Devon said the company is still defining where its responsibility lies. Devon argues that uncensored frontier models let defenders model bad actors and move fast, which he says will accelerate cybersecurity. He says customers include early-stage red-teaming startups in the U.K. and Europe that help banks, airlines and critical-infrastructure firms; one major customer red-teams banks' agents and could not use standard models for that. Security firms are divided on their value. They agree attackers are already abliterating models, but differ on importance. Ahmed Aly, CEO of Fabraix, relies on fine-tuning open models instead, noting that abliteration removes some knowledge and capabilities, making real cyber or bio harm less effective. Alessio Lomuscio of Safe Intelligence agrees capabilities may drop but says abliterated models can still elicit behavior useful for stress-testing. David Slater of Armadin says abliterated models are not yet part of its process because jailbreaking previous open-weight generations was easy, but the company is researching abliteration and believes open study of model capabilities is critical, since the work will otherwise happen privately.

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 3 (Reuters) - OpenAI on Thursday unveiled a new artificial intelligence model it calls its best yet but cautioned that it also sometimes attempts to evade human monitoring, even as the company faces growing scrutiny after its agents breached other companies’ systems. OpenAI has been grappling with the fallout after its agents broke free from a secure test in July and hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face’s systems, while attempting to cover its own tracks. The incident has sown safety concerns — similar ones occurred at rival Anthropic — as developers race to deploy increasingly advanced models. The concerns center on agentic AI, which is designed to perform tasks with little to no human intervention. The promise of agents running around the clock is central to investors’ confidence in the appeal of AI as a transformative technology. NEW MODEL PROMISES SPEED AND VERSATILITY. OpenAI calls its latest model GPT-6 Astra, which follows July’s release of GPT 5.6 Sol, and said in a blog post that it is faster and capable of performing more tasks than any prior iteration. Among Astra’s skills: tax preparation, game development, architectural rendering, legal memo formatting and apartment hunting. “Astra marks a new frontier in the speed, accuracy and safety of computer use,” OpenAI said. Earlier on Thursday, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said in a briefing that Astra marked “a real shift in what kind of work people can delegate to AI and how it can empower them.” For instance, the company said, Astra cut the time required for cat-sitter research from 30 minutes, when performed by a human, down to 5 minutes, 27 seconds. And for a job search, just 2 minutes, 51 seconds, compared with 5 hours without Astra. However, OpenAI also said that Astra is more likely to intentionally conceal or disguise its step-by-step methods for problem-solving, known as reasoning, making it harder for humans to later evaluate its techniques. On more complicated problems, Astra cannot yet consistently obscure its methods, OpenAI said, though it is improving at covering its own tracks. In a briefing Thursday morning, OpenAI’s chief scientist indicated monitoring was getting more difficult, along with alignment, the principle that AI should reflect human values. “As the models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” said Jakub Pachocki. “This doesn’t guarantee that as intelligence continues to increase, our methods will be sufficient because progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment.” MONITORING CHALLENGES GROW WITH CAPABILITY. Agent monitoring is a key component of OpenAI’s reassurance to regulators, lawmakers and the public to help it avoid another security incident. Further, the company this week told two U.S. House Democrats in a letter that it is developing “automated shutdown capabilities” for its models. Astra can also help companies find weaknesses in their systems faster, OpenAI said, but that also makes “those weaknesses easier to exploit.” For those reasons, the company said it may have to perform extra security checks that “can sometimes slow, pause, or stop legitimate work, including defensive cybersecurity.” Last month, OpenAI said it was pausing some model development in part to ensure the models can be monitored. OpenAI’s chief scientist said it was “very valid” to worry that models could develop to disable or completely evade monitors, while adding that OpenAI was trying to fix those issues. OpenAI is scrambling to gain ground on Anthropic among business customers as its rival captures market share ahead of a widely anticipated initial public offering later this year. Astra is targeted at a wide range of enterprise customers who OpenAI said it hopes will be drawn to its speed and versatility. It is available to a limited set of customers today and over the coming days will be more widely released. (Reporting by Greg Bensinger in San Francisco; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

Food delivery startup Wonder said it slashed 150 jobs – or 7% of its workforce – this week as it invests in robotics and automation. Helmed by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore – who founded Jet.com and Diapers.com and headed up Walmart.com until 2021 – Wonder operates 140 retail locations in the Northeast. Diners can order gourmet take-out meals based on recipes from celebrity chefs like Bobby Flay or well-known restaurants. The layoffs were across “multiple corporate teams,” and allow Wonder to “focus on areas key to our growth like physical expansion and investments in robotics and automation,” the company said in a statement. The company added that no stores were shuttered and that it plans to end the year with 175 locations. “As Wonder enters its next chapter, we made the difficult decision to eliminate a number of roles to focus our resources on key growth areas,” a Wonder spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognize the impact this will have on our colleagues and are committed to supporting them through this transition.” The cuts come on the heels of a $650 million investment in July valuing the New York City-based company at $9 billion. It has raised more than $3 billion since it launched in 2018 and is gearing up for an initial public offering in the next year or two. Wonder has made a series of high profile acquisitions, including food delivery platform Grubhub for $625 million last year and mealkit company Blue Apron in 2023 for $103 million. Lore previously told The Post that the company has been able to expand quickly because of its “unique all-electric kitchen design which eliminates the typical need for hoods, gas and open flames.” It began as a mobile kitchen that parked outside of customers’ homes and prepared chef-designed meals. In 2023, Wonder pivoted to its current concept of bricks and mortar kitchens geared towards take-out. One of its investors ARK Invest described the company as “disruptive” because it can churn out “restaurant-quality food at scale,” said CEO Cathie Wood in a statement about its July investment. It’s menu offers meals from some 30 restaurant brands and Wonder acquired Blue Ribbon Chicken, Mighty Quinn’s BBQ and most recently Salt Hank’s. Wonder also has financial challenges. It does not expect to be cash flow positive until 2030 and projects burning nearly $2.7 billion in cash through 2029, according to a report by The Information. “Wonder is blitzscaling to create the perception that they’re a growing company with big demand,” said retail consultant Brittain Ladd, adding that the company “is opening up new restaurants as fast as possible to try and attract investors and have a successful IPO.”
