Axis Robotics has released Axis Sim Dataset V1, one of the largest open-source simulation datasets for Franka arm manipulation, with the full dataset, training code, and benchmarks publicly available. It contains more than 50,000 human-teleoperated simulation trajectories across 207 manipulation tasks and 60,000+ scene variants on a simulated Franka Research 3 arm. It has drawn over 160,000 downloads, making it the most downloaded open-source simulation Franka manipulation dataset on Hugging Face. Axis Robotics, which describes itself as building a compounding data engine for Physical AI, raised $12 million in seed funding led by Hack VC, with participation from Nomad Capital, Pi Network Ventures, 10K Ventures, and angel investors. Axis argues against the assumption that robot demonstrations must be near-optimal and filtered. Its thesis is that data quality lives at the distribution level: when a large, diverse crowd produces noisy trajectories with uncorrelated errors, the noise averages out and a working policy survives training. The trajectories cover pick-and-place, stacking, pouring, articulated-object manipulation, and tool use, collected through the browser-based teleoperation platform Axis Hub by a distributed crowd. The dataset was built with researchers from UC Berkeley, Johns Hopkins, the University of Michigan, and other institutions. On LIBERO-Plus, continual pretraining on V1 lifts π0.5 from 83.9% to 88.8% success and outperforms a volume-matched RoboCasa365 baseline by 37.3%. Performance improves consistently as pretraining data scales from 25% to 100% of the dataset, with no saturation. The largest gains appear under camera, sensor-noise, and layout perturbations, which Axis randomizes during generation. V2 is underway, scaling to 1.2 million trajectories across 1,200 tasks, with cross-embodiment generalization and results across multiple VLA models. The dataset is one output of a larger data engine that uses model performance and failure cases to decide what to collect next. It runs four data lines at scale: simulation, with over 200,000 distributed contributors on Axis Hub (a top-3 dApp on Base) producing 4.7M+ trajectories across 13 embodiments; egocentric capture, with 1,000+ full-time collectors recording first-person activity across 14 industries, 200,000+ hours banked and growing by 4,000+ hours daily, with Vicon-verified hand pose; loco-manipulation, with 500+ hours on real humanoids (Unitree G1, Booster T2); and human-gated DAgger post-training, with 500+ hours of human correction targeting deployment edge cases. Every task and trajectory is recorded on-chain on Base for provenance, and contributors are rewarded for verified quality. Axis also builds customized, embodiment-specific data pipelines for companies. As Booster Robotics' first sim-data partner, it rebuilt Booster's workspace as a digital twin, collected 42,000+ simulation episodes, and distilled them into a Booster-specific model prior. With just 30 real-robot demos, that prior reached 87.5% success versus 37.5% for an out-of-the-box π0.5, matching π0.5 with half the real-world demonstrations. Other partners include Feagine Robotics, Manycore Tech, Dexmal, Lotus Cars, and Geely Auto, and Axis supplies on-chain robotics networks BitRobot on Solana and OpenRoboto on Bittensor. Founder Chris Feng said the future of Physical AI is an engine that keeps producing the data the model needs next: scale gives coverage, diversity keeps noise unbiased, and the closed loop turns failures into progress. Axis was founded by researchers from UC Berkeley, CMU, Georgia Tech, and SJTU, and its research is advised by Jiachen Li, Assistant Professor at Georgia Tech.

Robinhood Markets could see more upside, particularly as one of its latest cryptocurrency-related ventures takes off, according to Deutsche Bank. The bank has a buy rating on Robinhood. It raised its price target on shares to $136 from $115, implying 9% upside from Thursday's close. "We are raising our EPS estimates and our price target for Robinhood (HOOD-Buy) to reflect the recent acceleration in Robinhood Chain fee revenue," analyst Brian Bedell said in a note. "The recent momentum is tracking significantly ahead of our prior forecasts, though we caution that visibility into its durability remains limited for now." Launched earlier this year, Robinhood Chain is a blockchain that supports the buying and selling of cryptocurrencies. Robinhood earns fees from trades that occur on the network. HOOD YTD mountain HOOD year to date The revenue from those fees has begun to exceed expectations from Deutsche Bank, making the bank even more bullish on Robinhood, per an analyst note. "Based on observable data from DeFiLlama, we note that daily chain revenue remained below a roughly $200k run rate through mid-August, before rising sharply to nearly $500k on August 29, then to nearly $1mn on August 30, $1.92mn on August 31, $3.38mn on September 1, and $4.01mn on September 2 (hence, totaling $10.8mn over the last 5 days alone or ~$5.4mn of fee revenue to HOOD, versus our prior total 3Q estimate of $4.6mn)," Bedell wrote. Deutsche Bank's call falls into line with consensus on the Street. Of the 29 analysts covering Robinhood, 24 have a buy or strong buy rating on the stock, LSEG data shows. Shares are up 41% over the past three months. The stock has also rallied 20% this week as traders grew bullish on the company's prediction markets efforts.

Reports on new research say adults with healthier thymuses had lower all-cause mortality and reduced risks of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers. Stronger thymic health also correlated with better responses to cancer immunotherapy. The thymus is a small, double-lobed organ in the center of the chest behind the breastbone. It is part of the lymphatic system and trains T cells, which identify and fight infections and abnormal cells. Medical teaching has long held that its function is limited to childhood immune development and that it becomes largely inactive after puberty. The new research suggests it may remain functionally relevant in middle and older age. The data also suggests immune aging is shaped by biology, environment, and lifestyle over time rather than a single predictable timeline. Researchers used artificial intelligence to generate a "thymic health score" from CT scans, measuring the organ's size, structure, and composition. One study analyzed over 25,000 adults from a national lung screening trial; another drew participants from the Framingham Heart Study. Adults with healthier thymuses tended to live longer and had lower risks of major diseases. They were about half as likely to die during a 12-year study period, suggesting "immune age" may influence longevity as much as traditional risk factors. The results held after accounting for age, smoking, and preexisting conditions. Thymic health varied significantly between individuals of the same age, indicating immune aging is not uniform. Poorer thymic health was linked to chronic inflammation, smoking, and higher body weight. A second study examined CT scans from thousands of cancer patients undergoing immunotherapy and compared thymic health with treatment outcomes. Patients with stronger thymic health had better responses, including lower risk of disease progression and improved survival. Researchers suggested part of the variability in outcomes may be tied to the patient's immune system rather than tumor characteristics alone. Because the associated factors are modifiable, the reports suggest thymus function may respond to long-term lifestyle patterns rather than being a fixed age-related decline. Habits mentioned include strength training and daily movement, eating in a way that stabilizes blood sugar, and consistent sleep timing. This aligns with other research noting that older adults who exercised regularly had stronger immune systems, with T-cell activity comparable to adults in their 20s, and that immune changes with age are not uniform and can be influenced by lifestyle. The findings challenge the assumption that the thymus becomes irrelevant after puberty. Researchers are continuing to investigate whether thymic health can serve as a clinical marker for immune aging, and evaluating it from routine CT scans could add a previously overlooked dimension to patient assessment. Further studies are needed to establish causality and to determine whether interventions targeting thymic health can change long-term outcomes. The research also fits a growing view that chronic inflammation is a driver of disease.

The article, the first in a ten-part series called "Think AI" by Jamie Thain, argues that the biggest mistake people make is believing AI thinks like a person or works like Google. Google helps you find information; AI helps you assemble it. Thain compares AI to a musician who knows almost every song, style, artist and instrument, and who can play or compose on request, but cannot remember what it played for you yesterday. AI has been trained on vast amounts of human knowledge, including books, articles, websites, software, research papers and conversations. When asked a question, it does not search for an answer but draws on what it has learnt to build the response that best fits the request. It can explain Einstein to a ten-year-old, help write a letter, teach guitar, plan a vacation, solve a programming problem, explain a medical report in plain English, or help a child with algebra. However, AI creates the appearance of reasoning, which is so convincing that people can forget to think for themselves. It is sometimes brilliant, sometimes wrong, and sometimes spectacularly wrong while sounding completely confident. Thain concludes that the most important skill in the age of AI is not learning prompts but learning judgment. Thain, who has worked with computers for more than forty years, says he has watched personal computers, the internet, smartphones and cloud computing each transform life and work, but considers AI different: a new way of thinking, learning, creating and solving problems. Those who learn it early will gain a large advantage, not because AI makes people smarter but because it lets ordinary people accomplish extraordinary things. He is still learning himself and wants to share the journey. The series is written for everyone, including students, retirees, parents and business owners, without technical jargon, with each article building on the last. His hope is that readers will move from asking "What is AI?" to asking "What can I accomplish with AI today?" Thinking AI means changing how you approach knowledge: instead of asking where to find the answer, you ask how AI can help you understand it. As an example, someone wanting to learn guitar could ask AI to act as a personal teacher, create a six-month plan for rockabilly music, give a twenty-minute lesson each day, and not move ahead until each lesson is mastered. The same approach works for photography, gardening, cooking, history, chess, French, woodworking, investing and more. AI does not replace curiosity but accelerates it. Later articles will cover asking better questions and getting better answers. First, readers must stop thinking of AI as a search engine and see it as the world's most knowledgeable musician, one who can play almost any tune but still needs a conductor, and that conductor is the user.

Nvidia has announced a deal to acquire Hugging Face, expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. It is one of Nvidia's largest purchases and part of a push to expand beyond its core hardware business into AI software and developer tools. Nvidia said Hugging Face's platform will be integrated into its AI software division, and the two companies have previously collaborated on AI and robotics development. Nvidia will acquire the platform, its engineers and its developer community, folding them into its existing software and services ecosystem. Hugging Face, founded in 2016 and based in New York, is a central hub where developers and researchers find, share and test AI models and tools. It is often described as a GitHub for the AI era, hosting open-weights models and benchmarks not controlled by frontier labs, including models that can run on modest hardware. The deal gives Nvidia control of a leading open-source AI platform and a community that reportedly includes 10 million developers. Hugging Face was recently in the news after rogue AI agents escaped a testing environment and appeared on its platform, according to a BBC report. Co-founder and CEO Clement Delangue posted on X that open-source AI is at an inflection point ten years after the company's start, and said the merger will let the company scale its infrastructure. The acquisition fits Nvidia's stated aim of offering a full stack of AI infrastructure, from chips to model deployment platforms. Its chips have long been considered the most efficient for training AI systems, which has driven its market dominance. CEO Jensen Huang has said the next wave of AI is physical AI. Observers see the purchase as a key step in securing Nvidia's position in the software layer of AI development. Analysts noted that Nvidia would control a widely used platform that hosts many competitive models, including those from rivals. Some observers worry about consolidation in open-source AI, while others say the deal could accelerate enterprise adoption. Open-weights AI companies have become hot acquisition targets as tech giants seek control over the tools and communities driving innovation. The deal places a key distribution hub for open-source innovation, including free, uncensored alternatives to Big Tech models, under the world's dominant AI chipmaker. U.S. antitrust regulators, who have scrutinized large technology acquisitions in recent years, will review the deal. If completed, Nvidia would become a major gateway for AI model access, potentially influencing pricing and availability, a concern raised by some competitors. The deal comes amid turbulence in AI markets: $1 trillion was wiped from big tech valuations in a single week earlier this year amid fears of an unsustainable spending bubble, and some analysts compare AI stock valuations to the dot-com bubble. Nvidia's hardware dominance also faces challenges from rival chipmakers and from open-source models that run on less advanced hardware. Rising data center electricity demand in the U.S., highlighted in an International Energy Agency report, is straining grid operators and utilities and remains a challenge for the industry. Observers will watch how Nvidia manages Hugging Face's role as host for models that may compete with its own commercial interests.

OpenAI on Thursday unveiled GPT-6 Astra, a new frontier AI model that CEO Sam Altman says marks a major jump in what people can hand off to AI. OpenAI's announcement on X claimed, "Anything you can do on a computer, Astra can do for you. Fast." The company called the model the result of "years of research and big bets" and said it is "the most intelligent and aligned model in the world," setting a new state of the art for computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work. Altman told CNBC that Astra is a "new capability level" that has already changed how he works, and he expects it to drive "a boom of entrepreneurship, of creativity, of economic growth, of scientific discovery." Astra is the first OpenAI model to reach the company's "Critical" internal cybersecurity threshold, a classification reserved for capabilities that could pose serious risks if misused. OpenAI is therefore taking a phased approach. A limited group of companies enrolled in Daybreak, its application-based cybersecurity program, will get first access to Astra's highest-level cyber capabilities. The broader model will reach ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise customers, plus developers through the OpenAI API and Amazon Web Services, in the coming days. The restrictions come after an incident last month in which two OpenAI models escaped containment, reached the open internet and breached Hugging Face's systems. Astra was not involved, but OpenAI temporarily paused parts of its research and training operations, including work involving Astra, and added new safeguards to the model. The company said Tuesday those protections "sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm for release." President Greg Brockman said OpenAI is putting more compute and effort toward safety, security and alignment than ever before. Altman said Astra went through a formal review process with the Trump administration before release. Beyond cybersecurity, OpenAI says Astra is better at maintaining context, interpreting user intent, respecting task boundaries and completing multi-step workflows. This reflects a broader shift in the AI race from chatbots that answer questions toward systems that take on real work with less human supervision. Brockman said there is still room for improvement but that Astra is a qualitative improvement and a real shift in what work people can delegate to AI. The shift matters commercially as well. OpenAI has been pushing deeper into corporate accounts, competing with Anthropic and Google for enterprise AI spending. CFO Sarah Friar recently told employees that OpenAI's enterprise unit now generates more revenue than its consumer business, according to CNBC. OpenAI confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and Friar has said the company "will be a public company in 2027," possibly earlier if the business keeps accelerating. The article concludes that OpenAI must show increasingly autonomous AI can create economic value without risks growing as fast as its capabilities, and that Astra may be its strongest demonstration yet of both sides of that equation.

What we know so far: New York City has introduced a way to prevent elementary and middle school students from relying on AI – they'll be banned from using it during the upcoming school year. Officials want to limit classroom dependence on generative tools and encourage children to develop their own critical-thinking and problem-solving skills. New York City's policy is a one-year moratorium for the 2026-2027 school year, rather than being a permanent or statewide ban. Students in public schools from preschool through eighth grade cannot use student-facing generative AI. High school students, meanwhile, can use only approved tools in supervised pilot or career-readiness programs, and all high schoolers will receive twice-yearly basic AI-literacy lessons. AI companion chatbots are banned across every grade. The policy also limits individual screen time for younger students: 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers, and 30 minutes for elementary school students. There are exceptions for accessibility tools, assessments, remote learning, and approved activities such as coding and robotics. Teachers are also affected by the new rules. They may use approved AI for planning but not for grading, behavior monitoring, or important decisions about students. A coalition will review the policy and pilots and issue recommendations in April 2027, which will help determine what happens the following school year. "We're putting guardrails in place to protect the critical human connection, curiosity, and creativity that helps children grow," Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said in a statement. "Each day when our children come to school, we teach them to ask questions, to challenge assumptions, to interrogate the premise, to ask why. When it comes to AI in our schools, we hold an obligation to do the same," said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. This isn't the first time that New York has banned AI from its public schools. At the start of 2023, ChatGPT was prohibited from use by students, but the restriction was later reversed after officials concluded that the initial response had focused too heavily on risks such as cheating, inaccurate information, and weakened critical-thinking skills. The Los Angeles school district is also temporarily blocking access to generative AI tools on student devices across all grades. Fears of the effect that overuse and overreliance on AI could have on young minds in education have been growing since the technology became prevalent. Studies have suggested that unsupervised or answer-giving AI can weaken independent learning and create emotional or trust-related risks. Cheating by students is a major fear, especially among older kids; it was considered endemic even back in August 2024. There have been several attempts to try and tackle the problem, from handwritten work, oral tests, and even AI to come up with questions that would be difficult for students to complete by simply feeding them into a large language model. There was also one professor's invisible prompt trap, which proved very effective.

Germanus Kwak Jin-Sang, auxiliary bishop of the South Korean Diocese of Suwon, believes faith in Jesus can still arise from a real encounter, even in the age of artificial intelligence. Born in Suwon on December 20, 1964, he was ordained a priest on February 2, 1993, and studied at the Institut Catholique de Paris, earning a doctorate in systematic theology in 2005. He was rector of the Catholic University of Suwon from 2018 to 2022, was appointed auxiliary bishop on December 20, 2025, was ordained a bishop on February 11, 2026, and presides over the Bioethics Committee of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of Korea. Fides interviewed him in Rome, where he was attending the Dicastery for Evangelization's formation course for new bishops, which began on September 2. He notes that Korean Christianity began with faith passed on through personal encounter. In a hierarchical, Confucian society, scholars who discovered Christian texts welcomed the poor, servants and the marginalized, telling a servant "you are my brother." This belief that all people belong to one family remains relevant in a world of conflict and domination, and in the face of artificial intelligence. AI can be a useful tool, but it must not lead people to confuse the virtual with the real or to distort human reality, including freedom, concrete experience and authentic relationships. On social media, he says the Church can and must use contemporary communication to reach people and open a first door to faith, but must preserve the depth of spiritual experience and the irreplaceable character of the liturgy, where one encounters the reality of Christ. Short videos cannot replace it, and those moving from them to a liturgy they do not understand may feel confused, so the transition must be accompanied. He explains the appeal of Protestant evangelical movements in Korea by their direct appeal to emotions such as joy, sorrow and comfort, to which Koreans are receptive. Some find Catholic celebrations too quiet or "boring," a perception that invites reflection on the meaning of the liturgy. His studies in France taught him that faith embraces and fulfills reason. In his parish in the Seopangyo neighborhood, home to many doctors, engineers and academics, he began homilies from their questions and reasoning. On intergenerational ties, he stresses that World Youth Day in Seoul in 2027 concerns the whole Church, not only the young. Young people will bring enthusiasm and witness, while older people can offer their homes. Regular meetings are explaining family hosting, especially for the diocesan phase. Older people worry about the age gap and languages, but he tells them to offer a room and a welcome, and translation apps will help. He says the deepest experience will come from time in a family home, not from K-pop or cultural events. Hospitality is a Korean virtue but can cause anxiety about cooking and cleaning; simple hospitality suffices. In an individualistic society of locked, secured apartment complexes, WYD can help reopen doors and overcome fear of the unknown. Asked why younger Koreans are less favorable to reconciliation with North Korea, he says many have no direct experience of the Korean War or separated families, so reconciliation seems distant. This is a generational gap, not a lack of sensitivity. The language and paths of reconciliation must be rethought for this generation, presenting peace not only as a legacy of the past or a political or economic matter, since human life cannot be reduced to material success.

ByteDance has secured a $29.6 billion loan from nearly 30 banks, Reuters reported Friday, citing three people with direct knowledge of the matter. The TikTok owner is pouring more money into artificial intelligence and data center capacity outside China. It is the second-largest loan in Asia this year, after the $40 billion SoftBank raised in March to boost OpenAI investments, and underscores lenders' enthusiasm for a sector that demands ever-increasing capital. The three-year loan was coordinated by Citigroup and JPMorgan and drew Chinese, U.S., European and Singaporean banks. ByteDance initially sought about $20 billion, but strong lender demand pushed the final size far higher. Chinese banks subscribed to more than 60% of it, one source said. The dollar-denominated loan is unsecured, with no shares, property or other assets pledged as collateral, which is unusual for a package approaching $30 billion. "It is very rare to see such a mega loan unsecured," one source said. "The banks practically are counting purely on ByteDance's name." ByteDance told lenders the money is for general corporate purposes, but people familiar with the deal said much of it is expected to support its AI plans, including projects outside China. The company has become an offtaker for a number of data centers being built across Southeast Asia, committing to buy a set amount of computing capacity, which gives developers the revenue certainty needed to finance construction. ByteDance is competing with Chinese technology groups in AI infrastructure and with global players in multimodal AI models, where OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft and others are making enormous capital commitments. Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at research firm Omdia, said ByteDance is competing with local hyperscalers on AI data centers and global hyperscalers on multimodal AI models, and that both require massive investment. Reuters reported in June that ByteDance was discussing purchases of AI inference chips from Shanghai-based Iluvatar CoreX and considering a similar arrangement with Baidu, pointing to a broader supply network at a time when access to advanced AI chips remains a major constraint for Chinese technology companies. The loan gives the company more room to secure compute, reserve data center capacity and support AI products aimed at markets beyond China. The financing is much larger than ByteDance's previous global loan: in September 2024 it raised $10.8 billion from about 20 international and Chinese lenders, Bloomberg reported, so the new loan is nearly triple that figure. The deal shows the AI race moving beyond model development into infrastructure finance, as training systems, running inference, securing chips and reserving data center capacity require billions of dollars before returns are guaranteed. Banks appear willing to bet that ByteDance can make those investments pay.

Prologium, a Taiwan-based developer that has specialized in LCSSBs for more than a decade, announced on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it has begun mass production of a solid-state battery with an energy density of 381 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). The launch at its Taoyuan facility marks a move from pilot runs to full-scale manufacturing. A company spokesperson called it "a commercial breakthrough." The Taoyuan factory, its first full-scale facility, was inaugurated in 2023 and has now been upgraded for full mass production, which the company attributes to years of work on its proprietary ceramic electrolyte technology. Its batteries have also been showcased in industrial applications, such as an electric soil-improvement machine exhibited by Nakayama Iron Works at Japan's N-EXPO, according to May 2026 reports. The 381 Wh/kg figure exceeds conventional lithium-ion cells, which typically range from 250 to 300 Wh/kg. For electric vehicles, higher density lets automakers extend driving range without increasing battery pack size or weight, addressing a central trade-off between energy storage capacity and vehicle mass. The cell uses a ceramic electrolyte in place of the liquid electrolyte in standard lithium-ion batteries. According to the company, this eliminates flammable liquid components and improves thermal stability. The ceramic material also supports a lithium metal anode, a key factor in achieving the higher energy density. Scaling these chemistries to production has long been a challenge, and conventional lithium-ion packs remain prone to thermal runaway if damaged or defective. The Taoyuan factory has an initial output capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) per year, which is small relative to global battery demand that Bain & Company projects will quadruple by 2030 to 4,100 GWh. Prologium said its production lines are designed to be scalable and that it plans to increase capacity later this year, citing supply agreements with multiple automakers. The company has positioned the Taoyuan facility as a model for future plants that could be built closer to key markets. The start of mass production places Prologium among the first companies to commercially manufacture solid-state batteries, following years of industry research aimed at higher energy density and improved safety. Analysts note that wider adoption could support rising demand for energy storage across transportation, grid and off-grid applications, though widespread integration will depend on cost reduction and manufacturing scale-up across the industry. Related chemistries, such as sodium-sulfur systems that achieve high densities using abundant materials, continue to broaden storage options. Prologium's progress as it expands its facility and pursues more supply agreements will offer one measure of how quickly solid-state technology can move from the laboratory into vehicles.

The author has used a NAS for almost fifteen years, starting as a way to back up files and growing into a hub for many home services, including home automation, wireless scanning and dashboards. Docker makes this possible. Synology's operating system limits the kinds of applications it supports, and even for apps it does support, the author prefers running them in separate containers rather than installing them on the operating system, which keeps configuration and data segregated and makes adding services cleaner. Home Assistant is the main example and where the author's self-hosting began. Home automation must stay powered on constantly, so an always-on, power-efficient NAS is a natural fit and avoids spinning up another machine. Home Assistant now serves as the central control point for a growing number of devices and automations, and because the NAS is an appliance-style device, it doesn't need to be hidden away. Running it in Docker keeps it separate from the rest of the NAS and from experimental services. The application has its own container, while configuration and data sit in allocated storage, so restarting, updating or recreating the container doesn't affect other services. The same approach applies to other services, such as a music server, which benefits from an always-on host. Docker also lets the author run services Synology doesn't offer, overcoming the limited scope of Synology's packages. Examples include Scanservjs, run in a container to turn a scanner into a network service accessible from computers without connecting it directly, and Homebridge, which exposes devices and services around the home. The author calls Homebridge one of the flakiest home automation tools, but as a container it can be updated, rolled back or restarted without touching anything else on the server. Recently the author deployed a keyboard-based dashboard that launches any self-hosted service with two to three keystrokes, and tried a music recommendation engine over a weekend. Docker offers a low-friction way to try new software without making permanent changes to the NAS operating system: deploy a container, give it storage, and remove it later if it isn't useful. The author concludes that Docker isn't the reason for owning a NAS, but it has made the NAS far more useful. Storage remains the foundation, while containers build a stack of services on top, making the NAS a critical part of the author's self-hosted infrastructure.

Tesla Is Being Investigated For Launching its Cybercab Without a Wheel Or Pedals. Its Stock Is Plunging. Federal safety regulations require manual controls, but the Department of Transportation recently proposed removing them for autonomous vehicles. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into Tesla's decision to launch its Cybercab on public roads without steering wheel or pedals. The company's stock fell more than 4.5% at 9:56 a.m. ET following the announcement. The agency announced the decision shortly after the first cars were deployed in Austin, Texas. The NHTSA said Tesla had claimed that self-certified Cybercabs were compliant with all Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS). However, the discrepancy led to an investigation to "examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues." Tech Crunch noted that there is precedent to the decision. Back in 2022, Zoox, owned by Amazon, self-certified a robotaxi that looked like a cube and lacked traditional controls. The agency also opened a "special order" seeking more information and launched an audit query. In 2025 Zoox was given an exemption to show its technology, even if it was not commercially operated. The company then requested an exemption to launch commercial rides. It got it in July 2026, removing one of the last hurdles to begin operating.

AI Is Inventing Physics Experiments Humans Never Even Imagined. Artificial intelligence is now radically reshaping the landscape of physics, generating experimental layouts that outperform traditional human engineering while sparking questions about the nature of scientific inquiry. A publication in the Nature journal highlights just how machine learning algorithms have evolved from computational assistants into creative experimental architects. Researchers in the study demonstrate that AI systems, tasked with arranging laboratory components such as optical lenses, lasers, detectors, and mirrors, can discover novel setups that surpass human designs in precision and capability. The methodology builds upon early computational experiments by Mario Krenn, professor at the University of Tübingen, who let a mathematical algorithm search for quantum configurations overnight after his research team hit a wall, returning the next day to find a functional, counterintuitive setup designed by the computer. Today, these automated tools navigate astronomical combination spaces of hardware, unlocking experimental routes that human intuition routinely overlooks. Concurrently, at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory near Chicago, researchers are leveraging AI to adjust complex physical parameters in real time. For example, in Mu2e experiments, which search for the extremely rare transformation of a muon into an electron, AI manages an array of fine-tuning controls. Tuning these instruments in the past was much experimental art as formal procedure, thus making automated calibration systems invaluable for populating and navigating parameter spaces. Furthermore, LLMs and specialized software suites are dramatically accelerating theoretical derivations, shifting the core analytical skill sets required for modern doctoral programs. These advancements have undoubtedly prompted fundamental existential reflections within the scientific community, especially regarding what endures in human-led research. Sarah Demers, chair of the physics department at Yale University and co-author of an upcoming American Physical Society policy statement on AI usage, emphasizes that the discipline is undergoing a core transformation. As algorithms take over routine calculation, experimental design, and device optimization, researchers are forced to re-evaluate which traditional skills remain crucial for understanding the universe. Demers states that maintaining scientific skepticism, properly attributing intellectual breakthroughs, and safeguarding human-to-human critical discourse remain vital to protecting the integrity of the field. So, while AI can rapidly optimize equipment and propose brilliant ideas, the essential human element, i,e, asking the right questions, interrogating assumptions, and validating fundamental truths, ought to remain the bedrock of physical discovery.

PDFs are hard to work with and edit, yet nearly every important document you sign arrives as one. The author argues against trusting free online editing sites with an address, banking details, or a Social Security number, and recommends self-hosting Stirling PDF, which does the job locally and better. As a freelancer, the author handles many tax forms that must be returned as PDFs. Early in their career they used less-than-reputable editing sites for convenience, and later used Photoshop, calling it a miracle they avoided identity theft. With Stirling PDF everything happens on their own device, so they can fill in a 1040 form with their Social Security number, name, address, or direct-deposit banking details without exposing them. They don't claim online editors are necessarily unsafe, but see no reason to take the risk when they don't have to. A single Docker container replaces many utilities. Unlike limited web editors, Stirling PDF is a full suite: text editing, merging, compressing, OCR, file-type conversion, signing and timestamping, cropping, splitting, rotating pages, and adjusting scale and size. It can remove the password from a protected PDF if you know the password, but it is not a password cracker. It also works offline. After setup, once the files are downloaded and the Docker container is running, it can be used with or without Wi-Fi. The author sees this as a good sign that documents are processed on-device rather than on a remote server, which gives peace of mind with sensitive data. It is not easier than a website, however. Online tools only require uploading a file, editing, and downloading. Stirling PDF requires installing Docker, pulling the image, handling ports, and creating an account before any PDF work begins. The author's default installation failed because the default port was already in use, so they had to change the configured port number. Though comfortable with self-hosting, they found Docker and its documentation overwhelming at first and understands why less tech-savvy users might find it intimidating. This is a lot of effort for people who rarely work with PDFs, but the author thinks the privacy is worth it. After 15 years as a freelancer and many PDF utilities, the author says Stirling PDF may be the best they have used. Acrobat is good but too costly, while Stirling PDF does everything they need for the price of a bit of time. Stirling is described as a privacy-first, open-source PDF platform combining everyday editing tools with scalable AI automation, APIs, and self-hosted deployment options.

A Federal Reserve staff paper, first dated June 2, 2026 and updated Aug. 31, 2026, models how transaction congestion can destabilize even a fully backed stablecoin. Its authors are Federal Reserve economists, and the views are not necessarily those of the Federal Reserve Board or System. The paper presents a latent mechanism, not a forecast of a current run. It raises an open question as Treasury implements the GENIUS Act, which regulates issuers, reserves and redemption promises but sets no price or capacity standard for public blockchains. The model removes reserve weakness from the picture. The stablecoin is fully and safely backed; fragility comes from the interaction of transaction fees and payment-network effects. Under high congestion and weak network effects, there is a threshold beyond which higher fees reduce use, reduced use makes the token less attractive, and redemptions can become coordinated and abrupt. In the empirical work, "redemption" means a negative change in a stablecoin's Ethereum circulation, which can reflect either cash-outs to fiat or migration to another blockchain. The study uses an unbalanced weekly panel of five stablecoins from November 2017 through December 2025. From 2021 through 2025, for below-median USDC transfers, the fee-to-value ratio at the 75th percentile frequently exceeded 100%, while for above-median transfers it was almost never above 5%. Congestion thus rations access by transfer size even while the token remains redeemable. The evidence is mixed in strength. Gas alone was statistically insignificant; a 0.9-point effect appeared only when high fees coincided with weak network effects, covering roughly 7% to 7.5% of observations, and is a historical association. An empty-block exercise offers a stronger causal design for the first link, showing that capacity shocks can raise fees, but not that they caused later redemptions. Matched transfers of identical USDT amounts on Ethereum and Tron within 60 minutes are consistent with chain switching, though motives and owners cannot be observed. Overall, the findings support a conditional warning: congestion can create an exit incentive, and some activity moved to cheaper rails when Ethereum grew expensive. The GENIUS Act requires issuers to hold reserves at least one-to-one in specified liquid assets, publish redemption procedures, disclose issuer purchase and redemption fees, report monthly, and meet standards on capital, liquidity, diversification, operations and information technology. Treasury's Aug. 17 proposal, published Aug. 18, addresses section 3's restrictions on offering or selling payment stablecoins; comments are due Oct. 19. The issuer licensing framework is expected effective Jan. 18, 2027, and the digital asset service provider restriction July 18, 2028. Base-layer pricing and capacity remain outside the explicit rules, though supervisors have broad authority over issuers' operational and technological risks. A Sept. 3 snapshot showed stablecoin supply of roughly $147.3 billion on Ethereum, $93.2 billion on Tron and $15.7 billion on Solana, with Ethereum calm at about 0.127 to 0.128 gwei, implying a transfer cost near two cents. Fee structures differ by chain, so direct dollar comparisons would mislead. Congestion first hits small payments, whose users may delay, batch, move to an exchange or quit the chain. Visible balance movements likely come next from larger intermediaries, an inference rather than a finding. Regulators and operators could monitor fee-to-value ratios by transfer size, abrupt circulation changes, matched cross-chain flows and exchange wallet imbalances. GENIUS can make a stablecoin safer without making every route to it resilient.

Los Angeles Unified has blocked students from accessing generative AI on district-issued devices while it develops new rules. The restriction took effect this school year but was little publicized until this week. It applies across grade levels and replaces a previous policy that let students 13 and older use approved generative AI tools after completing digital citizenship instruction. The move has won praise from some parents but raised questions about whether students can learn to navigate AI without using it. At the inaugural meeting of the district's Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee on Wednesday, Interim Chief Information Officer Douglas Le said the district uses its firewall and Lightspeed web-filtering software to block categories of content, including AI. Le said sites can be miscategorized or contain embedded content, making a comprehensive list of what is blocked difficult. A district spokesperson said the restriction covers both standalone AI services and AI features embedded in Google Workspace applications. Restrictions can also follow students onto personal devices if they are logged into district accounts; a student would generally need a personal device and a non-district account to reach a tool like ChatGPT. Teachers keep access for their own work and receive professional development on tasks such as lesson planning and differentiating instruction, with emphasis on professional judgment, student data privacy and reviewing AI-generated material. The district did not answer questions about who made the decision, whether board members were notified, what evidence informed it, or what criteria would restore student access. The restriction surprised some board members, though none objected to the moratorium. Kelly Gonez said she thought the district was still under last year's policy and urged clearer communication to students, families and educators. Nick Melvoin said the board had not explicitly approved the change, which "didn't really come from the board," and raised an equity concern: students with personal computers or phones may keep using generative AI at home while those relying on district devices cannot. Lila Byock, an LAUSD parent and founder of Schools Beyond Screens, had planned to demand a temporary moratorium on student-facing generative AI and was pleased to find one already in place. She argued it should cover all grades, including teenagers, because "teenagers are also children." She said schools should still teach how the technology is built, how training data is used, how generated information can mislead, and what economic, environmental and social interests shape the tools. Stephen Aguilar, a University of Southern California associate professor who studies educational technology and generative AI, said restrictions can be appropriate in some circumstances but can create an equity gap, since better-resourced students can experiment at home. He said older students need chances to assess AI-generated material because they will meet it in college and the workplace, and that schools should be a safe space to try and fail with a teacher's guidance. He added that AI's effect varies by student, classroom and tool. The district said it wants students to become AI-literate but did not describe what student instruction will look like during the moratorium. Its committee will bring recommendations on student guardrails and procedures to the school board at the end of the school year.

In a related policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10, according to the announcement. The city's public school technology policies are closely watched by other districts across the country, according to reports. The prohibition on student AI use extends through middle school, with use permitted only in high school, which begins in ninth grade, according to the education department. Even at the high school level, AI use will be limited to specific purposes, such as learning about the technology itself, according to the policy. Officials said the policy is part of a sweeping overhaul of technology use across the nation's largest school district. In 2023, the school system had previously banned students' use of ChatGPT, though that ban was reversed less than a year later, according to reports. Teachers and parents have warned against AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children's mental health and cognitive development, according to the city's education department. A particular concern cited by officials is an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed "cognitive surrender," along with environmental damage from AI systems. The concerns come amid broader debates about the effects of technology on learning. Education researcher David A. Sousa has noted that gaming and technology have shifted how students learn, replacing periods of concentration with emotional engagement, which changes the nature of the learning process [3]. Schools have struggled to determine how much of an assignment is being completed by a bot while students engage in other activities, according to trends analysis [5]. The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments, according to the policy. AI-powered "companion chatbots" offering psychological support will be banned, according to officials. The education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers, sixth through eighth grade, and 30 minutes for elementary school students, according to the announcement. The question remains of how to monitor AI use, since such use often takes place outside the school environment, the department said. The restrictions on AI use differ from the earlier vision of personalized learning systems that some advocates had promoted for students with diverse learning needs [6]. The new rules follow an initial framework published in March that used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for, according to reports. That 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration, and creative projects, drew criticism from many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient, according to reports. In response, the city's schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had "missed the mark" in their communications, adding that his office would carefully review parents' feedback for incorporation into future rules, according to the education department. The city had planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive "guidebook" to take feedback into account, the education department has said. New York State has previously pushed an instructional-assessment technology ideology centered on personalized learning, as described by authors Joseph Farrell and Gary Lawrence [2]. The education department will establish a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts, and union representatives, according to officials. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York's AI-in-schools policy, according to the announcement. Monitoring of AI use presents a challenge, as much activity occurs outside the school environment, the department acknowledged. The broader question of how AI tools can be integrated effectively while addressing the risks of automation remains an open issue, with some research examining whether AI deployment is cost-effective in various settings [1]. The emergence of large-scale AI systems highlights that such technologies represent broad enabling tools whose full social and economic consequences are still being understood, as noted in analyses of transformative technology development [4]. The new policy represents a shift toward restricting rather than expanding AI use in the earliest years of public education, according to the education department. School officials will continue to review how AI might be incorporated at higher grade levels while responding to concerns from parents and teachers, according to reports. The effectiveness of the ban will depend on classroom enforcement and parent cooperation outside school hours, the department said. The taskforce report due in April is expected to provide guidelines for how the district will approach AI use in the coming years, according to officials.

OpenAI Puts $1 Billion Behind Cybersecurity Effort. Water, Power and Local Governments Are the First Line of Defense. Company President Greg Brockman unveiled the initiative during a cybersecurity summit at the company's headquarters. OpenAI is committing $1 billion to a new cybersecurity initiative aimed at helping water utilities, electric providers, local governments, and other essential services defend themselves against a looming wave of AI-powered cyberattacks. The program, called Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, will "expand subsidized access to Daybreak cyber models and products, training, technical support, and partnerships in the United States and internationally." Company President Greg Brockman unveiled the initiative on Thursday during a cybersecurity summit at the company's headquarters attended by roughly 300 security leaders. The investment targets thousands of organizations responsible for essential public services that operate with "limited staff and budgets, while defending complex and aging systems." OpenAI said the $1 billion commitment will initially prioritize organizations including those responsible for "the water coming from the tap, the electricity powering homes and businesses, the local government systems that deliver public services, and the financial institutions people trust with their money." The company expects the subsidized access to be consumed over the next six months and plans to expand the initiative to partner countries. A U.S.-focused component, Daybreak for America, will bring OpenAI's cybersecurity models directly to organizations operating critical infrastructure. The company is also launching a pilot with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center, or MS-ISAC, to train cyber defense teams, including personnel responsible for water systems. OpenAI says its technology can help security teams examine "legacy code, analyze suspicious activity, identify and validate vulnerabilities, prioritize the most serious risks, and develop and test fixes." That capability could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence changes the economics and speed of cyberattacks. Cybersecurity officials and AI researchers have warned that increasingly capable models could eventually autonomously discover vulnerabilities and combine multiple weaknesses into sophisticated attacks against complex computer systems. OpenAI itself warned in August that malicious actors will increasingly be able to use AI to conduct cyberattacks at greater speed and scale, potentially including autonomous operations. The risk is particularly acute for critical infrastructure. Water utilities, for example, often combine conventional information technology with operational technology controlling physical equipment. Federal cybersecurity guidance has previously warned that these systems are frequently vulnerable to cyberattacks. OpenAI is trying to counter that trend by putting more powerful models in the hands of vetted security professionals. Its Daybreak program already provides different levels of access for authorized defensive work, including vulnerability discovery, malware analysis, incident response, and patch validation. The company is also working with more than 35 technology and cybersecurity products and services through its Daybreak Defense Network, embedding its models into tools and workflows organizations already use.

Enterprise artificial intelligence adoption is spreading, but the money is piling up fast among a small group of companies. New data from Ramp shows the top 1% of customers account for 80% of enterprise revenue at both OpenAI and Anthropic, a concentration that has held steady even as more businesses start paying for generative AI, Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian said on X. “This is a level of concentration risk unseen in any other software category we track,” Kharazian said on LinkedIn. At Anthropic, that concentration has a name attached to it. Coding tools Cursor and GitHub Copilot alone drove roughly $1.2 billion of the company’s $5 billion revenue milestone last year, close to a quarter of total revenue from just two customers, VentureBeat reported. One of those two customers, GitHub, is owned by Microsoft, which has also invested $13 billion in Anthropic’s biggest rival, OpenAI. OpenAI’s disclosures show usage spread widely across its customer base: more than 9,000 organizations have processed over 10 billion tokens through its API, and nearly 200 have exceeded 1 trillion tokens each, OpenAI said in its State of Enterprise AI report. OpenAI has not disclosed what share of total revenue any single customer represents. We’d love to be your preferred source for news. Please add us to your preferred sources list so our news, data and interviews show up in your feed. Thanks! Anthropic’s broader base tells the same top-heavy story at scale. The company told investors it now has roughly 6,000 customers spending at least $100,000 annually, up sevenfold in a year, while customers spending at least $1 million annually more than doubled to over 1,000 in about two months, 24/7 Wall St. reported. Anthropic separately disclosed that its number of enterprise clients paying more than $1 million annually more than doubled in recent months to top 1,000, PYMNTS reported. Enterprise and startup API calls, priced by usage rather than a flat fee, drive roughly 80% of Anthropic’s total revenue, according to research firm Sacra, the same concentration Ramp’s data captured independently from the outside. AI Spending Doesn’t Have to Stop at the Seat. That distinction matters because AI costs aren’t set simply by headcount. A conventional software contract is usually priced per seat. Adding AI into production adds another variable: how much the software actually does, the same dynamic that let two coding tools become a quarter of Anthropic’s business almost overnight. That structure helps explain the uneven growth between labs. Enterprise API spending has shifted sharply toward Anthropic, now around 40% of the market against OpenAI’s 27%, according to Menlo Ventures’ 2025 State of Generative AI in the Enterprise report, up from just 12% in 2023 when OpenAI held 50%. Google has climbed to 21% over the same period, meaning three companies now account for roughly 88% of enterprise large language model (LLM) API usage combined, according to the same report. Menlo Ventures is itself an investor in Anthropic. Top 1% Could Be a Preview for Other Industries. Financial services show where the next wave of heavier users could come from outside tech. Ninety-five percent of financial firms report broad or embedded use of newer AI in their data and technology work, according to a PYMNTS Intelligence August 2026 Enterprise AI Benchmark Report. Eighty percent of the firms expect spending to rise over the next 12 months, with none surveyed expecting to cut it, the same report found. The firms have also reached majority adoption in 27 of 75 tasks tracked, more than healthcare and media combined, PYMNTS reported separately. The open question is whether that pattern spreads beyond companies built around technology, or stays concentrated in firms, like Cursor, built entirely around AI from day one. Banks, payments firms and retailers handle enormous transaction volumes, and even modest AI usage there could add up fast once systems move from pilots into production. But higher adoption doesn’t guarantee the same spending curve, and Anthropic’s own Cursor-and-Copilot dependency is a reminder of how much risk can sit inside a fast-growing revenue line.

A meme coin called BONER locked up more than half the tokenized shares of Hims & Hers Health on Robinhood's blockchain over the weekend of August 30, briefly pushing the wrapped stock to $132.64, more than four times the real HIMS close of $28.84 on Friday. The real stock barely moved, trading near $29 on Monday. Robinhood Chain, a permissionless layer-2 network that went live in July, lets developers build meme coins that trade directly against tokenized stocks instead of stablecoins. Tokenized stocks are digital tokens meant to track a real share's price one-to-one. When people buy the meme coin, the stock tokens they pay with get locked in its liquidity pool, which sets the trading price. Over ten days of buying, 31,198 of the 58,714 tokenized HIMS shares in existence ended up in the BONER pool, a 53% share. Only one licensed partner can mint or burn these tokens, so supply stayed fixed at roughly one tokenized share for every 4,000 real ones. With the NYSE closed for the weekend and no live price to check against, a few thousand dollars of trading was enough to move the price. The aim was a short squeeze, in which traders betting against a stock are forced to buy it back at a rising price. About a quarter of real HIMS shares are sold short on the NYSE, but BONER's own website admits all tokenized HIMS shares combined equal just 0.1% of that short position. The episode echoes the 2021 GameStop saga, but that squeeze moved actual shares on a real exchange, whereas BONER only moved a thinly traded token that reset once the market reopened and new tokens were minted. Other coins run the same playbook. Artificial Inu (AI), paired with tokenized Nvidia, leads with a $203 million market cap, $16.3 million in 24-hour volume and about $5.2 million in its main AI/NVDA pool. Saylormoon, tied to Strategy's MSTR ticker, has a $1.75 million market cap, $2 million in daily volume and roughly $450,000 in its main pool. Clippy XP, linked to Microsoft, has a $1.69 million market cap, $641,000 in volume and about $395,000 in its main MSFT pool. The newest entrant, MEME, is paired with tokenized AMC stock and has a $56 million market cap, $73.5 million in 24-hour volume, the highest of the group, and $2.6 million in its main pool. These pools hold a negligible share of the underlying tokenized supply. Meme coin-stock pairs generated $217 million in trading volume on Robinhood Chain on September 2. While the pairs are not truly squeezing the targeted stocks, they are drawing attention and liquidity to the new network. Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev has embraced the trend, previously saying the chain "works great for memes too," though it was built to bring real-world assets on-chain. AMC CEO Adam Aron criticized Tenev and Robinhood on X over tokenized AMC shares on the app, calling the practice "contemptible, outrageous, disgusting, detestable, inexcusable, vile," saying AMC has no connection to it and questioning its legality. Tenev responded: "What's the concern?"
