US schools are starting the year under a patchwork of inconsistent rules on generative AI chatbots, varying by state and even district. No one knows the best way to use the technology to help students learn, so some districts are pausing student use entirely. AI could tutor students on essays, explain math or help brainstorm projects, but it could also write essays or solve problems from a single prompt. Tools designed for education differ from general chatbots students can easily reach on phones and laptops, and teachers' own use of AI sparks a separate debate. New York City, the country's largest district, announced on Sept. 2 a "moratorium" on student-facing generative AI, along with a new screen-time policy. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the tech industry wants people to believe AI-powered early education is inevitable, but the city does not see it that way. Companion chatbots are prohibited for all grades, and other student AI tools are eliminated through eighth grade. About 5% of high schoolers will join five AI pilot programs, and all high schoolers will get AI literacy classes. The ban covers the 2026-27 school year while the city studies the effects. Los Angeles Unified announced on Sept. 3 that it would ban most AI use by students on district devices this year. That reverses its 2024 launch of a "pioneering" chatbot named "Ed," which collapsed within months amid turmoil with its creator company. Elsewhere approaches range from bans to explicit instruction in AI use. At least 35 states have issued AI guidance for public schools, and Maryland, Idaho, Oklahoma and Virginia passed new laws this year requiring such guidance. It mostly offers recommendations rather than mandates, addressing student data privacy, cheating, and human input and verification. Boston students from third grade can use approved AI tools under teacher supervision and must disclose AI use. Denver bans ChatGPT but authorizes the educational platform MagicSchool. Chris Agnew, director of Stanford's Generative AI for Education Hub, said districts should ask what capacities they want to develop in young people and whether AI helps or hinders them; outright bans may not be the answer. Research is limited and normally takes years. Studies show that immediate AI access can improve performance, but outcomes erode when the tools are removed. General chatbots that supply answers can remove the "productive struggle" students need, while narrowly designed, "Socratic" educational tools engage them in problem-solving. Education-specific tools like MagicSchool and Khanmigo are used as teaching assistants. Teachers often allow AI for brainstorming and editing but never for writing papers. Westchester fourth-grader Caroline Qian said copying AI output is cheating, but using it with your own knowledge and words is not. Teachers and administrators are increasingly authorized to use AI, and many policies stress human oversight, with some barring AI from decisions on discipline or special education plans. A Kentucky district faced backlash after student planners contained apparently AI-made resources with garbled spellings such as "Venecky" for Kentucky. Agnew said AI can cut lesson-planning time but requires skilled users and teacher training investments despite strained budgets. Missouri fourth-grade teacher Mandy Traub said it is useful for drafting permission slips and spelling lists.

The article argues that AI is helping, not killing, U.S. software companies. In early 2026, software stocks fell on fears that AI would replace IT services, software development and knowledge labor, in contrast to AI-infrastructure semiconductor makers. The picture changed as AI evolved from simple task automation to "agents" (AI secretaries). To be deployed inside a company, agents must connect to existing work systems, data and security processes, which are held by established software firms. Companies therefore have to pay Microsoft, ServiceNow, Salesforce and CrowdStrike for access. Shares of these four rose more than 20% each over the past month. Salesforce reported second-quarter fiscal 2027 sales of $11.34 billion, up more than 11% year-on-year. Its AI agent platform Agentforce, which did not exist before 2024, exceeded $1.5 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR), up 240%. A securities official said building an in-house AI platform requires considerable cost and expertise, so small and medium-sized companies rely on SaaS firms like Salesforce. The company completed 3.2 billion "agent work units" in the quarter. Shares jumped 22.6% after the August 26 report. Third-quarter revenue guidance of $11.42 billion to $11.5 billion was above Wall Street's $11.41 billion estimate. Microsoft's fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results beat expectations, with revenue and adjusted EPS exceeding forecasts by 2.7% and 11.8% respectively (adjusted EPS $4.74; the article's revenue figure, "$901 billion," appears erroneous). Paid Copilot seats exceeded 30 million, showing companies are now paying for and distributing AI to employees. Commercial remaining performance obligations (contracted future revenue not yet recognized) reached $678 billion, evidence of multi-year cloud and AI subscriptions. Copilot is built into products like Office 365, pushing customers toward higher-priced plans. CrowdStrike protects against new hacking channels opened when AI agents access corporate systems. Its net new ARR rose 51% year-on-year to a record $332.8 million in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, and AI detection and response ARR nearly tripled from the prior quarter. CEO George Kurtz raised annual guidance, saying the more companies adopt AI, the more they must buy AI-specific security platforms. ServiceNow, which automates corporate requests, approvals and processing, posted second-quarter fiscal 2026 sales of $3.99 billion, up 24%, with subscription sales up 24.5%. Its annual AI contract value exceeded $1 billion, and the number of customers operating agentic AI (AI that sets goals and completes multi-step tasks autonomously) rose nine times in nine months. Its 12-month current remaining performance obligation was $13.2 billion, up 21%, and it raised annual subscription revenue guidance to $15.76 billion to $15.78 billion. Valuations have risen with the rebound. Microsoft's expected price-to-earnings ratio climbed to 25.64 from 16.59 a year earlier, and Salesforce's rose from 9.2 to 15.39, meaning prices are rising faster than earnings. ServiceNow's estimated ratio is 36.25, considered overvalued, while CrowdStrike, above 184, is classed as ultra-high-risk.

At this year's Telluride Film Festival in Colorado, artificial intelligence intruded on the usually insulated event, which devoted two Saturday events to the subject. Festival executive director Julie Huntsinger, who said Telluride normally avoids political positions, made an exception: "AI is a threat." She acknowledged beneficial uses but urged the audience to engage in the debate. The festival is not treating AI as off-limits: its program includes "Love, Rendered," a short documentary directed by Liz Garbus and produced by Darren Aronofsky that uses AI to re-create the moment an elderly couple, confronting the husband's memory loss, met 70 years earlier. The first event, "The Humanity Dilemma," was an hourlong multimedia presentation by Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin, co-founders of the Center for Humane Technology, with artist Joy Mauthe and violinist Andrei Matorin. Mixing original songs with warnings and imagery, they argued that the race to build powerful AI is outpacing governments and the public, and that humans could eventually lose control of such systems. Raskin called AI "simultaneous utopia and dystopia," comparing it to "a nuke that could also solve cancer." Harris called for pausing frontier AI development and steering toward "a pro-human future." The second event, a panel titled "AI AI AI," featured Harris, Raskin, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and moderator Joshua Oppenheimer, director of "The Act of Killing" and "The Look of Silence." Gates, long focused on global health and poverty, said he now feels compelled to use his political influence to raise alarms about AI, which he said has advanced faster than he expected, notably in writing code, where "the AIs are superhuman." He cited five concerns: jobs, biotechnology, cyberattacks, psychosocial harms and loss of human control. Oppenheimer said he was "absolutely terrified" after researching the risks and read a ChatGPT estimate putting the chance of persistent dystopian outcomes at 25% to 40%, a civilization-scale catastrophe at 5% to 15%, and extinction or permanent loss of control at 5% to 10%. Gates also stressed AI's upside in medicine, education and aid to farmers in poor countries. Asked whether development should slow until safety measures catch up, he said he would likely support a credible plan to slow it or hold it in stasis for a period. He acknowledged that multiple developers in the U.S. and China are nearing the technological frontier but rejected the idea that competition makes regulation impossible, saying China does not want cyberattacks, bioattacks or loss of control. He called the next five years critical and warned that responses taking five or six years to begin could come too late. Harris offered "not naive optimism, but momentum," citing calls from AI-industry employees to limit more powerful systems and Meta's agreement to pay $17 billion to settle claims by 29 states that Facebook and Instagram harmed young users. Raskin suggested President Trump's desire for a Nobel Peace Prize might motivate a U.S.-China pause on more powerful AI; Gates called the idea "smart." Gates closed by noting that in movies about alien invasions the U.S. and China cooperate, adding, "believe me, the aliens are here." That night the festival screened "2001: A Space Odyssey."

Data centers are the largely unseen infrastructure behind modern life, powering apps, streaming, online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence. Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital that data centers have existed as long as technology has, and that anytime people use social media or email, the data is being processed in one. As more of the economy moves online, they have become essential infrastructure for everyday American life. The U.S. has roughly 4,000 operational facilities, with thousands more planned or under construction as demand for cloud computing and AI accelerates. The article lists eight ways they quietly power daily services: 1. Apps. From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind them. When a user opens an app, uploads a photo or sends a message, the phone connects to servers that retrieve and deliver the information in seconds. 2. Streaming and gaming. Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and similar platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to store huge content libraries and deliver them to millions of users without buffering. Online games use data centers to connect players, synchronize matches and reduce lag. 3. Photos and files. iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups are stored on physical servers, often with copies in multiple locations to prevent data loss, so a lost phone does not necessarily mean lost files. 4. Search. Search engines use data centers to sort enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second, locating webpages, images, maps and videos for each query. 5. Online shopping. Data centers manage inventory, process payments, make recommendations, track packages and update availability and pricing, and must handle surges during events such as Black Friday without crashing. 6. Navigation. Google Maps, Waze and similar services process traffic, route and location data in real time to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes around accidents or congestion. 7. Remote work. Video calls, cloud software, shared documents and messaging such as Zoom and Slack depend on servers that keep information synced among people in different locations. For many companies, data centers are as essential as office space, phones and electricity. 8. Next-generation technology. AI chatbots, image generation and AI-powered search require far more processing than a basic web search, which is why the tech industry is racing to build bigger data centers with specialized AI chips. Autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics and scientific research also need increasingly powerful computing infrastructure, and data centers help train the AI systems behind these tools and process large volumes of data.

Robinhood and AMC, both central to the 2021 meme-stock frenzy, are now on opposite sides of a dispute over whether Robinhood can create and sell blockchain-based products tied to public companies' stocks without those companies' approval. Robinhood has been pushing deeper into tokenization. Its Stock Tokens launched for eligible European customers in 2025, and it launched the mainnet for its own Robinhood Chain in July. More than 190 Robinhood Stock Tokens tied to U.S. companies and ETFs are available to eligible investors in more than 120 countries, trade 24/7, and can be used in DeFi applications. Robinhood says the tokens are tokenized debt securities issued by Robinhood Assets (Jersey) Limited, not shares issued by the referenced companies. They give economic exposure to a stock but no legal or beneficial rights in the company, including voting rights. AMC CEO Adam Aron was furious to find AMC stock among the tokenized assets. He called the practice "contemptible, outrageous, disgusting, detestable, inexcusable, vile," said AMC had "no connection to this at all," and said outside securities counsel would investigate. When Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev asked, "What's the concern?", Aron said the potential issues were "almost existential." He questioned how a U.S. company could set up an operation in Jersey and market a security appearing to represent AMC without complying with U.S. securities laws, and argued the structure could interfere with AMC's ability to raise capital and create shareholder-rights issues. He called the result a "quasi-fake market" that could further undermine confidence in financial markets, and demanded Robinhood voluntarily cease trading AMC tokens. Robinhood chief legal officer Dan Gallagher replied that the company knows U.S. securities laws and "will not 'DECIST,'" inviting AMC to send its lawyers. This is not the first such objection. In 2025, Robinhood offered European customers promotional "OpenAI" and SpaceX tokens, and OpenAI quickly disavowed its offering, saying the tokens were not OpenAI equity, it had not partnered with Robinhood, and any equity transfer required its approval, which it had not given. The fight comes as tokenization becomes a favorite crypto narrative. Proponents say tokens tied to real-world assets allow round-the-clock trading, wallet transfers, use as collateral, and broader market access. Robinhood and other major exchanges and institutions are selling that vision; the New York Stock Exchange has proposed a blockchain-based platform for 24/7 trading and faster settlement. Critics note that much of the industry involves centralized companies issuing tokens representing claims on traditional assets, which may rebuild the existing system on blockchain while leaving control in the same hands, a tension with crypto's original distrust of middlemen. The legal picture is murky. In January, SEC staff recognized that securities can be tokenized by third parties unaffiliated with the issuers. But Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo sided with Aron, saying he would not want offshore derivatives of his company's stock trading everywhere and citing an AMC-linked token that he said traded at roughly 60 times the actual stock price. Columbia Business School adjunct professor Omid Malekan argued that companies embracing "full on tokenization" could eventually have the lowest cost of capital. Crypto compliance lawyer Ana Ojeda noted that an AMC Stock Token buyer holds a promise from the Jersey issuer, not an AMC share. Robinhood may not need AMC's permission to create a derivative tied to its price, she said, but calling it a "stock token" does not give buyers shareholder rights and could cause confusion.

FBI probes potential data breach of millions of drivers’ licenses. WASHINGTON – The FBI is investigating the potential theft and sale of millions of drivers’ licenses on the dark web. Digital scans of more than 153 million drivers’ licenses belonging to people in the United States and Canada were advertised on the site Nexus. News of the breach was first reported by the blog Krebs on Security, run by former Washington Post journalist Brian Krebs, a cybersecurity expert. Krebs said he confirmed the authenticity of at least nine drivers’ licenses for sale on the site. Shortly after Krebs’ Sept. 2 story published, he said the Nexus site disappeared from the dark web. The FBI said in a statement it was “looking into the incident,” but could not comment due to the ongoing investigation. The source of the data breach remains unclear. Krebs pointed to Louisiana-based ID-verification company idscan.net as a potential culprit. The company provides services for a number of large organizations, including Hertz, Target, FedEx and the United States Coast Guard, according to its website. A spokesperson for the company told Krebs they were investigating the issue. USA Today has not been able to independently verify Krebs’ assertions and has reached out to idscan.net for comment.
