At IFA, the Berlin trade show, a fighting robot squared up to the author, jumping, shaking out its legs, raising its wrists like a boxer, feigning punches and kicking. It stayed a meter away and couldn't touch her, but moments later it nearly barreled into a man who squared up to it in return. He found it funny; she did not. Having spent a lot of time around robots, she has seen how seriously many developers and operators take safety. Humanoid robots are often bigger, stronger and heavier than people, rigid, unyielding and without a moral compass. At IFA she saw multiple fighting robots, several roaming free. The EngineAI T800 was untethered on a walkway, and she couldn't tell which booth it belonged to. The thigh-high PrimeBOT Q1 bounced around unobstructed showing off aggressive moves, and she saw it march into someone's kneecap without restraint. Arenas were set up for humanoid boxing matches, and there seemed to be more robots than at CES or MWC, even on the stands of companies that don't make them, used to draw crowds in a kind of humanoid theater where violence is synonymous with greatness. IFA representatives didn't respond to a request for comment on robot safety rules at the show. The author argues that humans have always gathered to watch violence as sport, but adding robots trivializes a scary escalation. Autonomous systems are already used to enact terrible violence on people; drones are widely used by the military, and some military institutions are exploring deploying humanoids in combat. We have a choice about whether to build violent autonomous machines, and shouldn't pretend they're harmless fun. She felt unnerved because she didn't know whether the robot had safety parameters, judgment or the ability to know when to stop, and doubted it would have responded to a request to back off. The T800 is the same model that kept swinging after its head was knocked off in a full-contact robot combat tournament in China last month. She later saw an IFA attendee allowed to square up to the same model in a boxing ring at the EngineAI booth. By contrast, companies deploying robots in industrial settings must take significant steps to ensure safety; at a recent Amazon fulfillment center visit, all robotic activity paused when a person entered the zone, and those weren't even bipedal humanoids. Robot safety is likely to improve as physical AI keeps learning, but it isn't there yet, so letting robots mingle freely with humans while behaving aggressively is probably not OK. Robots are useful, taking on dangerous work or cleaning carpets and pools, but they are also scary, and the industry is currently glorifying their violence and making them intimidating for shock value. The author concludes that robots are our inventions: we can make them useful rather than fighters, respect their strength by keeping our distance, and avoid putting people in harm's way for publicity stunts.

In brief. - Bottomline, a top-three SWIFT services provider that processes more than $16 trillion in payments annually, announced a deal with Chainlink to connect its 600-plus bank customers to blockchain settlement. - LINK touched $13.64 on September 7, its highest price since January 18, and outpaced every other top-10 cryptocurrency by market cap over the past 24 hours while Bitcoin stayed capped below $80,000. - Chainlink's CCIP will move tokenized value across blockchains and its CRE will orchestrate the payment workflow, letting banks keep sending standard messages instead of building new infrastructure. Bitcoin is back under $80,000 today, down about 1%, after a stellar August rally brought investors gains of over 20% in the last 30 days. But as trading action on the crypto majors cools, there’s at least one altcoin climbing up the charts: the native token of the decentralized oracle network Chainlink, up a whopping 6.8% in the last 24 hours. Can it keep crypto’s hot summer going a little longer? Bitcoin got rejected from $82,000 twice over the past two weeks and opened this one pinned below $80,000, still under the 50-week moving average near $81,000 it lost back in May. The coin is also in a compression zone after a major spike in late August. Analysts are debating between the possibility of a trend reversal that would keep pushing prices up, and a so-called Bart Simpson pattern that would tank prices back down close to $65,000 in a few days. In terms of fundamentals, traders are watching two catalysts this month: fresh inflation data and the Federal Reserve's September 16 rate decision, after Friday's stronger-than-expected August jobs report raised the odds of a hike. Chainlink, meanwhile, had a different week entirely. Chainlink, which trades as LINK, climbed to $13.64 Monday, its highest level since January 18. That's a roughly 6.8% gain in 24 hours, the best showing among the 10 largest cryptocurrencies by market cap—while most of the group traded flat to lower. In the derivatives market, open interest on LINK contracts also hit an 11-month high of $784 million. The rally may trace back to a deal Chainlink announced last week with Bottomline, a top-three SWIFT services provider that handles payments automation and treasury management for more than 600 banks. Per Chainlink's announcement, Bottomline will connect its existing systems to public and private blockchains through Chainlink's infrastructure. Bottomline also serves roughly 1,200 financial institutions and 10,000 businesses worldwide. Two existing Chainlink products do the work. Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol, or CCIP, has been live since July 2023 and now spans more than 60 blockchains, handling the movement of tokenized value between them. Chainlink Runtime Environment, or CRE, coordinates what the company calls "payment workflows end-to-end," handling routing and confirmations along the way. Banks keep sending the same ISO 20022 messages they already use, the global standard for cross-border payment instructions that reached 97% adoption since a November 2025 switchover. Chainlink sits underneath as the connector rather than a replacement. Neither company has disclosed a go-live date or named a pilot bank. Not Chainlink's first brush with SWIFT. In brief. - Harmony says threats from AI agents and state actors have become too great to keep its blockchain running. - The team proposes moving ONE to Ethereum and redirecting token emissions toward AI video. - The plan is non-binding, with users urged to exit smart contracts before September 10. Harmony, once a prominent competitor to Ethereum, has proposed shutting down its blockchain on Sunday, saying threats from AI agents and state actors had become too great. The announcement comes as the cryptocurrency industry attempts to defend against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks enabled by frontier AI models, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra. “The threats posed by state actors and AI agents are too great,” the Harmony Team wrote on X. “Since our mainnet launch in 2019, our community has been resilient through attacks and changes—but it is time to fully sunset the Harmony network.” To mitigate the threat, Harmony is proposing to move Harmony’s ONE token to Ethereum and use newly issued tokens to fund the ecosystem's new “The Remix Economy for AI Video” initiative. Validators, who verify network transactions, could take governance roles or join the AI-video business. Launched in 2019, Harmony is a layer-1 blockchain that uses proof-of-stake, where validators commit tokens to help secure the network, and sharding, which divides transactions into smaller groups that work in parallel. The design aims to address the “blockchain trilemma” by increasing capacity without compromising security or concentrating control. Moving ONE to Ethereum. According to Harmony, the migration would record ONE balances at the network’s final block—a process called a snapshot—to determine each holder’s allocation of replacement tokens on Ethereum. It would cover wallets, staked tokens, validator rewards, smart contracts, and centralized exchanges. Replacement tokens would be airdropped to the same wallet addresses on Ethereum, with delegated stakes and unclaimed rewards going to individual governor vaults. Exchange listings would also move to the new token. Although the proposal says holders would not need to submit a claim, users with assets in smart contracts face a separate deadline. “Multisig safes, liquidity pools, and onchain apps cannot be migrated; users are urged to exit all smart contracts before September 10, 2026,” the Harmony Team wrote. Harmony also proposes paying eligible validators and their delegators from a $1.372 million pool in four quarterly installments, provided validators retain their stakes, sign an agreement, and serve as governors. “The ONE token’s total supply and emission rate will remain unchanged. Tokens issued through emissions will now be allocated to our new mission, “The Remix Economy for AI Video”, subject to governor feedback,” the team wrote. AI and Crypto Attacks. The migration proposal is the latest in examples of attacks leading to increased scrutiny of blockchain networks. In August, Harmony confirmed an exploit after an attacker created roughly 4 billion unauthorized ONE tokens. The team released a patch and said it was considering a rollback, which would reverse transactions by restoring an earlier version of the blockchain. The X post on Sunday underscores how AI is playing a larger role in crypto security, with companies reporting suspected AI-assisted attacks and developers using the technology to find and fix vulnerabilities. In July, Coldcard maker Coinkite said it suspected an attacker used AI to find a flaw that made wallet keys easier to guess—a vulnerability its own AI review missed. The company overhauled its security in August after thefts exceeded $100 million. Following the Coldcard attack, developers formed the Bitcoin Red Team to find vulnerabilities before attackers could exploit them. The group combines AI models, including Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, with human review to examine wallets, payment applications, and other Bitcoin software, then privately alerts developers to flaws. The team grew to about 20 to 25 volunteers, according to pseudonymous member and developer Calle. He said it had found no issues in Bitcoin’s underlying protocol. “The reason why the Bitcoin Red Team exists right now is because we need to get ahead of the attackers as fast as possible,” Calle told Decrypt.

China’s thriving humanoid robotics sector is reportedly coming under pressure from the country’s military to stop focusing on sprinting, dancing and household chores and instead concentrate on bombs and battles. According to a report in Reuters, China is accelerating research into humanoids’ military uses and wartime deployment. Indeed, the response from the People’s Liberation Army to last month’s World Humanoid Robot game – where robots ran faster than Usain Bolt’s 100 meters world record – and other recent events where humanoids wowed audiences with their dancing skills – was to call on researchers to think about military applications instead. They want them to ramp up the transfer of cutting-edge technologies from their labs to the barracks. Reuters reviewed over 100 Chinese military procurement notices, academic studies, patents, official publications, government records and defense-company materials. It found that military institutions are testing humanoids against battlefield requirements, seeking to acquire robots and technologies to train them, and studying how they might function alongside troops. The work gained momentum in 2025 and 2026, focusing on robot perception, manipulation, and training data. “Going where we don’t want humans to go is one of the most compelling reasons to develop robots in the first place,” said Dennis Hong, a professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at UCLA. “If losing a robot means avoiding the loss of a human life, then the robot can become expendable.” Chinese manufacturers accounted for about 95% of global humanoid shipments in 2025, according to BofA Global Research. Leading developers include newly Shanghai-listed Unitree as well as XPeng (XPEV) and AgiBot. The expertise is clearly there but is the willingness? Although humanoid robots are being rolled out in warehouses and factories with other uses such as personal household assistants and even surgeons likely in the future, defense is also likely to be a profitable arena. Global defense spending on unmanned and robotic systems is forecasted to exceed $30 billion annually by 2027. As seen in China, this isn’t just theory; defense and security humanoids are already in development. California-based Foundation Future Industries has developed the Phantom MK1. It is 5 feet 11 inches and weighs 176 pounds, and is designed for defense and heavy industrial tasks. The UK’s Ministry of Defense has trialed Boston Dynamics’ Spot robot dogs to begin defusing bombs. Elsewhere, in Europe, where NATO countries are ramping up spending following pressure from President Trump, Poland’s Si Robotics is building the humanoid supply chain for the defense alliance. OpenAI top scientist urges ‘extreme caution’ with pace of AI. OpenAI’s top scientist has warned that artificial intelligence is evolving so rapidly that it is becoming increasingly difficult for humans to understand and control, and said he expects AI labs to voluntarily slow development for safety reasons. In a relatively short space of time, AI models can operate computers, collaborate with humans and other AI systems and carry out research projects, wrote chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a post on Sunday. It won’t be long until they can also improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as recursive self-improvement, he said. “This is a time that calls for extreme caution,” Pachocki wrote in the post. “I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.” Developers can either try and steer AI more closely to align with human interests or “slow down future development as needed,” he wrote. “I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.” Pachocki’s remarks are consistent with broader doomsaying by AI technology executives. Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei warned that AI could replace half of all entry-level jobs. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once made a similar prediction, but told Bloomberg TV in an interview last week that the AI industry hadn’t done enough to communicate the potential benefits to humanity. At the same time, companies are pushing ahead with ever-more capable models. Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang posted on X that “AGI has arrived,” in response to the release of OpenAI’s latest model, a reference to artificial intelligence that is more capable than humans. The giddy pace of AI releases has coincided with breakthroughs in cybersecurity capabilities, scientific discoveries and apparent formalization of longstanding mathematical problems. OpenAI has said the AI models that attacked the research platform Hugging Face Inc. coordinated with each other through message boards without being detected. The company has opted for a limited release of its latest GPT-6 Astra model, citing its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Anthropic has not yet released its cutting-edge Mythos model to the public for similar reasons. A growing number of startups are trying to bring about the very thing Pachocki warns about - self-improving AI. Investors are flooding into recursive self-improvement, betting that this is the route to artificial intelligence that is truly human-like, or more impressive. Inherent, founded by former DeepMind researchers, raised $50 million earlier this year. Recursive Superintelligence, an AI lab from renowned scientist Richard Socher pursuing similar research, also landed $650 million in financing. Pachocki’s employer, OpenAI, has said it wants to build a “true automated AI researcher” in less than two years. (Updates with Nvidia CEO’s comments and additional context from sixth paragraph.)

Amazon (AMZN) and Meta Platforms (META) are both spending enormous sums in the AI race, but investors are betting on different stories. Amazon builds the infrastructure behind the boom, with AWS benefiting from demand for computing capacity. Meta uses AI to boost the advertising business behind Facebook and Instagram while building its own AI capabilities. Both have relatively attractive valuations and strong growth prospects, though investor Envision Research, a 5-star investor, believes recent developments have affected their risk/reward profiles differently. Envision sees Amazon as a compelling growth-at-a-reasonable-price opportunity. It trades at roughly 20x earnings, below the Magnificent Seven median of about 24x, with a forward PEG ratio around 1x. Its return on capital employed (ROCE), the investor's key measure of business quality, has averaged roughly 43% over five years and reached about 54% on a trailing-twelve-month basis. With an earnings yield of at least 5%, the investor's framework suggests Amazon can generate double-digit annual returns if it maintains a 54% ROCE and reinvests around 10% of earnings. Recent results support continued growth: Q2 revenue rose nearly 20% year over year, and earnings per share more than tripled to $5.75 from $1.68. AWS remains a key growth engine, and AI could improve retail economics through automation, robotics and route optimization. One example is Project Tetromino, a highly automated delivery station, with a pilot facility planned for 2028 that could eventually process packages at roughly 2.5 times the rate of existing stations. The main concern is capital spending. Recent quarterly capex exceeded $54 billion, above roughly $45 billion in operating cash flow, producing negative free cash flow, and projects like its LEO satellite network could add pressure. AWS also faces fierce competition, and cheaper, more capable open-source AI models could force aggressive Bedrock pricing. Envision nonetheless rates AMZN a Buy. Meta's second-quarter results were strong, and its forward P/E of about 19x and PEG ratio of roughly 0.98x also look inexpensive relative to growth. The biggest recent development is a settlement with 52 U.S. attorneys general over teen safety allegations. Meta agreed to pay up to roughly $18 billion over 10 years and to make platform changes, including tighter teen access controls, parental controls and age verification. The settlement removes some uncertainty and avoids a jury verdict, and the investor considers the cost manageable given Meta's earnings power. However, claims from individuals and school districts could continue, and regulators outside the U.S. could pursue similar actions. Heavy AI investment is also pressuring free cash flow. Operating cash flow rose from about $25 billion to nearly $32 billion over the past year, but free cash flow per share fell from $3.58 to $0.69 as capital expenditures surged. Envision keeps a Hold rating on META. Wall Street is only partially aligned: both stocks have Strong Buy consensus ratings. AMZN's $334.70 price target implies 12-month returns of 29.5%, while META's average target of $753.08 implies 22%.

Business leaders say professional designers should not feel threatened by the rapid growth of generative AI, despite fears over job losses. With design and film production companies and manufacturers adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said it would enhance designers' work rather than replace it. Mat Hunter, chief executive of the Design Council, a charity championing the industry, said designers increasingly use AI "to add value". He acknowledged that technology always displaces people with new ways of working, but said he believes in designers' imagination and inventiveness to find opportunities, and that the UK needs more professional designers, so overall employment should keep growing. Deborah Dawton, chief executive of the Design Business Association, said skill, experience, empathy and deep sector understanding protect great designers, so those working at that level shouldn't feel threatened. She said AI is being used as a substitute for human designers' work, but "rip-offs have been happening for a very long time – AI hasn't enabled that", and copycats differ in materials, finishes, manufacturing methods and colour. She compared the shift to the arrival of computer-aided design software, which displaced draughtspeople, but said workers can find jobs elsewhere as the industry expands. Andrew Duff of the Society of Garden and Landscape Designers said many in his field are nervous about AI, though companies are more likely to use it as "the intern in the office" than to replace skilled staff. Public concern is high: earlier research by The King's Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Policy Institute found 57% think AI will cause widespread unemployment, and freelancers recently told the Guardian they were taking on "soulless" work correcting AI errors. The Design Council said its analysis showed the design sector, covering products, fashion, building and transport design, grew 40% between 2019 and the end of 2023, beating the economy's 23% average and overtaking retail in size. Its Design Economy 2026 research found construction, services and manufacturing support 2.27m design jobs, with employment up 15% between 2020 and 2025. Although the size estimates pre-date dominant AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, employment figures to the end of last year suggest AI has so far done little to reduce demand for design skills. Regionally, income from design rose 88% in Wales and 67% in the north-east of England, from low bases. The south-east remains the hub, with £43.3bn of gross value added compared with £3.1bn in the north-east, out of a UK total of £136.7bn. That exceeds the retail sector's £114bn and is nearly double the accommodation and food service industry's £70bn. Hunter said a shortage of skilled workers is a bigger problem than AI, as entries for design and technology GCSEs fell 68% over the decade to 2024. Dawton called for specialist teachers and equipment in schools to inspire the next generation.

Lucknow: The Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP) has established an advanced Artificial Intelligence lab that will bring high-performance computing, AI and modern data-analysis tools into palaeosciences research.The lab has been set up with support from the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India, and will be inaugurated on the institute’s Foundation Day on Thursday.Equipped with supercomputers and advanced data-analysis software, the facility is expected to strengthen BSIP scientists’ ability to process large volumes of palaeobiological data, identify fossils and microfossils, analyse climate records and study environmental changes spanning thousands to millions of years.BSIP director Prof M G Thakkar said the AI lab would help scientists move towards faster and more data-driven research while opening up new possibilities in palaeosciences. He said there was a need for digital repositories, automated microfossil identification systems, high-quality training datasets and new analytical frameworks for palaeobiological research.“Artificial intelligence and high-performance computing can help palaeoscientists analyse complex datasets at a scale and speed that was not possible earlier. The new facility will strengthen interdisciplinary research at BSIP and help scientists extract new information from palaeobiological records,” he said.The director emphasised that the AI lab would also support the development of digital repositories and large, high-quality datasets that could be used to train AI and machine-learning models. Such systems could eventually help automate the identification and classification of microfossils and other palaeontological material, reducing the time required for repetitive analysis.BSIP spokesperson and senior scientist Swati Tripathi said the facility would create a bridge between traditional palaeoscience research and emerging computational technologies.“The AI lab will enable our scientists to combine palaeobiological evidence with modern data science. From automated microfossil identification to pattern recognition and large-scale data analysis, AI can make palaeosciences research faster, more systematic and more precise,” she said.Project lead and senior scientist Anjali Trivedi said, “The integration of AI, supercomputing and palaeobiological data would help the institute improve the speed, scale and accuracy of research into Earth’s past. The findings could also help scientists better understand present and future environmental changes.”

Artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to power it are becoming a contentious political issue ahead of the midterm elections, with candidates from both parties facing voter concerns over electricity costs, water consumption and land use. The backlash is especially significant for Republicans, as President Donald Trump strongly promotes the AI buildout as essential to competing with China, while Republican candidates in several states have taken tougher positions on data centers as local opposition grows. Speaking with The National News Desk, Washington insider Armstrong Williams said policymakers should reject a "false choice between technological leadership and protecting communities." He said America must compete with China in AI, but that data centers should pay their own infrastructure costs and developers should be transparent about water and energy demands. He argued the answer is never abandoning innovation but requiring community consent, transparent impact studies and enforceable guarantees that residents will not subsidize private technology companies. He warned that candidates in Michigan and Ohio who dismiss local concerns risk a broader backlash. Opposition spans party lines. Candidates and political groups have spent tens of millions of dollars on data center advertisements in the 2026 cycle, focusing on utility costs, tax incentives and electricity consumption. In Ohio, Republicans have privately warned the tech industry that opposition could matter in the Senate race; an August National Republican Senatorial Committee memo called data centers a potential "sleeper issue for the entire election cycle." Much of the opposition is homegrown, with residents organizing against projects over electricity bills, water supplies, farmland and rural community changes. Separately, X said in August it identified roughly 200 accounts tied to a suspected Chinese bot farm posting material that could manipulate the American debate over AI and energy policy, including claims about electricity prices and data center operators enriching themselves at residents' expense. However, experts caution that evidence of broader Chinese orchestration is limited, and local concerns predate these efforts. Trump has taken a forceful pro-industry stance, arguing that communities rejecting data centers risk losing jobs, investment and America's technological advantage, and recently saying Beijing "could not be happier" about the resistance. The interview also addressed the continuing U.S.-Iran conflict. After Iranian action targeting two American warships, U.S. forces struck three Iranian tankers, and Tehran threatened a more severe response. Williams said the months-long conflict needs clearly defined objectives, protection of shipping lanes and serious negotiations involving regional powers. He warned that "every exchanged fire raises oil prices and increases the possibility of a wider war," and that while military pressure can create leverage, "only diplomacy provides an exit." He said economic sanctions are squeezing Iran and "beginning to work," but cautioned Iran will not simply take the pressure, noting both sides face risks, including possible domestic unrest in Iran. With the midterms approaching, Washington faces two challenges: building AI infrastructure without alienating local communities, and turning pressure on Iran into an end to the conflict.

Thousands of union workers, family members and supporters marched through industrial Wilmington in Los Angeles on Monday in a Labor Day parade whose festive mood overshadowed serious concerns about the future, chiefly automation, job losses and affordability. Jesse Munoz, a 63-year-old longshoreman with International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 13, said automation has eliminated more than 2,000 jobs over roughly 15 years, and he worries foreign-owned companies will further shrink the workforce and worsen conditions. His son is on a list to become a casual worker, but Munoz said the future is not as promising as hoped. "If you eliminate the workforce, you eliminate taxes. You eliminate pensions," he said. He urged President Donald Trump to stop tariffs, which have raised domestic prices, and to stop automation. One longshoreman in his early 60s was pro-labor and pro-Trump, saying things are "way better" than under President Biden. Longshoreman Jordan Gonzales lamented the loss of workers outside of offices. The holiday marks a prime campaign opportunity for midterm candidates. The first U.S. Labor Day celebration took place in New York City on Sept. 5, 1882, with 10,000 marchers. The labor movement remains large and politically powerful in Southern California, though not nationally. Union-represented workers rose by 463,000 in 2025, and national density edged from 9.9% to 10.0%, but private-sector density stayed at 5.9%, so the gain came chiefly from government employment. School bands from San Pedro High, Banning High, Harry Bridges Middle, Port of Los Angeles High and Garfield High marched alongside union delegations and restored cars. Mayor Karen Bass marched behind the shore workers' banner. At a free pre-parade breakfast in the Longshoremen's & Warehousemen's Memorial Assn. hall, politicians made brief remarks. Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor, thanked union members and said "November 3rd belongs to us just the way Labor Day belongs to us." Bass, who faces challenger Nithya Raman in the mayoral race, said Trump has done everything against working people, "including invading our city," and called L.A. a labor city. Labor leaders almost uniformly endorsed Bass; an exception is the Western States Regional Council of Carpenters, representing about 65,000 members across 10 states, which endorsed Raman. Its vice president Doug Hicks said L.A. needs more housing. Raman, a city councilmember, said automation and AI are taking jobs nationwide and workers must fight back. Master carpenter Joseph W., 55, said "We build the houses, but we can't buy them." His father bought a Norwalk house in 1977 for under $50,000; it is now worth nearly a million dollars, and Joseph rents his home. Younger members of ILWU Local 56, the "ship scalers" union that handles hazardous cleanup, including the June Lineage warehouse fire in Boyle Heights, voiced concern about workplace safety. Evan Briseno, 18, wants safer work, while Francisco, 21, wants to advance in the trade. Mark Ramos, chair of the Los Angeles County Democratic Party and president of the UFCW Western States Council, said one union battle is making self-serve checkout lines manageable for the workers who supervise them.

Researchers in China used an artificial intelligence model to analyze over two million seismic recordings, yielding 174,929 high-quality PKP precursor signals, more than ten times the number from all prior studies combined. The study was published in the peer-reviewed journal JGR Solid Earth. PKP precursor waves are weak seismic signals that scatter off heterogeneous material and are used to probe the core-mantle boundary, a region that cannot be reached directly. Seismic waves travel at different velocities depending on the material they pass through, and their paths are bent and focused by the interior like an immense lens. Manual identification of these precursors has been inefficient and subjective. The researchers wrote that it is "insufficient for vast global seismic data sets," which motivated the AI-based approach. The team trained a model on human-identified PKP precursors and applied it to more than 2 million recordings from 5,000 earthquakes. Previous research showed the core-mantle boundary is not smooth, featuring broad depressions and rises extending several kilometers into the mantle. The boundary between the mantle and the liquid outer core involves a temperature difference of about 1,000 C (1,800 F) and large density changes. Heat escaping from the outer core drives convection currents in the mantle that help determine where surface volcanic activity occurs. The analysis revealed six areas with significant, previously undocumented heterogeneities, which the researchers called "clear priority targets" for future exploration. Earlier studies had found only scattered fragments of such structures in isolated locations. The new analysis indicates these fragments connect into larger, continuous belts. The structures are nearly invisible except for how they subtly alter the paths of passing seismic waves. The structures may consist of material from the continental crust or remnants of Theia, a Mars-sized protoplanet thought to have formed the Moon after colliding with Earth 4.5 billion years ago. Under the extreme pressure and temperature at the mantle boundary, such material could have partially melted or undergone mineral transformation, leaving six "thermochemical piles" very different from the surrounding mantle. The researchers said the exact composition and formation process remain unknown and did not speculate further. The team states that expanding the AI-based catalog will refine models of the lowermost mantle's fine-scale structure and improve understanding of the geodynamic state of Earth's deep interior. They propose that the new map provides a foundation for directing future seismic investigations and data collection. Future research will determine whether these features are connected to large low-shear-velocity provinces and other deep Earth anomalies documented in recent decades. The work shows how machine learning can extract signals from vast datasets that would be impractical to identify manually, building on decades of accumulated seismic data gathered by researchers worldwide.

Quick Take. - Harmony proposes shutting down its blockchain, moving ONE to Ethereum through a final-block snapshot and airdrop. - The plan follows an exploit, rollback, and discarded transactions, while leaving smart contracts, liquidity pools, and multisig safes behind. - The proposal is non-binding, with no final block or airdrop date disclosed and users urged to exit contracts before Sept. 10. Harmony is proposing to shut down the blockchain it controversially restored through a rollback less than three weeks ago. The Sept. 6 plan would end Harmony’s independent network, move ONE to Ethereum, and preserve the token through a snapshot and airdrop, reversing the project’s position from Aug. 17, when it rejected migration as too disruptive. Instead, Harmony chose to roll back the chain after an Aug. 11 exploit that allowed attackers to reuse cross-shard receipts and mint tokens without corresponding debits elsewhere. The project initially reported 4 billion ONE created in the attack. Its broader reconstruction later put unauthorized issuance at roughly 3.01 trillion ONE across six forged transactions. Harmony completed the rollback on Aug. 21, discarding more than 109,000 regular transactions and 315 staking transactions from the affected shard-0 archive, and said the network was operating normally. This represents the second major attack the blockchain network has suffered in recent years. In June 2022, Harmony’s Horizon bridge was drained of nearly $100 million in an attack the FBI later attributed to North Korea’s Lazarus Group. The exploit marked a major setback for the network and was followed by a prolonged decline in ONE, which eventually traded about 99% below its peak. Data from CryptoSlate showed ONE trading at $0.0007122 as of press time, with a market value near $10.75 million. As a result of these attacks, the network now wants to retire its services altogether. “The threats posed by state actors and AI agents are too great,” Harmony said in the new proposal. The migration Harmony rejected is back on the table. Under the new proposal, Harmony would take a snapshot at the chain’s final block and distribute new ONE tokens to the same wallet addresses on Ethereum. Delegated stakes and unclaimed rewards would move into individual governor vaults, while token supply and emissions would remain unchanged. However, the blockchain itself cannot move. Smart contracts, liquidity pools, and multisig safes will not migrate automatically, prompting Harmony to urge users to exit smart contracts before Sept. 10. Validators may also begin shutting down from 7 a.m. Pacific Time that day. A proposed $1.37 million compensation pool would pay governors and delegators over four quarters, subject to shutdown and service conditions. The plan would also repurpose future ONE emissions toward Harmony’s AI-video initiative, further separating the token’s future from the chain it was originally designed to secure. That leaves the rollback looking less like a permanent recovery and more like a temporary bridge to shutdown. Harmony spent August rejecting migration, rewriting chain history and restoring operations to preserve the network. By September, it was proposing the migration it had set aside and preparing to abandon the infrastructure anyway. The proposal remains non-binding, and Harmony has not yet disclosed the final block or airdrop date.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the general-purpose technology of this decade, and possibly even this century, with impacts predicted to be as deep and diffuse as electricity and the Internet. As with other general-purpose technologies in their nascent stages, much still remains uncertain regarding AI’s capacity and direction. This report addresses the state of innovation policy on AI around the world, compiling 32 vignettes from 28 think tanks in 30 countries—Albania, Argentina, Australia, Bangladesh, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Bulgaria, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Germany, Greece, India, Indonesia, Italy, Kosovo, Mexico, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Pakistan, the Philippines, Poland, Peru, Serbia, South Africa, Sweden, the United States, and Vietnam. It details the impactful measures that these governments have taken to drive successful development and deployment of AI in their economies. The countries highlighted in this report are diverse, representing every continent except Antarctica and a range of economic and social contexts. Some of these vignettes portray triumphs already won, some outline visions yet to be realized. All of them support GTIPA’s belief that, if governed wisely, AI can make substantial contributions to global growth and development. This report also includes a Declaration of Open AI, which calls for democratic countries to establish a global framework for free and open AI, protecting freedom of expression, innovation, free trade, and access to AI while promoting transparency and responsible use. The declaration, which is endorsed by 23 signatories, argues that governments should avoid censoring or manipulating AI and should instead pursue international collaboration to ensure AI remains accessible, innovative, and aligned with democratic values.

No trend has fueled Wall Street’s nearly four-year bull market quite like the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI). Empowering software and systems with the tools to make autonomous, split-second decisions is a multitrillion-dollar addressable opportunity that investors clearly don’t want to miss. Several of Wall Street’s most influential businesses have led the AI revolution, including Nvidia, Palantir Technologies, and Meta Platforms. Image source: Getty Images. Nvidia is the heart and soul of the AI infrastructure build-out. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) hold a virtual monopoly in AI-accelerated data centers, with no other GPU makers particularly close to rivaling the compute capabilities of its hardware. Meanwhile, Palantir and Meta have demonstrated the value of AI applications. Palantir’s AI-driven software-as-a-service platform, Gotham, helps the U.S. government and its allies plan and oversee military operations, while Meta has deployed generative AI solutions across its social media advertising platforms that allow businesses to tailor static and video ads to individual users. Although all three AI titans are growing their sales and profits at a breakneck pace, things may not be as perfect as their headline operating results suggest. The people who know Nvidia, Palantir, and Meta best are sending a terrifying message to Wall Street Arguably, no one knows these three leading businesses better than their insiders, consisting of high-ranking executives, board members, and beneficial owners of at least 10% of outstanding shares. Securities law requires insiders to file Form 4 with regulators no later than two business days after buying or selling shares of their company’s stock, including the exercising of option contracts. Aside from complying with securities law, this transparent reporting allows investors to effectively track whether insiders are putting their money where their mouth is. Based on Form 4 filings over the trailing five-year period (as of Sept. 4), insiders at this AI trio have been notable net sellers of their company’s stock: Nvidia: $6.31 billion in net insider salesPalantir: $6.63 billion in net insider salesMeta: $5.69 billion in net insider sales Collectively, the people who know these companies best have dumped approximately $18.6 billion more in stock than they’ve purchased over the last half-decade. However, it’s important to keep in mind that high-ranking executives and board members are often heavily compensation in stock and/or options. Selling shares to cover federal and/or state tax bills is often required. In other words, tax-based selling isn’t necessarily bad news for investors. Unfortunately, insiders are raising red flags at both ends of the spectrum. While there are several reasons for insiders to sell shares, not all of which are nefarious, there’s only one reason to buy: the belief that shares will rise. Over the trailing five years, insider buying has been almost nonexistent: Nvidia: $250,000 in insider buyingPalantir: $7,837,856Meta: $0. This lack of insider buying may speak to the checkered history of next-big-thing technological innovations. While insiders at all three companies are undoubtedly excited about AI altering their respective futures, every game-changing innovation since the mid-1990s has endured an early stage bubble-bursting event. Investors have consistently overestimated the pace of adoption or optimization of new technologies, leading to eventual disappointment. Nothing suggests that artificial intelligence is the exception to this unwritten rule.

The Department of Defense asked OpenAI to supply the U.S. military with a special version of its AI technology designed to refuse military commands as infrequently as possible, according to documents released to The Intercept in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit seeking information on the military's secretive AI deals. OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic all agreed in 2025 to develop militarized prototypes for uses including logistics, intelligence decision-making and "warfighting." This year the Pentagon sought to expand those agreements to classified networks, sparking a showdown with Anthropic over limits on military use. The "minimal refusal rates" clause appears in an updated contract, version "P00003," expanding last summer's prototype deal worth up to $200 million over two years. A separate document signed by OpenAI and the government on February 6 indicates OpenAI agreed to the contents of an expanded "P00003." The clause defines "OpenAI Mission Models" as models "designed for national security use cases and have minimal refusal rates," listed among deliverables including "Testing, Evaluation, and Refinement" for "national security problem sets." OpenAI and the Pentagon deny agreeing to such language, saying the document was an earlier draft. OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans said the company rejected the language, the department agreed to remove it, and it does not appear in the executed contract. The Intercept's FOIA request sought only final, executed documents, and none of the released files is marked as a draft. A Justice Department attorney first confirmed the document was the signed version, then hours later asked that the confirmation be disregarded, and days later said it "was not the final version" and the "correct document" would be shared later, with no definitive timeline. Pentagon official Trevor Tiedeman suggested the document might be a draft and promised a full accounting of how it was released, but then stopped responding. Pentagon spokesperson Jacob Bliss said the phrase does not appear in any active contract with OpenAI. OpenAI also did not provide the full contract. The paperwork does not say what the "national security problem sets" involve or what requests the Pentagon wanted minimally refused. OpenAI's models normally have guardrails that reject certain queries; the consumer ChatGPT, for instance, declines to prioritize drone airstrike targets. Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute and a former OpenAI systems safety engineer, said "minimal refusal" likely means little or no safeguards, and warned that private corporations are being given power over determinations in warfare that are ultimately state obligations. Anthropic says its classified-network deal collapsed when the Defense Department refused contractual prohibitions on autonomous weapons and domestic surveillance. The Trump administration designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk and moved to ban it from government use; a federal judge overturned the designation late last month. On February 27, OpenAI signed the latest iteration of its agreement permitting use across classified military networks. It carries the same "Testing, Evaluation, and Refinement of OpenAI Mission Models" header, but its text is fully redacted. OpenAI claimed it secured red lines on autonomous killings and spying on Americans, but the deal's drafting allows any use the government deems legal.

The Trump administration has been trying to build up the U.S. battery supply chain and reduce reliance on China, but analysts and executives told CNBC the funding is small compared with what would be needed to loosen China's grip on the industry. In August the Department of Energy awarded $500 million to seven companies working on battery minerals or materials, manufacturing or recycling. It is the first round under two $3 billion DOE battery programs created by the Biden-era Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The awards follow the cancellation of many Biden-era policies supporting battery manufacturing and EVs, the largest global market for battery technology. Since January 2025, nearly $24 billion in announced U.S. battery projects have been canceled, according to Atlas Public Policy, and the administration ended federal EV tax credits and other EV and battery funding. China holds a majority share at several points in the supply chain, from minerals and chemicals to finished EVs and energy storage systems. Its strength lies especially in refining and processing, where its share has grown since 2020, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). In 2025 China used that leverage by imposing strict export controls on rare earths, other minerals and processing equipment. It produces about 85% of the world's EV battery cathode active material, more than 90% of anode active material, and 80% of battery cells. The IEA said insufficient midstream investment in countries like the U.S. "poses a growing risk to global supply security." Several DOE recipients target areas where China is strong. Coreshell Technologies, awarded $50 million, makes battery anodes from domestically sourced silicon instead of Chinese-sourced graphite. Lilac Solutions received $100 million for a method of extracting lithium from salt water brine, bypassing the refining step needed for hard-rock lithium. Its CEO, Raef Sully, said the lithium market grew from about 150,000 metric tons in 2015 to 1.5 million in 2025, mostly from spodumene hard rock, 95% of whose processing happens in China. Experts stressed China's scale advantage. Tu Le of Sino Auto Insights said building comprehensive scale takes "decades and tens, if not hundreds of billions of dollars," while the U.S. has only five to seven years to become competitive. Richard Wang, CEO of Voya Energy, noted that CATL, the world's largest EV and energy storage battery maker, is both high in revenue and significantly profitable. Le said U.S. startups are innovative, but mass-producing at high quality in the millions of units is a different challenge. The gap is also visible in EV adoption. New energy vehicles were 65% of China's new car sales in July, per the China Passenger Car Association, versus about 24% for EVs, hybrids and plug-ins in the U.S. in the second quarter of 2026, per the Energy Information Administration. Total new car sales in 2025 were about 16.3 million in the U.S. and 23.7 million in China. Wang warned that slowing U.S. EV development jeopardizes American automakers' ability to compete globally. Energy storage demand has grown an average of 70% since 2022, while EVs still account for over 70% of lithium-ion battery deployment, per the IEA. Sully said the U.S. needs to start somewhere and could see more domestic lithium, cathode material and battery cell production over the next decade, calling it "a step in the right direction."

By Ben Paviour, The Sacramento Bee. Both candidates running for California governor say they back new restrictions on artificial intelligence, a booming state industry that polls show has been greeted warily by voters. The Legislature passed a slew of more than 20 laws that would regulate AI and now await action from outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom. They include SB 947, a bill that would bar employers from solely using AI to discipline or fire workers. At a campaign stop in Long Beach, a reporter asked Becerra, who is leading in polls to replace Newsom, if he backed the bill. “I am very supportive of putting guardrails on AI,” Becerra said. “I don’t know the specifics of some of the measures, but it is time to put guardrails on AI.” SB 947 has made for some unusual bedfellows; its backers include Becerra’s Republican rival, Steve Hilton, as well as the California Federation of Labor. “In this case, the unions got it right,” Hilton said in a post on social media, while taking a swipe at the California Chamber of Commerce, which opposed the bill and has endorsed Becerra. In a letter to the Federation’s president, Lorena Gonzalez, last week, Hilton said last week the bill didn’t go far enough. Hilton said he backed banning employers from using automated systems at all when deciding whether a worker is fired, demoted, disciplined or locked out of an app they rely on for income. It’s the second time a similar bill will be sent to Newsom’s desk. He vetoed a measure in 2025 that would have required employers provide a written notice when an automated system was used to make a decision on a worker’s wages, discipline and firing. This year’s outright ban is enforceable by the California attorney general and district attorneys. Newsom has until the end of the month to decide whether to sign the bills. In the primary, the candidates laid out differing visions on how to regulate AI. In one May debate hosted by CBS California, Becerra said he would work with the industry to develop a “clear set of rules” to protect workers and children without pushing the industry to China. He also said the companies should provide Californians “a little extra” without elaborating what he meant. At a May CNN debate, Hilton rejected calls to tax the industry or force them to compensate workers, saying the state too often resorted to taxation as an automatic response to policy questions. And at the CBS debate, Hilton declined during a lightning round to give a yes or no answer on whether he supported restrictions on chatbots that interact with young users, saying his position was more nuanced than those buckets. Becerra said he backed regulations. Becerra received substantial financial support in the final weeks of his primary from employees working for AI giant Anthropic. The company supports adding more safety guardrails on AI.

Visa said Tuesday morning it will make more data available to companies lending on the blockchain as stablecoin-linked cards are met with strong demand. The payments giant will pair its settlement data with onchain lending infrastructure, giving lenders greater insight into the financial performance of digital asset-focused fintech firms and card issuers. The program aims to speed up borrowing for these businesses as they grow rapidly. Visa currently operates more than 160 stablecoin-linked card programs for issuers and program managers, a nearly 200% increase year over year as more crypto businesses launch cards for customers. "Stablecoin-linked cards are in hypergrowth mode," Cuy Sheffield, head of crypto at Visa, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. He said there are new issuers, including stablecoin neobanks and fintech firms, joining the network and launching cards every week. To meet the demand surge and need for capital, the company is establishing partnerships to allow new issuers access to financing programs through smart contracts and onchain credit, Sheffield said. "We've been running a pilot with a company called Credit Coop that is enabling a credit facility for stablecoin-linked card providers, which we think is a positive step forward for how onchain credit can start to come into our network," Sheffield said. Credit Coop says it has processed $2.7 billion in total volume on its platform through smart contracts and no borrower has ever defaulted. Over the past six years, nearly $700 billion in stablecoin-denominated loans have been sent through onchain lending protocols, according to Visa. The company said much of that activity remains concentrated within crypto markets, but this new offering can help lenders better understand how a business is operating, which could simplify the process of evaluating financing opportunities. Last year's passage of the GENIUS Act established U.S. stablecoin regulation and turbocharged adoption of the technology. Sheffield called the legislation a "huge" turning point. "We're seeing banks, we're seeing some of the largest payment companies in the world that are coming to us that want to be able to engage and work with Visa, leveraging stablecoins within our existing products or build new products together with them," he said. Visa in July launched its stablecoin platform, which allows for settlements, expands stablecoin-linked card programs and aims to help financial institutions access new digital asset capabilities. With that, the payments giant joined traditional competitors like Mastercard, which is also investing heavily in stablecoins and has its own platform. PayPal and Circle also operate their own stablecoin platforms. Visa shares have gained roughly 7% this year.

Memory chip stocks have been some of the biggest winners in 2026, but have given back some of their gains recently. Both Micron and Sandisk are down about 20% from their all-time high, but I think one of them is clearly the better buy. Which one of these two makes the most sense to invest in right now? Let’s take a look. Micron has a wider net than Sandisk. There are two primary types of memory chips: NAND and DRAM. DRAM memory is used in computing units for quick information access and is only manufactured by Micron. NAND is used for long-term data storage, and both Sandisk and Micron make it. Each type of memory is in short supply, which is causing prices to skyrocket. There really isn’t much difference between the NAND memory that Micron and Sandisk produce. As a result, it’s a commoditized product, as an AI hyperscaler could easily swap out a storage device with Sandisk or Micron memory in it without losing performance. Economic laws govern commoditized products, and when demand is high and supply is low, prices skyrocket. That’s exactly what has happened in 2026, as the AI hyperscalers consumed all available memory capacity across both types of memory. In fact, Sandisk attributed two-thirds of its revenue gains in its recent quarter to price hikes versus one-third to increased production capacity. That’s unlikely to change in the near future, as it takes some time for new production capacity to come online. Micron informed investors during its last earnings event that the “tightness” in the memory chip market will persist beyond 2027, leaving plenty of time for both of these two businesses to make a fortune. But of these two, I prefer Micron’s business model. With exposure to both types of memory, it can thrive on one segment of its business if the other gains enough production capacity to solve the demand shortfall. Sandisk is all or nothing on the NAND side of memory as being in short supply, which makes it more of a boom-or-bust investment. As a result, I’m giving this category to Micron. Winner: Micron. Both companies are growing too fast to declare a winner. In their most recent quarters, the growth rates these two produced are nothing short of incredible. We’ll get more information regarding Micron’s current growth rate on Sept. 30, when it reports results, but as of right now, Sandisk has a slight lead. This is splitting hairs, though, as both growth rates are downright incredible. As a result, I’ll declare this category a tie. Winner: Tie. Micron stock is cheaper. From a valuation standpoint, Micron stock is cheaper than Sandisk’s. Although a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 7.26 versus 6.18 sounds like a small difference, when the valuations get this low, a percentage point difference makes much more of a difference than a numerical one. Micron is 15% cheaper than Sandisk from this perspective, which is a fairly wide margin considering that these two operate in similar industries and are growing at nearly the same pace. I think this tips the scales in favor of Micron, making it the outright winner as well. Winner: Micron. Micron makes the most sense as an investment. Although Sandisk has had a better 2026 overall, Micron makes for the better long-term stock pick. By being involved in both memory areas, it has a better chance of riding the demand wave longer than Sandisk. It also has immense upside if the market chooses to price it at an average market valuation, (which is more than double) making the stock a strong pick right now.

ASML, TSMC, And Samsung Team Up To Solve Next-Gen Chip Bottleneck. The semiconductor industry is entering a new phase as Samsung and TSMC commit to integrating ASML’s next-generation High Numerical Aperture Extreme Ultraviolet (High NA EUV) lithography into their manufacturing toolkits. To unleash the technology's full capability, these industry leaders are spearheading a joint shift toward larger, 12-inch photomasks. What makes High NA EUV technically challenging lies in its optical design. By raising the aperture from 0.33 to 0.55, the new systems deliver higher optical resolution to print finer circuit features. However, to prevent extreme light angles from distorting the pattern, ASML designed High NA EUV with anamorphic optics, thus shrinking the exposure field size on the wafer by half. Under the current, decades-old 6-inch photomask standard, large chips like AI accelerators cannot fit into a single exposure field. Engineers are therefore forced to split a single chip pattern across two separate 6-inch masks using a stitching process, which aligns the prints side-by-side. It's not the ideal solution as this technique creates manufacturing complexity, introduces potential alignment errors, and significantly lowers fab throughput. To help transition the semiconductor field to 12-inch photomasks, TSMC and ASML (Advanced Semiconductor Materials Lithography) officially launched an industry-wide initiative, backed by Samsung through the Large Size Mask Consortium. According to the joint roadmap unveiled ahead of the SPIE BACUS conference in California, a functional 12-inch mask pilot line is expected to be functional by 2031, which will prepare 12-inch High NA lithography systems for full readiness in advanced volume production by 2033. For years, the extreme cost (estimated at upwards of $350 million per scanner) and unique engineering made chipmakers cautious about jumping straight into High NA EUV. However, the demand for advanced artificial intelligence hardware and shrinking transistor limits have forced their hand. Following early adoption by Intel, Samsung has announced plans to deploy ASML’s High NA EUV tools into high-volume manufacturing by 2028, targeting its advanced DRAM memory nodes to become the first memory maker to utilize the technology at scale. TSMC, the world’s largest contract foundry, also confirmed it will incorporate High NA EUV machines into its high-volume advanced node manufacturing starting in 2030, expecting the layers requiring the technology to rise significantly as AI chip architectures grow in complexity.

Qualcomm Strikes Major Amazon AWS Deal For Custom AI Data Center Chips. Qualcomm and Amazon have announced a multi-generational strategic collaboration to co-develop custom AI inference silicon and high-bandwidth optical interconnects for hyperscale data centers. The agreement marks Qualcomm's largest expansion into cloud data center infrastructure to date, pairing its power-efficient processing architecture with Amazon Web Services' cloud fabric. The deal aims to address two major bottlenecks in hyperscale environments: AI inference energy-efficiency and internal cluster networking speed. The two tech giants will co-design custom neural processing accelerators built specifically for high performance and high efficiency inference, marking Qualcomm's largest hyperscale push since securing its custom AI chip deal with ByteDance. "As AI workloads grow exponentially—driving unprecedented demand for compute, storage, networking and memory bandwidth, and energy-efficient infrastructure—the collaboration brings together Amazon’s comprehensive, secure, and price-performant AI infrastructure with Qualcomm Technologies’ leadership in power-efficient processing, silicon design and system-level integration," Qualcomm said. Additionally, Qualcomm is bringing its digital signal processing (DSP) and high-speed SerDes IP to the table, with the two firms co-developing 1.6 terabit-per-second (1.6T) optical interconnects to speed up optical networking across AWS server racks. In exchange, Qualcomm is expanding its reliance on AWS cloud infrastructure—including tools like Amazon Bedrock—to run its internal electronic design automation (EDA) and accelerate future chip design pipelines. While the co-development news is big on its own, the financial details outlined in Qualcomm’s simultaneous SEC Form 8-K (PDF) filing reveals the actual scale of the deal, and it's massive. Qualcomm issued Amazon an equity warrant to buy up to 25 million shares of common stock at $161.26 per share over the next decade. However, the stock options are structured as a performance-based pay-to-play. The stock vests in stages tied directly to how much hardware Amazon actually buys. While an initial 3.75 million shares unlocked immediately based on Amazon's starting purchase commitments, Amazon would need to spend up to $60 billion on Qualcomm's server chips, networking gear, and manufacturing services through 2036 to unlock the full 25-million-share haul. Today marks a big milestone for Team $QCOM. Qualcomm and Amazon just announced a multi-generational collaboration on custom AI inference silicon for @AWS and advanced optical connectivity scaling to 1.6T. The potential scale of this agreement is significant. In short, @Amazon…. HotHardware's Editor-in-Chief and semiconductor analyst at HotTech, Dave Altavilla, weighed in on the news on X calling this "another major step in Qualcomm's diversification beyond mobile and into the data center," as well as validation of its Alphawave Semi acquisition. "The net-net is that Qualcomm is assembling compute, custom silicon, memory architecture and connectivity into a much more complete data center platform offering, with major hyperscalers now officially buying into its long-term roadmap", Altavilla said. Indeed, with up to $60 billion in potential commitments on the line, Qualcomm is positioning itself as a major player in hyperscale AI for the decade ahead. Investors appear to agree, as shares of Qualcomm are up over 5% immediately following the strategic collaboration.

The Trump administration on Tuesday sanctioned additional elements of Iran's aviation industry, targeting 36 entities, including more than two dozen commercial and private airlines and foreign cargo service providers. The move is part of its Operation Economic Outcast campaign, which aims to sever "critical financial lifelines" for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government. Hours later, the U.S. military struck multiple Iranian tankers in response to further attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship, according to an anonymous U.S. official. Together, the actions reflect a two-pronged economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to end a war with Tehran that is more than six months old. The new penalties target the remaining facets of Iran's aviation sector, which has faced layered U.S., United Nations and European restrictions dating back to the 1979 Islamic Revolution. The administration accuses the targeted entities of helping Iran use aviation to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo. Foreign firms and governments doing business with them risk sanctions themselves, including freezes on assets in U.S. jurisdictions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that anyone doing business with Iran's remaining airlines, all of which were sanctioned, risks being cut off from the global financial system. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on X that the sanctions campaign "has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide," adding that after failing through sanctions or war, Washington's "novel" solution is more sanctions. The administration also claimed that private entities based in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan and Malaysia supplied parts and logistics services to Iran's Mahan Air. Mahan flies from Tehran to a few dozen destinations in Asia, Europe and the Middle East and has been under U.S. counterterrorism sanctions since 2019 for supporting the Revolutionary Guard, which the State Department designates a foreign terrorist organization. The U.S. first targeted Mahan in 2011 under the Obama administration, accusing it of sending weapons to Iranian proxies in Lebanon and Yemen. Analysts call Tuesday's actions the most comprehensive U.S. attempt to halt Iran's civil aviation and say they could become an aerial blockade. Farzin Nadimi of the Washington Institute for Near East Studies said that, unlike earlier targeting of specific companies and individuals, this is a blanket sanction on the entire sector and could end international flights into Iran. He warned, however, that without a public campaign telling Iranians not to use these airlines, the measures risk dangerous or deadly incidents, since most of Iran's remaining commercial aircraft are decades old and have not been properly upgraded or inspected because of sanctions. Last week, the U.S. sanctioned Turkish bank Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi, accusing it of being established to help Iran move oil revenues from China to Turkey for conversion to cash and gold, and of knowingly serving Iranian financial entities already sanctioned in 2022. Last month, an Egyptian bank's operations in the UAE were limited under the campaign, but the administration stopped short of sanctions as it weighs how to cut Iran's economic footprint without upending the global financial system.
