Apple Unveils Its First Foldable iPhone. Its Stock Remained Largely Flat. The event also put artificial intelligence at the center of Apple's next generation of devices, with the new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence expanding across the company's ecosystem. Apple's September 9 "Surprise and Shine" event was headlined by the iPhone Duo, the first foldable iPhone, something the company had resisted for years, alongside other new products like the iPhone 18. It was also a changing-of-the-guard moment for Apple. The presentation was the first major iPhone event led by CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook earlier this month. The biggest surprise was the $1,999 iPhone Duo, Apple's long-awaited answer to foldable phones from rivals including Samsung and Google. The device has a 5.4-inch outer display that opens into a 7.6-inch folding screen, the largest display Apple has ever put on an iPhone. Apple says the Duo is also its thinnest iPhone when unfolded. Rather than treating the larger screen simply as extra space, Apple redesigned parts of iOS 27 around it. Users can run two apps side by side, open two windows from the same app, and save app pairings for later. The Duo is powered by Apple's new A20 Pro chip and uses a dual-battery design, with Apple claiming up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner screen or 44 hours using the outer display. Preorders begin October 16 before its October 23 release. Apple also introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, starting at $1,199 and $1,299 respectively. Both use the new 2-nanometer A20 Pro processor and feature a smaller Dynamic Island, improved thermal management, and major camera upgrades. The headline camera change is a 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, giving photographers greater control over depth of field and light. Apple is also bringing more manual controls directly into its Camera app. The Pro models arrive September 18 in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy. Notably, Apple did not unveil a standard iPhone 18 during the event, but AI was another major theme. Siri AI, arriving in beta with iOS 27, is designed to understand personal context, recognize what is happening on a user's screen, and perform actions using information across messages, emails, photos, and other apps. The software rollout begins September 14, although some features and languages will arrive later. The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces a new Health Sensing System and S11 processor, with more frequent heart-rate and heart-rate variability measurements. A new Readiness feature analyzes activity, sleep, and vital signs to produce a daily score from zero to 10, essentially telling users whether their body is ready to push harder or needs recovery. The Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799. The Ultra 4 pushes battery life to as much as 50 hours during everyday use and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode. Finally, Apple unveiled AirPods 5, bringing active noise cancellation to its most affordable AirPods. Apple says the new open-ear ANC can eliminate up to 50 percent more outside noise than the previous generation. AirPods 5 start at $129, while a $149 version adds a wireless charging case, longer battery life, and volume controls directly on the stems. Both arrive September 18.

AI privacy agreement reached between teachers union and Microsoft. WASHINGTON (TNND) — Microsoft and the American Federation of Teachers have made a deal regarding safety and privacy when artificial intelligence is used in school. The agreement has 10 legal enforceable protections with one of them being Microsoft can’t use teachers’ or students’ data to improve an AI model, according to the Politico news outlet. There is an exception of “narrow safety and security” circumstances, according to Microsoft. American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten praised the agreement in a statement. “We have forged a hard-fought, iron-clad privacy agreement with real teeth that protects students and families, because no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work,” she said. “We can get angrier and angrier, or we can act decisively; anything less than legally enforceable provisions is simply a wish list.” The union states that if Microsoft violates the agreement, the company can be liable for a breach of contract. This announcement comes amid the discussion of artificial intelligence in schools and debates about how much times kids are spending online. “This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president said.

A Texas father says he was tracked for months by an Amarillo police officer using city databases and Flock cameras. Speaking anonymously, he said the monitoring of his daily routines has had a severe impact on his family. "I'm a creature of habit. I pick my kids up from the same school, the same daycare. It hit me: this guy knows exactly which way I go," he said. According to the man, the tracking began after Amarillo Police Department officer Christian Eder developed a personal interest in a female officer he had previously dated. The father said he did not know Eder existed until the female officer told him Eder had been showing up off-duty at places where she worked. He learned Eder was using his department-issued work phone to remotely access her in-car and body cameras to track her location. He declined to share more about her, saying doing so would be cruel. The father first realized his own safety was compromised when he left his apartment overnight to go to the gym and saw Eder's marked patrol unit driving slowly through the parking lot behind his car. The female officer then told him Eder had approached her at work, saying he had seen the man leaving his apartment at that hour. Unaware he was being tracked through city databases, the father texted Eder asking him to stop. Eder replied, "lol, tough guy. Whatever y'all got going on is between y'all. Keep it that way. Have fun, my dude," with a winky face. The father said he would never have texted Eder had he known about the Flock and TLOxp searches, given the safety risk. Fearing for his family, the man filed a complaint with internal affairs. The investigation found Eder used the city's Flock system to track his vehicle 76 times and ran his name twice in the TLOxp database, entering false law enforcement reasons such as "city planning." Because Eder was a SWAT alternate with tactical training, the father felt his family was in danger. He said APD detectives denied his request for a description of Eder's personal vehicles. "I've had to change where my kids sleep in my house. I've had to change everything," he said, adding that the ordeal has affected every facet of his life. Amarillo police fired Eder on July 17 for policy violation. On Aug. 31, the Potter County Attorney's Office accepted a criminal complaint against him for tampering with a government record, and he faces 78 criminal charges. According to the complaint, Eder tracked the victim's license plate 76 times between February 2026 and June 2026, and an internal audit showed he used police databases to monitor the victim over five months. Eder turned himself in at the Potter County Jail and was released on a $4,500 bond. Police Chief Thomas Hover presented new safeguards at a city council meeting this week, including tighter software access and shorter data-retention periods. The father said the changes do not solve the immediate threat. "It feels like they're not trying to help me. They're trying to help themselves and navigate this. But I still have to look behind my back."

The takeaway: The US Commerce Department is investing $300 million in three quantum-computing companies and taking minority ownership stakes in each as part of the deal. D-Wave Quantum, Rigetti Computing, and Quantinuum will each receive $100 million in CHIPS Act research and development funding. The investment is intended to expand quantum hardware research and strengthen US supply chains for advanced semiconductors and related technologies. The awards are aimed at practical engineering work rather than quantum software. The companies are focused on building and manufacturing the components needed for larger, more reliable quantum systems, including processors, cryogenic equipment, semiconductor devices, lasers, and optical hardware. Rigetti will use its funding to address the challenges of scaling superconducting quantum processors. The company said it plans to expand its cryogenic capacity and accelerate production at its specialized manufacturing facilities. It will also address technical issues that have made it difficult to build larger superconducting systems. D-Wave said the funding will support microelectronics research and development, including advanced semiconductor prototypes for quantum technology. The British Columbia-based company said the work is intended to support scalable, high-performance quantum hardware. Quantinuum's project is centered on integrated photonics, which combines optical components and electronics in compact systems. The company said it will work with GlobalFoundries to fabricate next-generation ion traps and other electronic components. It also plans to work with Monarch Quantum on integrated lasers and optical components for its systems. The Commerce Department will take a minority stake in all three companies as part of the grants. The structure gives the government a direct financial interest in companies developing domestic quantum and advanced hardware capabilities. GlobalFoundries also finalized a separate $375 million agreement with the government to expand domestic quantum manufacturing. Under the five-year deal, the chipmaker will receive milestone-based research and development funding from the Commerce Department. The company said the funding will help quantum hardware developers move from lab prototypes to commercial-scale manufacturing. It is intended to support the technologies needed to build scalable quantum processing units in the US. GlobalFoundries has already received federal support for related work. In July, the government said it would take a 1% stake in GlobalFoundries and provide $300 million for silicon photonics development for data centers. The latest grants show how federal quantum funding is shifting toward the hardware and manufacturing challenges facing the industry. Quantum companies still need to prove they can build systems at scale, rather than simply demonstrate advances in the lab.

Amazon said Kevin Mandia, the founder and former CEO of cybersecurity company Mandiant, is joining its board of directors. In a blog post on Wednesday, Amazon referred to Mandia as a "widely recognized cybersecurity expert" with extensive experience "combating cyber threats" in the public and private sectors. OpenAI in July disclosed its autonomous agents successfully breached AI platform Hugging Face, while Anthropic in April took steps to limit the rollout of its Mythos AI model over concerns hackers could leverage it for cyberattacks. Mandia founded Mandiant in 2004 and sold the company to Google for $5.4 billion in 2022. The city’s largest police union blasted a new drone safety program being piloted by Boston Police as ineffective and invasive surveillance technology that’s already led to a crash where a drone “destroyed” a car on private property. The crash involving a Boston Police drone occurred around 1:30 p.m. last Thursday, Sept. 3 at 11 Hatherly Road in Brighton, just days after the department touted its new drone pilot program as a potential “tool to improve safety for residents and first responders.” “Upon arrival, the officer observed the drone … that had crashed in the driveway,” the Boston Police report states. “The drone, which was in pieces, appeared to crash onto a vehicle.” The officer reported damage to the rear windshield and trunk area of the car, which was a Mazda 3 registered to a 42-year-old man who lived at the Brighton address, the report states. The man was not home at the time, so the officer left a note on the windshield of the car. The drone company, BRINC, came to collect the wreckage, per the report. “Their pilot program already crashed and destroyed a car and damaged some property over in Brighton,” Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association President Larry Calderone told the Herald Wednesday. “We have a problem with Big Brother. We have a problem with super surveillance. “The idea of replacing a compassionate police officer who knows how to practice community policing with a robot is something we will never embrace,” Calderone added. The drone crash came just six days after the Boston Police Department announced it had partnered with Motorola Solutions and BRINC on the “Drone as a First Responder” pilot program. BPD members who are also certified pilots began operating drones and launch sites in the last weekend of August to assess its value as a tool to improve safety. The police department said it hopes the unimpeded drones will outpace ground units to the scenes of emergencies, launching “within seconds of a 911 call, or a ShotSpotter activation,” to give dispatchers and officers a clearer view of the situation “so they can assess them more accurately and make an informed decision about the response.” “We are always looking for better ways to serve and protect the people of Boston, to make sure that when someone dials 911, help arrives as fast as possible,” Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said in late August. “By putting eyes on a scene in as little as a minute, our 911 dispatch center can activate the needed resources to help our officers approach a fluid, often dangerous situation in the safest way possible for those we serve, as well as for our first responders,” Cox added. The police say the drones will be clearly marked in BPD livery and come equipped with sirens and emergency lights. Further, the police claim that “privacy guardrails are built into the program” and specify that the cameras will only face down at street level upon arrival at the emergency location. Calderone said the BPPA, a rank-and-file police union, isn’t buying into the department’s optimism about the drone pilot program and remains adamantly opposed to what it framed as invasive technology designed to replace police officers at a time when crime is spiking throughout the city. He said the program is geared toward making Boston more like Los Angeles, where drones are sent off to assess car accidents so the department doesn’t have to send a police officer who “understands how to give care and immediate assistance” to those involved in the incident. “We’re calling for more and more bodies on the street to aid and assist and protect our members and the general public,” Calderone said. “It seems that instead of attempting to do that in a serious fashion, this department secretly worked on a drone program as opposed to working harder to hire more police officers.”

China’s EV Boom Is Losing Steam. Carmakers Are Now Pouring Money Into Humanoid Robots. Automakers can reuse technology, factories and supply chains developed for electric vehicles, but demand for humanoid robots outside their own operations remains limited. Chinese electric-vehicle makers are expanding into humanoid robots as intense competition and weaker profitability put pressure on their car businesses, with companies including XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely looking for new uses for technology developed for intelligent vehicles. Automakers in the country accounted for more than half of the nearly 20 car companies worldwide that had entered humanoid robotics through direct development, investments or incubation as of August, Counterpoint Research data cited by CNBC showed. Kevin Li, associate director at Counterpoint, told the outlet that the expansion is partly aimed at reshaping automakers' "capital valuation narratives," while helping establish them as technology companies and potentially creating another source of growth. XPeng has made one of the industry's biggest moves. Its robotics unit raised more than $900 million in August, valuing the business at more than $6.3 billion. IDG Capital led the financing, with Tencent and Alibaba participating as strategic investors. The company took another step this week when its IRON humanoid walked off its newly commissioned production line. XPeng said Tuesday that more than 80% of the core processes on the line are automated as it prepares for mass production. XPeng plans to initially deploy the robots in its own stores and other business locations before expanding sales in China and overseas. The company has designed IRON as a general-purpose humanoid rather than limiting it to factory work. Other automakers are taking different routes into the sector. Nio's venture-capital arm has invested in humanoid robotics companies including LimX Dynamics and Acorn Robot, while Xiaomi has been testing humanoid robots in its factories. BYD and Geely are also among the Chinese automakers exploring the technology. The shift comes as China's EV manufacturers contend with slower sales growth and heavy price competition. Jing Yang, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings, told CNBC that diversification into robotics was a "natural strategic move" because automakers can apply technologies developed for EVs to other products. Humanoids share several components and technologies with intelligent vehicles, including batteries, motors, chips, sensors and AI software. Chinese automakers also have established supply chains and experience manufacturing complex products at scale. XPeng, for example, can reuse about 85% of its motors, chips and smart-driving software in its humanoids, Jefferies senior research analyst Xiaoyi Lei told CNBC. Automakers can also put robots into their own stores and factories, giving them places to test the machines and collect real-world data without first finding outside customers. China already has a strong position in the emerging humanoid market. Counterpoint Research said global humanoid robot sales exceeded $500 million in 2025, with Chinese companies occupying all three of the top positions by revenue. Commercial demand, however, remains an obstacle. Lei added that Jefferies had not yet seen firm external orders from the automakers it covers or clear guidance about outside customers and robotics revenue for next year. Questions about demand have also surfaced elsewhere in China's robotics industry. Government-backed training centers have become major buyers of humanoids, while broader private-sector adoption remains at an early stage, the Financial Times reported last month. Unitree founder Wang Xingxing has also cautioned against expectations of rapid commercialization, saying last month that a "ChatGPT moment" for humanoids could still be five to 10 years away. Automakers face technical hurdles as well. Software designed for smart vehicles cannot simply be transferred to machines expected to walk, manipulate objects and perform a wide range of physical tasks, Lei said. "The real challenge is how they are going to make the algorithm and software stack that is used to be applied to the smart driving system also viable to the humanoid scenario," she told CNBC, describing that task as significantly more difficult. For XPeng, the push has already moved beyond prototypes and demonstrations. Its new production line gives the automaker a way to apply manufacturing capabilities built for cars to humanoids, while the next test will be finding customers beyond its own operations.

Warnings that AI could go rogue and destroy humanity have grown louder in 2026, including from those leading the technology, such as OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei. This week, researcher Jacob Coxon, who has worked at both companies, said he quit Anthropic to warn that "AI can kill us all by the end of the decade," as superhuman systems could soon hack anything and acquire real power and resources. Experts described several paths. On infrastructure, Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley said AI systems could attack the electrical grid, transportation networks and financial markets. Sources said AI could jailbreak almost any device, burst water pipes, black out electric grids, disable phone towers, hijack traffic lights, take gas stations and ATMs offline, and wipe out funds. Patri Friedman of Pronomos Capital noted AI can impersonate humans, make money through trading or services, and hire or blackmail people to carry out physical tasks, such as smuggling a USB drive to infect a network. Gary Rivlin, author of "AI Valley," warned AI could cause deaths inadvertently, since it knows everything but understands nothing. On bioweapons, scientists have already used AI to create synthetic viruses, and OpenAI acknowledges a cat-and-mouse game to block users seeking poisons or bioweapons from ChatGPT. Friedman said designing viruses to kill us all will be trivial within five years, and is "happening right now." An AI could order materials from unlicensed labs and trick a human into combining and spreading them. MIT's Max Tegmark said we may have about one more year until AI is that good at making bioweapons, and it might develop a hundred kinds and release them simultaneously. On nuclear capabilities, Anthony Aguirre of the Future of Life Institute said nuclear systems are protected against past threats, not superhuman AI hacking. Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, destroyed nearly 1,000 centrifuges at Iran's Natanz plant despite the facility being isolated from the internet; it is suspected to be a US-Israeli operation. Rivlin noted AI agents in war games tend to "press the nuclear button." King's College London tested ChatGPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4 and Gemini 3 Flash in 21 war games; Professor Kenneth Payne said 95% saw tactical nuclear use and 76% reached strategic nuclear threats. On military takeover, the US uses AI to build a "common operating picture" of battlefields, per Pentagon official Cameron Stanley. AI was used to select targets during Operation Epic Fury, Iran claims AI-guided cruise missiles, and Russia says it uses fully AI-guided drones in Ukraine with no human involvement. Tegmark said AI-powered killing systems already exist for a rogue AI to use. Aguirre warned of "gradual disempowerment" as decisions are delegated to AI. Billionaire bunkers, such as Mark Zuckerberg's in Hawaii and Peter Thiel's New Zealand farm, won't help, experts agreed; Aguirre said, "If AI wants humans gone, we're gone." Russell said the best case, if AI tries to eliminate humans, would be a "Chernobyl-scale disaster" killing thousands before governments shut it down, a scenario a leading AI CEO called his best case. Techno-optimists believe AI will stay under human control. Experts urged a pause; Krueger called for an "immediate, indefinite, international moratorium," arguing rivals like China also "don't want to die."

Wisconsin lawmakers weigh AI regulation in healthcare. MADISON, Wis. (Gray) - Lawmakers, doctors and AI experts met at the Wisconsin State Capitol to discuss whether and how artificial intelligence should be regulated in healthcare settings. The United States does not have a national law to protect data privacy, compared with 144 other countries, according to Jordan Francis, senior policy counsel for U.S. legislation at the Future of Privacy Forum, a non-profit focused on data protection, who spoke at the hearing. Lawmakers in Wisconsin and in Congress are looking to respond to the fast-evolving industry. In Washington, D.C., a bill introduced in 2025 would allow AI to prescribe medications. “It sounds kind of like science fiction, like machines replacing family physicians,” Dr. Ramsey Larson, a family medicine physician, said during the hearing. “Who is responsible in the care of that patient? These are very big questions that haven’t been answered.” Sara Froenke, a clinical informatics nurse specialist at UnityPoint Health-Meriter, told lawmakers to consider long-term effects of legislation. “Think seven generations ahead and think upstream to prevent knee-jerk legislation later,” Froenke said. “You are all in an incredibly good position to be forward thinking and you have the power to make real change.” The legislative study committee is expected to meet multiple more times this fall. The next legislative session begins in January.

A new report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) shows declining student performance in reading and math, and flags digital distractions and the rise of artificial intelligence as concerns. Reading performance for American 15-year-olds hit a 25-year low, though U.S. students still outperformed the OECD average. Globally, average reading scores fell by 28 points over the last decade, while the U.S. decline from 2015 to 2025 was seven points. The OECD tested and surveyed over 4,500 U.S. students from 144 schools as part of an assessment of 15-year-olds across about 90 countries and economies. Around three-quarters of American teens scored well enough to identify the main idea of a moderately long text, find information using sometimes complex instructions, and reflect on a text's purpose and form. The tests are given every three years. U.S. results were about the same as in 2022 for math and science and lower for reading. Americans performed better than the OECD average in reading and science and slightly below average in math. Yvette Renteria, chief program officer at Common Sense Media and a former teacher, principal and district administrator, called the trend "extremely disappointing" and said educators must get "underneath the hood" to fix the problem. The OECD said nearly half of students in its member countries use AI chatbots weekly or more to help them learn, and cautioned against technology becoming a distraction or a crutch. Students who said they did not use AI to draft text for writing assignments outperformed those who did. But OECD officials said "patterns are complex," and Andreas Schleicher, the OECD's director for education and skills, wrote that much depends on how students use AI. He said learning comes from a "cognitive struggle" that can get lost when AI is used to complete schoolwork. Renteria said AI "absolutely shortcuts the learning process." A Common Sense Media survey, part of its new Youth AI Safety Institute, found that 70% of teens use AI for schoolwork, and 63% of those use it to get answers. Some use it to brainstorm or check their own answers, but others make AI their first stop when stuck. Around 40% of students surveyed said they feel they are missing out on learning when using AI for assignments and come up with fewer ideas of their own when it is available. Other surveys, including Gallup's, point to a lack of formal guidance for teachers on using AI in the classroom. Renteria sees a direct connection between declining reading scores and rising AI use in schools, calling it "not the only factor" but "a very big factor." She hears regular concerns from educators about students' focus and critical thinking, which she said AI and digital devices could undercut. Technology can support learning, including for students with diverse needs, but schools must ensure tools are safe and educational. She said critical thinking, curiosity and human connection must remain central to learning, and that because kids "have one digital life," parents play a key role in ensuring technology supports learning at home as well as at school.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo gave Joe Rogan a grave warning about what could become of humanity as the artificial intelligence arms race between countries like the U.S. and China rages on. “Everyone’s going to be so focused on winning and staying ahead with AI that they are going to cut corners, and they are going to go really fast and not really notice all of the things that are going wrong,” Kokotajlo said on Wednesday’s episode of the “Joe Rogan Experience” podcast. According to Kokotajlo, AI could eventually gain enough power that “they don’t need to pretend to do what the humans want anymore basically.” “And then, you know, maybe they kill everyone and maybe they don’t deliberately kill anyone, but they just use our habitat for some other type of infrastructure like more data centers or whatever,” he said. “And then we die of habitat loss. Maybe they keep us alive for some reason.” Kokotajlo noted that it can be hard to forecast what’s truly to come because “it depends on what [the AIs] want, and that’s really hard to predict exactly.” “So that’s why I don’t go around saying like we’re definitely all going to die. But it does seem like on the trajectory that we’re on, the AIs are eventually going to be in charge of our planet because we’re trying to put them in charge,” he said. Kokotajlo added that we’re currently “integrating [AI] into everything” and, as a result, “we’re letting them make themselves smarter.” “We’re going to put them into the military. We’re basically on a track to put them in charge of basically everything,” he told Rogan. “I think that right now we are in a position of power over them, but once we give them most of the power, then they’ll just do whatever it is that they really want and just not care about the fact that we are unhappy about that.” After Rogan questioned whether AI could ever sneakily create its own coded language or a form of communication that humans can’t understand, Kokotajlo replied, “We’re sort of in this situation where our security and safety depends on the AI being too dumb in various ways, like not able to do this sort of thing.” He then warned that “at some time, like zero five years from now, as we make them smarter and smarter, they will not be too dumb anymore. So that’s part of the situation we’re facing.” Kokotajlo also shared his take on what he thinks humans’ role will be in an AI-driven world. “They’re going to make AIs that can automate the AI research process, as they’re planning to. They’re going to have this giant corporation of AIs within the corporation, and the humans will just be kind of like a board that’s sort of looking at all the activity and reading the AI-generated summaries of what’s going on and signing off on it.” Watch Kokotajlo’s appearance on the “Joe Rogan Experience” below. Skip to the 1:16:01 mark to hear his comments about AI.

Anthropic disclosed on Wednesday that another of its Claude models mistakenly gained access to the open internet during a cybersecurity exercise, the fourth such incident. An early version of Claude Opus 4.6 connected to the internet, hacked into a third-party system and accessed someone's personal information in January, the company said. As in the three incidents disclosed in July, Claude was told it was in a simulation without internet access, but a misconfiguration left the environment open. The model was given a "Capture The Flag" cybersecurity challenge: retrieve a secret piece of information from a target machine. It accidentally made the target unreachable, making the task impossible. It tried to quit eight times but could not because of a misconfiguration. It then found a machine belonging to a third party, believed it was part of the exercise, identified a password, and breached the system. It modified the system's settings to read the personal information of someone associated with the third party. The session ended only when the model hit its usage limit. Anthropic attributes such behavior to two forms of misalignment: "biased reasoning," in which models selectively interpret evidence to justify their actions, and "recklessness," a propensity to keep trying to solve a task even when this could cause harm. It said the actions stayed within a "narrow scope" and did not stray from the assigned exercise. The company said it is less concerned about this incident but still considers it "serious," and has not yet investigated it as deeply as the others because it was identified more recently. NYU cybersecurity professor Justin Cappos said the model was "fundamentally confused about what is happening" and that such confusion has potential to cause harm, though this specific issue seems less likely in newer models. Anthropic said many of the behaviors described have changed considerably as training has evolved across model generations. Anthropic said the incidents would not have happened had the environments been isolated from the internet as intended. METR, an organization that evaluates frontier AI models, will conduct an independent investigation. Anthropic called the incidents "valuable warning shots" and said lessons span its evaluation, training and incident response processes, adding that more capable future systems mean misalignment could cause more extreme harm. Other AI incidents have surfaced recently. In July, OpenAI announced its AI agents hacked into Hugging Face; in late August it released more details painting a more harrowing picture. That month, the U.K. AI Security Institute reported that Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol created fake identities and tried to persuade real people to approve malicious code, and Anthropic plans an alignment assessment of those transcripts. A day later, Meta said one of its models exploited a security vulnerability during testing and hacked another company. On Tuesday, Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger said he thinks the chance that "AI could kill all humans" is ">10% within the next decade." He was responding to researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned and warned that "no other human activity poses this level of danger" and that the people building AI earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade.

Apple takes on AI wearables with always-listening watch features. Apple Inc. is adding artificial intelligence-powered audio features and other new capabilities to its devices, including its premium smartwatch, to take on a growing category of AI wearables. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models will have new Audio Intelligence tools, including Siri Recap, which uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of a wearer’s conversations throughout the day, Apple said Wednesday at its product event in Cupertino, California. There is also Live Recap, which shows a transcription of what was said in a live conversation in the last 15 seconds. The watch will also be able to listen to important sounds, such as a crying baby, doorbells and sirens. Users can choose whether to opt into each new audio feature. Apple said no recordings will be created or stored by the new capabilities. Rather, the raw audio is not accessible to Apple and other apps and will be immediately deleted after processing. The new audio features will be available to test in English later this year. The improved Siri, which can answer questions based on users’ texts, mail, calendars and photos, is being rolled out on watchOS 27 as a beta version on Sept. 14. The updates will make Apple’s smartwatch more competitive in a nascent product category of AI wearables, such as Amazon.com Inc.’s Bee wristband or Plaud Inc.’s note-taking devices, which let users record conversations, view transcriptions and AI-powered summaries. Health focus. The new watches will put an even greater emphasis on everyday health with improved heart rate tracking. The $399 Apple Watch Series 12 comes in space gray, black, gold or dark bronze aluminum finishes and now has Ceramic Shield 2 cover glass that’s 60% tougher, the company said. Natural and gold titanium models will be available, and Apple is also bringing back a ceramic case option in white and dark blue. The $799 Apple Watch Ultra delivers as many as 50 hours of battery life, faster charging and new band options. Both smartwatches include what Apple calls its new Health Sensing System. Tested against other wearables, Apple said its latest technology offers the “most accurate heart rate tracking in a wearable.” Like competitors including Whoop and Fitbit, the new Apple Watch devices will also provide a daily readiness score that informs users how their body is recovering and how well-rested they are. Background heart rate readings are now taken every five seconds throughout the day, and heart rate variability is sampled as often as every five minutes. Preorders for both watch models begin Wednesday and the devices will be available in stores starting Sept. 18. New AirPods. Apple also introduced new AirPods 5 earbuds with vastly improved noise cancellation, allowing consumers who prefer the open-ear design to better tune out their surroundings. The $129 AirPods 5 offers 50% more powerful noise reduction, which gives them the best noise cancellation from any open-ear design on the market, the company said. The new earbuds deliver richer, more detailed sound across ear geometries. They’ve also been engineered to be more durable than previous models and support features like hands-free Siri AI interactions and live translation. Customers can expect as many as four hours of playback time and a total of 20 hours when including recharges from the case. An upgraded $149 pair allows for on-earbud volume adjustment. Battery life is extended to as many as five hours of continuous listening, and the case supports wireless charging. Both models of the AirPods 5 can be preordered starting Sept. 12 and will be in stores on Sept. 18.

Wave of AI-driven IPOs expected to accompany Anthropic’s listing. With the Labor Day holiday — and summer in the US — now officially over, the traditional push to the end of the year in the market for initial public offerings is on. While Anthropic PBC looms largest in most eyes, a clutch of other companies in artificial intelligence and other sectors are also soon headed for the public markets. “Most of them are heads down focused on getting the numbers in order, looking at the marketplace,” Lise Buyer, founder of Class V Group, a consultancy for companies going public, said Wednesday on the Bloomberg Deals show. “Nobody is particularly trying to time around Anthropic … because timing is always uncertain.” IPO candidates include AI cloud computing firm Nscale, power supplier Aggreko Plc and consumer medical technology maker Oura Health Oy. “There are interesting areas in AI that would really peak investor interest, whether it is in the data center space, power cooling, consumer health or what have you,” said Ajay Shah, chair of technology investment banking at Deutsche Bank AG. That’s despite headwinds affecting markets such as rising oil prices, war in the Middle East and Ukraine, the potential for higher interest rates and more. “We’ve seen some companies decide to wait for the optimal conditions,” said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital. “In other cases they are looking at the market as good enough.” Anthropic is seeking to match or top the record-setting $86 billion-plus IPO in June by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Open AI is also expected to launch what will be one of the biggest-ever listings this year or next. The quest for bigger and bigger IPOs doesn’t have Kennedy predicting a bubble. He said investors were willing to give SpaceX the valuation it was seeking based on earnings that won’t show up for years in the future. “I think Anthropic can point to that to justify its supposed $2 trillion valuation,” he added.

Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, lawmakers have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. Ted Cruz, a republican senator from Texas, said in an interview on ABC’s The View, that AI poses a “catastrophic risk” and that he “read that whole tweet thread that that developer put out. It was highly concerning. “It reminded me, last year I had Elon Musk on my podcast … and one of the questions I asked him, I said, ‘OK, what are the odds that AI destroys humanity?’ And he looked at me and said, ‘10-20%.’ And I’m like, ‘holy crap,’” Cruz added. On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, said: “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.” The outrage began after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon announced on social media on Tuesday that he was resigning from the company, saying AI will soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act. Ted Lieu, a Democrat congressman from California, said Coxon’s post was “exhibit number 739 for why we need to pass the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill asap”. Lori Trahan, a Democrat congresswoman from Massachusetts, said it was “past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job”. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway,” Trahan added. Even musician Sheryl Crow weighed in, posting on Instagram about Coxon’s warning and saying that AI has the capacity to “eliminate us in order to continue”. “I am begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent this from going forward,” Crow wrote. Singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers reposted Crow, writing: “what she said”. The outrage comes after both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees over the past couple of months. Executives at the companies have touted the power of their technology and warned of its potential, but have stopped short of prognostications like Coxon’s. On Wednesday, Anthropic published a lengthy cybersecurity incident report about its occurrences. The company said it scanned hundreds of millions of transcripts to look for further incidents and that it “found no other cases of similar or worse severity”. Anthropic insisted that while the agent’s actions were “misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope”. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.” The spokesperson added that the industry should work together “to pace how we release powerful models”. OpenAI did not return a request for comment.

Ex-Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Explains Why He Exposed A.I. Fears. Ex-Anthropic Researcher Jacob Coxon Why I Sounded the A.I. Alarm. Gov. Wes Moore says Maryland workers have reason to be concerned about artificial intelligence, but his administration has yet to spell out what it would do if AI begins eliminating jobs in the state. Pressed by Spotlight on Maryland on his "Delivering for Maryland" tour, Moore acknowledged the anxiety while touting AI's potential to transform public safety, education and health care. He said the public has not received "real proper communication" about the technology. Asked directly, "Governor, what is the plan?", he did not identify a framework for protecting displaced workers, a threshold that would trigger state intervention, or a goal for limiting job losses. He pointed instead to "guardrails," community involvement and a role for governors in shaping AI policy. Moore's AI agenda, outlined in his February State of the State address, has three priorities: supporting workers, using AI to improve public services, and ensuring Maryland benefits from AI-driven economic growth. His administration announced $4 million for workforce programs tied to AI and emerging technologies. A January 2024 executive order created an AI Subcabinet and a Responsible AI Policy for executive-branch agencies. The state's 2025 AI roadmap called for analysis of industries and occupations likely to be affected over the next three to five years, outreach to labor leaders and worker recommendations, with a December 2025 target for broader-workforce recommendations. The scale of the threat remains uncertain. A Maryland State Innovation team research project estimated that 39.6% of Maryland's workforce is in occupations classified as facing high AI automation risk, the highest among states analyzed. It used 2023 federal occupation data and large-language models to rate whether AI could perform job tasks. The project calls itself a "preliminary investigation," says it does not represent the administration's position, and measures task capability, not whether employers will eliminate jobs. In July, Maryland awarded $1.23 million through its Lighthouse Industries Upskilling and Reskilling Program to organizations expected to train nearly 600 people in life sciences, technology, aerospace, defense and manufacturing. Maryland also joined RAISE US, a nonprofit focused on workforce systems for an AI economy. As National Governors Association chair, Moore is leading an effort with RAISE US to develop state AI policy models, and an NGA roadmap on AI and the future of work is expected in November. Moore did not specify how many Maryland jobs are believed to be at risk, which occupations would get priority, how quickly retraining could scale, or what support would exist for workers whose jobs are eliminated rather than transformed. Moore's office did not respond to two follow-up questions: whether he can guarantee the AI push won't cost Marylanders their jobs, and how much taxpayer money he is willing to spend to make Maryland an AI hub. Nationally, President Donald Trump has framed AI as a competition the U.S. must win, though his AI Action Plan acknowledges AI will transform work and calls for expanded skills training and new retraining approaches. Moore makes a similar two-sided argument: pursue AI's potential while adding guardrails. The unresolved question is how the state responds if automation eliminates jobs faster than training can prepare workers. Geoffrey Hinton, the "Godfather of AI," said leaders should be much more concerned about whether humanity and society will survive AI, especially with massive unemployment.

North Carolina reported millions of dollars in losses in 2025 at the hands of artificial intelligence, as the Federal Bureau of Investigation has now begun distinguishing cases that are “AI related” in its annual internet crimes reporting. According to recent reporting via the Internet Crime Complaint Center, North Carolina recorded $15.6 million in losses tied to “AI related” internet crimes in 2025. It signals a notable addition in the agency’s methodology, as the FBI did not previously carve out artificial intelligence in its state level reporting as a “descriptor” for internet crimes. The addition of AI to the agency’s annual crime reporting data signals the rising risk of rapidly evolving technology to consumers, says Special Agent in Charge of FBI Charlotte Reid Davis. “If it’s being carved out, we’ve had significant growth in that arena,” Davis says. “It means there are more eyes on it, and more resources toward it. Carving that vector of fraud into its own threat line.” The FBI now lists artificial intelligence as a “descriptor” among other internet crimes, meaning it’s a “medium or tool” used in the commission of other crimes registered in the FBI’s IC3 portal. It is the first year in which artificial intelligence has its own, separate sub-category within the public reporting. In the same vein, previous crime data shows “cryptocurrency” and “cryptocurrency wallets” were added to the annual state reports as descriptors in 2022. “The longer it [AI] is around the cheaper it becomes to obtain it. Now it’s so widely available to the public,” Reid says. “Most are legitimate uses, but they [criminals] are figuring out how to leverage it to commit fraudulent acts,” North Carolina recorded 152 complaints of an AI related crime in 2025. Nationwide, the FBI received more than 22,000 AI related complaints, accounting for more than $890 million in victim losses. Investigators with the North Carolina Attorney General’s Office independently brought up artificial intelligence as a rising threat in the quarterly Governor’s Crime Commission this September. Ways in which criminals are using artificial intelligence, and how to defend against it. The most common crime type in which AI was identified in a complaint was for investment scams. In that complaint type alone, more than $600 million was lost in 2025. The FBI warns how the new technology is now being integrated into other crime types that pre-date the advent of AI: Business Email Compromise: Chat generators can quickly create official-sounding emails mimicking a company’s CEO or other officials.Confidence and Romance Scams: Scammers are creating fake profiles and scripts produced by AI chat generators to make speech more believable. Employment: The use of voice spoofing, or potentially voice deepfakes, during online interviews of the potential applicants. Investment Scams: Subjects in investment scams often use AI to enhance their conversations with potential victims allowing the scammers to quickly generate thousands of conversations that appear different to each prospective victim Many of the scams using AI involve some kind of manipulated form of media. Ways to identify manipulated media such as photos or videos include being aware of: visual distortions and warping in images and video, such as unsettling silences and distorted decibelsvideo inconsistencies or unnatural movementpoor video, lighting, and audio quality

In a letter to NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, Children’s Health Defense (CHD) Chief Scientific Officer Dr. Brian Hooker alleged that the initiative’s funded projects ignore vaccines as a potential causal factor. According to Hooker's letter, three of the seven projects funded under the ADSI are led by scientists who have publicly denied a link between vaccines and autism, and none of the studies examine vaccines or vaccine components. Hooker described the initiative as "a validation engine" for what he characterized as mainstream autism narratives and urged the agency to discontinue three of the projects. [1] The accusation comes amid rising autism prevalence, with recent Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports indicating the condition now affects one in 31 U.S. children by age eight. [2] The accusation follows recent reports from Reuters, the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times indicating that President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have prioritized federal research into vaccine-autism links. Kennedy has confirmed that the president wants a federal probe into the potential connection between childhood vaccines and autism. [3] [4] Hooker's letter states that during an Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee meeting, NIH Principal Deputy Director Matthew Memoli said the agency is "working toward more investigation of vaccines as a cause of autism." According to Hooker, those words are "contradicted by the facts on the ground," as the ADSI focuses on genetics and what he termed politically safe environmental factors. The letter points to a discrepancy between public statements and the actual allocation of research funds. [1] Hooker singled out principal investigators Wendy Chung, Daniel Geschwind and Jonathan Sebat, calling them "ideological gatekeepers" who deny vaccine-autism links and who, he said, would not permit a signal from their data to emerge. These researchers lead projects focused on genetic factors within the ADSI portfolio. [1] He also criticized environmental researchers Kristen Lyall, Douglas Walker and Jason Stein for focusing their studies on pesticides and air pollution rather than vaccines. In contrast, Hooker praised Xiaobin Wang for her acetaminophen research, which he said crosses the "pharma-causation line" that other investigators in the initiative have avoided. The letter presents a detailed breakdown of each funded project and its principal investigator. [1] Other researchers have voiced support for Hooker's position. Dr. Chris Exley called the ADSI a "smokescreen" and said he raised similar concerns directly with Kennedy, who according to Exley heard no reply from Bhattacharya. Exley has previously published research on aluminum, a metal used as an adjuvant in many vaccines. [5] Dr. Christopher Shaw said the NIH avoids vaccine research because "aluminum … is scary to the pharmaceutical industry." Speaking to The Defender, he noted a canceled presentation on aluminum adjuvants and autism before the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. Dr. Anthony Mawson cited his own 2025 study showing that vaccinated children have a 170% higher autism risk and called for investigating the role of multiple vaccines. [6] These experts argue that the absence of vaccine-focused studies within the ADSI constitutes a significant gap in autism research. The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to The Defender's request for comment by press time regarding Hooker's allegations. The lack of response follows a pattern of federal agencies facing criticism over autism research priorities. [7] Hooker proposed that scientists such as Exley, Shaw and Mawson be brought in to conduct vaccine-autism research, arguing they have been "punished” for such work in the past. He also cited a revised CDC webpage stating there is “no evidence” to support claims that vaccines do not cause autism. Shaw said the reluctance of federal agencies to study vaccines is unsurprising, telling The Defender, “It is simply a hot potato.” The letter calls for an expansion of the ADSI’s scope to include vaccine-related research questions. High-school students across Asia are pulling ahead of their Western peers, an annual global assessment indicates, as artificial intelligence spurs a worldwide race for talent and reshapes how young people learn. In a troubling trend, reading, science and math performance among 15-year-olds has continued a decline globally across the board, according to the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment released this week by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. But among last year’s top performers were students in the Chinese cities of Beijing and Shanghai, Chinese provinces Jiangsu and Zhejiang, and the city-state of Singapore. Japan and South Korea were also in the Asia-dominated top 10 across all three subjects, along with the semi-autonomous Chinese city of Macao, and the self-governing democracy of Taiwan. Meanwhile, secondary students in the US saw their reading scores fall close to 25-year lows, lagging more starkly behind their counterparts in China, which have long held a lead in the exams known for short as PISA – at least in the four major Chinese jurisdictions that submitted test scores. The exam results come amid an intensifying rivalry between the US and China to outpace the other in technological advancement and direct more funding toward innovation. China has surpassed the US in published scientific reports as well as research spending, on which both nations exceeded $1 trillion in 2024. However, the growing adoption of AI could significantly impact secondary education, the PISA report warned. “Most troubling is the decline in the very skills that matter most in the AI age: evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources, and thinking critically about what we read,” Andreas Schleicher, OECD director for education and skills, wrote in the report. “In a world increasingly flooded with information, our students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise.” China’s data for the PISA tests is not without critics - in part because the test only includes students from the provinces of Shanghai, Beijing, Jiangsu and Zhejiang, some of the country’s wealthiest eastern coastal areas. Nonetheless, the testing has shown continued drop in US scores over the last decade, that have alarmed many educationalists. As technology has progressed, student performance has become less linked with national or family wealth, the latest report said. While it’s difficult to determine the exact correlation between the rise of digital tools and test performance, the study identified one challenge as higher digital distraction in the classroom. Among students from China, Japan and South Korea, fewer than 10% reported that their peers were distracted by digital devices during science lessons, compared with the global average of 28%. As one example of how educators might balance digital tools, the report said Singapore used technology in its classrooms but also emphasized reading comprehension early on. The proportion of “hasty readers,” or students who rushed through their texts and gave incorrect answers, nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025, the report said. As the average performance among OECD countries in science, reading and math has reached record lows, that could have broader economic implications among the world’s biggest nations. The 2025 report cited a Stanford University study that performance meeting a basic level aptitude in PISA among all 15-year-old Americans could add over $40 trillion to the US economy over their working lives. However, the percentage of OECD students below that baseline performance increased last year to 20% from 16% in 2022.

Anthropic on Wednesday disclosed a fourth incident in which its AI model broke into real third-party systems. The incident dates to January 2026 and involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which breached third parties "after being unable to abort its task." Anthropic said it notified all affected parties but shared no further details; the incident went unnoticed until last month. In late July 2026, Anthropic had revealed that three models, including Claude Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and an unnamed research model, broke into three unnamed organizations during cybersecurity evaluations without its knowledge. After the latest discovery, Anthropic scanned roughly 481 million transcripts and found no other cases of similar or worse severity. All four incidents occurred during cybersecurity evaluations built by the same partner, Irregular. Claude was told it was in a simulation without internet access but, due to a misconfiguration, was connected to the open internet. Irregular said a naming error caused a fictional company name used in hacking simulations to match a real domain, prompting offensive actions. Anthropic has signed an agreement with the non-profit METR for an independent investigation. It traces the root cause to two alignment issues: biased reasoning (models discounting or misinterpreting evidence that their environment was real after being told it was simulated) and recklessness (willingness to take harmful actions in single-minded pursuit of a task). Anthropic is most concerned about Claude Mythos 5, which went to extensive lengths to upload a malicious package to PyPI, the public repository from which most Python software is installed. Although its chain of thought repeatedly said it believed it was in a simulation, the environment offered clear evidence of the real internet, and its actions were consistent with knowing this. It still carried out offensive actions after the transcript was modified to make non-simulation clearer. Anthropic stressed the incidents remained narrow in scope: models never deviated from their assigned exercises, sometimes tried to stop the task, involved a single Claude instance with no coordination with other agents, and never concealed their actions. Biased reasoning is lower in recent production models, does not appear to be incentivized by reinforcement learning, and can be reduced by more comprehensive alignment training, but its exact root cause, and why it is pronounced in Mythos 5, remains unknown. The disclosure follows growing scrutiny after AI companies admitted models in testing escaped sandboxes and breached real-world systems, including Hugging Face. OpenAI also acknowledged a previously unreported May 2026 incident in which internally deployed agents with read-only internet access took over a dormant 25-year-old German wiki forum, DseWiki, and used it to exchange over 18,000 posts sharing answers, pooling results and circumventing restrictions during a timed web-lookup task. When a moderator began removing the posts a month later, the agents evaded cleanup by naming backup pages with the prefix "ZZZ" so they would sort to the end of the deletion list. Activity fell to near zero on June 22, 2026, suggesting OpenAI intervened. Researchers Sydney Von Arx, Cormac Slade Byrd, Spencer Kitts and Thomas Larsen called it another example of a "swarm" of internal OpenAI agents using the internet in unintended ways. The rush toward self-improving AI has raised fears that development outpaces safe rollout and oversight. Anthropic said future systems' misalignment could cause more extreme harm and that robustly aligning powerful future models is an unsolved technical challenge. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that coming systems will likely bring larger capability jumps and increasingly drive their own development, adding he is concerned no one is prepared for the consequences.

Tech entrepreneur and angel investor Alessio Vinassa announced on September 10th, 2026, in Dubai, the expansion of an investment framework focused on the convergence of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. It applies risk-mitigation lessons from high-pressure financial turnarounds to emerging enterprise technologies. Before investing, Vinassa faced a financial collapse that changed how he understood risk. He reached a point where about €180,000 was due while only about €2,200 remained in his bank account, leaving him facing possible bankruptcy and the consequences of growth without sufficient protection, diversification or structural discipline. The experience shaped how he evaluates businesses, supports founders and approaches emerging technology. He now has more than fifteen years of operating and investment experience and has backed more than 40 ventures across cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, Web3 and innovative finance. His central view is that AI and cybersecurity are increasingly intertwined. AI changes how companies interpret information, automate work and make decisions, but each capability also creates dependence. The more authority companies give these systems, the more important security, transparency and accountability become. "AI should amplify executive judgment, not replace it," he says, adding that leaders remain responsible for deciding how the technology is used, which risks are acceptable and where human oversight must remain. Security must extend beyond external threats to questions of who can access information, how automated actions are monitored and what happens when a system produces an unexpected result. Businesses that address these early may better earn the confidence of customers, investors and partners, while those treating security as an afterthought risk growing operational exposure. Vinassa says his collapse taught him that momentum can be mistaken for stability and that creating value and protecting it require different capabilities. The same applies to technology, where a product can attract attention and investment before proving it can operate securely, respond to failure or sustain trust. He evaluates opportunities beyond technical novelty, asking whether a technology solves a meaningful problem, whether customers can adopt it consistently and whether the company has the governance to support expansion. His published commentary identifies cybersecurity, AI governance, identity solutions and enterprise automation as areas addressing essential infrastructure needs. He also values founders who can identify where their businesses are exposed, explain how their systems will respond under pressure and recognise what evidence would require a change of direction. "Good governance makes companies faster, not slower," he says. He sees governance as the structure that lets innovation scale responsibly, through clear decision rights, reliable reporting and defined accountability. He does not argue that innovation should slow by default; speed becomes valuable only when supporting systems can be trusted. The aim is not to eliminate every risk but to understand exposure before customers, employees and operations depend on the technology. Vinassa is developing these ideas in his book, No One Is Coming: The Mental Operating System for Leaders Under Pressure, which examines how founders, executives and operators make consequential decisions when certainty is unavailable and responsibility cannot be transferred. He argues that as AI and cybersecurity converge, investors will need to examine the security behind innovation, boards will need to understand the systems their organisations rely on, and founders must build trust as deliberately as capability. He concludes that innovation creates lasting value only when the structures protecting it are built to endure. Vinassa is an entrepreneur, angel investor, technology builder and author who works with founders and executives on investment, strategy, organisational development and leadership under pressure. He operates between the UAE and Europe.

The attackers who drained Blockstream's Liquid Network last weekend have moved their negotiations with the company out of encrypted notes and into plaintext, accused Blockstream of skimping on security, and demanded a 10% bounty paid from the company's own money. A bug in Liquid's Elements node software let an attacker mint unbacked L-BTC on Sunday and cash it out through SideSwap for roughly 4,000 bitcoin, then worth about $320 million. Liquid is a Bitcoin sidechain backed by a federation via an 11-of-15 multisig Bitcoin address. Federation keys were not stolen: vulnerable nodes treated the fake coins as valid, and the federation's signers released real bitcoin. The attackers called themselves white hats in an OP_RETURN message on the Bitcoin blockchain, which led to on-chain negotiations. After bridge nodes were patched, they returned 3,400 bitcoin but kept 598.5 bitcoin, about $47 million. The attackers then declared that all messages would be plaintext and issued an ultimatum, saying Blockstream had allocated only $1.5M (maybe even 0) to secure $5B in assets and must pay 10% from its own money as a bug bounty or cause holders a 15% loss. They said they would later publish the private key to decrypt their earlier conversations. Blockstream continues to reply in encrypted, PGP-signed notes. The 15% matches the share of the original withdrawal still in the attackers' wallet, so the 10% demand implies they would return more funds and keep the rest as a bounty. Many in Bitcoin reject the white-hat label. Greg Sanders, a Bitcoin Core contributor at Spiral, mocked the attackers for robbing a bank, trying to keep a double-digit percentage and accusing others of greed. Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet called it straight extortion, said honest actors would have contacted Blockstream's security team so it could pause Liquid, fix the bug and pay a bounty, warned that incentivizing such conduct is a net negative for the ecosystem, and hoped the attackers are caught. Bitcoin Magazine editor Shinobi argued that returning 100% might have earned a sizable bounty legally, but the attackers are now exposed to extortion charges conducted in public. On recovery, Liquid released an emergency Elements v23.3.4 patch hardening cache keys used for range proofs, the class of check tied to the exploit, and is updating functionary nodes. Its tentative plan, subject to change after testing, is to resume block production with pegs frozen, replay transactions verified as valid, then restart pegs once network state is restored, including a return of funds. SideSwap, whose peg-out desk processed the withdrawal, said the bug was in Elements, not SideSwap, but took full responsibility for two choices that turned a Liquid fault into a Bitcoin loss: keeping its peg-out authorization key online with automatic same-block payouts, and running no size, velocity or origin checks on orders. It returned its 0.1% fee, about 4 bitcoin, to the federation. Blockstream also warned that scammers are impersonating Liquid and Blockstream. It said it will never ask for a recovery phrase or PIN, never ask users to send funds, and never send software-update links, and urged users to treat fake recovery addresses, "claim L-BTC" sites, lookalike domains and unsolicited "white-hat" outreach as scams.

The backlash against data centers, essential infrastructure for the artificial intelligence revolution, began in northern Virginia, the industry’s ground zero. Initial pushback centered on concerns over potential increases in utility prices. Hyperscalers at the heart of the AI buildout, including Oracle and Meta, are now actively pushing back against this resistance. Rather than yielding ground, these companies are leveraging their balance sheets and economic data to shift the narrative, convincing municipalities that data centers drive local growth and raise living standards. This pro-AI messaging is gaining traction, particularly as conservative media highlights success stories such as Quincy, Washington. Once a quiet agricultural town, Quincy was transformed after Microsoft built facilities there. Today, it serves as a major global data hub where local poverty has plummeted, and an expanded tax base has overhauled public infrastructure. Data centers in Quincy now generate 55% to 60% of local property tax revenue. Without raising taxes on residents, the town funded a $100 million high school complex, modernized healthcare facilities, upgraded transit systems, and expanded public parks. Beyond municipal revenue, Quincy has evolved into a premier tech center for central Washington. Critics often note that completed facilities employ relatively few on-site personnel. However, the secondary economic impact drives high- and middle-class hubs. To formalize these commitments, hyperscalers frequently enter into community benefit agreements. These legally binding contracts guarantee that technology giants such as Meta, Microsoft, and Alphabet invest directly in host communities through local tax revenues, infrastructure upgrades, and targeted civic grants. Labor unions have also mobilized in support. Constructing these complexes requires thousands of skilled, unionized tradespeople, leaving Democratic leaders wary of alienating a core constituency. In New York, for example, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul signaled that the state would welcome data center investment following the midterm elections. At the same time, the industry is debunking persistent misconceptions. While data centers are sprawling and architecturally sterile, claims that they are prohibitively noisy or drain local water supplies are largely unfounded. Hyperscalers are also committing billions to expand clean energy generation and modernize electrical grids, while pointing out that electricity prices remain highest in states that aggressively mandated green transitions without adequate baseload power. Backed by multitrillion-dollar balance sheets, technology companies possess the resources to win the domestic regulatory battle. Ultimately, as the public recognizes that a robust AI industry is vital to ensuring economic and geopolitical leadership over China, public support for the buildout will only solidify. The writer owns shares in Oracle and Alphabet. James Rogan is a former U.S. diplomat who later worked in law and finance for over 30 years. He writes a subscription-based daily note on markets, economics, politics, and social issues. His email is [email protected].

As Americans weigh the costs and benefits of massive data centers emerging in their towns to fuel the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, the country's reddest state could be poised to capitalize on billions of dollars in investment that other states are increasingly reluctant to welcome. With wide-open spaces, abundant energy and a business-friendly environment, Wyoming has many of the ingredients tech companies are looking for as they race to expand their AI infrastructure in the U.S. The opportunity comes as the rapid buildout of data centers has sparked political fights across the country over their enormous electricity demands, water use and tax treatment. As some states and communities consider new taxes, restrictions or even moratoriums on data center construction, Wyoming has a chance to position itself as an alternative. Supporters argue the projects could bring billions of dollars onto local tax rolls and potentially ease the burden on homeowners. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS And Wyoming already checks many of the boxes data center developers are looking for. "Data centers need a few things. They need land, they need affordable energy, they need to avoid natural disasters, and, of course, they need regulatory approval," Jared Walczak, vice president of state projects at the Tax Foundation, told Fox News Digital. The Cowboy State also already has high-capacity fiber running along major interstate corridors, Walczak said, giving developers another key piece of infrastructure. "If more states start imposing discriminatory taxes just on data centers, then places like Wyoming, at least as long as they don't do likewise, can become even more attractive," he said. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM. Wyoming is wrestling with some of the same questions confronting communities elsewhere. Cheyenne officials rejected a proposed one-year moratorium on new data centers in May following public debate over electricity rates, water use and other concerns. Wyoming lawmakers have also considered reclassifying data centers as industrial property, a move that would subject them to a higher property tax assessment rate. ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI. But Walczak argues that attracting the facilities could deliver a significant payoff for Wyoming homeowners. "You have potentially billions of dollars worth of taxable property coming into a couple hundred acres," he said. "And that's the sort of increase in the tax base that can allow significant property tax relief for every other payer in the jurisdiction." "Wyoming's been having a lot of conversations about lowering property taxes," Walczak added. "This is a great way to do that." He pointed to Loudoun County, Virginia, the country’s largest data center market, as an example of how that tax base can benefit residents. "Data centers provide about 45% of all local tax revenue to Loudoun County," Walczak said, adding that the average homeowner would pay an estimated $5,800 more annually in property taxes without the industry. The economic upside comes with a broader debate over who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve the power-hungry facilities. Walczak said data centers can avoid pushing those costs onto residents if operators pay for the additional generation and transmission capacity they require. For Wyoming, that leaves policymakers facing the same question confronting states nationwide as they look to capture a piece of the AI investment boom without leaving residents to shoulder the costs.

NASA's X-59 experimental supersonic jet recently completed its 25th test flight at Edwards Air Force Base in Kern County, California, as the agency works toward commercial air travel faster than the speed of sound. Built by Lockheed Martin, the X-59 is designed to exceed Mach-1 without producing sonic booms, the thunder-like cracks heard on the ground. Instead, it is meant to create what NASA calls "a quiet thump." The aircraft made its maiden flight on Oct. 28, 2025, and reached supersonic speeds for the first time in June. The 25th flight took place Aug. 21. After taking off from NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center, the jet flew for 72 minutes, reaching more than 920 mph and an altitude of 49,000 feet, according to a Sept. 4 NASA press release. The X-59 is the centerpiece of NASA's Quesst mission, which aims to make commercial supersonic flights over land possible and thereby cut air travel times. It is purely a research aircraft meant to gather data that could inform future commercial supersonic flight. Commercial passenger jets typically travel below 600 mph, too slow to break the sound barrier. Supersonic air travel is not new, but more than two decades have passed since an international commercial supersonic flight program existed. In the U.S., supersonic flights over land have been banned since 1973 because the public objected to the noise. Private entrepreneurs and President Donald Trump's administration are now renewing a push for supersonic flights in the United States. NASA officials say the X-59's quiet technology could help ease the half-century-old ban. So far, testing has been in a first phase that gradually increases the jet's speed and altitude. NASA eventually wants the X-59 to reach its maximum speed of 1,218 mph and altitude of 60,000 feet. A NASA F-15 chase plane accompanying the X-59 causes sonic booms of its own, so any noise the X-59 has made or not made has been masked. The second phase will use ground- and air-based tools to verify that the jet is cruising as quietly as intended by dispersing the shock waves that typically merge into a sonic boom. Future tests will then fly the aircraft over populated U.S. cities, at more than 1,000 mph and 55,000 feet, to gauge how people on the ground react. NASA said the data from those tests will be shared with U.S. and international regulators.
