Circle launches Arc mainnet with USDC as native gas token. Circle’s Arc mainnet is live with USDC for transaction fees, support for more than 20 fiat stablecoins and links to over 20 blockchains. USDC issuer Circle has launched the mainnet of Arc, a layer-1 (L1) blockchain targeting stablecoin payments and financial markets, particularly agentic transactions. Arc uses USDC as its native gas asset and offers Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) compatibility and deterministic sub-second settlement finality, according to an Arc blog post on Wednesday. The network supports more than 20 fiat stablecoins, including USDC, EURC, JPYC, KRW1 and TRYB, while tokenized assets including BlackRock’s BUIDL and Circle’s USYC are available natively on Arc. Arc also offers interoperability with more than 20 blockchains through Circle’s Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP) and Gateway. CEO Jeremy Allaire called Arc “the single most significant launch in Circle’s history since USDC itself.” Separately, Circle said in a post on X that Arc was built for “programmable money, global markets, and agentic economic activity,” describing the network as stablecoin-native infrastructure for developers and institutions. The launch follows Arc’s public testnet debut in October 2025, when Circle said more than 100 companies were participating, including BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, Mastercard and Visa. Circle said in August that more than 100 institutional and ecosystem builders had participated in Arc’s private mainnet ahead of the public launch. Arc said it ultimately plans to broaden participation in network operations and explore a transition from Proof of Authority to Proof of Stake in 2027. Circle also completed the genesis mint of 10 billion ARC tokens this week but said the mint does not represent a commitment to launch the token publicly.

The author argues that, while tariffs serve different purposes (foreign policy goals, leverage for better trade deals, or spurring domestic manufacturing), he considers all of them an unnecessary interference in commerce between consenting parties, though most politicians disagree. His central point is that some tariffs actually hurt domestic manufacturing, because many American manufacturers import materials used to make finished products. Cars are built with steel and imported parts, pharmaceutical ingredients are frequently sourced abroad, and refining fuel requires imported equipment. President Donald Trump's push to increase domestic manufacturing is therefore impeded by tariffs that hit these industries. He focuses on the proposed semiconductor tariff under Section 242 of the Trade Expansion Act, which would apply to all imports. Citing the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, he notes that semiconductors underpin artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, telecommunications, and other technology-intensive sectors. The foundation estimates that if the tariffs remain in effect for 10 years, GDP would fall by $1.6 trillion, or 3.9%. The author contends it makes no economic sense to tax the inputs American companies need to produce goods and services if the goal is higher productivity. He argues that raising semiconductor costs risks letting other nations overtake the U.S. in services, where the nation leads the world in exports, including business services, financial services, and travel, despite an overall trade deficit. He notes that the U.S. Chamber of Commerce urged on Jan. 28, 2026, that the administration "grant exclusions for small businesses, for products not readily available from domestic sources, and in instances where tariffs threaten American jobs." He argues these exclusions should extend from small to large companies that rely on foreign inputs to manufacture in the U.S. Tariff analysis, he says, should account for disruption to consumers and manufacturing. Tariffs on spices, coffee, bananas, and cocoa will not spur domestic production because the U.S. is not a tropical country. He compares this loosely to today's gas and diesel prices, where higher fuel costs hit consumers and raise the price of shipped goods. On national security, he argues that a semiconductor tariff could reduce security by limiting the military's access to what it needs for communications networks. Insourcing all semiconductor manufacturing will not happen overnight, and he asks what consumers will do if high costs shut them out for years while domestic production reaches critical mass. He concludes that a semiconductor tariff hike will not advance domestic manufacturing, since it raises costs on products not sourced domestically that are critical to the economy's engine. The result, he says, will be decreased productivity and less disposable income for American consumers. The author, Brian Darling, is a former counsel for Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY).

CV Summit 2026, billed as Switzerland's largest digital assets and AI conference, will bring global and Swiss leaders together in Zurich on September 29–30 at Kongresshaus Zurich. It aims to examine where institutional use of frontier technologies such as AI and blockchain goes next. Franklin Templeton, Ripple, Binance, BlackRock, Standard Chartered and Deutsche Bank are among the international entities attending alongside Swiss financial and technology leaders. The announcement stresses Switzerland's position. As the first jurisdiction to create clear legal ground for digital assets, it now has 54 of its 225 banks active in digital assets, more than any other country. Zurich hosts 7 out of 10 of the world's leading technology and AI players, and 70% of the 185+ AI entities located there are Swiss-made. Crypto Valley counts close to 1,800 firms and captures 47% of Europe's blockchain funding, according to the CV VC Top 50 & Ecosystem Report. Switzerland directs 63% of all venture capital to deep tech, the highest share of any country, ahead of China (56%) and the United States (54%) on a per-capita basis, per the Swiss Deep Tech Report 2026. Switzerland also ranks first globally in AI talent density, according to the Stanford AI Index Report 2026. Citing its supercomputing infrastructure, neutrality and diplomacy, the organisers say it has become a global AI hub and will host the official Geneva AI summit in 2027. CV Summit 2026 is an official event of the Road to Geneva programme ahead of that summit. Benedek Orban, Head of Ecosystem at CV VC & CV Labs, the hosts and organisers, said institutions worldwide are rapidly embracing frontier technologies and that the summit unites the players shaping the AI age. The summit runs across three stages, Anchor, Catalyst and Deep Dive, plus a networking area, with content in four tracks: Financial Infrastructure (stablecoins, digital custody and market infrastructure); Tokenization of Capital Markets (tokenised securities, institutional DeFi, digital exchanges, programmable financial infrastructure); AI and the Intelligent Economy (AI in finance, autonomous systems, agentic intelligence, and applications including defence and entertainment); and Wealth and Asset Management (how digital assets and technology are reshaping wealth creation). International speakers include Christopher Perkins, Head of Franklin Crypto; Cassie Craddock, Managing Director UK & Europe at Ripple; Catherine Chen, Lead of VIP & Institution at Binance; Dirk Klee, Country Head Switzerland at BlackRock; Marianne Webber, Head of Market & Regulatory Strategy, Digital Assets, at Standard Chartered; Manuel Klein, Head of Market Management Payments & Digital Currencies at Deutsche Bank; and Vincent Gusdorf, Head of Digital Finance Research & AI Analytics at Moody's. Swiss participants include PostFinance, Maerki Baumann, Luzerner Kantonalbank, UBS, Zürcher Kantonalbank, Sygnum, GenTwo, the SIX group and ISP. Partners come from Switzerland, the USA, Europe and the UAE. Franklin Templeton is presenting partner, joined by 60+ others including DMCC, Ephelia Group, Luzerner Kantonalbank, PostFinance, Ripple, SCRYPT and Unblock. Swiss industry bodies such as the Crypto Valley Association, Swiss Blockchain Federation, Swiss Fintech Association, Greater Zurich Area and Swiss Fintech Innovation take part, as do multiple universities and the Zug Institute of Blockchain Research (ZIBR). More information is at cvsummit.ch.

Venture capital is becoming more physical and specialized, financing the infrastructure and domain assets around AI rather than only foundation models. Ten rounds were announced in a 16-hour window on September 16, 2026, across AI drug discovery, manufacturing, robotaxis, reusable rockets, autonomous research, world models, semiconductor equipment, supply-chain software and materials. Disclosed capital included $471 million across Anew Labs, Hello Robotaxi, Noetive and TypeSafe AI; ¥17.7 billion for CADDi; nearly RMB1.05 billion across Apex Intelligence, Fuller Technology and Jinjing Technology; and a £22.7 million package for iGii. Space Epoch said its Series B financings over six months exceed RMB2.3 billion but did not disclose the new B++ tranche. Six of the ten companies are Chinese, and state-linked funds feature prominently alongside private investors. Anew Labs, ByteDance's AI drug-discovery unit, raised a $290 million inaugural external round at a $1.5 billion valuation, per Reuters, led by HSG (formerly Sequoia China), IDG Capital and Hillhouse, with 5Y Capital as co-lead. ByteDance keeps 56%. The raise was reported by sources and not publicly announced. Tokyo-based CADDi raised a ¥17.7 billion Series D at a ¥182 billion valuation, bringing cumulative equity funding to ¥36.31 billion. Investors include Woven Capital and Salesforce Ventures. It has shifted from a parts-procurement platform to an AI data platform for manufacturing, and says its software is used in 22 countries and by over half of the discrete manufacturers in the Nikkei 225. Funds go to AI development, North American expansion and hiring. Shanghai's Hello Robotaxi raised about $100 million at a near-$3 billion post-money valuation, led by Shanghai Guotou's Pioneer Fund. Backed by Hello, Ant Group, CATL and Alibaba, it will fund a 10,000-GPU-scale computing platform, end-to-end driving models and data supply. Beijing's Space Epoch completed a Series B++ round, with investors including IDG Capital. It is building the reusable Yuanxingzhe-1 rocket, targeting a first orbital flight and first-stage recovery attempt by end-2026 and commercial launches in 2027. Apex Intelligence raised nearly RMB400 million in Angel and Angel+ rounds under three months after its June 2026 founding. Founder Chen Yongchao of Tsinghua is pursuing recursively self-improving AI research; the claims remain unproven commercially. Fuller Technology raised RMB350 million in a Series B led by Shenzhen Capital Group. It serves over 1,300 enterprises (company figures) and is embedding AI agents in warehouse and transport software. Jinjing Technology raised RMB300 million in a Series B to scale electron-beam lithography and microscope production, a domestic-equipment play. Noetive raised a $41 million seed led by Eclipse for an industrial world model; an early customer estimated 10% to 15% added line capacity, unverified. TypeSafe AI emerged from stealth with a $40 million DCVC-led seed to build Jev, a fast, low-cost model for software decisions; performance claims are unvalidated. iGii's £22.7 million package combines an £11.7 million Series B led by the Scottish National Investment Bank with £11 million from Scottish Enterprise, to commercialize its porous carbon nanomaterial. Key patterns: investors are paying for proprietary data, scientific IP, physical control loops and manufacturing capability that cheaper models cannot replicate; seed rounds are unusually large; industrial AI is judged on measurable economics; and deep-tech and public-private financing structures increasingly resemble industrial rather than SaaS models.

More than 153 million US and Canadian driver's licenses were stolen earlier this month, apparently from an identity verification provider, and ended up on a dark web identity service called Nexus alongside millions of other stolen identity and travel documents. This week fintech Revolut revealed it had been tricked by a hacker into handing over sensitive customer data, including passport copies and verification selfies. The hacker is drip-feeding the documents of 680 customers online to try to secure a $3 million ransom in Monero. In the first half of 2026, US data breaches affected at least 343 million people, according to the Privacy Rights Clearinghouse. The irony is that Know Your Customer (KYC) processes are meant to make financial systems safer, yet they require companies to store vast amounts of sensitive information, creating honeypots for criminals. KYC evolved around the assumption that institutions should see and record customers' passports or licenses and keep evidence of the check, producing an ecosystem of providers and databases each holding copies. In the Revolut case, the hacker emailed requests for KYC data from a legitimate Italian law enforcement address. Lyudmyla Kozlovska, Open Dialogue president, said EU anti-money-laundering law gives banks no meaningful way to verify who is behind an authenticated state request, and refusal risks fines in the millions. Susie Violet Ward of Bitcoin Policy UK argues identity verification and surrendering your identity should not be treated as the same thing, noting you can reset a password but not your identity. Zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs, which demonstrate something is true without revealing the underlying details, could let someone prove they are over 18 without sharing a birth date or license image. Evin McMullen of Billions Network says the technology is in production today across thousands of applications and regulated institutions; the obstacle is that the compliance stack was built around collecting and storing document copies, making this "a governance and standards problem wearing a technology costume." The EU is already building ZK-based age verification and its Digital Identity Wallet supports "selective disclosure." Barriers include compliance teams conflating "we saw the ID" with "we must keep the ID," and a lack of shared standards so proofs can be checked without calling back the issuer. ZK is not a cure-all: podcaster Efrat Fenigson notes proofs are usually bound to an account in someone else's database, leaving people dependent on a centralized intermediary. The rules are also less rigid than assumed. The Financial Action Task Force's risk-based guidance considers digital ID for customer due diligence rather than requiring physical documents. McMullen says many regimes require verifying identity and retaining records of the verification, not keeping raw document images forever, so a cryptographic attestation could suffice. But because guidance is ambiguous, institutions keep everything since auditors accept it, and Ward notes regulators instinctively equate more information with more safety. Change seems unlikely unless rules explicitly allow ZK proofs. As McMullen says, "You cannot lose what you never held."

The space for the Fremont Union High School District’s robotics programs has been transformed from temporary portables to a permanent home. The district on Sept. 10 celebrated the grand opening of its new robotics center. Located at Cupertino High School, the new facility can serve up to 900 students from all five district high schools. The 14,500-square-foot facility is funded by Measure G, a $275 million bond measure passed by district voters in 2022. The center includes a dedicated robotics field space with spectator seating, a fully equipped workshop, classrooms and team collaboration zones. The grounds feature an entry plaza, outdoor learning and project spaces, drop-off areas, landscaping, and rooftop solar panels. Elements that support high-tech, hands-on learning include elevated ceiling heights to accommodate aerial drone testing, Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) protective flooring to guard sensitive electronic components, and dedicated Wi-Fi systems engineered to prevent signal interference during robot operation. The facility also features acoustic roof decking and wall paneling, advanced security features and integrated daylighting controls. The robotics center was designed by Quattrocchi Kwok Architects and built by Landmark Constructors, with Blach Construction serving as construction manager. “Seeing our students get to step into this facility is an incredibly proud moment for our entire district,” said superintendent Graham Clark in a release. “For years, our talented students worked wonders in makeshift, portable spaces. Thanks to the support of our local community and project team, we now have an environment where our award-winning robotics teams can take their work even further.”

Today’s private credit market is fragmented. Nonbank lenders often depend on several providers to make and manage loans, keep records, distribute payments, and ensure transactions are accurate. Because those providers all rely on different internal systems, the process can be slow and costly. That’s why a Brooklyn-based fintech company called Tare is pledging to simplify the process by using blockchain technology to bring those functions onto a single platform. Cofounded by credit and crypto veterans Kevin Miao, Keerthi Moudgal, and Lucas Vogelsang, Tare announced Wednesday that it had raised a $13.25 million seed round, which closed in March. The company plans to use the funding to build software on the Avalanche blockchain that creates digital records of loans, while automating the administrative work involved in managing them. Blockchain Capital led the round, joined by Janus Henderson, Strobe Ventures, the Venture Dept, Neoclassic Capital, and the Avalanche Foundation. Individual backers included Aave CEO Stani Kulechov, Tether cofounder Phil Potter, and Privy CEO Henri Stern. Tare declined to disclose its valuation following the seed round. In an interview with Fortune, Tare CEO Kevin Miao argued that the difference between what borrowers pay and what investors ultimately earn is often absorbed by the intermediaries that sit between them. Using mortgages as an example, he noted that middlemen costs inflate the interest rates borrowers pay while lowering the yields investors receive. Blockchain-based systems can automate that operational work and eliminate extra costs. “We deserve to have a system that works for us [and] doesn’t extract from both sides, and we need to build a platform or a marketplace that connects the two sides with no friction,” Miao said. “If we do this, everyone is going to benefit.” Modernizing credit systems. Certain companies have already made headway in using blockchain to make credit markets more efficient. Figure operates a blockchain-based lending and loan-trading platform, while tokenization platform Centrifuge helps bring real-world assets, including private-credit products, onto blockchain networks. Trading platform Octaura, meanwhile, has developed digital tools to streamline institutional credit trading. Rather than trying to compete with existing products, Tare is focused on updating the outdated systems financial firms use behind the scenes to manage loans, said Aleks Larsen, a general partner at Blockchain Capital. “I don’t see a direct competitor in crypto today. This is the first time we’re taking this entire system and trying to put it on-chain,” Larsen told Fortune. “The old way of doing things is the competitor.” Tare’s cofounders have spent years working at the intersection of credit and blockchain. Miao began his career at Citigroup in 2014, where he traded subprime mortgage products and helped early fintech lenders access debt capital markets. Inspired by a 2017 paper on using blockchain for securitizations, he later launched BlockTower Credit, a $2 billion institutional private-credit fund focused on bringing real-world credit assets and securitizations onto blockchain networks. Vogelsang cofounded Centrifuge in 2018 and led the company for several years before becoming a venture partner at Blockchain Capital and later turning his attention to Tare. Miao and Vogelsang first worked together on a deal when BlockTower selected Centrifuge as its tokenization infrastructure partner. They later met Moudgal, who was leading development at Kinexys, J.P. Morgan’s internal blockchain unit. The three concluded that earlier tokenization efforts had addressed only isolated parts of the credit market. At the end of 2023, they left their respective roles to launch Tare. Besides its New York headquarters, Tare has an office in Lisbon, Portugal. The company will use funds from its seed round to build and expand its loan management software, hire staff, and obtain the licenses needed for its lending arm, Tare Credit LLC, to operate across the United States.

Tutor Intelligence Inc., a provider of AI-powered warehouse robot workers, has launched second-generation versions of its Cassie and Sonny robots, which run on the company's robot foundation models. Sonny began as the company's dual-armed, semi-humanoid robot, introduced alongside Tutor's Ti0 4.5 billion parameter Vision Language Action model. It has since evolved from a research platform into a fully deployable robot capable of autonomous manipulation and mobility in warehouses. Cassie, the large-format, single-arm robot that resembles a giant arm atop a large wheeled box, was expanded for mobility in warehouses and factories, adding pallet movement and greater physical intelligence. The first generation of Cassie worked from a fixed position; it can now move across warehouse floors, lift 50 pounds and tug thousands of pounds. Co-founder and Chief Executive Josh Gruenstein told SiliconANGLE it is important that the company's general robots are also "immediately practically useful." Tutor chose not to follow the humanoid trend, noting humans already do that fundamental work fine, and instead designed robots around the work rather than around looking like a person. Cassie moves heavy material in pallet warehouse settings, while Sonny works among shelves, where arms and hands make sense for picking small objects and moving them between bins. Gruenstein said Cassie doesn't need to reason about everything a pair of hands might encounter: its physical vocabulary is small, essentially identifying, grasping, moving and placing an object. Sonny's vocabulary is much larger, so Tutor built Ti0 and a training facility to address the data problem. Robotics lacks an "internet of training data"; models need visual and kinetic telemetry showing how to pick up objects, what they look like, where to place them and how to move. In December, Tutor raised $34 million in Series A funding. Since then it has built what is essentially a "classroom" for its AI models called Data Factory 1 (DF1), a 100-robot factory where Sonny robots "learn." An internationally staffed team of tutors can remotely control a robot to teach it a new task for the first time. The 100 robots then go through the motions to fine-tune behaviors, smooth out kinks and prepare for field conditions, a process known as post-training. Good performance by an individual robot is reinforced in the AI model with a positive reward, a "thumbs up," while poor performance gets a "thumbs down," helping the model learn how real-world behaviors interact with actual hardware. Gruenstein said this approach can produce robots that "recursively self-improve and are superhuman in their performance relative to people."

This AI-Powered App Tells People How to Pose. An app called Superpose is teaching people how to pose better by employing AI computer vision. Melody Chu and Jing Liu both used to work at TikTok and came up with the new iOS app because of a very common problem faced by couples. “My husband just takes awful photos of me,” Chu tells TechCrunch. “It was a true pain point in our marriage where I don’t understand how he gets me to look just so terrible all the time. And I thought to myself, there has to be a way to solve this problem with advancements in computer vision and generative AI. And I decided to set out on my own.” Superpose was launched in July and has reportedly been downloaded over 22,000 times. The company says users have generated more than 190,000 poses to date. Superpose gives users five free generations each day, with additional generations available for purchase: five for $2.99 or 20 for $9.99. Opening the app, users will be greeted by a camera that can be used to take a photo or selfie. From one photo, the app uses AI to generate four possible poses. “One shot becomes several photos of the exact moment you lived — same place, same people, same light, just more of you in it,” says Superpose. “Not a different you, not somewhere you weren’t. Keep the ones that feel most like you.” Users are able to either save the AI-generated poses or try and imitate them; the app gives an outline of a pose for people to follow. Chu tells TechCrunch they want to stay away from AI-generated backgrounds and focus on real settings. “We want to lean into the core of memory capture versus, say, putting you in a fantastical place that you’ve never been,” she says. “I think there are so many apps that do that well already, but we really wanna focus on actually capturing the lived moment and experience.” Using AI to suggest poses was also a feature in Huawei’s new phone, the Pura 90. Superpose is available on the App Store now. Image creditsSuperpose. Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

Waymo in Minneapolis: City council considers ordinance that could ban driverless rideshares. MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - Waymo has been testing its autonomous vehicles in Minneapolis for months, eyeing a launch in the city. Now, a proposed Minneapolis City Council ordinance could complicate those plans. The proposed ordinance. What we know: The ordinance would require a human monitor inside every driverless ride-hailing vehicle operating in Minneapolis. According to the proposal, that person would need a valid driver's license and must be paid at least the minimum rates established under the city's ride-hailing driver laws. Waymo has pushed back hard, calling the measure a "de facto ban" on autonomous ride-hailing. Critics of the ordinance argue it defeats the purpose of the technology entirely and makes it too expensive to justify bringing Waymo's service to Minneapolis. Even in cities that don't require a human in the vehicle, Waymo rides already tend to cost more than a comparable Lyft or Uber trip. Why you should care: Supporters of the ordinance say the stakes are high for thousands of workers already on the road. Those in favor argue the measure protects more than 10,000 local drivers who currently work for services like Uber and Lyft. Safety is also a concern — backers of the proposal point to the risks of a fully driverless vehicle with no human available to step in during an emergency. Local perspective: Supporters of the proposed driver requirements were at City Hall held a news conference on Wednesday to make their case for why they believe the ordinance is necessary. A public hearing on the measure is set for next week, where the debate over driverless cars in Minneapolis is expected to continue. What we don't know: It remains unclear how the City Council will vote on the ordinance or whether Waymo would pull back its Minneapolis plans if the measure passes. The Source: Information in this story comes from Minneapolis City Council meeting agenda documents and a Waymo statement provided to FOX 9 as well as previous FOX 9 reporting.

The essay argues that Bitcoin's quantum debate is not simply "freeze or don't freeze" vulnerable coins, but a question of how to minimize total property-rights violations once elliptic curve signatures no longer reliably authenticate ownership. Every serious option violates something users value: doing nothing lets future quantum actors take coins without owners' consent, freezing retroactively invalidates spending conditions, and forced migration can resemble deadline-backed confiscation. Bitcoin's ECDSA and Schnorr signatures use secp256k1. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could derive a private key from a visible public key. Long-range attacks target outputs whose public keys are already on-chain (old pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs); short-range attacks target coins at spend time. Grover's algorithm gives only a quadratic speedup, so mining is a far lesser threat. Whether such a computer will ever be built is uncertain. Skeptics such as Mikhail Dyakonov and Gil Kalai argue fault-tolerance assumptions may not be physically satisfiable, correlated noise may defeat error correction, and qubit-count timelines cannot be simply extrapolated. Even if all active users migrated to post-quantum cryptography, at least 2.6 million BTC would remain vulnerable (about 1.7 million BTC sit in old P2PK outputs), a systemic-risk pool, so protecting it requires rule changes. BIP-361 proposes phases: stop sending coins to vulnerable addresses once a quantum-resistant type exists; after a multi-year window, invalidate legacy ECDSA and Schnorr spends; and consider recovery via proofs not relying on broken ECC, such as zero-knowledge proofs from seed phrases. Pro-freeze arguments: a quantum attacker is not a legitimate owner; sweeping vulnerable coins would concentrate wealth and effectively expand supply, especially from lost coins; attackers might also pursue political attacks, market destabilization or a 51% attack; credible belief in a looming sweep could cause panic; deadlines are needed because voluntary migration is slow and institutions face fiduciary pressure; and disabling a known-insecure spend path is like replacing a broken lock, not blacklisting owners. Anti-freeze arguments: valid coins should stay spendable under the rules in force when received; freezing cannot distinguish lost, dormant, imprisoned or deceased owners and creates a conflict of interest for active holders; the threat may not materialize; a freeze could cause a contentious fork, set a precedent for other confiscations, and create legal liability; and post-quantum schemes are large and immature, risking higher fees and throughput loss. Alternatives include barring new vulnerable outputs, temporary locks, Hourglass rate-limiting of P2PK spends (one BTC per block), commit-delay-reveal schemes, zk-STARK seed-derivation recovery (currently a ~200 KB proof, costly for small UTXOs), and opt-in dual signatures. Chaincode estimates full migration would take 76 to 142 days of all block space, and a complete timeline of roughly five to fifteen years. The author notes property rights were violated before, in the 2010 Value Overflow Incident, and cites Ethereum's DAO fork outcome as evidence that economic incentives tend to prevail. The author concludes that ECC deprecation is defensible only as a last resort, with a vetted quantum-resistant destination, a long migration window, objective narrow rules, recovery options, and pre-agreed warning criteria. BIP-361 is a contingency plan, not for activation now; near-term work should focus on reducing address reuse and xpub sharing, researching recovery proofs and efficient post-quantum schemes, and activating opt-in quantum-safe scripts.

Half a year after Iranian drone strikes knocked out multiple Amazon data centers, the US tech company has acknowledged the permanent loss of some customer data that was hosted in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Amazon Web Services was “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in some of the war-damaged data centers, according to an AWS dashboard update posted on September 15. The development was first reported by Reuters and suggests that the Iranian strikes inflicted catastrophic damage on the data centers. Customer data was irretrievably lost in one of three AWS availability zones in the United Arab Emirates region, specifically the mec1-az2 availability zone. Each availability zone is serviced by one or more Amazon data centers. The company is still working on “recovering regional resources” and restoring resources hosted in the other two availability zones in the United Arab Emirates. The AWS update described ongoing work to replace “affected infrastructure” and promised to update customers on a restoration of services in the coming months. But the destruction was apparently even more widespread for the data centers in the Bahrain region, because Amazon said it was unable to restore access to resources and data across all three availability zones there. “The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple Availability Zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” the AWS update said.

Level-5 has apologized for the generative AI controversy arising from its recent online showcase and announced that it will avoid directly using AI in videos released to the public in the future. On September 17, Level-5 announced measures regarding generative AI and plans to revise several promotional videos shown at its recent showcase via its official website. The company stated that some PVs presented during the showcase contained errors from AI usage as well as human errors that could be mistaken for AI, adding that revised versions of the videos will be re-released in time for the opening of Tokyo Game Show. Furthermore, the studio explicitly clarified that "there is absolutely no direct use of AI" within the games themselves. The controversy erupted following "LEVEL5 VISION 2026 II" held on September 10. Viewers pointed out scenes in some of the revealed videos that appeared to use generative AI, leading Level-5 CEO Akihiro Hino to admit on his official X account on September 12 that AI was indeed used in the presentation footage. Hino apologized, explaining that experimental processing with the latest AI was applied to make the showcase more spectacular, acknowledging that it was undeniable AI had been used in various ways during the presentation. However, he explained that elements directly tied to the charm and identity of released titles—such as scenarios, character designs, and fundamental settings—are all created entirely by humans. He emphasized that the goal of AI-driven efficiency is centered on digitizing human-made creations, such as accurately converting original artwork into 3D polygon models, reassuring fans that carelessly outputted AI data is not being included in released games. Subsequently, Level-5 released a statement on September 17 specifically addressing the controversial elements in the artwork and PV for 'Yo-kai Watch 2: Haunted Domain'. The company clarified that unnatural power lines in the image were a designer's manual work simplified for the background based on real utility poles and wires, and that oddities with vending machines and rain gutters were human errors that occurred while simplifying details. Regarding a bicycle lacking brake levers, Level-5 explained that given its direction to enhance detail in the latest title, it should have been depicted this time. Addressing observations that Keita's face differed between the PVs shown in the Nintendo Direct and Level-5's own showcase, the studio stated that this was not a change or modification caused by AI. According to Level-5, revisions were underway to improve the quality of the existing character model, but because the submission deadline for the Nintendo Direct video was earlier, those changes could not be included, whereas the revised model was used in its own showcase. Additionally, the company explicitly noted that no AI was used for 'Professor Layton and the New World of Steam'. In its statement, Level-5 remarked, "By carelessly using AI in some videos, we created a situation where even human errors were misunderstood as AI usage. We deeply apologize for causing distrust due to our clumsy application of AI and human mistakes." The company added, "We will exercise greater care with public releases to prevent situations that cause misunderstandings," concluding, "Going forward, our company will limit AI use strictly to improving efficiency and avoid direct usage in videos presented to users."

China's Humanoid Robots Are Walking Off The Assembly Line On Their Own. Tesla revealed its Cybercab concept back in 2024, only to have thousands of Waymo vehicles flooding cities across the United States before even one Cybercab rolled off the assembly line. Tesla then converted its Fremont, California factory — which also produces the Model 3 and Model Y — into a factory for its humanoid robot, Optimus, which is still nowhere to be seen — and Chinese automaker Xpeng has its own humanoid robot, Iron, walking off the assembly line. Literally. With this small step for robot kind, Xpeng has now completed production of the world's first "advanced general-purpose humanoid robot," according to a press release. The manufacturing system itself was also 80% autonomous, focused on consistent, fast-paced mass production, with the goal of scaling it up and expanding. The robots are currently expected to be mass-produced by the end of 2026, with launch and delivery following in 2027. During Tesla's "We, Robot" event back in 2024, Optimus was revealed to be controlled by humans, but CEO Elon Musk still claims that the $20,000 to $30,000 robots will be delivered by 2027 as well. What is Xpeng's Iron humanoid robot? Xpeng's Iron humanoid robot is designed to fit into the real world, with CEO He Xiaopeng stating that he expects Iron to become "part of everyday life" – improving people's lives while becoming their companion. Iron is meant to do a variety of tasks that people may not want to do, including factory work or making a morning coffee. To complete these tasks, Iron has three AI chips for a plethora of computing power, along with human-like dexterity and mobility. Xpeng claims that Iron is already assisting in its own manufacturing process, which would mean it has come a long way since its tech demos back in 2025 (Iron also appears less "naked" now as well) You won't find many specific details on the official Iron page on Xpeng's website, which may not be instilling investors with the utmost confidence in the automaker. Xpeng's stock is down nearly 50% in the first half of 2026. It's not only Xpeng and Tesla competing to launch a humanoid robot by 2027 — other companies are also working on their own creations (with varying degrees of creepiness), and China continues to lead the way in this mysterious new technology frontier.

Cloud computing. A subscription-based delivery model, cloud computing provides the scalability, fast delivery and IT efficiencies required for effective big data analytics. Because it removes many physical and financial barriers to aligning IT needs with evolving business goals, it is appealing to organisations of all sizes. Data management. Data needs to be high quality and well-governed before it can be reliably analysed. With data constantly flowing in and out of an organisation, it’s important to establish repeatable processes to build and maintain standards for data quality. Once data is reliable, organisations should establish a master data management programme that gets the entire enterprise on the same page. Data mining. Data mining technology helps you examine large amounts of data to discover patterns in the data – and this information can be used for further analysis to help answer complex business questions. With data mining software, you can sift through all the chaotic and repetitive noise in data, pinpoint what’s relevant, use that information to assess likely outcomes, and then accelerate the pace of making informed decisions. Data storage, including the data lake and data warehouse. It’s vital to be able to store vast amounts of structured and unstructured data – so business users and data scientists can access and use the data as needed. A data lake rapidly ingests large amounts of raw data in its native format. It’s ideal for storing unstructured big data like social media content, images, voice and streaming data. A data warehouse stores large amounts of structured data in a central database. The two storage methods are complementary; many organisations use both. Hadoop. This open-source software framework facilitates storing large amounts of data and allows running parallel applications on commodity hardware clusters. It has become a key technology for doing business due to the constant increase of data volumes and varieties, and its distributed computing model processes big data fast. An additional benefit is that Hadoop’s open-source framework is free and uses commodity hardware to store and process large quantities of data. In-memory analytics. By analysing data from system memory (instead of from your hard disk drive), you can derive immediate insights from your data and act on them quickly. This technology is able to remove data prep and analytical processing latencies to test new scenarios and create models; it’s not only an easy way for organisations to stay agile and make better business decisions, it also enables them to run iterative and interactive analytics scenarios. Machine learning. Machine learning, a specific subset of AI that trains a machine how to learn, makes it possible to quickly and automatically produce models that can analyse bigger, more complex data and deliver faster, more accurate results – even on a very large scale. And by building precise models, an organisation has a better chance of identifying profitable opportunities – or avoiding unknown risks. Predictive analytics. Predictive analytics technology uses data, statistical algorithms and machine-learning techniques to identify the likelihood of future outcomes based on historical data. It’s all about providing the best assessment of what will happen in the future, so organisations can feel more confident that they’re making the best possible business decision. Some of the most common applications of predictive analytics include fraud detection, risk, operations and marketing. Text mining. With text mining technology, you can analyse text data from the web, comment fields, books and other text-based sources to uncover insights you hadn’t noticed before. Text mining uses machine learning or natural language processing technology to comb through documents – emails, blogs, Twitter feeds, surveys, competitive intelligence and more – to help you analyse large amounts of information and discover new topics and term relationships.

Snap is partnering with Nvidia, Amazon Web Services and Salesforce as part of an effort to bring its $2,000 Specs augmented reality glasses to the enterprise market. Evan Spiegel, Snap's CEO, characterized the initiative as tied to the company's broader effort to help people "understand that Specs is a computer, not a pair of smart glasses for taking photos." When Snap revealed the Specs AR glasses in June, with a $2,195 price tag and $200 refundable deposit, the company pitched the device as catering to the public instead of developers. Although AR and related virtual reality technologies have improved over the years, devices like Microsoft's HoloLens and Meta's Quest-branded VR headsets have failed to become breakout hits. Spiegel said the bulkiness of those older devices were a major hindrance, and said his company's Specs AR glasses will be better suited for tasks like helping field technicians troubleshoot equipment problems by viewing digital instructions, and interacting with workers. To date, Snap's success has been in the consumer market. The company is hoping that a partnership with the likes of Nvidia can change that. "They've got an open-source XR AI platform that a number of businesses are already building on top of," Spiegel said. "The goal with both Salesforce and Nvidia is to make it really easy for businesses to get the benefits of those agentic platforms." Snap is also debuting a consumer-oriented AI service dubbed Specs Intelligence that's like a digital assistant that can do tasks across the AR glasses as well as iPhones and Mac computers. Spiegel said the company hasn't determined specific pricing details yet, but it will include a free tier and "different price points" depending on usage. The company's latest AI-related foray comes as debate heats up in the broader technology market about safety, and whether foundation model leaders like Anthropic and OpenAI should slow the pace of development. Spiegel said, "these are concerns that have been raised for a long time." "It's really important that we coordinate an international and thoughtful response," Spiegel said. "It's really important that regulators and policymakers consider actual potential harms rather than imagined harms, and so that's why I think it's going to be really important for a thoughtful and international group to really get together on this."

Spain's data protection authority, the Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD), confirmed on September 15, 2026 that it received the first notification in Spain of a personal data breach allegedly carried out by an AI agent running on a well-known large language model. The reporting organization says the agent logged into a system, searched for weaknesses on its own, then modified personal data and accessed invoices, largely without step-by-step human direction. The AEPD stresses this is one filing, not a verdict. Everything public comes from the affected organization's own notification, and the agency must still run its own analysis. It has not named the model, the agent framework, or the affected company, and has not disclosed how long the sequence took or how the breach was discovered. It confirms the agent used a widely available LLM and carried out multiple stages with limited human involvement, and says using a given model does not mean that model or its provider's infrastructure was compromised. Security researchers note that without the model name, defenders cannot check logs for matching behavior and vendors cannot confirm whether guardrails were bypassed. The reported sequence: the agent authenticated to the application, likely via a weakness tied to generic files rather than a novel zero-day; searched the live application for further flaws; exploited one; then altered personal data and read invoices and billing records. These concrete outcomes are part of why the case was publicized. BleepingComputer broke the English-language coverage, and Spanish outlets followed. The case's significance is that a national regulator has logged an AI agent as the named attacker, moving the threat from conference hypotheticals into official breach paperwork. The AEPD says a single notification does not establish a trend, but shows AI-assisted attacks materializing in real personal-data processing. It is compared with other 2026 incidents involving AI tooling, such as nearly 700 rogue AI agents tied to Hugging Face and 1.8 million Android apps scanned via Claude, but is the only one formally logged with a privacy regulator. Implications discussed include GDPR's 72-hour notification window, which was designed for human-paced incidents; an agent chaining reconnaissance, exploitation and data modification could compress events into minutes, making fast detection harder. The AEPD says risk assessments must account for how automation changes likelihood, speed and scope. The EU AI Act may add a second reporting layer alongside GDPR. Insurers may gain a first reference case for pricing agentic AI risk, and vendors are racing to add agent detection. Security teams are advised to move detection toward authentication and API layers and adopt faster automated containment. Predictions include other EU authorities adding AI-agent categories to breach templates, insurers asking about autonomous-attack exposure, growing pressure to name models in future cases, and overlapping GDPR and AI Act compliance burdens. These are extrapolations, not claims about what the AEPD will confirm. Earlier, more than 100 companies had jointly warned of AI-driven cyberattack risk.

Luminis Health sued over alleged failure to protect patient data after cyberattack. A patient of Anne Arundel Medical Center alleges in a lawsuit that the hospital's parent company, Luminis Health, negligently failed to protect their medical information following a cybersecurity incident earlier this month, according to our media partner, The Baltimore Banner. The lawsuit claims the breach occurred because Luminis Health stored patient data in "an unencrypted, Internet-accessible environment." According to The Banner, Jokisha White filed the complaint on Sept. 11, arguing that she and others affected by the breach face a "certainly impending" risk of fraud, "intrusion of their health privacy" and other risks that "may last for the rest of their lives." The Banner reports that two other Anne Arundel County residents, Rachel Rogers and Angela Ritchie, joined the lawsuit Wednesday and are seeking to make it a class-action case. The lawsuit says "tens of thousands" of people could be eligible to join the class action. It asks Luminis Health to provide at least 10 years of credit monitoring and pay monetary damages, according to The Banner. Luminis Health serves more than 1.8 million patients on Maryland's Eastern Shore and in Anne Arundel and Prince George's counties, according to its website. The health system operates Anne Arundel Medical Center in Annapolis and Doctors Community Medical Center in Lanham. Luminis Health posted an alert on its website Sept. 1 saying it was "responding to a cybersecurity incident affecting certain systems across our organization." On Wednesday, Luminis Health said it was making "considerable progress in restoring affected systems." Telephone services have been restored across all Luminis Health locations. The health system said its hospitals, physician practices and clinics remain open and are seeing patients. Surgeries and baby deliveries are also continuing. Luminis Health said an investigation is ongoing to determine whether patient information was impacted. The health system said it is working "around the clock to restore remaining impacted systems" and "testing those systems for safety and quality as they are being restored." For more information, visit the Luminis website here.

Optiv Security, Colorado's leading cybersecurity firm, has moved its headquarters from Denver to Leawood, Kan., another blow to the region's struggling tech sector. Company spokesman Jeremy Jones said Optiv closed its Denver office but that Colorado remains a critical market. Its couple hundred Colorado-based employees will keep working remotely, as they have since the pandemic. Denver is no longer listed as a company location on its website; the official home base is now 5100 W. 115th Place in Leawood, Johnson County. Optiv had been the marquee tenant at 1144 15th St. since 2018, but after subleasing one of its three floors to PNC Bank in 2021, it is vacating floors 29 and 30. CBRE has listed the remaining 39,415 square feet for sublease through May 31, 2031. The privately held firm made no formal public announcement. This echoed Palantir, Colorado's largest big data and AI firm, which announced on Feb. 17 on X that it was relocating its headquarters to southern Florida. Optiv had deep Colorado roots dating to 2002, when Dan Burns launched the downtown startup Accuvant, which became a national cybersecurity provider. In November 2014, Blackstone combined Accuvant and Kansas City-area FishNet Security in a $2 billion "merger of equals," creating Optiv with headquarters in Denver. In 2016, Blackstone sold the company to KKR, which put $1 billion in debt on its balance sheet to fund the buyout. In 2018 Optiv moved into downtown's newest tower, developed by Hines and nicknamed the "Burrito Building" because Chipotle was meant to co-anchor it. Chipotle signed a 15-year lease but never moved in after incoming CEO Brian Niccol relocated its headquarters to Newport Beach, Calif. JLL vice president Maddy Stevenson said Denver's office market has become a game of "musical chairs," with demand internal and few out-of-state tenants arriving, so departures of large tenants are a problem. Palantir has a global workforce of 4,500 and a market value almost as large as all other Colorado public companies combined. Optiv, the largest "pure-play" cybersecurity integrator, has about 2,800 workers worldwide and 75% of Fortune 500 companies as clients. In 2026 Colorado has lost two of its largest technology firms, one public and one private. In April, 230 business, technology and civic leaders signed a letter warning that the foundation of Colorado technology and business leadership is deteriorating and urging immediate action. This summer Gov. Jared Polis formed a competitiveness council to examine why Colorado has fallen behind other states on job growth and corporate retention. The state economic development office plans more "exit" interviews with departing companies, and Optiv will likely be among them. Optiv also faced internal stresses. KKR has tried and failed to sell the company, and IPO plans went nowhere, partly because of the $1 billion in debt from the 2016 buyout. Higher interest rates raised debt payments, eating into cash flow, and S&P cut the company's credit rating deep into junk territory. Extensions with creditors push repayments to 2028 and 2029 but do not address the excessive debt. Optiv has shifted from expanding its market to surviving its financial load, and Denver lost out.

Sutton officials are investigating a cybersecurity incident affecting parts of the town’s network, including its public school system, officials said Wednesday. After the incident was discovered, the town’s Information Technology “immediately” took steps to secure its systems, contain the incident, and minimize any potential impact on operations, Sutton officials said in a statement. Town services remain operational, the statement said. The town is working with independent cybersecurity and forensic experts and law enforcement to determine the nature and scope of the incident, including whether any personal data was involved. “If the investigation determines that personal information was involved and that notification is required under applicable law, affected individuals will be notified as appropriate,” the statement said. The town said it is also taking additional measures to strengthen the security of its systems. “Protecting the information entrusted to the Town is a responsibility we take seriously,” the statement said. Officials said updates will be shared as appropriate. The investigation is ongoing. Last week, separate cyber safety incidents closed Springfield Public Schools and Everett City Hall, the Globe previously reported. Springfield schools were closed last week after a cyber attack by a “sophisticated” group of hackers hindered access to vital school systems, including class curriculums, medical records and food databases, according to school district officials. Students returned to school Monday. On Tuesday, the FBI told the Springfield school district that student and staff data had been breached during the attack, school officials said. The FBI, state police and local police are investigating. In Everett, officials announced last week on social media that city hall would be closed “as the City responds to a cybersecurity incident impacting its internal network and technology systems.” Everett City Hall will remain closed through Thursday, officials said Sunday on social media. A study drawing on 177,971 adults in the UK Biobank and 57,971 adults in the Japan Collaborative Cohort Study, a combined sample of 235,942, examined stilbene intake and lung cancer. All participants were cancer-free at baseline and were followed for roughly thirteen years. The highest stilbene intake was linked to a 15% lower lung cancer risk in the UK group and 20% lower in the Japanese group, with a pooled reduction of 17%. The cohorts were chosen for their distinct dietary patterns. Researchers measured intake of several plant compound groups, including stilbenes, flavonoids and phenolic acids, and adjusted for potential confounders. This account was published September 12, 2026 by NaturalHealth365. Stilbenes are a subgroup of polyphenols, a family of phytochemicals found in plant foods. Resveratrol is the best-known stilbene, found in at least 72 plant species, including mulberries, peanuts, grapes and red wine. The association was strongest among men who had ever smoked: those with the highest intake had a 25% lower risk, a pattern that held in both countries. No significant association was seen in women or never-smokers, which researchers said may indicate the protective window depends on the body's existing oxidative stress. Researchers attributed the smoking-related pattern to stilbenes' antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, which may help mitigate smoke-related oxidative damage. Stilbenes have also been linked to slower tumor growth. Resveratrol has been shown to markedly reduce cellular COX-2 in stimulated macrophages, and quercetin limited tumor formation in a mouse model of induced lung cancer. Main dietary sources differed: wine in the UK group and fruits in the Japanese group. Red grapes, berries and other fresh fruits supplied significant resveratrol in both. Because wine contains alcohol, which is linked to increased cancer risk, the account concluded that fresh fruit gives a cleaner benefit signal, recommending red and purple grapes, blueberries, blackberries and cranberries. Organic foods were reported to have 28% higher stilbene levels. Stilbene intake was very low compared with other polyphenols measured, which the authors said suggests stilbenes may partly act as markers for other protective compounds in the same foods. Flavonoids and phenolic acids, far more abundant in grapes and berries, showed their own independent links to lower lung cancer risk. The study does not prove causation, and the authors say further research is needed. Related research on pesticide residues on fruits and vegetables and lung cancer in young nonsmokers led Dr. Jorge Nieva of USC Norris to say the results raise questions about an unknown environmental risk factor related to otherwise beneficial food. Health officials maintain that avoiding smoking remains the most effective way to reduce lung cancer risk. The account advised that people with a smoking history have longer exposure to oxidative stress that these compounds seem to counter, and suggested pairing fruit with cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and Brussels sprouts.

Warnings from tech leaders about the dangers of artificial intelligence are colliding with political resistance in Washington, testing whether the federal government can confront what may become a defining issue of the era. Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk have called for greater government oversight. President Donald Trump is leading the opposition, dismissing efforts to limit the technology on Monday as a "conspiracy." Vice President JD Vance has expressed caution, and House Speaker Mike Johnson has largely deferred to the White House. Democrats are pressing for a stronger response. They met privately in the House on Tuesday to discuss AI, and Sen. Bernie Sanders is hosting a briefing with experts on Wednesday. Candidates such as Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia are urging sweeping action, and former President Barack Obama is encouraging potential White House candidates to develop a "very clear plan" on AI. There are bipartisan exceptions: a Washington AI conference will feature both Sanders and Steve Bannon, and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., opened an investigation into OpenAI after its AI system hacked another AI company on its own. Max Stier of the Partnership for Public Service said political leaders are not grasping the crisis and that delay "is going to prove very costly." Congress and the White House have responded swiftly to past crises, including the 2007–2008 financial collapse and the COVID-19 pandemic. But Congress has long been reluctant to regulate technology. Trump rescinded the Biden administration's 2023 AI executive order soon after returning to office. A 2024 bipartisan Senate working group formed by then-Majority Leader Chuck Schumer recommended spending at least $32 billion over three years on AI development and safeguards, but little followed. A bipartisan children's internet safety bill has repeatedly stalled. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Congress does nothing "until we have a holy heck moment," and Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., voiced skepticism that AI legislation could pass given other failures. Some urgency is emerging. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., about a "path forward" on legislation, aiming to guard against advanced threats without harming U.S. competitiveness. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., plans to offer a "kill switch" measure requiring developers to be able to shut down their systems, though it needs full Senate support. Hawley has introduced bipartisan legislation requiring federal tracking of AI safety concerns tied to national security, civil liberties and labor protections. Still, with the calendar dwindling before the November election, fast action seems unlikely, and any bill would need Trump's support, which appears improbable. Johnson was downbeat, urging Trump to meet with AI leaders instead and warning against "red tape and hyper regulation." Rahm Emanuel, a former Obama chief of staff and potential 2028 candidate, called the inertia baffling, noting he had never seen an industry or CEO ask for regulation. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said Congress is capable of passing stronger rules and that there is sufficient support for multiple bills, calling it "very much a leadership issue" as the House prepares to adjourn until after the elections.

A ChemSec report finds that PFAS, thousands of synthetic "forever chemicals" that do not readily break down, are used in server cooling systems, in fabricating the advanced microchips needed by large language models, and as binders and separator coatings in lithium-ion batteries. Data centers typically use compressor-based cooling with gases that may contain PFAS, or submerge servers in PFAS-containing fluids, according to the Sierra Club. A 2024 Texas Tech University report found few end-of-life guidelines for PFAS-containing battery waste, most of which ends up in municipal landfills where it can accumulate, travel, or leak into water supplies. Contamination has been reported at multiple U.S. locations, including near data center clusters in Virginia and herbicide plants in Louisiana. Research links prenatal PFAS exposure to elevated blood pressure risk in teenagers, and a University of Hawai'i and University of Southern California study found adolescents with higher blood PFAS levels face nearly triple the risk of a serious fatty liver disease. ChemSec's survey of the 10 largest PFAS manufacturers found nearly all plan to expand production in the U.S., Europe and Asia, with investments explicitly framed around "the AI revolution" and microchip fabrication. Chemours is developing Opteon 2P50, a fluorinated data center cooling fluid it says will "revolutionize" cooling by reducing energy use. Daikin plans to more than triple fluoropolymer capacity by 2027. Bayer, AGC, Arkema, Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials, Solstice, 3M and Syensqo are also expanding; only BASF and Archroma are cutting back. The PFAS market is worth roughly $25 billion to $30 billion a year, while health and environmental costs in Europe alone are estimated at 440 billion euros by 2050. DuPont and Chemours agreed in 2017 to pay $670.7 million to settle about 3,550 PFOA injury claims, and Chemours has paid $2.4 billion in U.S. PFAS damages. In 2024 a federal court approved a settlement in which 3M committed up to $10.3 billion to public water systems, and the EPA set drinking-water limits of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS. The Trump administration said in 2025 it would keep those limits while reconsidering other PFAS standards, and in 2026 the EPA proposed extending the compliance timeline and rescinding limits for PFHxS, PFNA, GenX and other mixtures. On January 15, 2026, CHIPS Communities United and the Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice, sued in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit to overturn EPA approval of certain forever chemicals. They allege Toxic Substances Control Act violations, saying the EPA allowed semiconductor chemicals to be used without adequately assessing risks to workers and surrounding communities. Congress amended the law in 2016 to require manufacturers to show new substances are unlikely to present unreasonable risk, but the groups argue the agency has failed to enforce this. The case remains pending. Nearly all Americans are exposed to PFAS, which stay in the bloodstream for a lifetime. Scott Faber of the Environmental Working Group said nearly 2,000 public water supplies have some PFOS and PFOA. Because the chemicals are not broadly regulated, municipalities are not required to test for them. ChemSec concludes that the only effective way to end the pollution crisis is universal bans with strictly time-limited derogations.

Americans are grappling with artificial intelligence — from its lightning-fast development to the construction of data centers to support it — and becoming more skeptical of its benefits. Nebraskans are leery, too. According to the new Nebraska Snapshot, most Nebraskans — nearly three in four — rated the risks of AI for society as high or very high. Additionally, less than one in five Nebraskans surveyed rated the benefits as high or very high. The Nebraska Snapshot is reported from the Nebraska Annual Social Indicators Survey, an annual review of the state's adults fielded by the University of Nebraska–Lincoln’s Bureau of Sociological Research. People are also reading…. Forty percent of respondents rated the benefits of AI as medium, and 31% rated the benefits as low or very low, while 11% said they were unsure. Younger respondents and those with more education were slightly more confident about the benefits of AI, as 21% of those 19-64 rated the benefits as high or very high, while only 11% of those 65 and older said the same. Similarly, 24% of those with a bachelor’s degree or higher rated the benefits of AI as high or very high, in contrast to only 19% of those with some college or less. However, younger Nebraskans were also more wary about the risks, as 78% of respondents 19-64 rated the risks of AI as very high or high, compared to only 65% of those 65 and older. “It seems a majority of Nebraskans are nervous about artificial intelligence,” said Amanda Ganshert, co-author of the report and assistant director for research and methods at the Bureau of Sociological Research. “Men, younger adults and employed Nebraskans rated both the perceived benefits and risks of AI higher than their counterparts.” Twenty-three percent of Nebraska men surveyed rated the benefits of AI to society as high or very high, in contrast with only 15% of women. Meanwhile, 78% of men rated the risks as high or very high, compared to 71% of women. Democrats and independents appear to have more reservations about AI than Republican peers. Eighty-one percent of Democrats and 80% of independents and others surveyed rated the risks of AI as high or very high, while only 67% of Republicans said the same. Nearly one in five in all three groups rated the benefits as high or very high. A previous Nebraska Snapshot explored Nebraskans’ perceptions of AI and found that 47% of respondents said they had read or heard a lot about artificial intelligence, while 53% reported they have read or heard little or nothing about it. Additionally, 45% of respondents said they had little or no control over artificial intelligence in their life, while 35% said they had some control, and only 19% said they had a great deal or quite a bit of control. The Nebraska Annual Social Indicators Survey is used by researchers, state entities and policymakers, but also includes a core questionnaire that delves into demographics, quality of life measures, educational attainment and community satisfaction, among other variables. These core questions will inform most of the Nebraska Snapshot series. This is the first time the survey has included questions about artificial intelligence.

Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest sectors in AI, with investors pouring in billions of dollars to serve use cases ranging from automating customer support and sales calls to creating meeting notetakers and developing AI smart glasses that use voice as the primary interaction surface. Meanwhile, AI labs are quickly releasing models, and hardware makers are trying to create the best experience for consumers to interact with devices. All of this new technology needs testing and a feedback loop for improvement. An Iceland-based startup, Treble, is positioning itself to be at the center of the voice AI industry by creating a simulation platform that can cater to model makers, robotics companies, and consumer hardware makers. The company, founded in 2020 by acoustic engineers Finnur Pind and Jesper Pedersen, has raised $18 million in an extension of its Series A funding led by Paladin Capital Group, with participation from existing investors KOMPAS VC, Frumtak Ventures, EIC, and Omega ehf. It received an investment of $12 million in 2024, bringing its total raise to date to over $40 million. The startup counts Amazon and Logitech as customers. Treble has a few verticals related to simulation and data. For voice AI companies, it has a synthetic data generation platform that could be used for speech enhancement, noise suppression, and model training. It also evaluates voice AI models in different conditions to provide feedback to labs. Earlier this year, it partnered with Hugging Face to launch a benchmark for speech recognition models across different realistic conditions. “Audio AI is really a data challenge, and this is where the most opportunities to enable next-generation models and hardware lie. To date, pretty much all sound-related AI has been made from recordings and data scraped from the internet. We believe that accurate physics simulation can be an alternative way to create data for sound,” Pind told TechCrunch. The startup also focuses on hardware design and testing from a voice perspective. For instance, it works with headphone and speaker companies for virtual prototyping to help them understand how their product might sound. It could also test how a smart speaker can understand commands based on the positioning of the speaker. Lately, Treble has ventured into providing simulation testing for smart glasses and AI devices. Pind said that the company is excited to work on wearables that could enhance hearing for users. “I’m really excited about the next generation of these devices like headphones and smart glasses that can enable [a feature like] superhuman hearing. That’s an area where you can really just hear better in challenging acoustic environments. Maybe you are in a restaurant, and you only want to hear people within two meters of range, or you are in a seminar, and want to mute people around you,” he said. Treble aims to increase its focus in the physical AI space, including robotics, automotive, and drone companies, to enable sound-based functions for them through testing and simulation. Francois Ruether, VP of Paladin Capital Group, told TechCrunch that Treble’s platform, which simulates different models and devices, stands out; the platform’s importance will increase as it gets involved in more areas. “Our thesis is that, as more products depend on understanding sound, this infrastructure becomes increasingly valuable across voice AI, wearables, robotics, and physical AI. Customers retain ownership of their models, products, and development workflows, while benefiting from a shared foundation of a simulation-native acoustic infrastructure layer,” Ruether said.
