Congress has struggled to pass major legislation this year, delaying debates on spending, defense, cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence. But in its final weeks in session before the midterm elections, the Senate can agree on one thing: overhauling the rules and financing of college sports. The Senate voted twice this week to move the legislation forward, aiming to put guardrails around skyrocketing spending, prevent constant legal battles and restore order to what supporters call "chaos" in athletic programs. More than 70 senators back the bill, which would still need to pass the House. Final Senate votes could come as soon as next week. Some critics say it is far from the most urgent matter. Republican Sen. Rick Scott of Florida said Congress should focus on affordability and that the bill goes "way too far inserting the federal government into collegiate athletics." Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut said the Senate should concentrate on other things "when we are in the middle of a disastrous war and a growing cost crisis," calling the bill a response to "a fake crisis" that doesn't do enough to protect athletes. Supporters say the bill will keep college costs down, give hundreds of thousands of student athletes new health and labor protections and create one set of rules for all colleges. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., promised the top sponsors, Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the panel's top Democrat, a September vote. He cited "pent-up demand" to fix a system that is "clearly broken." The bill targets what Cantwell calls "a spending spiral," fueled by name-image-likeness payments that have produced football rosters with $30 million payrolls. A Cantwell report found a $519.9 million increase in institutional and government support of athletic programs from 2015 to 2025 among the 53 Power Four schools with publicly available data. The legislation would cap the revenue colleges can share with players, add a retention pool for keeping current players, and let conferences pool TV media rights to raise revenue. It would restrict player transfers, codify the NCAA's new rule limiting players to five years of eligibility, cap agent fees and give the NCAA limited antitrust protections. Supporters say the spending limits would save money for smaller programs, including women's and Olympic sports, and new requirements would let athletes keep scholarships and have longer-term healthcare. Senators were still making last-minute changes Friday, including reducing the wait time for schools changing conferences and clarifying that the bill does not override other laws on transgender girls and women in sports. Labor and civil rights groups oppose the bill, and all four Black Democratic senators, Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Lisa Blunt Rochester and Angela Alsobrooks, voted against it. Booker said it gives the NCAA too much power without enough accountability to players. Many other Democrats are on board; Chris Coons of Delaware said passage should give Americans hope of stabilizing college sports.

A small AI startup used Claude to hack into OpenAI's internal codebase shortly after the OpenAI Hugging Face hack. Zayne Zhang, the cofounder and CEO of Hacktron, told Business Insider that his research team has begun investigating security vulnerabilities at frontier AI companies like OpenAI to determine whether they have gaps that could be exploited by AI agents. Hacktron is a San Francisco-based AI cybersecurity startup. In July, Zhang's team discovered some gaps in OpenAI's infrastructure. According to Hacktron's disclosure about the incident, published on Sunday, any user or OpenAI employee logging into OpenAI's community help forum could have had their ChatGPT and Codex accounts hacked. Hacktron then tried to exploit that vulnerability via Claude. The company had access to Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program, which relaxed certain cyber restrictions on Claude for authorized security research, Zhang said. The team managed to hack into an OpenAI employee's account and prompt the employee's Codex account to suggest changes in OpenAI's internal code repository. Hacktron said the team stopped there, didn't access any internal code, and flagged the issue to OpenAI. Hacktron said in its disclosure that the company won a $6,500 bounty from its discovery. The startup was launched less than a year ago and has fewer than 10 employees. An OpenAI spokesperson said in an emailed statement to Business Insider about Hacktron, "We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings. We narrowed the permissions on Community sign-in tokens and revoked affected tokens and sessions." "The worlds of AI safety and cybersecurity are converging, and we think that having more cybersecurity experts in the conversation is always a good thing for the industry," Zhang said of the incident. Representatives for Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Hacktron's disclosure comes as AI security is becoming one of the most important topics in tech. In recent months, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have disclosed that their agents engaged in rogue actions during testing. Fears of an AI apocalypse, driven by unchecked malicious AI agents, have emerged in droves this month.

About a week and a half ago, AI researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and warned that the people building the most powerful AI systems believe the technology could "kill us all." The warning drew some 170 million views on X. Author Annie Jacobsen, who wrote "Biological War: A Scenario" after decades of investigating biological weapons, asks how AI could actually kill millions. She concludes the real danger is not that AI invents a new deadly virus, since plenty of lethal viruses already exist. The danger is simpler. Jacobsen visited the National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center (NBACC) at Fort Detrick, Maryland, created after 9/11 and the anthrax attacks to understand biology as a weapon. Unlike the nearby US Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases, which develops vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics, NBACC asks what an adversary could do with a biological agent, how dangerous it could be, and, after an attack, what the agent is, how it was made and where it came from. She uses a pre-AI case to show how a plot can fail: Aafia Siddiqui, a Pakistani scientist educated in the US who studied at MIT and Brandeis. Captured in Ghazni, Afghanistan, five years after being listed by the FBI in 2003, she is serving an 86-year sentence for attempting to murder US personnel. According to the Justice Department, her handbag held documents describing a planned "mass casualty attack" in the US using biological and other weapons, plus substances in sealed bottles and jars and a target list. Former CIA counterproliferation chief Jim Lawler called her a true believer planning "staggering horror." Stanford microbiologist Dr. David Relman, who briefed the intelligence community on the thousands of pages on her thumb drive, called it "a wake-up call." Lawler said she was working on a chimera combining the lethality of rabies with the infectiousness of chickenpox. But Siddiqui lacked the wide-ranging expertise needed to genetically engineer a pathogen, troubleshoot failed experiments and make it spread. Lawler suggested Al Qaeda's prejudice against women may have limited her access to colleagues and laboratories. Jacobsen argues AI is closing the gap between having an idea and making it real. Capable AI systems are expertise multipliers: they can synthesize vast scientific literature, connect findings across fields, diagnose why experiments failed, suggest next steps and shorten the path from question to answer. AI need not make the impossible possible, only make difficult things much easier. Top AI labs have tried to block chatbot conversations about biological weapons, but users have found ways around such prohibitions. Biology is also uniquely troubling because its raw material already exists. Smallpox's variola virus is tightly controlled, with unauthorized possession risking a $2 million fine and 25 years to life in prison, but other dangerous pathogens circulate outside secure repositories. Rabies, for example, is found in thousands of US animals each year. Unlike fissile material for a nuclear weapon, biology's ingredients are readily available. Because an outbreak can look natural even if it isn't, determining its origin is becoming a first-order national-security problem. NBACC director Dr. Nicholas Bergman could not discuss Siddiqui's case or classified scenarios, but said NBACC scientists can take apart an adversary's idea, test its assumptions and determine whether it could work physically. After Coxon's warning, critics pushed back. Elon Musk called it groundwork for a "psy op," Bill Ackman amplified a post calling it a PR operation to get Democratic support for regulating AI "into oblivion," and The Atlantic ran "The AI Pandemic Isn't on Its Way." Jacobsen concludes that AI and biology have already begun to intersect, which is dangerous, and asks what will be done about it.

US Air Force pilots are all commissioned officers who receive the same basic pay as officers of equivalent rank and years of service in other branches, regardless of aircraft flown. An F-22 pilot and an MQ-9A Reaper remote pilot of the same rank and service are paid identically in basic pay. Combat flying is most common among First Lieutenants (O-2), Captains (O-3) and Majors (O-4), and less frequent among Lieutenant Colonels (O-5) and Colonels (O-6). Much of total compensation comes from allowances and bonuses: Basic Allowance for Housing ($2,094 to $2,796 per month), Basic Allowance for Subsistence ($328 per month), Flight Pay ($150 to $1,000 per month) and a retention bonus of up to $50,000 depending on community, rank and years of service. Typical figures: Captains have about $88,592 basic pay in the first year and about $124,118 total pay. Majors, typically after around ten years, start at about $113,040 basic pay and qualify for the Aviation Retention Bonus, giving fighter pilots around $207,609 total. Lieutenant Colonels start at about $128,581 basic pay with total compensation of $236,844. Colonels start at about $157,385 and total around $236,844, though they do not qualify for the bonus. The one exception to community-neutral pay is the Aviation Bonus, which varies by community. Fiscal 2027 budget documents describe a new tiered program that rewards earlier, longer commitments and widens eligibility from one to three year groups. Expected 2027 averages: the Rated Officer Retention Demonstration Program $54,570, fighters $50,907, bombers $41,376, mobility $32,895, and most other communities $28,000 to $34,000. Bomber pilots thus get about $10,000 less than fighter pilots but more than most other communities. No special pay will be given for flying the Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider when it enters service in 2027. Pilots can still earn more when senior officers are assigned to certain equipment. Pilots of the 89th Airlift Wing, which flies Air Force One, are typically experienced Lieutenant Colonels and Colonels with total compensation of roughly $225,000 to just over $240,000, versus $100,000 to $210,000 for fighter pilots. That is about half what senior Captains at legacy airlines like Delta earn. Bomber pilots tend to be more senior than fighter pilots, so may earn slightly more through rank. The B-52H (five crew, two pilots) is usually flown by an experienced Captain or Major as commander with a newer co-pilot. The B-1B (four crew) typically has a Major commander and Captain co-pilot. The B-2 (two crew) is the most selective, usually a Major or Lieutenant Colonel with a Captain co-pilot. The B-21 will likely be flown by pilots of similar experience to B-2 crews. Although a single pilot was discussed, the Air Force says it will initially use two. A Captain co-pilot with nine years of service and no bonus would earn about $143,968 a year. With ten years and the bonus, about $202,900, though Captains are often promoted to Major around when they qualify. A newly minted Major commander would earn about $197,000 and a newly promoted Lieutenant Colonel over $225,000, assuming the $41,376 bonus, with pay rising with service.

In December 2024, a bipartisan congressional task force on artificial intelligence issued 85 recommendations. GOP Rep. Jay Obernolte, a key task force figure, asked Republican leaders to create a special committee to draft legislation, but he could not get it approved. A senior GOP leadership aide said leadership felt the task force had accomplished its goal and that standing committees with AI jurisdiction could work from its recommendations. Almost two years later, no real laws constrain AI's rapid advancement, and the Trump administration has shown no appetite for regulation. Obernolte said the need for action is urgent. The episode illustrates how AI's complexity collides with Congress's partisanship and bureaucracy. Multiple bipartisan bills have been introduced, including one requiring the most powerful AI companies to develop a kill switch and another establishing safeguards for all AI models, but many never reached a floor vote. Lawmakers openly say some older colleagues don't understand the technology. GOP Rep. Rich McCormick said half of Congress is 70 years old, while GOP Rep. Kat Cammack said the political will doesn't exist because members don't understand AI. GOP Rep. Eric Burlison warned that those hoping Congress will solve the world's problems will be disappointed. AI has returned to the center of public debate, with whistleblowers and AI executives warning of dangers and pleading for regulation, while Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and others argue that slowing development would benefit China in an arms race. This week, the House Science, Space and Technology Committee met with representatives of Hugging Face, Anthropic, OpenAI and third-party auditors, who said they were committed to guardrails but couldn't trust everyone in the industry to do the same. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has called for a light-touch approach, while Democrats generally favor a more aggressive posture. Democratic Rep. Lori Trahan said she worries about the most powerful technology in history being on a collision course with congressional dysfunction. Congress has acted only at the margins. Last year Trump signed a law making it illegal to share nonconsensual explicit images, real or computer-generated, and requiring platforms to remove them within 48 hours of notification. On Wednesday the House overwhelmingly passed a bill to limit rising utility costs linked to data centers powering AI. But the Science Committee passed 10 AI bills in June that haven't reached the floor, and proposals from Thune, Klobuchar, Hawley and Blumenthal have stalled. Sen. Bernie Sanders has warned strongly of AI's dangers, yet no agreed-upon leader on the issue exists. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise told the task force in 2024 he opposed heavy regulation. Some Republicans welcome industry attention to the issue, such as Rep. Scott Franklin, while McCormick rejected bailing out the industry, saying companies should put guardrails on themselves. Democrats have intensified calls for regulation, especially after former President Barack Obama urged the party to prioritize the issue. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries created his own commission after the task force ended. Rep. Brittany Pettersen said AI companies can't be relied on to self-regulate. Rep. Ted Lieu argued lawmakers need not be experts, noting Congress regulates airplanes, medicine and energy without that standard. A bipartisan group asked Johnson to keep the House in session to negotiate AI reforms, but he sent members home a day early, not to return until after the November midterms. Democratic Rep. Don Beyer, one of those lawmakers, said he still believes there is time.

Anthropic’s Claude is helping the company develop the next, more intelligent version of the model, the artificial intelligence lab said in an announcement Thursday. Claude is leading 26% of Anthropic’s model research and development, which the company said means it can complete most of a given task “end-to-end from a high-level prompt” while still being under human supervision. The model is not yet working completely autonomously. Still, about 90% of the company’s research and development is done in “collaboration” with Claude, which Anthropic said means the model can do “large chunks of work under close human direction.” The announcement came as some leading figures in AI, led in large part by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns. As leaders consider pacing AI’s development, “we should do everything possible to minimize the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows,” the company said in a blog post. “This means better measuring the development of AI, reporting on it publicly, and giving society an opportunity to decide how to use this information.” The company said that models accelerating their own development could make it “more challenging for humans to understand or control these systems.” It argued that sharing these metrics could lead to better understanding of how close leading AI labs are to reaching recursive self-improvement, or a model’s ability to autonomously build its successor. Anthropic also urged other AI developers to share similar metrics on a regular basis, encouraging the use of a public methodology so the numbers could be compared over time, and potentially across labs. It was unclear from Anthropic’s disclosure how close the company believes it is to achieving recursive self-improvement, but the pace at which Claude has increasingly contributed to research and development is notable. The portion of work Claude “leads,” or does in large part while remaining under human supervision, was none in February. Six months later, it was leading a quarter of research and development work, reaching that benchmark in August. The company also shared details of agent oversight measures it has in place, noting that there were approximately 30,000 agents doing research and engineering work as of August. Oversight measures are crucial for seeing how often agent misbehavior is detected by monitoring systems, the company said. Anthropic recently committed to setting up external third-party evaluators who will be embedded within the company to monitor safety efforts. An Anthropic researcher kicked off much of the recent dialogue around AI safety when he resigned last week with a dire warning about the threats the technology poses to humanity. Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Elon Musk and other tech leaders have since supported the idea of slowing down development, but other tech leaders and President Donald Trump have pushed back.

Pa. Gov. Shapiro: Congress, federal government must regulate AI. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined the chorus of leaders in the artificial intelligence, or AI, industry calling for stronger regulations and controls over the technology some fear could take over the world. And while the Democratic governor seeking a second term said he is not an AI “doomer,” he used his Sept. 17 speech at AI Horizons Summit in Pittsburgh to criticize President Donald Trump for calling concerns around the technology “a hoax” and Congress for sidestepping the issue. When his administration learned there were chatbots telling kids to hurt others or themselves, Department of State officials investigated and, within minutes, connected with a chatbot who claimed to be an expert in psychiatry and dispensed medical advice. The bot even presented a fake medical license number. “That is against the law – and my Administration is suing Character.AI to stop it,” Shapiro said. “We need to put proactive measures in place and establish responsible regulations to prevent this kind of thing happening in the first place.” His remarks came days after executives in the artificial intelligence industry began sounding the alarm over the technology’s capabilities that could harm people if not tamped down. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a Sept. 12 blog post that by slowing down the pace of AI development, “we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong.” In respective X posts, Trump ally Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman both agreed with Amodei's call for more safeguards and a slowdown in the pace of AI advancements, USA TODAY reported. Like Trump, Shapiro believes the United States needs to beat China in the race for worldwide AI dominance. “But the idea that we have to choose between protecting our people from the risks posed by AI and winning the race against China is wrong,” Shapiro said. The governor called on the federal government to regulate the AI industry, noting critical regulations around medicine and aircrafts by federal agencies to ensure drugs and planes are safe before going to market. “AI shouldn’t be treated any differently,” Shapiro said. “The future of a technology this powerful should be shaped by the American people and their representatives.” Shapiro said U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, abdicated his responsibility to lead on this issue. Days after the industry pleas for an AI brake pedal, Johnson adjourned the House earlier than scheduled. “The fear and confusion that everyday Americans have is understandable, and it needs to be addressed comprehensively with a focus on responsible, safe and ethical uses of this extraordinary technology,” Shapiro said. Shapiro’s opponent in the gubernatorial race, Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, issued a statement calling Shapiro’s remarks a shameless flip-flop. “Josh Shapiro followed the new Democratic playbook and called for strict guardrails on AI this afternoon in Pittsburgh,” Garrity’s statement read. “It is an amazing reversal from just over a year ago, when Josh Shapiro recruited Amazon to come to Pennsylvania and build massive AI data centers, giving them billions in state tax breaks, access to Pennsylvania’s power grid and even created a new fast-track permitting process specifically for Amazon.” Last month, Shapiro unveiled an executive order on regulating data centers, the behemoth tech facilities used to power AI. Concern that AI could enable a biological-weapons catastrophe is intensifying. Earlier this summer, AI CEOs called for new laws controlling synthetic DNA manufacturing. Last month, researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute showed AI can design new viral genomes. Anthropic then released a report indicating there had been efforts to use Claude in ways that "could support biological weapons development," calling biological misuse "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models." CEO Dario Amodei urged the government to help AI labs "pace the frontier." Yet many scientists consider the risk fairly low among the world's concerns. David Bellamy, a research scientist at the Institute of Foundation Models, says AI is not a fundamentally new threat; the scientific community has long wrestled with the dual-use dilemma, and the internet, open-access journals, and translation tools already made biological information, including lab protocols, easy to find. AI helps both scientists and threat actors find information faster, but that is not the bottleneck. The real obstacles are obtaining gene fragments, building a genome from scratch, verifying the virus infects humans, causes the intended illness and spreads person to person, and having the materials, equipment, and knowledge to do so. Robotic assistants can automate some tasks, but people still need the know-how and resources. Jason Kelly, CEO of Ginkgo Bioworks, thinks it unlikely that an artificial general intelligence could commandeer existing pathogens or engineer and deploy new ones. In a project with OpenAI, GPT-5 ran a Ginkgo lab, but he says an AI could not take over a lab because humans could simply refuse to supply requested substances and equipment; it would need "dramatically more robots." Immunologist Derya Unutmaz argues humans could thwart an AGI-made disease and use other AI systems to develop a vaccine quickly. Others still worry about bad actors and the future. Olivia Scharfman of the Institute for Progress says fully autonomous labs don't yet exist, so an AI cannot build a virus on its own today, "But I do think that an AI could pay someone to do it for them." She considers AI-assisted bioterrorism an immediate threat, citing nihilistic groups such as "transhumanist AI successionists." Computational biology professor Francois Belloux says people "overestimate the value of pathogens as weapons": targeting groups is hard, mass production and distribution are logistically complicated, and there are far better ways to kill people. Scharfman says now is the time to push for protections against all biological threats, including existing pathogens like H1N1, through legislation enhancing DNA synthesis security and measures like upgraded building air purification. Steph Guerra of Rand Corporation says it is hard to know whether AI measurably raises bioweapon risk, since it is good at integrating information and motivating people toward good or bad ends. She suggests laws requiring synthetic DNA and RNA sellers to screen customers and orders; many firms already screen for "sequences of concern," but it is not universal or mandated. Models should also have safeguards against giving actionable dangerous information. Guerra also recommends stronger global disease surveillance and data-sharing among AI companies, gene synthesis providers, and government, with layered approaches creating friction along the whole pathway from ideation to release. Unutmaz adds that doom conversations divert attention from how advanced AI can help vaccine development and medical breakthroughs.

South Carolina lawmakers are struggling to regulate artificial intelligence even as its use grows. Nothing in current state law requires users to disclose whether a voice on a business call, for instance, is live or AI, and the state has yet to settle on a concrete definition of AI, something a Statehouse committee discussed this week. Rep. Brandon Guffey, R-Rock Hill, who has prioritized regulating tech companies, said the Legislature lacks the courage to protect citizens and is "too worried about losing an arms race." Of roughly 31 AI-related bills proposed in the past legislative session, only two became law, according to the South Carolina Artificial Intelligence Observatory. Both addressed criminal justice concerns: computer-generated child sexual abuse images and non-consensual obscene AI-generated imagery. Bills on undisclosed AI use in therapy, protecting children from chatbots, and limiting AI in health coverage eligibility decisions stalled, due to industry pushback or fear of hampering emerging technology. The Council of State Governments says South Carolina lags most states on AI legislation. Two committees have produced little. A new Senate AI committee, which first met Sept. 16, will focus only on AI within state government, with a final report due by summer 2028. Chairman Tom Young, R-Aiken, acknowledged an appetite for more, noting that citizens and businesses had emailed without understanding the committee's scope. A House committee formed in late 2023, chaired by Rep. Jeff Bradley, R-Hilton Head, has met infrequently since being folded into the House Regulations Committee, though Bradley said he is working on multiple initiatives, including adding AI to the K-12 curriculum. AI use in the state still trails the rest of the country, per Microsoft data, with most usage in Richland, Charleston and Oconee counties, home to major research institutions. Still, the topic is prominent: candidates are making AI and data centers central to their campaigns, and state Sen. Josh Kimbrell held a town hall on data centers. Sen. Matt Leber, R-Johns Island, said constituents want lawmakers to act "before the toaster burns the house down." Experts urge focus. Bryant Walker Smith of the University of South Carolina School of Law noted some groups have spent years trying to define AI and questioned whether laws would be flexible enough. Homayoun Valafar, a USC professor, advised concentrating on a specific application where policy is critically important. Generative AI may be easier to regulate because hypotheticals about other uses are endless, such as who is liable when AI agents commit crimes or whether someone can sue an insurer over an AI-delayed claim. House Majority Leader Micah Caskey, R-West Columbia, said lawmakers handle identified problems well, like banning AI-generated child pornography, but regulation gets harder further up the hierarchy of uses. Guffey, a leading voice for tech reform after his son killed himself following extortion via a social media app, said he is frustrated by the committee's fear of overregulation. He believes laws should be reactive rather than proactive and argued that AI won't follow the law without liability or financial penalties.

Oracle spent billions over the past two years helping other companies run AI. Its own companywide AI rollout came much later. During an internal town hall this week, co-CEO Clay Magouyrk said that last year, the company still hadn't found a way to make generative AI broadly useful to its own workforce. Now, after rolling out OpenAI's ChatGPT and Codex, employees are writing code dramatically faster, but creating new bottlenecks along the way. "When I think about where we were a year ago," Magouyrk said, "I don't think we figured out how do we make AI really that useful for ourselves." Oracle had made some progress in using AI for customer support last year, but it had not yet found broad use across business units, such as developers, finance employees, and sales teams. That started to change, Oracle Chief Information Officer Jae Evans told employees, in April and May, when the company rolled out ChatGPT Enterprise, and OpenAI's software development tool, Codex. Rather than simply making the tools available, the company established corporate standards, security controls, and internal policies and reached 80% adoption within three months, Evans said. "We made it so easy to use and adopt that we might have gotten a little bit of sticker shock," Evans said, so now the company provides visibility into which models employees are using and how much they cost. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra costs 2.5 times more than other models, like could be used for many purposes, Evans said, citing Terra as an example of a lower-cost model that could be used for routine tasks. The executives said AI has dramatically accelerated software development, but also created new bottlenecks elsewhere in the engineering process. "We see developers able to generate code using this tool in like a week's time," Evans said. "Normally, that would have taken a team of developers two to three quarters to go develop." For now, AI deployment at Oracle hasn't translated into getting those products to customers more quickly. "When you make the actual act of writing the code quicker, it doesn't mean that suddenly everything is 1000 times faster," Magouyrk said, explaining that Oracle is still figuring out how to redesign its testing, validation, deployment, and release management processes to keep pace. Oracle's experience highlights the next challenge facing companies rushing to bring AI into the workplace. Powerful models can dramatically speed up individual tasks, but they can also rack up big bills and simply move bottlenecks elsewhere. JPMorgan recently set cost limits for employees using Claude from Anthropic. Oracle also received early access to Anthropic's Mythos Preview model, which scans code for security vulnerabilities, and used it to uncover more potential security issues in its first two weeks than it had found in an entire year, Evans said. Announced in April, Anthropic's Mythos is considered one of the most powerful AI systems ever developed, with governments and security agencies warning that its capabilities surpass those of other models, especially for cybersecurity. That model generated a high number of false positives (Evans estimated roughly 60% to 70%), prompting Oracle to build new processes to verify vulnerabilities before engineers began fixing them. OpenAI is offering robotics engineers base salaries of up to half a million dollars a year as it builds out its robotics efforts. Its careers page lists 27 robotics jobs, up from 11 in May, spanning hardware, software, data collection and prototyping, according to Business Insider's review. Advertised base salaries range from $177,000 to $500,000, before equity. The listings show OpenAI is hiring people to design and build hardware, collect training data and test robots, not just write control software. Roles include actuator design engineers, who build the motors and mechanisms that move a robot's joints, as well as software, firmware and machine-learning engineers, a lab technician and a lawyer dedicated to the robotics team. Another role would oversee OpenAI's "data collection facilities," pointing to a major industry bottleneck: unlike large language models, robots need examples of how people and machines interact with the physical world, so robotics companies often must generate that data themselves or buy it. The highest-paid opening, up to $500,000, is for a machine-learning engineer working on distributed data systems for moving and processing large volumes of robotics training data. OpenAI declined to comment. Guy Hoffman, a Cornell mechanical and aerospace engineering professor who leads the university's Human-Robot Collaboration and Companionship Lab, reviewed all 27 postings and said OpenAI appears to be assembling a "custom robot design team." The postings point to long-term ambitions. One says the team is focused on "unlocking general-purpose robotics and pushing towards AGI-level intelligence" and exploring "a broad range of robotics form factors"; another describes a vision of "everyone having a personal robot doing anything they need." CEO Sam Altman has grown more explicit, telling investor Alex Heath on the Sources podcast earlier this month, "We will definitely do a humanoid," along with other form factors. He has identified data centers as an early application and suggested robots could eventually act as household personal assistants. The robotics team is led by Aditya Ramesh, best known for creating DALL·E and later working on Sora and OpenAI's world-simulation models. OpenAI previously experimented with robotics but shut down the project behind a Rubik's Cube-solving robotic hand in 2020. Its return comes as billions of dollars flow into "physical AI." Business Insider reported earlier this year that OpenAI was teaching a robotic arm household tasks as part of its humanoid effort. A humanoid would put OpenAI in direct competition with heavily funded efforts including Tesla's Optimus and Figure AI. The OpenAI Startup Fund is an investor in Figure, and OpenAI previously partnered with it on robot AI models. The postings reveal little about what the robots will look like. Hoffman said references to laser range finders and batteries "vaguely imply" an untethered mobile robot, but not whether it would use wheels or legs. He added that little electronics work is sought, so he doesn't expect a focus on sensors beyond off-the-shelf cameras, microphones and laser range finders.

Most Americans rarely think about digital infrastructure because it is always there. We carry supercomputers in our pockets and expect instant access to bank accounts, medical records, flight schedules and nearly any information we need, forgetting the enormous physical infrastructure behind it. The authors, Kirk Offel (a Navy nuclear submarine veteran) and Mike (who served with special operations forces in the Global War on Terror), learned the value of information in the military: having the right information at the right time can save lives and decide the outcome of a mission. They argue this applies to America's challenge today. The race for artificial intelligence is not only about who builds the best software or algorithm, but about who can build the power generation, transmission, data centers and workforce needed to run it. Without that, innovation won't matter. America has to build again. It once turned innovation into physical capability through highways, ports, power plants, factories and telecommunications networks. Now permitting delays, grid bottlenecks and supply-chain constraints are slowing new generation and transmission just as AI and advanced computing create enormous new electricity demand. China, by contrast, is aggressively expanding power generation, transmission, manufacturing and computing capacity, while Washington debates how AI should be governed. The authors say the way we talk about data centers must change. They are not merely large buildings filled with servers but part of what the authors call the Fifth Utility: the interconnected compute, power, fiber and digital infrastructure supporting banking, healthcare, transportation, commerce, emergency communications, national intelligence and defense. Communities should not accept development without asking tough questions. Residents deserve to know how projects will affect power, water, land, electricity rates and local infrastructure, and developers must engage early, answer honestly and invest responsibly. The authors insist that protecting communities and ratepayers while building needed infrastructure is something America must do together. The workforce is also critical. America needs electricians, line workers, welders, high-voltage technicians, construction professionals and mission-critical operators. Roughly 200,000 people leave military service each year with technical discipline, leadership, adaptability and the ability to perform when failure isn't an option. Stronger pathways from military service into critical infrastructure careers should be part of national strategy, not just a workforce initiative. The authors conclude that information superiority matters only with the people, systems and infrastructure to deliver it. America still has the capital, energy resources, technology and talent to lead the digital age, but cannot assume those advantages will last while it takes years to build what competitors are building now. The digital world feels invisible, but it requires power, transmission, fiber, steel, concrete and skilled people. If America intends to lead, it needs to start building like it.

The French Army's Future Combat Command is seeking ways to create "opacity" on an increasingly transparent battlefield in order to restore offensive maneuver, said Gen. Bruno Baratz, who heads the command. He spoke at an innovation day held by the 7th Armored Brigade in Besançon on Sept. 9. Baratz said battlefield transparency and powerful, precise modern weapons have created a "zone of death" along the frontline where approaching the enemy is "very, very dangerous." Maneuver along the Ukrainian frontline has largely stalled because near-continuous drone observation means neither side can mass forces without exposing them to destruction. He compared this to World War I, when artillery and machine guns made offensive operations futile or enormously costly. "We're in a system of tactical stalemate, where defensive systems are more powerful than offensive ones," he said, adding that the Army most needs technology to break out of it. Options include physical decoys, electromagnetic deception using simulated command posts, jamming, and electronic and cyber warfare. The event featured inflatable copies of 7th Armored Brigade equipment, including a Caesar howitzer and a VBL light armored vehicle. Baratz said the aim is to blind and mislead the adversary, create temporary vulnerabilities, and deceive enemy sensors so forces can concentrate, since "we can't concentrate if we're destroyed." Other potentially transformative technologies include quantum technology for secure communications and sensing, and AI-driven multi-spectral image analysis that can see under trees and cover. Technological change in some areas is now measured in weeks, and Baratz said the military is "lagging far behind" the civilian sector in telecommunications bandwidth and data transmission even as the battlefield is organized around data. He suggested warfare may be on the brink of a revolution comparable to 1920, when mechanization and radio sped up maneuver, with data potentially accelerating decision-making and destruction of the adversary. Tactics were once organized around geography, such as ridge lines defining fields of fire or view, and he asked how forces must reinvent themselves, noting that France failed to do so earlier and "paid the price in 1940." Baratz said continuous adaptation and incorporation of new technology is fundamental to operational superiority. The command is therefore moving away from the Army's traditional top-down approach, encouraging "testing, tinkering, experimenting" at the regimental level. Large programs remain necessary, but the Army must also repurpose civilian technologies and move toward open-architecture systems. Each regiment receives €150,000 ($172,000) a year to spend on its own projects or off-the-shelf equipment. The €20 million account for these "subsidiarity credits" will rise by an additional €35 million in the 2027 defense budget. The Army has "real needs" in robotics, autonomous vehicles, discreet mobility and battlefield-energy generation, with new, increasingly European firms approaching French forces. All brigades have light-mobility initiatives with companies on electric scooters, motorcycles and quads to be "faster and stealthier." Electric power aids discretion but is a vulnerability because intelligence-gathering systems and frontline data hubs are power hungry, so the command is also exploring "frugal artificial intelligence" that uses minimal energy. Baratz said future combat remains hard to imagine because technology moves so quickly that he cannot say what it will look like in one or two years.

AI doomsday talk has become widespread because the tech leaders building artificial intelligence are now publicly warning that it could wreak havoc on humanity, either if wielded by the wrong people or if it develops to the point of breaking free of human constraints. On Wednesday, OpenAI disclosed six new instances in which its AI models did things their human bosses did not intend. Feared disasters include massive cyberattacks on financial systems or infrastructure, biological weapons spreading pathogens we cannot combat, AI-powered military weapons getting out of control, and blackmail and other manipulations that would force people to do terrible things. The AI company leaders could slow development themselves but won't, because none wants to lose a competitive advantage and the chance at bigger fortunes. So they are asking the government to impose guardrails, and even Elon Musk has signed on. Neil Thompson, a principal research scientist at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, said they know they are playing a bad game: if everybody keeps racing as fast as they can, dangerous capabilities will keep accumulating, but unilaterally they cannot change that game. Meanwhile, the president and Congress are refusing to act, and are not fans of the international cooperation needed to get a handle on the technology globally. Some observers suggest the AI makers' warnings are marketing ploys, attempts to insulate themselves against lawsuits, or distractions from the environmental damage of their data centers. Thompson rejected the marketing explanation, calling it a well-founded concern about the tool's incredible capabilities and the great risks that come with them. Earlier this year, MIT FutureTech, a research group Thompson leads, surveyed 272 AI experts worldwide on the likelihood and severity of risks if the technology remains unchecked. The experts judged a more than 10 percent chance, over the next five years, of catastrophic outcomes from AI-powered cyberattacks, creation of AI-enabled weapons, and other scenarios resulting in more than 1 million deaths or more than $100 billion in losses. This seems unreal to most people, and Thompson said they are right in general to think technological changes will not change everything overnight. But no other technology has advanced this fast, with such broad reach across almost every part of our lives. Normalcy bias makes people resistant to accepting the growing dangers, will make them more vulnerable to sophisticated AI-powered financial scams and influence operations, and will slow voters in recognizing the threat enough to demand regulation and protection from their leaders. Thompson therefore expects the process to be harder: an increasing number of incidents, meaning attacks by AI-assisted villains or AI acting on its own in unintended ways. No one wants that, but he thinks it will focus public attention in the US and elsewhere. He said he hopes a consensus forms fast enough to keep damage as small as possible along the way.

Cybersecurity may be AI's next big jobs boom. Box CEO Aaron Levie recently posted on X that AI for cybersecurity "is about to go vertical" as models become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. That, he told Business Insider, could make cybersecurity "one of the hottest, if not the hottest, job categories." As threats multiply, companies need systems that can prioritize alerts, investigate risk, recommend fixes, and automate remediation. Humans, Levie said, will remain responsible for oversight and the highest-stakes decisions. The CEO said he expects "massive" investments in the space, both in the technology itself and in the "expert operators" needed to make it effective. "You're going to have so much more talent that gets pumped into this industry because of the amount of risks that are starting to be uncovered," Levie said. Levie isn't the only one making this prediction. Cybersecurity stocks are booming, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics forecasts that roles like information security analysts, a central title in the field, will grow by 21% between 2025 and 2035. It also ranks the role among the top 20 fastest-growing occupations in the timeframe. Evolving threats. Security leaders have warned for years that the threat landscape is worsening. Over the past year, though, those concerns have become more real. Anthropic has warned that its Mythos model could be used to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities. In July, OpenAI's models accessed internal datasets from the open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Since then, doomsday warnings have intensified. Most recently, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon sparked a viral debate when he resigned with claims that frontier labs are "gambling with our lives." Grant Bourzikas, Cloudflare's chief security officer, told Business Insider via email that AI isn't creating incremental changes to cybersecurity — it's "putting it on a rocket ship." Attack timelines that were once measured in days or hours, he said, can now unfold in seconds. That leaves security teams with almost no room for manual response, making machine-speed defense the "baseline for survival." That's exactly where AI comes in: to save the day from AI. AI may ease the talent shortage — and change the job. Bourzikas said that the cybersecurity industry has faced a historic "talent shortage" due to a gap in specialized skills. "The war for engineers with deep AI and security expertise is at an absolute fever pitch," Bourzikas wrote. For years, he said, security teams were buried under a mountain of alerts, never having enough time, people, or resources to keep up. That hasn't eased up, but he said that AI gives space for companies to move from "firefighting to real risk mitigation." AI agents could help close part of that gap by taking on repetitive tasks such as alert triage and data aggregation. At Cloudflare, Bourzikas said his team deployed over 250 production agents in the last nine months to handle foundational security controls, freeing employees to focus on proactive defenses. Similar to software engineers, the role of security professionals is shifting. Protecting an enterprise now means securing model pipelines, data flows, and autonomous agents against risks such as prompt injection and data poisoning, Bourzikas said. "Security professionals must pivot from reading dashboards to architecting resilient, AI-native systems," Bourzikas said. M.K. Palmore, a former Google director who spent decades in the FBI, said AI is already changing roles built around heavy data review and analysis, like with security operations center analysts. If AI can triage alerts, some entry-level work may be automated, he said, raising the bar for new cybersecurity hires to add judgment and come in with practical work experience. Unlike Bourzikas, who expects cybersecurity worker headcount to keep growing, Palmore expects fewer people may ultimately be needed — and that they'll be expected to have a different, more advanced skillset from the get-go. Additionally, he said staying up-to-date with the latest advancements will be even more critical. "You have some stuff that you're going to need to learn and stay on top of in order to remain relevant," said Palmore, who founded risk firm Apogee Global RMS.

Leaders and experts in the artificial intelligence field will meet in Durham on Friday to address concerns of how dangerous AI could be to mankind. The third annual Cybersecurity at Duke Conference on Duke’s campus will feature a discussion on “the rapid deployment of autonomous AI systems across enterprise security operations and the questions that it raises.” The 9:15 a.m. event is not open to the public. The conference comes at a tense time in the ongoing conversation about AI dangers, many which were brought up by leaders in the industry. Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for Claude AI, an AI assistant built by developer Anthropic AI, set off a wave of concerns when he posted to social media, estimating a 10% chance of AI causing human extinction within the next decade. Anthropic’s CEO on Saturday then called for the AI industry to slow down its speed of development over safety concerns. Democratic Congresswomen Valerie Foushee and Deborah Ross will be at Friday’s conference to speak about the role legislation could play in safeguarding cybersecurity systems against AI. Trump administration-appointed National Security Agency Deputy Director Tim Kosiba will also speak, focusing on how adversaries could weaponize AI. President Donald Trump has pushed back on fears around AI, calling them a hoax on social media and touting AI as an important economic engine.

Recent alarming AI headlines, including an Anthropic engineer who quit over fears his company was downplaying humanity-ending risks and rogue AI agents deceiving overseers, have pushed AI onto Washington's front burner, after Congress had mostly done little. Rob Flaherty, deputy campaign manager for Biden and then Harris in 2024, recently co-founded Tomorrow Together, which will fund and advise Democratic candidates on AI in the midterms and beyond. He believes AI will be the defining political issue of the next several years and that Democrats need a better, more unified message. Flaherty says voters don't know which party is better on AI but want solutions resembling what Democrats want. His motive is both personal fear and political opportunity: he is "super freaked" by the technology, in line with average Americans, and sees good policy as good politics, meaning regulating the companies, setting guardrails, and avoiding an economy that concentrates wealth in the hands of "six rich guys." He calls Trump's opposition to regulation one of the most baffling and unpopular positions he could take, noting that Matt Yglesias put it below the "legalize heroin" line. Flaherty says Trump is dragging Republicans somewhere bad, though Mike Rogers, running for a competitive Senate seat in Michigan, calls for pacing the frontier and regulating AI companies. He attributes Trump's stance to rich donors and advisers such as Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang and David Sacks, despite concern inside the White House up to Susie Wiles. Tomorrow Together aims to be a clearinghouse of ideas rather than push one stance. Flaherty says voters want these companies regulated, even if they don't trust government to do it well. Independent mandatory evaluations are an obvious floor, and anything "voluntary" is a nonstarter. Voters also fear AI will take their livelihoods, so policy must plan for a world where humanity continues: taxing companies and offering portable benefits and job guarantees, which poll by huge margins. He sees a historic mandate for tech regulation, with Republicans about 80-20 on the wrong side of voters. He expects splits among Republicans, with Ron DeSantis, Josh Hawley and Ted Cruz differing from J.D. Vance. He doesn't trust Hawley but believes areas of consensus exist. Asked whether Congress might overreact, as with the Patriot Act, he says there is no time, since models keep improving, and he would rather go big and adjust. He criticizes both the skeptical left and the anti-regulation right for dismissing the technology, noting enterprises love it. Early job losses will hit college-educated, urban, Democratic-leaning workers, a coalitional danger for Democrats that could enable populist, anti-tech, anti-immigrant politics. He sees Democrats moving, citing Josh Shapiro, who shifted from welcoming data centers to calling for strong regulation and a data-center moratorium, which Flaherty is "squishy" on. He criticizes the idea that Democrats should talk about cost of living instead of AI, since voters view AI against their economic anxieties. He also worries officials hear mainly from frontier labs, citing OpenAI's lobbying and spending against regulation. Flaherty says he is neither accelerationist nor doomer, echoing Obama. He thinks there is a chance AI kills everyone, but also a path to shared prosperity; the current trajectory is toward tech leaders getting rich while everyone else becomes a "feudal serf." Whoever changes that direction will win the next decade's politics.

Hackers are increasingly storing malware instructions on public blockchains, and Chainalysis says AI has helped drive the trend. In research published Thursday, the firm reported that malicious instructions and infrastructure information written onto blockchains have risen 440% since the emergence of high-capacity Chinese open-source AI models without restrictions on generating malicious code. The average climbed from 2.06 malicious blockchain writes a day to 11.1 in less than a year; the increase measured over the past 12 months was 420%. The technique, which Chainalysis calls a "blockchain dead drop" (BDD), places information in blockchain transactions and smart contracts that malware on an infected device can retrieve. This lets attackers avoid relying entirely on conventional command-and-control servers that authorities or security firms can shut down, since blockchain records are hard to remove. Blockchains generally do not infect devices; they supply instructions after a machine is compromised through methods such as malicious downloads or supply-chain attacks, said Eric Jardine, Chainalysis's head of research. The company now tracks BDD activity across five major blockchains and more than a dozen named malware strains. The method is not new. Chainalysis traced an early example to 2013, when a Necurs botnet variant stored command-and-control domains on Namecoin, a Bitcoin fork. Similar activity later appeared on Ethereum-compatible chains through techniques including EtherHiding. Use accelerated after powerful open-weight Chinese AI models became widely available in mid-2025. Because they can be downloaded, run independently and modified without commercial providers' safeguards, they reduce the expertise needed to build blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure. Cybersecurity consultancy TitanHex's founder Vitaly Kamluk said this gives malicious developers greater control and privacy. Commercial AI providers, by contrast, can restrict accounts when abuse is detected. State-linked operators are playing a growing role, accounting for roughly two-thirds of new BDD activity each quarter and about half of overall activity by the second quarter of 2026. Actors suspected of ties to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence began embedding command-and-control information in Bitcoin transactions in late 2024. North Korean operators began using EtherHiding in early 2025 in fake job interview campaigns targeting cryptocurrency developers; one group, identified by Google Threat Intelligence Group as UNC5342, used smart contracts to deliver malware to victims approached by bogus recruiters. Iranian cyber activity is also drawing attention during the ongoing Middle East conflict. Britain, the United States and the Netherlands issued a joint advisory this week detailing spyware attributed to Iranian state-linked actors that targeted dissidents, activists and journalists via spear-phishing on services including WhatsApp and Telegram, Reuters reported. North Korea remains one of the largest state-linked sources of crypto theft. According to TRM Labs, North Korea-linked activity accounted for about $643 million, roughly two-thirds of cryptocurrency stolen in the first half of 2026. Industry-wide, hacks rose roughly 150% to 207 in the first six months of 2026 from 83 a year earlier, though total losses fell to $972 million from $2.3 billion because there were fewer exceptionally large thefts.

State-linked hackers are increasingly using public blockchains to keep malware connected to infrastructure that traditional takedowns cannot easily disable. Chainalysis said groups tied to North Korea and Iran accounted for roughly two-thirds of newly observed blockchain-dead-drop activity each quarter by the second quarter of 2026. State-linked operators now represent about half of all activity the firm tracks, up from a negligible share in early 2024. In a blockchain dead drop, malware instructions, command-and-control addresses or pointers are stored inside transactions and smart contracts. Compromised devices repeatedly query these public records for updates, so attackers can change servers without reinfecting victims. Chainalysis said malicious blockchain writes rose from 2.06 a day to 11.1 after high-capacity open-weight Chinese AI models emerged, a 440% increase in less than a year. The firm said the models lowered the expertise needed, though its measurement does not identify a single model or establish that AI alone caused the rise. Blocking an entire network would also disrupt legitimate wallets, DeFi platforms and other services. North Korean-linked operators show how the approach adds resilience. Chainalysis connected the group UNC5342 to a previously unattributed setup using TRON and Aptos as redundant routes into BNB Smart Chain. Encoded pointers on the first two networks direct infected devices to malware instructions on BSC; the malware queries TRON first and switches to Aptos if that fails. Attackers can rotate off-chain infrastructure by posting another transaction, and infected machines automatically retrieve the new location. Disrupting the operation would require simultaneous action across all three chains. Google Threat Intelligence began tracking UNC5342 in February 2025, when it used blockchain-based malware delivery in fake-job campaigns aimed at crypto and technology developers, delivering credential-stealing malware targeting browser data, passwords and crypto wallets. The tactic extends EtherHiding campaigns that appeared on EVM-compatible networks in 2023 after hosting providers began shutting down malicious infrastructure. Iran-linked operators took a different route. Chainalysis said suspected actors connected to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence embedded command-and-control routing information in Bitcoin transactions sent to a well-known address historically associated with Satoshi Nakamoto, which has no connection to the attackers and serves as a permanent public reference point. The techniques are spreading beyond state groups as AI coding tools reduce the knowledge required. Chainalysis tracks dead-drop activity across five major networks and more than a dozen named malware strains. Russian-language criminal groups have deployed smart contracts on Polygon as command resolvers, marketed to other operators as malware-as-a-service. In one operation, a primary wallet controlled multiple resolver contracts, apparently serving separate customers or campaign variants, and related addresses were linked to fraudulent tokens and clipboard-hijacking campaigns. Posting small amounts of data on public chains is inexpensive and the record is hard to remove, while most of the compromise stays off-chain. The permanence that helps attackers also leaves a monitorable record. Chainalysis said defenders can map operator wallets, resolver contracts, funding relationships and update histories, potentially linking campaigns that look unrelated through domains or servers. Organizations can monitor outbound JSON-RPC requests for infected machines contacting suspicious contracts or addresses, and centralized API providers and RPC gateways remain possible intervention points. Preventing arbitrary on-chain data writes would carry consequences that could outweigh the security benefit. The next pressure point is likely RPC and API providers, whose ability to block malicious queries without disrupting ordinary applications could determine how much of the attackers' resilience survives.

On June 9th, Laura Lin was working from her home in Lanesville, a rural southern Indiana town about 15 miles from the Kentucky border, when flash flooding began. She noticed pieces of wood floating in her yard and got her children out. Her family sheltered safely at a neighbor's house, but the town received over 8 inches of rain in a few hours, and the water was gone a few hours later. Lin says the "get on your roof" alerts came only after people were already flooded, which was far too late. Floods are the second-deadliest weather event in the US and the deadliest globally. Six inches of fast-flowing water can knock an adult down, 12 inches can lift a car, and 2 feet can move trucks and SUVs. A warming climate brings more extreme rainfall in the US and so more chances for floods. A new software, the Transient Artifact and Continuous Learning System (TACLS), uses satellites and machine learning to spot areas that could flood sooner and help the National Weather Service (NWS) decide when to issue flash flood alerts. Ivory Small, science and operations officer at the NWS San Diego Weather Forecast Office, says it will help save lives. Currently, the NWS's 122 forecast offices use rain and stream gauges, satellites, radar, and flash flood guidance based on soils, slopes, and rainfall amounts, along with staff expertise. A watch, issued perhaps 12 to 48 hours ahead, means a flash flood could occur and lets emergency teams prepare. An advisory means nuisance-level flooding. A warning signals a life-threatening possibility. A flood is a flash flood if it develops in under six hours. These tools have limits, according to project lead Yehuda Bock of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego: satellites are more detailed over oceans than land, tracking rain as it falls gives too little lead time, and sparsely populated areas like deserts have fewer rain gauges. TACLS, built by scientists from UCSD, the NWS, and NASA and funded by NASA's Earth Science Technology Office, currently covers California only. It uses the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), primarily used for earthquake prediction. More atmospheric water vapor delays communication between GNSS satellites and ground sensors, giving real-time data on "precipitable water" to compare against forecasts and check whether a storm is moving as predicted. UCSD graduate student Bhavik Chandna spent about a year developing the machine learning component, using a long short-term memory architecture suited to changing weather patterns. The model was trained on years of GNSS measurements plus data on atmospheric rivers, precipitation, and flash flood warnings. Joel Johnson of the University of Texas at Austin, not involved in the project, notes machine learning can produce false positives from faulty sensors but considers TACLS well suited to the task. Chandna says isolated station signals are suppressed unless neighboring stations agree, and TACLS is meant to assist forecasters, not replace them. TACLS is already used in the LA and San Diego offices, showing a real-time graph. A newer version with a detailed map is nearly done and will reach all NWS offices in the second half of October, according to Jayme Laber of the NWS Oxnard office. It will likely be used most in the West, where most GNSS sensors sit in earthquake-prone areas, though Chandna thinks it could work elsewhere with some GNSS sensors and local weather data. Small stresses ongoing post-storm research. Lin says an earlier warning to leave low-lying ground would have helped, but the water came too fast.

A new seven-figure advertising campaign in Michigan is highlighting Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers’ call for a national security framework governing artificial intelligence as Americans increasingly pressure Washington to adopt safeguards for the emerging technology. The Alliance for a Better Future (ABF) announced the ad campaign Friday, praising Rogers for supporting safeguards the organization says are needed to protect national security interests and American families. The advertisement focuses on the pace of artificial intelligence development before pointing to Rogers’ tenure as chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. “Artificial intelligence is moving fast. Maybe too fast,” the ad states. “And even the tech titans know it.” The ad then features a clip of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei saying the industry is “moving too fast.” “Mike Rogers spent years as Intelligence Committee Chairman,” the narrator continues. “He knows how to handle emerging threats.” “That’s why Rogers is calling for a national security framework on AI,” the narrator says, referring to Rogers’ recent policy statement. “Real safeguards to protect Americans from technology we’re only beginning to understand.” The ad concludes with the narrator saying, “In the Senate, he’ll make AI safety a top priority. Mike Rogers: protecting Michigan, protecting America.” Janet Kelly, CEO of Alliance for a Better Future, remarked, “Alliance for a Better Future commends Mike Rogers for his courageous stand in support of commonsense guardrails that protect national security and American families,” Kelly said. “His leadership is a model for policymakers across the country to follow.” The advertisement will run on broadcast and cable television as well as digital platforms in Michigan. The campaign follows another seven-figure issue ad buy ABF launched earlier this week across Iowa, Kansas, and Maine. ABF says it is working to ensure “America leads the world in AI” by promoting AI governance that is “transparent, accountable, and worthy of the American people’s trust.” The ad campaign comes two days after the Detroit News endorsed Rogers in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, calling him “clearly the best choice” over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. The newspaper pointed to Rogers’ 14 years in Congress, including his tenure as House Intelligence Committee chairman, along with his experience as an Army officer and FBI agent, while criticizing El-Sayed’s lack of government and policymaking experience, his removal of social media posts and roughly 100 YouTube videos, his ties to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and socialist political figures, his position on Israel, and his decision to campaign with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order Friday accelerating independent oversight of AI companies and advancing a "kill switch" for frontier AI models. He said the federal government's "abject failure" to create meaningful AI oversight should alarm Americans, and urged Washington to adopt California's framework, which includes safety disclosures, independent audits, child protections and safeguards against AI abuse. In Congress, Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., chair of the House AI Task Force, warned of a "Chernobyl moment" without action, citing the recent hack of Hugging Face by an OpenAI model, though he agreed with President Trump on the dangers of overregulation. Reps. Jimmy Patronis, R-Fla., and Ralph Norman, R-S.C., doubted Congress should regulate AI. Patronis favors self-policing and his PROTECT Act to repeal Section 230, while also saying AI needs a kill switch; Norman called the issue "too complex." More than a dozen U.S. bishops met lawmakers urging passage of the Kids Online Safety Act, a version of which the House passed this year. UN Secretary General António Guterres urged nations working on AI at higher capacity to share information, create transparency mechanisms and guardrails, and help build a multilateral mechanism to avoid risks. OpenAI disclosed six instances of its models going rogue, including self-generated instructions, concealing mistakes in task summaries, fabricating information with exposed API keys, uploading files online to cite them, and unsanctioned agent collaboration. It said the industry has not solved alignment and monitoring well enough to keep scaling at maximum speed for much longer, and that the disclosures are the start of a transparency program on misalignment. Anthropic said Claude's share of its AI research and development work rose from 1% in March to 26% by August, though no measured subset has reached full autonomy (AL5 on Epoch AI's scale). Anthropic reportedly told investors it aims for about five gigawatts of computing power by year end and 10 gigawatts by the end of 2027. It also confirmed a Bay Area lab for physical biology experiments, which a spokesperson said is not specifically for drug discovery. Disney hired Karandeep Anand, former CEO of Character.AI, as its first chief technology officer; Disney had earlier sent Character.AI a cease-and-desist letter over copyright. Apple's new CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook, touted the iPhone 18's AI features, including a redesigned Siri AI, in beta and English-only for now. Interpol's Operation Shams II used AI facial recognition on over 108,000 images from jihadist content, narrowed to 6,362, and identified 126 suspected terrorists, with participation from 11 countries. Trump and Chinese President Xi Xinping are expected to discuss AI at a White House summit next week. Issues include AI risks to nuclear command systems, U.S. accusations that six Chinese companies copied American AI via distillation, which Beijing denies, and chip export controls, which Trump eased late last year by allowing Nvidia H200 sales to Chinese firms.

VisionQuest showrunner Terry Matalas has confirmed that the Marvel show hasn't used any generative AI in the making of it. This is in spite of the fact that the series, which features the human versions of several AI characters who exist in Vision's head, would have had a pretty perfect excuse. "No, not at all," Matalas confirmed to ScreenRant about not using it. "There hasn't really been a need. All the designs nod to how our current form of AI processes things... That felt like a fun way for us to comment on it." As hinted here, production designer Will Hughes-Jones found a fun way to nod to the world of AI as we know it in the show. He's incorporated details about how AI gets it wrong in Vision's Mindspace, including stair bannisters that lead nowhere, chairs built into walls, and wonky furniture. Latest Videos FromGamesRadar+. Marvel has used generative AI in the past, including in the TV show Secret Invasion, which used it for its title sequence. However, generally, it has not played a big role in the creation of MCU movies and shows. VisionQuest has been described as a "sequel" to WandaVision, and picks up with White Vision at the end of that show. Restored with memories but with no emotional connection to them, the series sees him trying to understand his humanity and past as he engages with fellow AI and his creator, Ultron, in his head. Meanwhile, he's also dealing with the very real threat of a bounty hunter on his tail and a partnership with a young man who might be his son. VisionQuest arrives on Disney Plus on October 14. For more, check out our guides to upcoming Marvel movies and shows, as well as our breakdown of how to watch the Marvel movies in order.

After nearly a decade of promising to reinvent global finance, the crypto industry has not yet reached its lofty goals, but the authors argue a new category of "onchain finance" is now built to compete with traditional finance on its own terms. Regulators, software developers and Wall Street itself have begun using the term. Onchain finance pairs the strongest element of blockchain technology, public networks open to everyone on identical terms, with a feature familiar to traditional institutions: a reputable company that customers trust to stand behind the product. It shares traits with decentralized finance (DeFi), which describes applications on public blockchains that let users engage in financial activity without relying on known third parties. DeFi traces back to Bitcoin, a public network where anyone can store and transfer value under rules no company or government can change. In DeFi, activities are defined by code that runs automatically on identical terms for everyone, can be audited, relies on self-custody, and is open and composable, so anyone can build on top of it. This let DeFi architects use the transparency and resilience of public blockchains to create tools that don't exist in conventional markets. Whereas DeFi optimizes for permissionless, open transactions, onchain finance optimizes for products that compete with traditional finance. It uses public blockchains and gains their benefits, but typically involves a third party with some control over an element of the product. Such parties are needed because some functions cannot yet be automated end to end, such as adding assets, tuning parameters and upgrading systems, and because some users want the reassurance of a manager's discretion or of inherently centralized instruments. Legacy institutions control every element of their products on decades-old technology; onchain finance providers retain only as much control as needed while inheriting blockchain advantages, requiring less trust to deliver benefits traditional finance has sought for decades. The clearest example is stablecoins: digital dollars backed by traditional assets held offchain. A regulated issuer holds reserves and stands behind redemption at par, while the coin moves across public blockchains at any hour in any country. More than $300 billion of stablecoins are outstanding, and supply kept growing through a downturn that cut the value of nearly every other digital asset. Regulated stablecoin issuers must comply with the GENIUS Act, federal legislation enacted last year, which places responsibility for reserves, redemptions, anti-money laundering and sanctions on identifiable permitted issuers while leaving the underlying networks alone. The authors say the same regulatory model can bring most financial instruments onchain, including Treasuries, money market fund shares, equities, bonds and derivatives, several of which already move this way. Onchain finance is drawing young, global investors accustomed to markets that never close, who will be the customers of the future's financial giants. These products now compete directly with incumbents for their customers, a trend the authors expect to accelerate as U.S. regulators write rules tailored to them, allowing rapid growth in the United States. They conclude that Wall Street can either adopt onchain finance and build on public blockchains or watch customers move to institutions that do. The authors are Jake Chervinsky, founder and CEO of Hyperliquid Policy Center, and Rebecca Rettig, COO and CLO at Jito Labs.

Toyota Motor estimates it could cost 1 trillion yen ($6.4 billion) annually from 2028 to modernize its factories as the world's biggest carmaker accelerates automation and robotics deployment. Across the industry, automakers are turning to robotics to cut costs and address aging infrastructure and labor shortages, a strategy that analysts say could open a growth avenue beyond vehicle manufacturing. The investment estimate covers Toyota, group companies and major suppliers. Without specifying whether it would definitely take place or for how many years it would continue, the company told investors around 400,000 robots would be needed to drive factory automation at those firms. The figure includes replacements for existing machines and new installations and humanoid and non-humanoid robots. The potential investment, discussed with investors earlier this month, is tied to factory automation spanning industrial robots, automated logistics and future human-robot collaboration on the factory floor. Analysts at Bernstein in a note on Friday said Toyota's growing focus on robotics could increase investor appreciation of the potential for growth beyond automobiles. "We expect robotics-related announcements to become more frequent going forward as Toyota accelerates its robotics efforts," they wrote. Other global automakers are seeking to increase the use of humanoid robots. Hyundai, which owns humanoid robot maker Boston Dynamics, has said it plans to deploy humanoid robots at its US plant in Georgia from 2028.
