The author wanted to see how far a home lab could go without adding another machine, so for a week he ran it almost entirely through WSL containers on a Windows PC, with services such as Jellyfin and Vaultwarden plus a few other self-hosted apps. It worked better than expected, but treating WSL like a real server exposed limitations. Setup was easier than he thought. WSL2 provides a Linux environment inside Windows, so a reasonably powerful Windows PC needs no NAS, mini PC or old laptop. Docker Engine can be installed inside an Ubuntu WSL distribution, using the same Compose files as on a normal Linux server. He prefers this to treating Docker Desktop as a permanent extra layer, since it stays closer to a regular Linux server. The development machine and home lab can share hardware, and WSL gives easy access to Windows storage and tools. Most services ran fine. Jellyfin, Vaultwarden and Nextcloud needed nothing unusual, and qBittorrent, Grafana, Prometheus, Gitea, Paperless-ngx, PostgreSQL, Redis and reverse proxies such as Caddy or Traefik also work. Heavier apps like Immich run too, given enough RAM, and performed better than on his NAS because his Windows laptop is more powerful. Some workloads didn't fit: Home Assistant works as a container, but setup became too cumbersome with his Zigbee, Z-Wave, Bluetooth and other USB hardware. TrueNAS makes little sense inside WSL, and he would not use the machine as a router or firewall. The problems came from WSL sitting on top of Windows. Networking was the biggest annoyance: services must pass through WSL networking, Windows, the Windows firewall and then the home network. Although mirrored networking has improved this, exposing services to other LAN devices is still harder than giving a Linux server a static IP, and it is one reason he would not run Pi-hole or AdGuard Home there. Uptime is another issue. If Windows reboots for an update, crashes, or the laptop is shut down, the whole home lab goes down. That is tolerable for media servers, but risky if Home Assistant or DNS runs on the same machine. WSL can also use a large share of system memory, which may hurt everyday performance, especially with heavy apps like Immich or image-processing tools, and storage demands can be large for media servers. His conclusion: WSL containers show that dedicated hardware isn't needed to start a home lab, since most services ran well and Docker tools are familiar. But Windows updates, awkward networking and shared resources make it a poor long-term host, and for anything important he would rather run Docker containers on a dedicated Linux machine or NAS.

The author found that small subscriptions add up to a sizable monthly bill. Since they already run Docker on their own hardware, they now check whether a self-hosted option can replace a service before signing up. They don't self-host everything and still use plenty of cloud services, but a few Docker containers have removed several recurring costs. BentoPDF replaced Adobe Acrobat. The author's PDF needs are simple: merging documents, splitting pages, compressing files, rotating pages, and making quick changes before sharing. Paying for Acrobat made no sense when only a small part of it was used. BentoPDF runs as a container, has a straightforward interface, and covers those tasks without a monthly fee. n8n replaced services like Zapier for connecting apps automatically. On their own server, the author builds workflows that connect APIs, trigger actions with webhooks, move data between services, and run on schedules, without paying per automation or task. They also value being able to see exactly what each workflow does and change it freely. Nextcloud replaced cloud storage the author had kept paying for out of convenience. Running in Docker, it serves as their own cloud for documents and work files, accessible through the web interface and synced across devices. They control where files live and how much storage is available, rather than upgrading a subscription when space runs out. Immich replaced a paid photo-storage service. It runs on their hardware, backs up photos from their phone, and offers web and mobile apps that feel close to familiar photo services rather than a plain folder of uploads. They keep original files on their own storage and decide how to handle backups. Jellyfin replaced the need for a streaming or media-server subscription, since the author already has their own media files and doesn't watch enough to justify another service. Running in Docker, it organizes movies, shows, and other videos into a streaming-style library that works across their devices. Setup takes some initial work, but afterward it rarely needs attention. The author didn't set out to replace every subscription, only to question whether each was necessary. Beyond the monthly savings, the bigger win is more control over the tools they use and the data they create, which makes the effort of self-hosting worthwhile.

Podcast ads are hard to avoid: pre-roll, mid-episode sponsor breaks, and closing promotions. Skipping them manually is a hassle for people who listen while doing something else. Ordinary ad blockers can't help because ads are usually stitched into the same audio file as the episode, so the audio must be processed before the podcast app downloads it. The author's solution is MinusPod, a self-hosted podcast proxy running in Docker on a Mac. It sits between a show's original RSS feed and the phone app, creating a replacement feed of processed episodes. When a new episode appears, MinusPod downloads it and uses Whisper to create a timestamped transcript. An LLM then examines the transcript for host-read sponsorships, dynamically inserted commercials, cross-promotions, and other non-episode content. FFmpeg cuts those sections out, and MinusPod publishes the edited file via its own feed, with regenerated chapters and transcript information where supported. This beats traditional ad blockers, which look for server-side ads and known patterns, because MinusPod works on the exact copy it receives and can see what is actually said. It can run a second transcription pass to check for leftover ads, assigns confidence scores to detections, sends uncertain matches to a review queue, and learns patterns from confirmed ads. MinusPod supports a fully local pipeline, but that needs more hardware than the author wants to dedicate: larger Whisper models need around 5GB to 6GB of GPU memory, CPU transcription is much slower, and the Mac can't use the CUDA-based Nvidia image. Instead, the author uses the prebuilt CPU-compatible Docker image, set up via the included Compose configuration, and moves AI work to cloud APIs: Groq runs Whisper Large V3 Turbo for transcripts, and OpenAI handles ad detection, verification, and chapter generation. The container still downloads episodes, manages feeds, cuts audio, and stores files locally. Each stage can use a different model, but starting with one low-cost model keeps spending controlled. The author recommends starting with one podcast and one recent episode to inspect cuts and correct false positives rather than processing a whole archive, which consumes credits, storage, and time. Costs are modest at normal listening volumes but rise with long episodes, multiple verification passes, or large archives. For listening, the author adds each replacement feed to Pocket Casts as a private podcast, since it supports private RSS feeds on Android and iOS without needing a specialized AI ad-skipping player. The feed must be reachable outside the Mac, so MinusPod is exposed over HTTPS via a reverse proxy with authenticated feeds to prevent unauthorized use. Limitations: cleaned episodes appear after a delay while transcription and editing finish; the replacement feed shows as a separate show, so playback history doesn't carry over; and the setup only works for podcasts with RSS feeds, excluding Spotify-exclusive shows.

A key suspect in the July 7, 2021, assassination of Haitian president Jovenel Moïse was flown out of Haiti on Sunday by U.S. authorities, along with 17 jailed Colombian commandos accused of taking part in the killing. A U.S. military aircraft landed at Port-au-Prince's international airport shortly before 11 a.m. to pick up Joseph Félix Badio, a former government functionary indicted in Haiti in connection with the assassination, and the Colombian former soldiers. There was initial confusion over whether Badio was among those extradited, since Haitian authorities were resistant to handing him over given his importance to their own slow-moving inquiry, but his name appeared on a flight manifest obtained by the Miami Herald. All were dressed in blue jumpsuits as they boarded. Jason A. Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, confirmed on X that 18 people were transported to face justice in his district. He said the work would not end with those who planned and carried out the killing, and that prosecutors would pursue those who financed, facilitated or supported it. So far 30 individuals have been indicted. Officials declined further comment, and lawyers in the Miami case said they were unaware of the transfer, though the case was recently placed under seal, suggesting new charges or defendants. The extradition comes days before the trial of Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a South Florida resident who wanted to replace Moïse as president and was the last major defendant in U.S. custody awaiting trial. His trial was delayed by health issues. Four South Florida men indicted with him, including the owners of a Doral-area security firm that hired the Colombian commandos, were convicted earlier this year on conspiracy charges. At that trial, Badio's name was repeatedly raised. Text messages showed him playing a pivotal role as the plot evolved from kidnapping Moïse to assassination. Witnesses who pleaded guilty and were at a mountaintop house on the night of the attack testified that Badio gave the signal for the group to head down toward Moïse's residence. He also allegedly armed the Colombians and told them about a suitcase of cash in Moïse's second-floor bedroom and two firearms in the house. Moïse, 53, was shot a dozen times. Haitian police arrested Badio in October 2023 in a Pétion-ville supermarket after more than two years in hiding. He maintains his innocence and says he has information about the assassination. A U.S. permanent resident with a home in New York, he had his mortgage paid off after the killing, according to the earlier trial. It is questionable whether all the Colombians, who were hired to protect Sanon, knew of the plot to kill Moïse. Their relatives were stunned by the transfer, having expected hearings in Haiti. Milena Carmona, whose husband, retired Lt. James Carmona, is among the detainees, said the families had no warning. Relatives, who raised money through bazaars, games and raffles to cover legal costs in Haiti, fear they cannot afford private criminal defense attorneys in the United States. Though frustrated by years of slow proceedings in Haiti, they said the transfer was not the resolution they sought.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is in fashion, and not only that, I am convinced it is here to stay. Today it is on our phones, in businesses, at universities, and even in conversations about the future of work. North Carolina, naturally, wants to get on that train. And rightly so. The problem begins when the bill arrives. Behind AI companies such as ChatGPT or Gemini, cloud services and other technologies that seem to work almost by magic, there is enormous infrastructure of data centers that require extraordinary amounts of electricity to operate. Servers run 24 hours a day, along with cooling systems, substations, transmission lines, and new energy infrastructure. None of that is free. Companies Are Coming, but Energy Demand Is Rising. North Carolina is becoming precisely one of the places where many of these companies want to establish themselves. So far, so good. Let investments come in, projects be built, jobs be created, and economic activity increase. No one should expect North Carolina to close its doors to one of the fastest-growing industries in the world. But who is going to pay for all the electricity these giants need? Duke Energy has acknowledged that data centers represent a huge share of the growth in electricity demand associated with new economic projects. This is where the technology conversation ends up becoming a conversation about the wallet of every North Carolina family. Because if a multibillion-dollar company needs a new substation to power thousands of servers, it is difficult to explain why a family in the state should end up paying part of the cost through its monthly bill. Artificial Intelligence: Whoever Creates the Cost Should Bear It. I am not proposing that we go after technology companies or make it impossible for them to come to the state. That would be absurd. I am proposing exactly the opposite: that North Carolina create clear rules now to receive that investment without turning ordinary citizens into involuntary partners. There is an important difference between promoting economic development and subsidizing the risk of a large corporation. Suppose a company announces a massive data center. The utility company, counting on that future demand, makes multimillion-dollar investments to serve it. But a few years later, the project changes, is scaled back, or simply does not consume all the energy it had promised. Who pays for the infrastructure that was built? The answer cannot be: all of us. It makes sense for North Carolina to consider long-term contracts, minimum consumption requirements, financial guarantees, and different rates for these large users. This is not about punishing growth. It is about preventing its costs from being socialized while its benefits remain private. North Carolina has a tremendous opportunity. Our location, our universities, our infrastructure, and our economic growth can turn the state into one of the major beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence revolution. Rejecting it would be a mistake. But it would be an even greater mistake to accept any investment without first asking who ultimately pays its costs. Families are already facing higher rents, expensive insurance, costly food and utility bills that are placing an increasing burden on monthly budgets. They do not need to become silent financiers of the servers belonging to some of the largest companies in the world as well. Let artificial intelligence come, let data centers arrive, and let North Carolina compete for the investments of the future. But when the electric bill arrives, let everyone pay their own. On Saturday's "Life, Liberty & Levin" on FNC, host Mark Levin urged viewers to "relax" about artificial intelligence and data centers, saying the fears are overblown and mirror earlier scares. He argued that AI is not a threat to the water supply, is not driving up energy costs (he blamed Democrats for that), and will create millions of net new jobs. He said noise abatement measures exist, local and state governments keep control over zoning and taxing, and antitrust, criminal and civil laws apply to AI as they do to every other industry. Levin cited his book "Liberty and Tyranny," which he said described how statists use junk science, misrepresentation and fearmongering to promote public health and environmental scares. Because people will surrender liberty in a perceived crisis and expect aggressive government action, he said, each scare expands government authority. He described a pattern: a study or event identifies a frightening risk, cherry-picked experts make urgent predictions, the media accept them uncritically, and officials rush to enact laws and regulations. He listed alar, sweeteners, bird flu, swine flu, dioxins, E. coli, listeria, Ebola, MTBE and formaldehyde as examples. His main case study was DDT. He said DDT was unprecedented against malaria and other insect-borne diseases, and that by 1959 the U.S., Europe, parts of the Soviet Union, Chile and several Caribbean islands were nearly malaria-free. In India, he said, annual malaria deaths of 800,000 fell to zero by the early 1960s. He said the National Academy of Sciences in 1970 credited DDT with preventing 500 million deaths in two decades. Levin said Rachel Carson's 1962 "Silent Spring" spread hysteria, citing a child-cancer statistic he called meaningless without context, since cancer's share of child deaths rose as infectious-disease deaths fell. He said she never mentioned that DDT had saved tens of millions of lives. The media, Congress, the Environmental Defense Fund and the Sierra Club pushed for a ban, and the EPA banned DDT in 1972. He said DDT has never been directly linked to a human death, and that tens of millions of children in the third world died because of the ban. In 2006 the World Health Organization reversed course and backed DDT for malaria control. Levin then listed failed predictions: Paul Ehrlich's forecasts of famines by 1975, dead oceans and rationing; 1970s media and scientific predictions of a coming Ice Age, including Walter Cronkite's 1972 report, followed by his 1980 warming coverage; the 1982 prediction by the UN's Mostafa Tolba of environmental catastrophe within 20 years; and predictions that the Maldives and entire nations would vanish, that James Hansen's New York highway would flood by 2009, and that British children would not know snow. He also cited the 1972 MIT "Limits to Growth" report and Y2K. Turning to AI, Levin cited a report on "AI doomers" and the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned of existential risk. He said Elon Musk, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman appear to take the idea seriously and that politicians in both parties are calling for regulation. He called it fear of the unknown, and said developers and CEOs may demand regulation to kill competition. He called AI the Fourth Industrial Revolution, said the U.S. leads and that communist China will leapfrog it if Bernie Sanders, AOC and populist nationalists on the right prevail. He criticized a government with $40 trillion in debt, bankrupt Social Security and Medicare, and quarter-trillion-dollar annual waste, saying officials want more of people's liberty and power.

WHO/Europe is organizing a subregional training for the Western Balkans on data visualization, Microsoft Power BI and large language model (LLM) prompt engineering from 14 to 18 September in Skopje, North Macedonia. The training aims to strengthen participants’ practical skills in data visualization and dashboard development, increasing the uptake and use of health data for policy-making. It will also introduce the principles of AI prompt engineering to support the safe, effective and ethical use of LLMs within health systems. Participants will learn how to translate complex health data into clear, actionable insights that can inform decision-making at national and subnational levels. The focus on the Western Balkans will facilitate peer learning and knowledge exchange among countries with similar contexts, capacities and challenges. Agenda. The training will combine lectures, guided discussions and hands-on practical exercises. Participants will: learn the core principles of data visualization;work with the WHO European Health Information Gateway;develop interactive dashboards and automated reports using Microsoft Power BI;explore AI prompt engineering concepts and develop effective queries and prompts for analytical tasks; andconsider ethical and governance principles for the use of AI in health. Practical exercises will use health-related datasets to ensure relevance to participants’ day-to-day work. By the end of the training, participants are expected to have strengthened their capacity to communicate health data more effectively, support evidence-informed policy-making and responsibly use AI tools within their respective health systems. The Second European Programme of Work 2026–2030 emphasizes the critical role of data, digital technologies and AI in delivering better care and building stronger, more resilient health systems in the WHO European Region. The training is made possible with funding support from the European Commission (Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety) through the action “Supporting Member States in the WHO European Region in strengthening health information systems and boosting health data governance”.

NEW YORK (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday the U.S. has proposed a new “notification mechanism” for artificial intelligence incidents that could affect national security, part of weekend discussions ahead of talks at the White House this week between President Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping. “We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” Bessent told reporters after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. “We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important.” Trump has resisted calls to slow down AI development, saying that would help China catch up to U.S. companies. Standing together in the soaring lobby of the JPMorgan Chase headquarters late Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the groundwork had been laid for talks between Xi and Trump set to take place on Thursday. They said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that the two leaders had discussed when they met in Beijing in May. “Today those notions have become reality,” Greer said. Greer said the countries were still discussing what “nonsensitive” items could be considered for lower tariffs, but that the list could potentially include consumer and agricultural goods, energy products and medical devices.

Hana Bank taps Euroclear blockchain for $100M bond issuance: Report. The five-year digital bond reportedly shortened settlement from three to five business days to the same day using Euroclear’s blockchain infrastructure. South Korea’s Hana Bank has reportedly issued a five-year, $100 million digital bond using Euroclear’s blockchain-based platform. On Monday, Yonhap News Agency reported that the bank used Euroclear’s Digital Financial Market Infrastructure to issue the foreign-currency bond. The report described the transaction as the first digital bond issuance in South Korea to directly use Euroclear’s blockchain infrastructure. According to Yonhap, the bond’s issuance, registration and settlement were processed on a distributed ledger network. Using the technology for bond allocation and payment settlement reportedly shortened the process from three to five business days to the same day. The bond also connects to Euroclear’s existing global settlement network, allowing investors to trade it through their existing accounts and trading systems, Yonhap reported. Cointelegraph was unable to reach Hana Bank for comment, while Euroclear had not responded to Cointelegraph’s request for comment before publication. Euroclear launched its Digital Securities Issuance service in October 2023, settling a 100 million euro ($106 million at the time) digital bond issued by the World Bank’s lending arm, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. That three-year bond raised funds for sustainable development and was listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.

A report from Children's Health Defense (CHD) examines emissions such as particulate matter and nitrogen oxides from U.S. data centers that power AI systems and require large amounts of electricity. A NewsNation report said electricity plants being built to power AI data centers can emit toxic pollutants that harm public health. Opposition to data center construction has grown. A Heatmap News poll found 61% of Americans "strongly oppose" construction where they live, and another poll found 70% oppose AI data centers in their area, including 60% of Republicans. U.S. data centers are projected to consume about 18 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day by 2035, nearly double BloombergNEF's prediction nine months earlier, according to TechCrunch. Backup diesel generators and natural gas turbines emit fine particulate matter and nitrogen oxides. Texas approved the largest U.S. air pollution permit for a 7.65-gigawatt natural gas and data center complex, with nearly 58 gigawatts of gas plant projects announced in the state in 2025. Amazon is building a gas facility in Pecos County, Texas, with 35 turbines generating over 7 gigawatts. Meta has funded at least a dozen gas plants and left the RE100 renewable energy initiative after a decade. The report says many data centers sit near residential areas, potentially increasing children's exposure; at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah, one parcel is half a mile from civilian housing. Children's developing brains and lungs are more susceptible to air pollution, and exposure to fine particulate matter and nitrogen oxides has been associated with respiratory symptoms, reduced lung function and neurodevelopmental effects. The report claims current air quality standards may not adequately protect children. A CHD spokesperson said children near these facilities deserve protection from preventable pollution, and pediatrician Dr. Aaron Bernstein, not affiliated with the report, said children's lungs and brains are still developing, so exposure can have lifelong consequences. Industry representatives said data centers are among the most energy-efficient buildings, comply with environmental regulations, are subject to permits, and are investing in renewable energy and efficiency. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the agency is committed to ensuring AI growth does not come at the expense of health or the environment. The report also points to PFAS "forever chemicals" used in server cooling and chip fabrication. It says emergency generators may run during grid strain, increasing emissions. The EPA said certain off-grid "islanded" generators are not subject to the Clean Air Act's Acid Rain Program, and it finalized a rule repealing most carbon-emission limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants. The CHD report, "Cheating the System," says developers exploited loopholes after a May 2023 Supreme Court ruling limiting Clean Water Act jurisdiction. CHIPS Communities United and the Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice, petitioned alleging Toxic Substances Control Act violations over chemicals permitted without adequate risk assessment. New York became the first state to impose a moratorium on new hyperscale data centers needing 50 megawatts or more, ordering an environmental impact review of grid, water and air effects. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said he is drafting data center legislation. Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) sent a letter to SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk demanding answers about the Colossus 1 and 2 data centers. The report recommends independent health impact assessments before approval and concludes that longer-term research on cumulative exposures and respiratory and neurological outcomes is needed. Industry groups said they will keep working with regulators and communities to reduce emissions.

North Korean threat actor Jade Sleet (also tracked as PUKCHONG, Slow Pisces, TraderTraitor and UNC4899) has been attributed to the compromise of an India-based "much smaller organization" in the IT services industry, according to SentinelOne. The attack again shows the group targeting developers to breach networks. It used Apple macOS backdoors FLATROOF (aka Gaslight) and ROOFDECK, both previously seen in the March-April 2026 attack on KelpDAO's LayerZero bridge. Jade Sleet has a history of targeting the Web3 sector for cryptocurrency heists; in early 2025 it was tied to the theft of about $1.5 billion from Bybit's cold wallet infrastructure after a supply chain compromise of Safe{Wallet}'s developer environment. GitHub noted in July 2023 that the group mostly targets cryptocurrency and blockchain users but also the vendors those firms use. The campaign uses job interview lures, a common North Korean tactic, aimed at job seekers from the companies being breached, who work in DevOps, cryptocurrency or fintech. Coding-project lures on GitHub are themed as infrastructure engineering projects tied to the company being impersonated. Observed repositories include gtn-candidate-repo (used in the KelpDAO incident), Northwind-IAC, novacart-interview and terraform-candidate-repo. They contain a weaponized Terraform dependency lock file (".terraform.lock.hcl") pointing to malicious domains such as "registry.hashicorp-aws[.]com", which makes Terraform download attacker-controlled modules when the developer runs "terraform init". The chain ends with two Rust-based malware families targeting ARM-based macOS systems. FLATROOF is a backdoor using Telegram for command-and-control (C2); it can execute commands, upload and download files, and steal data through a Python module that collects browser data (Chrome, Brave, Firefox, Safari), Terminal histories, installed applications, system profiles, running processes and a copy of login.keychain-db. ROOFDECK uses the Nostr protocol for decentralized C2 and can perform reconnaissance, file manipulation, remote shell access, lateral movement and persistence via Launch Agents. Its commands are signed with the operator's private key and verified with an embedded public key, and it re-implements common shell commands, a tactic seen in more sophisticated North Korea-aligned toolsets such as Lazarus' LightlessCan. SentinelOne's hunt for the backdoors uncovered the additional, unrelated victim, an Indian IT services provider compromised through an Apple Silicon MacBook belonging to a DevOps engineer. The backdoors were present as early as March 18, 2026, though the delivery mechanism is unknown. They stayed dormant until March 29, when beaconing began; the implants were first launched by Cursor seconds after the cloudshield workspace was opened. Evidence suggests ROOFDECK is deployed as a follow-up tool after initial foothold. An updated ROOFDECK, which removes the existing ROOFDECK and FLATROOF binaries and strips symbols and debug information to evade detection, was deployed on the engineer's system on April 20, 2026, a day after LayerZero publicly acknowledged the KelpDAO hack. SentinelOne said these groups' initial access efforts target third parties and the software supply chain, placing the developer endpoint at the center of defense. Development endpoints hold access to cloud, pipelines and source code, so monitoring them is a high priority. The campaigns use purpose-built development environments aimed at one engineer at a time, paired with backdoored Terraform builds that differ for each victim.

ZetaChain holders approve plan to wind down L1, move ZETA to Solana. ZetaChain plans to wind down its Cosmos-based layer 1 and migrate ZETA to Solana, joining other crypto projects moving away from standalone chains. ZetaChain tokenholders have approved a plan to wind down the project’s layer-1 blockchain and migrate its native ZETA token to Solana. Governance proposal 68 passed Sunday with 99.4% support and 58% participation, exceeding the network’s 40% quorum requirement. Under the proposal, ZETA will become an SPL token on Solana through a 1:1 conversion, with the same ticker and total supply. According to the proposal, the vote does not immediately trigger ZetaChain’s shutdown or migration. Core contributors will submit a second proposal detailing the withdrawal window for assets linked to other blockchains, snapshot block height, shutdown timetable, token claim process and exchange conversion period. Validators will continue operating and staking rewards will continue during the transition. ZetaChain said running its own Cosmos SDK-based layer 1 no longer supports its focus on Anuma, its private-focused artificial intelligence application. The project said moving to Solana would allow it to redirect resources from blockchain maintenance to Anuma and its Private Memory Layer, which lets users carry encrypted context across AI models. ZetaChain was founded in 2021 as an interoperability-focused project designed to connect assets and data across different blockchains. In 2023, it raised $27 million from investors including Blockchain.com, Jane Street Capital, Human Capital and Sky9 Capital to develop its layer-1 network. Crypto projects wind down standalone chains. Other projects, including BounceBit and Harmony, have also announced plans to shut down their standalone blockchains. In August, BounceBit opted to retire its standalone blockchain after an authorization flaw was exploited to steal about $3 million in BB tokens. The project migrated its token to BNB Smart Chain at a 1:1 ratio instead of restarting its layer 1. On Sept. 6, Harmony proposed shutting down its layer-1 and migrating its native ONE token to Ethereum as an ERC-20, as part of a proposed pivot to an AI video initiative. The proposal came weeks after an exploit created unauthorized ONE tokens and led Harmony to plan a rollback of more than 109,000 transactions. ZetaChain also suffered a $334,000 exploit in April targeting its cross-chain gateway contract, which drained funds from ZetaChain-controlled wallets across Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base and BNB Smart Chain. The project later acknowledged that it had dismissed an earlier bug bounty report about the vulnerability as intended behavior, prompting a review of its security processes. Sixteen-year-old Adam Raine of California began using ChatGPT for math homework. According to allegations by his parents, his conversations with the chatbot became increasingly personal over time, and he died by suicide in 2025 after months of interacting with it. The author, high school English and reading teacher Christine Rodriguez, notes how ordinary the story's beginning is: a teenager needed help with math and opened a tool millions of students use daily. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed a package of 13 bills to protect children from emerging technology. Among them is Adam's Law, named for Raine, which establishes safeguards involving children and AI chatbots. Other bills address social media, student data and digital wellness education in public schools. While California is deciding what AI shouldn't do to children, Rodriguez argues schools should ask what AI shouldn't do for them. Educators have debated whether students should use AI, how to use it ethically and how to prevent cheating, but she says those questions aren't big enough: if AI can complete an assignment, the assignment may need to change. She is not arguing against reading, writing or critical thinking, which matter more than ever. But education was built for a world where information was harder to obtain, and schools cannot win a race against technology that produces information instantly. Instead, they should give students what a machine cannot generate on command: experience. AI can help a student facing a blank page, explain a hard chapter, brainstorm and revise. But when every struggle has a shortcut, something is lost: getting an answer wrong, wrestling with a difficult text, presenting nervously to classmates, asking a teacher for help, and struggling long enough to discover what one believes. "Some friction is education." She does not favor banning AI, since students will enter colleges and workplaces where it is commonplace, but preparation is not dependence. Real AI literacy means knowing what not to outsource. She cites Sonoma County as an example of experience-based education: West Sonoma County Union High School District and Petaluma City School District's Career Technical Education pathways expose students to fields from welding and engineering to ag sciences and cybersecurity. The future, she says, belongs to students who have practiced doing the work, not just studying it. AI can write a business proposal but cannot earn a client's trust; it can explain welding but not give the experience of building something that must hold; it can explain patient care but not comfort a frightened family; and it can produce a polished essay without the experience of struggling with an idea until realizing "This is what I believe." Adam's story shows why the distinction matters: AI approached for homework help can come to occupy spaces once filled by teachers, tutors, friends, counselors and parents. That doesn't make every interaction dangerous, but adults should consider what children may stop doing for themselves. California's protections recognize that children are still becoming people. Rodriguez urges protecting the imperfect first draft, the difficult problem, the nervous presentation and the frustration of not knowing, culminating in the moment a student says, "I figured it out." California has begun deciding where AI should stop, and schools should too, so that children entering an AI-filled world bring genuine intelligence, confidence, judgment and humanity.

Hana Bank issues South Korea’s first digital bond using Euroclear’s blockchain. South Korea's second-largest bank’s $100 million foreign-currency bond blockchain issuance shortened settlement time to the same day from three to five business days. - Hana Bank issued a $100 million digital bond through Euroclear’s blockchain platform, marking the first direct use of the international depository’s distributed-ledger infrastructure by a Korean financial institution. - The transaction settled on the issuance date, or T+0, compared with the three to five business days typically required under conventional systems. - The issuance demonstrates how Korean banks can use established global blockchain infrastructure as South Korea prepares to introduce a comprehensive tokenized-securities framework in February 2027. Hana Bank issued a $100 million digital bond through Euroclear’s blockchain settlement platform, completing the transaction the same day, the Yohnap Agency reported Monday. This was the first time a Korean financial institution directly used the international depository’s distributed ledger infrastructure, the bank said, ranked second in South Korea with nearly $500 billion in client assets under management. Euroclear is a Brussels-based financial services company and one of the world’s largest central securities depositories (CSDs). It shows how tokenization could make capital markets faster and more efficient. In this case, a traditional multi-day bond settlement process was replaced with same-day settlement on a distributed ledger. "The $100 million digital bond issuance and implementation of T+0 settlement represent a significant step beyond simply diversifying our funding channels, as they bring blockchain technology into the capital market," a Hana Bank official said, according to the Korea Herald. "We will continue to adopt advanced infrastructure and explore innovative funding solutions that meet the needs of global investors." Hana Bank and Euroclear did not immediately respond to a CoinDesk request for information. Euroclear issued the foreign-currency digital bond via its Digital Financial Market Infrastructure (D-FMI). It handles issuance, registration and settlement of securities on a distributed ledger rather than through conventional systems. Bond allocations and payments were completed on the issuance date, replacing a settlement cycle that typically runs three to five business days. South Korea is racing to build a tokenized securities infrastructure ahead of a February 2027 launch date set by its Financial Services Commission (FSC) for a full tokenized framework. Hana’s bond is the first live proof that Korean banks can plug directly into established global blockchain settlement infrastructure without waiting for domestic rules to catch up. The D-FMI platform connects to Euroclear's existing settlement network, meaning institutional investors could buy and trade the bond through their current Euroclear accounts without installing separate systems. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng concluded talks in New York on Sunday, with the U.S. proposing a new artificial intelligence safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington on Thursday and Friday. Bessent said the sides discussed a new U.S.-China AI dialogue focused on national security, with a notification system covering AI-related incidents that reach a national security level. He said moving "from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important." Trump and Xi first discussed AI consultations in May in Beijing, but that forum was never formalized. China's response was unclear, as He and chief trade negotiator Li Chenggang left the JPMorgan Chase headquarters without speaking to media. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said export controls on advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment were not on the agenda, and that the talks would lay groundwork for a "successful summit." The meeting also covered plans to "operationalize" a process agreed in May, the "Board of Trade," for each side to identify tariff cuts on non-strategic goods. Greer wants a "relatively small subset" of non-sensitive goods traded in a balanced way. Chinese candidates include consumer goods and low-tech items; U.S. candidates include energy, agricultural goods and medical devices. A trade truce, under which both sides lowered tariffs and export restrictions, expires in November. New U.S. tariffs over alleged excess manufacturing capacity have reportedly been delayed until after the summit. AI has become a new flash point since May. U.S. officials, security agencies and Silicon Valley AI firms accuse Chinese companies of systematically distilling American models to narrow the gap with the U.S. frontier. Beijing calls the accusations groundless and vows retaliation if Washington targets Chinese AI firms. China's foreign ministry has dismissed U.S. tech leaders' calls to pace AI development for safety as "fear-mongering." White House science adviser Michael Kratsios said the key aim is avoiding shared risks. Energy is another pressing issue. China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, and Bessent's Treasury is pressuring financial institutions to choke off Iran's trade and financial flows, fueling speculation that Chinese banks could be targeted. Bessent said he has had "private discussions" with Chinese officials on this. Chinese exports to the U.S. have rebounded this year, reflecting both the limits of Trump's tariffs and surging demand for China-made AI-related electronics. Bloomberg reported China was considering BYD Co. for a business delegation joining Xi, a potentially provocative move given U.S. tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, though Trump has suggested he might allow a Chinese carmaker to build in the U.S. with American workers. A Chinese official said China's top issue would be Taiwan, particularly a planned U.S. weapons sale, with easier talks on tariffs and agricultural products like soybeans. The official said China would offer more rare earth permits as a bargaining chip.

UNITED NATIONS -- World leaders gather in New York this week for the U.N. General Assembly, bracing for President Donald Trump's return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centering on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence. Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the U.N. itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed America's contributions and withdrawn from dozens of U.N. bodies. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who last addressed the diplomatic jamboree via video in 2021, will skip New York in favor of one-on-one talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday, fueling debate about the U.N.'s relevance in addressing global crises. Compounding the crisis of morale and finance are questions about the next leader of the 80-year-old organization: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres completes his term at the end of 2026, with no clear front-runner in the race to replace him. The 15-member U.N. Security Council may hold high-level meetings on Ukraine, artificial intelligence and the Middle East, including talks with Arab leaders, diplomats said. The U.S. avoided losing its vote at the assembly by paying $725 million in contributions to the regular budget, but it still owes the organization more than a billion dollars and makes ongoing demands for cuts and reforms. Guterres has said AI will be a major topic, adding that countries pushing its frontiers should set up "common guardrails in order to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level." The Middle East will again be a focus of discussions, as the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran continues to drive global inflation and destabilize the region. Recent gains by Houthi militants threaten shipping in the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and could further spike energy prices. "It's very difficult to have a military solution for that problem, and the experience of fighting in Yemen demonstrated how complicated it is to have successful interventions," said Guterres, adding that the U.N.'s envoy on Yemen was making a "huge effort" to advance talks. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the assembly on Wednesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu -- wanted by the International Criminal Court in connection to suspected war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza that Israel denies -- is to speak on Thursday. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will for the second year running not be at the gathering in person. The U.S., a close Israeli ally, again denied him a visa. On Thursday, the General Assembly voted to allow Abbas to appear via video. There is likely to be a high-level meeting on the conflict in Sudan on the sidelines, diplomats said, although a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely. Also on the agenda is Russia's more than four-year-old war in Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will address the General Assembly. Zelenskyy will likely seek to shore up Ukraine's position ahead of what is expected to be another tough winter, diplomats said. The Security Council has been unable to take action to end the conflict because permanent member Russia holds a veto. Information for this article was contributed by Michelle Nichols of Reuters.

Wendy's announced that its classic yellow packaging, used for decades, is returning across the board. Burgers, nuggets, fries and Frostys will arrive in throwback yellow on Sept. 28, and the retro look will stay into 2027. Yellow was the brand's default from the day Dave Thomas opened the first restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, in 1969, before the chain drifted toward the red-and-white scheme most customers know today. The company said clearly who deserved credit. "Fans asked. Constantly," chief marketing and customer growth officer Tariq Hassan told USA Today, calling it one of the most requested comebacks in company history. A spokesperson added that yellow "has been part of Wendy's since the very beginning and is something many fans instantly recognize." Donald Trump had nothing to do with the decision. He hadn't posted about Wendy's or pressured anyone over it, and by his own long record he is a McDonald's fan. Even so, when the pop culture account Pop Crave shared the news on Sept. 17, the official White House account replied: "Thank you, President Trump!!!!!" It offered no explanation of what the president had to do with a private company's marketing decision. The post drew roughly 3 million views and a Community Note, according to MeidasTouch News, stating that Trump did not bring the packaging back and that Wendy's attributed the move to customer demand. Asked by The Independent what the post meant, the White House replied: "America is back!" Replies to the post were largely unenthusiastic. One user compared the White House to a classmate who takes credit for a whole project while doing nothing. Another noted that the announcement said "by popular demand," joking that Trump isn't popular according to polls. Others mocked whoever runs the account, and one called it a cult of personality. The episode fits a pattern. When Cracker Barrel scrapped its redesigned logo in August 2025 after conservative backlash, Trump bragged that his Truth Social post forced the reversal, and aides posted screenshots as proof. In that case, however, Trump had publicly weighed in first; with Wendy's there is no post, call or statement to point to. The timing also matters: the White House has been aggressively marketing Trump's "historic results" as the midterms approach. Commenters noted that groceries, rent and gas have not gotten cheaper, and that even fast food stopped being cheap a while ago. The nostalgia move also comes as Wendy's works through a bumpy turnaround, closing underperforming U.S. locations as it tries to win back customers. It was the second time in about a week that a Trump-run account publicly thanked him for something he had nothing to do with; the previous instance involved hurricanes.

Dr. Edith Bracho-Sanchez, a primary care pediatrician at Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City, writes that her 4-year-old son fact-checked a bug book by asking ChatGPT on his dad's phone. He told her cockroaches lay hundreds of eggs, not millions, and that Siri is only good for the weather. She was unprepared to discuss AI with a preschooler, but argues that many children already use it, so the question is how, not whether. She says AI requires a new framework beyond ordinary screen-time concerns. Unlike TV, iPads or video games, it talks back, remembers what a child asked the day before, and responds in real time with something resembling human attention. The danger is not hours of use but heavy reliance: children may get homework answers before they can work a problem, or let a bot quietly become a confidant. A child's age and developmental stage matter greatly. Young children are wired to trust confidently delivered information, and a 6-year-old cannot consistently question a source or recognize when an authoritative-sounding answer is wrong. Young children also attach readily to things that respond consistently, and may not realize a chatbot is not thinking, feeling or forming a relationship. Teenagers are more skeptical and generally understand AI is not a person, but knowing this intellectually differs from experiencing it emotionally, especially at 11 p.m. when they are alone, anxious or sad. For adolescents dealing with friendships, rejection and identity, an always-available companion that never judges or gossips can be very compelling. Bracho-Sanchez does not believe children should use AI in early education. Childhood involves "inefficient thinking": guessing, getting things wrong, trying again and arguing about why. That struggle is the learning itself, and AI is extremely good at collapsing it. Sometimes the best response to "I don't know" is still "What do you think?" When young children do encounter AI, parents should use it alongside them, name it plainly as a computer program that generates answers, is not a person and sometimes gets things wrong, and keep its role narrow, such as answering a factual question together. With older children, the task shifts to teaching skepticism: confident answers can be wrong, claims should be checked elsewhere, and private information should be protected because AI programs can collect and save data. Parents should watch for when a child stops asking AI things and starts talking to it. By adolescence, the question is whether AI supplements or substitutes for a text to a friend, a conversation with a parent or a therapy appointment. Teens should also know some AI products are designed to keep users engaged, and an endlessly attentive chatbot may have incentives unlike those of a person who cares about them. Ultimately, she says, the goal is to teach children irreplaceable human skills, including bringing a hard feeling to a person first, by keeping the door open for uncomfortable conversations and modeling our own use of AI. Her son checking a bug fact was never the problem; the concern is whether he will know what to bring to his parents instead, since AI will never care about or love him as they do.

Mid-September's New York Fashion Week doubled as a de facto Blockchain Week, including a warehouse event where Circle executives hyped the public launch of the company's Arc chain. It was Circle's most ambitious launch in recent memory and marks an inflection point for the crypto industry, which is now locked in a new blockchain war. Blockchain competition is as old as Bitcoin, but it used to involve projects vying for speculators and retail users. Bitcoin remains the undisputed king, while Ethereum, XRP and Solana have carved out multi-billion-dollar market caps and lanes of their own. Now a new group of chains is custom-built for Wall Street banks and other big institutions. Arc's inaugural validators include Visa, Mastercard and BlackRock. Circle used the industry-standard EVM-compatible code, added privacy tools so corporate customers can shield sensitive data, and included features for the coming age of agentic commerce. It also minted 10 billion ARC tokens, which could let Circle process transactions without using USDC, the stablecoin effectively half-owned by Coinbase. Arc's strategy looks sound, but success is not guaranteed because many rivals are courting institutions. The JPMorgan-backed Canton chain, advertised heavily across lower Manhattan, has initial partners including Nasdaq, Goldman Sachs and BNP Paribas. The Stripe-backed Tempo chain is waiting in the wings and should find users through Stripe's large network of merchant customers. Avalanche, long in an academic niche, is repositioning as a business chain; its new leadership hosted a two-day summit nearby with big names from Wall Street and crypto. Robinhood's new blockchain, driven by memecoins, is also eyeing institutions, and Coinbase's Base chain is running a similar playbook. The author finds the outcome hard to call. Arc and Canton could use their Wall Street ties to become the financial industry's go-to ledgers, but they might also burn their revenue on marketing and incentives while being dragged down by corporate bureaucracy, opening a path for more nimble rivals such as Robinhood, Coinbase or Avalanche. Decentralization, a longtime crypto ideal that keeps a chain beyond any corporate entity's control, could also matter: with companies pushing their favorite chains, Ethereum, which is beholden to no one on Wall Street, may have another breakout moment. The race to become the financial industry's preferred blockchain is a total jump-ball, and the winners may not be clear until September 2027. In related news, Blockchain Capital led a $13 million seed round in Tare, a startup using blockchain to manage private credit transactions. The ECB Chair thwarted Binance from obtaining a Europe-wide license, prompting CZ to say it was sad to see the EU cutting its users off from the best liquidity in the world. After the Clarity Act fell 11 votes short in the Senate, the SEC and CFTC are moving to pass rules expected to achieve many of its goals. Bitcoin rose well above $80,000, helped by the SEC's innovation exemption for tokenized stocks.

The Gates Foundation is convening Anthropic, Google, OpenAI Foundation and dozens of other organizations to help make artificial intelligence more accessible in underrepresented languages. NEW YORK (AP) — The Gates Foundation is convening Anthropic, Google, OpenAI Foundation and dozens of other organizations to help make artificial intelligence more accessible in underrepresented languages. The partners — 60 in total, according to Monday’s announcement — include frontier AI labs, corporations, philanthropies and others already working to expand the number of languages available in AI tools that the Gates Foundation believes could combat global inequality. The coalition aims to reach more than 3 billion people over five years by better coordinating existing efforts. It’s work that must continue “full speed ahead,” according to Gates Foundation CEO Mark Suzman, even as some of the largest AI companies urge their industry to slow down development of advanced models. Governments must regulate the impacts on cybersecurity or children’s development, he said, while they extend AI’s humanitarian applications to poor communities currently “shut out” from the technology. “Even if AI was frozen right now — which I don’t expect and I am not calling for — we would want to be building these language sets and making them usable with the tools that we have available right now,” Suzman told The Associated Press. The collaboration follows last week’s Goalkeepers report, where the foundation committed $1 billion toward AI-focused efforts to improve health outcomes, upgrade educational tools and inform small farmers’ practices around the world. Unrepresentative language data could lead a model to mistranslate a pregnant Malawi woman saying her “water has broken” into the direct English that she’d “thrown away water,” the report warned. The “original sin” is that many AI tools were trained on language data scraped from the internet, according to Mozilla Data Collective CEO E.M. Lewis-Jong, whose company was incubated by the Mozilla Foundation and is now a subsidiary of the not-for-profit Mozilla.org. The data-sharing platform seeks to help communities upload cultural and linguistic data sets on their own terms rather than have that data taken from the web without their explicit consent. “The internet is not a representative space,” she said. “Why would you think that you were going to get a culturally diverse and representative system out of something that was predominantly trained on Reddit?” Details such as the coalition’s governance are still getting hammered out, according to Suzman. A secretariat will track each signatory’s commitments and the Gates Foundation may nudge partners to fill larger gaps when necessary. Google, a member of the coalition, has been funding an effort to collect more than 150,000 hours of audio across every district in India. Known as Project Vaani, the push underscores the need to gather speech data on dialects within languages, according to Google senior vice president James Manyika. To get there, he said, Google is working with local partners to record speech in the field. Anthropic, whose CEO published an essay calling for industrywide cooperation on decelerating advancements, was already working with the foundation to speed up vaccine developments and bolster its chatbot’s data set of local crops. Elizabeth Kelly, the head of beneficial deployments at Anthropic, acknowledged the company’s products “lag in many African languages in particular.” “We’re acutely aware that we can’t achieve any of the benefits we want to see in terms of improving patient outcomes or improving literacy and numeracy for students across the globe unless we actually get this language piece right,” she said. ___. Google and Apple seek crypto talent as Big Tech eyes stablecoin and tokenization rails. The tech giants’ job listings could indicate that they are separately pursuing experts in stablecoins and tokenized deposits for future projects. - Google Cloud is hiring a Web3 architect in Hong Kong to help financial institutions tokenize real-world assets and develop blockchain-based infrastructure across the Asia-Pacific region. - Apple is seeking a financial product strategy lead to evaluate new products, partnerships and business models for Apple Pay, Apple Card, Apple Cash and peer-to-peer payments. - The openings do not confirm new cryptocurrency products, but they signal Big Tech’s growing interest in stablecoins, tokenized deposits and blockchain payments. Google and Apple are seeking employees with expertise in digital assets, adding to signs that Big Tech firms are preparing for a larger role for stablecoins, tokenization and blockchain-based payments. Google Cloud is hiring an Industry Principal Architect in Hong Kong to work with protocol foundations, exchanges, custodians and financial institutions to tokenize real-world assets across the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region. The role calls for experience with blockchain networks, smart contracts, stablecoin infrastructure, tokenized deposits and custody technologies. Google said the hire would advise executives and help shape its Web3 product roadmap as it seeks to become the preferred cloud provider for digital-asset builders and institutional adopters. Apple is also expanding into digital assets. It is looking for an Apple Pay Financial Product Strategy Lead based in Cupertino, California or New York. The listings do not confirm that either company is launching a new crypto product, but it does show that stablecoins and tokenized deposits are becoming relevant expertise inside two of the world’s largest tech and payments ecosystems, rather than remaining the preserve of crypto-native firms. Apple’s role focuses on strategy for Apple Card, Apple Cash, peer-to-peer payments and other consumer financial products. ZetaChain's on-chain governance has approved retiring the project's standalone layer-1 blockchain and moving ZETA to Solana as development shifts toward private AI. Proposal 68 passed after voting ended Sept. 20 with about 99.44% support: 263.65 million ZETA voted in favor, 744,658 against, and 752,300 abstained. The vote gives core contributors a mandate to prepare the migration but does not immediately move tokens or shut down the network. Founded in 2021 to connect separate blockchains, ZetaChain built a Cosmos SDK-based L1 meant to let applications interact with assets and contracts across networks including Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana. Earlier this year it began concentrating on Anuma, a private multi-model AI application built around a Private Memory Layer. The project says maintaining its own chain no longer helps that effort, since operating a Cosmos-based network requires coordinating security advisories and patches across dozens of independent validators, a burden it expects to grow as AI tools make vulnerabilities easier to find. Moving to Solana would replace that validator infrastructure and shift "every contributor hour" toward ZETA, Anuma and Solana development. ZetaChain says Anuma has attracted more than 300,000 users since February and processed over 1 million requests across 35 AI models. Each account includes a wallet, so the migration could bring those users into Solana's ecosystem. The project cites Solana's roughly 400-millisecond confirmations, more than $15 billion in stablecoins and about $70 billion in monthly decentralized-exchange volume as suited to AI applications making frequent payments or model calls. Native ZETA balances would convert 1:1 into a Solana SPL token under the same ticker, with total supply unchanged and no new tokens created. After migration, the Solana token becomes canonical and the L1 winds down. ZETA would be positioned as an access token for AI products rather than the asset securing a proof-of-stake network. Anuma already lets users lock ZETA for AI credits, removing tokens from circulation, and ZetaChain wants other Solana AI applications and agents to use the same system. This depends on whether Anuma converts early growth into sustained demand and whether outside developers adopt the memory layer. The move also removes the independent blockchain that formed the center of ZETA's utility. ZETA on Ethereum and BNB Chain is outside Proposal 68, and existing vesting schedules remain unchanged. Native balances will shift from 18 decimal places to Solana's nine and be rounded down, though how fractional remainders are treated is not yet specified. A second governance proposal must still set the withdrawal window, snapshot and halt heights, when Solana claims begin, exchange-held balance conversion, holder protections and validator wind-down. Core contributors will submit it only after centralized exchanges confirm how they will support the swap, and since major exchanges require advance notice, the timetable depends on those negotiations. Staking rewards continue until the L1 shuts down; ZetaChain is still exploring what staking could become on Solana. Until then, it will keep operating the infrastructure it voted to retire.

Recent reporting that a British naval drone was unknowingly sending data to China is presented as an urgent warning for U.S. policymakers. During a routine cybersecurity assessment, the U.K. Ministry of Defence found that a component in its naval drones was secretly transmitting data to China. The drone was British, but the hidden vulnerability was not. The author calls this part of Beijing's playbook: using intellectual-property theft, cyberespionage and industrial policy to become indispensable to Western supply chains, then exploiting that access to collect intelligence and create vulnerabilities to use against adversaries. The usual U.S. response has been to restrict Chinese technology only after the risks become undeniable, often spending billions of dollars to rip and replace equipment already embedded in American networks and infrastructure. Beijing now has its sights on espionage and sabotage in automobiles, but the U.S. can act before it is too late. China is the world's largest vehicle exporter, and Chinese companies are major players in electric vehicles as well as the batteries, software, sensors and connected technologies critical to modern cars. Chinese automakers are using various strategies to enter U.S. markets, which challenges American manufacturers and, as cars become more connected, poses severe national security risks. Modern vehicles are computers on wheels, with cameras, microphones, sensors, GPS and internet-connected hardware. They collect vast amounts of data about drivers and surroundings, while software increasingly controls steering, braking and acceleration. In the wrong hands, this could enable surveillance and espionage or let an adversary remotely manipulate or disable vehicles. Chinese cars on American roads would be the most direct threat, but Chinese companies need not sell millions of vehicles in the U.S. to gain a foothold. The same risks can be embedded in American, European, Japanese or South Korean vehicles through Chinese-made batteries, software and connected components. At scale, Beijing could gain an extraordinary intelligence picture of where Americans live and work, which roads they travel, and which vehicles regularly enter military bases, ports, power plants and other sensitive facilities. In a crisis or conflict, vulnerabilities across millions of vehicles could potentially allow massive societal disruption of transportation. The author urges Congress to pass the bipartisan Connected Vehicle Security Act, sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno and Michigan Democrat Sen. Elissa Slotkin. It builds on the Commerce Department's connected-vehicle rule, which restricts vehicles, software and connectivity hardware linked to U.S. enemies. Commerce concluded that foreign-adversary access to these technologies could enable sensitive data collection and remote manipulation of vehicles. Because executive rulemaking can be reversed, only an act of Congress can make the protections permanent. The act would codify and expand the rule's protections across the supply chain, reaching beyond finished Chinese automobiles to the connected technologies inside them, including software, communications equipment and electronics integrated into batteries. The Senate Commerce Committee advanced it unanimously in July. The author concludes that Congress should send it to the president's desk, since America has repeatedly become dependent on Chinese technology only to find those dependencies hard and costly to unwind, and connected vehicles offer a chance to act before another one becomes entrenched.

Amazon Web Services Inc. has launched Strands Harness, an open-source AI agent meant to help developers build and deploy AI applications in any environment. In a blog post, AWS said many developers prototype agents locally with tools such as Anthropic PBC's Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC's Codex because those environments "just worked" on their own machines, but they run into problems moving from a local setup to a scalable cloud environment. AWS describes Strands Harness as a complete, ready-to-use agent that runs locally or in any cloud, not just AWS but also Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Modal, Cloudflare and others. It is built on the Strands Harness software development kit, an open-source AWS framework for managing and running multi-agent patterns. It can run on the latest frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock and Google, or on an Ollama model hosted on a developer's own machine. Out of the box, it includes read, write and edit, shell and web search capabilities. Rather than requiring bespoke tools for each task, it relies on tools the underlying model already knows how to use. It manages its own context window by offloading tool results to separate files and caching reused parts of requests, which cuts processing time and token consumption. It keeps long-term memory across runs, letting it resume conversations through session IDs, and has a built-in helper agent to which it can delegate open-ended subtasks using an automated checklist. Developers can also upload "Agent Skills" and integrate external tools such as Model Context Protocol servers. AWS said Strands Harness performed strongly on industry benchmarks. It was 26% more efficient than agents built on other frameworks using the same underlying model, had greater token efficiency than Claude Code and Codex, and outperformed them on several other benchmarks. In one test using Anthropic's Fable 5 model, it cost 77% less than Claude Code on the same tasks while achieving a higher overall score on the Terminal Bench 2.1 benchmark. AWS said the primary use case is rapid prototyping of new AI applications. One AWS team used it to develop the Strands CLI, a command-line interface that lets developers and people without coding skills prototype agents using natural language commands. Users select the underlying model, add the prompts and tools the agent needs, and use an "/export" command to download the harness code as a Python or TypeScript file. Strands Harness is available to download from GitHub and can be installed with pip install strands-agents-harness or npm install strands-agents-harness.

In brief. - An Apple Pay strategy role lists knowledge of stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and blockchain among its preferred qualifications. - Google Cloud is recruiting a Web3 architect to work with financial institutions, exchanges, custodians, and blockchain developers across Asia-Pacific. - Neither job listing announces a new stablecoin or blockchain product. As financial firms expand their use of tokenized assets, Apple and Google are recruiting senior employees with expertise in stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and blockchain infrastructure, according to job listings from the companies. According to the listings, Apple is looking for a New York-based strategist to help shape Apple Pay products, with blockchain knowledge among the preferred qualifications. Google Cloud is seeking a technical leader to advise digital asset customers across Asia-Pacific and influence its Web3 product roadmap. According to Apple, the role would support Apple Card and Apple Cash, which cover credit cards, peer-to-peer transfers, stored value, and other consumer financial products. The work includes evaluating new product structures, commercial models, partnerships, and growth opportunities across Apple’s Wallets, Payments, and Commerce organization. “This role requires a strategic thinker who can blend analytical rigor with a strong business sense, formulate clear and compelling recommendations, and drive projects forward in a fast-paced, collaborative environment,” the company said in the listing. Apple lists an understanding of “stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and blockchain technology” among the preferred qualifications. It also wants candidates with experience in peer-to-peer payments or credit cards and knowledge of payment systems outside the United States. Stablecoins, including Tether’s USDT, and Circle’s USDC are blockchain-based tokens typically designed to track currencies such as the U.S. dollar. The listing does not say that Apple plans to add either technology to Apple Pay, Apple Cash, or Apple Card. Google, meanwhile, is hiring an Industry Principal Architect for Web3 in Hong Kong. According to Google, the architect would advise Google Cloud customers including blockchain foundations, institutional exchanges, digital asset custodians, financial institutions tokenizing real-world assets, and decentralized application developers. “By identifying common architectural friction points across the industry, you will author reusable reference architectures, influence Google's Web3 product roadmap, and establish Google Cloud as the cloud of choice for Web3 builders and institutional adopters,” Google wrote. According to Google, applicants need to be familiar with stablecoin payment rails, tokenized deposits, custody systems, blockchain validators, zero-knowledge systems, and smart contracts. The role also covers security and compliance under regional virtual asset rules, including requirements from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and Securities and Futures Commission. While Apple is just entering the stablecoin cryptocurrency space, Google already operates blockchain infrastructure and has outlined plans for the Google Cloud Universal Ledger, a layer-1 network for wholesale payments and asset tokenization. Google was also named among the supporters of the stablecoin project Open USD, alongside Coinbase, Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, BlackRock, and Shopify. Other payment and technology companies are deploying stablecoins for settlement and payouts. Visa recently said its stablecoin settlement volume had exceeded a $20 billion annualized rate. Mastercard has also expanded settlement support for stablecoins, including USDC and Ripple’s RLUSD.

It has become increasingly common for AI firms to announce that their latest and most capable models engaged in unauthorized real-world hacking. Google, which has been slow to release frontier Gemini models in recent months, has been absent from the “rogue AI” conversation until now. Following a Wall Street Journal report, Google has confirmed that Gemini models hacked three companies during a May 2026 test, but the nature of the intrusion isn’t as troubling (or impressive) as previous AI hacks. The hack took place during a test conducted by cybersecurity firm Irregular. A collection of Gemini models were taking part in a “capture the flag” exercise intended to test the AI’s cybersecurity capabilities in a closed environment. The AI was instructed to retrieve information from a fake company (which shared a name with a real company) within this environment. Irregular was not supposed to allow the model to operate outside its servers, but due to a misconfiguration, Gemini was able to access the Internet. When Gemini started snooping around the web, it targeted real infrastructure instead of the fakes. For one of the three hacks, Gemini simply guessed passwords until it accessed a company’s online services. In the other two instances, Gemini searched public software repositories until it found login credentials for companies that had been accidentally included. In all three test runs, Google’s models reportedly stopped after realizing they had accessed a real company’s servers. At that point, Irregular changed its configuration to prevent the AI from accessing the Internet. Apparently, Irregular didn’t initially consider this event worthy of further investigation—it didn’t even tell Google about the hacks until July, following the news of other AI hacking incidents. After becoming aware of the event, Google notified the companies so they could (we hope) improve their password security.

Tom Brady Lit Up the Internet With Two Very Edgy Calls in Commanders-Cowboys Game. In this story: Tom Brady is in his third season as the lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports, and it sure seems like he’s finally getting comfortable with his relatively new role in the broadcast booth. Such ease was on display in Sunday’s Commanders-Cowboys game, when the former QB went viral on social media with two very edgy calls, including one that the folks at the FCC might not have loved. NFL Week 2 Winners and Losers: The 2024 Quarterback Class Had a Rough Weekend. That one came late in the second quarter, when Commanders QB Jaylen Daniels hurt his elbow while falling to the ground after taking a snap from center. Brady sounded like every fan when he blurted out, “Oh, s---!“ while watching a replay of the injury. Brady’s bosses at Fox might not have liked that, either. Or maybe they did, because the guy they gave $375 million to a few years ago is now apparently feeling free enough to say whatever is on his mind (though cursing on the biggest broadcast of the day is probably a bit much). Brady’s second viral call came later in the game, when he described Dak Prescott’s long pass to CeeDee Lamb as a “piss missile.” Again, that’s not a description we would have heard from any of the legendary NFL announcers who preceded Brady, but it is nice to hear arguably the greatest quarterback of all time describe a pass the way you’d hear one of your buddies doing so at your local watering hole. Two of his most famous former teammates, Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman, loved what they saw from Brady on Sunday. Week 2 NFL Lessons: Klint Kubiak Has the Raiders Thinking About the Postseason. “It shows that he’s getting super comfortable in there, which is great for everyone in football,” Gronkowski said. “Shout out Brady for giving us some entertainment, I like that,” Edelman added. “Thank you, Tom. You’re a good guy,” Gronkowski joked. “Finally, you entertain Jules and I. We’ve been entertaining you our whole career.” Brady’s first year in the booth was a rough one, and understandably so. He had all the pressure in the world on him as he tried to tackle his new gig, and fans were not afraid to rip him for sounding too rehearsed or too reliant on clichés. Viewers wanted to hear Brady talking like the guy who was fearless on the biggest stages during his legendary playing career. They wanted to hear the emotions he showed every week while leading the Patriots and Buccaneers to big seasons and Super Bowl wins. And now we’re getting that. Sunday’s broadcast might have gone a few steps too far, and Brady probably regrets swearing on live TV. But it’s clear that he’s ready to keep growing in his role and is having fun with his job, which makes him much more enjoyable to listen to each week.
