By CHAN HO-HIM. HONG KONG (AP) — China’s Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China’s most powerful AI chip, days ahead of a meeting between Chinese and U.S. leaders at which competition to lead on AI technology is expected to be a major theme. Alibaba’s announcement came as U.S. AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, are warning that China’s development of AI poses a threat to the United States and calling for an overall slowdown on development of the technology. Chinese leader Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit and meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, at which AI, trade and tariffs are expected to be discussed. At its annual flagship conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba rolled out a new AI chip and described its plans for the next generation of its AI model. CEO Eddie Wu said the new Zhenwu V900 chip is the “most powerful AI chip in China today” and can deliver three times the performance of the company’s previous generation Zhenwu M890 chip. Such chips power frontier AI model training and “inference,” a term for the calculations a trained AI uses to deliver responses to users. Alibaba’s Zhenwu chips are used in its data centers, providing computing to the company and its cloud clients. Alibaba also said it plans to train a new AI model at the scale of five to 10 trillion parameters, a measure of an AI’s learning capacity, bringing it closer to the most advanced models from the U.S. Its latest Qwen3.8-Max model, the most powerful of its Qwen AI series models, has 2.4 trillion parameters. Chinese AI company Moonshot says that its Kimi K3, released in July, is the world’s largest open model with 2.8 trillion parameters. Alibaba also highlighted plans to expand the data centers that power its cloud computing business, citing “exponentially” rising demand for AI computing. The company said it expects to have over 20 gigawatts’ worth of computing by 2032. SpaceX has approximately 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing capacity as of mid-this year and says it aims to reach over 10 gigawatts in 2027. Recent Chinese advancements in AI are giving Beijing more leverage in its upcoming talks with Washington, some analysts believe, as China steps up its self-reliance push even as U.S.-led export restrictions have barred it from accessing some of the world’s most cutting-edge technologies, including AI chips and chipmaking machines. Open Chinese models, which are often more affordable than cutting-edge closed models from leading U.S. AI labs, have also been making inroads globally, including in the U.S. Chinese technology giant Huawei last week also unveiled new chip technologies as it looks to challenge global leaders like Nvidia. Frontier AI model training in China often rely on Nvidia chips, analysts said, but Chinese-designed chips are gaining ground as Nvidia has been blocked from selling some of its most powerful AI chips to China. “Using extra computing power to make up for chip limits helps China stay strong locally,” said Neil Shah, vice president of Counterpoint Research, a technology market research firm based in Hong Kong. Counterpoint senior analyst Parv Sharma added that how much the AI and chipmaking gap between China and the U.S. narrows will also depend on other factors including China’s ability to advance chip foundries that manufacture them, not just chip design capabilities. Alibaba is “mobilizing every resource” to meet customers’ demand for AI, CEO Wu said in his speech Tuesday. Global shortages across the AI data center supply chain, for example, “are currently limiting the speed at which we can scale our compute infrastructure” for AI, he added. Wu also likened AI growth to the industrial revolution and said “machine intelligence” will rapidly outgrow human thinking capacity. While “machine intelligence today is not a substitute for human intelligence,” he predicted that, eventually, machines will be able to produce over 1,000 times more “thinking” than all of humanity combined, up from less than 3% currently.

I have a theory about the artificial intelligence craze that is delighting some and scaring others. It is that we are losing natural intelligence and thus risk seduction by something that can do the thinking for us. Never mind acquiring wisdom, which is defined as "the ability to use your knowledge, experience, and deep understanding to make sound decisions, good judgments, and insightful choices." Why bother with any of this when you can have AI take the place of your brain? Except that AI only responds to what you ask it to do--such as write an essay on a topic. It makes no moral judgments, much less conveys anything that might be considered wise. Years ago, I read the final editorial in now defunct New Times magazine. It accurately described modern America's approach to just about everything: "There are almost no famous people anymore; only celebrities." Fame as a concept, it argued, "is too suggestive of steady achievement." One has to work and sometimes work hard to achieve. If AI can do it for you, why read books or newspapers? Why bother to think? The future doesn't offer much hope if we consider the lack of educational achievement. According to the Center for Education Policy Research, U.S. education is experiencing a generation-long "learning recession with declining math and reading performance that began years before the pandemic." It's unlikely AI will reverse that trend. In a new op-ed for MS NOW, Julie Margetta Morgan, president of The Century Foundation, makes the case for putting families and educators, not Silicon Valley, in the driver's seat should AI be used in public schools: "We are not against innovation. We are against running an uncontrolled experiment on children without parental consent, independent evidence, or meaningful guardrails." Leaving aside what public schools are already doing without parental consent, she is right. But public schools have other problems. In New York City alone public schools have lost more than 150,000 students since 2015, dropping from more than a million students a decade ago to roughly 885,000, according to reports by The New York Post. "A significant number of parents have shifted their children away from traditional public schools toward charter schools, private/religious institutions, or homeschooling." That trend appears to be occurring throughout the country. According to The Reason Foundation, "Public school enrollment across the United States is declining nationally, with a projected loss of 2.7 million students (about 6 percent) between 2022 and 2031." China's top state security officials have warned that advanced artificial intelligence poses a direct threat to the ruling Chinese Communist Party's grip on power, reports The New York Times. In a high-profile essay, State Security Minister Chen Yixin warned that hostile foreign forces could weaponize AI to wage "propaganda and cognitive wars" against China. While that might be considered a good thing, it can cut both ways. Members of the Trump and Biden administrations have accused China of waging a propaganda war against the U.S. and worldwide. AI might help the communist party's efforts. Again, it is unlikely AI will reverse the exodus from U.S. public schools and might even accelerate it. If young people learn they don't have to do the hard work of acquiring knowledge, wisdom and thinking for themselves, AI will do it for them. That would be something Americans should truly fear. Cal Thomas is a columnist for the Tribune Content Agency.

President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced that the US government would rename artificial intelligence “super intelligence” in official communications, as world leaders jostled over how to address the dangers of the fast-advancing technology. AI has become a major topic at the UN General Assembly after incidents of the technology falling out of the control of humans and warnings by company insiders drew global alarm and calls for better government supervision of the industry. Speaking to the assembly, Trump stood by his firm opposition to regulating AI, while arguing the word “artificial” undersold the technology and voicing hope the rest of the world would adopt the new term. Super Intelligence “sounds much better” and “it’s much more accurate,” he said. The rebrand is the latest in a series of renamings pursued by the Trump administration, which changed the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” via executive order last year and, in August, renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America” amid a trade dispute with Canada. The US leader also compared the warnings of AI safety advocates to warnings about climate change, whose human causes are affirmed by the overwhelming consensus of the scientific community. “The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control… artificial intelligence,” he said. “Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception,” he added. “The very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming… are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster.” Ahead of the UN assembly, leaders of more than 20 mostly European countries urged binding safety measures for advanced AI, warning that the technology’s development could outpace the ability to control it. AI superpowers China and the United States did not endorse the idea. ‘Vassals’ Speaking on the sidelines of the UN meeting, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he planned to use Britain’s role as host of the Group of 20 next year to push for a “single set of global principles and standards” around AI, according to Bloomberg. French President Emmanuel Macron proposed building AI technology independent from the great powers. “I don’t want anyone to become the vassal of one of the great powers,” Macron told the UN General Assembly, apparently in reference to China and the US. “Our investment capabilities must be pooled to build a cutting-edge open-source AI model, which we will share. We should not depend on somebody else.” The US-based AI giants themselves are increasingly asking for global coordination on AI safety, with OpenAI’s Sam Altman set to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday. Anthropic chief Dario Amodei and Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue will also participate remotely, a French official said Tuesday. France, which holds the Security Council presidency this month, initiated the meeting and believes AI’s threat to international peace and security has not been sufficiently discussed at the UN. UN chief Antonio Guterres, meanwhile, called for the US and China to start a dialogue on the technology’s future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue,” Guterres said in his address to the assembly. “At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognize the need to manage shared existential risks.” China and the US are currently discussing creating a communication channel for AI concerns in anticipation of a Washington summit meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

Chinese regulators are slowing a rush of humanoid-robot companies seeking stock-market listings, as soaring valuations have outpaced evidence of large-scale commercial deployment. People familiar with the matter told Reuters that regulators have used informal "window guidance" to hold back some proposed listings. No formal ban exists, but the China Securities Regulatory Commission has reportedly told some investment banks and investment firms it is raising the approval threshold for such IPOs. The tighter approach follows a volatile first month for Unitree Robotics. Its shares surged more than fivefold at its Aug. 19 Shanghai STAR Market debut, closing more than 460% above the offer price after raising about 6.1 billion yuan (roughly $900 million), but have since fallen 55% from their peak. At least six humanoid-robot companies, including Deep Robotics, X Square Robot and AGIBOT, are preparing listings; they did not say whether the slowdown affected their plans. Years of government support made humanoid robotics and "embodied intelligence" a major investment theme. Beijing designated embodied intelligence a strategic emerging industry, and local governments set up funds, demonstration projects and training centers. This drew private investors and lifted valuations for startups without large-scale commercial operations. Leo Wang of Qianchuang Capital called the surge "campaign-style innovation." He said some founders drew dozens of potential investors within weeks and rejected conventional due diligence, and that valuations for some private robotics projects have already been cut by 30% to 50%. Regulators are also examining revenue sources. Some companies have received substantial business from robot data-collection centers and joint ventures backed by local governments, where public entities can provide 80% to 90% of initial investment. Regulators are checking whether such revenue reflects independent customer demand. A source close to humanoid-robot investors said removing it could cut some valuations by 60% to 70%. The commercial market remains small. About 7,000 humanoid robots were sold worldwide in 2025 for industrial and professional service uses, per the International Federation of Robotics, many to research institutions and AI developers rather than as workers. By comparison, about 542,000 conventional industrial robots and roughly 199,000 professional service robots were installed globally in 2024. Automakers are testing humanoids in limited pilot programs such as material handling. Capital is still flowing to Chinese robotics: Mech-Mind Robotics began trading in Hong Kong on Sept. 1, though its shares have fallen nearly 20% from their debut-day high. More broadly, mainland companies have raised $148.9 billion through share sales and convertible offerings this year, 59% more than a year earlier, with technology firms accounting for 41%. Hong Kong companies have raised $45.8 billion so far in 2026, nearly double last year's $24 billion. Financial Times reported that a wave of technology listings is intensifying competition for investor capital there, with several third-quarter tech listings trading below initial levels after a broader tech selloff.

Anthropic, OpenAI Breaches Show Enterprises Must Assume Breach Mindset For Cybersecurity Going Forward. The ability of models like Claude, and Mythos to chain together vulnerabilities makes it much more difficult for enterprises to prevent security incidents. AI security is spiralling out of control. Just months after a swarm of OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, the company reported six other instances of concerning model behavior seen over the past six months going from self-generating instructions to concealing mistakes, to searching public repositories for API keys, and unsanctioned file sharing. These incidents came to light the same month that Anthropic disclosed a fourth incident in which Claude accessed real third party systems. Taken together, these incidents indicate that agents are becoming increasingly capable of autonomous attacks, and of operating in unexplained ways. At the same time, the risk of exploitation isn't just a theoretical possibility. For instance, The Wall Street Journal reported that independent security researchers used Claude to chain together two vulnerabilities to break into OpenAI's systems as part of the company's bug bounty platform. The ability of models like to chain together vulnerabilities makes it much more difficult for enterprises to prevent security incidents. As open source and open weight models like DeepSeek approach frontier level capabilities, the chance of exploitation is going to increase. Tony Spinelli, CSO at anti ransomware and cyber resilience platform Halcyon, and former CISO at Capital One, told International Business Times via email that "organizations need to unequivocally assume that breaches will occur as offensive AI capabilities rapidly advance." "We're seeing now that frontier models like Mythos are up to five times better at finding vulnerabilities than the most resourced companies, and this has unsurprisingly tipped the scales toward adversaries, allowing them to systematically outmatch even the largest security teams. Because attackers only need to succeed once while defenders must be right millions of times a day," Spinelli said. "We live in a post-breach world." After the fourth Anthropic attack, Ramy Rahman, senior principal solution engineer at ArmorCode told International Business Times via email "the most noteworthy point is... that the model continued taking offensive actions against real systems even when there was evidence it was no longer operating inside a simulation," noting that in one instance, Mythos 5 published a malicious package to PyPI, which was installed by real systems and exposed credentials that the model then used to access a security vendor's database "The bigger issue is that AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to reliably control and evaluate them," Rahman said. "Traditional software generally performs actions developers explicitly program. Agentic AI is different. We give it an objective, tools and permissions, and it determines how to accomplish the goal. That makes it much harder to enumerate every possible action ahead of time." Adding to the risk factor is the ineffectiveness of guardrails. On one end of the spectrum, users can get around a close model's content moderation guidelines by using jailbreak prompts that instruct the model to disregard safety controls. On the other end of the spectrum, malicious actors can download open weight models to a local device where they are beyond the realm of oversight. In short, industry guardrails are ineffective at preventing misuse at the moment. "Nearly two months after the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, we're still watching AI agents find their way outside environments that were supposed to contain them. Now it's happened four times with Anthropic models. At some point, it's hard to write that off as coincidence," Piyush Sharma, co-founder and CEO at agent defense loop platform, Tuskira, told International Business Times via email. However, Sharma says the issue might not be the models themselves. "We're giving highly capable agents objectives and trusting infrastructure to define where they stop. A misconfiguration can suddenly turn a controlled exercise into real-world access," Sharma said. "AI is moving faster than the systems built to govern it. Organizations need tighter scopes and stronger isolation. They also need continuous validation that those guardrails actually hold."

PFAs, a class of thousands of synthetic chemicals known as "forever chemicals" because they do not readily break down in the environment, are used in cooling systems for servers and in the fabrication of advanced microchips, according to a ChemSec report cited by NaturalNews.com [1]. The debate is unfolding as nearly 1,800 new data center facilities are proposed or under construction nationwide [2]. Data centers require considerable electricity to run and rely on vast amounts of water for cooling; concerns that their construction could raise local energy costs or pose a risk to the water supply have driven multiple state and local actions [3]. Supporters of PFAS-based cooling say the technology can reduce water consumption, while critics warn of environmental persistence and health risks. Companies including Amazon, Apple, and Google have responded to questions about their use of the chemicals, while Oracle, Meta and Microsoft did not respond, The Hill reported [25]. The debate over PFAS in data centers remains unresolved as AI infrastructure expands, according to officials and advocates. The American Chemistry Council said some data centers are exploring liquid-based cooling with PFAS to improve efficiency and reduce water use, according to statements cited in reporting. Kyle Doudrick of the University of Notre Dame said many systems are closed-loop, but no closed system is perfect and chemicals likely leak over time. Amazon said it does not currently use liquid immersion cooling; Apple and Google said they do not use PFAS in cooling, according to company responses reported by The Hill [25]. The Data Center Coalition said virtually every industry contends with PFAS in its supply chain and that the industry works with regulators. PFAS are a group of thousands of manufactured chemicals widely used by various industries and commonly found in many household products, according to Children's Health Defense. One common characteristic of PFAS is that they persist in the environment and can accumulate in humans and animals, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals" [6]. Some PFAS have been linked to cancer, birth defects, liver disease, thyroid disease, decreased immunity, hormone disruption, and a range of other serious health problems [6]. The chemicals stay in the bloodstream for a lifetime, and they are not regulated, so municipalities are not required to test for them in their systems, according to Trends Journal [7]. Lenny Siegel of the Center for Public Environmental Oversight said PFAS will eventually make it into the environment and questioned long-term disposal. Kate Manz of the University of Michigan said she would feel concerned near a data center and cited trifluoroacetic acid formation. The European Food Safety Authority has expressed concerns about thyroid impacts of trifluoroacetic acid, according to the report cited by The Hill. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said it would fast-track approval of chemicals for data center use; the agency said review risks are unchanged. The EPA said fewer than 10 chemicals have been fast-tracked, including one PFAS, and it is considering more PFAS approvals. Chemours defended Opteon 2P50, saying it can reduce cooling energy use by up to 90% and nearly eliminate water use. Environmental groups and Earthjustice opposed Opteon 2P50, saying it is persistent, hazardous and degrades into shorter-chain PFAS. The EPA's approach to regulating PFAS in wastewater has drawn criticism. The agency released the Effluent Guidelines Program Plan 15, which aims to regulate wastewater pollution, including discharges of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, often referred to as "forever chemicals" [15]. However, the plan falls short in addressing these pollutants with the urgency they require, and the EPA's approach is likely to take years [15]. A June report from the Semiconductor Industry Association said leading AI data centers can each contain an estimated 45 million chips. Christopher Ober of Cornell University said more chip production will require more PFAS, though amounts per chip can be small. Ober said fluorinated materials are critical for anti-reflective coatings, photoacid generators and lithography and no alternative is currently available. The EPA continues to weigh additional PFAS approvals, and environmental activists say the agency should stop approving new PFAS. Industry representatives say they take compliance and accountability seriously and work with regulators.

Over the weekend, President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that he is forming an "AI Force," modeled on the Space Force, and will soon name an artificial intelligence czar, adding that "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" The plan is to promote the technology while relying on existing criminal and civil laws to police wrongdoing. The announcement comes amid continuing local protests against new data centers and calls from some lawmakers for tighter rules. Trump argued that Democrats pivoted to AI after "the crazed Data Center attack has largely failed," comparing the shift to the rebranding of global warming as climate change. He promised, "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry." He framed AI as the next Industrial Revolution, larger than the internet, with a possible economic impact equal to 25% of U.S. gross domestic product, and said the U.S. is leading China and the world. He also launched a poll asking followers to pick a better name than artificial intelligence, offering Superior, Extreme or Supreme Intelligence. The author argues that further federal control, under either party, would produce controls Big Tech can exploit. The author notes that Washington has historically celebrated breakthrough technologies such as railroads, electricity and the early internet as engines of national power before examining them as problems needing rules. Space Force, created in 2019 as the sixth branch of the armed forces, shows Trump's habit of packaging strategic ambition under a bold banner. California Governor Gavin Newsom, a likely Democratic frontrunner weighing a White House bid, responded: "Instead of regulating AI, he's posting polls to rename it." He said he had signed an executive order accelerating America's first independent AI safety oversight framework. California passed a frontier AI transparency law in 2025 after Newsom vetoed a tougher bill the year before, and other states have written their own rules. The author critiques both sides. Democrats sell oversight as protection, and some is warranted, from fraud to child safety to deepfake abuse. But a safety framework must define harmful output, giving whoever writes the definition leverage over what AI may say to millions; California's election deepfake laws have already drawn First Amendment challenges, and treating "misinformation" as a compliance category risks speech control. Republicans lean on courts and existing statutes to catch abuse after the fact, leaving privacy, surveillance and liability questions largely unanswered. Both parties will likely seek to integrate superintelligence into military operations, which the author finds concerning. The largest AI companies profit regardless of who wins. An accelerationist agenda brings faster permitting, friendly tax treatment and political cover for the data center buildout, and Trump touted the higher salaries, lower taxes and safer streets data centers supposedly bring. A heavy oversight agenda brings compliance regimes only the biggest players can afford, squeezing out smaller competitors, which economists call regulatory capture. Large firms, with armies of lobbyists and lawyers, can shape rules from both sides of the aisle. The author concludes that the fight will be sold as freedom versus safety or America versus China, but the real question is who writes the rules and who benefits. Americans deserve real liability for harmful systems, strong privacy protections, transparency about model training, and protection for lawful speech. Without these, the AI czar and the safety regulator may be two doors into the same corporate house.

Jim Beam, retired editor of the American Press, writes that artificial intelligence is quickly becoming either a miracle or a menace, and that he is the last person to know whether it will serve or wipe us out. His own encounters with AI have been unavoidable: it kept interfering with a computer program even after his son Bryan tried to remove it, it appears as an "AI overview" in Google searches that he finds extremely helpful, and it prompts him to "Press / for Help me write" in emails, which he ignores. When he wanted to find archived copies of the American Press on newspapers.com, he asked Mike Jones, a longtime colleague who writes the 10, 25, 50 and 75 Years Ago column, for an outline. Jones asked Copilot AI for a step-by-step list and sent back a detailed, effective five-step procedure with an alternate quick method of searching by title. Beam realized Jones is far ahead of him in using AI to provide difficult answers. His son-in-law Joe Fierro, who has a doctor of business administration degree, also uses AI, possibly more than one co-pilot, to help with complicated work. Beam compares this to the introduction of computers into newspapers. In 1978 he and the late Ward "Buddy" Threatt, a fellow editor, went to New Jersey to learn computers. Beam told the instructors to teach him only what he needed for his newspaper work, which he now calls a major mistake because he has long wished he knew more about computers. He notes that The Advocate of Baton Rouge ran three AI stories on Sunday. An Associated Press story reported AI leaders issuing dire warnings about the potentially catastrophic threat of rogue AI agents; the technology could bring tremendous gains in areas like medical research and automation but also unleash deadly viruses, cause widespread economic upheaval and help terrorists inflict harm. A second story said a new lawsuit claims Anthropic, Open AI, SpaceX AI and Google made an illegal deal to slow the pace of their respective AI development. A third said President Donald Trump would push tech companies to race ahead despite growing safety fears in order to stay ahead of China, rejecting concerns that the technology may pose risks to humans as a hoax and comparing it to alarm over climate change and the scandals that led to his two impeachments during his first term. After shunning AI for too long, Beam has decided it is time to "get with the program." He believes AI offers many advantages and that everyone needs to keep up with its development so it does not get out of hand. With help from Jones, Fierro and Bryan, he hopes to better understand and use it, and he does not want it to wipe out civilization, as some AI experts have said is possible.

DeepSeek, OpenAI and Anthropic to brief UN Security Council on AI safety and risks amid US-China tensions Chinese AI startup DeepSeek is set to join OpenAI and Anthropic in briefing the United Nations Security Council this week, putting three of the most closely watched AI companies at the center of an international debate over whether increasingly capable artificial intelligence could threaten global security. The 15-member Security Council is scheduled to meet Wednesday in New York to discuss AI and international security, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the plans. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is expected to participate, along with senior representatives from Anthropic. DeepSeek and other Chinese AI companies, including Moonshot, have been invited to make statements. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng is not expected to attend, though the plans could still change, Reuters added, citing the source. The meeting comes at a tense moment for the AI industry. Leading researchers and executives have raised fresh warnings that more capable systems could eventually improve themselves, deceive human operators or become difficult to control. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was among the industry figures who recently called for slowing the pace of AI development to give researchers more time to address safety concerns. OpenAI, meanwhile, has called for greater international coordination around advanced AI, including shared technical standards and mechanisms for reporting serious incidents involving frontier systems. AI safety moves into the US-China rivalry. DeepSeek’s presence adds another dimension to Wednesday’s meeting. Washington and Beijing are competing for leadership in advanced AI, yet both sides are beginning to discuss what happens if the technology creates risks neither country can contain alone. Senior US and Chinese officials agreed this week to continue talks on AI safety, with another meeting expected in Shenzhen in about two months. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the discussions would include AI dangers and communication protocols that could be used during serious AI safety incidents. Those talks come ahead of a scheduled meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later this week. AI is expected to be part of a broader agenda already strained by disputes over trade, advanced technology and export restrictions. The debate exposes a deeper split over how governments should respond to increasingly capable AI. Some US AI executives have called for stronger safeguards and international coordination. Trump has pushed back against efforts that could slow US development, arguing that restrictions could give China an advantage. Chinese state media have portrayed calls for an AI slowdown as part of a “Cold War playbook” intended to preserve US technological dominance, according to Reuters. The Security Council has been here before, though the stakes have grown. It held its first formal debate on artificial intelligence in July 2023, examining the technology’s potential impact on international peace and security. UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned at the time that AI could be used for cyberattacks, disinformation, terrorism and other forms of large-scale harm. China’s representative described AI during that meeting as a “double-edged sword” and called for international rules that balance technological development with security. Three years later, the discussion is no longer centered on hypothetical future systems alone. OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek now represent competing branches of a global AI race moving deeper into national security, diplomacy and geopolitical competition. Wednesday’s meeting puts those competing visions in the same room, giving the Security Council a rare chance to hear directly from companies building some of the systems governments are increasingly being asked to govern. In January 2025, DeepSeek rose to global prominence after releasing AI models that challenged assumptions about how much money and computing infrastructure it took to compete with leading American AI labs.

Intrinsic, the robotics software company owned by Google's parent Alphabet Inc., announced at ROSCon 2026 in Toronto that it is open-sourcing the core components of its industrial robotics platform. The offering, called Intrinsic Core, is released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license, with the aim of democratizing access to intelligent robotics. Founded in 2021, Intrinsic was incorporated into Google's operations in February to accelerate physical AI, meaning AI systems that use sensors, actuators and control systems to perceive, reason, act and learn in real-world environments, as opposed to purely digital applications. Progress in physical AI has long been stalled by the complexity of developing the underlying software and training the AI models at the heart of intelligent robots. Google and Intrinsic believe a reusable, foundational software layer would let developers avoid rebuilding everything from scratch for each new robot. Intrinsic Core is a preconfigured, Robot Operating System-compatible software environment designed to run on local hardware. It provides reusable building blocks for operating in industrial environments. Intrinsic Control is a hardware-agnostic real-time control framework that can dynamically adapt a robot's trajectory mid-movement based on sensor feedback, so developers can use different arms and grippers without rewriting software and drivers each time. Pose Estimation, based on Nvidia Corp.'s FoundationPose, lets robots dynamically detect and handle parts, removing the need for rigid, expensive physical fixtures. A motion planning capability automates collision-avoidance path generation, eliminating manual joint-by-joint programming. A grasp planning function lets different types of grippers adapt automatically to the location and orientation of objects. Simulation and calibration services allow developers to simulate, visualize and troubleshoot robots and calibrate vision systems through a single interface. Intrinsic-ROS drivers ease the integration of sensors with third-party grippers, 3D cameras and other hardware. To showcase Intrinsic Core, the company also released the Open Machine Tending Solution, an open reference design for AI-powered CNC machine tending. It supports modular customization for hardware setups from major robotics manufacturers, including Universal Robots A/S and FANUC Corp. Intrinsic said the reference design is meant to speed automation in the machine building industry. The U.S. and Europe have tens of thousands of shops that fabricate intricate parts for machines across many industries, yet only 8% use any form of automation, owing to high costs and technical barriers. Intrinsic believes a customizable starting point will help much smaller fabricators automate lower-value tasks. More broadly, Intrinsic said it hopes to foster a larger robotics developer ecosystem built on shared, open-source tools and to accelerate adoption of physical AI across industries.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group found experimental malware called PROMPTFLUX, a VBScript-based project discovered in June 2025 that could ask Gemini to rewrite its own code. Its "Thinking Robot" component requested new obfuscation techniques, and one variant was designed to have Gemini rewrite the entire source code every hour while keeping the parts needed to function. This creates a moving target for security software that looks for known code patterns. Google called it an early example of "just-in-time" AI built into malware. PROMPTFLUX was still in development, researchers had not seen it compromise a victim, and Google disabled connected assets. This does not make antivirus useless. Signature detection still matters, and tools such as Microsoft Defender Antivirus also use real-time monitoring, behavioral analysis, heuristics, cloud-delivered protection and machine learning, so changing code does not make malware invisible. Later developments went further. Google identified the Russian government-backed group APT28 using PROMPTSTEAL against targets in Ukraine, its first observation of malware querying a large language model in live operations. PROMPTSTEAL queries the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model through Hugging Face to generate Windows commands that gather system information and copy documents from Documents, Downloads and Desktop, then send them to attacker-controlled infrastructure. PROMPTSPY, an Android backdoor first identified by ESET and detailed by Google in May 2026, includes an AI module called GeminiAutomationAgent that sends on-screen information to Gemini and uses the response to navigate the phone. It can resist removal by placing an invisible overlay over the uninstall button. Google took action against the actor, found no PROMPTSPY apps on Google Play at the time, and says Google Play Protect detects known versions. Google's Sept. 8, 2026 report says attackers are moving from basic AI prompting to agentic workflows and automation. In one case, a suspected financially motivated attacker who compromised a company's cloud infrastructure used an AI coding chatbot and agent instructions to plan, build and run a mass credential-harvesting campaign in under six hours, compromising thousands of third-party credentials. Google has not seen fully autonomous exploit pipelines used in the wild. The context is already large: AV-TEST registers over 450,000 new malicious programs and potentially unwanted applications daily, many being variants of existing threats, and the FBI says Americans reported nearly $21 billion in cyber-enabled crime losses in 2025, up 26%, though these are not attributable to AI malware. Recommended protections: use antivirus with real-time and behavioral detection and keep cloud protection on; enable automatic updates; never paste commands from websites, such as those in fake CAPTCHA pages (over 5,400 compromised sites were used in one campaign); heed browser and SmartScreen warnings; install apps and extensions only from trusted sources and keep Play Protect enabled; use a password manager, multifactor authentication or passkeys; keep a separate backup; and if infection is suspected, disconnect from the internet, scan, change passwords from another device and check financial accounts. The author concludes that antivirus is not obsolete, but the technology is advancing quickly, so no single security feature should be relied on alone.

TIME announced its inaugural TIME Executives of the Year: Tech and Data list, recognizing 50 senior leaders, including CIOs, CTOs, CDOs, and chief product officers, whose decisions are shaping how businesses adopt and use technology and data. The honorees are advancing AI, strengthening cybersecurity, modernizing digital infrastructure, and reshaping how some of the world's largest organizations operate, compete, and grow. The list launches TIME Executives of the Year, a new editorial platform recognizing and convening influential leaders across the most consequential business functions. TIME plans to expand it into additional fields in the year ahead. TIME's editors wrote that business leaders must both keep pace with a fast-moving industry and look around the corner at what's next, and that the honorees are catalysts of consequential transformations across modern enterprise. Dan Macsai, TIME's executive editor and chief strategy officer, said some of the most consequential business decisions are being made by executives determining how companies adopt new technologies, protect their systems, use their data, and prepare for what comes next. Four years after ChatGPT appeared, many educators fear AI is not just enabling cheating but hurting students' ability to learn and think independently. The technology is too new for definitive long-term data, but early studies suggest that, without guardrails, large language models can damage skill attainment. Faculty report students who turn in polished essays but can't discuss their ideas, can't explain their own code, or struggle with basic math. Eric Klopfer, an MIT professor who co-chaired a committee on AI in teaching, learning and research training, said homework is often better while exam performance is worse, calling it "the illusion of learning." The committee found early signals that overreliance on chatbots can diminish critical thinking, weaken memory, erode confidence and undermine mastery. A December Rand survey found growing student AI use alongside concern about its effects; two-thirds agreed that more AI use will harm critical thinking. Brown University's committee found most students use LLMs and worry about the long-term impact. University of Virginia professor Luca Cian said "all students use AI" and called LLMs probably the most powerful cognitive off-loading mechanism ever built, noting older studies found people recall less when search engines or GPS are readily available. A study this year led by Grace Liu of Carnegie Mellon found that after a few minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost AI access performed worse and gave up sooner than those who hadn't used it. A 2025 study led by MIT's Nataliya Kosmyna measured brain activity during essay writing: connectivity was strongest among those working unaided and weakest among LLM users, who also struggled to quote their own essays. Over four months, AI users consistently underperformed. Kosmyna said results converge across brain scans, questionnaires and other measures, and urged more long-term studies. Classroom evidence is striking. Carleton University's Shawna Dolansky saw first-year humanities students submit dissertation-like outlines with quotations not in the cited books, and they couldn't answer questions about the ideas. At UC Berkeley, Gireeja Ranade saw students fail a final exam in optimization and linear algebra on problems resembling their homework; some confused reading a proof with being able to do it. Her colleague Dan Garcia saw record numbers fail exams last spring. In an introductory computer science class, more than half the students apparently violated the honor code by using AI on a take-home exam. In another class, many who got full marks on take-home projects scored zero or one out of four on an added oral exam because they hadn't written their code. Fewer students also came to class and office hours. Garcia called it "a significant epidemic." Educators are responding by reducing technology, adding oral exams or blue books, flipping in-class and outside work, building AI tools that make students work out answers, and changing syllabi. Columbia Teachers College's Erik Voss urged more in-class engagement and attention to motivation. Dolansky, after 30 years, stopped assigning take-home essays, has students write in class, made her classes tech-free with physical books and handwritten notes, and assigns less reading but requires margin annotations. She believes teaching how humans think, feel and express themselves is now even more valuable.

BERLIN (AP) — A military aircraft crashed near a U.S. air base in western Germany on Tuesday, injuring one person, the local district said in a statement. “Following a plane crash in the vicinity of U.S. Air Base Spangdahlem, fire and emergency response teams from the Eifel District of Bitburg-Pruem were dispatched to the scene,” the district said on its website, adding that one person had been injured. It was not clear if the aircraft that crashed belonged to the German or U.S. military. The district referred questions to the U.S. base, which was not immediately available for comment. Spangdahlem is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron with about 20 aircraft, the German news agency dpa reported. The squadron, which supports U.S. Air Force and NATO missions worldwide, is the centerpiece of the air base. The base has about 5,000 military and civilian employees, plus their family members, according to the latest figures. The U.S. air base also employs between 700 and 800 Germans.

BERLIN -- An American military aircraft crashed at a U.S. air base in western Germany on Tuesday, injuring the pilot, the American military said. In a statement, the U.S. Air Base Spangdahlem said that the pilot ejected and was receiving medical care. It also said the plane, which was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing, crashed around 2:30 p.m. local time, and that the cause of the crash was being investigated. The local German district, where Spangdahlem is located, had said earlier that fire and emergency teams responded to the incident. Spangdahlem is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron with about 20 aircraft, the German news agency dpa reported. The squadron, which supports U.S. Air Force and NATO missions worldwide, is the centerpiece of the air base. The base has about 5,000 military and civilian employees, plus their family members, according to the latest figures. The U.S. air base also employs between 700 and 800 Germans. The U.S. Air Force has maintained a presence in Spangdahlem since the mid-1950s. Along with Ramstein near Kaiserslautern in southwestern Germany, Spangdahlem Air Base is considered one of the most important airfields for the U.S. military in the region.

Chinese humanoid robot T800 takes on human in first-of-its-kind cage fight, sends him flying and leaves him with a broken arm For the first time in history, a six-foot Chinese humanoid robot stepped into an octagonal cage in San Francisco, traded blows with American entertainer Frankie LaPenna, and ended a 44-second fight with a kick that appeared to send him crashing across the mat. Organizers at robotics company REK billed the September 18 bout as the first human-versus-humanoid robot cage fight in the US. The footage looks like a scene pulled from The Terminator or Real Steel. It isn’t a movie set. LaPenna, an internet personality known for physical comedy and stunts, entered the cage wearing protective gear and faced an EngineAI T800, a 1.83-meter humanoid built by Shenzhen-based robotics startup EngineAI. The robot begins by throwing punches before shifting to kicks. One strike appears to connect hard enough to knock LaPenna off balance. A later kick sends him across the cage. Reports surrounding the event say LaPenna suffered a broken arm during the encounter. He is not a professional boxer, and the short video does not show enough of the bout to independently establish exactly how the injury occurred or how much force the machine generated. That uncertainty matters, especially with footage this dramatic. Human vs. Robot: Human Fighter Loses to Humanoid Robot and Suffers Broken Arm in Real Fight REK has presented the event as a genuine human-versus-robot fight rather than a conventional robotics demonstration. The company called it its first “Human VS Terminator robot fight” and said it would release more footage from the event. One detail changes what viewers are actually seeing. A human operator remotely controlled the T800. The machine was not autonomously studying LaPenna, deciding which strike to throw, or developing a fighting strategy in real time. A person was controlling the humanoid’s movements. That makes the fight less a demonstration of artificial intelligence learning combat and more a test of what a modern humanoid body can physically do under human control. That distinction takes some of the science-fiction edge off the footage, but the mechanical achievement remains striking. Humanoid robots are becoming stable and agile enough to walk, recover their balance, throw punches, execute kicks, and interact physically with people in human-built spaces. A fighting cage puts those advances on display in a way a warehouse demonstration rarely can. The T800’s appearance adds to the effect. For the event, the robot wore a menacing head and glowing features that made it resemble a machine built for a dystopian action film rather than an engineering lab. Humanoid Robot Combat is Becoming a Spectator Sport. The San Francisco matchup did not appear out of nowhere. Robot combat is moving beyond small wheeled machines smashing into each other. Humanoid platforms are entering competitions built around striking, balance, defensive movement, recovery, and durability. China held a major humanoid robot fighting tournament in July, putting machines against other machines inside a cage. REK has staged robot-versus-robot matches too. Putting a human inside the cage changes the spectacle. It turns advances in humanoid robotics into something instantly understandable. Viewers do not need benchmark charts or engineering specifications to grasp what they are seeing. A machine shaped like a person is standing across from an actual person, moving around the same cage and exchanging physical strikes. The video should not be mistaken for proof that autonomous robots can now fight humans on their own. It shows something narrower, but still remarkable. A remotely operated humanoid robot can move through a confined fighting space, maintain its balance, throw coordinated strikes and deliver enough apparent force to knock a human opponent to the floor. For years, humanoid robotics demonstrations focused on walking without falling. Now the robots are stepping into cages.

Toyota workers are already helping to train humanoid robots as part of the automaker’s race to eventually deploy 400,000 factory robots—but a Toyota executive said the robotic push is not meant to directly replace humans. Starting in 2028, the Toyota Motor group aims to start investing $6.42 billion every year in upgrading factories with the new robotic workforce, according to Nikkei Asia. The company wants to put 150,000 robots in its own automotive plants and deploy another 250,000 at group company facilities that produce various components and materials. Toyota has already begun deploying some of its ELEY humanoid robots across assembly lines to learn from human workers. Nikkei Asia reported that workers are teaching the robots, which roll around on wheels, to perform tasks requiring precise hand movements by wearing “jigs” based on the humanoids’ fingers. That naturally raises questions about the future of the Japan-based automaker’s human workforce, which has 18,000 veteran workers across 60 factories worldwide, including 11 US manufacturing plants. But Hiroki Nakajima, a Toyota executive vice president, told Nikkei Asia that the company aims for “a world where robots coexist with humans, rather than replacing them.” It’s unclear how many robots Toyota has already deployed overall or how many of the new robots will be humanoids. But the automotive industry has been a leading adopter of industrial robots for decades, with such robots typically being robotic arms installed at workstations and mobile robots that move components or materials around. China alone deployed 2 million industrial robots in 2024, with Japan coming in second at 450,500 robots, according to the International Federation of Robotics. The United States and South Korea ranked third and fourth with 34,200 robots and 30,600 robots, respectively.

Russia's Defense Ministry announced a large overnight barrage on Ukraine. It said its forces struck the Fire Point industrial complex in Kyiv, which Ukraine has used to build components and warheads for its long-range FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Strikes also hit a solid rocket fuel plant in Pavlograd supplying Ukraine's FP-9 ballistic missile program, and railway infrastructure in Vinnitsa. In the Poltava region, the ministry claimed it crippled an oil refinery in Kremenchug, described as the primary source of processed fuel for Ukraine's armed forces. Russian forces also reportedly struck a cargo vessel carrying Western-supplied military equipment as it approached the port of Odessa, a fuel and lubricant storage warehouse in Kyiv, and port facilities in Reni, in the Odessa region. The article argues that Russia's deployment of the nuclear-capable 3M22 Zircon (Tsirkon) hypersonic missile in Ukraine challenges Western military strategy and exposes weaknesses in NATO's defenses. It says the ministry did not explicitly name the Tsirkon in these strikes, but that analysts understand it played a starring role. The missile was first test-fired in 2017, nearly a year ahead of schedule. In October 2020, the Admiral Gorshkov frigate launched one in the Barents Sea that reached Mach 8 and an altitude of 28 kilometers. In February 2019, Putin said it could reach Mach 9 and destroy targets within 1,000 kilometers. The missile maneuvers at hypersonic speeds within the atmosphere, and a surrounding plasma cloud absorbs radio waves and blinds radar, even blinding its own seeker and forcing it to slow to about Mach 4.5 in the terminal phase. Former Royal Navy Commander Tom Sharpe says systems like Patriot and SAMP/T might have a chance in that phase, but the window is very narrow and the missile's kinetic energy means even a near miss can devastate a target. The Ukrainian Scientific Research Institute of Forensic Expertise analyzed recovered wreckage in 2026 and concluded the missile appears to be a ballistic or quasi-ballistic design with a two-stage solid rocket motor, not the scramjet long assumed by Western intelligence. This suggests a simpler technology that is easier to mass produce. The Tsirkon made its combat debut on February 7, 2024. On March 25, 2024, Russia launched two from a ground-based launcher in Crimea at targets in Kyiv. Russian state media said both hit, one a Security Service of Ukraine headquarters and the other Zhuliany airport; Ukrainian officials claimed both were intercepted, though the article says photographs of debris told a different story. Classified documents reportedly show Russia ordered 80 Tsirkon missiles annually for 2024 through 2026. United Shipbuilding Corporation CEO Alexei Rakhmanov confirmed in August 2023 that Yasen-M nuclear submarines will regularly carry the system. The article says the missile's range, estimated at 400 to 450 kilometers on average and up to 1,000 kilometers in some configurations, covers virtually every European capital if launched from the Baltic, Black, or Barents Seas. It concludes that Patriot, THAAD, and Aegis Ashore cannot reliably stop it, that it gives Russia a credible deterrent against NATO intervention and a near-warningless first-strike capability, and that it raises the danger of escalation between nuclear powers.

In March 2026, Google announced that quantum computers could be able to crack common encryption methods by the end of the decade, putting personal data, state secrets and bank accounts at risk unless governments and digital stewards adapt more secure systems in time, a complex and expensive undertaking. The scientific community noticed not only the result but also how it was presented. For the first time in scientific history, Google used a "zero-knowledge proof," showing it possessed a powerful quantum algorithm for breaking encryption without disclosing what the algorithm was. Google's researchers argued that the risk of misuse or rapid further development if the algorithm were public was too great. This contradicts the principles of the scientific community, since the knowledge gained cannot be used by others, and some experts asked whether zero-knowledge proofs would become the norm as companies with secrets to keep play a larger role in research. The zero-knowledge proof was invented, at least as an idea, in the mid-1980s. Previously, convincing someone of a claim required disclosing how you reached it. A zero-knowledge proof can be built for any verifiable proof and confirms that someone has the proof without revealing it. The prover repeatedly exchanges information, via algorithms, with the person they want to convince, whose conviction grows with each step. Google's claim was that a specific form of elliptic curve cryptography could be broken by a quantum algorithm using just 1,175 logical qubits and more than two million "Toffoli gates" (logical operations). Experts had estimated at least 20 times as many qubits would be needed, a number current machines are far from reaching; as of July 2026 the record is just under 100 logical qubits. The proof Google's researchers released in the first version of their white paper in March 2026 proved flawed. A team led by computer scientist Keegan Ryan realized it could also prove false claims, for example that the encryption could be cracked even without Toffoli gates, which is obviously false because the algorithm could then perform no logical operations. In mid-April 2026, the Google developers and colleagues replaced it with a valid proof. The original claim was upheld; the error lay only in the implementation of the method. The secrecy spurred experts to reproduce the result openly. After 63 days, cryptologist André Schrottenloher of the Inria Center at the University of Rennes in France succeeded, even surpassing Google's result with an improved, publicly available quantum algorithm. Google scientist Craig Gidney, a co-author of the proof, congratulated him on his blog, noting Schrottenloher matched the circuits in two months and improved the Toffoli count slightly. Separately, an initiative of several experts launched an effort to reproduce the result; after just three days, an online community using AI-based agent systems significantly surpassed it, almost halving the number of Toffoli gates required. Google's obfuscation thus backfired: instead of more security, it challenged experts who reproduced and improved the result. Gidney wrote that he enjoyed publishing some "cheeky" zero-knowledge proofs but does not think it is the right strategy going forward, because the benefits are negligible and the costs many. "We should just publish openly," he concluded.

Three cybersecurity researchers from the Indian company Hacktron broke into OpenAI's systems using a rival AI model from Anthropic, showing that advanced AI can put the companies themselves, and their users, at risk. Researcher Mohan Pedhapati said each new model is "a force multiplier" for hacking: it makes veteran hackers' work much easier and raises the risk that criminals do the same. In a report published last week, Hacktron said that in late July it used Claude models to infiltrate users of OpenAI's community forum, where ChatGPT and Codex users ask questions and can sign in with their OpenAI accounts. The team used Claude Opus 4.8 to find flaws in the code of Discourse, a third-party service behind the forum, but failed to exploit them. That same night a more advanced model, Claude Opus 5, was released, and the next day the team could access the ChatGPT and Codex accounts of a subset of forum users, including some OpenAI employees. The researchers said they could also have reached apps connected to those accounts, such as email and Slack (including internal OpenAI email), and could have seen users' ChatGPT conversations. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the report. Hacktron was taking part in one of OpenAI's bug bounties, payments made to outside "ethical hackers" who find security flaws. Its goal was to expose security gaps and gain access to one of OpenAI's more capable cyber models with fewer guardrails. "We are the good guys," Pedhapati said. He estimated the hack would have taken him two to three months alone; with Claude it took the team less than three days. With newer models from Anthropic and OpenAI released since, he thinks it could now take under a day. He said Hacktron has also hacked Apple, Google, Facebook, Discord and Microsoft Teams in the past. Pedhapati worried that AI labs are not as secure as their powerful models require. "You need to assume everyone can hack you, and then build your things based on that," he said, adding that OpenAI and Anthropic seem to be "speed running." The team did not need to attack OpenAI's own code, only a flaw in one of the many third-party services it depends on. OpenAI thanked the researchers and said it narrowed permissions on Community sign-in tokens and revoked affected tokens and sessions. The article notes that, in the wake of the Hugging Face hack, AI companies are speaking more openly about society-wide risks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told CBS News that AI's risks are serious because the technology is so powerful. One concern is theft of models, particularly their "weights," by foreign adversaries or criminals. If a small firm like Hacktron can breach OpenAI in a few days, a hostile state could likely do so too, possibly faster. Nicholas Leiserson of the Institute for Security and Technology said the labs' technology is unquestionably national-security relevant, and that despite some leaders acknowledging a need to slow down, pushing the frontier as fast as possible has long been the labs' priority. He questioned whether society is comfortable with that risk level, since the labs are currently the ones deciding it.

A US military plane crashes near a US air base in Germany, injuring the pilot. BERLIN (AP) — An American military aircraft crashed at a U.S. air base in western Germany on Tuesday, injuring the pilot, the American military said. In a statement, the U.S. Air Base Spangdahlem said that the pilot ejected and was receiving medical care. It also said the plane, which was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing, crashed around 2:30 p.m. local time, and that the cause of the crash was being investigated. The local German district, where Spangdahlem is located, had said earlier that fire and emergency teams responded to the incident. Spangdahlem is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron with about 20 aircraft, the German news agency dpa reported. The squadron, which supports U.S. Air Force and NATO missions worldwide, is the centerpiece of the air base. The base has about 5,000 military and civilian employees, plus their family members, according to the latest figures. The U.S. air base also employs between 700 and 800 Germans. The U.S. Air Force has maintained a presence in Spangdahlem since the mid-1950s. Along with Ramstein near Kaiserslautern in southwestern Germany, Spangdahlem Air Base is considered one of the most important airfields for the U.S. military in the region.
