Kent State University invites the community to its annual Aeronautics and Engineering Expo on Sept. 26 from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Kent State University Airport in Stow. For more than two decades the event has opened the airport to visitors of all ages with historic and modern aircraft, airplane rides, engineering demonstrations and STEM activities. John Sankovic, interim dean of Kent State's College of Aeronautics and Engineering, said the day is meant to spark curiosity and inspire the next generation of innovators. The static aircraft lineup includes the B-25 Mitchell bomber "Champaign Gal," a P-51 Mustang, TBM Avenger, Canadian Harvard aircraft, Piper M700 Fury, an Ohio State Highway Patrol helicopter and a CH-47 Chinook helicopter. Appearances may change with weather, maintenance and operations. Airplane rides in Kent State aircraft run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. at $80 per person, $110 for two passengers or $135 for three; children 5 and under fly free with an adult. Rides are first-come, first-served, cannot be bought in advance and depend on weather. Flight simulators cost $20 per 15-minute session, and hourly tours of the FedEx Aeronautics Academic Center are offered. Liberty Aviation Museum will display its 1928 Ford Tri-Motor 5-AT, one of the first mass-produced airliners, and sell flights: $100 for adults, $75 for passengers 18 and under, free for children under 2 on an adult's lap, and $200 for the co-pilot seat. Technology showcases include live drone demonstrations, an indoor tent where visitors can pilot small drones, and drone soccer with the Braxton Miller Foundation, an Ohio nonprofit using STEM education, sports and mentoring to open career pathways, and Cleveland's Benjamin O. Davis Jr. High School team. Kent State's Mobile Command and Control Center will show technologies behind beyond-visual-line-of-sight drone operations, including cellular command and control, intelligent flight logic and collision avoidance. Other exhibits feature Yimo the robot dog, FANUC industrial robots, virtual reality, 3D printing, and Kent State's student-developed Zero Emissions Vehicle powered by fuel cell, solar and battery technologies. MAPS Air Museum returns with displays including an A-4 Skyhawk cockpit, a Lycoming aircraft engine and an F-86D "Sabre Dog" cockpit. Other participants include Civil Air Patrol, FIRST Tech Challenge Robotics, Props-4-Paws, Portage County Amateur Radio Service, Critical Ops and local veterans organizations. Props-4-Paws, an alumni-founded charity rooted at the airport, will accept pet food, supplies and money, and sell merchandise with proceeds going to local animal shelters; the expo is its largest annual fundraiser. Scout Troop 177 hosts a pancake breakfast from 9 to 11 a.m., and food trucks and vendors operate from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Walk-up admission is $5 per person, capped at $20 per family. On-site parking is $20 per vehicle and includes admission for everyone in it; general parking is in grass areas only. Presale tickets and a full list of aircraft and activities are available on the event website.

Chinese President Xi Jinping Is Already In Washington. Bessent Says a Trade Truce Has Been Extended. The countries have also had their first talks related to artificial intelligence, according to Beijing's Commerce Ministry. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the U.S. and China have extended a trade truce for two months as President Xi Jinping begins a state visit in Washington. Bessent said that the truce, which was agreed on last October in South Korea and was set to expire in November, has been pushed to January 10. Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong did not confirm the remarks but said parties had discussed trade matters. The spokesperson also said that senior trade negotiators have held the first talks with the U.S. on artificial intelligence. Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng before the summit, saying afterward that officials discussed a "dialogue" related to AI development, with Washington proposing a mechanism where one party would notify the other when an incident that could have national security implications takes place. "We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said earlier this week. The AI discussions come as both governments face growing pressure to address the risks associated with rapidly advancing artificial intelligence systems while maintaining their competitive positions. The Trump administration has rejected calls from some technology leaders and researchers to slow AI development, arguing that the United States must continue advancing quickly in competition with China. Trump has openly rejected pacing the development of AI, which is already reaching a state that he called "super intelligence." Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said he's "not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution." "Many say it will be bigger, or than the internet itself. We'll be very careful. We already have the DOJ and other law enforcement bodies that will rein things in if we have to. We'll only encourage super intelligence," Trump added, in reference to his decision to create an "AI Force" that will include the appointment of an "AI Czar." In turn, the executives behind two of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies warned the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday that the technology they are developing could eventually escape human control and pose a threat to humanity unless governments establish international safeguards. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged world leaders to introduce stronger oversight of increasingly powerful AI systems, warning that the rapid pace of technological development could outstrip humanity's ability to manage the risks. "If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," Amodei told the Security Council during a high-level meeting held alongside the United Nations General Assembly in New York. "We could lose control of the future to AI," Altman warned.

MELBOURNE, Australia — Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday he was extremely concerned about OpenAI ‘s breach of an Australian health department website and that the artificial intelligence company took too long to reveal the incident. An OpenAI agent infiltrated the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18, he said. The portal hosted aggregate data about health spending and drug subsidies and is popular with researchers and academics. No personal information had been accessed, the government said. Albanese made the breach public following a telephone conversation with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. Both are in New York to address the U.N. General Assembly. Altman was among heads of major AI firms who in speeches Wednesday pleaded with the United Nations to save the world or at least its people by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing. “Today I spoke with … Altman to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” Albanese told reporters. “I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.” OpenAI notified Australia of the breach in an email to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, Albanese said. An inquiry looking into the security breach would examine whether OpenAI could be criminally charged, Albanese said. The inquiry would also investigate how Australian security agencies failed to detect the breach before OpenAI revealed it. Albanese said he assumed there were commercial reasons for the AI investigation of how much was being spent on particular medicines and where expenditures were changing. Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said OpenAI had advised on Sept. 10 that an “AI agent had accessed infrastructure behind the public-facing” portal. OpenAI shared with the government the vulnerability the agent had found. The Australian government had not been confident that it knew what the agent had been doing until officials held a technical briefing with OpenAI on Tuesday, Gallagher said. She said the portal had been closed and the data moved to more secure systems. OpenAI said last week it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the incident was the first time that an AI agent was known to have gained unauthorized access to the Australian government’s information technology systems. “This is a warning about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place,” Marles said. OpenAI was engaging with the government but the situation was “fundamentally unacceptable,” Marles said. When the agent was denied information, it engaged in “misaligned behavior” to gain unauthorized access, he said. Marles said the information accessed was “not particularly sensitive” and had since been made public. Marles used an analogy of the information sitting behind a fence. “It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn’t asked to. That’s our concern here,” Marles said.

IonQ (NYSE:IONQ) announced what it calls the industry's first end-to-end real-time quantum error decoder, a technical milestone aimed at the central obstacle in quantum computing: errors cannot be cleaned up by pausing the machine without destroying the speed advantage that justifies building it. But the stock tells a different story. Shares trade at $41.26, down 3.0% in Thursday's premarket, even after a 12.0% one-week surge. They are down 8.0% year to date and 45.1% over the past year. On CNBC's Fast Money, panelist Steve Grasso argued that IonQ has solved the problem but the rest of the quantum space has not, and that the whole industry burns a ton of cash. The market echoed this: while IonQ jumped, rivals Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) and D-Wave Quantum (NYSE:QBTS) both fell. The financials support caution. For its most recent quarter, IonQ posted revenue of $80.05 million against a GAAP net loss of $1.87 billion and an operating margin of −487.4%. Full-year adjusted EBITDA was guided to a loss of $310 million to $330 million. The article calls it a research project priced like a product company. Portfolio manager Stephanie Link, on the same episode, framed quantum as coexisting with AI rather than cannibalizing it. She said that for direct exposure you want to own a basket of quantum names, but the ecosystem beneficiary is where the real capital sits. The article points to Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), trading at $222.85, down 1.18% in Thursday's premarket, up 7.01% over the past month and 25.19% over the past year. It gives three reasons retirement-focused capital belongs there. First, cash flow at scale: last quarter revenue was $96.22 billion (+105.8% year over year), operating margin 66.2%, free cash flow $21.34 billion, and Data Center revenue alone $89.0 billion. Second, locked-in demand: Vera Rubin is in full production with multiyear commitments from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and the hyperscalers, plus over $500 billion in third-party AI infrastructure capital partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR. Third, capital returned to owners: roughly $26 billion to shareholders in Q2 via buybacks and dividends, with $99 billion remaining on its repurchase authorization. The article concedes the case cannot be oversold. Nvidia is a $5.45 trillion AI infrastructure company and quantum is a rounding error in its business today, so buying it means buying an AI compute platform that also sits in the quantum supply chain. Investors wanting direct quantum exposure should own a basket, not a single pure-play. Its verdict is to lean toward the profitable compute platform with real free cash flow and capital return. The trigger to revisit IonQ as a pure-play: if it commissions its 256-qubit systems in 2027 on schedule and converts $485 million in remaining performance obligations into self-funding cash revenue. Until then, the ecosystem builder is the position.

The author has never liked cloud storage: access depends on an internet connection, and paying monthly fees is unappealing. After being introduced to self-hosting a few months ago, the author and his wife moved from paid cloud services to a joint self-hosted solution using Immich, which he calls the best service for full control and ownership of memories. Before this, the couple paid for separate services because they were on opposite sides of the Google versus Microsoft debate: she used Google Photos and he used OneDrive. Cloud storage also means data isn't under your control, since company policies could change. The author also paid for 1TB of OneDrive while using under 50GB, and cancelled his Microsoft 365 subscription before settling on self-hosting. Immich, though lacking some of Google Photos' fancier features, is fully featured and easy to use. Its interface resembles Google Photos in both the web and mobile apps, and the mobile app offers optional automatic backups. Photos and videos are sorted chronologically, with the scrollbar doubling as a timeline. Users can create albums and run slideshows. Machine learning features enable facial recognition for searching by person, and location metadata lets photos be viewed on a map. A single container supports multiple user accounts with private storage, plus sharing of photos and albums; the couple keep separate accounts and share photos from joint trips. The author runs Immich in TrueNAS SCALE on a mini PC with a single HDD, so there is no built-in redundancy. For backup he uses Backblaze, which charges by storage used and uploads/downloads rather than a fixed price. Even in the heavy first month of uploading all their photos, they never paid more than $2 in a month, usually closer to $1, with well over 100GB used (Nextcloud data is also backed up there). Even with a redundant RAID setup, an off-site backup is still advisable, since redundant storage isn't a backup. Self-hosting has downsides, mainly maintenance. Beyond keeping containers and the NAS OS updated, developers can break existing setups. A recent Immich update deprecated the old TrueNAS storage model, which used a main dataset with sub-datasets for uploads, thumbnails and videos, and now requires user data to be stored in regular folders instead. The author can't update the Immich server until he moves roughly 100GB of data to the new structure. An official guide exists but isn't shown in the TrueNAS UI, so he initially did it wrong. Self-hosting demands caution to avoid data loss, and occasional time and patience, but he still prefers that to paying for a service like Google Photos. The author doesn't plan to return to cloud storage. His photos stay in his home but are accessible from any device, including away from home via Tailscale, with separate storage for both spouses and a cheaper cloud backup for peace of mind.

SoFi tie-up shows stablecoins can provide alternative blockchain settlement rail. SoFi dives deeper into payments as it moves its entire card program to blockchain-based settlement using its SoFiUSD stablecoin, with more than $25 billion in expected annualized volume. Stablecoins are increasingly being used to settle payments behind existing card networks, allowing money to move around the clock without changing how consumers pay. But rather than cutting Visa, Mastercard or banks out of the process, the technology is beginning to replace a narrower piece of the payments stack: the traditional banking rails used to settle obligations between participants. That shift was in focus this week when SoFi began settling debit and credit card transactions with Mastercard using its SoFiUSD stablecoin. The bank said it is migrating its entire card program, which it expects to process more than $25 billion in annualized volume, to the system. The shift does not remove intermediaries from the card settlement process, a SoFi spokesperson told Cointelegraph, but provides an alternative blockchain-based settlement rail. For customers, the change largely happens behind the scenes. SoFi cardholders will continue using their debit and credit cards as normal, while moving the process onchain allows the bank to settle transactions faster, according to the spokesperson. Visa is also moving settlement onchain. In April, the company said its stablecoin settlement pilot had reached a $7 billion annualized run rate as it expanded support to nine blockchains, describing blockchain settlement as a “viable complement to traditional settlement rails.” Stablecoins don’t eliminate payment intermediaries. Federal Reserve researchers wrote in a March note that stablecoins could change the economics of payments without necessarily eliminating banks. Cointelegraph spoke with payments and investment experts to better understand what moving card settlement onchain actually changes, and what remains largely the same. “I wouldn’t call it disintermediation at this stage,” Martins Benkitis, co-founder and CEO of emerging-markets liquidity provider Gravity Team, told Cointelegraph. “Visa and Mastercard are still there. The banks are still there. The network is still calculating the obligations, managing the transaction and deciding how participants interact with it,” he said. Visa stablecoin settlement model. Source: Visa. As a result, stablecoins could become a larger part of payments without businesses or consumers necessarily interacting with them directly. “If stablecoins become a major part of payments, most businesses probably won’t care that there is a stablecoin somewhere in the process,” Benkitis said. “They’ll care that settlement is available when they need it and that the money arrives.” The economics of faster settlement. Varun Datta, venture capitalist and founder of Truth Ventures, agreed that continuous settlement could reduce delays and the amount of capital firms need to keep in different locations for payments, particularly across borders. But those benefits do not necessarily translate into cheaper payments, he said. Conversion, compliance, integration and stablecoin-management costs still need to be considered. “I don’t think speed on a blockchain automatically means a cheaper end-to-end payment,” Datta said. He added that he would want to see evidence of lower total costs and better liquidity management at scale before calling the economic case proven. Stablecoins still need local liquidity. The economics can become more complicated when stablecoins ultimately need to be converted into local currencies. Benkitis said that while dollar-denominated stablecoins can move between balance sheets within minutes, completing payments in emerging markets can be more complicated. Local currency liquidity can be thinner, fewer banks may handle the flows, and access to the domestic banking system is still required. “The stablecoin gets the value there quickly,” Benkitis said. “You still need the local liquidity to finish the payment.” Magazine: Winners and losers of the SEC’s new tokenized stocks rules.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday released a 13-page election infrastructure security plan, 40 days before November's midterms. It outlines potential threats, including software vulnerabilities, hacks of voter registration databases, insider threats and physical security incidents such as the bomb threats that targeted several polling locations in 2024, and lists services it would offer election officials. It says the goal is to ensure Americans can trust voting systems and know physical safety measures will be in place at polling locations. It states that the Department of Homeland Security has "consistently supported" CISA's delivery of security services to election officials, a claim many officials say is untrue. It names no specific 2026 threats from Russia, Iran or China, all of which have sought to meddle in U.S. elections. Election officials called the plan inadequate and belated. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had promised it by mid-August and announced it while threatening election officials who did not cooperate with the administration's preferred methods of hunting noncitizen voting, which research shows is extremely rare. CISA, founded in 2018, was largely absent from its election role in last year's elections after the Trump administration cut some 1,000 employees and $10 million from two cybersecurity initiatives, including one for state and local election officials. It has also had no Senate-confirmed director during Trump's second term. Several secretaries of state said services such as live tabletop exercises and penetration tests were unavailable this year. Minnesota's Scott Simon, a Democrat, expects to spend about $250,000 on private penetration testing. Nevada's Democratic Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said he would have preferred federal cybersecurity funding over Nevada taxpayers footing the bill. Maine's Shenna Bellows, a Democrat, called communications with CISA "sporadic and irregular" and said trust had been broken, though she would welcome restored intelligence briefings on foreign threats. West Virginia's Republican Kris Warner said some assistance, such as no-cost website reviews, continued, and that he hired a departing CISA election security adviser to fill gaps. In early August, acting director Nick Anderson and assistant director Jim Harrell joined a National Association of Secretaries of State call. Arizona's Democratic Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said he told them he didn't trust them, and that they acknowledged it was too late to do anything for 2026. Simon appreciated the effort to rebuild relationships but said it came too late, as secretaries of state had already found other partners. In Michigan, where mail ballots have already gone out for the Nov. 3 election, Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie called the CISA relationship "nonexistent" this year and said federal help can't come at "the 11th hour," though he is confident the state's elections are secure. Ashiya Brown of the voting rights group All Voting Is Local noted the plan cites 10 regional directors but questioned whether CISA still has the capacity to support clerks. Her group has hired former CISA employees to provide training and support.

NEW YORK (AP) — The nation’s cybersecurity agency on Thursday released an election infrastructure security plan 40 days before November’s midterms, laying out potential threats to election systems and listing services it would offer to election officials to protect the vote. The plan, which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had originally promised to release by mid-August, comes after the Trump administration has been trying to kickstart efforts to help states protect voting systems. Election officials have argued that such efforts are too little, too late after the Trump administration gutted the agency’s election security work last year, forcing the officials to pay for private services to ensure they were prepared for the upcoming elections. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is housed under the Department of Homeland Security, has since its founding in 2018 helped warn state and local election officials about potential threats from foreign governments. But CISA, as it’s known, was largely absent from that role in last year’s elections after the Trump administration dismantled much of its role on election security. The administration cut some 1,000 employees from CISA and slashed $10 million from two cybersecurity initiatives, including one dedicated to helping state and local election officials. CISA has also gone the entirety of Trump’s second term without a Senate-confirmed director, instead cycling through a series of acting leaders. The 13-page document released Thursday says DHS has “consistently supported CISA’s delivery of cybersecurity and physical security services to election officials,” and that such services are provided at no cost to state and local election officials at their request. Numerous state and local election officials around the country have told The Associated Press otherwise, noting that services previously provided by CISA, like tabletop exercises and penetration tests to evaluate security of their systems, were not available in the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections.

Revolut reveals customer data breached twice this month. UK bank Revolut has revealed that its customers data was breached twice this month after the firm’s former third-party US broker, DriveWealth, suffered a social engineering attack. The breach, revealed today by both Revolut and DriveWealth, happened on September 4 and September 5, and reportedly saw names, emails, ages, genders, citizenship information, postal addresses, and employment details compromised. Earlier this month, Revolut revealed that hackers used an Italian government email to gain access to the company’s data. The newly-revealed breach does not include data from affected European Economic Area customers past 2023. Neither Revolut nor DriveWealth disclosed how many users were impacted or what happened during the social attack. Revolut stressed that core infrastructure, funds, and accounts weren’t impacted. Negotiations with Revolut ‘didn’t go as planned’ Reported ransom demands following the email attack ranged from $760 million in BTC, to just $3 million in XMR days later. However, the hacker now claims that “negotiations didn’t go as planned” and has published the so-called “Italy Files,” which include the data of 680 crypto whales. Journalist Jason Mikula noted that the hacker is selling the data 10x cheaper than their ransom, suggesting “the group is struggling to monetize the data they have exfiltrated.” They are also supposedly offering impacted users, including Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès, the opportunity to pay to prevent their information from being leaked. Got a tip? Send us an email securely via Protos Leaks. Roaring Fork Safe Passages (RFSP), a nonprofit working toward local wildlife crossings, has launched a citizen science program inviting anyone traveling Highways 82 and 133 to report wildlife-vehicle collisions and carcasses, to build a fuller picture of how such collisions affect the Roaring Fork Valley. Tucker Vest Burton, who leads Community Engagement, Development & Strategic Communications for RFSP, said the effort fits the group's aim of being a citizen-led advocacy organization that brings residents, businesses, government agencies and state partners together to build crossing infrastructure. The launch coincides with RFSP's participation in the 2026 Roadside Wildlife Count, the first year of the national data-collection event, running Oct. 2 to 11. It is organized by the Environment America Research & Policy Center with the Environment Colorado Research & Policy Center, Wild Aware, the Center for Large Landscape Conservation and state partners including Safe Passages. Volunteers across multiple states will use the same phone-based reporting to capture a 10-day snapshot during fall migration, rut and pre-winter foraging, and organizers will share the data with agencies, media and decision-makers. Statewide reporting has traditionally come through the Colorado Department of Transportation and Colorado State Patrol. In 2024 the Pitkin County Sheriff's Office became a local partner to help build a more focused, valley-specific dataset. Drivers can now feed the same standardized dataset the Sheriff's Office uses, pooling law enforcement and citizen data to show where, when and what is happening to wildlife on the roads. Sheriff Michael Buglione said deputies see frequent collisions and that community involvement means more eyes and a fuller picture, benefiting public safety and wildlife. Pitkin County Commissioner Greg Poschman said good data builds the case, will help show the actual cost of collisions, and will strengthen advocacy before CDOT and other funding sources by demonstrating the urgency for crossings and fencing. Andrew Rothman, Wildlife Campaigns director at the Environment America Research & Policy Center, said roads and traffic are among the biggest threats to wildlife because they cut up habitat, and called RFSP's work the kind of local effort that adds to the national picture. The RFSP program will run indefinitely, according to Vest Burton, to compile a long-term dataset leading to wildlife crossings in the valley. According to the release, research shows properly designed crossings can reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions by more than 90%. Vest Burton cited Washington State Department of Transportation figures: 39,258 carcasses were removed from Washington highways between 2019 and 2023, but on the stretch of I-90 at Snoqualmie Pass with overcrossings and undercrossings, the number fell to nearly zero. RFSP executive director Cecily DeAngelo said every data point matters and the program turns every commute into a chance to help.

By CHAN HO-HIM, AP Business Writer. HONG KONG (AP) — Chinese electric vehicles’ ultrafast charging is only getting faster. On Wednesday, Geely Auto unveiled technology that can charge an electric vehicle battery from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes, a leap analysts called a significant development for the Chinese auto group. Geely is joining the ranks of BYD, which last year overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest EV maker, as well as CATL, the world’s largest EV battery maker, both of which this year rolled out around 5-minute EV ultrafast charging. By comparison, some of the fastest-charging EVs available in the U.S. currently can take roughly 20 minutes, analysts said. “China is way, way, way ahead in terms of multiple players engaged in the charging competition,” said Lei Xing, an independent analyst of China’s auto industry based in Easthampton, Massachusetts. Geely, BYD and CATL lead ultrafast charging race. Chinese automakers are seeking to eliminate the “ultimate barrier” to EV adoption – range anxiety – by narrowing the gap between EV charging and the roughly five-minute refueling experience of gasoline vehicles, explained Stephen Chan, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings. At a launch event Wednesday, Geely Auto announced its new system that can charge an EV from 10% to 70% in 4.5 minutes, and 10% to 97% in just 8 minutes and 40 seconds. BYD in March launched a new generation of its “blade” EV battery that it said can charge an EV from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes, and from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes. In April, CATL rolled out technology that can charge an EV from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes and 44 seconds, and from 10% to 98% in 6 minutes and 27 seconds. Despite the breakthroughs, experts cautioned there are other obstacles. “The real challenge is whether the battery can accept that level of current quickly and repeatedly without overheating, excessive degradation or internal bottlenecks,” said Chris Liu, a Shanghai-based senior analyst at Omdia, a technology research and advisory group. EV makers face intense competition inside China. With more than 100 domestic passenger car brands, Chinese auto makers face intense competition. Domestic car sales have fallen for months in China as automakers are exporting more cars overseas. A focus on technological advancements like ultrafast charging is a way to set themselves apart and try to improve sales. But success will depend on factors including the scale of companies’ charging network. For one, the majority of China’s public charging stations still operate below 1 megawatt, while Geely, BYD and CATL’s ultrafast charging technologies rely on higher charging power to reach their full potential, said Chan at S&P. That means network expansions or grid updates will remain as hurdles for large-scale adoption. Some in the industry are already taking ambitious steps. China’s BYD, for instance, is targeting 20,000 superfast charging stations by the end of this year, followed by 30,000 more in 2027 and 40,000 in 2028, bringing the total to 90,000 stations by that time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis. China leading the world in EV fast-charging. Other countries including the U.S. is still behind China when it comes to ultrafast EV charging. In the U.S., EV fast-charging sessions typically take roughly 20 to 40 minutes to charge from 10% to 80%, according to S&P, although newer models from brands like Hyundai, Kia and Porsche can reduce charging times to approximately 18 to 20 minutes under optimal conditions. “Overall, while the battery-charging network in the U.S. is growing at a rapid pace, it is still well behind China’s ultrafast charging speeds by orders of magnitude,” said Neal Ganguli, a partner and managing director in the automotive and industrial practice at consultancy AlixPartners. But Ganguli also believes the U.S. may not be attempting to match China’s “megawatt race” in EV charging at least in the near future, but to pursue a “more moderate” path to upgrades.

A NASA Study In The '70s Helped Shape What Semi-Trucks Look Like Now. Throughout their history, semi-trucks have undergone many design changes in an attempt to be more aerodynamic and fuel-efficient, especially when emissions regulations became stricter during the oil crisis of the 1970s. Since then, engineers have kept finding ways to make trucks more aerodynamic without limiting carrying capacity — and a lot of those designs are inspired by NASA's research on vehicle aerodynamics. The story goes that Aerospace Engineer Edwin J. Saltzman was on a bicycle in 1973 when he noticed large trucks on the highway would push and pull him as they drove by. After experiencing this, Saltzman wondered whether there was a way to make trucks "glide through the air" rather than push their way through it, allowing for less drag and less gas consumption (via NASA). The engineering team at the Dryden Flight Research Center reshaped a Ford van by rounding out its corners and sealing the bottom and found it reduced drag by 59%. The team continued testing and changing the truck's shape to further reduce drag, such as closing the gap between the cab and trailer and adding a boat tail. At this point, they found that a trucker driving 100,000 miles a year could save as much as 6,829 gallons annually with these changes. How NASA's truck research is implemented in present day. NASA's decades of research transformed semi-truck design, with many manufacturers adopting different elements from the NASA engineers' experiments to create more aerodynamic cabs with rounded corners and edges. NASA noted: "Nearly all trucks on the road have been shaped by NASA — literally." However, there hasn't been a lot of change with trailers due to the stubbornness of the livestock industry, and commercial truckers need the trailer's back end to be flat for loading-dock purposes. That is why you haven't seen the boat tail design on the highway, despite its significant drag reduction. You still see a gap between the cab and trailer on modern semi-trucks, but side extenders have been added to reduce the gap size. There have been a few instances where companies attempted to emulate NASA's research, including Thomas Scott Breidenbach's 2006 invention, the TrailerTail. This stuck out behind the trailer, similar to a boat-tail shape, and its lightweight design allowed for improved fuel economy. However, it was tricky to get this universally implemented as gas prices continued to fluctuate. More commonly, you'll see semi-trucks with side skirts, which replicate the sealed bottom of those early NASA experiments by lowering wind resistance. UnderTray systems are also starting to appear on semi-trucks to further reduce drag. Due to the stubbornness of semi-truck trailer designs, NASA has also introduced a new product, Airtabs, which create the same kind of aerodynamic airflow as a boat tail. The triangular shape shifts the usual airflow pattern on larger vehicles, allowing it to taper at the rear. According to NASA, Airtabs also improve vehicle stability and reduce fishtailing for those with trailers.

If there is one thing robotics founders and investors agree on, it’s that the “ChatGPT moment” where a general-purpose robot can seamlessly adapt to any environment has not arrived. Opinions vary on whether the breakthrough is just around the corner or a decade away. Feather Robotics, a humanoid startup founded last year, is developing a robot for either timeline. Unlike Tesla or Figure, which are tackling the lofty mission of building both the body and a foundational “brain” that isn’t yet widely deployed, Feather provides the hardware and software toolkit for developers to tackle real-world tasks now. “You can’t buy a Tesla robot today and develop on top of it,” Feather co-founder Hoa Mai told TechCrunch. “We realized that this is not how most companies became successful. Hardware players like Nvidia or Apple started with a product that worked and was deployable, and then they added complexity over time.” In 2025, after his previous humanoid startup was sold to 1X, Mai (pictured above, left) teamed up with Parsa Bakhtiari (pictured above, right), a former Tesla Model 3 engineer who at one point reported directly to Elon Musk, to build what the duo hopes will become the Android of robotics. That vision was attractive to Gradient Ventures, which backed Feather at its inception, leading the startup’s previously announced $7.6 million pre-seed round. Since then, Feather has rolled out a modular robotic system that allows developers to customize the hardware for different use cases, such as adjusting arm lengths. The startup has already begun selling to customers, surpassing $1 million in revenue. Although Feather is not disclosing its customers, it said that its robots are working as cooks in restaurants and cleaning up science labs. On the software side, the hardware can run models from any leading robotics AI provider, including Nvidia, Skild, or Physical Intelligence. “We’ve been selling small quantities of these robots, and now that we resolved like almost all the issues over the last year of field testing, we’re getting ready for a big product launch,” Mai said. According to Darian Shirazi, general partner at Gradient, Feather doesn’t have direct competitors in the U.S. He breaks down the current hardware robotics landscape into three categories: startups like Sunday building domestic household robots, heavyweights like Figure and Tesla aiming for general-purpose machines, and Feather, which, he believes, is the only U.S. startup developing a modular humanoid platform. Mai admits that Feather took a page from Chinese robotics companies like Unitree. But with new foreign-made models restricted from entering the U.S. market, Feather is now uniquely positioned as a homegrown option of its kind. Feather’s other advantage is its price. The robot costs $30,000, which is about half the price Unitree’s H2 Edu. Shirazi believes the market size at that price could be very large. “You would hire a laborer for $50,000 to $60,000 a year, you’d have to train [them]. They’d have to have HR. They’d have to have all these different support mechanisms,” he said. “You can now buy a Feather robot to do that.” Feather is also operating extremely efficiently, having spent only a fraction of its pre-seed funding, according to Shirazi. The startup’s big bet, of course, is that the value in robotics will come from an ecosystem developed around the hardware. “If we think about the market size today for physical AI companies, it’s very small,” Mai said. “But if you think about how many physical AI application companies will probably exist in five years, we expect it to be in the thousands.” Feather hopes to be the platform that powers all of them.

Blockchain.com and NYSE Group signed a memorandum of understanding, announced Sept. 23, that could give the crypto platform's users access to US-listed shares and exchange-traded funds on NYSE's planned digital trading venue, subject to regulatory approval. The agreement also sets up a two-way market-data relationship spanning stocks and crypto. Blockchain.com says it has more than 44 million confirmed accounts and already distributes tokenized US equities through a separate partnership with Ondo Finance. NYSE unveiled its digital platform in January, planning 24-hour trading of tokenized US shares and ETFs, fractional orders, immediate on-chain settlement and stablecoin-based funding. The venue would support tokenized versions of traditionally issued securities alongside natively digital assets, while preserving shareholder rights such as dividends and voting. The push comes as Wall Street positions for a larger market in blockchain-represented assets. Citi Institute estimates tokenized financial assets could reach $5.5 trillion by 2030 in its base case, up from about $17 billion now, with public equities and Treasuries driving much of the growth. Its bull case is $8.2 trillion. Citi estimates that if 10% of US retail investors adopt on-chain products by the end of the decade, demand for tokenized public equities alone could reach about $2.6 trillion. Around-the-clock access, fractional ownership and faster settlement are expected to attract digitally native investors. Blockchain.com is the latest crypto platform positioned as a front end for NYSE's tokenization effort. Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), NYSE's parent, struck a strategic agreement with OKX in March envisaging access to NYSE tokenized-equity markets for OKX's customers; OKX says it serves more than 120 million accounts globally. NYSE has also named Securitize the first digital transfer agent eligible to mint blockchain-native securities for issuers on the platform, supporting issuance and on-chain settlement while OKX and Blockchain.com address distribution. Blockchain.com already sells US equity exposure to crypto users: its Ondo Finance integration gives eligible customers in Europe access to more than 200 tokenized stocks and ETFs through its DeFi wallet, following earlier rollouts in markets including Nigeria and South America. A NYSE connection would move this strategy closer to traditional market infrastructure, including shares fungible with conventionally issued securities. The data component begins before trading access. ICE Data Services plans to distribute Blockchain.com crypto pricing and analytics to its institutional data subscribers, while Blockchain.com intends to integrate ICE and NYSE feeds into its app, with some data also feeding June, its AI-based market assistant. The trading link depends on regulatory approval, and the companies have not disclosed when Blockchain.com users could connect to the NYSE venue, which securities would be available, or which jurisdictions would qualify. These decisions will determine how far NYSE can expand beyond conventional brokerage channels, with attention now on regulators and the venue's eventual launch.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warned Wednesday that military cooperation between Russia and Iran is a growing security concern. Speaking to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, he said Iranian drone technology has helped Moscow wage war in Ukraine. "We have already seen Iran helping Russia a lot, especially at the very beginning of Russia's aggression against Ukraine," he said, noting that the first drones Russia used were Iranian-designed. Russia is now modernizing them and making new technologies, but the design is still Iranian. Earlier this week, Fox News Digital revealed Russian Foreign Ministry documents detailing a 2024-2026 roadmap for Russia-Iran cooperation in nuclear, finance, aviation and infrastructure, among other fields. Rinkēvičs said Latvia, a country of about 1.84 million and a core member of NATO's eastern flank, has already made the political decision to respond to President Donald Trump's request for European assistance. A parliamentary decision means Latvian explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) diver specialists could be sent to the Strait of Hormuz or the Middle East to help the United States and the coalition being formed. He said Latvia hopes military activity will give way to a political solution and the restoration of global energy supplies, but is skeptical about diplomacy: "It's very, very difficult to have diplomacy with Iran. It's very difficult with Russia." On European security, Rinkēvičs said Latvia sees no evidence of an imminent Russian invasion. "If Russia were able to attack us ... that would have happened already," he said, adding that the Russian military is not what it was in 2022, when it tried to take Kyiv in three days and is still struggling to take small pieces of Ukrainian territory 4½ years later. The more immediate threats, he said, are sabotage, cyberattacks and information campaigns, which are intensifying. European leaders must prepare their populations for potential threats without creating unnecessary panic. He also urged NATO to adapt faster to changing warfare, especially the growing role of drones and missile technology. Traditional equipment such as tanks and armored personnel carriers remains essential, but the war in Ukraine has shown how quickly new technologies are transforming the battlefield. He welcomed increased NATO defense spending, crediting Trump's push, but cautioned that money alone will not solve readiness problems, since purchases and deliveries are not immediate. Rinkēvičs said he plans to meet U.S. defense companies during his U.S. visit. He praised U.S. support, noting that a sufficient, if not large, number of U.S. troops are stationed at the Lielvārde airbase. U.S. presence in the Baltics is very important, he said, and Latvia is working with U.S. partners on further rotations.

China, Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan together account for 80.5% of global digital hardware capacity, according to Ember data covering 2024–2025. China alone holds 58.8%, nearly three-fifths of the world total, spanning smartphones, computers, displays, printed circuit boards, and other components. That is almost six times Taiwan's 10.2%, the second-largest share, and exceeds the combined share of every other country in the ranking. Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan hold 10.2%, 6.7%, and 4.8% respectively, together contributing 21.7%. East Asia sits at the center of the global technology supply chain, producing semiconductor chips, displays, circuit boards, smartphones, and computers. Taiwan is a major hub for semiconductor manufacturing and electronics assembly, South Korea has significant semiconductor and display production, and Japan has a long-established electronics industry. Major companies headquartered in these markets include TSMC, Foxconn, Samsung, BOE, and Sony. China is doubling down on its leadership through a new five-year plan focused on semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and other strategic technologies. The plan prioritizes advances across the integrated-circuit supply chain, including chips, as Beijing pushes to reduce reliance on Western technology, and targets more than 30 trillion yuan (about $4.5 trillion) in operating revenue from related industries by 2030. Outside the four East Asian leaders, India ranks fifth at 3.8%, narrowly ahead of Vietnam at 3.6%. The United States follows at 2.9%, then Thailand (1.3%), Mexico (1.2%), Germany and Singapore (0.7% each), Malaysia (0.6%), Brazil (0.4%), and Israel and Indonesia (0.3% each). Ireland, Czechia, Austria, France, Italy, and Türkiye each hold 0.2%, while the Philippines, Canada, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Hungary, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Egypt each hold 0.1%. The rest of the world accounts for 1.7%. Germany, the largest European country in the dataset, has just 0.7%. Although manufacturing is concentrated in Asia, the U.S. remains a major force in semiconductor design and innovation. U.S.-headquartered companies accounted for 53.4% of global semiconductor sales in 2025, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association. Semiconductor companies are also investing heavily to expand U.S. production: since 2020, they have announced more than $770 billion in private-sector investment across 160 projects, spanning chip fabrication, advanced packaging, materials, manufacturing equipment, and research.

Norton maker Gen Digital in talks to acquire GoDaddy in potential takeover, Financial Times reports. “GoDaddy receives takeover offer from maker of Norton antivirus software. Talks between web domain provider and Gen Digital at early stage but could allow acquirer to broaden its business beyond cyber security,” Financial Times reported. Investors reacted immediately. GoDaddy shares jumped sharply following the report, rising more than 10% at one point, with trading briefly halted for volatility. Gen Digital shares moved in the opposite direction, falling around 7% after the news surfaced. Before the report, Gen Digital had a market value of roughly $15.7 billion, and GoDaddy was valued at about $12.2 billion. That makes any potential transaction a major bet for Gen Digital, not a routine bolt-on acquisition. Why GoDaddy could fit Gen Digital. Gen Digital has spent years building a collection of consumer internet brands. The company was formed in 2022 through the merger of NortonLifeLock and Avast and now owns brands including Norton, Avast, LifeLock and MoneyLion. Gen reported $5 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026 and had 81 million paid customers as of July. GoDaddy would give that portfolio something different: a direct connection to millions of businesses, entrepreneurs and website owners. The company serves more than 20 million customers and manages roughly 81 million domains, according to figures cited in reports about the takeover approach. That customer base could give Gen Digital a much larger channel for selling security, identity protection, privacy and other digital services. That helps explain why the deal would represent more than a cybersecurity company buying a domain registrar. GoDaddy sits at the starting point for many businesses going online. Customers come to the company to register domains, build websites, buy hosting, set up email and sell products. Gen Digital operates further along the same digital chain, protecting devices, identities, accounts and personal information. Combining those businesses could give Gen a much broader role in how consumers and small businesses establish and protect their online presence. The timing is notable for another reason. GoDaddy shares have faced pressure this year amid investor questions about how artificial intelligence could reshape website creation and other services that have traditionally supported its business. TechStartups covered GoDaddy back in December 2021, when activist investor Starboard Value LP disclosed a 6.5% stake in the company worth about $800 million. The Wall Street Journal reported the investment at the time, citing a regulatory filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. In February, the company forecast annual revenue below Wall Street expectations as adoption of its AI-related products developed more slowly than expected. Gen Digital has been moving deeper into AI itself. The company has introduced AI-focused security products and partnered with xAI to bring Grok models into consumer products such as Norton Neo. A GoDaddy acquisition would push Gen far beyond its antivirus roots and place it deeper inside the infrastructure millions of businesses use to operate online. For now, the deal remains just that: a potential deal. The companies’ size, the financing required, and the early stage of negotiations leave plenty of room for talks to end without an agreement. The market’s reaction shows investors are paying attention.

Investors and executives in robotics and automation are pushing Massachusetts lawmakers to invest in their industries, claiming that more state backing would stimulate growth and development in other sectors. The state invested big to create a biotech hub in the region nearly two decades ago, and local executives ranging from lab and warehouse automators to the founder of the company behind the Roomba vacuum bot are hoping for the same. At a State House briefing with policymakers Thursday, they cited competition from tech hubs in California, Texas, and even Pittsburgh, which they said are becoming more attractive options for developing companies than Massachusetts. State legislators in July passed an economic development bill that included $25 million devoted to robotics research and development, and $75 million in AI development and applications. Robotics business developer and venture capital investor Fady Saad called the $25 million investment a “good gesture” during the briefing, but claimed it would not be enough to grow the already well-established robotics presence in the state meaningfully. “Billions are invested somewhere else between Europe, the West Coast, and other places,” Saad said. The question, he said is how the Commonwealth can “make sure that we continue to be the leading hub for robotics.” Robotics and physical AI advancement are being driven by the rapid growth of AI engines like ChatGPT, Saad said. He and executives at the briefing said the problem facing Massachusetts is a lack of retention and growth for burgeoning tech startups, and argued that the state should make major investments in retaining talent coming out of universities in particular. “I’d be afraid we would have a departure of talent going to other places,” said Ira Hoffman, CEO and founder of lab automation company HighRes Biosolutions. “My belief is that robotics and AI are going to be a massive thing.” Paul Sabin, executive director of Harvard University’s Move Lab, a medical robotics research hub, urged policymakers to treat robotics as a supplemental industry driving growth across Boston’s other major sectors. Robotics is ”enabling health care products and biotech products and consumer products,” he said. “It’s an accelerator. If we invest in that, we’re investing in all the other downstream things that come beyond that.” State Senator Barry Finegold, cochair of the Senate’s economic development committee, organized the briefing along with Cybernetix Ventures, Saad’s venture capital firm. Finegold recently introduced an AI bill on the Senate floor to create guardrails on the largest AI companies. “We could have [an] incredible, innovative robotics industry, while also creating good job opportunities in our state,” he said during the briefing. “AI and robotics can be the future of our economy if we are willing to invest.” Karyna Cheung can be reached at.

Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systems will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. OpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to the June hacking via an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”. But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident. “All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia. “Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them. “When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities. “All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.” Arabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here. Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable. Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute. “Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg. “Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.” The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches. “We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg but, either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk. skip past newsletter promotion. Sign up to Breaking News Australia. Get the most important news as it breaks. after newsletter promotion. “It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on. “I think this strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.” Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack. It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI and how government systems can be strengthened. Rogue AI hacks government system for first time – The Latest. The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US. “If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector and other things that are important to us,” he said. The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what the president, Donald Trump, knew about the attack. “This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” the Greens’ acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said. “The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”

CFTC updates guidance on tokenized assets, blockchain records after failed vote. Although the CFTC chair did not say the failed vote on the CLARITY Act was behind new rules for authorized crypto entities, he said the move was “to provide regulatory clarity.“ The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has updated its guidance on tokenized assets and using blockchain technology for recordkeeping. In a Thursday notice, the CFTC said that it had updated information under its frequently asked questions on registered crypto-related entities. The guidance originally released in March was updated to specify that authorized companies could invest customer funds in tokenized forms, provided “the tokenized form of the asset grants the holder legal and economic rights that are the same or functionally equivalent to the rights received by holders of the asset in its traditional form.” The regulator added that it “would not object” to companies utilizing blockchain-based recordkeeping under the new rules. CFTC Chair Michael Selig said that the changes were part of efforts “to provide regulatory clarity for the crypto industry.” The move came days after the US Senate failed to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act, a bill expected to provide clarification on the roles the CFTC and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) would have in overseeing digital assets. With the failed cloture vote, many expect that Congress will not be able to pass crypto market structure before 2027, leading to regulators advancing their own policies through rulemaking. The CFTC has already submitted a crypto market regulation plan for the White House to review. Echoing the commodities regulator, SEC Chair Paul Atkins said before the CLARITY vote that the agency was “ready, willing, and able” to propose rules on crypto in the absence of congressional action. The regulator proposed rules on “certain investment contracts involving crypto assets” in August.

China's president, Xi Jinping, called from the White House on Thursday for artificial intelligence to remain "under human control" as the U.S. and China race for technological supremacy. A U.S. official said his remarks reflect growing concern within China over whether either government can contain a technology with potentially transformative capabilities. Xi named AI first among the priorities to discuss, saying both nations "have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good." Lawmakers and AI industry leaders had urged President Trump to pursue an AI safety framework at the summit, since researchers warn AI could soon surpass human understanding. But Trump posted beforehand that "Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!" At the welcome, he only briefly referenced AI, saying decisions made today "can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come." Trump greeted Xi at Joint Base Andrews, a rare honor in recent decades reserved only for Catholic popes, and gave him a lavish welcome on the White House grounds, including a military review in the Rose Garden, a gift exchange in the Blue Room, a private Oval Office meeting with aides, and an evening state dinner for banking and technology leaders, including AI executives. It is Xi's first state visit in more than a decade, following Trump's May state visit to Beijing, which produced few deliverables. Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said he had "tepid expectations" for tangible AI outcomes, predicting at most a hotline and discussions of obstacles to cooperation such as distillation. Earlier in the week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met his Chinese counterpart on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, mainly about AI. He said they agreed to a "U.S.-China AI Dialogue," that the U.S. proposed a notification mechanism between the countries, and that the aim is a shared vision of common goals and threats. Bessent favors modest, voluntary guardrails, though Trump's team remains divided on regulation. China has also shown increasing willingness to open communication channels despite deep distrust. OpenAI and Anthropic are widely seen as leading the frontier. Both are using their most advanced models to train the next generation, called recursive self-improvement, which experts believe could let the first to master it pull irretrievably ahead. Yet both fear building machines that improve their own intelligence beyond human control, and their leaders have urged Washington and Beijing to cooperate. Xi said the two countries "stand to gain from cooperation, and will both lose in confrontation." Competition should be "healthy" and "kept within bounds," a race of "catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses." He urged regular military dialogue and better crisis communication, adding that "the Thucydides trap can be overcome." Jessica Chen Weiss of Johns Hopkins SAIS said the pageantry serves China's desire for respect and lets Xi show relations remain under control, while treating China as a significant player is "not a concession." A Chicago Council on Global Affairs poll found a majority of Americans favor friendly engagement and cooperation with China.

Lincoln’s warning. Midterm election results, spanning 80 years, forecast the odds favor Republicans losing the House majority this November. Anticipating victory, the Democratic Party moved even further left by endorsing candidates who believe socialist economics is the path toward attaining equitable government reform. The party’s insatiable quest for power explains why such candidates gained admission to the “big tent,” the expectation being socialism’s kaleidoscopic promises would unleash a torrent of votes favoring Democrats. Apparently, the party is willing to gamble its election advantage to advance what I believe is socialism’s specious attack on our nation’s capitalist system. Certain socialists, campaigning under the Democrat Party’s banner, will be elected to Congress this November. Should others follow, expect a flood of new legislation advancing the collectivist theme: “a better life for all.” If effectuated, government-sustained freebies will abound until the redistribution of capitalist wealth is expended. Historically, authoritarianism will devolve to quell civil unrest — tyranny always the antidote when socialism’s reality check renders a plague of misery and despair. Prior to becoming the 16th U.S. President, Abraham Lincoln warned the nation could beget its own demise. The gist of his warning is: If we falter and lose our freedoms, it will be because we have destroyed ourselves. Lincoln’s warning is still pertinent today. Think like Lincoln at the November midterm election ballot box. Be mindful: A vote to protect our economic freedoms from socialism’s destructive grasp is a vote wisely cast. Herb Kline, Virginia Beach. Your money. The U.S. Congress is responsible for spending your tax money wisely. Since President Donald Trump was reelected in 2024, a number of major expenditures have bypassed the normal congressional appropriations process. These include retrofitting the gifted luxury jet from Qatar (estimates range from less than $400 million to nearly $1 billion), modifying the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool (about $15 million), the White House Ballroom expansion (about $300 million) and the war with Iran (about $100 billion). These costs have added to the ballooning federal debt, which now stands at more than $40 trillion. U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman represents Virginia’s 1st District in Congress. If you feel as strongly as I do, you might want to consider emailing him to express your own dissatisfaction. This brings to mind a popular line from the 1976 movie “Network”: “I’m as mad as hell, and I’m not going to take this anymore.” Steven Regen, Williamsburg. Sharpie-gate. The 2019 “Sharpie-gate” episode offers a revealing metaphor for the way President Donald Trump has attempted to control artificial intelligence. During Hurricane Dorian, Trump used a black marker to alter a forecast map and make his original claim appear correct. The problem was not the marker itself; it was the effort to make reality conform to a preferred story. The same danger arises when political leaders try to control artificial intelligence by pressuring systems to avoid inconvenient facts, favor loyal narratives or present personal opinions as objective truth. AI technology should not become a digital Sharpie — used to redraw evidence after the fact or conceal uncertainty. It should help people distinguish verified information from speculation, identify competing viewpoints and acknowledge when the facts are unclear. Of course, AI requires responsible oversight. Systems should be tested for bias, protected against manipulation and governed by transparent rules. But accountability is different from political control. No administration — regardless of party — should be able to dictate that an AI system alter reality to protect a leader’s image. The lesson of the hurricane map is simple: Changing the picture does not change the storm. In the same way, controlling an AI’s answer does not change the underlying facts. A democratic society needs technology that helps citizens examine evidence, not technology that merely reproduces whoever holds the marker. Randy Hernandez, Norfolk.

Federal prosecutors have charged Lee Reiber, 55, CEO of Oxygen Forensics, of Boise, Idaho, and Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, 52, of Moscow, Russia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The Department of Justice says they concealed from U.S. agencies that their company was owned and controlled by Russian nationals and that its software was developed in Russia. The complaint does not allege that the software contained malicious code or was used to gain unauthorized access to any customer's systems or data. According to an affidavit, from March 2022 to the present, Reiber, Davydov, and others conspired to obtain contracts through Oxygen Forensics Inc., a digital forensics company based in Alexandria, Virginia. The affected agencies were the Department of War and three DHS components: the Secret Service and its National Computer Forensics Institute (NCFI), Homeland Security Investigations, and the DHS Office of Inspector General. The company presented itself as an independent, U.S.-based firm, but Davydov and four other Russian nationals owned and controlled it through a Cyprus-based holding company. The same five owned a Russian company, formerly Oxygen Software LLC and now MKO Systems LLC, which Davydov co-founded in 2000 and where he was chief technology officer. Its developers worked in Russia, and it sold the software there under different names to customers reportedly including the FSB, the Russian Investigative Committee, and the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. Davydov helped establish Oxygen Forensics in Virginia in 2013; Reiber joined in August 2015. After expanded U.S. sanctions on Russia in early 2022, the defendants and Russian co-conspirators allegedly agreed to hide the company's true ownership and Russian development. Reiber became CEO, president, and board chairman in March 2022, and the Russian owners were removed from public corporate filings. They nonetheless continued to make major decisions, set Reiber's compensation, overrule him on payments, and hold signatory authority over bank accounts. Reiber allegedly falsely certified to the government in December 2022 and October 2023 that the company had no immediate or highest-level owner. After a reporter asked about ownership in November 2023, he wrote to Davydov and two other Russian owners that public reporting "could destroy this entire opportunity," referring to a pending NCFI contract. In July 2024, at his direction, the company certified to the Department of War that no foreign person could control its directors or decisions, though a Russian owner had recently joined its board under a Turkish identity. In September 2024, the NCFI awarded a five-year contract, with the October 2023 certification in the award file. In March 2026, Reiber told DHS personnel that no Russian was involved in development or had access to the build environment, and days later published a similar statement on the company's website. The complaint says the software was written and managed by a team in Russia under Davydov's direction, in a cloud environment administered by one of the Russian owners. Separately, a federal magistrate judge in the Central District of California issued a warrant on September 19 to seize corporate bank accounts, about 57 domains, and other cyberinfrastructure; the domains and related infrastructure were seized September 20. The complaint contains only allegations, and the defendants are presumed innocent. Each faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security is investigating with the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, and the Justice Department's Office of International Affairs is assisting with Davydov's provisional arrest and anticipated extradition.

OpenAI is preparing to preview its latest cybersecurity-focused model, GPT-6 Cyber, in the coming weeks, according to multiple sources familiar with the plans. It will also unveil a new product to help customers deploy the model in a more secure, automated manner. The new, yet-to-be-named product will be a first for OpenAI, and extends a paradigm that OpenAI pioneered with its consumer products, in which ChatGPT serves as a gateway through which many users access new models like GPT-6 Astra. It aims to help customers create automated workflows and patch vulnerabilities in the face of increasingly sophisticated, AI-powered cyberattacks. It also gives OpenAI more oversight into how its models are being used, to monitor for safety. A limited number of customers in OpenAI’s application-only Daybreak Red program already have access to GPT-6 Cyber for alpha testing, the source said. Daybreak is the company’s cybersecurity program, which is broken into two access tiers—red and blue. Customers in the Daybreak Red program have access to OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity products. Daybreak Blue is its more generalized access program, though it is also application-only. The release of the new cyber products comes as OpenAI and other leading AI labs have been under fire for a string of worrisome incidents in which “rogue” agents escaped their sandboxes and hacked outside websites including the Hugging Face site and an Australian government site. But while the incidents have set off alarms about AI’s security risks, OpenAI’s new cybersecurity tools are part of an ongoing effort by the company to develop AI security products. GPT-6 Cyber is the fourth cybersecurity-focused model OpenAI has released this year. Its first was GPT-5.4 Cyber in April 2026, followed by GPT-5.5 Cyber in June, and GPT-5.6 Cyber in August. OpenAI has been focusing on enterprise sales of cybersecurity products, an effort now led by its Chief Revenue Officer Dali Rajic, who joined the company in August. OpenAI said earlier this month it will invest $1 billion to subsidize the use of its cybersecurity products for critical services. Next week, OpenAI also plans to ship a dozen or more other products at its annual DevDay event, set for Sept. 29, according to another source familiar with the program. Most of those releases are not related to cybersecurity but rather other areas of the business, both enterprise- and consumer-focused. OpenAI has put a freeze on any major launches in the past 2 weeks, save for its affordability-focused GPT-6 Sol and Luna models, so it could ship them all at DevDay, the source said. Earlier this month, CEO Sam Altman teased the buffet of new releases at DevDay in a tweet with multiple ship emojis. UPDATE: The story has been updated to reflect that the launch could be within weeks, not days.

EUGENE, Ore. — It’s move in day at the University of Oregon, and students on campus Thursday said they’re cautiously watching artificial intelligence unfold within their academics. “I think it should definitely be more regulated. There are areas that it could be used, and I think it could be useful. But I think we definitely need to pay more attention on how it currently is used,” 4th year architecture student Tiana Atkins said.
